books.title: Business Law and Practice · SQE Notes（26页版）

pages.heading: CHOICE OF BUSINESS MEDIA · INTRODUCTION:
pages.text:
BLP – SQE notes | Page 1 of 26 
CHOICE OF BUSINESS MEDIA 
 
INTRODUCTION: 
 
Businesses are set up to make a profit (except for non-profit 
organisations). A business generates income by selling products and/or 
services. 
 
Business can be incorporated or unincorporated. 
Unincorporated businesses: 
× 
Few formalities are required. You must still register for VAT if 
the business reaches the threshold. 
× 
No need for registering these businesses. 
× 
Examples: sole traders and general partnerships. 
 
Incorporated businesses: 
× 
You must formally register the business at Companies House. 
× 
Examples: private limited companies and limited liability 
partnerships. 
 
Companies House: 
The Registrar of Companies in the UK. In this module, you will learn what 
information must be filed at Companies House and how to register a new 
company. 
 
CHOICE OF BUSINESS MEDIA: 
 
When the client is choosing business media, consider the advantages 
and disadvantages of each business media. 
 
Depending on the what the business owner is trying to achieve, 
different business media will prove to be beneficial. 
 
Most common types of business media: 
1. 
Sole traders 
2. 
General partnerships 
3. 
Limited Partnerships 
4. 
Limited liability partnerships 
5. 
Companies limited by shares 
 
Sole trader 
 
A sole trader is a person who owns all the assets in the business. The business 
is not a separate entity from its owner so the sole trader business cannot run 
if the sole trader dies. The sole trader is liable for all the business losses and 
will make all the decisions in relation to the business. 
 
Key characteristics: 
• 
Number of persons needed for set up: 1 person. Cannot form sole 
trader business for less/more than 1. 
• 
Control and management: Sole traders have complete control over the 
running of the business. This gives sole traders flexibility but pressure 
if working without support. 
• 
Liability: Not limited – Unlimited personal liability. 
• 
Expenses when setting up: No formalities so no setting up costs 
• 
On-going expenses after the business is set up: None necessary, 
although usually accountants will be involved in keeping accounts 
• 
Methods of financing: Sole trader can borrow from a bank but cannot 
create floating charges nor raise finance by share issue. 
• 
Profits: All profits go to the owner. 
• 
Tax: Owner pays tax as an individual (income tax + capital gains tax) 
• 
May trade immediately? Yes. 
 
 
General partnership 
 
s.1(1) Partnership Act 1890 Partnership = persons carrying on business with 
a view of profit. It is based on an agreement between the parties. – May form 
a partnership irrespective of contrary intention. 
 
No separate legal identity. The partnership is unable to own property or enter 
into contracts. Instead, it is the individual partners who will sue, own property 
jointly, and enter into contracts jointly. If partnership goes insolvent, creditors 
can enforce debt against the partners personally. 
 
Key characteristics: 
• 
Number of persons needed for set up: Min. 2 persons 
• 
Expenses when setting up: None, although it is beneficial to have a 
Partnership Agreement drawn up by lawyers (this may be expensive). 
• 
On-going expenses after the business is set up: None necessary, 
although must pay for accountants 
• 
Management structure of the business: In accordance with the 
Partnership Agreement, however if no agreement, the default 
provisions in the PA 1890 step in. 
• 
Methods of financing: Partners can borrow but cannot create floating 
charges. They also cannot raise finance by issuing shares. 
• 
Liability: Each partner has unlimited personal liability. 
• 
Publicity: Fewer requirements than for other options, easier to 
maintain privacy. No disclosure required 
• 
May trade immediately? Yes. 
 
 
 
 
 
Limited Partnership 
 
Limited Partnerships Act 1907 The act governing limited partnerships. 
 
Two types of partners in these partnerships: *You need one of each* 
1. General partners – manage the business and have unlimited liability. 
These partners will be the ones entering into contracts on behalf of the 
partnership. 
2. Limited partners – invests capital in the business and has limited 
liability. Their liability is limited to the amount they have spent on the 
business. 
 
These types of partnerships must be registered at Companies House. 
 
 
Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) 
 
An LLP is a hybrid as it has the flexibility of a partnership with the added 
advantage of limited liability for its members. – Common for Law firms. 
 
Limited Liability Partnerships Act 2000 The act governing limited liability 
partnerships. 
 
An LLP is a separate legal entity from its members. But for tax purposes, it is 
treated as a partnership and the members will be taxed as partners, each 
being liable to pay tax on his share of the income of the LLP. 
 
The members of the LLP are not personally liable and their liability will be 
limited to their investment similarly to companies. 
 
These types of partnerships must be registered at Companies House. 
 
Key characteristics: 
• 
Number of persons needed for set up: 2 persons min. 
• 
Expenses when setting up: Low costs but must pay legal fees for 
Partnership Agreement. 
• 
On-going expenses after the business is set up: Accounts must be 
prepared by accountants annually. File a Confirmation Statement 
minimum once a year. Higher costs due to regulation and disclosure 
rules. 
• 
Management structure of the business: Apart from a few default 
provisions, the LLPA and regulations leave matters of governance to a 
partnership agreement – if one exists. Pros of an LLP is the few 
formalities for management procedures. 
• 
Methods of financing: LLP can borrow and create floating charges. If 
any financing is underwritten by a member's personal guarantee, 
limited liability is removed. Cannot raise finance by issuing shares. 
• 
Publicity: No privacy. Similar disclosure rules as for companies. 
• 
May trade immediately? No, as LLPs must be registered. 
 
 
Companies Limited by shares 
 
A company has a separate legal identity from that of its owners. The company 
may therefore own property, enter into contracts, sue, and be sued in its own 
name. The owners of shares in the company are known as shareholders or 
members. 
 
Companies must be registered at Companies House. 
 
Two types of companies: 
1. Private companies – these companies are privately owned and the 
public cannot purchase its shares. 
2. Public companies – higher regulatory requirements as these 
companies can offer their shares to the public. 
 
Key characteristics: 
• 
Number of persons needed for set up: Min. 1 person 
• 
Expenses when setting up: Higher set up costs as there will be legal 
costs incurred in dealing with the company's constitutional documents, 
etc., as well as incorporation fees due to Companies House. 
• 
On-going expenses after the business is set up: Accounts must be 
prepared by accountants annually. High on-going administrative costs 
because of the greater regulation and disclosure rules. 
• 
Management structure of the business: Meetings of the directors and 
the shareholders are held in accordance with the Companies Act 2006 
and the articles. 
 
• 
Methods of financing: Company can borrow + create floating charges. 
Again, if members give personal guarantees, limited liability is lost. Can 
raise finance by issuing shares – ie. will be easier for a limited company 
to obtain financing. 
 
• 
Liability to third parties: The shareholders' liability to third parties is 
limited to the amount, if any, paid on their shares. 
• 
Publicity: No privacy. Onerous disclosure requirements.

pages.heading: GENERAL PARTNERSHIPS · FORMATION:
pages.text:
BLP – SQE notes | Page 2 of 26 
GENERAL PARTNERSHIPS 
 
FORMATION: 
 
A partnership is formed when: s.1 Partnership Act 1890 
1. 
Two or more persons 
2. 
Carry on business in common 
3. 
With the intention to make a profit 
 
Persons = includes companies, so two companies may form a 
partnership, or a human may form a partnership with a company. 
 
Business = buying/selling goods or providing services for a fee. 
 
In common = operating the business together. 
 
Intention to profit = does not include intention to form a partnership, 
simply to make a profit. 
 
Any number of partners may be involved. 
 
A partnership is NOT formed when: 
1. 
Parties jointly own property even if they share profits from the 
property 
2. 
Simply sharing the gross returns on something does not create 
a partnership 
 
Existence of partnerships: 
No formality is needed to establish a partnership so a partnership can 
be formed without the specific intent of the parties to form one. 
 
Profit sharing is prima facie evidence of a partnership. Even if it is 
unclear whether a partnership has formed or not, the partnership will 
be deemed to have been formed if there is profit sharing. 
 
KEY CHARACTERISTICS: 
 
Many partnerships are professional partnerships such as lawyers, 
accountants, surveyors and architects. 
 
Key characteristics of a partnership: 
• 
Tax transparent 
• 
Allows for a high degree of confidentiality 
• 
Min of 2 people 
• 
PA 1890 does not distinguish between actual and legal persons, 
so a company could be a partner. 
 
Care needed: 
• 
Very easy to create unintentionally, the partners do not need 
to use the word “partnership” to form one. 
• 
Unlimited joint liability 
• 
The firm will be bound by the actions of anyone authorised to 
act on the firm's behalf. Each partner is an agent of the firm 
and will bind the firm and other partners by contracting with 
third parties. 
• 
All partners share a fiduciary relationship and have a duty not 
to compete with the firm by carrying out a similar business 
without the permission of the other partners. 
 
Advantages: 
• 
It costs nothing to create a partnership. 
• 
May start as a partnership before converting to limited 
company. 
• 
Cheaper administrative costs as no need to file profits 
• 
Tax transparency – taxes flow through to the partners 
 
RULES/PROCEDURES OF PARTNERSHIPS: 
 
The default position without a Partnership Deed: 
• 
Profit-sharing Ratio: partners are to share the profits equally 
profits even if the partners have not contributed equally. 
• 
No salary to partners 
• 
Cannot expel a partner 
 
Authority to bind the partnership: 
 
The partnership will be bound by a partner's acts if: 
• 
The partner had authority to act 
 AND 
• 
The partner shows intention to bind the partnership 
 
Two types of authority: 
• 
Actual authority: 
1. 
Express 
2. 
Implied – where the partner regularly acted, and the 
other partners did not stop it. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
• 
Apparent/ostensible authority: 
When a partner acts in the usual way of business, their act will 
bind the partnership unless: 
* 
The partner had no authority to act 
 AND 
* 
The person with whom the partner dealt with knew that 
the partner had no authority to act or did not know that 
the person they dealt with was a partner. 
 
Decision-making: 
 
Decisions are made by simple majority. However, for changing the 
partners' mutual rights and obligations, unanimous consent is required 
(can be express or inferred). 
 
Partnership Property: 
 
Each partner owns a share in the partnership property. An individual 
partner does not have a right to partnership assets. 
 
The partners cannot use partnership property for personal use, these 
items/money can only be used for the purposes of the partnership. 
 
Because of this, it is very important for you to be able to identify 
whether a property in question is partnership property. 
 
 
 
Partnership property includes: 
* 
All money contributed by the partners. 
* 
All money the partnership has earned throughout its life. 
* 
Any property brought into the partnership by the partners for 
the purposes of the business. 
 AND 
* 
Any property purchased with partnership money. 
 
In order for property to become partnership property, the owner of the 
item must intend for the property to become partnership property. 
 
If one of the partners allows the other partners to use an item for the 
purposes of the partnership, this does not make item partnership 
property. 
 
If an item did not become partnership property, the partner may take 
the item when they leave the partnership. 
 
Personal liability for partnership debts: 
 
Each partner is personally bound under the firm's contracts. 
 
Contractual Liability: Every partner in a firm is liable jointly with the 
other partners for all the debts and obligations of the firm incurred 
whilst he is a partner. 
Tortious Liability: joint and several. 
 
A new partner will not automatically be liable in relation to any debts 
incurred by the partnership before he joined. 
A partner will still be liable after he retires in respect of debts incurred 
by the partnership whilst he was a partner. 
 
Unless: 
1) 
The creditor agrees 
2) 
You specifically absolve them 
3) 
You novate the contract 
 
Dissolution of partnership: 
 
If no Partnership Agreement, use default provisions in PA 1890: 
* 
Automatic dissolution: 
1. 
Expiry of fixed term 
2. 
Death/bankruptcy of partner 
 OR 
3. 
If the partnership business becomes unlawful 
 
* 
Dissolution of partnership at will (ie. with no fixed duration) 
by notice from any partner 
 
Where a partnership is wound up, once all debts and liabilities have 
been paid, any money/assets left will be distributed so that each 
partner is paid back his/her original capital first. 
 
COMMON PROVISIONS IN PARTNERSHIP 
AGREEMENTS: 
 
If no Partnership Agreement, PA 1890 default provisions (fall-back 
provisions) will apply. Default provisions are disadvantageous so advise 
your client to set up a Partnership Agreement. 
 
Partnership Deed/Agreement provides certainty and thus low risk. 
 
Profit-sharing Ratio: 
Set a ratio for profit sharing to reflect how much each party has 
contributed.

pages.heading: Salary: · Allow for the partners to receive a salary and set out how much this
pages.text:
BLP – SQE notes | Page 3 of 26 
Salary: 
Allow for the partners to receive a salary and set out how much this 
would be. 
 
Decision-making: 
Set out the requisite majority required for certain decisions. 
Common provision: unanimous consent requirement for expenditure. 
 
Dissolution of partnership: 
Under the fallback provisions, when a partner leaves, the partnership is 
dissolved. – But the other partners will not get their investment back. 
 
Common provisions: 
* 
Clause stating that the remaining partners get their money back 
and the partnership stays as it is (Buy-out). 
* 
Clause stating that the partnership will not dissolve when a 
partner leaves. 
* 
Clause allowing for partners to be expelled. 
 
Winding up partnership: Collecting in/distributing assets: 
 
Common provision: a clause dealing with the proportion in which any 
surplus assets are to be shared out following dissolution. This is called 
the asset surplus ratio (ASR). 
 
If there is no agreed ASR then surplus assets are shared in accordance 
with the agreed profit sharing ratio (PSR). 
 
If there is no PSR then they are shared equally.

pages.heading: LIMITED LIABILITY PARTNERSHIPS · An LLP is a hybrid as it has the flexibility of a partnership with the added
pages.text:
BLP – SQE notes | Page 4 of 26 
LIMITED LIABILITY PARTNERSHIPS 
 
An LLP is a hybrid as it has the flexibility of a partnership with the added 
advantage of limited liability for its members. – Common for Law firms. 
 
Limited Liability Partnerships Act 2000 The act governing limited 
liability partnerships. 
 
An LLP is a separate legal entity from its members. But for tax purposes, 
it is treated as a partnership and the members will be taxed as partners, 
each being liable to pay tax on his share of the income of the LLP. 
 
The members of the LLP are not personally liable and their liability will 
be limited to their investment similarly to companies. 
 
FORMATION: 
 
An LLP is formed when the partnership is registered at Companies 
House. – even though limited liability may be desirable to the partners, 
if the partnership is not registered, the partners liability will not be 
limited. 
 
If there is no Partnership Agreement, the default provisions in the LLPA 
2000 will apply to the partnership. Once an LLP Agreement is drafted, 
its provisions will override the act. 
 
When registering, submit: 
• 
The name of the LLP (must end with LLP/limited liability 
partnership) 
• 
LLP's registered office address 
• 
Member's names and addresses 
• 
Details of people with significant control 
 
People with significant control – any of the below: 
1. 
The person holds (directly/indirectly): 
• 
more than 25% of the surplus assets on winding up 
• 
more than 25% of the voting rights in the LLP 
 
 OR 
2. 
The person holds the right (directly/indirectly) to appoint or 
remove a majority of those involved in the management of the 
LLP. 
 
 OR 
3. 
The person exercises/has the right to exercise significant 
influence or control over a firm which meets any of the other 
two conditions above in relation to the LLP, or would do so if it 
were an individual. 
 
KEY CHARACTERISTICS: 
 
Key characteristics of an LLP: 
• 
LLPs have a separate legal personality – the partnership will not 
cease if a member exits the partnership or goes bankrupt. 
• 
Min of 2 people – may have only 1 member for the first 6 
months, but they will be liable for the debts of the LLP. 
• 
Members must have access to the books and records of the LLP. 
• 
The members will not be liable for any acts/omissions of the 
other members committed while conducting the business. 
• 
The LLP will be liable for the acts/omissions of its members. 
 
RULES/PROCEDURES OF PARTNERSHIPS: 
 
Standard rules – Unless there is contrary provision in the LLP 
Agreement: 
• 
Members share the profits and assets of the LLP equally. 
• 
Each member may take part in the management of the 
business. 
 
An LLP must indemnify its members in relation to: 
1. 
Payments made in the conduct of business 
2. 
Liabilities incurred in the conduct of business 
3. 
Anything done to preserve the business/property of the LLP 
 
Duty to account: 
1. 
If a member is conducting business in competition with the LLP 
without the LLP's consent, that member must account for the 
profits made in that business. 
2. 
Members must account to the LLP for personal benefits derived 
from any transactions concerning the LLP, without the LLP's 
consent. 
 
Duty to make certain documents publicly available: 
• 
The LLP's annual accounts 
• 
Annual confirmation statement 
• 
The appointment/removal of members 
• 
Changes to the details of members 
• 
Changes to the registered office/name of the LLP 
 
 
Liability for debts: 
• 
The LLP is a separate entity and the liability of members is 
limited to the amount owed to the creditors. 
• 
The members may be held liable for wrongful and fraudulent 
trading – Insolvency Act 1986 
• 
Clawback provisions: if a member has withdrawn any property 
from the LLP within 2 years before it goes into insolvent 
liquidation and when he withdrew the property, he know or had 
reasonable grounds to believe that the LLP was/was going to be 
unable to pay its debts, the court may make an order 
compelling the member to contribute to the assets of the LLP. 
 
Termination: 
• 
Voluntary striking off/dissolution: 
– 
A majority of the members may apply to Companies 
House for the LLP to be struck off/dissolved. 
– 
Members must notify the creditors in the London 
Gazette. 
– 
The LLP cannot be struck off if it has carried on 
business/changed its name in the last 3 months. 
 
• 
Insolvency: an LLP can be liquidated (voluntarily/compulsorily) 
or put into administration. 
 
Taxation: 
• 
Tax the trading profits (income tax) and capital gains (capital 
gains tax) 
• 
Income tax/capital gains tax is paid by the partners. 
• 
The taxation of partners is based on their profit sharing rights. 
• 
Stamp duty exemption: no Stamp duty land tax (SDLT) is due if 
property is transferred within the first year of incorporation if 
the transfer was made by a partner.

pages.heading: THE NATURE OF COMPANIES · BASIC CONCEPTS OF COMPANY LAW:
pages.text:
BLP – SQE notes | Page 5 of 26 
THE NATURE OF COMPANIES 
 
BASIC CONCEPTS OF COMPANY LAW: 
 
The internal structure of a company: 
 
THE COMPANY 
 
 Shareholders Directors 
Secretary (if any) 
 Role: Investors Role: Managers 
 
 
 
 
 
 Board of directors 
 General meeting Board meeting 
 
 
Employees (if any) 
 
 
 
 
The company will have shareholders and directors. It may also have 
secretaries and employees. 
 
Shareholders: 
 
Shareholders (members) = owners of the company. Shareholders invest 
a lump sum in the company and in return they receive a shareholding. 
 
s.112(2) CA 2006 Membership begins when the member's name is 
entered in the company's Register of Members. 
 
Subscribers = the first shareholders of the company who become 
shareholders when the company forms. 
 
Shareholders pay for their shares and are entitled to profits on their 
shares. They usually also have the right to vote. 
 
However, company properties and assets are owned by the company, 
not the shareholders. Change in the shareholders does not affect the 
property. – eg. Tesco owns a number of retail sites and buildings, but the 
shareholders are not entitled to those. 
 
Directors: 
 
Directors = appointed managers who deal with the day-to-day 
operations of the company. – they may also be shareholders, but they 
need not be. 
 
Directors together constitute the board of directors. 
 
TYPES OF COMPANIES: 
 
Companies Act 2006 The act governing companies. 
 
Main types of companies: 
 
 
Company 
 
 
 Limited company 
 
Unlimited company 
 
 
 
 Limited by shares 
Limited by guarantee 
 
 
 
Public company 
Private company 
 
 
 
Unlimited companies: 
* 
Rare type of company 
* 
Its members are personally liable for the debts of the company 
* 
It does not need to publish its accounts – higher degree of 
confidentiality 
 
Companies limited by guarantee: 
* 
Used for non-profit organisations 
* 
Instead of shares, the members pay a fixed amount (guarantee), 
usually £1 to be paid out if the company is wound up. 
* 
No shareholders, members only. Must have at least one 
member. 
 
 
Companies limited by shares: 
* 
Most common form of company 
* 
The members have a limited liability – limited up to the amount 
they paid for the shares. 
* 
Companies limited by shares may be private or public. 
 
Differences between a private and public company: 
 
 
Private company 
 
Public company 
Name 
Must end in ‘Limited' or 
‘Ltd' 
Must end in ‘Public Limited 
Company' or ‘Plc'. 
 
Minimum 
shareholding 
No minimum share capital, 
so it could be incorporated 
with just 1 share of 1p. 
Must have at least 1 share. 
 
Must have a share capital 
with a nominal value of 
min. £50,000. – the setup 
costs are high. 
 
Minimum 
number of 
directors 
1 
2 
 
Company 
secretary 
May choose to have a 
company secretary but it is 
not obliged to have one. 
 
Must have a company 
secretary. 
 
Certificate 
required 
before start of 
trading 
Certificate of incorporation. 
 
Can commence business as 
soon as incorporated. 
Certificate of 
incorporation. 
 
Cannot commence 
business until a trading 
certificate is issued by 
Registrar. 
 
Annual general 
meetings 
Need not have to hold an 
AGM although they can 
hold 1 if they want to. 
 
Must have min 1 annual 
general meeting each year. 
Method of 
payment and 
minimum 
amount 
payable for 
share capital 
No restriction on method 
of payment. Shares can be 
issued without immediate 
payment. 
Payments in cash only or 
where consideration has 
been independently 
valued. 
 
25% of nominal value must 
be paid on allotment plus 
the whole of any premium. 
 
Regulation 
Prohibited to sell its shares 
to the public. 
Audited accounts must be 
filed within 6 months of 
the accounting reference 
date. 
 
FSMA imposes 
considerable restrictions. 
 
 
The main difference between public and private companies: 
Only public companies can offer their shares to the public (hence the 
name). This is done through listing on the London Stock Exchange. 
 I 
Listed companies: 
• 
It is not the company that is listed but the shares 
• 
Enables companies to raise large amounts in funds 
• 
Client must convert the company into a plc first and then apply 
for a listing on a stock exchange by making sure that they comply 
with all the relevant listings regulations. 
 
SEPARATE LEGAL PERSONALITY: 
 
Companies have a separate legal personality, meaning that they form 
a legal person from the date of incorporation. Due to this separate 
personality, the shareholders are protected from liability and their 
liability will be limited to the amount they paid for the shares. 
 
A company is an entity that is distinct from its shareholders, directors, 
creditors and employees. It has a separate legal personality. A company 
continues to exist even if its shareholders and/or directors change. 
 
Directors owe their duties to the company, not to the shareholders. 
Shareholders have rights against the company, rather than against the 
directors. Third party contractors also have rights against the company, 
even though the directors sign the contract because they sign on behalf 
of the company. 
 
The acts/omissions of the director will ultimately be the acts/omissions 
of the company and the company will be liable for such acts, not the 
director. However, the director can also be liable in certain situations. 
 
The body corporate is able to exercise the functions of an incorporated 
company from the date of incorporation. 
 
Date of incorporation = the date when all the necessary documentation 
is submitted to Companies House (the Registrar).

pages.heading: Owning property: · Must own property in its own name
pages.text:
BLP – SQE notes | Page 6 of 26 
Owning property: 
• 
Must own property in its own name 
• 
Shareholders have no right to property. 
 
Contracts: 
• 
Must contract in its own name 
• 
Directors must make the decision on behalf of the company 
whether or not to enter into a contract 
 
Suing and being sued: 
• 
A company as a legal person can take action to enforce its legal 
rights. – eg. if there is a customer who has failed to pay an 
invoice, the directors can take action in the company's name to 
enforce the payments. 
• 
Company can be sued for breach of its legal duties. – eg. the 
company delivers faulty goods to a customer, then the 
customer can bring a claim against the company. 
 
Lifting the veil of incorporation: 
 
Lifting the corporate veil = disregarding the separate legal personality 
of a company. It is essentially an exception to limited liability and it 
means removing the veil of incorporation so that shareholders are 
liable for the debts and other obligations of the company. Different 
synonyms: lifting, penetrating, piercing the veil. 
 
Narrow jurisdiction: the court can only lift the veil when it is deemed 
absolutely necessary – piercing the veil is very rare in practice. The 
reason for this is to maintain certainty and that the courts do not wish 
to undermine the purpose of incorporation. 
 
Having incorporated therefore the company have a reasonable 
expectation that the courts will not dispute the separate legal 
personality of the company and will apply the rule in Salomon v 
Salomon. Therefore, they expect that the liability of the shareholders 
will be limited. 
 
Even when the veil is pierced, the courts will only do this to the extent 
necessary to address the particular circumstance. 
 
Lifting the veil: 
1. Fraudulent and wrongful trading: if the director continues to 
trade while the company is insolvent, they may be liable for 
fraudulent/wrongful trading. 
 
2. Public limited companies trading without a Trading Certificate 
 
3. If company group accounts are not filed: this is only necessary 
for group companies.

pages.heading: COMPANY FORMATION AND CONSTITUTION · FORMATION:
pages.text:
BLP – SQE notes | Page 7 of 26 
COMPANY FORMATION AND CONSTITUTION 
 
FORMATION: 
 
Promoters: 
 
The promoter is the person arranging the incorporation. They will be 
the ones registering the company with Companies House. 
 
Companies cannot enter into contracts until incorporated. 
If the promoter enters into contracts pre-incorporation, they will be 
personally liable for paying/fulfilling those contracts. 
 
Protection for promoters: 
* 
Prepare the contract as a draft and only sign it once the company 
is formed. 
* 
Enter into a novation agreement after incorporation. – a 
novation agreement is a contract between the promoter, the 
contractor and the company where the parties agree that the 
promoter is to be substituted with the company. 
* 
Assign the benefit of the contract to the company after 
incorporation in return for the company agreeing to indemnify 
the promoter if the promoter is to be held personally liable 
under the original contract. 
 
Incorporation methods: 
 
Two incorporation methods: 
1. 
Incorporating a new company from scratch 
 OR 
2. 
Purchasing an existing shelf company 
 
Incorporation from scratch: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Send to the Registrar of Companies at Companies House: 
1. 
The application form (Form IN01) with the relevant fee 
 
2. 
Articles of association: 
× 
Model articles apply automatically 
× 
Company may entrench articles: notify the registrar 
× 
A company may choose to alter the articles 
 
The IN01 application form must contain: 
• 
Name of the company 
• 
Registered office 
• 
Memorandum of Association 
 
• 
A statement of capital setting out the following: 
1. Total number of shares for the subscribers 
2. Aggregate nominal value of the shares 
3. Total number of shares in each class 
4. The amount to be paid up on each share 
5. Details of all subscribers 
 
• 
Initial shareholdings + list of directors and their addresses 
• 
If company limited by guarantee, details of the guarantee. 
• 
Statement of compliance 
 
Applications may take the Registrar of Companies up to five days to 
process, but you can pay a higher fee for same-day incorporation. 
 
Once approved, the company receives a certificate of incorporation 
containing: 
1. 
The name of the company 
2. 
The date of incorporation 
3. 
The company's registered number 
 
The company becomes a legal entity from the date of incorporation. 
 
 
 
 
 
Shelf company: 
 
In this case, a shelf company has been set up in advance by a law firm 
ready to tailor it to the client's requirements. This was used to speed up 
the process of setting up a company, although now with online 
registration, this is becoming obsolete. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
When a client requests a new company, change the following via 
shareholder resolution: 
* 
Articles – s.21(1) CA 2006 
* 
Members, directors and company secretary 
* 
Shares held by subscribers (those working at the law firm) are 
to be transferred to client 
* 
Client's representatives are appointed as directors 
* 
The first directors resign 
* 
Registered office 
 
Company name: 
 
* 
The name cannot be misleading. 
* 
Name cannot be offensive 
* 
Name cannot suggest an association to government 
* 
Name cannot use sensitive words. 
* 
A private company's name must end with limited or ltd. 
 
Name should not be the same as another company's name: 
*Check at Companies House if the name is free* 
– 
Companies with a goodwill can object 
– 
SoS may require change of a similar name 
 
CONSTITUTION: 
 
All companies must have articles of association (articles for short). The 
main purpose of this document is to regulate the relationship between 
the shareholders, directors and the company. 
 
The articles do not need to be filed at Companies House as these are 
supplied by the Registrar. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
When advising a client, a lawyer must check the articles first. 
 
Types of articles a company may adopt: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
A company is free to choose its articles, as long as they do not 
contravene the CA 2006. 
 
A private company incorporated under the CA 2006 will have the 
Model Articles by default, unless it chooses otherwise. 
 
 
 
 
 
Advantages 
 
* 
Traditionally slower, now with the advent of online 
incorporation services, difference in speed is now 
negligible, however incorporation can only take place 
during Companies House opening hours even if 
incorporated online. 
 
* 
Easier to prepare tailor-made articles, but then it would be 
more expensive due to legal costs and it would take longer. 
 
* 
Costs: Companies House fees, no legal fees involved 
Advantages 
 
* 
The conversion of a shelf company retains the advantage of 
being available all the time on every day of the year. 
 
* 
If the client requires complex tailor-made articles: usually 
shelf companies are incorporated with Model Articles which 
will require a special resolution to change the articles – this 
may delay the company's start date for trading by 14 clear 
days unless the procedure can be shortened. 
Example provisions: 
* 
Method of appointment of directors 
* 
Special rights attaching to shares 
* 
Powers of directors 
* 
Voting rights and how voting takes place 
Model Articles 
 
 
These are a 
standard set of 
articles and there 
is a version 
available for 
private 
companies or 
public companies. 
 
Amended Model 
Articles 
 
You might want 
to adopt the 
model articles but 
amend them 
slightly. This is 
good if the model 
articles are good 
for a starting 
point. 
Bespoke articles 
 
 
The articles have 
been drafted from 
scratch and they 
would have been 
specifically 
tailored to your 
company.

pages.heading: Objects of the company: · Objects of a company mean its objectives – eg. to operate an
pages.text:
BLP – SQE notes | Page 8 of 26 
Objects of the company: 
* 
Objects of a company mean its objectives – eg. to operate an 
educational platform. 
* 
If the objects of a company are restricted, the directors must 
adhere to those restrictions and cannot operate the business to 
achieve an alternative objective. 
* 
If the articles do not restrict the company's objects, then the 
directors are free to operate the business as they see fit. 
 
Relationship between CA 2006 and the articles: 
 A company may include procedures in the articles which are more 
onerous than the procedure set out in CA 2006. – eg. A Ltd could provide 
in its articles that it requires 5 directors voting in favour in its board 
resolutions, and so would need to comply with this requirement in its 
articles. 
 
Exception – CA 2006 provisions overriding anything in the articles: 
The right to demand a poll vote at a general meeting 
 
Alteration of the articles: 
1. 
By special resolution 
2. 
Entrenched articles can be amended by agreement of all 
members or by a court order. 
3. 
Any alteration must be made bona fide in the best interests of 
the company as a whole. 
4. 
Alteration may adversely affect minority interests if it was made 
in good faith in the best interest of the company. 
 
Entrenchment: 
* 
When voting on changing the articles, a special resolution (75% 
or more shareholders voting in favour of the change) is 
required. 
* 
Certain provisions of the articles may be entrenched by the 
articles requiring a higher majority to change those provisions. 
– eg. unanimous decision. 
* 
Alteration of the articles cannot be completely prohibited. 
* 
The company must notify Companies House that its articles 
are entrenched. 
 
SHAREHOLDERS' AGREEMENTS: 
 
Shareholders' agreement = A contract between some/all of the 
shareholders in their personal capacities, in which they can agree 
between themselves how to regulate their company's affairs. 
 
Shareholders' agreements are not a requirement when setting up a 
company, however, many shareholders choose to enter into one. 
 
Why to enter into a Shareholders' Agreement? 
• 
The provisions of the articles are subject to CA 2006 limits. 
• 
The shareholders may include commercially sensitive clauses 
unlike the articles. 
• 
Shareholders' agreements are easier to enforce and will allow 
the shareholders to make a claim for breach of contract 
• 
Shareholders' agreements may remain private while the articles 
are submitted to Companies House.

pages.heading: DIRECTORS AND OFFICERS · Officers of the company:
pages.text:
BLP – SQE notes | Page 9 of 26 
DIRECTORS AND OFFICERS 
 
Officers of the company: 
1. 
Directors 
2. 
Company secretary 
3. 
Company auditors 
 
COMPANY AUDITORS: 
 
CA 2006 Large companies must hire specialist accountants (auditors). 
 
The accounts of small companies need not be audited; however the 
directors may appoint an auditor to audit the accounts. 
 
COMPANY SECRETARY: 
 
A public company must have a company secretary. 
 
A private company is not required to have a company secretary unless 
the articles require so. – If a private company does not have a company 
secretary, the directors may do anything the secretary was required or 
authorised to do. 
 
Main duties: *No prescribed duties* 
– 
Keep the company books and records up to date 
– 
Produce minutes of board and general meetings 
– 
Make sure all necessary filings are made at Companies House 
 
The acts of the company secretary will bind the company even if they 
were not authorised to act. 
 
Qualification requirements of secretaries (public companies only): 
Must have at least one of the below qualifications: 
– 
Has been the secretary of a public company for at least 3 of the 
5 years immediately preceding their appointment 
– 
Is a member of a specified list of accountancy/secretarial bodies 
– 
Is a UK barrister/solicitor 
– 
Is a person who, due to their experience or being a member of a 
professional body appears to the directors to be capable of being 
a secretary. 
 
DIRECTORS: 
 
Directors are responsible for the day-to-day management of the 
company. 
 
Directors must be natural persons; a company cannot be a director. 
 
Director = any person occupying the position of director, by whatever 
name called. What is important is that they should fill in the role of a 
director. – eg. some articles refer to governors or managers, but they 
will still held to be directors. 
 
Minimum age limit of 16 for directors. 
Model Articles Directors may delegate specific powers. 
 
The roles of directors and shareholders differ, even though they may be 
the same person. 
 
Appointment: 
 
Private companies must have at least 1 director. 
Public companies must have at least 2 directors. – with at least one of 
the directors being a natural person. 
 
Procedure to appoint new directors: 
• 
This will be set out in the articles. 
• 
Directors are appointed by ordinary resolution of the 
shareholders (see later) – Model Articles 
 
Notice of change: 
Companies must notify Companies House within 14 days of the 
appointment of new directors and the changes of their details. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Types of directors: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Powers of directors: 
 
Model Articles The directors must act collectively as a board and have 
the power to do all acts necessary for the management of the company's 
business. – The board must not exceed their powers. 
 
Provided that the third party is acting in good faith, they are entitled to 
rely on the authority of the directors. 
 
Power of an individual director to act on behalf of the company: 
Model Articles The board is able to delegate. The board of directors do 
not always have to act collectively as a board. 
 
TYPES OF AUTHORITY 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Director acting without actual authority: 
May have apparent authority whereby they don't need to have express 
authority to act. 
 
If not, the director could be liable to the company for any losses. 
May have decisions ratified if the act benefited the company. 
 
If the act was within the powers of the board: it could be ratified after 
the act by board resolution. 
If the act was outside the powers of the board: ratify it by ordinary 
resolution of the shareholders. 
 
Actions by the director which are outside both actual and apparent 
authority will not bind the company. In this case, third party may have 
a personal remedy against the director for breach of warranty. 
 
Execution of documents: 
 
Companies execute documents by: 
1. 
The signature of two directors 
2. 
The signature of a company secretary and a director 
3. 
Affixing their company seal to the documents 
 
 
Actual express 
authority 
 
 Authority to act 
regarding a specific 
transaction given 
formally by a board 
resolution. – eg. 
evidence of express 
authority is a copy 
of the board 
minutes granting 
the authority. 
 
 
Actual implied 
authority 
 
 Directors can bind 
the company in 
acts which is usual 
for the director to 
be acting. 
 
 Apparent/ostensible 
authority 
 
 
If the principal's 
words/actions 
reasonably lead a 
third party to believe 
that the director had 
authority, then the act 
of the director will 
bind the company. 
 
 
Executive directors 
 
Directors who have been 
appointed to executive office. 
They are both an officer and 
employee of the company. 
 
De jure directors = formally 
appointed directors. 
De facto directors = directors 
in practice with no formal 
appointment. 
Non-executive directors 
 
An officer but not an employee 
of the company. They do not 
take part in the day-to-day 
running of the company but 
rather provide independent 
guidance and advice. 
 
Shadow directors 
 
s.251 CA 2006 Shadow 
directors = someone with 
significant influence over the 
actions of a company without 
having been appointed to a 
leadership position. 
 
Alternate directors 
 
Not included in MA but may be 
provided for in articles. They 
act in the director's place if 
they are incapacitated, 
otherwise engaged, or out of 
the country. 
 
Becoming obsolete as it is now 
possible to hold board 
meetings over the phone and 
pass board resolutions in 
writing. 
Nominee directors 
 
Appointed to represent the 
interests of a particular 
shareholder.

pages.heading: Directors as decision-makers: · Directors will make day-to-day decisions as to the management of the
pages.text:
BLP – SQE notes | Page 10 of 26 
Directors as decision-makers: 
 
Directors will make day-to-day decisions as to the management of the 
company. Shareholders are the owners of the company and thus, 
certain, more important decisions will require their approval. – eg. 
decisions where the articles are to be altered or where a director have 
an interest in a transaction. 
 
Resolutions = company decisions. 
 
Two types of resolutions: 
• 
Board resolutions 
• 
Shareholder resolutions: ordinary resolution and special 
resolution 
 
CA 2006 Lists decisions that require shareholder resolution. In addition 
to these decisions, the articles may also set out decisions that require 
shareholder resolution. 
 
Board meetings: 
 
Board meetings are conducted by the directors. The Model Articles 
govern the way board meetings are conducted. Can be held without 
great formality. 
 
Board meetings are called to: 
1. 
Make day-to-day decisions that don't require a General meeting 
(Ordinary resolution or special resolution) 
 AND/OR 
2. 
Call General meetings where ordinary resolution or special 
resolution is needed. 
 
Right to compensation and expenses: 
* 
Model Articles The board may determine what is fair 
compensation of the directors. 
* 
The company must also pay reasonable expenses, the directors 
incur in relation to attending meetings.

pages.heading: DIRECTORS' DUTIES AND REMOVALS · DIRECTORS' DUTIES:
pages.text:
BLP – SQE notes | Page 11 of 26 
DIRECTORS' DUTIES AND REMOVALS 
 
DIRECTORS' DUTIES: 
 
Statutory duties found in: CA 2006, Insolvency Act 1986, common law 
and equity. 
 
All of the statutory duties apply to directors, shadow directors and 
directors will be held liable even if they are no longer directors. 
 
Provisions in the articles/a contract attempting to exempt a director 
from liability arising from breach of duty/negligence/breach of trust in 
connection with the company is void. 
 
Basic fiduciary duty: 
Directors have a fiduciary duty under the common law to act in good 
faith and the best interest of the company as a whole. 
 
Duty to act within powers: s.171 CA 2006 
Director must act within its powers (within the constitution) 
 
Duty to promote the success of the company: s.172 CA 2006 
Codified the previous common law duty requiring directors to act bona 
fide in the interests of the company. 
 
Encompassed the ‘Enlightened shareholder value'. Attempted to 
balance running a company to make profit (long-term interests) and the 
shareholder interests (short-term gains). 
 
A director is required to have regard to the matters below: 
1. 
The likely long-term consequences of any decision 
2. 
The interests of the company's employees 
3. 
The need to foster the company's business relationships with 
other stakeholders (= suppliers, customers, wider community) 
4. 
The impact of the company's operations on the community and 
the environment 
5. 
The desirability of the company maintaining a reputation for high 
standards of business conduct 
6. 
The need to act fairly between the members of the company. 
 
Duty to exercise independent judgment: s.173 CA 2006 
Directors must exercise independent judgement by making decisions in 
relation to the company. 
 
Duty to exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence: s.174 CA 2006 
 
Examples: 
* 
They must not be negligent in making decisions in relation to the 
company. 
* 
They must make sure that they are on top of the company's 
finances and operations. 
 
For the judging reasonability, take into account the knowledge, skill 
and experience: 
* 
That may be reasonably expected of a director (objective test) 
 AND 
* 
That the director actually has (subjective test) 
 
Duty to avoid conflicts of interest: s.175 CA 2006 
The interests of the director or that of a connected person should not 
conflict with the interests of the company. – eg. if the director has a 
second business selling furniture making a decision on whether or not 
the company should sign a contract for buying furniture from that 
business will give rise to conflict of interest. 
 
The duty is not infringed if: 
× 
The situation cannot reasonably be regarded as likely to give rise 
to a conflict of interest 
 OR 
× 
The director discloses their interest in the transaction and the 
directors authorise the transaction despite the conflict of 
interest. 
 
Secret profit: 
The directors should not be making unauthorised profits from the 
company. – If authorised, then this won't be a breach. 
 
Duty not to accept benefits from third parties: s.176 CA 2006 
A director cannot accept benefits from third parties if those benefits are 
given to them because they are a director or doing anything as a director. 
 
Exception: 
Duty is not breached if the acceptance of a benefit cannot reasonably be 
regarded as likely to give rise to a conflict of interest. 
 
Duty to declare interest in the proposed transaction: s.177 CA 2006 
Must declare nature and extent of interest to other directors. 
 
This duty includes a duty to disclose interests in existing transactions 
or arrangements. Very common when a new director joins the board. 
 
Director must disclose their interest by: 
• 
Written notice 
 OR 
• 
Oral notice at the board meeting 
 
Model Articles The director interested in the actual/proposed 
transaction with the company cannot form part of the quorum at the 
board meeting where the decision is made. 
 
Exception – The director need not declare their interest if: 
* 
A conflict of interest in unlikely 
* 
The other directors are already aware of it 
 OR 
* 
It concerns the director's service contract 
 
Loans to directors: 
 
Directors must obtain shareholder approval before: 
1. 
Entering into a loan/guarantee with the company. 
 OR 
2. 
Giving security for a loan with a third party. 
 
Shareholder approvals: 
 
Shareholder approval in advance: 
Shareholders may support a director's proposed action, and be prepared 
to approve it in advance, even if it would otherwise be a breach of the 
general duties. 
 
Shareholder approval after the act (Ratification): 
Shareholders can absolve a director of liability by ratifying the director's 
actions after it happened. – so it is always an option for directors to seek 
ratification. 
 
Shareholders by ordinary resolution can ratify the following conduct of 
directors: 
× 
Negligence 
× 
Default 
× 
Breach of trust 
× 
Breach of duty 
 
If a director holds shares, then votes to ratify their breach attaching to 
shares held by him/connected persons will be disregarded. 
 
DIRECTORS' REMOVAL AND DISQUALIFICATION: 
 
Directors are personally liable to indemnify (reimburse) the company for 
the loss caused and to account for any gain they made from their 
wrongdoing. 
 
A breach of duty could be grounds for: 
1. Termination of an executive director's service contract or 
2. Disqualification 
 
Removal: 
 
CA 2006 Director may be removed by the ordinary resolution of the 
shareholders. 
 
The shareholders must serve Special notice. 
Special notice = 28 clear days between the notice of the removal 
resolution and the GM to pass the resolution. 
 
Written resolution cannot be used to remove a director. 
 
A director cannot be removed by fellow directors unless the articles are 
amended to provide for this. 
 
Power usually may not be overridden: 
 
Bushell v Faith It is possible for the articles to provide enhanced voting 
rights to a director at his removal resolution. This director cannot be 
removed irrespective of the number of shares he holds. 
 
Steps a director can take to protect himself: 
 
× 
Claim compensation as director's service contract is breached by 
their removal. 
× 
The director may argue his case at the general meeting. 
 
Retirement by rotation – for public companies: 
 
Model Articles At the first annual general meeting, all directors must 
retire from office. 
 
At every subsequent annual general meeting, the directors may be 
reappointed. – This is called the system of retirement by rotation.

pages.heading: Disqualification: · Company Directors Disqualification Act 1986 Directors can be
pages.text:
BLP – SQE notes | Page 12 of 26 
Disqualification: 
 
Company Directors Disqualification Act 1986 Directors can be 
disqualified from office for misconduct/unfitness. 
 
Insolvency Act 1986 Directors can be disqualified for wrongful 
trading/because they are bankrupt. 
 
General misconduct: 
– 
Conviction of an indictable offence in relation to the promotion, 
formation, management, liquidation, striking off of a company, 
receivership of company property, being an administrative 
receiver. 
– 
Breaches of company legislation in relation to filings at 
Companies House 
– 
Fraud/fraudulent trading 
– 
Summary conviction of an offence in contravention of/failure to 
comply with company legislation in relation to filings at 
Companies House 
 
Unfitness: 
– 
Directors can be disqualified under this heading for 2-15 years. 
– 
Secretary of State may apply to the court for an order if it is in 
the public interest that a disqualification order is made.

pages.heading: DIRECTOR TRANSACTIONS · SUBSTANTIAL PROPERTY TRANSACTIONS:
pages.text:
BLP – SQE notes | Page 13 of 26 
DIRECTOR TRANSACTIONS 
 
SUBSTANTIAL PROPERTY TRANSACTIONS: 
 
Make sure to note down the Net asset value, type of articles, names of 
the shareholders and directors with their respective shareholdings after 
reading your question. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
State the general rule in s.190: 
 
An arrangement requires ordinary resolution if the asset is a 
substantial non-cash asset and: s.190(1) 
1. 
Company sells the asset to a director/connected person – 
s.190(1)(a) 
 OR 
2. 
Company buys from a director/connected person – s.190(1)(b) 
 
Is the transaction with a director or a connected person? 
 
Director = includes shadow directors and former directors. 
 
Connected persons = wide definition: 
* 
A member of the director's family: can be a spouse, partner, 
child, stepchild, parent – not nephew/siblings. 
* 
A company in which the director/connected person holds at 
least 20% of the shares either alone or together. 
 
Is the asset substantial non-cash asset? 
 
Where there are a series of transactions, the board only needs to obtain 
one ordinary resolution. 
 
Non-cash asset = property/interest in property excluding cash. – a loan 
is not a non-cash asset. 
 
Substantial non-cash asset = 
An asset worth £0 < x < £5,000 is not a substantial asset. 
An asset worth £100,000 < x is a substantial asset. 
For multiple assets, use their aggregate value. 
 
An asset worth £5,000 < x < £100,000 is a substantial asset only if it is 
worth more than 10% of the company's NAV. 
 
Is there a defence/exemption? 
 
s.195(7) If the connected person or director had no knowledge that the 
company's rules were not complied with, the person will not be 
personally liable for the losses caused as a result of the transaction. 
 
s.192(b) If the connected person is a connected company that is the 
wholly-owned subsidiary of another company, the holding company 
will need to obtain the resolution, not the subsidiary. 
 
What if the director fails to obtain approval? 
 
Shareholder approval in advance reduces the risk of breach. 
 
The transaction will be voidable by the company unless: s.195(2) 
* 
The asset is now in the hands of a bona fide purchaser for value. 
* 
The shareholders affirm the transaction by ordinary resolution 
within a reasonable period. – 
 
Directors who authorised the transaction would be liable to account for 
any loss/pay damages. 
 
Duties triggered? 
 
s.175 – Conflict of interest 
s.177 – Declare that interest 
 
MA 14 An interested director cannot vote and cannot count in the 
quorum for board resolutions to approve that transaction. 
 
s.172 – Promote the best interest of the company 
 
 
 
 
LOANS TO DIRECTORS: 
 
Ordinary resolution is required before a company can make a loan 
(including quasi-loans/credit transactions) or give a guarantee to a 
director. 
 
The ordinary resolution can be obtained: 
* 
Before the transaction is entered into 
 OR 
* 
After the transaction has been agreed 
 
Exemptions: 
 
In any of the following situations no need shareholders' approval: 
 
* 
The funds were used to meet expenditure incurred on behalf of 
the company. Max. total amount of £50,000 or less. 
 
* 
Minor and business transactions: Loans or quasi-loans to a 
director up to £10,000 can be given without shareholder 
approval. This figure rises to £15,000 for credit transactions. 
 
* 
A money-lending company 
 
Defence for any connected person and director who authorised the 
transaction if they can show they had no knowledge of the 
circumstances constituting the contravention. 
 
Sanctions for non-compliance and for which persons? 
 
The transaction will be voidable. 
 
The arrangement can be affirmed by the shareholders of the company 
and the holding company (where relevant) by ordinary resolution within 
a reasonable time. 
 
Must account for any gain made directly or indirectly from the 
transaction and indemnify the company for any loss or damage resulting 
from the transaction. 
 
Statutory duties? 
 
Directors must always comply with their duties. – ss.172 and 177 
 
 
 
 
Example: 
 
The directors of UCF Ltd decided to give a car worth £35,000 to one 
of the company's directors, Holly. The Net Asset Value of the 
company is £904,500 and the unamended model articles have been 
incorporated. 
 
Shareholders: Max, Sam, others 
Directors: Max, Sam, Agnes, Holly 
 
Will Holly need to obtain ordinary resolution for the gift to go ahead?

pages.heading: SHAREHOLDERS · INTRODUCTION:
pages.text:
BLP – SQE notes | Page 14 of 26 
SHAREHOLDERS 
 
INTRODUCTION: 
 
Shareholders (members) = owners of the company. Shareholders invest 
a lump sum in the company and in return they receive a shareholding. 
 
Membership begins when the member's name is entered in the 
company's register of members. 
 
Subscribers = the first shareholders of the company who become 
shareholders when the company forms. 
 
A shareholder can be a company or an individual. 
 
Wholly owned subsidiary = company A owns 100% of shares in company 
B. In this case, A is B's parent or holding company. B will be included in 
A's accounts as an asset. 
 
Subsidiary = company A owns shares in company B, however, it does not 
necessarily own all the shares. 
 
Shareholders pay for their shares and are entitled to profits on their 
shares. They usually also have the right to vote. 
 
However, company properties and assets are owned by the company, 
not the shareholders. Change in the shareholders does not affect the 
property. – eg. Tesco owns a number of retail sites and buildings, but the 
shareholders are not entitled to those. 
 
By becoming a member of the company, shareholders acquire certain 
rights and powers. 
 
Shareholder rights and powers: 
 
* 
Right to vote on certain decisions 
* 
Right to receive dividend *potential right* 
* 
Right to receive a distribution on winding up *potential right* 
* 
Right to make a claim if their membership rights are not upheld. 
 
Person with Significant Control: 
 
Since 1 Apr 2016, UK companies are required to identify people with 
significant control. The purpose is to increase transparency and combat 
terrorist financing/tax evasion. 
 
Person with significant control (PSC) is any individual who: 
• 
Owns more than 25% of shares/voting rights in the company 
• 
Has the power to appoint/remove a majority of its board 
 OR 
• 
Otherwise exercises significant influence or control. 
 
Relevant Legal Entity (RLE) = a company that would qualify as a PSC of a 
company if it was an individual. 
 
Companies must take reasonable steps to identify their PSCs and RLEs. 
Failure to do so is a criminal offence. 
Penalty: a fine or up to 2 years' imprisonment. 
 
PSC register must be filed at Companies House alongside a confirmation 
statement. 
 
DIVIDENDS: 
 
Dividend = a return on the shareholder's investment. 
 
Whether the shareholder has right to receive dividend will depend on 
the class of shares they hold. 
 
CA 2006 Before paying a dividend, a company must check its relevant 
accounts to establish it has sufficient distributable profits and it cannot 
pay a dividend if it does not have enough distributable profits. 
 I 
This rule relates to the rules on capital maintenance, which sets out that 
the capital that the shareholders invested in the company is not be 
returned to them. 
 
Distributable profits = profits – losses made in the same year. – eg. if a 
company made £15,000 in profits, but made £2,000 losses, the amount 
of distributable profits available for paying dividends is £13,000. 
 
Two types of dividends: 
 
Interim dividends: 
Can be declared without 
shareholder approval and can be 
cancelled by the directors prior to 
payment. 
 
Final dividends: 
Paid following the end of a 
company's accounting year and 
require shareholder approval. It 
becomes a debt payable once 
declared at GM. 
 
 
Class rights: 
 
There are different classes of shares with different rights attaching to 
them and these will be set out in the articles – eg. different types of 
ordinary share, each carrying different rights such as voting or no voting 
rights 
 
The different shares provide varying rights to dividend: 
 
1. 
Ordinary shares are the most basic type of shares. They all rank 
equally on insolvency. 
 
2. 
Preference shares include the right to receive dividends and the 
holders of these shares will have priority over common 
shareholders when receiving dividends. 
 
Features: 
* 
Holder receives a preferential right to receive 
dividend/recover capital on insolvency. 
* 
This type of share may or may not include a right to vote. 
* 
May be cumulative – this is where if dividend is not paid 
for a particular year, the right to that dividend will carry 
over to the next year. 
* 
May be participating – this is where the shareholders are 
able to participate in ordinary dividend distribution. 
 
3. 
Cumulative preference shares include the right to dividend 
which accumulates, and the amount will be carried forward if 
not paid in any given year. 
 
4. 
Redeemable shares are shares which allow the company to 
decide to redeem these shares at a later date. Beneficial for the 
company as they can reduce the amount they owe. 
 
Procedure: 
 
Model Articles The decision to pay interim dividend rests with the 
directors. – the articles might set out something different. 
 
For final dividends, a two-stage process: 
1. 
The amount of a final dividend must be recommended by the 
board of directors. – Model Articles 
 AND 
2. 
It must be declared in a general meeting by way of an ordinary 
resolution at which the relevant accounts will also be approved. 
Shareholders may decide to pay less but not more. 
 
Payment of dividends: 
* 
Shareholders entitled receive the dividend will be those 
appearing in the Register of Members at the time of declaration. 
* 
If a company decides to pay dividend, it must pay to all 
shareholders holding the same class of share. 
* 
The articles will determine how dividends are to be distributed. 
* 
If the articles are silent on this, the dividend must be paid in 
proportion to the nominal amount of the shares. 
 
Unlawful dividends: 
If the dividend that was distributed was unlawful and the shareholder 
receiving it has a reason to believe it was unlawful, they will be liable to 
repay the dividend to the company. 
 
Dividend is unlawful if: it was paid out of funds other than distributable 
profits. – eg. if it was paid out of capital. 
 
RESOLUTIONS: 
 
Shareholders hold General meetings where they make decisions on 
matters that affect the company's business. 
 
General meetings (GMs) are called to: 
1. 
Make decisions that require Ordinary resolution 
 AND/OR 
2. 
Make decisions that require Special resolution 
 
Ordinary resolution = Simple majority, so more than 50% 
Special resolution = 75% or more. 
 
Ordinary resolution is required for matters that are less onerous and the 
required majority is also lower. Decisions that require special resolution 
will be more important and therefore, will require at least 75% of the 
voting rights to pass such a resolution. – eg. if only 60% of the votes will 
be in favour of the decision, then the proposed action cannot go ahead. 
 
How do you tell which decisions require ordinary or special resolution? 
You must look at CA 2006 or the Articles to find what the shareholders 
will be deciding on and these will set out if ordinary or special resolution 
is required.

pages.heading: DERIVATIVE CLAIMS: · A shareholder who believes that a director has/is about to breach their
pages.text:
BLP – SQE notes | Page 15 of 26 
DERIVATIVE CLAIMS: 
 
A shareholder who believes that a director has/is about to breach their 
duty and against whom the board of directors will not enforce the 
company's rights to prevent/remedy the situation, may apply to the 
court to bring a derivative action against the director. 
 
Requirements for a derivative claim: 
* 
Only a shareholder or a person who received shares may bring a 
derivative claim. 
* 
The claim must show a prima facie case for the relief sought. 
 AND 
* 
The claim must promote the best interests of the company. 
 
Any damages received in a derivative claim will belong to the company, 
so the shareholder will not receive any damages. However, they may be 
indemnified for the expenses they spent on pursuing the claim. 
 
SHAREHOLDERS' RIGHTS: 
 
Shareholders have the right: 
a) 
To inspect the directors' service contracts. – these service 
contracts must be kept at the registered office of the company 
for at least a years after the director leaves. 
 
b) 
To inspect the Register of Members – this will also be kept at 
the registered office. The company must comply with a request 
to inspect the company's Register of Members within 5 days. 
 
PROTECTIONS OF MINORITY SHAREHOLDERS: 
 
You would use these claims as a last resort. 
 
This is also a good option for directors that have been removed that 
are also minority shareholders. 
 
Unfair prejudice: 
 
If a minority shareholder believes that the way in which the company's 
business is being conducted is unfairly prejudicial to that shareholder, 
they may make a petition to the court for a remedy. 
 
The court will use the objective test to determine whether the conduct 
has been unfairly prejudicial. 
 
Examples that could amount to unfairly prejudicial conduct: 
* 
Being excluded from decision-making 
* 
Being excluded from management where the shareholder had a 
legitimate expectation that they would be involved in the 
management of the company 
* 
Majority shareholders paying themselves excessively 
* 
Breaches of the articles 
 
Difficult, expensive and time-consuming to bring a successful claim for 
unfair prejudice. – A negotiated settlement is the preferred option. 
 
Winding up the company: 
 
A shareholder may apply to the court for a winding up order which will 
wind up the company if the shareholder can prove that it would be 
equitable for the court to do so.

pages.heading: COMPANY DECISION-MAKING · Board meetings – meeting of the directors
pages.text:
BLP – SQE notes | Page 16 of 26 
COMPANY DECISION-MAKING 
 
Board meetings – meeting of the directors 
General meetings – meeting of the shareholders 
 
Decisions are made through board and shareholder resolutions. 
 
If correct procedure is not followed: 
× 
Resolutions passed may be invalid 
× 
Potential criminal sanctions 
 
BOARD MEETINGS: 
 
Can be passed without great formality. 
 
Board meetings are called to: 
1. 
Make day-to-day decisions that don't require a General meeting 
(Ordinary resolution or special resolution) 
 AND/OR 
2. 
Call General meetings where ordinary resolution or special 
resolution is needed. 
 
Who calls? 
Model Articles Called by any director 
 
Notice period? 
Reasonable notice. 
 
Quorum? 
Quorum = Number of people required to attend a meeting in order for 
the meeting to be valid. 
 
Model Articles The quorum may be fixed from time to time by the 
directors but must never be less than 2 and unless otherwise fixed, it is 
2. 
Model Articles If the company only has 1 director, then the quorum is 1. 
 
Decision-making? 
Model Articles Decisions at BM are made by board resolutions passed 
either: 
• 
On a simple majority 
 OR 
• 
By unanimity 
 
Simple majority = more than 50% 
Count 1 vote per director unless that director abstains. 
 
Model Articles If there is only one director, they can take decisions on 
their own. 
Model Articles Decisions are made on a show of hands unless a poll is 
demanded. 
 
Casting vote? 
Model Articles Under the Model Articles, the chairman, if one is 
appointed, will be able to use their casting vote if there is a deadlock. – 
eg. If there are 4 directors, 2 votes for a decision and 2 votes against it, 
then the director who is also the chairman will be given an additional 
vote to decide the resolution and break the deadlock. 
 
What if someone abstains? 
If a director abstains from voting on a decision, he will not be counted 
towards the number of people voting on that issue. – eg. If a board has 
6 directors, and 1 abstains, count the votes out of 5. To get a majority, 
you would thus need 3 out of 5 voting in favour. 
 
Alternative procedure – unanimity: 
1. 
Unanimous decision of the directors 
Directors can make decisions by unanimous agreement without 
having to hold a Board meeting 
2. 
All directors must indicate to each other that they share a 
common view “by any means”. – eg. a written resolution, 
telephone conversation. 
 
SHAREHOLDERS' MEETINGS/GENERAL MEETINGS: 
 
Matters are referred to the shareholders: 
× 
Where a matter is outside of the powers of the directors – eg. 
making amendments to the articles 
 OR 
× 
A matter within the power of the directors but requires prior 
approval of the shareholders – eg. making a loan to a director 
 
General meetings (GMs) are called to: 
1. 
Make decisions that require Ordinary resolution (OR) 
 AND/OR 
2. 
Make decisions that require Special resolution (SR) 
 
Ordinary resolution = Simple majority, so more than 50% 
Special resolution = 75% or more. 
 
 
How do you tell which decisions require OR or SR? 
You must look at CA 2006 or the Articles to find what the shareholders 
will be deciding on and these will set out if OR or SR is required. 
 
Notice of GM: 
 
For a private company: call GM on 14 clear days' notice. 
This notice excludes the day on which notice is given and the day of the 
meeting. – the 14 days must be ‘clear' days.

Notice GM 
 
 
If the notice is posted: 
If the notice is posted, it is deemed to have been received by the 
recipient 48 hours after it was posted. These 48 hours only include 
working days. 
Working day = not weekend/bank holiday. 
 
Shorter notice: 
GM may be held by shorter notice if agreed by: 
• 
A majority in number of the members who have a right to attend 
and vote the GM. 
 AND 
• 
This majority must together hold not less than 90% the shares 
(95% for non-trading public companies). 
 
Quorum? 
The quorum is 2. 
If the company has only 1 member, 1 qualifying person present is 
sufficient. 
 
Decision-making? 
Decisions are made on a show of hands unless a poll is demanded. – if 
you have 2 shareholders with a large shareholding, he is likely to demand 
voting by poll as this is more beneficial for them. One shareholder is not 
enough to demand a poll unless he is also a director. 
 
Show of hands: each shareholder present at the meeting will be entitled 
to 1 vote, regardless of the number of shares held by that shareholder. 
Poll: every shareholder has one vote in respect of each share. 
 
Model Articles A poll can be demanded before the meeting or at the 
meeting either before or immediately after a show of hands has taken 
place. 
Model Articles The chairman, the directors, 2 or more shareholders, or 
any member with not less than 10% of the voting rights of those entitled 
to vote on the resolution can demand one.

DIRECTORS DECLARING INTEREST IN THE 
TRANSACTION: 
 
Directors must declare their interest in any existing/proposed 
transactions, and this must be done by giving notice to the other 
directors. 
 
Form of notice: 
– 
No prescribed form for giving notice. 
– 
Disclosure to the members is not sufficient. 
– 
CA 2006 Notice may be given orally, in writing or by giving 
general notice. 
– 
CA 2006 Notice must include the nature and extent of the

with which we are dealing. 
 
Quorum:
