will not be counter towards the quorum on that decision.

pages.heading: DIFFERENT TYPES OF PROCEDURES: · Full notice procedure:
pages.text:
BLP – SQE notes | Page 17 of 26 
 
DIFFERENT TYPES OF PROCEDURES: 
 
Full notice procedure: 
 
This is the standard procedure. In this case, we must give 14 days notice 
for the GM which is the full notice. 
 
Structure: 
* 
Board Meeting I 
* 
General Meeting 
* 
Board Meeting II 
* 
Post-meeting matters 
 
Post Meeting Matters: 
* 
If the resolution held at the meeting affects any information filed 
at Companies House, a copy of the changes must be filed at 
Companies House within 14 days. 
* 
Meeting minutes to be kept for all meetings. 
 
* 
File forms at Companies House: 
- 
Appointing new directors/company secretary/auditors 
- 
Terminating the contract of existing directors/ 
company secretary/auditors 
- 
Changing the company name/address (whichever is 
relevant) 
 
* 
Update the register of members/director (whichever is relevant) 
* 
Issue new share certificates (if relevant). 
 
Short notice procedure: 
 
You can only use the short notice procedure if consent for short 
notice is obtained. 
 
Approval for short notice must be given by: 
× 
The majority in number of the members of the company – eg. 
out of 6 shareholders, a minimum of 4 must consent. 
× 
Who together hold at least 90% of the shares of the company. 
 
Structure: 
1. 
Have the Board Meeting, then adjourn it. 
2. 
General Meeting 
3. 
Reconvene the same Board Meeting on the same day 
4. 
Post-meeting matters 
 
Post Meeting Matters: 
* 
If the resolution held at the meeting affects any information filed 
at Companies House, a copy of the changes must be filed at 
Companies House within 14 days. 
* 
Meeting minutes to be kept for both meetings. 
* 
Consent to short notice document must be filed at Companies 
House. 
 
* 
File forms at Companies House: 
- 
Appointing new directors/company secretary/auditors 
- 
Terminating the contract of existing directors/ 
company secretary/auditors 
- 
Changing the company name/address (whichever is 
relevant) 
 
* 
Update the register of members/director (whichever is relevant) 
* 
Issue new share certificates (if relevant). 
 
Written resolution procedure: 
 
Only private companies may pass a shareholders' resolution by way of 
a written resolution. 
 
If this is approved, the company will hold a written resolution instead of 
a General meeting. 
 
Structure: 
1. 
Have the Board Meeting, then adjourn it. 
2. 
Written resolution 
3. 
Reconvene the same Board Meeting on the same day 
4. 
Post-meeting matters 
 
The directors must circulate the written resolution to all eligible 
members. 
 
If there is a company representative: they can indicate agreement to the 
resolution by signing a copy of the draft written resolution. 
 
A written special resolution must state it is a special resolution. 
The written resolution document must be signed, dated and returned by 
each member. 
All votes on written resolution are on a poll. 
 
 
 
 
Post Meeting Matters: 
* 
If the resolution held at the meeting affects any information filed 
at Companies House, a copy of the changes must be filed at 
Companies House within 14 days. 
* 
Board meeting minutes to be kept. 
* 
Keep a record of the written resolution. 
 
* 
File forms at Companies House: 
- 
Appointing new directors/company secretary/auditors 
- 
Terminating the contract of existing directors/ 
company secretary/auditors 
- 
Changing the company name/address (whichever is 
relevant) 
 
* 
Update the register of members/director (whichever is relevant) 
* 
Issue new share certificates (if relevant). 
 
REQUIREMENTS FOR DIFFERENT MATTERS: 
 
Matters requiring shareholder approval by ordinary resolution: 
* 
Appointment of auditors 
* 
Appointment/reappointment of directors 
* 
Removal of a director 
* 
Removal of an auditor 
* 
Adoption of annual accounts 
* 
Adoption of directors'/auditors' reports 
* 
Declaration of dividends 
* 
Allotment of shares 
* 
Approval of a substantial property transaction involving 
directors with a personal interest in it 
* 
Ratification of a director's breach of duty 
* 
Entering into a service contract with a director for a term of more 
than 2 years 
* 
Making a loan to a director 
* 
Giving a director loss of office payment/gift after leaving office 
 
Substantial property transactions: 
 
If a director buys/sells property from/to the company for less than 
£5,000, the transaction will be considered de minimis, and will not need 
shareholder approval. 
 
If the value of the property purchased/sold is more than £100,000, it 
will be automatically considered a substantial property transaction. 
 
If the value of the property is between £5,000 and £100,000, you need 
to look at the value of the company (Net Asset Value) to determine 
whether the transaction will amount to a substantial property 
transaction. If the transaction exceeds 10% of the company's Net Asset 
Value, then it will be deemed to be a substantial property transaction. 
 
Matters requiring shareholder approval by special resolution: 
* 
Any decision relating to the buyback of company shares 
* 
Changes to the company's articles 
* 
Changes to the company's name

pages.heading: COMPANY RECORDKEEPING AND FILING · RECORDKEEPING:
pages.text:
BLP – SQE notes | Page 18 of 26 
COMPANY RECORDKEEPING AND FILING 
 
RECORDKEEPING: 
 
Registers: 
Companies Act 2006 Companies must keep a number of registers 
available to the company's members for inspection for free or the public 
for a fee: 
* 
A register of members 
* 
A register of directors 
* 
A register of secretaries 
* 
A register of charges against the company's assets 
 AND 
* 
A register of people with significant control (PSC) 
 
Minutes: 
* 
Minutes of all general meetings must be kept and available for 
inspection by members of the company for at least 10 years. 
* 
Minutes of board meetings 
 
Directors' service contracts: 
Copies of service contracts must be kept and made available for 
inspection by the members for at least one year beyond the term of the 
contract. 
 
COMPANIES HOUSE FILING: 
 
Companies must file at Companies House the following each year: 
1. 
Confirmation statement 
2. 
Company accounts 
3. 
Directors' report – medium and large companies only 
4. 
Strategic report – medium and large companies only 
 
Medium and large companies = companies with more than 50 
employees or a turnover of £10 million or more. 
 
Annual confirmation statement: 
 
The annual confirmation statement must confirm that the information 
at Companies House is up to date. 
 
It is a criminal offence to fail to file the confirmation statement within 
14 days of the end of the company's review period. 
 
Company accounts: 
 
Private companies must file their accounts at Companies House no later 
than 9 months after the relevant accounting reference period. 
 
Public companies must file their accounts at Companies House no later 
than 6 months after the relevant accounting reference period. 
 
The accounts must include a Balance Sheet, Profit and Loss Account 
giving a true and fair view of the company's financial year. 
 
The directors must approve the accounts verifying their belief that they 
are satisfied that the accounts give a true and fair view of the company. 
 
Annual directors' report: 
 
*Medium and large companies only* 
 
Medium and large companies must file an annual directors' report 
which names the directors and state the amount that the directors 
recommend should be paid as dividend (if any). 
 
Annual strategic report: 
 
*Medium and large companies only* 
 
Medium and large companies must file an annual strategic report to give 
the members a comprehensive view of the development/performance 
of the business so the members may assess the directors' performance. 
 
BUSINESS LETTERHEADS: 
 
The letterhead of a company must disclose: 
* 
Its registered name 
* 
The part of the UK in which the company is registered 
* 
The company's registered number 
* 
The address of the company's registered office 
* 
If a company choose to display the name of any director on its 
letterhead, it must include the name of every director on the 
letterhead. 
* 
A change in name requires approval by special resolution. 
 
 
 
 
 
The letterhead of a partnership must disclose: 
* 
The name of the partnership 
* 
The name of each member of the partnership 
 AND 
* 
The partnership's business address 
 
A sole trader's letterhead must include: 
* 
The individual's business name 
* 
The individual's real name if that is different from the business 
name 
 AND 
* 
The business address.

pages.heading: RAISING FINANCE · Equity finance:
pages.text:
BLP – SQE notes | Page 19 of 26 
RAISING FINANCE 
 
Equity finance: 
 
Equity finance = money raised by issuing shares. In return of their 
purchase money towards the shares, the shareholders have certain 
expectations which are the benefits of these types of investments. 
 
Benefits to the shareholders 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Debt finance: 
 
Debt finance = money raised by borrowing money from the bank/other 
lenders in the form of a loan. 
 
Types of debt finance: loan finance and debt securities. 
 
EQUITY FINANCE: 
 
Shares and their features: 
 
Nominal or par value: 
 
Shares must have a fixed nominal value – eg. 1p, 5p or £1 
 
Nominal value = the minimum subscription price for that share. It 
represents a unit of ownership rather than the actual value of the share. 
Market value = often higher than the nominal value and it constantly 
changes. 
Eg. a share's nominal value may be £1, but it maybe sold on the market 
for £2.50. 
 
The excess over nominal value is the ‘premium' – eg. Market price 
(£2.50) – Nominal value (£1) = £1.50 
 
Issued, allotted, paid-up and called-up shares: 
 
Issued share capital = the total amount in value (nominal and premium) 
of all shares in issue at any point in time. – This is the amount of share 
capital that will be shown in the company's accounts. 
 
Issued share capital is made up of: 
× 
Subscriber shares = shares purchased by the first members of 
the company. 
× 
Further shares will be issued once the company has been 
incorporated. 
 
Allotment = shares are ‘allotted' when a person acquires the 
unconditional right to be included in the company's register in respect 
of those shares. 
 
Issue of shares = shares are only issued, and only form part of a 
company's issued share capital once the shareholder has been 
registered. 
 
Paid-up share capital = the amount paid on shares. 
 
Called-up share capital = the outstanding payment on shares that has 
been demanded by the company. 
 
Transfer of shares: 
 
Shareholders may decide to sell their shares to third parties. The right 
to transfer the shares is governed by the articles. 
 
Model Articles for private companies The company directors have the 
absolute power to stop the shareholders from selling their shares. 
 
Issuing new shares: 
 
Generally, the directors have the power to allot new shares if the 
company has only one class of shares and there is no restriction 
removing this power in the articles. – There is no such restriction in the 
Model Articles. 
 
To issue new shares in any other situation, directors must seek 
ordinary resolution from the shareholders. 
 
General procedure for issuing shares: 
* 
Directors will decide on the price and number of shares to allot 
and will hold a resolution to allot shares. 
* 
Shares are issued in exchange for cash in general, but the 
directors may accept property for shares as well. 
* 
The full value of the shares must be paid to the company on 
allotment. – Model Articles 
* 
If the shares have a nominal or par value, the money received 
on account of the value will be added to the company's share 
capital. 
* 
The premium amount must be recorded separately in the Share 
Premium Account. 
* 
The new shares must be first offered to the existing 
shareholders, unless the articles provide otherwise (the Model 
Articles do not). – this is because existing shareholders have a 
pre-emption right. 
 
Pre-emption rights and related rules: 
* 
The shares must be offered on the same terms for which the 
shares would be offered on the open market. 
* 
The existing shareholder must be given at least 14 days to 
accept. 
* 
The pre-emption right does not apply to shares issued for noncash consideration. 
* 
The pre-emption right may be disapplied by special resolution. 
 
DEBT FINANCE: 
 
Two types of loans: 
– 
Unsecured loan: 
A contractual promise to repay the money borrowed. 
 
– 
Secured loan: 
A contractual promise to repay the money borrowed where the 
Lender receives the right to take collateral (property) if the loan 
is not repaid as specified in the Loan agreement. 
 
* 
Mortgage: The security provider retains possession of 
the asset but transfers ownership to the creditor. 
 
* 
Charge: The Lender gets an equitable interest in the sale 
proceeds of an asset. As well as this equitable 
proprietary interest, the charging document will give 
the lender contractual rights over the asset. – eg. to 
appoint a receiver or administrator to take possession 
of it and sell it, if the debt is not paid back. 
 
1. 
Fixed charge: a charge taken over a specific 
asset – eg. a machinery. 
 
2. 
Floating charge: a charge taken over a class of 
assets that are frequently changing. – eg. stock. 
This charge, on crystallisation, becomes fixed on 
the assets and is enforceable as a fixed charge. 
 
Charges and mortgages against a company asset must be 
registered at Companies House within 21 days of creation. 
 
Debt security = a document which serves as evidence of the loan made 
to the company. This document may be traded. 
 
 
 
Dividends: 
A share in the 
company's profits. 
 
However, 
dividends can only 
paid out of profits. 
 
Capital return: 
Increase in share 
value. If the shares 
sell for a greater 
amount than the 
amount the original 
purchase price, the 
shareholder keeps 
the difference. 
Voting rights: 
This keeps the 
shareholders 
involved in the 
running of the 
company.

pages.heading: INSOLVENCY PROCEDURES · Insolvency = where a person/business is unable to pay its debts.
pages.text:
BLP – SQE notes | Page 20 of 26 
INSOLVENCY PROCEDURES 
 
Insolvency = where a person/business is unable to pay its debts. 
 
DIRECTORS' DUTIES ON INSOLVENCY: 
 
When the directors become aware that insolvency is a possibility, they 
must take action to assess if the company should continue to trade. 
 
On insolvency, directors should: 
* 
Seek advice from a financial advisor/insolvency practitioner 
* 
Have regular discussions (possibly daily) to assess the company's 
financial position and decide whether or not to cease trading. 
They should voice concerns, suggesting reduction on liabilities at 
BM and keep minutes of these meetings to demonstrate that 
they have complied with their duties. 
* 
Not take on more debt as this would be a breach of duty or even 
wrongful trading 
* 
Pursue debtors rigorously 
 
Once there is a prospect of insolvency, the directors' duty to promote 
the success of the company will be subject to any law requiring directors 
to protect the interests of the creditors instead. 
 
If the directors continue trading when there is no reasonable prospect 
that the company will be able to avoid insolvency, they may be 
personally liable for any losses. – see Voidable Transactions below. 
 
PRE-INSOLVENCY MORATORIUM: 
 
Corporate Insolvency and Governance Act 2020 A pre-insolvency 
moratorium is now available for companies in addition to the existing 
moratorium procedures (administration and CVA). 
 
Moratorium = a period stopping all insolvency/legal proceedings against 
the company. It allows for the directors to negotiate with the creditors 
or to propose a CVA/restructuring plan/Scheme of arrangement. 
 
While the moratorium is in effect: 
× 
No enforcement of security is allowed by floating charge holders. 
× 
An administrator cannot be appointed. 
× 
A floating charge cannot crystallize into a fixed charge. – This is 
different to other types of moratorium. 
 
Requirements: 
1. 
The company must be in financial difficulty to apply and must 
intend to use this time to agree a long-term solution with its 
creditors. 
2. 
The court will only grant a pre-insolvency moratorium if it is likely 
that the company can be rescued as a going concern. 
3. 
The moratorium can only continue if it is still likely that the 
company can be rescued as a going concern and the company is 
also able to pay its moratorium debts and pre-moratorium debts 
when due. – Monitor will constantly check the company's 
finances and if the requirements cease to exist, the monitor 
must bring the moratorium to an end. 
 
Length: 
20 days which may be extended once for another 20 days. 
 
For further extension up to 12 months in total: extension must be 
approved by at least 50% in value of the secured and unsecured creditors 
or court order. 
 
INFORMAL NEGOTIATIONS: 
 
The directors may enter into informal negotiations with the creditors. 
 
During the negotiations, the company will seek: 
To restructure its debt on more favourable terms or refinance the debt 
by entering into a new contract – a Restructuring Agreement. 
 
In return the company may have to do the following: 
* 
Grant new/additional security 
* 
Sell subsidiaries to raise cash 
* 
A debt for equity swap: issue new shares to the creditors 
 
SCHEME OF ARRANGEMENT: 
 
The directors may enter into a Scheme of Arrangement (SoA). 
 
Scheme of Arrangement = an agreement binding all creditors 
(including dissenting/unknown creditors). 
 
Can only be made by preferential and unsecured creditors, fixed and 
floating charge holders will not participate in a scheme of arrangement 
because they can simply enforce the security under the terms of the loan 
agreement. 
 
 
Use SoA: 
* 
in group insolvencies and restructuring. 
* 
if a company wishes to compromise secured liabilities and it does 
not have 100% agreement among creditors. 
 
COMPANY VOLUNTARY ARRANGEMENT: 
 
The directors may enter into a Company Voluntary Arrangement (CVA). 
 
Company Voluntary Arrangement = an agreement allowing the 
company to settle its debts by paying only a portion of the monies owed. 
This agreement will bind all creditors (including dissenting/unknown 
creditors). 
 
Can only be made by preferential and unsecured creditors, fixed and 
floating charge holders will not participate in a scheme of arrangement 
because they can simply enforce the security under the terms of the loan 
agreement. 
 
Setting up a CVA: 
1. 
The directors prepare a written proposal for repayment 
nominating a licensed insolvency practitioner (nominee) as the 
supervisor. 
2. 
The nominee will seek creditors' approval using a permitted 
decision-making procedure. 
3. 
The compromise must be agreed by 3/4 in value of the creditors. 
4. 
The nominee must call a separate shareholder meeting passing 
an ordinary resolution. 
5. 
Must be sanctioned by the court. 
6. 
If the company does not fulfil its obligations under the CVA, the 
company will be wound up. 
 
7. 
Creditors can challenge a CVA within 28 days on grounds of: 
× 
Unfair prejudice 
× 
Material irregularity (procedure was not followed) 
 
Moratorium: 
* 
Enter into administration before a CVA to get a moratorium. 
* 
Protects the company from creditor claims 
* 
Directors of small companies can apply to the court for a 28day moratorium. 
 
A company is a small company if it satisfies two or more of the below: 
* 
Its turnover is not more than £6.5 million 
* 
Its Balance sheet is not more than £3.26 million 
* 
It does not have more than 50 employees 
 
Pros and cons of a CVA: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
ADMINISTRATION: 
 
If enforcing a floating charge – use the Administration procedure. 
 
Debenture = the document setting out the floating charge. The 
debenture will include a provision giving the charge holder the right to 
appoint an administrator/administrative receiver if the company 
defaults. – if the debenture contains this provision, the floating charge 
will be a qualifying floating charge. 
 
Procedure: 
 
Court procedure: 
The shareholders, board of directors, any creditor, liquidator or 
supervisor of a CVA can apply to the court to appoint an Administrator. 
 
Out-of-court procedure: 
Only the company, directors or a qualifying floating charge holder 
(QFCH) can appoint an administrator using the out-of-court procedure. 
 
1. 
If a QFCH appoints the administrator/administrative receiver: 
× 
They can appoint an administrator/administrative 
receiver if the charge was created before 15 Sep 2003. 
× 
An administrator cannot be appointed if one has already 
been appointed. 
Pros for creditors: 
× Could carry out 
profitable trading during 
the moratorium, so may 
get more than on 
insolvency 
× CVA costs less than 
insolvency proceedings. 
× For floating charge 
holders, no risk of 
avoidance. 
 
Cons for creditors: 
× Supervisor has 
no power to 
challenge past 
transactions 
unlike a 
liquidator or 
administrator 
× Many 
companies will 
not qualify for a 
moratorium. 
Pros for directors: 
× Supervisor has 
no power to 
challenge past 
transactions 
× Directors retain 
control of the 
company 
× The company's 
goodwill is 
preserved

pages.heading: To appoint, file a notice of appointment at court, serves · notice on any prior QFCH and the appointment
pages.text:
BLP – SQE notes | Page 21 of 26 
× 
To appoint, file a notice of appointment at court, serves 
notice on any prior QFCH and the appointment 
commences on the date of the filing. 
 
2. 
If the directors/the company appoint the administrator: 
× 
File notice of intention to appoint an administrator at the 
court 
× 
Serve it on any QFCH giving them 5-days' notice. 
× 
QFCH may appoint their own administrator within 5 days 
× 
The directors will file a notice of appointment with the 
court within another 5 days. 
 
Once the administrator/administrative receiver is appointed: 
 
Administration procedures allow for a statutory moratorium arising 
immediately when the administrator is appointed. 
 
No winding up petitions/other claims can be made and no steps can be 
taken to enforce any security. 
 
Administrator's appointment terminates automatically after 12 months. 
 
Administrators' duties: 
* 
The administrator runs the company – directors can make no 
decision without consent. 
* 
The administrator is an officer of the court, with a duty to the 
court to act in the interest of all creditors. 
* 
They can pay a dividend to secured creditors and can now pay 
the prescribed part dividend to unsecured creditors. The 
administrator will seek court permission to make the dividend 
payment or will propose a CVA or SoA to be able to pay. 
 
Pros and cons of Administration: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
RECEIVERS: 
 
The directors may decide to call in a receiver. 
 
Types of receivers: 
 
a. 
Fixed charge receivers: 
Appointed by the holder of a fixed charge. A fixed charge 
receiver becomes the receiver only of the property charged and 
is only entitled to deal with that property. 
 
b. 
Administrative receivers: *Most common* 
The receiver is appointed under the debenture's terms which 
includes a floating charge security. This security must cover the 
whole/substantially the whole of the company's property: 
* 
ARs have their powers set out in the debenture 
document unless they are expressly excluded. 
* 
There is no moratorium period here 
* 
Only an option for Pre-15 Sep 2003 QFCHs. 
 
LIQUIDATION: 
 
The directors might decide to go into liquidation and wind up the 
company. 
 
Go into liquidation and wind up the company to realise and distribute 
the company's assets in the order of priority. 
 
The company is dissolved within 3 months. 
 
Three types of liquidation: 
* 
Compulsory liquidation 
* 
Members' voluntary liquidations (solvent liquidations) 
* 
Creditors' voluntary liquidations (insolvent liquidations) 
 
 
 
 
Compulsory liquidation: 
 
A petition to the court can be issued by any creditor, Administrator, 
AR, Supervisor of CVA or the company itself through its directors or 
shareholders (where there are insufficient assets to fund a voluntary 
liquidator). 
 
Because a QFCH may appoint an administrator out-of-court if the 
company defaults on the loan repayments, it is usually an unsecured 
creditor who will apply to the court for a winding up order. 
 
The only ground for a liquidation petition is that the company is unable 
to pay its debts. 
 
 
Proof of inability to pay debts: 
1. 
Statutory demand (£750 < x) unpaid for 3 weeks 
2. 
Unsatisfied judgment against debt owed 
3. 
Cash flow test 
 OR 
4. 
Balance sheet test – more onerous than the cash flow test. 
 
Cash flow insolvency = the company has insufficient income to pay for 
its debts. 
Balance sheet insolvency = the company has insufficient assets to pay 
for its debts. 
 
Creditors' voluntary liquidations: 
 
This is a form of insolvent liquidation commenced by resolution of the 
shareholders but controlled by the creditors. 
 
The shareholders will pass: 
* 
A special resolution to approve the CVL 
 AND 
* 
An ordinary resolution appointing a liquidator but within 14 days 
a creditors' meeting will be convened to either approve the 
liquidator or put forward their own choice of liquidator. 
 
The liquidator is the de facto agent of the company. The directors lose 
their powers upon the liquidator's appointment. 
 
The liquidator's function: 
1. 
To realise the company's assets for cash 
2. 
To identify the company's creditors and the amount owed to 
them and then pay a dividend to the creditors proportionately 
3. 
To maximise the assets available for distribution to the 
company's creditors by: 
* 
Challenging voidable past transactions or to sue the 
directors for wrongful/fraudulent trading. 
* 
Disclaiming onerous property available equally in both 
solvent and insolvent liquidations. – lease of land. 
 
Liquidator: will usually sell assets on a piece-meal basis rather than 
selling the assets and business as a going concern. 
 
Where there is a dividend to be paid to unsecured creditors, companies 
may enter into liquidation after the administration comes to an end. In 
such a case, the purpose of the liquidation will be payment of a dividend. 
 
 
 
 
Pros for a QFCH: 
× May avoid bad 
publicity 
× Will prevent the 
other creditors 
from taking action 
× Past transactions 
can be challenged 
Cons for a QFCH: 
× Costs of court order 
and fees of 
administrators 
× 5 days delay whilst 
administrator is 
appointed 
× QFCH does not 
control whether 
floating charge 
assets will be sold 
× unlike for a CVA the 
website and 
communications of 
the company must 
state that it is in 
administration. 
Pros for a company: 
× The aim of an 
administrator is 
to save the 
company while 
the aim of an 
administrative 
receiver is to 
maximise assets 
to repay the 
creditor.

pages.heading: STEPS ON INSOLVENCY · If the directors conclude that the company is unlikely to be able to
pages.text:
BLP – SQE notes | Page 22 of 26 
STEPS ON INSOLVENCY 
 
If the directors conclude that the company is unlikely to be able to 
trade out of its difficulties, they have several options: 
* 
Do nothing – however, directors might be held liable for 
wrongful/fraudulent trading and could be disqualified. Directors 
may be in breach of their statutory duties. 
* 
Enter into pre-insolvency moratorium 
* 
Enter into informal negotiations with the creditors 
* 
Enter into a Creditors' Voluntary Arrangement 
* 
Enter into a Scheme of Arrangement 
* 
Go into administration 
* 
Call in a receiver 
* 
Go into liquidation and wind up the company 
 
The company may also need to bring in new management and/or 
replace existing directors. 
 
SELECTING THE RIGHT PROCEDURE: 
 
 
Directors selecting the procedure 
 
If the directors want to 
save the company 
 
Enter into a consensual agreement 
binding only on those creditors which 
agree to it. No insolvency procedure will 
be needed. 
 
 
If the directors want to 
seek compromise with 
creditors 
 
 
Enter into a pre-insolvency moratorium 
or go into administration prior to 
entering into a Scheme of arrangement 
or Creditors' Voluntary Arrangement. 
 
 
If the directors need time 
during which creditors 
cannot force insolvency 
 
 
Enter into a pre-insolvency moratorium 
or go into administration. 
 
 
If the company cannot be 
saved, but its business can 
be saved 
 
 
Enter into a pre-insolvency moratorium 
or go into administration to protect the 
business from creditor action. 
 
 
If neither the company nor 
its business can be saved 
 
 
Enter into administration, then 
liquidation. 
 
 
 
Secured creditors selecting the procedure 
 
If the creditor wants a 
compromise with the 
company 
 
 
Enter into a consensual agreement with 
the company binding only on those 
creditors which agree to it. No 
insolvency procedure will be needed. 
 
 
If the creditors want to 
enforce a floating charge 
 
Enter into administration. 
 
 
 
If the creditors want to 
enforce a fixed 
charge/mortgage 
 
 
Appoint a fixed charge receiver. 
 
 
If the creditors want to 
enforce a pre-15 Sep 2003 
qualifying floating charge 
 
 
Enter into administration or 
administrative receivership. 
 
 
If the creditor is a high 
street bank 
 
 
Send a reservation of rights letter and do 
nothing. 
 
 
 
 
Unsecured creditors selecting the procedure 
 
If the creditor wants a 
compromise with the 
company 
 
 
Enter into a consensual agreement with 
the company binding only on those 
creditors which agree to it. No 
insolvency procedure will be needed. 
 
 
If the creditor wants a 
compromise where all 
creditors are bound 
 
 
Enter into a Creditors' Voluntary 
Arrangement or Scheme of 
Arrangement. 
 
 
If the creditors want to 
take over the running of 
the company in the 
creditors' interests 
 
 
Enter into administration. 
 
 
If the creditors serve a 
statutory demand which 
is not paid 
 
 
Petition to the court for Compulsory 
liquidation 
 
 
If the creditors sue, obtain 
judgment which remains 
unpaid 
 
 
Enforce the judgment debt 
 
 
 
PROCEDURE MAP: 
 
KEY: FIRST → THEN – eg. A CVA becoming Administration. 
 
CVA → ADMINISTRATION 
An administration is unlikely to follow a CVA but may follow if the 
creditors vote down a CVA proposal or a CVA terminates. 
 
CVA → ADMINISTRATIVE RECEIVERSHIP 
A QFCH would usually have the right to enforce its security and appoint 
an AR under a pre-Relevant Date floating charge if the debtor proposes 
a CVA to its unsecured creditors. 
 
CVA → LIQUIDATION 
Unlikely but if a company does not fulfil its obligations under the CVA, 
the supervisor will petition the court for a winding up order. 
 
ADMINISTRATION → CVA 
Possible. The administrator (but not the directors) may propose a CVA 
during the administration. 
 
ADMINISTRATION → ADMINISTRATIVE RECEIVERSHIP 
Not possible. 
 
ADMINISTRATION → LIQUIDATION 
May occur only after administration has come to an end. 
 
ADMINISTRATIVE RECEIVERSHIP → CVA 
Possible in theory but in practice it does not happen. 
 
ADMINISTRATIVE RECEIVERSHIP → ADMINISTRATION 
Only possible with a court order. 
 
ADMINISTRATIVE RECEIVERSHIP → LIQUIDATION 
Possible. Following the conclusion of an administrative receivership, the 
company will usually go into liquidation. 
 
LIQUIDATION → CVA 
Possible. The liquidator (but not the directors) may propose a CVA in the 
course of the liquidation. 
 
LIQUIDATION → ADMINISTRATION 
Not possible. 
 
LIQUIDATION → ADMINISTRATIVE RECEIVERSHIP 
Possible. Usually a petition to appoint a liquidator in an event of default. 
This would entitle a QFCH to appoint an AR. If an AR is appointed, the 
liquidation and receivership will run concurrently. 
 
ORDER OF PRIORITY ON WINDING UP: 
 
Order of priority = the order in which a company's assets are distributed 
when it is wound up. 
 
Order of priority: 
1. 
Liquidator's fees/expense 
2. 
Amount due to fixed charge creditor 
3. 
Other costs/expenses of the liquidation 
 
4. 
Preferential creditors: 
× 
Holiday pay due to employees 
× 
Wages due to employees in the last 4 months 
× 
HMRC in relation to unpaid VAT, PAYE and NI 
contributions 
 
5. 
Create the prescribed part fund from floating charges for 
unsecured creditors 
Must be paid to unsecured creditors in full if under £10,000. 
If more than £10,000, then 50% of the first £10,000 and 20% 
thereafter up to £600,000 is set aside for the unsecured creditors 
and the rest goes to floating charge holders.

pages.heading: Creditors with floating charges · Two people has the same charge – share equally (pro rata).
pages.text:
BLP – SQE notes | Page 23 of 26 
 
 
6. 
Creditors with floating charges 
Two people has the same charge – share equally (pro rata). 
Two charges: If there is a deed of priority – pay out according to 
it. If no, then the charge that is created first (if registered within 
21 days) 
 
7. 
Unsecured/trade creditors (including payment of the 
prescribed part) 
Ordinary trade creditors, secured creditors who did not get fully 
paid, taxes (Crown debts), employees' outstanding pay 
Rank and abate equally. 
 
8. 
Interest from the start of the winding up proceedings owed to 
unsecured creditors. 
9. 
Shareholders – Preferential shareholders are in priority to 
ordinary shareholders.

pages.heading: BANKRUPTCY · Bankruptcy = a judicial process in which the assets of the person who
pages.text:
BLP – SQE notes | Page 24 of 26 
BANKRUPTCY 
 
Bankruptcy = a judicial process in which the assets of the person who 
is bankrupt are passed to a third party called the trustee in bankruptcy. 
 
The trustee in bankruptcy will liquidate the assets and use the money 
from the liquidation process to pay off as many of the debtor's debt as 
possible. 
 
BANKRUPTCY PROCESS: 
 
1. 
A bankruptcy application should be made: 
* 
Bankrupt may make a bankruptcy application online. 
* 
One/more of the debtor's unsecured creditors owed at 
least £5,000 can submit a petition for a bankruptcy 
order. 
 OR 
* 
The supervisor of an Individual Voluntary Arrangement 
can petition for a bankruptcy order if the debtor is in 
default of the Individual Voluntary Arrangement. 
 
2. 
After the application is made, the debtor's creditors cannot 
continue to chase after the debtor and the debtor will be 
discharged from most of their debts after one year. 
 
3. 
If an application is made by the creditors: 
* 
The application must prove that the debtor is unable to 
pay their debts by showing that: 
× 
The debt is payable immediately and that the 
debtor does not have funds to pay. 
 OR 
× 
The debt is payable in the future and the debtor 
has no reasonable prospect of being able to pay. 
 
* 
If the debtor owes a liquidated debt for £5,000 or more, 
the creditor may make a statutory demand for 
payment. – If the debt is not paid within 3 weeks, or the 
debtor does not apply to set aside the statutory 
demand within 3 weeks, the debtor will be deemed 
insolvent. 
 
* 
If the debtor owes a future liability of more than 
£5,000, the creditor may serve a statutory demand for 
a proof of ability to pay and if the debtor does not show 
a reasonable prospect of being able to pay the debt 
when it falls due or apply to court to set aside the 
statutory demand, the debtor will be deemed insolvent. 
 
* 
If the debtor owes a judgment debt of more than 
£5,000, the creditor can seek to execute on the 
judgment, if the attempt fails, the debtor will be 
deemed insolvent. 
 
4. 
After the bankruptcy order is made, an official receiver is 
appointed who will act as the trustee in bankruptcy unless the 
creditors seek to appoint their own nominee. 
 
5. 
The debtor's properties will automatically vest in the trustee, 
except for the following, which is kept by the bankrupt: 
* 
Anything necessary for day-to-day living 
* 
Tools required for their job 
* 
Their salary 
 
6. 
During the bankruptcy proceedings, the bankrupt cannot: 
* 
Apply for credit over a prescribed amount. 
* 
Act as a company director 
* 
Be a partner 
* 
Trade under another name 
 
7. 
The trustee must pay creditors in this order: 
* 
Costs of the bankruptcy 
* 
Preferential debts, including employee wages for 4 
months and money owed to HMCR for taxes and NI 
contributions 
* 
Ordinary unsecured creditors 
* 
Postponed creditors (spouse/civil partner) 
 
8. 
A bankrupt who has caused the bankruptcy by their own 
dishonesty, negligence or recklessness is considered culpable 
and can be subject to a court bankruptcy order for up to 15 
years. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
PARTNERSHIPS: 
 
If the bankrupt is a partner in a general partnership: 
1. 
If the partnership is at will – it will be dissolved on the 
bankruptcy of the partner and the partner's share of assets will 
be turned over to the trustee. 
2. 
If the partnership is for a specified term/undertaking – it will 
continue and commonly, the remaining partners purchase the 
insolvent partner's interest. 
 
If the bankrupt is a member of an LLP: 
They cannot participate in the management of the LLP. 
 
If the general partnership itself is insolvent: 
It will be wound up using bankruptcy proceedings. 
 
If an LLP is insolvent: 
It will be wound up in the same way as a company.

pages.heading: PERSONAL LIABILITY OF DIRECTORS · ON INSOLVENCY
pages.text:
BLP – SQE notes | Page 25 of 26 
PERSONAL LIABILITY OF DIRECTORS 
ON INSOLVENCY 
 
Company Directors Disqualification Act 1986 Disqualification from 
acting as a director for up to 15 years. 
 
FRAUDULENT TRADING: 
 
Elements of the claim: 
 
Insolvency Act 1986 Fraudulent trading is a civil claim. 
 
The claim can be brought by: 
* 
A liquidator 
* 
An administrator 
 
Both liquidators and administrators need the sanction of the 
creditors/court to bring a claim. 
 
Brought against a director or any other person. 
Who is party to the carrying on of any business of the company for any 
fraudulent purpose. 
 
Actual dishonesty is required – a high standard of proof – likely to be 
extremely difficult to establish. 
 
Defence: 
 
It is a defence if the director genuinely believed that things would get 
better. 
 
Sanctions: 
 
The director will be personally liable to make such contributions to the 
company's assets as the court thinks fit. 
 
Company Directors Disqualification Act 1986 Disqualification order is 
likely. – with disqualification for up to 15 years. 
 
Criminal sanctions can also be brought. 
 
WRONGFUL TRADING: *POPULAR EXAM Q* 
 
Elements of the claim: 
 
Test: the company becomes insolvent and at some point prior to that 
the director knew/ought to have known that there was no reasonable 
prospect that the company would avoid insolvent liquidation or 
administration. – easier to prove than fraudulent trading. 
 
Liquidators and administrators may bring a claim – but only with the 
sanction of the court. Claims can be brought against directors. (This 
includes shadow directors, de facto and non-executive directors). 
 
Insolvency for wrongful trading purposes is judged solely on the 
balance sheet test and not on the “cash flow test”. 
Balance sheet test = the value of the Company's assets are less than its 
liabilities. 
 
Defence: 
 
The ‘every step' defence: The director will have a defence if they can 
show that, from the time they noticed that the company is likely to 
become insolvent, they had taken every step to minimise the potential 
loss to the Company's creditors. 
 
The court will apply the reasonably diligent person test and apply the 
higher of the two standards: 
 
1. 
Objective test: 
The general knowledge, skill and experience reasonably 
expected of a director carrying out the same functions as the 
direction in question. – The general knowledge of a managing 
director/finance director etc. 
 
 OR 
 
2. 
Subjective test: 
A higher subjective standard due to the director's actual skill, 
knowledge and experience. – Have they been a director of 
another company before becoming a director here? Does the 
director have any relevant qualifications? Do they have any kind 
of financial qualifications? 
 
The every step defence – do one/more of the following: 
* 
Persuade the other directors to commission a detailed financial 
review without delay. 
* 
Ensure that the company has adequate financial monitoring 
systems in place to enable constant review of the company's 
finances. 
* 
Calling regular – possibly weekly – board meetings to review the 
Company's financial position and the director should voice and 
have minuted their concerns. 
* 
Suggesting savings options for the company in the running of the 
business. 
* 
Requesting that the board take steps to avoid incurring new 
credit and/or reduce current debts. 
* 
Suggesting to the board that to take professional independent 
advice from an insolvency practitioner and/or that insolvency 
procedures be considered/initiated. 
* 
Communicating their concerns to shareholders to get them on 
their side. 
 
Although a director cannot escape liability by resigning, it might be 
appropriate for the director to resign if the other directors do not listen 
to their concerns or take any actions which would amount to 
wrongful/fraudulent trading. 
 
Sanctions: 
 
The director will be personally liable to make such contributions to the 
company's assets as the court thinks fit. 
 
Company Directors Disqualification Act 1986 Disqualification order is 
likely. – with disqualification for up to 15 years. 
 
Such claims are not brought in every case because of the risk that the 
creditors will get even less after the court and liquidator's extra fees. 
 
MISFEASANCE: 
 
Elements of the claim: 
 
Use where liability is already established. 
Any creditor/liquidator (but not an administrator) may bring a claim for 
repayment, restoration, or contribution to the company's assets. 
 
A claim can be brought against: an (ex-)officer of the company. 
 
Misfeasance includes: 
1. 
Misapplication of the company's money/assets 
2. 
Transactions at an undervalue 
3. 
Preferences 
 
4. 
Breach of any statutory duty/directors' duty: 
a. 
Unlawful loans to a director 
b. 
Not disclosing their interest in a loan 
c. 
Not informing of substantial property transaction 
d. 
A director failing to act within their powers 
e. 
Negligence 
 
Shareholder ratification is not possible where the company is on the 
brink of insolvency. 
 
Sanctions: 
 
Company Directors Disqualification Act 1986 Disqualification order is 
likely. – with disqualification for up to 15 years.

pages.heading: VOIDABLE TRANSACTIONS (CLAWBACK) · INTRODUCTION:
pages.text:
BLP – SQE notes | Page 26 of 26 
VOIDABLE TRANSACTIONS (CLAWBACK) 
 
INTRODUCTION: 
 
If the company, sole trader or partner is struggling financially, the 
directors of the company or the affected individual might try to move 
assets to safety to “hide” them from the liquidator or trustee in 
bankruptcy. 
 
Once the bankruptcy or insolvency/administration has commenced, 
these past transactions may be challenged. 
 
The court's sanctions: 
* 
An order reversing the transaction 
* 
An order providing for financial restitution to restore the 
company to the position it would have been in had the 
transaction not occurred. 
 
Insolvency Act 1986 Bona fide purchasers for value without notice who 
were not a party to the original transaction are protected. 
 
Voidable transactions: 
* 
Transactions at an undervalue – eg. the directors selling 
company stock/assets to someone for half price. 
* 
Preferences – eg. paying unsecured creditors before insolvency 
to avoid paying secured creditors. 
* 
Avoidance of floating charges – eg. where a new floating charge 
is given on an existing loan/overdraft facility. 
 
 
 
DEFINITIONS 
 
 
Persons connected with the company = the company's director, 
shadow directors, or their associate or the company's associate. 
 
Associates of director = includes their spouse/civil partner, their 
relative, spouse/civil partner's relative, employees, anyone they own 
a partnership with. 
 
Onset of insolvency = includes Administration and Liquidation. 
 
Insolvency = company's inability to pay its debts. 
 
Relevant time = the time period before the onset of insolvency that 
will be investigated by the liquidator/administrator. This time period 
changes based on the type of transaction. 
 
 
 
TRANSACTIONS AT AN UNDERVALUE: 
 
Elements of the claim: 
 
Transaction at an undervalue = a gift/sale at an undervalue. 
A liquidator or administrator can bring a claim. 
 
The transaction is voidable if: 
1. 
It took place 2 years prior to the insolvency (Relevant time). 
2. 
The company must have been insolvent at the time of the 
transaction or have become insolvent as a result. 
3. 
This will be presumed if the transaction is with a connected 
person – otherwise it has to be proven. 
 
There is a rebuttable presumption that an acquisition by a subsequent 
purchaser was not in good faith. 
 
Defence: 
 
Acting in good faith and for the purpose of carrying on the company's 
business. They acted in good faith if they had reasonable grounds for 
believing that the transaction would benefit the company. 
 
Sanctions: 
 
The court may make such order as it thinks fit. 
 
If you are claiming transaction at an undervalue, also look at voidable 
preference as this may be relevant. 
 
PREFERENCES: 
 
Insolvency Act 1986 A liquidator/administrator can prevent a creditor 
obtaining an improper advantage over the other creditors by applying 
to the court for an order to set aside the preference. 
 
The transaction must have been with a creditor and by making the 
payment, the company must have put that creditor in a better position 
than it would have been if that payment has not been made. 
 
Elements of the claim: 
 
The transaction is a preference and thus voidable if: 
1. 
If the transaction is with an unconnected person: the transaction 
is a preference if it took place within the 6 months (Relevant 
time) before the onset of insolvency/bankruptcy. 
2. 
If the transaction is with a connected person or an associate of 
the bankrupt: the transaction is a preference if it took place 
within the 2 years (Relevant time) before the onset of 
insolvency/bankruptcy. 
 
 AND 
 
3. 
The company must have been insolvent at the time of the 
transaction or have become insolvent as a result. 
 
4. 
The company must have been influenced by a desire to prefer 
that creditor (subjective test). – This desire to prefer is presumed 
if the transaction is with a connected person. 
 
Sanctions: 
 
The court may make such order as it thinks fit. 
 
AVOIDANCE OF FLOATING CHARGES: 
 
Insolvency Act 1986 A liquidator or administrator can simply avoid a 
floating charge – where an unsecured creditor has obtained a floating 
charge to secure an already existing charge for no new consideration. 
 
Elements of the claim: 
 
A floating charge can be avoided if: 
1. 
If the charge is granted to an unconnected person: the floating 
charge can be avoided if it was granted within the 1 year 
(Relevant time) before the onset of insolvency. 
2. 
If the charge is granted to a connected person: the floating 
charge can be avoided if it was granted the 2 years (Relevant 
time) before the onset of insolvency. 
 
AND 
 
3. 
The company must have been insolvent at the time of the 
granting of this charge or have become insolvent as a result, 
unless the charge was granted to a connected person. 
 
The floating charge can only be over the new amount – Only additional 
amount is valid, not the full amount. 
 
Automatically invalid – no need for proceedings. 
 
A floating charge is void if it is not registered with Companies House 
within 21 days. 
 
A floating charge granted to a creditor may also be voidable as a 
transaction at an undervalue or preference.

pages.heading: BASIC PRINCIPLES OF TAX · INTRODUCTION TO TAXES:
pages.text:
Taxes SQE Notes | Page 2 of 13 
 
BASIC PRINCIPLES OF TAX 
 
INTRODUCTION TO TAXES: 
 
On the SQE, taxes are only examined in relation to the following 
subjects: 
1. 
Property Practice 
2. 
Business Law and Practice 
3. 
Will and Administration of Estates 
 
Examinable taxes: 
1. 
Income Tax: paid by individuals (employees, sole traders, 
partners in a partnership, company directors). 
2. 
Capital Gains Tax (CGT) 
3. 
Corporation Tax 
4. 
Value Added Tax (VAT) 
5. 
Inheritance Tax (IHT) 
6. 
Stamp Duty Land Tax (SDLT) 
 
Types of taxes: 
 
Direct taxes: 
Direct taxes = taxes imposed by reference to a taxpayer's circumstances. 
Eg. Income tax, CGT, IHT and corporation tax. 
 
Indirect taxes: 
Indirect taxes = taxes ismposed by reference to transactions. 
Eg. VAT and SDLT. 
 
THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN INCOME AND CAPITAL: 
 
When working through a tax calculation problem, start by collecting all 
your figures and highlighting them. 
 
Each figure will fall into one of four categories: 
* 
Income receipts 
* 
Capital receipts 
* 
Income expenditure 
* 
Capital expenditure 
 
Work out which category each of the figures will fall into. – any amount 
will fall into one of these categories and cannot fall into more than one 
category. 
 
Income receipts: 
Receipt of money that originates from regular income generation, 
income received on a recurring basis. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Income receipts: 
Receipt of money that originates from regular income generation. 
 
Capital receipts: 
Falls into this category if there is an income receipt and that income is 
due to a sale that is not part of a regular activity. Capital receipts are 
‘one-off' transactions. 
 
Example: 
* 
Selling your car if you don't sell cars as part of a business. 
* 
Selling a painting if you don't sell paintings as part of a business. 
 
Income expenditure: 
If the expense is incurred due to the day-to-day trading activities of a 
business, it will be classed as income expenditure. 
 
Example: 
* 
Payment of rent – for business premises. 
* 
Paying bills – eg. staff wages, heating, lighting, rent or 
marketing/stationery expenses. 
* 
Paying for repairs of business premises/business vehicle etc. 
 
Capital expenditure: 
If you spend money on a new capital asset or enhancing an existing asset 
as part of the business, it is ‘capital' expenditure. Capital expenditure is 
a ‘one-off' transaction. 
 
Example: 
* 
Buying new large equipment/machinery. 
* 
Buying new property. 
* 
Spending money on enhancing existing equipment/machinery/ 
premises. 
* 
Paying bills – eg. staff wages, heating, lighting, rent or 
marketing/stationery expenses. 
* 
Paying for repairs of business premises/business vehicle etc. 
 
ASSESSMENT OF TAX: 
 
Tax assessment for individuals – based on Tax year 
Tax assessment for companies – based on Financial year (although 
companies may choose a different period for tax assessment purposes, 
called the accounting period) 
 
Both the tax year and financial year are different to the calendar year. 
 
Tax year: starts 6 April, ends 5 April the next year. 
Financial year: starts 1 April, ends 31 March the next year. 
 
HOW IS TAX COLLECTED? 
 
HMRC collects tax from individuals and businesses via the selfassessment system. 
 
In some cases, income tax is deducted at source, meaning that the payer 
of a taxable sum deducts the tax and accounts for it to HMRC on the 
recipient's behalf before the net amount is paid out. The recipient 
therefore receives the sum net of tax. One example of this is the Pay As 
You Earn (PAYE) system. The employee receives the wage/salary net of 
income tax. 
 
 
Example: 
* Salary 
* Trading profits of a 
business will be the 
income of the owner 
* Interest charged on loans 
will be the income of the 
lender 
(whether 
paid 
monthly/quarterly) 
* Rental income paid to 
landlord will be the 
income of the landlord. 
 
Other income that will fall in this 
category: 
* Pension earnings 
* Interest on savings 
* Dividend 
* Benefits in kind given to you 
by the company you work 
for (health insurance, a 
company car and lowinterest or interest-free 
loans of more than 
£10,000).

pages.heading: INCOME TAX – GENERAL RULES · INTRODUCTION TO INCOME TAX:
pages.text:
Taxes SQE Notes | Page 3 of 13 
 
INCOME TAX – GENERAL RULES 
 
INTRODUCTION TO INCOME TAX: 
 
Who pays income tax: 
 
Income tax is paid by individuals and not companies. 
 
This includes: 
* 
Employees 
* 
Sole traders 
* 
Partners in a partnership 
 AND 
* 
Company directors 
 
Deceased persons: 
 
People who are deceased will also need to pay income tax if the tax 
relates to a period when they were working prior to their death and on 
any income received on their estate. – eg. rental income generated by 
the house that forms part of the estate. 
 
This will be paid by their personal representatives as part of the 
administration of their estate. 
 
What is taxable for income tax purposes? 
 
Income tax is paid on receipt of money that originates from regular 
income generation (income profits). Capital profits will not be taken 
into account for income tax purposes. 
 
Foreign income: 
 
Foreign income = income originating from abroad. 
 
If the individual is a UK resident, they must pay tax on foreign income 
they receive during the tax year. 
 
The taxpayer will be deemed to be a UK resident if they have spent at 
least 183 days in the UK during the relevant tax year. 
 
ASSESSMENT AND COLLECTION OF INCOME TAX: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Self-employed/partners – Self-assessment: 
 
Self-employed: 
 
Directors and self-employed people are always required to complete a 
self-assessment tax return. In this case, it is up to the individual to 
calculate the tax bill and not HMRC. 
 
Individuals might be both employees and self-employed to account for 
any additional income they may have received during the tax year via 
different means and this income will be called a trading income. – eg. 
side hustle, rental income, dividend or savings income. 
 
If you are self-employed, you must also register with HMRC as selfemployed within 3 months of starting the business. 
 
Deadlines for submitting tax return: 
1. 
If submitted online – must be filed by 31 January 
2. 
If submitted in paper form – must be filed earlier, by 31 October 
 
Partners in a partnership: 
 
If your client is a partner in a partnership, their share of the 
partnership's profit must be included in their tax return. 
 
Partnership profits, unlike company profits are distributed in accordance 
with the rules of the partnership or the partnership agreement (if any), 
and each partner will receive a share. 
 
The partners must pay income tax on this share they are receiving, this 
is also, similarly to sole traders, called a trading income. 
 
The partnership itself does not pay income tax, and the partners will 
have to nominate a partner who will file a Partnership Tax Return form 
with HMRC, essentially reporting on the income of the partnership, 
showing any expenses and deductions and each partner's share. 
 
 
 
 
Overlap profits: 
 
A business (partnership or sole trader business) may decide to have an 
accounting period that is different from the tax year. 
 
Because HMRC calculates tax based on the tax year, HMRC will set a 
“basis period” for the tax year ending with 31 December and as a result, 
some of the profits earned in the first year will be taxed twice. These are 
called overlap profits. 
 
This tax paid will not be returned until the business ceases trading or if 
their accounting period changes to the official tax year. When this tax is 
returned, this is called overlap relief. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Employees – Deduction at source: 
 
Employed individuals are not required to complete a self-assessment 
tax return because their tax is collected via the PAYE system (the tax is 
deducted at source – receives income net of tax). 
 
PAYE system procedure: 
 
* 
The employer can set a payroll period for their employees. 
 
* 
For each period, the employer is required to calculate the 
income tax payable by the employee for that period. 
 
* 
If the employee earns more than £184 per week, the employer 
must deduct the income tax alongside the National Insurance 
contributions. 
 
* 
On or before payday, the employer will be required to send a Full 
Payment Submission (FPS) report to HMRC showing the amount 
that has been deducted. 
 
* 
The payments must be sent to HMRC every month. If an 
employee receives less than £1,500 per month, then the 
employer may make these payments every quarter instead. 
 
* 
The employer may report to and pay HMRC online, if that is the 
case, the report and payments must be received by HMCR by the 
22nd of each month. 
 
* 
If a report and/or payment is submitted late, HMRC may charge 
interest and may issue a penalty charge to the employer. 
 
DIFFERENT TYPES OF INCOME: 
 
There are three different categories of income and individual may 
receive: 
1. 
Savings income 
2. 
Non-savings income 
3. 
Dividend income 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The tax year for income tax purposes is 6 April to 5 April the 
following year. 
Example: 
 
A sole trader has an accounting period running from 6 October to 6 
October the next year. Their business is going well so they cease 
trading on 1 Mar 2025 and become an employee of the limited 
company they register at Companies House. 
 
What is the amount of overlap relief that will apply. 
 
6 Oct 2022 – 5 Oct 2023 Their trading income is £34,000. 
6 Oct 2023 – 5 Oct 2024 Their trading income is £49,000. 
6 Oct 2025 – 1 Mar 2025 Their trading income is £21,000. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 6 Oct 2022 6 Apr 2023 6 Oct 2023 31 Dec 2023 
 (year-end) 
 
Year 1 taxes 
Year 2 taxes 
Savings income will 
include: 
* Interest from 
savings accounts 
 
* Interest from 
government and 
company bonds 
 
* Income from 
credit union 
accounts 
Non-savings income 
will include: 
* Salaries and 
bonuses 
 
* Trading income 
from a business 
 
* Pension earnings 
 
* Rental income 
 
 
Dividend income will 
include: 
* Dividends received 
on shares.

Partners and sole traders will receive trading income instead of a salary, 
however for individuals who receive both a salary and a trading income, 
both can be included in their tax calculations. 
 
SUGGESTIONS FOR PAYING LESS TAX: 
 
 
Transfer the money on deposit or the shares to spouse 
if they have one of the following: 
 
 
 
Personal allowance 
of £12,570 
Personal savings 
allowance 
If they would only 
pay tax at a basic 
rate. 
 
 
Client may try to: 
* 
Increase their personal pension contributions to benefit from 
tax relief and reduce their Net Income 
* 
Apply for marriage allowance. 
* 
Make contributions to tax-efficient savings vehicles such as 
ISAs. 
* 
If they are partners/sole traders, use Loss Relief. 
 
Loss Relief: 
If a sole trader or partnership has made a loss in one tax year, the loss 
can be deducted from next year's profits to reduce the income tax 
payable. 
 
Loss relief can be used before applying any available personal 
allowances, reducing the total income. 
 
Any excess loss that remains after loss relief has been used to reduce 
the net income can be used to reduce any capital gains made within the 
same tax year. 
 
Sole trader: 
 
Tax year 2021-22: Made £5,000 in loss (If I spent £8,000 on advertising 
and made only £3,000) 
Tax year 2022-23: Made £15,000 profit 
 
Income tax calculations for tax year 2022-23: £15,000 - £5,000 = £10,000 
 
ANTI-AVOIDANCE RULES: 
 
Tax legislation has been developed to stop loopholes exploited by 
taxpayers seeking to reduce/eliminate their taxes. HMRC and the courts 
are increasingly cutting down tax avoidance schemes. This legislation 
has introduced the general anti-abuse rules (GAAR). 
 
In relation to income tax: 
 
* 
HMRC will be able to look behind tax arrangements if the 
arrangement cannot be reasonably regarded as a reasonable 
course of action by the taxpayer. This is called the double 
reasonableness test. 
 
* 
If HMRC finds such an arrangement, they may tax the taxpayer 
amount they should have bene taxed without the arrangement. 
This will be done if this is just and reasonable under the 
circumstances. – rather than sending out a new tax bill, HMRC 
will make an adjustment to the amount payable. 
 
* 
Under the rules, taxpayers cannot reduce their income tax 
liability by making gifts of income-producing items. – eg. 
dividend or interest-paying shares to their children. 
 
* 
The income will be treated as remaining with the taxpayer 
making the gift.

INCOME TAX CALCULATIONS 
 
Start by collecting all your figures and highlighting them. Separate each 
figure into separate categories. 
 
To calculate the total income, use income receipts in your calculation. 
 
Also highlight income expenditure and capital expenditure as these 
might be deductible. 
 
STEP 1: TOTAL INCOME: 
 
Next, we will calculate the Total Income. 
 
 
 
 
 
Income: 
Receipt of money that originates from regular income generation. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
If some of the amount you have been given is not for a year, make sure 
to adjust the period for each income to one year. 
 
If you have to calculate the trading income: 
 Calculate the gross income received by the business for its accounting 
period and deduct the expenses of the business. – if the taxpayer in your 
question is also receiving a salary from employment, then make sure 
that the period covered by the salary is the same as the accounting 
period. 
 
Business expenses may only be deducted if they have been incurred 
wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business. If only a 
proportion of an expense has been used for business purposes, you can 
deduct that proportion. – if for example, the taxpayer pays for 
broadband and uses the internet for the business 40% of the time, and 
the other 60% of the time, he uses it for his own private purposes, then 
only 40% of the broadband cost is deductible as an expense. 
 
Capital expenses such as plant and machinery can also be deducted if 
the cost is within the Annual Investment Allowance figure: £1 million. 
 
Not income: 
* 
Gifts 
* 
Trivial benefits in kind max. £50 (except cash) 
* 
Capital receipts from one-off sales which are capital receipts 
 
Exempt income: 
* 
Interest from an Individual Savings Account (ISAs and NISAs) 
* 
Interest from National Savings Certificates 
* 
Gambling or lottery wins 
* 
Winnings on Premium Bonds 
* 
Personal injury claim damages 
* 
Redundancy pay-outs or damages max. £30,000 
* 
Child Benefit, Child Tax Credit, Working Tax Credit, Universal 
Credit, Housing benefit 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
STEP 2: LESS PENSION AND INTEREST ON 
QUALIFYING LOANS: 
 
Next, we will calculate the Net Income. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Pension contributions and Interest on Qualifying Loans are subject to Tax 
Relief so they are deducted before taxing income. 
 
Pension contributions: 
One may pay contributions into a pension scheme – either an 
occupational pension scheme (set up by their employer) or a personal 
pension scheme. Both types must be deducted from the Total Income. 
 
Qualifying loans: 
1. Loans to a partnership or loans to contribute capital to a 
partnership. 
2. Loans to buy shares in a close company (a small company with 5 
shareholders or less). 
 AND 
3. Loans taken on by Personal representatives to pay inheritance tax 
on the estate. 
 
Make sure that the loan you have in your scenario is a qualifying loan. 
Don't deduct interest that comes from loans that don't meet this 
criteria. 
 
 
STEP 3: LESS PERSONAL ALLOWANCE: 
 
In step 3, we will calculate the Taxable Income. 
 
 
 
 
 
Net income – £12,570 = Taxable income 
 
Above £100,000 Net income: 
 
If the Net income is more than £100,000, the personal allowance is 
reduced (tapered). 
 
The personal allowance will be reduced by £1 per every £2 of income 
that goes above £100,000. 
 
Marriage allowance: 
 
Couples may transfer part of their personal allowances between each 
other to obtain a more favourable tax position. The maximum 
transferrable amount is £1,260 for the tax year. 
 
Marriage allowance conditions: 
1. 
The couple must be married/civil partners. 
2. 
The transferring party's income must be below the personal 
allowance amount. 
 AND 
3. 
The receiving party must be a basic rate taxpayer before the 
transfer. 
 
STEP 4: SPLIT: 
 
In step 4, we will split the Taxable income into different categories. 
 
Add up all income coming from dividends = Dividend Income. 
Add up all interest coming from savings = Savings Income. 
Taxable income – Savings Income – Dividend income = Non-savings 
Income 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Add up all sources of income = Total Income. 
 
Total Income – Pension contributions – Interest on Qualifying 
Loans = Net Income 
 
Net Income – Personal Allowance (£12,570) = Taxable Income

partnership)

Taxes SQE Notes | Page 8 of 13 
 
CAPITAL GAINS TAX (CGT) 
 
Start by collecting all your figures and highlighting them. Separate each 
figure into separate categories. 
 
CGT is paid on receipt of money that originates from one off sales. 
 
Foreign sale: 
 
Foreign sale = sale of an asset situated abroad. 
 
If the individual is a UK resident, they must pay tax on foreign capital 
gains they receive during the tax year. 
 
The taxpayer will be deemed to be a UK resident if they have spent at 
least 183 days in the UK during the relevant tax year. 
 
Taxpayers who are not resident in the UK do not pay tax for assets sold 
in the UK. 
 
 
STEP 1: CALCULATE THE SALE PROCEEDS OF EACH 
ASSET: 
 
 
 
 
 
If the asset is transferred as a gift, sold at an undervalue or sold to a 
connected person, instead of the sale proceeds, use the market value 
 
Capital receipts: 
Falls into this category if there is an income receipt and that income is 
due to a transaction that not part of a regular activity. Capital receipts 
are ‘one-off' transactions. 
 
Example: 
* 
Selling your car if you don't sell cars as part of a business. 
* 
Selling a painting if you don't sell paintings as part of a business. 
* 
Selling a house. 
 
Exempt capital: 
1. 
Principal private residences: this one applies for first homes if 
the house is primarily used as a first home (Private Residence 
Relief). 
2. 
Cars for private use – incl. vintage cars. 
3. 
Any tangible moveable property worth less than £6,000 
4. 
Disposal of some investments – such as government securities, 
National Savings certificates, ISAs and life assurance policies. 
5. 
Disposals to charities 
6. 
Spouses transferring assets to each other. 
 
STEP 2: LESS DISPOSAL EXPENDITURE: 
 
 
 
 
 
Disposal expenditure = Costs of disposal – eg. agents' commission. 
 
STEP 3: LESS INITIAL AND SUBSEQUENT 
EXPENDITURE: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Initial Expenditure: 
1. 
The cost price of the asset – base cost, costs of original purchase. 
 AND 
2. 
The costs of acquisition – surveyors' and lawyers' fees. 
 
Subsequent expenditure: 
1. 
Subsequent expenditure if enhances asset's value – repairs and 
general maintenance are not subsequent expenditure. 
 AND 
2. 
Money spent on defending title to the assets 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
STEP 4: LESS LOSSES CARRIED FORWARD AND 
ANNUAL EXEMPTION OF £6,000: 
 
 
 
 
 
If any net capital losses were made in previous years, carry those 
forward to reduce the Taxable Chargeable Gain 
 
If the losses are more than the Total Chargeable Gain in the same tax 
year, any unrelieved losses are set against gains in future tax years i.e. 
carried forward until used up. 
 
STEP 5: APPLY THE TAX RATES: 
 
The rates depend on the rate calculated for taxable income. If an 
amount spills into the higher rate band, apply the higher rate amount. 
 
For basic rate taxpayers – taxed at 10% 
(18% for gains on sales of residential property) 
For higher and additional rate taxpayers – taxed at 20% 
(24% for gains on sales of residential property) 
For all taxpayers with Business Asset Disposal Relief – taxed at 10% 
 
If there are more than one capital gains, assets for which the Business 
Asset Disposal Relief (BADR) applies must be taxed and used up first. 
 
Conditions of Business Asset Disposal Relief to be satisfied: 
1. 
The company would need to be a trading company. 
2. 
Client must own (and be able to vote in relation to) at least 5% 
of the ordinary shares in the company and must be involved in 
running the company as an officer or employee. 
3. 
Client must be entitled to receive at least 5% of the dividends 
and 5% of the assets on winding up. 
4. 
Client will need to have met the above conditions for at least 2 
years immediately prior to the disposal, and Client must not 
have exceeded their £1 million lifetime limit in relation to 
Business Asset Disposal Relief. 
 
The taxpayer must apply for Business Asset Disposal Relief on or before 
the first anniversary of the 31 Jan following the tax year in which the 
disposal is made. 
 
STEP 6: CALCULATE THE TOTAL TAX PAYABLE: 
 
If Rollover or Holdover relief applies, then no tax is payable now on 
that gain. 
 
 
 
 
 
Rollover relief: 
 
This applies where the sale proceeds of the asset are used to buy a new 
asset. Rollover relief defers Capital Gains tax until the replacement is 
sold and no new qualifying replacement asset is purchased. 
 
This applies to land and buildings and fixed plant and machinery. 
 
The new asset need not necessarily be of the same type as the old one. 
It merely needs to be within the list of qualifying assets. 
 
Holdover relief: 
 
This applies where a donor gifts a qualifying asset, then the liability to 
Capital Gains tax is transferred to the donee (receiving the asset) and 
deferred until the donee sells. 
 
The sale proceeds will be the market value of the asset. 
 
Both donor and donee must jointly elect to claim hold-over relief. 
 
Qualifying assets: 
1. 
Assets used by a company in which the transferor owns at least 
5% of the shares. 
2. 
Shares in the transferor's company or an unquoted trading 
company. 
3. 
Assets qualifying for agricultural property relief. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Sale proceeds – Disposal expenditure = Net Sale Proceeds 
Net sale proceeds – Initial expenditure – Subsequent expenditure = 
Total Chargeable gain 
Total Chargeable Gain – Losses carried forward – Annual 
Exemption (£6,000) = Taxable Chargeable gain 
 
Capital income = income from one-off sales. 
 
To calculate the total tax payable, add up all the tax liability.

ANTI-AVOIDANCE RULES: 
 
Taxpayers cannot reduce their CGT liability by creating and using 
artificial losses. 
 
Taxpayers cannot lie and avoid tax by stating that they are not resident 
in the UK when in fact, they are. 
 
 
Example: 
 
Carrie owns shares in a shoes company, Sparkly Toes Limited (STL), 
which are currently valued at about £450,000. Carrie acquired these 
shares for £13,000 when STL was first set up 10 years ago. She is 
considering giving them to her friend, Charlotte. 
 
This would work as follows:

Gross gain = £437,000 
 
Carrie will not need to pay any CGT on the £437,000 gain. Instead, 
Charlotte will take Carrie's base cost of £13,000 and on a subsequent

gain following the date of the gift from Carrie (subject to the usual 
deductions and exemptions). Carrie cannot use her annual 
exemption to reduce the gain being held over.

to a family friend. The company manufactures plastic clips and sells

100 ordinary shares of £1 each (his brother owns the other 50%) and 
each had 50% of the voting rights. 
 
Hardeep was a director of the company since he set up Clip Clops 
Limited with his brother many years ago and Hardeep resigned from 
his position at the same time as selling the shares. He sold the 
shares in July 2024 for their market value of £200,000, and made no 
other gains or losses. 
 
Hardeep has not used any of his £1m lifetime Business Asset 
Disposal Relief allowance. Hardeep is a higher rate taxpayer.

year.

expenditure) of £36,000. Helen has no losses available to set off 
against any gain and is not entitled to Business Asset Disposal Relief. 
Her taxable income is £22,000. 
 
How much CGT will she pay for this tax year?

Taxes SQE Notes | Page 10 of 13 
 
CORPORATION TAX 
 
Start by collecting all your figures and highlighting them. Separate each 
figure into separate categories. 
 
 
 
 
Tax assessment for companies – based on Financial year (although 
companies may choose a different period for tax assessment purposes, 
called the accounting period) 
 
Both the tax year and financial year are different to the calendar year. 
 
Tax year: starts 6 April, ends 5 April the next year. 
Financial year: starts 1 April, ends 31 March the next year. 
 
STEP 1: WHAT IS INCOME? WHAT IS CAPITAL? 
 
Work out which items are income, and which are capital. Refer to the 
notes on Income tax and CGT for further examples. 
 
Income receipts: 
Receipt of money that originates from regular income generation. 
 
Dividend received by the company is exempt income. 
 
Example: 
* 
Salary 
* 
Trading profits of a business will be the income of the owner 
* 
Interest charged on loans will be the income of the lender 
* 
Rental income paid to landlord will be the income of the 
landlord. 
 
Capital receipts: 
Falls into this category if there is an income receipt and that income is 
due to a transaction that not part of a regular activity. Capital receipts 
are ‘one-off' transactions. 
 
Example: 
* 
Selling your car if you don't sell cars as part of a business. 
* 
Selling a painting if you don't sell paintings as part of a business. 
 
Income expenditure: 
If the expense is incurred due to the day-to-day trading activities of a 
business, it will be classed as income expenditure. 
 
Example: 
* 
Payment of rent (for business premises) 
* 
Paying bills (eg. staff wages, heating, lighting, rent or 
marketing/stationery expenses) 
* 
Paying for repairs of business premises/business vehicle etc. 
 
Capital expenditure: 
If you spend money on a new capital asset or enhancing an existing asset 
as part of the business, it is ‘capital' expenditure. Capital expenditure is 
a ‘one-off' transaction. 
 
Example: 
* 
Buying new large equipment/machinery 
* 
Buying new property 
* 
Spending money on enhancing existing equipment/machinery/ 
premises 
* 
Paying bills (eg. staff wages, heating, lighting, rent or 
marketing/stationery expenses) 
* 
Paying for repairs of business premises/business vehicle etc. 
 
STEP 2: CALCULATE TRADING INCOME PROFITS: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Deductible Expenditure: 
 
• 
Incurred “wholly and exclusively” for trading purposes 
• 
Not prohibited by statute – entertainment, provisions for 
doubtful debts, only actual debts are allowed to be deducted. 
• 
If of an income nature – eg. rent, wages. 
 
Not deductible: dividend 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Capital Allowances (allowable expenditure): 
 
Expenditure on plant and machinery, is allowable expenditure. 
 
YEAR 1 Plant and Machinery costs £1,400,000 
 
1. 
Calculate the allowance claimed: 
Annual Investment Allowance: £1,000,000 each year. 
£1,000,000 
 + 
Deduct 19% of reducing balance 
£400,000 x 19% = £76,000 
 
 
Total Year 1 Allowance: AIA + 19% 
£1,000,000 + £76,000 = £1,076,000 
 
2. 
Calculate the tax written down value (TWDV): 
Deduct the Total year 1 allowance from the cost: 
£1,400,000 - £1,076,000 = £324,000 
 
YEAR 2 
 
3. 
Calculate the allowance claimed: 
19% of Year 1 TWDV 
£324,000 x 19% = £62,320 
 
4. 
Calculate the tax written down value (TWDV): 
Deduct the Year 2 allowance from Year 1 TWDV: 
£324,000 - £62,320 = £265,680 
 
Trading Losses: 
 
Previous year: 
Net loss = Old loss MINUS Old income 
 
Current year: Carry forward that Net loss to the current year 
Income Profits = Current Income MINUS Current loss 
 
Deduct the previous year's net loss from the current income profits. 
 
 
STEP 3: CALCULATE TAXABLE CHARGEABLE GAIN: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Disposal costs, initial and subsequent expenditure: 
 
This is calculated the same way as for individual CGT. 
 
Disposal expenditure = Costs of disposal – eg. agents' commission. 
 
Initial Expenditure: 
1. 
The cost price of the asset – base cost, costs of original purchase. 
 AND 
2. 
The costs of acquisition – surveyors' and lawyers' fees. 
 
Subsequent expenditure: 
4. 
Subsequent expenditure if enhances asset's value – repairs and 
general maintenance are not subsequent expenditure. 
 AND 
5. 
Money spent on defending title to the assets 
 
Rollover relief: 
 
Available to a company which uses the proceeds of sale of a capital 
asset to fund replacing it with a similar qualifying asset within 12 
months. 
 
Qualifying assets: 
1. 
Land and buildings 
2. 
Fixed plant and machinery 
 
Exercise: 
 
Where replacement asset costs MORE than the original asset:

LESS Indexation allowance

£30,000 
This is going to be the roll-over gain below. 
 
 
 
All Income receipts – Deductible Expenditure – Capital Allowances 
– Trading losses = Trading Income Profits 
Total sale proceeds – Disposal costs – Initial and subsequent 
expenditure – Indexation allowance – Roll-over relief – 
Chargeable Losses = Taxable chargeable gain 
TTP = Chargeable gains + Income profits (trading profits)

If “Original Asset – Replacement asset” is GREATER than the Chargeable 
gain: no Rollover Relief. 
 
Trading Losses: 
 
If all the income has been set off by trading losses, you can use the 
remaining amount to set off capital profits next. 
 
Capital losses: 
 
Capital losses can be carried forward indefinitely within the company 
but capital losses cannot be carried back. 
 
Calculation: 
 
(i) 
Previous year: Where the old loss exceeded the old profits: 
 
Net loss = Old loss MINUS Old profits 
 
(ii) 
Current year: Carry forward that Net loss to the current 
 
Capital Profits = Chargeable gain MINUS Net Loss 
 
(iiI) 
Note that any remainder may be carried forward for next year. – ie. the 
old net loss last year was greater than this year's Chargeable gain, it 
will reduce the current Income profits to £0 and whatever is left over 
can be used next year as in sub-step (ii) above. 
 
Exercise:
