Substantial Shareholding Exemption (SSE): 
 
Corporation tax liability can be cancelled out altogether by the SSE. 
 
This is only relevant to private company acquisitions. SSE only applies 
to Share sales. 
 
Conditions to be satisfied for SSE: 
1. 
The Seller must have owned at least 10% of the ordinary share 
capital of the Target company's shares. 
2. 
For at least 12 consecutive months in the previous 2 years. 
 AND 
3. 
Both companies must be trading companies/part of a trading 
group for the 12 months up to the date of the sale. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
STEP 4: CALCULATE TOTAL TAXABLE PROFIT (TTP): 
 
 
 
 
STEP 5: CALCULATE CORPORATION TAX PAYABLE: 
 
If the TTP is £50,000 or less, it will be taxed at 19%. (Small Company 
Rate) 
 
If the TTP is more than £50,000 but less than £250,000, it will be taxed 
at 25% but the Marginal Small Companies Relief will apply. 
 
If the TTP £250,000 or over, it will be taxed at 25% applying to all profits 
 
Example: 
Company A has TTP of £250,000 
All TTP is taxed at the corporation tax rate of 25% = £62,500 
 
STRADDLING: 
 
Companies are assessed corporation tax by reference to the financial 
year (1 Apr – 31 Mar) and the company's accounting year may not 
coincide with this. The company's accounting period may straddle two 
Financial Years (the 2022/23 and 2023/24 tax years). 
 
CORPORATION TAX SELF-ASSESSMENT: 
 
TTP of £1,500,000 or less: 
1. Company estimates its tax liability and pays HMRC within 9 
months and one day of the end of the accounting period. 
2. Company must file (electronically) a tax return within 12 months 
of the end of the accounting period, together with its accounts. 
3. Unless HMRC examine or make enquiries into the tax return to 
establish whether or not the correct tax has been paid, the 
company's tax computation will usually be regarded as finalised 12 
months after the filing date for the tax return. 
 
Interest will accrue on any under or over-payments. 
 
TTP of more than £1,500,000: 
Companies with TTP of more than £1.5m are required to pay their tax 
bills in four instalments over the course of the relevant accounting 
period and the next one. 
 
PRACTICE QUESTION:

= Trading Income Profits = £368,000 
 
STEP 3: Calculate the Chargeable gain:

STEP 4: Calculate the TTP: 
Income Profits + Chargeable gains = TTP 
£368,000 + £135,000 = £503,000

Calculate Happy Paws' corporation tax liability.

pages.text:
Taxes SQE Notes | Page 12 of 13 
 
STEP 5: Calculate the corporation tax: 
£503,000 Taxed at 25% = £125,750 
 
CLOSE COMPANIES: 
 
Close companies are subject to special tax treatment. The close company 
regime is an example of anti-avoidance legislation. 
 
Definition: 
 
s.439 CTA 2010 A company is a close company if it is under the control 
of 5 or less participators or any number of participators if they are also 
directors. 
 
Company with 3 shareholders: Yes, close company 
Company with 11 shareholders: No 
Company with 11 shareholders but all of them are also directors: Yes, 
close company. 
Company with 11 shareholders, one of them is also a director: no, not a 
close company. 
 
Participator = a person having a share/interest in the company's 
capital/income. – eg. shareholders, some creditors. 
 
Control = the ability to exercise control over the company's affairs by 
voting rights/possession of: 
i) issued share capital allowing the greater part (50%+) of income 
of the company if distributed 
 OR 
ii) the greater part of the company's assets on winding up. 
 
Taxation effect: 
 
Loans to Participators: 
 
Loans = All advances of credit except: 
a) 
Credit given by a company in respect of goods/services normally 
supplied in the course of business if the duration of credit is not 
more than 6 months/company's normal limit 
b) 
A loan made in the ordinary course of the company's business – 
this includes money lending. 
 OR 
c) 
A loan to a borrower which, together with other loans made by 
the company to that borrower, does not exceed £15,000 and the 
borrower is a full-time worker for the company and does not 
have a material interest in the company. 
 
Material Interest = indirect control of 5%+ of the company's ordinary 
share capital or an entitlement on winding up of 5%+ of the assets. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Distributions: 
 
Distribution = includes living accommodation, other benefits in kind 
provided to participators (if not provided by reason of employment). 
 
Inheritance Tax Implications: 
 
Only individuals pay IHT, so some may form a company to make a 
transfer through it. A transfer by a close company will result in the value 
of the gift being distributed between its shareholders. 
 
Transactions in Securities rules: 
 
The transactions in securities rules apply to transactions involving a close 
company if the transaction gives someone a tax advantage by changing 
an income receipt into a capital receipt. Where they apply, the rules 
counteract the tax advantage. 
 
When a transaction may fall within these rules, apply to HMRC for 
advance clearance. HMRC would then state if they are satisfied that the 
provisions do not apply here. 
 
 
 
Tax effect for the company: 
 
The company must pay 
corporation tax on the loan. 
This is calculated at the rate of 
income tax payable on 
dividends by higher rate 
taxpayers. This must be paid 
within 9 months and 1 day 
after the end of the accounting 
period for the loan. 
 
Claim a refund of the tax paid 
if the loan is repaid/satisfied/ 
written off/waived. 
Tax effect for the recipient: 
 
If the loan is written off/ 
waived, the participator is 
deemed to receive a dividend 
equal to the amount of the 
loan. 
 
No tax effect for the 
participator if he pays back 
the loan in full.

pages.heading: VALUE ADDED TAX (VAT) · Legislation introducing VAT is Value Added Tax Act 1994.
pages.text:
Taxes SQE Notes | Page 13 of 13 
 
VALUE ADDED TAX (VAT) 
 
Legislation introducing VAT is Value Added Tax Act 1994. 
 
s.4 VATA 1994 VAT is charged on any supply of goods or services made 
in the UK where it is a taxable supply made by a taxable person in the 
course of any business carried on by him. 
 
s.5 Supply of Goods or Services = any supply made in the UK of goods or 
services done in return for consideration. 
 
s.4 Taxable supply = any supply made in the UK which is not an exempt 
supply. 
 
s.3 Taxable person = a person who is, or is required to be, registered for 
VAT purposes. 
 
Person = individuals, partners, companies, unincorporated organisations 
 
Registration: 
 
Businesses are required to register for VAT if their VAT taxable turnover 
exceeds the current registration threshold. 
 
The 2024 threshold is £90,000. Registration thresholds change annually. 
 
A person can also register voluntarily. 
 
Sched 1 VATA 1994 A person must be registered: 
1. 
If the value of their VAT taxable turnover exceeds the current 
registration threshold. 
 OR 
2. 
If there are reasonable grounds for believing that their VAT 
taxable turnover will exceed the threshold in the next 30 days. 
 
De-registration: 
Any registered person may apply for de-registration and cease to be 
taxable if the value of their future annual taxable supplies will not exceed 
the VAT registration threshold. 
 
Output and input tax: 
 
s.24 VATA 1994 Output tax = the VAT chargeable by a business when 
making a supply of goods/services. The VAT relates to the output of the 
business. 
 
s.24 Input tax = The VAT paid by a person on goods or services supplied 
to the person. The VAT relates to goods/services bought by the person. 
 
A VAT registered business offsets input tax against output tax it has 
charged customers and only accounts for the difference to HMRC. 
 
Examples: 
Billy makes and sells furniture. 
Buy the logs. – Mary sells logs for £80: VAT on £80 is £16. Billy will pay 
£80 + £16 
Buy screws. – Amanda sells screws for £20: VAT on £20 is £4. Billy will 
pay £20 + £4 
 
Billy will pay £20 in input tax. 
When Billy sells the table he makes for £200 plus VAT (£40) 
Because Billy has already paid £20 in VAT, now Billy will only send £20 to 
HMRC. 
 
 
Rate of VAT: 
 
The rate of VAT will depend on the type of supply. 
 
The standard rate of VAT is 20% 
 
s.19 VATA 1994 The price of any product/services is deemed to be VAT 
inclusive unless stated otherwise. 
 
Price + VAT (20%) = 1.2 x Price 
 
The seller must account for the VAT element amount to HMRC. 
 
Types of Supply: 
 
A business can make four kinds of supply: 
1. 
Standard Rated – s.2 VATA 1994: 
The standard rate is 20%. A supply by a business will be standard 
rated unless it falls within one of the other three categories. 
 
2. 
Reduced Rated – Sched 7A VATA 1994: 
The reduced rate is 5%. 
 
Examples of reduced-rated supplies: 
* 
Domestic heating/power supply 
* 
Installation of elderly mobility aids 
* 
Stop-smoking products 
* 
Children's car seats 
 
3. 
Zero Rated – Sched 8 VATA 1994: 
Some supplies are zero rated for public policy reasons. 
 
Examples of zero-rated supplies: 
* 
Some basic food items 
* 
Export items 
* 
Farming inputs 
* 
Books/newspapers 
* 
Construction of new houses 
* 
Public transport 
* 
Children's clothing. 
 
Zero rated supplies are also taxable supplies so when a VAT 
registered business makes zero rated supplies, it can recover any 
VAT suffered on its inputs. 
 
4. 
Exempt – Sched 9 VATA 1994: 
 
Examples of exempt supplies: 
* 
Insurance services 
* 
Financial services 
* 
Education/health services 
 
Record-keeping: 
 
As from Apr 2019, businesses that have a turnover above the VAT 
registration threshold must keep their VAT records and make VAT 
return online. 
 
Smaller businesses may also choose to do this. 
 
VAT registered businesses that have a turnover below the registration 
threshold must make their VAT return online, with the first return 
starting on/after Apr 2020.

pages.heading: OFFER · Formation of a contract: *Does the contract exist?*
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Notes | Page 1 of 16 
OFFER 
 
Formation of a contract: *Does the contract exist?* 
• Parties in agreement (Offer and acceptance) 
• Consideration 
• Intention to create legal relations 
• Capacity 
 
Contracts do not need to be in writing, can be made orally. 
 
Exception – important contracts that must be in writing: 
• Contracts to Sell Land 
• Contracts of Guarantee 
• Consumer Credit Agreements 
 
Key types of contracts: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
MAKING AN OFFER: 
 
The parties will be in agreement when one person makes an offer and 
the receiving party accepts it in response. 
 
Offeror = person making the offer. 
Offeree = person on the receiving end of an offer. 
 
An offer must: 
1. 
Be certain – the offeror must know what is being offered. 
2. 
Be addressed to the Offeree 
3. 
Show intention to create legal relations – this may be implicit or 
explicit. 
 AND 
4. 
Must be communicated to the Offeree (in writing, orally or by 
conduct) 
 
Types of offers: 
 
* 
Bilateral offers: offering something in return for a promise. – 
eg. Andrew promising to sell his car in return for £4,500. 
 * 
Unilateral offers: offering something in return for the 
performance of a prescribed act. – eg. Lily promising to pay £3 
million to anyone who finds the cure to cancer. 
 
Offer to the world = when you make an offer that 
anyone can accept by performance. 
 
INVITATIONS TO TREAT: 
 
If you have an expression that might be an offer but it does not fit the 
criteria of an offer, it is an invitation to treat. 
 
Invitations to treat are an expression of willingness to negotiate by 
inviting offers from others. Because these are not offers, they cannot 
be accepted. 
 
Invitations to treat: 
1. 
Displays of goods 
2. 
Advertisements 
 
Display of goods: 
 
Displays of goods are not offers but merely invitations to treat. 
 
In relation to display of goods, the offer is made by the buyer when they 
take the goods to the checkout. 
 
Advert: 
 
Advertisements are not offers but merely invitations to treat (inviting 
customers to make an offer). – this is because if everyone seeing the 
advert responded to it, the person who placed the advert would be out 
of stock soon, but would still be obliged to perform the contract. 
 
Exceptions: 
 
Unilateral offers: 
If the advertisement contains a prescribed act and it is sufficiently clear, 
it may be a unilateral offer. 
 
 
 
Limitless supply: 
 
If an advert is clear, certain and shows an intention to be bound and 
there is no problem with supply the normal rule would not apply. 
 
Invitations to tender: 
 
By inviting tenders, you are not making an offer. 
 
Invitation to tender = expression of willingness to invite people to make 
offers with the price. If the invitation to tender is also a unilateral offer, 
there will be a unilateral contract formed if the prescribed act is 
performed. 
 
If the invitation to tender sets out that they would accept the highest/ 
lowest bid, then the promisor must do so. 
 
Auctions: 
 
An auctioneer inviting bids is an invitation to treat and the bidders make 
the offer. The acceptance at the auction is made once the auctioneer 
drops the hammer. If a person has made an offer that person is also 
entitled to revoke that offer as long as it has not been accepted. 
 
TERMINATING AN OFFER: 
 
An offer will stay open until terminated by: 
1. 
Rejection of the offer 
2. 
Revocation 
 OR 
3. 
Lapse 
 
An offer cannot be revoked if it has been accepted. 
 
Rejection: 
 
Counter-offer: 
 
Rejecting the original offer and making a new offer. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Requests for further information: 
 
A request for further information is not a rejection, it is simply asking 
for clarification of the terms. 
 
Lapse: 
 
An offer may lapse by: 
1. 
Passage of time 
2. 
Death 
3. 
Non-fulfillment of a condition 
 
Passage of time: 
 
Offers only stay open for a reasonable time. 
What is reasonable will depend on the circumstances. – eg. if someone 
makes an offer to you to sell a newspaper for 50p this offer is not going 
to be open for a whole year. But the offer for a house will likely be 
reasonable to stay open for longer. 
 
Revocation: 
1. 
Auctions – Revocation is effective if it has been done before 
the offer is accepted. 
 
2. 
Only effective once received 
 
3. 
Third party revocation – An offer can be revoked by a third 
party if that third party is authorised by the offeror. 
 
4. 
Revocation of unilateral offers: 
A unilateral offer is revoked once the act set out in the offer is 
performed. A unilateral offer may not be revoked if someone 
has started performance. 
 
The offeror cannot prevent the offeree from performing the 
prescribed act. 
 
Offers to the world: 
For announcing revocation, the offeror must use a method 
similar to how the offer was made. 
 
 
Example: 
 
If there was an offer for the sale of land, for £1,000. The buyer said 
that he will pay £995. The seller then sold the land for someone else. 
When the buyer wanted to force the buyer to sell the land to him 
for £1,000, the court disagreed as he has already rejected that offer. 
Bilateral contract = 
one person makes 
the offer and other 
person says that 
they accept. – there 
is an exchange of 
promises. 
 
Unilateral contract = 
one person makes a 
promise to do 
something in return 
for the performance 
of a prescribed act. 
 
⇒ 
Collateral contract = 
where there is a 
contract between two 
parties, a separate 
(collateral) contract 
may exist which 
relates to the original 
contract.

pages.heading: AGREEMENT · An agreement forms when an offer is accepted with intention to create
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Notes | Page 2 of 16 
AGREEMENT 
 
An agreement forms when an offer is accepted with intention to create 
legal relations where both parties had the necessary capacity to enter 
into the contract. 
 
ACCEPTANCE: 
 
Acceptance must be: 
1. 
A mirror image to the offer 
2. 
Made by the offeree 
3. 
Made in response to an offer 
4. 
Communicated 
 
Communicated: 
Silence does not constitute acceptance. 
 
If acceptance is communicated by conduct: it is still valid. – eg. In 
relation to taking out loans, if the person who took out the loan 
deposits the loan amount in their bank account, this will be acceptance 
by conduct. 
 
Exception to the rule on communication: 
* 
Unilateral offers – accepted by performance. 
* 
Offeror's fault – The person accepting must ensure that their 
message goes through. 
 
Prescribed acceptance: 
If the Offeror specified what amounts to acceptance, then the Offeree 
must follow the rules of acceptance. – eg. if the offer states that 
acceptance happens by saying “yes”, then you cannot accept by saying 
“I accept”. 
 
The postal rule: 
 
If acceptance has been sent by post, use this rule, unless: 
* 
Letter was not properly posted (not properly addressed/ 
stamped) 
* 
It was unreasonable to accept by post. – eg. a postal strike so 
the letter won't arrive or the sale is regarding a scoop of ice 
cream which will melt in the meantime. 
 OR 
* 
The Postal rule was excluded by the Offeror. 
 
If accepting via post, then acceptance happens as soon as you put the 
letter in the letter box. 
 
If the letter was properly posted but lost or destroyed, acceptance is 
still valid. 
 
Instantaneous communications: 
 
Use this rule only where acceptance has been sent by email/telex. 
 
The receipt rule: acceptance must have been received. Communication 
will be deemed received within office hours. 
 
If the message was sent outside of office hours, the message will be 
deemed received the first thing when the office opened again. 
 
There is no universal rule on office hours, the court will always look at 
the circumstances of the case. 
 
Prescribed mode: 
 
Use this rule only where the offeror has set out a prescribed method of 
communication for the acceptance. – eg. please accept by letter or 
please don't accept by post. 
 
Prescribed mode will only be binding if it is explicitly mandatory and 
rules out all other modes. If the offeror does not rule out any other 
mode then all he did was state a preference. – eg. ‘Please contact me 
by telephone, not by email.' or ‘Please contact me by telephone, and 
only telephone.' 
 
If the prescribed mode does not rule out other modes, then as long as 
the other mode is as fast as the prescribed mode, it will be valid. The 
other method should not disadvantage the offeror. 
 
If the offer was sent by an instantaneous method, it will be implied that 
the acceptance must be sent by an equally instantaneous method. 
 
If the method was prescribed for the convenience or benefit of the 
sender then the sender can waive the prescribed method. – eg. if the 
prescribed method was tracked post, this is always done for the benefit 
of the sender so that they have a receipt and can see once the post has 
been received. In this case the sender can simply send the post by 
normal post, and this will not invalidate the acceptance. 
 
 
LEGAL INTENTION: 
 
Intention to create legal relations (ICLR) = ‘to create a contract there 
must be a common intention of the parties to enter into legal 
obligations, mutually communicated expressly or impliedly.' – This is an 
objective test. 
 
Presumptions: 
Presumptions in law are the starting point and will be upheld unless 
proven wrong. 
 
In commercial situations: 
 
There is a presumption of ICLR. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
If the agreement was made as a social arrangement, there is there is no 
ICLR. – eg. Where the parties promised to divide earnings in a pop 
group. 
 
If the contract signed contains a clause saying that there is no ICLR, the 
court will uphold this even in the business context. 
 
In domestic situations: 
 
There is a presumption of no ICLR. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Presumption of no ICLR between married couples. 
Presumption of no ICLR between a parent and their child. 
Presumption of ICLR between separating couples. 
Presumption of ICLR where there was mutuality of obligations. 
 
Previous conduct can rebut the presumption of no ICLR in social 
settings. 
– 
eg. 
Friends 
sharing 
jackpot 
winnings 
in 
an 
organized/business-like manner. 
 
CAPACITY: 
 
A contract entered into by someone without capacity renders the 
contract voidable by them when the disability ends. – in this case, the 
person who lacked capacity may choose to ratify the contract or leave 
it (in this case, the contract will be void). 
 
People who lack capacity: 
1. 
Minors 
2. 
People with mental incapacity 
3. 
Intoxicated people 
 
Minors: 
A contract between an adult and a minor (under 18) is not binding on 
the minor, unless the minor ratifies the contract once they reach 18. 
 
Exceptions: 
1. 
Contracts for ‘necessaries': 
• 
Minors are bound where a contract supplies them with 
‘necessaries', or everyday goods. 
• 
Sale of Goods Act 1979 A reasonable price must be paid 
for goods. 
• 
Fancy waistcoats were not necessary for a student 
who was sufficiently clothed. 
 
2. 
Beneficial contracts for service: 
Minors are bound where a contract supplies them services 
which are deemed beneficial to them. 
 
3. 
Contracts for continuing obligations 
 
Mental incapacity: 
 
Someone will lack capacity if: 
1. 
He is ‘unable to make a decision for himself in relation to the 
matter at the time the contract is made' 
2. 
It is not relevant whether the impairment is temporary/ 
permanent. 
3. 
He will still be liable to pay for ‘necessaries'/everyday items. 
 
 
Example: 
 
A company hiring a cleaner will likely intend to be in a legal 
relationship so the cleaner will be able to sue the company if they 
don't pay her. 
Example: 
 
A mother asking her daughter to wash the dished will not likely 
intend to enter into a legal relationship so the daughter will not be 
able to sue her mother if she doesn't pay her.

pages.heading: CONSIDERATION · Consideration = an element of exchange, whereby both parties provide
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Notes | Page 3 of 16 
CONSIDERATION 
 
Consideration = an element of exchange, whereby both parties provide 
something valuable to the contract. Consideration is what makes 
contracts enforceable. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Two types of consideration: 
 
1. 
Executory consideration – promise to do something in the 
future. – eg. contacting a massage parlour that they would give 
you a massage in the future. 
 
2. 
Executed consideration – performing what is due under the 
contract. – eg. if you turn up at the massage parlour asking for 
a massage, they could give you the massage immediately and 
you would then pay either before or after. 
 
RULES OF CONSIDERATION: 
 
The rules of good consideration refer to whether consideration will be 
legally valid in the circumstances. 
 
Promisor = person making the promise 
Promisee = person that is being promised something. 
 
Consideration must: 
1. 
Not be past 
2. 
Move from the Promisee – the Promisee must communicate it. 
 AND 
3. 
Be sufficient but need not be adequate 
 
Must not be past: 
 
Past consideration = Where one party has already provided a benefit, 
and that party is now asking for a promise in return for that benefit. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
A promise made after the agreement has formed is not a binding 
promise. 
 
Exceptions: 
 
* 
It was understood that payment would be due: 
 
If there was an understanding between the parties that 
payment would be due for the services from the beginning, 
then the paying party cannot get out of the contract by arguing 
past consideration. – eg. if the service was provided in the 
course of a business. 
 
This is the case even if there was no discussion as to the amoun 
that would be due. All that is necessary for good consideration 
is an understanding that some sort of payment would be due. 
 
* 
Contract made by deed: 
 
If a contract is made by deed, then the rules of good 
consideration will not apply. Any consideration will be accepted 
and deemed valid by the court. 
 
Deed = a document set out in a prescribed form. 
 
Must be sufficient (good consideration): 
 
Consideration must be sufficient but need not be adequate. 
 
The law expects both sides on the contract to make some sort of effort 
as consideration for the contract, they must provide some value. – 
Paying one apple in return for a TV may not be adequate. The apple has 
a lower market value than the TV, however, it is sufficient. 
 
However, illusory consideration will not be sufficient. This includes any 
consideration that is too vague and hard to define and enforce. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
PRE-EXISTING OBLIGATIONS: 
 
Making a promise to do something you are already obliged to do is not 
good consideration. 
 
Exceptions: 
1. 
Going over and above the existing obligations 
 OR 
2. 
By entering into an agreement, the paying party obtains a 
practical benefit. 
 
Going over and above: 
If the Promisee can show that they have gone over and above their 
existing obligations, that will count as good consideration. – eg. this 
could be done by doing a better job. 
 
Practical benefit: 
If the Promisee agrees with the Promisor to carry out the works at some 
time (without clarification as to when), then the Promisee calls the 
Promisor and tells him he would pay more to carry out the works 
tomorrow, the Promisee would earn a practical benefit from the 
agreement. – This would amount to good consideration. 
 
Even though there was already a contract to carry out the works, the 
works have now become urgent, so you earn a practical benefit from 
agreeing to do the works tomorrow rather than at some time in the 
future. 
 
PART-PAYMENT OF DEBT: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Debtor = the person who owes money. 
Creditor = the person who is owed money. 
 
General rule: 
 
Payment that is less than the debt will not discharge the obligation to 
pay the full amount. 
 
Common law exceptions: 
 
Pinnel's case Promises to accept less can be binding if there is new 
consideration in the form of a different thing, place or time. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Promises to accept less can be binding if the payment is made by a 
third party. 
 
However, if the debtor is in debt because the creditor did work for them 
and the debtor later finds out that the work was not done to the 
standard expected, then agreeing to pay less will mean that the debtor 
agreed to waive their right to litigate the matter. 
 
 
Example: 
 
You owe me £500. You don't have that money at the moment, but 
you promise to pay me £500 later on once you have the money. You 
do have £350 on hand and promise to pay me £350 now to discharge 
the debt. Is this promise enforceable? 
Examples: 
* 
Promises to provide goods/services. 
* 
Promises to pay a certain amount. 
* 
Promises to not sue someone. 
* 
Promises to not do something. 
Example: 
 
An aunt provided childcare for her niece in the past is now asking 
for payment in return for the work she has carried out. At the time 
when she agreed to care for her niece, she agreed to care for her for 
free. She can't then turn around and change her mind saying that 
she now wants payment for that past work. 
Examples of sufficient 
consideration: 
* 
Giving up a legal right. 
* 
Promising not to sue 
someone. 
* 
Paying a peppercorn 
as rent. 
NOT sufficient consideration: 
* 
Giving up 
complaining 
* 
Promising to pay at a 
rate which the 
promisor will decide 
at a later date – 
promisor has too 
much discretion. 
Different thing: 
If you want a debt of £500 to be discharged for £350, you need to 
offer something else in addition, eg. £350 and a cup of tea. It doesn't 
matter if the new consideration does not need to be adequate, 
merely sufficient. 
 
Different place: 
If you want a debt of £500 to be discharged for £350, you can offer 
to pay the £350 at the house of the promisor to give him an 
advantage. 
 
Different time: 
If you want a debt of £500 to be discharged for £350, you can offer 
to pay the £350 at an earlier date.

pages.heading: PRIVITY OF CONTRACT · GENERAL RULE:
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Notes | Page 4 of 16 
PRIVITY OF CONTRACT 
 
GENERAL RULE: 
 
Privity of contract = asks the question who can sue under a contract 
and who can be sued. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
A claimant can only make a claim in relation to a contract if he is the 
one who has given the consideration. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
If there is a contract made between two parties to benefit a third party, 
that third party cannot enforce the benefit they were to receive under 
the general rules, if the original parties to the contract refuse to 
perform their obligations. 
 
However, this case will likely fall within the exception under the 
Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 which we will look at 
below. 
 
EXCEPTIONS: 
 
If you have a client who wants to make a claim under a contract to 
which they are not a party, they must look at whether one of the 
exceptions apply. 
 
Main exceptions: 
1. 
Trusts 
2. 
Agency 
3. 
Collateral contract 
4. 
Assignment 
5. 
Contracts (Rights of Third parties) Act 1999 
 
Agency: 
 
A third party to a contract may make a claim relying on agency if one of 
the parties to the contract acted as their agent. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
In this case, the agent will simply be acting on the third party's behalf 
and while in theory, the contract is between the agent and the other 
party, the third party is the true party to the contract. 
 
Once the contract is signed, the agent will not be acting on behalf of the 
third party and the third party becomes a party to the contract. 
 
 
 
 
Collateral contract: 
 
Creative solutions by the courts to avoid the unfair result that is created 
by strictly following the rules of privity. 
 
The court may find that there is another contract which has not been 
expressly stated between the parties. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
In this case, the court must find that both parties intended for there to 
be a contract between them. 
 
Assignment: 
 
If you have a right, you can assign (pass on) the right to a third party. 
 
Two parties have a contract. One of the parties then assigns some or all 
of the rights from his contract to a third party. That third party can now 
sue the original party on the basis of breach of contract if they refuse 
to pay. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Contracts (Rights of Third parties) Act 1999: 
 
Third parties can now sue for a benefit of the contract. 
 
Third party will be able to benefit from a contract if: Contracts (Rights 
of Third Parties) Act 1999 
• 
The contract expressly provides that they could 
 OR 
• 
The contract purports to confer a benefit 
 
However, the act can be expressly excluded so look out for clauses 
excluding it. 
 
Trust: 
 
In some cases, a third party might be able to successfully argue, that the 
original party to the contract was holding the promise on trust for 
them. 
 
If so, the third party could instruct the party to the contract to enforce 
the promise. Once the money is paid to the party to the contract, that 
money must be paid to the third party, who will be the beneficiary of 
the trust in this case. 
 
The word “trust” need not have been used to create a trust in this case. 
 
 
 
Example: 
 
I need my room painted so I reach out to Katy, my gardener and ask 
her if she could do the work for me. If she agrees to paint my room, 
then me and Katy will both be parties to the contract. 
 
If she decides not to take on the work, she may refer me to her son, 
Thomas, the local handyman. If I make a contract with Thomas, then 
Thomas and I will be parties to the contract. – Katy will not be a party 
to the contract in this case. 
 
PARTY 
 
THIRD 
PARTY 
 
PARTY 
contract 
help third 
party 
PARTY 
(AGENT) 
 
THIRD 
PARTY 
 
PARTY 
contract 
help third 
party 
Example: 
 
Thomas paints my room and I owe him £500 for the job he has done. 
He asks me to pay him £300 and pay £200 to his mother, Katy, as he 
owed her £200. 
 
In this case, Thomas assigned some of the benefit of the contract to 
his mother.

pages.heading: TERMS · EXPRESS TERMS:
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Notes | Page 5 of 16 
TERMS 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
EXPRESS TERMS: 
 
Representation or express term? 
 
Look at factors: 
 
1. 
Timing: The longer the time between the representation and 
signing the contract, the less likely that the representation was 
meant to be a term. 
 
2. 
Importance: The parties must have placed importance in the 
truth of the statement. If they did, it is likely that the statement 
was a term. 
 
3. 
Specialist knowledge: 
If one of the parties have specialist knowledge/they are expert 
in the subject matter of the contract, then the court will usually 
decide against them. 
The court will always make sure that the expert party loses out 
in these circumstances. 
 
4. 
Checks: 
If a seller tells the buyer not to carry out checks, then this is 
effectively a promise that what they are telling the buyer is true. 
This does not generally apply to auction sales. 
 
The Parole Evidence rule: 
 
Parole evidence rule = extrinsic evidence may not be taken into 
account to vary an express written contract. If the contract is in 
writing, you cannot use what was said around the time of making the 
contract to deny or dispute the written terms of the contract. 
 
Exceptions: 
• 
Contracts not wholly written: 
If the contract is one which is part-written, part-oral, then the 
parole evidence rule doesn't apply. 
 
• 
Collateral contracts: 
There was another contract formed, varying or altering the 
original contract. This other contract might be an oral contract. 
 
• 
Onerous terms: 
Onerous terms must be very obvious/pointed out the other 
party, otherwise invalid. 
 
Entire agreement clauses: 
Entire agreement clauses are inserted into the agreement to exclude 
the parole evidence rule and will be upheld by the court. 
 
IMPLIED TERMS: 
 
The courts/statute will only imply terms into the contract if the parties 
must have intended the term to be a part of the contract, as it was 
necessary for business efficacy. 
 
Implied by the courts: 
 
Different types of implication by the courts: 
* 
Implied as a one-off to ensure business efficacy. – eg. if a car is 
being sold, the car must have four wheels. 
* 
Rules of trade custom – will be implied terms. 
* 
Previous course of dealing – will imply the terms in the new 
contract as used in the old contract. 
 
Implied by statute: 
 
Sale of Goods Act 1979: 
 
s.12-15 Sale of Goods Act 1979 Rely on this act if the contract is for the 
sale of goods and it is a contract between two businesses (Businessto-business). 
 
Implied terms: s.12-15 Sale of Goods Act 1979 
* 
The seller must have good title to the goods so they are able to 
legally transfer them to the buyer. 
* 
The items sold must be of satisfactory quality. 
* 
The items sold must be fit for the buyer's particular purpose, if 
the buyer told this to the seller. 
* 
If the sale is sale by sample: then the goods must correspond 
with the sample. 
* 
If the sale is sale by description: then the goods must 
correspond with the description. 
 
Consumer Rights Act 2015: 
 
Consumer Rights Act 2015 Rely on this act if the contract is for the sale 
of goods and the buyer is not a business (Business-to-Consumer). 
 
Implied terms: 
* 
Right to supply 
* 
Description 
* 
Satisfactory quality 
* 
Reasonably fit for a particular purpose 
* 
Sample 
 
Same provisions as for the SGA 1979 above, just use a different statute. 
 
CLASSIFICATION OF TERMS: 
 
Types of terms: 
1. 
Conditions 
2. 
Warranties 
3. 
Innominate terms 
 
Conditions = a term in the contract that goes to the root of the contract 
(an important term). 
 
Warranties = a term in the contract that is less important. 
 
Innominate term = a term where it is not possible to tell if the term 
goes to the root of the contract. – this will become clear when breach 
happens. Once decided whether the term goes to the root of the 
contract, it will then be treated as a condition or warranty. 
 
Conditions: 
 
The word condition carries a specific legal meaning in this case which is 
an important term to the contract. 
 
Can be defined by: 
• 
Statute 
• 
The parties 
• 
Courts 
 
Statute: 
 
Sale of Goods Act 1979: 
 
Sale of Goods Act 1979 Rely on this act if the contract is for the sale of 
goods and it is a contract between two businesses (Business-tobusiness). 
 
Sale of Goods Act 1979 s.12-15 are all classed as conditions. 
 
s.15A Sale of Goods Act 1979 The breach of these conditions may be 
treated as a breach of warranty if: 
• 
If both parties are businesses 
• 
There is a slight/technical breach of ss.13, 14 or 15 
 AND 
• 
Rejecting the goods would be unreasonable 
 
Consumer Rights Act 2015: 
 
Consumer Rights Act 2015 Rely on this act if the contract is for the sale 
of goods and the buyer is not a business (Business-to-Consumer). 
 
CRA does not classify its terms as either conditions or warranties. 
 
Parties: 
* 
If a term is defined as a condition in the contract, the courts will 
give effect to this. 
* 
If a term is defined as a condition, but this leads to an 
unreasonable result, the parties must be particularly clear in the 
contract that this is the result they want. 
 
Courts: 
* 
'Expected readiness to load' clause will always be a condition. 
This clause means that one party must inform the other when 
the ship is in the dock ready for the goods to be loaded onto it. 
 
* 
Time of performance is always a warranty except when the 
contract says ‘Time is of the essence' in which case it becomes 
a condition. 
 
 
 
Terms = 
describe the 
meaning and 
effect of a 
contract by 
setting out 
the rights and 
obligations 
contained 
within it. 
Representat
ions = precontractual 
statements 
of fact. Not 
terms to the 
contract. – 
eg. The 
horse is not 
vicious. 
Express terms 
= terms which 
the parties 
agreed that 
they should 
form part of 
the contract. 
Typically 
written terns. 
 
Implied terms 
= terms that 
have not been 
agreed by the 
parties 
expressly but 
they also form 
part of the 
contract.

pages.heading: EFFECT OF BREACH: · Breach of condition:
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Notes | Page 6 of 16 
EFFECT OF BREACH: 
 
Breach of condition: 
 
The innocent party has a choice (right of election) to: 
• 
Terminate the contract and claim damages 
 OR 
• 
Affirm the contract and claim damages 
 
Breach of a warranty: 
The innocent party can only claim damages. 
 
Breach of an innominate term: 
Rights of the innocent party are uncertain. It depends on how the court 
decides. If the innocent party believes that this was the breach of a 
condition and decides to terminate the contract, then the other party 
can sue them for wrongful termination. 
 
VARIATION OF TERMS: 
 
Both parties must agree to the variation, preferably in writing. 
 
Unilateral variation (ie where only one party can make a change) is only 
valid under specific circumstances if this has been agreed in advance. 
 
Methods of varying a contract: 
 
1. 
Written variation 
 
2. 
Oral variation: 
Valid, however, it can be difficult to enforce. Making a recording 
of the oral variation/having witnesses helps enforcement. 
 
3. 
Variation by conduct: 
Often seen in construction contracts or where a contractor has 
deadlines to meet. However, this can lead to an implied change 
in the contract. 
 
In some cases, sustained minor breaches, if the other party 
acquiesced (said nothing), may also lead to an implied change 
of terms, incorporating the conduct amounting to the breach 
into the contract. 
 
4. 
Unilateral variation: 
Generally invalid. However, if both parties agree in the contract 
that unilateral variation is an option, then such variation will be 
valid. This will likely only apply to certain specified terms. 
 
Waiver: 
One party may waive (give up) certain rights under a contract for a set 
period of time. This can be done orally or in writing. Once they have 
agreed to do so, the waiver is binding. 
 
Sustained minor breach: 
If one party consistently accepts minor contractual breaches, and a 
dispute then arises regarding these breaches, previous acceptance will 
be taken into account by the court.

pages.heading: EXEMPTION CLAUSES · INTRODUCTION:
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Notes | Page 7 of 16 
EXEMPTION CLAUSES 
 
INTRODUCTION: 
 
Definition: 
 
An exemption clause is a clause that will change a party's obligations to 
pay damages. 
 
Exemption clauses = ‘a term which excludes or modifies an obligation, 
whether primary [or] general secondary.' 
 
Two types of exemption clauses: 
1. 
Exclusion clause – this will exclude liability completely 
2. 
Limitation clause – this will limit a party's liability, so that party 
will only pay a part of the loss. 
 
These types of clauses are put into contracts by a party that has more 
negotiating power over the other. These are usually seen to be added 
by large businesses where the consumer is not able to negotiate the 
terms of the contract as they have weaker bargaining power. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
INCORPORATION: 
 
In the past, the courts have not been able to cross out clauses that they 
deemed unfair so when encountering these clauses, they wanted to 
make sure that these clauses were really a part of the contract and have 
been properly incorporated. 
 
Incorporation may happen by: 
* 
Signature 
* 
Notice 
* 
Previous course of dealings 
* 
Trade custom 
 
Incorporation by signature: 
 
General rule: 
If an agreement is signed, in the absence of fraud, it will be immaterial 
whether both parties have read the terms of the agreement. 
 
Exceptions: 
1. 
If there is an overriding oral assurance. 
2. 
If the document given to you is not reasonably expected to have 
a contractual effect, then it won't. – eg. Timesheets. 
3. 
'Non est factum': if you are incapacitated from understanding 
what is in the document, you will not be bound even if you 
signed it. 
 
Incorporation by notice: 
 
Notice = bringing to the attention of the other party what the contract 
will contain. 
 
Reasonable notice: the party relying on the clause must take 
reasonable steps to bring the clause to the other party's attention. 
 
Referring to the term is usually enough for the terms to be 
incorporated. 
 
If the term is particularly onerous terms, then the party relying on the 
term must take more effort to make sure that the other party 
understand the term. 
 
Incorporation by previous course of dealings: 
 
If there had been previous dealings between the parties, then it can be 
assumed that the new contracts will be on the same or at least similar 
terms to the past contracts. 
 
In order to establish previous dealings: 
1. 
The dealing must be consistent 
 AND 
2. 
Regular – Contracting 3-4 times in 5 year was not regular 
enough. 5 similar contracts made in 13 months was regular 
enough. For big contracts, a lower frequency will be enough. 
 
Incorporation by trade custom: 
 
If there is a recognized custom in that industry to use some specific 
implied terms, the court will take those into account. 
Other key considerations: 
 
Timing: 
The clause must be a part of the contract before it is signed. 
The clause must be shown to a carpark customer before the automatic 
barrier. 
 
Nature of document: 
If the nature of the document is not one to be expected to be legally 
binding, then it is unlikely to form part of the contract. 
 
CONSTRUCTION: 
 
Would a reasonable person construe the clause as such that it would 
cover the breach? 
The court will interpret the clause using its ordinary, natural meaning. 
Would the clause cover the breach? 
 
Contra proferentem rule: 
If there is any ambiguity in the exemption clause, the clause will be 
construed against the person relying on the clause. 
 
Example: 
If there is a clause in a contract for purchasing a car, that the 
manufacturers limit liability if the car carries a “load in excess of that 
for which it was constructed”, and this is set out to be 5 people, the 
court will interpret load to mean weight and not the number of people. 
 
When interpreting a clause, the starting point of the court is the 
ordinary meaning of the words. 
 
When excluding liability for negligence, you must state that you are to 
exclude liability for negligence, otherwise the wording may be 
construed to mean something else. 
 
If one of the parties purports to exclude negligence, this is not 
something that the general public would agree to so the wording on 
this must state that what is being excluded is negligence, otherwise the 
court will construe it to mean something else. 
 
If the limitation clause in the contract is sensible about the limit, the 
court is more likely to uphold the clause. 
 
STATUTORY CONTROLS: 
 
First, differentiate between Business contracts and consumer contracts 
as different rules apply depending on the type of contract you are 
dealing with. 
 
Business to business – Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 
Business to consumer – Consumer Rights Act 2015 
 
UCTA 1977: 
 
The test under the act is that of reasonableness, not unfairness as the 
name would suggest. 
 
Scope: 
• 
Only deals with business-to-business contracts 
• 
Only deals with exemption clauses and does not deal with any 
other terms 
• 
Deals with business liability (contractual and tortious) 
• 
Deals with non-contractual notices – eg. where the premises 
have signs trying to limit liability. 
 
It controls clauses which tries to limit/exclude liability for: 
• 
Negligence 
• 
Breach of a contractual term 
• 
Breach of a term implied by SGA or SGSA 
 
Negligence: 
 
Negligence = is a ‘breach of any express or implied contract term to take 
reasonable care or exercise reasonable skill'. 
Eg. A breach of s.13 Supply of Goods and Services Act 1982. 
 
If the term is trying to exclude personal injury or death caused by 
negligence, the exemption clause will be invalid. 
 
If a term is excluding ‘other loss or damage', then the exemption clause 
must be reasonable in order to be valid – look at s.11. 
 
Breach of a contractual term or an implied term: 
 
Breach of a contractual term: 
This means express terms. 
 
If the parties are dealing on the basis of standard terms of business, 
then the reasonableness test in s.11 applies. 
Common law controls: 
* 
Incorporation 
* 
Construction 
 
 
Statutory controls: 
* 
Unfair Contract Terms 
Act 1977 
* 
Consumer Rights Act 
2015

pages.heading: If the parties are not dealing on the basis of standard terms of business, · and the contract is negotiated, then the court will presume that the
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Notes | Page 8 of 16 
If the parties are not dealing on the basis of standard terms of business, 
and the contract is negotiated, then the court will presume that the 
terms are reasonable. 
 
If the general terms of the main agreement are not negotiated, even 
if the other related agreements are negotiated, means contracting on 
general terms. 
 
Breach of a term implied by SGA or SGSA: 
This is an implied term, that cannot be excluded/limited. 
 
Breach of any other implied term: 
Go through the reasonableness test in s.11. 
 
The Reasonableness Test – s.11: 
 
The test for reasonableness must be considered in the circumstances 
existing at the time of contracting. 
 
What is reasonable is a question of fact to the court. 
 
Also look at the non-exhaustive list of guidelines in Schedule 2. 
 
Schedule 2 Guidelines – indicative ‘Grey List': 
These have a general application to the requirements of 
reasonableness. 
 
The guidelines include: 
a) 
The strength of bargaining positions of the parties 
b) 
Whether the customer received an inducement to 
agree to the term 
c) 
Whether the customer knew/ought to reasonably have 
known of the existence and extent of the term 
d) 
If exemption clause relies upon some condition not 
being complied with and whether that was reasonable 
to expect 
e) 
Whether the goods were manufactured/processed or 
adapted to the special order of the customer 
 
Limitation clauses have other rules that apply to them. Court must 
have regard to resources of the party and whether they had insurance 
available to them. 
 
The proferens (= party seeking to rely on the clause) must prove 
reasonableness. 
 
What is reasonable is decided on a case-by-case basis: 
 
There could be no appeals made on reasonableness, the finding of 
which is at the discretion of the court. 
 
If businessmen dealing with large companies with equal bargaining 
power would believe that the terms are reasonable, then the courts 
will not intervene. 
Unless the court is satisfied that one of the parties is taking unfair 
advantage of the other or the terms are so unreasonable that they 
would not be properly understood/considered, then the court will not 
interfere with the agreement of the parties. 
 
If the clause is so unreasonable that it contradicts a basic assumption 
of responsibility. 
 
Definitions: 
 
A party is dealing as a consumer if it is not dealing in the course of its 
business and the other party is. 
 
A company may be a consumer if the purchase is not integral to their 
business. 
 
Business = includes a profession and the activities of a public and local 
authority. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
CRA 2015: 
 
Scope: 
Only deals with business-to-consumer contracts but applies to any term 
in the contract, not only exemption clauses. 
 
All terms must be transparent, legible and fair. 
 
Certain exclusions are unfair such as: 
- 
Excluding or limiting liability for death/personal injury caused 
by negligence 
- 
Excluding or limiting the conditions implied by the CRA 
 
If a term is unfair then will not be binding on the consumer. 
 
A term is not binding if it tries to restrict liability for any of the implied 
terms in the Act: 
1. 
Right to supply the goods 
2. 
Goods of satisfactory quality 
3. 
Goods to be fit for a particular purpose 
4. 
Goods to be as described 
5. 
Goods to match any sample examined 
 
Excluding liability when providing services: 
 
An exemption clause is not binding if it is to exclude trader's liability 
arising under s.49 for negligently performing the service. 
 
If the clause is only limiting liability for breach of s.49: then it may be 
binding if it meets the below conditions: 
• 
It does not limit liability for death/personal injury caused by 
breach of duty of skill and care 
• 
It does not limit liability below the purchase price 
 AND 
• 
It passes the fairness test of the act.

pages.heading: VITIATING FACTORS · Vitiating elements/factors:
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Notes | Page 9 of 16 
VITIATING FACTORS 
 
Vitiating elements/factors: 
• Misrepresentation 
• Mistake 
• Unfair contract terms 
• Duress and undue influence 
• Illegality 
 
DURESS: 
 
Duress = ‘some form of coercion or threat to the person, property, or 
to a person's financial interests.' 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Effect of duress, if proven: 
The contract will be voidable (different from void), and the court can 
set it aside. 
 
Voidable = the innocent party has a right to choose whether to keep 
the contract in place or set it aside. If they choose not to go ahead with 
the contract and they then mak an application to the court, the court 
will set the contract aside as per their right. 
 
Void = the contract is void from the beginning and the innocent party 
has no choice whether to keep the contract. Proving mistake will render 
the contract void (not voidable). 
 
Types of duress: 
1. 
Duress to the person: 
• 
This is their contract was entered into by one party 
because of threats made to their person. 
• 
Threat to the person need not be the only reason for 
entering into a contract, but it must be one of the 
reasons. 
 
2. 
Duress to goods: 
• 
This comprises of the unlawful detention of someone's 
goods. 
• 
Test for duress to goods is the ‘but for' test. But for the 
threat, would the innocent party have signed the 
contract. This is a higher requirement that we have seen 
in relation to duress to the person (must be one of the 
reasons). 
 
3. 
Economic duress 
 
 
 
Economic duress: 
 
The test for economic duress: Pakistan International Airline Corp v 
Times Travel (2021) 
1. 
There is a threat/pressure made to the victim. – they may have 
other choices, but those choices would not be practical 
2. 
The threat/pressure is illegitimate, and the Defendant knows it 
is illegitimate. – pressure must be illegitimate, but differentiate 
this from rough negotiations which are acceptable 
3. 
The threat/pressure caused the victim to enter into the 
contract. 
 AND 
4. 
The victim had no reasonable alternative option but to give in 
to the threat/pressure. 
 
Factors to decide whether there has been illegitimate pressure: 
1. 
Pressure is a threatened breach of contract – if so, likely 
illegitimate 
2. 
Pressure is applied in bad faith – if so, likely illegitimate 
3. 
The victim protested – if so, likely illegitimate 
4. 
The victim affirmed – if so, unlikely to be illegitimate 
 
The victim protested or did not affirm the contract: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Waiting for 8 months affirms the contract. 
As soon as the invoice is sent, paying the original amount and refusing 
to pay the rest is a sign of protest. 
 
Significant cause: 
This is a ‘but for' test. But for the pressure, the victim would not have 
entered into the contract. 
 
UNDUE INFLUENCE: 
 
An equitable doctrine to ensure that when a party enters into a 
contract, their decision has not been unduly influenced. 
 
If undue influence is proved, the contract will be voidable and the 
innocent party may choose to rescind it. 
 
Similar to duress, however, duress is concerned with pressure while 
undue influence is concerned with whether the innocent party made 
their decision through their own free will. 
 
Types of undue influence: 
1. 
Actual undue influence by overt acts 
2. 
Presumed undue influence as a result of the relationship 
between the parties. 
3. 
Third-party undue influence. 
 
Actual undue influence: 
Undue influence must have been a factor for entering into to the 
contract, however, it need not be the only factor. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Presumed undue influence: 
 
Elements of presumed undue influence: 
1. 
A relationship of trust and confidence between the parties. 
2. 
When viewed objectively, the resulting transaction requires an 
explanation 
 
This relationship will be presumed in fiduciary relationships: 
• 
Parent and child 
• 
Two partners in a partnership 
• 
Doctor and patient 
• 
Solicitor and client 
 
In most other situations, the relationship of trust and confidence must 
be proven. – eg. in relation to spouses. 
 
Once the presumption of undue influence arises, the burden of proof 
shifts onto the other party. 
 
ILLEGALITY: 
 
Contracts may be void for illegality. – eg. a contract to carry out criminal 
behaviour is illegal and void. 
 
Contracts illegal by statute: 
Where the contract provides for the performance of an act that is 
against a rule set out in a statute. 
 
Contracts illegal at common law: 
- 
Any agreements to commit a crime is illegal under common law. 
– may also be illegal under the provision that sets out the crime. 
- 
Any agreements to commit a tort are also illegal. 
 
Contracts damaging to the government: 
Any agreements to trade with the enemy during war times would be 
illegal. 
 
Contracts that interfere with justice: 
Any agreements to conceal a crime would be illegal and also any 
agreements to undermine the court's jurisdiction. 
 
 
 
Example: 
Where one person threatens that the other will be harmed, they will 
damage something they own or make them bankrupt. This last one 
is a special form of duress called economic duress. 
Example: 
 
Protesting after signing the contract is evidence that you were put 
under pressure to sign the contract. You should protest as soon as 
possible and the longer you wait the less likely that your protest will 
be viewed as good evidence. 
 
In particular, the latest you could protest is as soon as the pressure 
has been lifted. 
Example: 
An elderly woman is told by her daughter to sign a contract in 
relation to a family trust or face legal proceedings. She is afraid of 
her daughter and dislikes confrontation. Even though the threat is 
lawful, the contract will be set aside for undue influence.

pages.heading: VITIATING FACTORS – MISREPRESENTATION · INTRODUCTION:
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Notes | Page 10 of 16 
VITIATING FACTORS – MISREPRESENTATION 
 
INTRODUCTION: 
 
Misrepresentation = a misleading/false statement made to a party to 
the contract before signing the contract that made then enter into it. 
 
Effect: 
Misrepresentation makes the contract voidable. 
Court may undo the contract by rescission. The remedy of rescission is 
available for all types of misrepresentation. 
 
Rescission = an equitable remedy that takes the innocent party to the 
start before the contract was made. 
 
Distinguish from other statement: 
• 
Mere puff 
• 
Terms 
• 
Representations 
• 
Statements of fact – these are somewhere in between mere 
puff and representations. 
 
ELEMENTS OF MISREPRESENTATION: 
 
Actionable Misrepresentation: 
1. 
Unambiguous – the statement should have only one meaning. 
2. 
False – If the statement is not substantially correct, then it is 
false. 
3. 
Statement of fact/law 
4. 
Addressed to the party misled (directly or indirectly via a third 
party) 
5. 
Induces the contract 
6. 
Causes loss 
 
Statement of fact: 
‘A representation is not an undertaking to do, or not to do something. 
It is a statement asserting a given state of affairs.' 
 
Examples of statements of fact/law: 
 
Conduct: 
• 
Conduct could amount to a statement of fact. 
• 
Deliberate concealment of a defect amounted to a false 
statement of fact if the seller did not disclose the defect. 
 
Opinion: 
• 
Opinion could amount to a statement of fact. 
• 
If the party expressing their opinion is an expert or holds out to 
be an expert, then their opinion will be a statement of fact. 
 
Future intention: 
• 
Future intention is not a fact. 
• 
No duty to inform of change of future intention. 
• 
Dishonest statement of intention will amount to misrep. 
 
Silence: 
Silence cannot be a statement of fact. There is no general duty of 
disclosure. 
 
Exceptions: 
• 
Contracts uberrimae fidei: you must disclose all material 
matter when purchasing insurance. 
• 
Fiduciary relationships: you must disclose the truth even if not 
asked. 
• 
Half-truths = something that is true but gives the wrong 
impression. 
• 
Continuing representations = something that is true at the time 
but with the false representation that it will continue to be true. 
 
Is the statement material? 
• 
Material statement = statement relating to an issue that would 
influence a reasonable man. 
• 
Use the objective test. 
• 
If the statement is material – then inducement is inferred. 
• 
If a reasonable person would be influenced by this statement, 
then the court will infer that the Claimant was actually induced. 
• 
Inducement is inferred unless Defendant can prove Claimant 
was not induced (subjective test). 
• 
If the statement is not material – then there was no inducement 
unless the Claimant proves that they were induced (subjective 
test). 
 
Inducement: 
• 
The misrep statement need not be the only inducement. 
• 
No inducement if the Claimant did not see/hear the misrep. 
• 
No inducement if the Claimant did not rely on the misrep. 
 
 
 
 
TYPES OF MISREPRESENTATION: 
 
The reason why a Claimant will argue misrepresentation is because they 
want to get out of the contract (rescission). 
 
Four types: 
1. 
Fraudulent – The tort of deceit 
2. 
Negligent misrepresentation – Misrepresentation Act 1967 
3. 
Innocent misrepresentation – Misrepresentation Act 1967 
4. 
Negligent Misstatement – Tort of negligence, use this is the 
statement was made by a third party. 
 
Fraudulent misrep: 
 
A false representation is made: knowing it was untrue or without 
belief in its truth or reckless as to its truth. 
 
Reckless as to the truth of the statement = the person making the 
statement closing its eyes as to the truth of the statement. 
 
Remedies: 
• 
Rescission, Damages (extensive) and possible indemnity. 
• 
Sometimes rescission is not enough, and damages can be 
claimed. 
• 
Damages for fraudulent misrepresentation are extensive, 
meaning that these damages will put the innocent party back 
into the position before the contract was made. 
• 
If, due to the misrep, the innocent party has accrued 
responsibilities to pay to another party, then they can also claim 
indemnities. 
 
Measure of damages is as for the Tort of deceit: 
• 
All loss must be ‘directly flowing' from the transaction 
• 
Does not need to be foreseeable 
• 
But cannot be rendered too remote by Claimant 
 
Negligent misrep: 
 
The court is willing to make a finding of negligent misrepresentation. 
 
Elements of negligent misrep: 
1. 
False statement 
2. 
No reasonable grounds to believe in its truth 
3. 
No need for actual negligence 
 
Burden of proof is on the Defendant to show reasonable grounds for 
belief, effectively disproving negligence. 
 
Remedies: 
• 
Rescission or that is not possible, then damages are possible in 
lieu of rescission and if applicable, indemnity. 
• 
Calculation of damages is the same as for fraudulent 
misrepresentation. 
• 
Claim losses that flow from the misrepresentation (not the 
same as for fraudulent misrep which calculated on losses that 
flow form the transaction). 
 
Innocent misrep: 
 
The person who made the false statement can prove that they believed 
that the statement was true and they had reasonable grounds to 
believe that the facts represented were true. If this cannot be proved, 
then they will be liable for negligent misrep. 
 
Misrepresentation Act 1967 Burden is on the misrepresentor to prove 
that he: ‘had reasonable grounds to believe up to the time the 
contract was made that the facts represented were true.' 
 
Remedies: 
• 
Rescission or that is not possible, then damages in lieu of 
rescission and if applicable, indemnity. 
• 
However, no right to substantive damages so you cannot claim 
the losses you have accrued. Your best outcome will be 
rescission. 
• 
Must inform the other party of intention to rescind. 
 
Negligent misstatement: 
 
Difficult to prove, only use it if you cannot claim for misrepresentation 
and you don't need rescission, only damages. 
 
May also use this claim if the false statement that induced you into the 
contract was not the seller but a third party. 
 
Hedley Byrne v Heller Claimant must prove: 
• 
Reliance reasonably foreseeable 
• 
Relationship of proximity between parties 
 AND 
• 
Fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty

pages.heading: REMEDIES TO MISREPRESENTATION: · Rescission:
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Notes | Page 11 of 16 
REMEDIES TO MISREPRESENTATION: 
 
Rescission: 
 
Bars to rescission: 
* 
Third party rights: If a third party acquired rights in the contract 
innocently, then rescission will not be allowed. 
 
* 
Affirmation: Even if a person doesn't want the contract, they 
can affirm it by conduct indicating that they don't wish to 
rescind. 
 
* 
Impossibility: Court cannot allow for rescission if it is 
impossible. – eg. selling a company that no longer exists. 
 
* 
Lapse of time: Court will not allow for rescission if a long time 
has passed. – eg. 5 years may be too long. 
 
Indemnity: 
 
Indemnity is relevant if, after entering into the contract, the wronged 
party wasted money on a service so this amount is to pay off that party. 
– eg. if you purchase a car under misrep and then you make a contract 
for parking arrangements, you can claim indemnity on the parking 
arrangements. 
 
Indemnity is an equitable remedy.

pages.heading: VITIATING FACTORS – MISTAKE · INTRODUCTION:
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Notes | Page 12 of 16 
VITIATING FACTORS – MISTAKE 
 
INTRODUCTION: 
 
Types of mistake: 
 
• 
Mutual mistake: Both parties are mistaken in different ways. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
• 
Common mistake: Both parties are mistaken in the same way. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
• 
Unilateral mistake: Only one party is mistaken. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Effect: 
 
Mistake renders the contract void ab initio. The parties believed that 
they have made a contract but there was never a contract to begin with. 
This is different from a contract that is voidable, because even if ends 
up voided, that contract have run from the date it was made until the 
date if was voided. 
 
Mutual and Unilateral mistake – Finding of mistake may mean that 
there was no agreement in fact. 
 
Common mistake – Or it may mean that the mistake destroys the 
nature of the agreement. 
 
The mistaken facts must exist before the conclusion of the contract. 
 
MUTUAL MISTAKE: 
 
There must have been such ambiguity that no agreement could be 
found. 
The test for agreement is objective. 
 
COMMON MISTAKE: 
 
Can arise in two ways, res extincta and res sua. 
 
Res extincta: 
 
At the time of the contract, both parties believe that the item for sale 
exists which is not in fact the case. 
 
If there is a mistake as to the existence of goods, that will fall within the 
claim of common mistake. 
 
Sale of Goods Act 1979 Where there is a contract for specific goods 
and the goods, without knowledge of the seller, perish, the contract 
is void. 
 
Res sua: 
 
At the time of the contract, the buyer already owns the thing they are 
trying to purchase. 
 
Mistake must be operative and affect a fundamental quality of the 
contract. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Examples: 
1. 
There was an auction of napkins that were said to have 
belonged to Charles I. Later it turned out that they were not, so 
their value dropped. 
2. 
There was a painting which was painted by the painter 
Constable, but it turned out to be wrong. No mistake here, as 
the court held, the buyer wanted a painting of a cathedral and 
that is what they have received. 
 
3. 
There was a ship that was struggling on sea and they made a 
contract with the Great Peace to help the crew. Later it turned 
out that the Great Peace was not as close by as they thought 
they were and wanted to terminate the contract. Held: The test 
was slightly reformulated to be: did the mistake affect an 
essential quality of the contract. 
 
UNILATERAL MISTAKE: 
 
Unilateral mistake can be made due to the expression of intention. 
Unilateral mistake can be made due to the nature of document. 
 
Defence – Non est factum: 
 
Incapacity: where the person signing a document does not understand 
the nature of the document. 
 
Fraud: if a document is signed by fraud, the party signing will not be 
held to it. – eg if A man was senile and could not recognize his own 
signature. He was induced to sign a document by fraud and he was not 
held to it. 
 
Fraud cannot be argued if there had been negligence. – eg if A lady has 
lost her glasses prior to signing some documents. The court will find 
that she was negligent and could not argue fraud. 
 
Fraud: if a document is signed by fraud, the party signing will not be 
held to it. – eg if A son was buying a farm and the father signed a 
document to guarantee that his son will be able to pay for the farm. The 
son actually asked him to sign a guarantee for all of his debts. The father 
was illiterate. 
 
Unilateral mistake as to identity: 
 
Unilateral mistake as to identity = where one person mistakes the 
identity of another. 
Eg. A person misrepresenting their identity when making a purchase on 
credit. 
 
Only the identity of the buyer can be essential to the contract, not 
their credit-worthiness. 
 
Distance sales: 
* 
In distance sales, the identity of the buyer is what is essential 
and so mistake will be allowed. 
* 
Mistake will not be allowed if merely the credit-worthiness of 
the buyer is essential to the contract. 
 
Face-to-face sales: 
* 
Mistake will not be allowed if merely the credit-worthiness of 
the buyer is essential to the contract. 
* 
If the wronged party looked up the identity of the buyer, then 
their identity was essential to the contract. – Unlikely to be 
followed. 
* 
Mistake will not be allowed if merely the credit-worthiness of 
the buyer is essential to the contract. 
Example: 
If one party wants to sell some coke, the drug, and the 
other person understands coke, the drink. 
Example: 
If one party wants to sell a car, but while making the sale, 
the car is burnt down. Both parties are mistaken as to the 
current state of the car. 
Example: 
If one party is lying about their identity and they know 
about the lie, but the other party doesn't. 
Example: 
Lever Bros owned a subsidiary in Nigeria. Mr Bell and Mr Snelling 
were chairman and vice chairman of Lever Bros and they paid them 
to resign as they did not want them to continue to be officers. Later 
the company found out that these officers breached their contracts 
and they could have been fired without payment. The company 
sued claiming mistake. The claim failed.

pages.heading: TERMINATION · Every contractual obligation gives rise to a corresponding contractual
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Notes | Page 13 of 16 
TERMINATION 
 
Every contractual obligation gives rise to a corresponding contractual 
right. Thus, where the obligation of one party is discharged, the 
corresponding right of the other party is extinguished. 
 
Where all obligations arising from the contract are discharged, all rights 
are thus extinguished, a contract is discharged. 
 
A contract may be discharged by: 
1. 
Performance 
2. 
Agreement 
3. 
Breach 
4. 
Frustration. 
 
TERMINATION BY PERFORMANCE: 
 
Entire obligations rule: a contractual obligation is discharged by 
complete performance. Where the promisor is unable or unwilling to 
give more than partial performance, there is no discharge of the 
contract – this is the case especially for lump sum contracts. 
 
Exceptions: 
1. 
If partial performance is accepted voluntarily by the innocent 
party, the party in default will be entitled to a quantum meruit. 
He must be compensated for the value of the work done 
without profit. 
 
2. 
If the innocent party has no choice but to accept, no payment 
is due. This may be due to: 
* 
A subsequent binding contract (new contract) 
* 
A term in the original contract (condition precedent or 
condition subsequent) 
 
Condition subsequent: 
A contract may contain a condition subsequent upon 
the occurrence of which obligations are discharged. – 
eg. “If my son dies, the contract is discharged.” If the 
event occurs, the contract is automatically discharged. 
Facts: the term of the contract was that the horse must 
hunt with a prescribed type of hound. 
 
Condition precedent: 
A contract may contain a condition precedent upon the 
occurrence of which obligations would commence – eg. 
“If my son is born, the contract commences.” If the 
event never occurs, the contract never comes into 
existence. 
 
A subsequent binding contract: 
* 
An agreement to discharge is effective if 
supported by consideration, if these obligations 
are wholly executory, then it is a mutual waiver. 
Only relevant if none of the parties started the 
performance. 
* 
Pinnel's case If partially performed, then an 
effective agreement to discharge is a deed on 
accord of satisfaction. Part-payment of debt can 
only 
be 
discharged 
by 
providing 
new 
consideration. 
* 
A simple part-performance does not discharge a 
contract. 
 
3. 
An equitable waiver may discharge a contract in certain 
circumstances. – eg. the cases on promissory estoppel. 
 
4. 
Performing the obligations in a way that was completely 
wrong did not amount to substantial performance. 
 
Other rules: 
 
Divisible obligations will allow the contracted party to receive 
payment for each obligation completed. If the contract sets out that 
each individual obligation will warrant the payment of money, then 
even if not all the obligations are performed, payment will be due. – eg. 
there is a difference between a contract saying: ‘I will pay you if you 
paint five paintings' and ‘I will pay you for each painting.' 
 
Performance by third party is not allowed if the person of the party 
carrying out the contract is important. 
 
TERMINATION BY BREACH: 
 
Breach of contract = Where a party, without lawful excuse fails or 
refuses to perform what is due under the contract or performs 
defectively or incapacitates himself from performing. 
 
 
 
 
Types of breach: 
1. 
Breach of condition: In this case, the innocent party has: 
* 
“Immediate right of election” 
* 
A choice to terminate or affirm the contract 
* 
An also claim damages 
 
2. 
Breach of warranty: In this case, the innocent party has the 
right to sue for damages only. 
 
3. 
Breach of an innominate term: In this case, the innocent party's 
rights will depend on the seriousness of the breach. 
 
Anticipatory breach: 
 
Anticipatory breach = a type of breach whereby prior to performance 
one party informs the other they will not fulfill their obligations. In this 
case, the innocent party should argue frustration. 
 
Anticipatory breach may be express or implied by words or conduct. 
 
Right of election – Affirmation: 
 
When an innocent party is faced with a repudiatory anticipatory breach, 
he is under no obligation to sue at once, but can elect to affirm the 
contract and wait for the time of performance. 
 
The innocent party is allowed a period of time to decide between 
affirmation and termination. If after the affirmation, the other party 
continues to refuse to perform, the innocent party can revoke the 
affirmation and terminate the contract. 
 
Once the decision is made, it must be clear and unequivocal. 
 
Obligations and rights remain on both sides, so the innocent party 
needs to carry out their obligations on their end. 
 
Limitations on affirmation: 
* 
Where the other party's cooperation is required, affirmation 
may not be possible. – eg. to let the other party into the gardens 
to carry out the services. 
* 
Affirmation is only allowed if the affirming party has a 
legitimate interest in affirming the contract. 
* 
Legitimate interest means: not wholly unreasonable. 
* 
The legitimate interest test will only be applied in ‘extreme 
cases'. Extreme cases: where it would be unreasonable to 
affirm and damages would be an adequate remedy. 
 
Risks of affirmation: 
* 
Advise your client on the risks of affirmations. 
* 
Client may subsequently breach the contract and may then be 
sued. 
* 
Client may subsequently frustrate the contract and lose their 
rights to damages. 
 
FRUSTRATION: 
 
Frustration is a defence to a claim of breach of contract. 
 
Before going to look at frustration in a question, go through the part on 
terms of contract where you establish the breach and whether a 
condition or warranty has been breached. Then look at frustration as a 
defence. 
 
Definition of Frustration: Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943 
* 
A supervening event – event arising after the formation of the 
contract 
* 
Unforeseeable 
* 
At no fault of either party 
* 
Which renders the contract impossible/illegal/otherwise 
radically different 
 
Effect of frustration: By operation of law, all future obligations will be 
discharged. 
 
Examples of frustration: 
 
Impossibility: 
 
Destruction of the thing: 
1. 
Destruction of the music hall 
2. 
Destruction of a thing that is closely connected to the contract. 
– eg. the factory, where machinery should have been installed. 
 
Unavailability of a thing: 
1. 
This is a matter of degree so set out a ration of unavailability. 
Look at the length of unavailability and how long this is relative 
to the contract. 
2. 
Unavailability for 5 months out of a 1 year contract was able to 
frustrate the contract. 
3. 
There was no time limit in the contract, but the contract implied 
a reasonable time.

pages.heading: The time approach is only the starting point of the court. · Unavailability of a person:
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Notes | Page 14 of 16 
4. 
The time approach is only the starting point of the court. 
 
Unavailability of a person: 
1. 
Incapacity: performer was not able to perform his contract due 
to being called to service. 
2. 
Death 
 
Illegality: 
A contract to do what it has been illegal to do cannot be legally 
enforceable. 
 
Government intervention: 
Where the resources were requisitioned by the government, the 
contract was held to have been frustrated. 
 
Frustration of purpose: 
The ‘Coronation cases' However, it must be the common purpose of 
the parties. 
 
Coronation cases: 
1. 
Krell v Henry (1903) 
Facts: Henry hired a flat to watch the procession for the king's 
coronation. The coronation was cancelled so he did not want to 
pay the rent. The court held that the contract was frustrated. 
Krell advertised the flat to watch the coronation and the flat 
was only for day-time hire so this was evidence of his intention. 
 
2. 
Chandler v Webster (1904) 
Facts: Chandler hired a ship so that they could watch the king 
look at the fleet. The court held that the contract was not 
completely frustrated as the fleet was ‘well worth to look at' by 
itself. 
 
3. 
Herne Bay Steamboat (1903) 
Facts: Cab hire ahead of time to make sure that the hirer could 
get to the racecourse. The court held that the cab did not know 
why they were taking the hirer to the racecourse and do not 
usually ask or care. 
 
Leases: 
* 
Leases can never be frustrated even if someone else is 
occupying it. 
* 
There would be some instances when the lease could become 
frustrated. 
* 
In principle, leases can become frustrated, but the court will 
‘hardly ever' make such a finding. When looking at frustration 
of leases, consider ratio of unavailability to total length of lease. 
 
Not frustration: 
 
Commercial impracticality: 
Frustration cannot be used to defend against commercial 
impracticability. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
‘Self-induced' frustration: 
* 
Contracting without having confirmed outcome on the licencing 
where that is required for the contract is self-induced 
frustration and not upheld by the court. 
* 
If the party in breach exercised a choice in any way, they cannot 
argue frustration. 
 
Event foreseeable: 
* 
Government intervention such as the introduction of new 
legislation may be foreseeable if – eg. there are public 
discussions regarding the intervention. 
* 
If there is a provision in the contract dealing with the event that 
happened, then frustration does not apply. 
* 
Many contracts now contain a force majeure clause which lists 
common intervening events and suspends the contract on one 
of the events listed. Other contracts also contain a price 
variation clause. 
 
Consequences of frustration: 
 
At common law: 
 
Claiming consideration: 
 
In cases of partial failure of consideration, money that has already 
been paid cannot be claimed back. 
Partial failure of consideration = cases where parts of the contract 
were satisfied. 
If there was additional consideration provided, then the full amount will 
be due. 
 
In cases of total failure of consideration, the amount paid is 
recoverable. 
 
Expenses: 
 
Expenses incurred before the frustrating event: recoverable only at the 
court's ddiscretion, however, they must have been incurred in 
preparation for the performance of the contract. 
 
Expenses incurred after the frustrating event: no recoverable. 
 
Legislation: 
 
If either party achieved a valuable benefit after the frustrating event 
then a ‘just sum' may be awarded. – eg. in a building contract, although 
the building works were not finished, the job was partially completed 
which the hirer will not have. 
 
Calculate the price of the valuable benefit and the courts will decide
