what would be fair to award in the circumstances. The courts have a 
wide discretion. 
 
Example: 
Contract to ship ground nuts in November. They were to go through 
the Suez Canal but the canal was being nationalised. If it was 
written in the contract that the ship must go through the Suez 
Canal, then the contract will become frustrated due to 
impossibility. Also if the goods are perishable then the longer route 
would not work and a claim would also succeed on frustration.

pages.heading: REMEDIES · ACTING FOR THE CLAIMANT:
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Notes | Page 15 of 16 
REMEDIES 
 
ACTING FOR THE CLAIMANT: 
 
Damages that a Claimant may claim: 
1. 
Liquidated damages and penalties 
2. 
Compensation 
 
Liquidated damages and penalties: 
 
Liquidated damages = where the parties agree on the damages in case 
of a breach beforehand and set it out in the contract. 
 
This is beneficial as the parties will know what to expect and this 
reduces the risk of potentially paying out a higher amount than what 
have been agreed. This will also ensure that both parties can take out 
insurance. 
 
Penalty clauses: 
Liquidation clauses could be struck out if they are found to be a penalty 
clause. 
 
Legitimate interest test: Ask if the detriment to the contract breaker is 
out of proportion to the legitimate interest of the other party. Look at 
this in the context of the agreement. You will need to find a legitimate 
interest of the party for the clause and it will be valid if proportionate. 
 
Compensation: 
 
If there is no valid liquidated damages clause, then ‘unliquidated 
damages' will be calculated. 
 
The aim in the UK is compensation, not punishment. 
 
Damages aim to put the innocent party into the position they would 
have been in had the contract been performed. 
 
You can claim either expectation loss, reliance loss or restitution. 
 
Expectation loss: 
 
Damages aim to put the innocent party into the position they would 
have been in had the contract been performed. – Forward looking 
measure. 
 
3 measures: 
1. 
Difference in value – eg. because of the contract, you have now 
lost out on money. Having a car worth £3,000 but the car would 
have been worth £5,000 due to the contract, the innocent party 
can be awarded £2,000 to reflect the diminution of value. 
2. 
Cost of cure – eg. an amount awarded to reflect how much it 
would cost to fix the defect. 
3. 
Loss of amenity – eg. an amount awarded to reflect the fact that 
the Claimant lost access to something. 
 
Ask for the highest amount and any other available options in the 
alternative. 
 
The court may award loss of amenity if the money to remedy the 
defect would be disproportionate for the benefit achieved by fixing 
the problem. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Other examples: 
• 
Farley wanted a peaceful country residence and contracted 
Skinner to find the ideal property for him. Once he moved in, he 
realised that the area was very noisy due to airplanes constantly 
landing nearby. He was also awarded a loss of amenity. 
 
• 
Loss of amenity is not available in a commercial context. 
 
• 
McGlinn demolished a property built with cosmetic defects, he 
then rebuilt it and sued for cost of cure. This was seen as 
excessive and only loss of amenity was awarded. 
 
Reliance loss: 
* 
These losses aim to put the innocent party back in the position 
had they not made the contract. – Backward looking measure. 
* 
You cannot use reliance loss to get out of a bad bargain. 
* 
Losses that are too speculative will not be allowed under this 
head of loss. Calculating the amount a Claimant could have 
made from a project is too speculative and such compensation 
will not be allowed. 
* 
Pre-contractual expenses could be allowed by the court if any. 
 
Restitution: 
* 
A measure depriving the contract breaker from their profits if 
they made profits from breaching the contract. 
* 
Restitution is only available in exceptional circumstances, 
where contractual damages would be inadequate. 
* 
If you breach your contract as you would make a better deal 
elsewhere, this is allowed, as long as you pay damages. 
 
Damages for mental distress: 
 
This is generally not available. 
The innocent party will always be upset when a contract is breached. 
 
Exception: 
If the contract was for pleasure/relaxation/peace of mind. 
Pleasure/relaxation/peace of mind must have at least been a ‘major 
object of the contract'. 
 
Loss of reputation: 
Claims for loss of reputation can be allowed. 
 
Loss of chance: 
Losing the chance of winning can be claimed. 
 
Quantum meruit: 
Paying for partially completed work will usually be only paying for work 
that had been done. 
 
ACTING FOR THE DEFENDANT: 
 
Limiting damages: 
1. 
Causation – D might agree to a breach but argue that the loss 
was not caused by the breach 
2. 
Remoteness – D might agree that the loss was caused by his 
breach but the loss was too remote 
3. 
Mitigation – D might agree that the loss was caused by his 
breach but claim that C did not mitigate which could have 
reduced its losses. 
4. 
Contributory Negligence – D might argue that his breach of 
contract was due to negligence and may then say that C was 
also negligent so he is not responsible for all the damage 
caused. 
 
Causation: 
 
There must be a causal link between the breach of contract and the 
loss claimed. 
 
The breach must be an effective cause of the loss. 
 
If there is a novus actus interveniens (break in the chain of causation), 
the cause that happened closer to the loss will be deemed to cause it. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Example: 
Mr Forsyth wanted to get a swimming pool built and contracted some 
builders. He wanted the pool to be 7 foot 6 inches deep. When the 
works were completed, it turned out to be 6 foot 9 inches deep only. 
 
Contract price 
 
£20,000 
Cost of cure 
 
£21,560 
Difference in value 
£0 – he wouldn't get more money for a 
deeper pool 
Loss of amenity 
 
£2,500 
 
Held: The court was not sure if he was going to use the money to 
remedy the defect. The amount awarded this way would have also 
been disproportionate for the benefit achieved by making the 
swimming pool deeper. 
Example: 
 
A farmer had a trailer which had a faulty coupling. Because of this, 
it went on the other side of the road and caused an accident. The 
farmer argued that the loss was caused by the breach of contract 
by the manufacturer of the trailer. 
 
Held: The loss was not caused by the manufacturers as the farmer 
knew that the trailer was broken when he decided to use it.

pages.heading: Remoteness: · Some losses are too remote.
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Notes | Page 16 of 16 
Remoteness: 
 
Some losses are too remote. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Hadley v Baxendale When looking at remoteness of a loss, apply the 
two-limb test. 
 
Two-limb test: 
1. 
C can claim for a loss arising naturally in the usual course of 
things. 
Imputed knowledge is required (objective) – eg. mill owners 
should be expected to keep a second mill shaft. 
 
2. 
Reasonably in the contemplation of both parties 
Actual knowledge (subjective) – What did the parties actually 
know about? The claimants in this case should have told the 
defendants at the time of contracting that they did not have 
another mill shaft. 
 
Must be in the contemplation of both parties at the time of 
contracting. 
 
The second limb is not satisfied if the other party to the contract did not 
know about the big contract coming up. 
 
Was the loss one which was ‘not unlikely' to occur? If the loss occurred 
because of a drop in market prices, this was deemed to be 
unforeseeable. 
 
Mitigation: 
 
Strictly speaking no obligation to mitigate, but losses resulting from 
failure to mitigate are unrecoverable. 
 
Only reasonable steps are required to mitigate. 
No need to litigate to mitigate. 
If cost-effective, innocent party may need to renegotiate the contract. 
Mitigation not ‘weighed in nice scales'. Court will not expect the 
innocent party to count pennies. 
 
Contributory negligence: 
 
Contributory negligence may be available if the other party or a third 
party was also negligent and their negligence contributed to the 
damages caused. 
 
Contributory negligence is available where there is: 
i. 
Breach of a contractual duty 
 AND 
ii. 
The breach is also a tort 
 
Equitable remedies: 
 
Specific Performance: 
Specific performance = compelling the other party to perform the 
contract. 
Only in rare cases and when damages would be insufficient. 
 
Specific performance will not be granted if: 
1. 
Performance would cause undue hardship/unfairness to the 
party in breach 
2. 
Consideration agreed in return for performance is inadequate 
3. 
The innocent party themselves has outstanding obligations 
under the agreement. 
4. 
The contract is an employment contract/contract for personal 
services – the court will not force a person to work for someone. 
5. 
The order would require court supervision. 
 
Injunction: 
To stop a person from doing something. – eg. prohibiting a party from 
contracting customers. 
 
Rescission 
 
Rectification: 
If there is a mistake on the contract, the court can correct the document. 
 
 
 
INDEMNITIES AND GUARANTEES: 
 
Indemnities: 
Indemnity = a contractual obligation by which one party agrees to keep 
another protected from a specific loss. Liability under an indemnity 
arises not because of a breach but because the parties have stipulated 
that one shall pay another in specified circumstances. 
Eg. if A is sued because of the low quality of the product provided by B, 
B indemnifies A for the lawsuit. 
 
The scope of an indemnity will depend on its wording. 
 
Guarantees: 
Guarantee = a contractual promise made by the guarantor to ensure 
that another person, who is a party to the contract will perform their 
obligations. 
 
UNJUST ENRICHMENT (RESTITUTION): 
 
Restitution is a concept that is separate from contract law. Restitution 
exists to prevent unjust enrichment. 
 
Unjust enrichment = one party has obtained a benefit at the expense of 
another by mistake, duress or undue influence. 
 
Restitution could be an alternative to contractual damages, however, it 
only applies once the contract has been set aside. Restitution is only 
awarded if other remedies are inadequate. 
 
Requirements: *Awarded to innocent parties only* 
1. 
Innocent party shows a legitimate interest in preventing the 
other party from keeping any of the profits. 
2. 
The other party must have been enriched/benefited 
3. 
The enrichment must have been at the expense of the innocent 
party 
4. 
The enrichment must have been unjust 
5. 
There are no defences. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Remedies: 
* 
Money or property 
 OR 
* 
An order that the party in breach returns any gains they have 
made to the innocent party 
 OR 
* 
If restitution in relation to services: quantum meruit award – an 
order requiring payment of reasonable remuneration for the 
works carried out. 
 OR 
* 
If restitution in relation to goods: quantum valebat award. 
 
 
 
Example: 
If you fall asleep while driving and drive into another car causing an 
accident, then even if no one dies, the other driver might end up in 
hospital. Because he broke an arm and was in hospital, he was not 
able to do his job as a shelf stacker at Tesco. Because he was not 
able to work, he lost out on money and was not able to buy his 
daughter a textbook she needed to study Contract law. Because she 
did not get the book, she failed the class and gave up on studying 
law. At some point, these losses will be too remote. 
Examples: 
1. 
Work has been carried out but there was no contract 
2. 
One party failed to provide consideration – eg. because one 
of the parties terminated the contract before they have 
done anything at all. 
3. 
If a contract is only partially performed, the innocent party 
then accepts partial performance, however, no price is 
actually agreed 
4. 
Money paid out by mistake 
5. 
Rescinding a contract where there is an outstanding amount 
remaining with the wrong party 
6. 
Transfer of property due to threat/pressure 
7. 
Undue influence

books.title: Contract Law · SQE Prep Notes（30页版）

pages.heading: INTRODUCTION TO CONTRACTS · DEFINITION OF A CONTRACT:
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 1 of 30 
INTRODUCTION TO CONTRACTS 
 
DEFINITION OF A CONTRACT: 
 
Treitel (academic) Contract = an agreement between two or more 
parties which includes one/more promises that the law will enforce. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Formation of a contract: *Does the contract exist?* 
• 
Agreement (offer and acceptance) 
• 
Consideration 
• 
Intention to create legal relations 
• 
Certainty 
• 
Capacity 
• 
Privity of contract 
• 
Rights of third parties 
 
Contracts do not need to be in writing and can simply form by entering 
into an oral agreement. 
 
Agreement: 
The parties will be in agreement when one person makes an offer and 
the receiving party accepts it in response. 
 
Consideration: 
The parties must also provide something of value to the other under 
the agreement. – this may be a promise to carry out works, supply a 
product or make a payment. 
 
Exception – important contracts do need to be in writing: 
*Popular exam q* 
• Contracts to Sell Land 
• Contracts of Guarantee 
 AND 
• Consumer Credit Agreements 
 
KEY TYPES OF CONTRACTS: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
You will find that the words “unilateral” and “bilateral” come up quite 
often during your legal studies, so it is important to know what they 
mean. 
 
Unilateral = performed on one side, affecting one side only. 
 
Bilateral = performed on two sides, affecting two sides. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
ENFORCEABILITY OF CONTRACTS: 
 
Void (void ab initio) = a contract is void (“void from the beginning” or 
“null and void”) where it is deemed by the court that there was no 
contract between the parties. 
 
Voidable = if a contract is voidable, then the contract will be valid and 
enforceable until it is avoided by one of the parties. Most contracts are 
not voidable, however, they may become voidable in certain 
circumstances. 
 
Unenforceable = if a contract is unenforceable, it is valid, however, the 
courts are unable to enforce it. In this case, it is up to the parties to 
decide whether to perform the terms of the contract. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Example: 
 
A contract is made when you get on a bus. You pay for your ticket 
and there will be an agreement between you and the transport 
company to take you to your destination. 
Bilateral contract = your 
typical contract, where one 
person makes the offer and 
other person says that they 
accept. 
 
The enforceability of these 
types of contracts is based on 
exchanged promises. 
 
Unilateral contract = one 
person makes a promise to do 
something in return for the 
performance of a prescribed 
act. 
 
These offers are accepted by 
performance of the act and 
the contract will become 
enforceable in that moment. 
Collateral contract = where there is a contract between two parties, 
a separate (collateral) contract may exist which relates to the 
original contract. 
 
In the original contract, there may be a promise to enter into the 
collateral contract or the collateral contract may simply be a 
contract affected by the original contract. 
Example – collateral contract: 
 
Abby is a sole trader operating an Airbnb. She designs some images 
online showing what she imagines her redesigned room to look like 
after some renovations. She receives a payment of £1,000 booking 
the room for March. Abby hires Cillian to carry out the renovations 
to make the room look just like her design. 
 
When Cillian fails to complete the renovations on time and to the 
required standard, Abby will have to cancel the booking and refund 
the £1,000 (this booking was the collateral contract in this situation. 
Example – unilateral contract: 
 
Peter posts an offer in a newspaper to give £17,000 to the first 
person to send him a picture of the Lock Ness monster taken in 
2024. 
 
Isha sees this advert during her stay in Scotland and she has already 
taken some pictures of Loch Ness the week before (in February 
2024) and found that one of the photos had something on it which 
could have been the Loch Ness monster. When Isha sends these 
pictures to Peter, a unilateral contract will have formed.

pages.heading: AGREEMENT · OFFERS:
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 2 of 30 
AGREEMENT 
 
OFFERS: 
 
Offeror = person making the offer. 
Offeree = person on the receiving end of an offer. 
 
Offer = “an expression of willingness to contract on specified terms 
made with the intention to become legally binding as soon as it is 
accepted by the person to whom it is addressed.” 
 
An offer must: 
1. 
Be certain – the offeror must know what is being offered. 
2. 
Be communicated to the Offeree 
 AND 
3. 
Show intention to create legal relations – this may be implicit or 
explicit. This will be a separate topic later on in the course. 
 
Certainty of the offer and its terms: 
 
Certainty means: 
* 
Certainty as to the terms of the contract 
* 
Complete 
 
Certainty as to the terms of the contract: 
 
An offer must be clear and certain as to the key terms of the contract 
and its subject matter. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Gibson v Manchester CC An offer must be certain and the word “may” 
in an offer is not sufficiently certain. 
 
Scammell v Ouston The terms of the agreement must be clearly 
ascertainable for the contract to be enforceable. Using trade practice 
and the course of dealings between the parties is not possible to 
ascertain what the terms of the contract may have been, the court will 
only look at the actual terms of the contract. 
 
Complete: 
 
The offer must be complete, including all key terms without any of the 
terms to be determined in the future. 
 
May and Butcher v R If an offer states that key terms of the contract, 
such as the price and date of payment under a sale of goods contract 
are to be “agreed upon from time to time”, it is not a valid offer as it 
is incomplete without including the relevant key terms. 
 
The offer must also be communicated to the Offeree: 
 
In order to have the ability to accept the offer, the Offeree must know 
that the offer existed, and therefore, the offer must be communicated 
to the Offeree. 
 
Communication can be done: 
* 
In writing 
* 
Orally 
* 
By conduct 
 
The accepting party must also communicate acceptance in response to 
the offer in writing, orally or by conduct. 
 
Types of offers: 
 
* 
Bilateral offers: offering something in return for a promise. 
These promises are made to a specific person or a specific class 
of people. – eg. Andrew promising to sell his car to Jimmy in 
return for £4,500. 
 * 
Unilateral offers: offering something in return for the 
performance of a prescribed act. These promises may be made 
to a specific person or “to the world” and are valid irrespective 
of acceptance and the identity of the person performing the act. 
– eg. Lily promising to pay £3 million to anyone who finds the 
cure to cancer. 
 
Offers to the world: 
 A subset of unilateral offers, where the unilateral offer 
is made to the world. 
 Offer to the world = when you make an offer that 
anyone can accept by performance. 
RESPONSES TO REQUESTS FOR INFORMATION (NOT 
AN OFFER): 
 
Responses to requests for information in relation to a potential contract 
do not amount to offers, and will simply be statements to provide 
further information regarding the terms of the potential contract. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
INVITATIONS TO TREAT (NOT AN OFFER): 
 
If you have an expression that might be an offer but it does not fit the 
criteria of an offer, it is an invitation to treat. 
 
Invitations to treat are an expression of willingness to negotiate by 
inviting offers from others, inviting the other party to begin 
negotiations or make an offer. When unsure whether a statement is an 
offer or an invitation to treat, it is useful to look at the intention behind 
the statement. 
 
An invitation to treat has no legal status. It is merely the opening step 
in negotiations and because it is not an offer, it cannot be accepted. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Invitations to treat: 
1. 
Displays of goods 
2. 
Advertisements 
3. 
Requests for further information 
 
Display of goods: 
 
Fisher v Bell Displays of goods in shop windows or the shop floor are 
not offers, but merely invitations to treat. 
 
In relation to display of goods, the offer is made by the buyer when 
they take the goods to the till/checkout. The offer is accepted when the 
shop assistant enters the sale into the cash register or scans the 
product. 
 
Adverts: 
 
Partridge v Crittenden Advertisements are not offers but merely 
invitations to treat. An offer is made by the person contacting the 
sellers to buy the products or sign up to the services advertised. – this 
is because if everyone seeing the advert responded to it, the person 
who placed the advert would be out of stock soon, but would still be 
obliged to perform the contract. 
 
Price lists also amount to advertisements, and therefore, the Seller 
producing the price list will not be obliged to sell the products that 
appeared on the price list. 
 
Exception 1 – Unilateral offers: 
 
Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co. If the advertisement contains clear 
terms and a prescribed act, it may be a unilateral offer. The 
advertisement must show intention to create legal relations, and this 
can often be inferred from how detailed the advertisement is. – the 
more detailed, the more likely that a court will find it to constitute a 
unilateral offer. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
⇒ 
Example: 
 Vimal says the following to Christopher: “I will sell you my used 
laptop for £560.” This amounts to an offer. 
 
On the other hand, if Vimal says to Christopher: “I will potentially 
sell my used laptop, it is probably worth around £600. Would you 
buy it for £600?” This is simply an invitation to treat. There is no 
clarity as to the intention to sell and no clarity as to the purchase 
price. 
Example: 
 Ewan promising to sell his hamster for £30 will have made a clear 
offer, as both the subject matter of the sale (hamster) and the price 
(£30) as clear and certain. 
 
On the other hand, Ewan promising to sell a hamster for £30 is 
unclear, as the offeree would not know which hamster was to be 
sold. 
Example: 
 Nicholas sees an advertisement for a boat in the window of his local 
off-licence. He texts the number and his text includes the following 
message: “Please text me the lowest price for the boat.” Beca's 
response is the following: “£6,500 is the lowest I would go.” 
 
Nicholas' message amounted to a request for further information 
and Beca's message amounted to a response, rather than an offer. 
As a result, if Nicholas were to text her saying: “I accept the offer.”, 
Beca would not be bound to sell his the boat for £6,500 because her 
statement did not amount to an offer. 
Example: 
 An advertisement for teeth whitening strips states that if the strips 
do not whiten someone's teeth by three shades when used for 5 
consequtive nights according to the user manual, that person shall 
receive £7,000. If the ad also states that this amount has already 
been deposited in the seller's bank ready to pay out, this will be 
sufficient clarity to amount to a unilateral offer.

pages.heading: The advertisement does not amount to a unilateral offer if it is an · obvious joke.
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 3 of 30 
 
The advertisement does not amount to a unilateral offer if it is an 
obvious joke. 
 
Exception 2 – Limitless supply: 
 
If an advert is clear, certain and shows an intention to be bound and 
there is no problem with supply the normal rule would not apply. 
 
Exception 3 – Invitations to tender: 
 
By inviting tenders, you are not making an offer. 
 
Invitation to tender = expression of willingness to invite people to make 
offers with the price. – eg. you need to get some work done and you 
contact people who may be interested, you give them the details of 
what needs to be done. They will then reach out to you with the price. 
 
If the invitation to tender is also a unilateral offer, there will be a 
unilateral contract formed if the prescribed act is performed. 
 
If the invitation to tender sets out that they would accept the highest/ 
lowest bid, then the promisor must do so. 
 
Exception 4 – Auctions: 
 
Payne v Cave An auctioneer inviting bids is an invitation to treat and 
the bidders make the offer. The acceptance at the auction is made once 
the auctioneer drops the hammer. 
 
If a person has made an offer that person is also entitled to revoke 
that offer. But, the offer can only be revoked as long as it has not been 
accepted. Once the offer is accepted the contract is formed. 
 
In case of without reserve auctions the offer of the highest bidder will 
be automatically accepted. 
 
TERMINATING AN OFFER: 
 
An offer will stay open until terminated by rejection of the offer, 
revocation or lapse. 
 
An offer can be revoked before it has been accepted, but not after 
acceptance. 
 
Rejection: 
 
Counter-offer: 
 
Rejecting the original offer and making a new offer. This will be the 
case where any of the terms of the original offer are altered. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Battle of the forms: 
 
Two companies, both wanting to contract on their standard terms. 
None of them ever agreeing. In this case, the last shot approach will 
apply. Whoever will finally accept unequivocally, that will be the agreed 
final contract. 
 
BUT! Requests for further information: 
 
This is not a rejection, simply asking for clarification of the terms on 
which the offer is made. 
 
Lapse: 
 
An offer may lapse by: 
1. 
Passage of time 
2. 
Death 
3. 
Non-fulfilment of a condition precedent 
 
Passage of time: 
 
Offers only stay open for a reasonable time. 
What is reasonable will depend on the circumstances. – eg. if someone 
makes an offer to you to sell a newspaper for 50p this offer is not going 
to be open for a whole year. But the offer for a house will likely be 
reasonable to stay open for longer. 
 
Death: 
 
If the offeror dies before the offer has been accepted, then the offer 
will lapse. 
 
Non-fulfilment of a condition precedent: 
 
Condition precedent = a condition before the offer can come into force. 
 
If this condition is never fulfilled, then the offer will lapse. 
 
Revocation: 
 
An offer can be revoked before it has been accepted, but not after 
acceptance. 
 
Byrne v Van Tienhoven Revocation is only effective once received by 
the Offeree. 
 
Third party revocation: 
 An offer can be revoked by a third party if that third party is authorised 
by the Offeror. Revocation does not necessarily need to be done by the 
Offeror themselves. 
 
Auctions: 
 Payne v Cave Revocation is effective if it has been done before the 
hammer falls. 
 
Revocation of unilateral offers: 
 A unilateral offer is revoked once the act set out in the offer is 
performed. 
 
A unilateral offer may not be revoked if someone has started 
performance. If someone has started performance and it thus becomes 
unfair to revoke the offer, the offeror must give a chance to the offeree 
to finish the performance. 
 
The offeror cannot prevent the offeree from performing the 
prescribed act. 
 
Offers to the world: 
 
For announcing revocation, the offeror must use a method similar to 
how the offer was made. 
 Difficult to revoke unilateral offers made to the world as there would 
be a problem in communicating the revocation. In this case, revocation 
will be effective if the offeror uses a method that is “equally notorious” 
as the method whereby the offer was made. – eg. if the offer was made 
in a newspaper ad, the revocation should be made the same way to be 
effective. 
 
AUCTION SALES: 
 
Auction sales attract special rules. 
 
English auction: 
 
English auctions = auctions where the item/property is sold to the 
highest bidder subject to the reserve price set by the seller. The reserve 
price will be the opening bid which will be announced by the auctioneer 
before taking bids. 
 
If your question on the exam does not specify the type of auction, it 
simply states that there is an auction in the scenario, it is safest to 
assume that the auction is an English auction, as this is the standard 
and most common type used in the UK. 
 
The auction catalogue (advertisement): 
 Payne v Cave The listings in the catalogue do not amount to offers, but 
merely invitation to treat. 
 
Request for bids (invitation to tender): 
 Payne v Cave When the auctioneer makes a request for bids, this is also 
not an offer but an invitation to treat. 
 
Bids: 
 Blackpool and Fylde Aero Club v Blackpool The offer is made when the 
bidders make a bid. 
 
Knocking down the hammer: 
 Payne v Cave When the auctioneer brings down the hammer, that is 
when the offer is accepted. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Example: 
If there was an offer for the sale of land, for £1,000. The buyer said 
that he will pay £995. The seller then sold the land for someone else. 
When the buyer wanted to force the buyer to sell the land to him 
for £1,000, the court disagreed as he has already rejected that offer. 
Example: 
 Winnie is at an auction house, bidding for various items. A statue 
catches her eye, which she believes is particularly valuable. During 
the bidding process, she notices as the other bidders do not see the 
value in the statute as much as she does. She ends up being the 
highest bidder and she withdraws her offer in a state of panic before 
the hammer drops. 
 
She will have successfully withdrawn her offer in this case, as her 
offer has not yet been accepted when she withdrew it.

pages.heading: Auction without reserve: · Auctions without reserve = auctions where the item/property is sold
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 4 of 30 
Auction without reserve: 
 
Auctions without reserve = auctions where the item/property is sold 
to the highest bidder even if the price is lower than the Seller expected. 
These auctions also called absolute auctions or no reserve auctions. 
 
At an auction without reserve, the auctioneer must accept the highest 
bid regardless of the price. 
 
The auction catalogue (advertisement): 
 
Warlow v Harrison The advertisement of a no reserve auction, while an 
invitation to treat in relation to the sale, contains a promise that the 
item/property will be sold to the highest bidder. This will create a 
collateral contract between the bidders and the seller/auction house. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Request for bids (invitation to tender): 
 Payne v Cave When the auctioneer makes a request for bids, this is also 
not an offer but an invitation to treat. 
 
Bids: 
 Blackpool and Fylde Aero Club v Blackpool The offer is made when the 
bidders make a bid. 
 
Knocking down the hammer: 
 Payne v Cave When the auctioneer brings down the hammer, that is 
when the offer is accepted. 
 
 
Example: 
 Reggie is selling a lesser known Leonardo Da Vinci painting as a no 
reserve auction, thinking that he would be able to sell the painting 
for a stellar price. 
 
During the auction, it appears that there is not as much demand for 
the painting as Reggie had hoped, so he starts bidding to the 
painting himself as soon as he sees that another bidder, Julia, is also 
interested. Reggie ends up being the highest bidder and the painting 
is sold to him. 
 
Julia learns that Reggie was actually the owner of the painting and 
she sues him for breach of contract. She is right in doing so, as she 
had rights under a collateral (related) contract with Reggie and the 
auction house. This contract included a promise that each 
item/property would be sold to the highest bidder and she will have 
accepted the offer when she took part in the auction.

pages.heading: ACCEPTANCE · OBJECTIVE TEST:
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 5 of 30 
ACCEPTANCE 
 
OBJECTIVE TEST: 
 
Whether a contract has formed, will be decided by an objective test. 
Objective test: whether a reasonable person listening to the 
negotiations between the parties agree that a contract has been made? 
 
If a man conducts himself in a way that any reasonable man would 
believe that he was agreeing to the terms, then he will enter into the 
contract, even if his real intentions were not to be bound. 
 
But the court will not allow buyers to ‘snatch a bargain'. 
 
REQUIREMENTS: 
 
Acceptance must be: 
1. 
A mirror image to the offer 
2. 
Made by the offeree 
3. 
Made in response to an offer 
4. 
Communicated 
 
If there are multiple acceptances to the same offer, then the 
acceptance that reaches the offeror first will form the contract, and 
the other acceptances will not have bene successful. 
 
Communicated: 
 
Entorres v Miles Far East Acceptance is effective on receipt. 
 
Felthouse v Bindley Silence does not constitute acceptance. 
 
If acceptance is communicated by an authorised third-party: it is still 
valid. 
 
If acceptance is communicated by conduct: it is still valid. – Butler 
Machine Tool v Ex-cell-o Corporation – eg. In relation to taking out 
loans, if the person who took out the loan deposits the loan amount in 
their bank account, this will be acceptance by conduct. 
 
Exception to the rule on communication: 
• 
Unilateral offers – Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball 
Unilateral offers are accepted by performance. No need 
to state: ‘I accept the offer.' 
 
• 
Offeror's fault 
The person accepting must ensure that their message 
goes through. What if the offeree believes that the 
message had gone through but in fact it never did? – eg. 
if the acceptance was sent in an email but the offeror 
inadvertently deletes the email without reading it, this 
will be the offeror's fault. 
 
If it was the offeror's fault that the message did not go 
through, they cannot then rely on the communication 
rule saying that acceptance was not communicated, 
even if done inadvertently. 
 
• 
The Postal Rule – Adams v Lindsell 
If accepting via post, and posting is done properly, then 
acceptance happens as soon as you put the letter in the 
letter box. The letter need not actually arrive. 
 
Prescribed acceptance: 
 
If the Offeror specified what amounts to acceptance, then the Offeree 
must follow the rules of acceptance. – eg. if the offer states that 
acceptance happens by saying “yes”, then you cannot accept by saying 
“I accept”. 
 
Mirror image to the offer: 
 
Hyde v Wrench The terms of the acceptance must match the offer. If 
the acceptance is in relation to different terms compared ot the offer, 
then the acceptance will amount to a counter offer. 
 
THE POSTAL RULE: 
 
General rule: 
 
Use this rule only where acceptance has been sent by post. 
 
If accepting via post, then acceptance happens as soon as you put the 
letter in the letter box. 
 
 
 
 
 
Exceptions to the rule: 
 
The Postal rule does not apply if: 
* 
Letter was not properly posted (it was misaddressed or not 
properly stamped) 
* 
It was unreasonable to accept by post. 
 OR 
* 
The Postal rule was excluded (ousted) by the Offeror. 
 
If the letter was properly posted but lost or destroyed, acceptance is 
still valid. 
 
Letter was not properly posted: 
 
In this case, acceptance is received once it actually reaches the offeror. 
 
There can still be a contract in these cases but the commencement of 
the contract may be delayed. 
 
If, during that time period, someone else has accepted the offer, then 
the contract will have never formed. 
 
If the reason for the wrong address was the fault of the offeror, the 
Postal rule will still apply. 
 
It was unreasonable to accept by post: 
 
It will be deemed to be unreasonable to accept by post if posting causes 
a ‘manifest of inconvenience and abserdity'. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Where the Postal rule is ousted: 
 
This can be done by the offeror indicates that actual communication is 
required or saying that they want ‘notice of acceptance', ‘letter to be 
received'. 
 
Consequences of the Postal rule: 
 
Not beneficial for offerors as there may be people out there who have 
already accepted the offer, but the offeror would not know until the 
acceptance is received. 
 
The post may have been lost or destroyed and the offeror will not know 
that a contract has already been formed. The position of the offeror is 
therefore very uncertain. 
 
Revocation of offer is invalid after acceptance. 
This is true even if the revocation was sent by a faster method than the 
acceptance and the offeror did not know that the offer has already been 
accepted. 
 
INSTANTANEOUS COMMUNICATIONS: 
 
Use this rule only where acceptance has been sent by email/telex. 
 
The receipt rule: acceptance must have been received. 
 
Communication will be deemed received within office hours. 
 
If the message was sent outside of office hours, the message will be 
deemed received the first thing when the office opened again on the 
next working day. 
 
There is no universal rule on office hours, the court will always look at 
the circumstances of the case. 
 
If there is evidence that the office usually operates until late into the 
evening, then the deemed office hours will include those hours. 
 
PRESCRIBED MODE: 
 
Use this rule only where the offeror has set out a prescribed method of 
communication for the acceptance. – eg. please accept by letter or 
please don't accept by post. 
 
Prescribed mode will only be binding if it is explicitly mandatory and 
rules out all other modes. If the offeror does not rule out any other 
mode then all he did was mention what his preference would be as to 
communication. – eg. ‘Please contact me by telephone, not by email.' 
or ‘Please contact me by telephone, and only telephone.' 
Examples where acceptance by post is unreasonable: 
 
* 
There is an ongoing postal strike so the letter will not arrive. 
 
* 
If the subject matter of the purchase is a freshly cooked meal 
which may spoil by the time that the post arrives. 
 
* 
If the parties are talking to each other face to face then the 
accepting party runs off to write a letter without verbally 
accepting the offer first.

pages.heading: If the prescribed mode does not rule out other modes, then as long as · the other mode is as fast as the prescribed mode, it will be valid. The
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 6 of 30 
 
If the prescribed mode does not rule out other modes, then as long as 
the other mode is as fast as the prescribed mode, it will be valid. The 
other method should not disadvantage the offeror. – eg. if asked to be 
telephoned, an email may put the offeror at a disadvantage eg. if the 
offeror is blind and cannot read the email. 
 
If the offer was sent by an instantaneous method, it will be implied that 
the acceptance must be sent by an equally instantaneous method. 
 
If the method was prescribed for the convenience or benefit of the 
sender then the sender can waive the prescribed method. 
 
 
 
 
Example: 
If the prescribed method was tracked post, this is always done for 
the benefit of the sender so that they have a receipt and can see 
once the post has been received. In this case the sender can simply 
send the post by normal post, and this will not invalidate the 
acceptance.

pages.heading: CONSIDERATION · Consideration = an element of exchange, whereby both parties provide
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 7 of 30 
CONSIDERATION 
 
Consideration = an element of exchange, whereby both parties provide 
something valuable to the contract. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Enforceability: 
 
Consideration is what makes contracts enforceable. 
 
Enforceable = something that is recognised by the court. If a contract is 
unenforceable, one or more of the parties can decide to walk away from 
it and the other party will not be able to make a court claim to enforce 
the contract terms. 
 
Two types of consideration: 
 
1. 
Executory consideration: 
Consideration may be a simple promise to do something, but 
the obligations have not yet been performed. These 
considerations are valid and the agreement will form a binding 
contract. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
2. 
Executed consideration: 
Consideration may be actually performing what is due under 
the contract. Once the obligation is performed, consideration 
will have been executed. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
RULES OF CONSIDERATION: 
 
The rules of good consideration refer to whether consideration will be 
legally valid in the circumstances. 
 
This is not a moral judgement on consideration whether or not 
consideration was proper, acceptable and providing market value. That 
will be up to the parties to decide. 
 
Promisor = person making the promise 
Promisee = person that is being promised something. 
 
In a contract, there is one Promisors and one Promisee. – one promisor 
will promise to pay, the other promisor will promise to perform 
obligations. 
 
General rule: 
 
Consideration must: 
1. 
Not be past 
2. 
Move from the Promisee 
 AND 
3. 
Be sufficient but need not be adequate 
 
Promises to carry out existing obligations is not usually seen as good 
consideration. 
Part-payment of a debt will not constitute good consideration. 
 
Must not be past: 
 
Past consideration = Where one party has already provided a benefit, 
and that party is now asking for a promise in return for that benefit. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Past consideration is not enforceable. 
 
A promise made after the agreement has formed is not a binding 
promise. 
 
Exceptions: 
* 
It was understood that payment would be due 
* 
Contract made by deed 
 
It was understood that payment would be due: 
 
If there was an understanding between the parties that payment would 
be due for the services from the beginning, then the paying party 
cannot get out of the contract by arguing past consideration. 
 
In commercial situations, it will be understood that payment would be 
due. This is unlikely to be the case in domestic situations. – eg. if the 
service was provided in the course of a business, however, there is not 
going to be an expectation to make a payment in a domestic situation 
where you are simply asking your brother to prepare a meal for you. 
 
This is the case even if there was no discussion as to the amount that 
would be due. All that is necessary for good consideration is an 
understanding that some sort of payment would be due. 
 
Three-stage test to see if past consideration could be valid: Pao On 
1. 
Consideration must be at the request of the promisor 
2. 
It must have been understood that payment would be due 
 AND 
3. 
Apart from this issue, contract must be enforceable – eg. 
nothing done that is illegal will count as good consideration. All 
the usual elements of a contract must also be satisfied. 
 
Contract made by deed: 
 
If a contract is made by deed, then the rules of good consideration will 
not apply. Any consideration will be accepted and deemed valid by the 
court. 
 
Deed = a document set out in a prescribed form. 
 
Must move from the Promisee: 
 
A claimant can only make a claim in relation to a contract if he is the 
one who has given the consideration. 
Anyone who has privity can enforce a contract. 
 
s.1 Contracts (Rights of Third parties) Act 1999 Despite this, any person 
may enforce a contract if the contract expressly sets out that he may 
enforce it or any of the terms confers a benefit to him. 
 
Must be sufficient: 
 
Rscorla v Thomas Chappell v Nestle Consideration must be sufficient 
but need not be adequate. It is sufficient for the rules of consideration 
to provide something of a small value in return. – eg. paying £1 for a car 
will be sufficient, need not be market value. 
 
Sufficient consideration is sometimes called “good consideration” and 
you might hear this terminology used in your reading or a question. 
 
However, illusory consideration will not be sufficient. This includes any 
consideration that is too vague and hard to define and enforce. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The law expects both sides on the contract to make some sort of effort 
as consideration for the contract, they must provide some value. 
 
Paying one apple in return for a TV may not be adequate in that the 
market value of the apple is a lot lower than the market value of a TV, 
however, the court is not going to step in to make the contract 
unenforceable in these cases. 
 
 
Examples: 
* 
Promises to provide goods. 
* 
Promises to pay a certain amount. 
* 
Promises to not sue someone. 
* 
Promises not to compete. 
* 
Promises to not do something. 
* 
Promises to provide services such as carrying out work or 
looking after someone's dog. 
Example: 
 
An aunt provided childcare for her niece in the past is now asking 
for payment in return for the work she has carried out. At the time 
when she agreed to care for her niece, she agreed to care for her for 
free. She can't then turn around and change her mind saying that 
she now wants payment for that past work. 
Examples of sufficient 
consideration: 
* 
Giving up a legal right. 
* 
Promising not to sue 
someone. 
* 
Promises to not drink, 
smoke, swear or play 
cards. 
* 
Paying a peppercorn 
as rent. 
NOT sufficient consideration: 
* 
Giving up 
complaining 
* 
Promising to pay at a 
rate which the 
promisor will decide 
at a later date – this 
gives too much 
discretion to the 
promisor. 
* 
Promising to sell any 
goods the promisor 
wants. – again gives 
too much discretion 
to the promisor. 
Examples: 
You might agree when contacting a massage parlour that 
they would give you a massage at a given date, and you 
make a payment at the time of booking. The massage takes 
place at a later date and therefore is is going to be 
executory consideration. 
Examples: 
If you turn up at the massage parlour asking for a massage, 
and they have an empty slot there and then, they could give 
you the massage immediately and you would then pay 
either before or after. Consideration will be executed when 
the contract is formed.

pages.heading: Peppercorn consideration: · Peppercorn = commonly used metaphor in contract law meaning a very
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 8 of 30 
Peppercorn consideration: 
 
Peppercorn = commonly used metaphor in contract law meaning a very 
small amount of cash or nominal consideration. – eg. £1 or £10 
 
Chappell v Nestle Peppercorn consideration is still valid consideration. 
 
Why to use peppercorn consideration in contracts? 
 
1. 
To hide the true value paid under the contract: 
 This provides confidentiality as to the price. While the 
peppercorn consideration ensures that the contract remains 
valid, it will allow for the exact amount paid to stay hidden and 
will not be included in public records. 
 
2. 
To satisfy the requirements for leases: 
 
Peppercorn rent is a nominal amount paid for rent in long 
leaseholds of 99 years or over (virtual leaseholds), where a 
large premium is paid to purchase the leasehold estate, 
however, the satisfy the requirements for a valid lease, 
peppercorn rent is paid on an annual basis thereafter. 
 
Usually ground rent is paid annually for community expenses 
but this is then reduced to peppercorn rent once the lease 
expires and is extended. 
 
This may also be used to reduce the Capital Gains Tax on the 
property by claiming that the property should be valued at a 
lower price since it could only bring in a low amount in rent. 
 
3. 
To satisfy the requirements for land contracts: 
 Peppercorn payment is also used for land contracts to convert 
a gift of property into a valid sale. This is achieved by adding in 
a peppercorn consideration clause in the deed what effect the 
sale. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Why to use peppercorn consideration instead of gifting land? 
 
* 
Selling the land instead of gifting will ensure that the 
person making the gift cannot change their mind after 
the transaction.- “Equity will not assist a volunteer.” 
 
* 
Free of inheritance tax: gifts are subject to inheritance 
tax if the person making the gift dies within 7 years of 
making it. Selling the property for peppercorn 
consideration ensures that the property does not 
attract inheritance tax. 
 
 
 
PRE-EXISTING OBLIGATIONS: 
 
Existing public duty: 
 
Making a promise to do something you are already obliged to do is not 
good consideration. 
 
Police: 
Existing police duty amounts to good consideration if the police goes 
over and above their usual duties. 
 
Parental: 
Keeping a child happy and giving them the choice who to live with is 
going over and above normal parental responsibilities and can 
constitute good consideration. 
 
Legal: 
Attending a hearing as a witness is not good consideration as it is an 
existing legal duty. 
 
Existing contractual duty: 
 
General rule: 
Performing existing contractual duties will not count as good 
consideration. 
 
Exceptions: 
1. 
Going over and above the existing obligations 
 OR 
2. 
By entering into an agreement, the paying party obtains a 
practical benefit. 
 
 
 
 
 
Going over and above: 
 
If the Promisee can show that they have gone over and above their 
existing obligations, that will count as good consideration. – eg. this 
could be done by doing a better job. 
 
Practical benefit: 
 
If the Promisee agrees with the Promisor to carry out the works at some 
time (without clarification as to when), then the Promisee calls the 
Promisor and tells him he would pay more to carry out the works 
tomorrow, the Promisee would earn a practical benefit from the 
agreement. – This would amount to good consideration. 
 
Even though there was already a contract to carry out the works, the 
works have now become urgent, so you earn a practical benefit from 
agreeing to do the works tomorrow rather than at some time in the 
future. 
 
This rule applies where: Roffey Bros 
1. 
There was a contract to supply goods/services 
2. 
B has to have a reason to doubt that A will complete their 
obligations (on time as needed or at all). 
3. 
B makes a promise to pay A extra in order to complete on time 
when the works are needed. 
 AND 
4. 
B obtains a practical benefit by making this promise. – eg. 
because of this payment, the builders avoided the payment of 
late fees. 
 
By promising to complete on time, the paying party obtains a practical 
benefit which I s that the original deadline will be met and the late fees 
could be avoided. 
 
Obligations owed to a third party: 
 
Performing existing obligations to a third party could be good 
consideration. 
 
This is the case even if the obligations already existed, because it was 
the right of the Promisor to decide not to carry out their obligations 
under the promise. 
 
If a third party then pays the Promisor to keep their promise under the 
original contract, then that is going to be good consideration and the 
contract will be valid. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
PART-PAYMENT OF DEBT: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Debtor = the person who owes money. 
Creditor = the person who is owed money. 
 
General rule: 
 
Foakes v Beer Payment that is less than the debt will not discharge the 
obligation to pay the full amount. 
 
Common law exceptions: 
 
Pinnel's case Promises to accept less can be binding if there is new 
consideration in the form of a different thing, place or time. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Example: 
 
You owe me £500. You don't have that money at the moment, but 
you promise to pay me £500 later on once you have the money. You 
do have £350 on hand and promise to pay me £350 now to discharge 
the debt. Is this promise enforceable? 
Example: 
 
Andrew has to fix the sink in Janet's home under an agreement they 
had earlier this week. Andrew got exceptionally busy during the 
week, and told Janet that he could only fix her sink after 3 weeks 
due to the long waiting list. 
 
Janet's brother, Kyle is a good friend of Andrew, and he decides to 
call him up and promise to pay him £100 if he could fix Janet's sink 
by the end of this week. Kyle accepts the £100 in return for this 
promise and this will be a valid contract. 
Example: 
“The Parties agree to comply with the terms of this 
Agreement in consideration of the payment of £1 by the 
Buyer.”

pages.heading: Promises to accept less can be binding if the payment is made by a · third party.
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 9 of 30 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Promises to accept less can be binding if the payment is made by a 
third party. 
 
However, if the debtor is in debt because the creditor did work for them 
and the debtor later finds out that the work was not done to the 
standard expected, then agreeing to pay less will mean that the debtor 
agreed to waive their right to litigate the matter. 
 
QUESTION 1: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Correct Answer: D) There is a contract in this case, as sufficient 
consideration was promised in return for the watch. 
 
Tom's immediate purchase of the antique watch represents executed 
consideration, and Barbara's promise to hand him the watch later is 
executory. 
 
 
Executory consideration is still valid, and the fact that Tom did not pay 
market value will not negate the contract. The £34 will be sufficient 
consideration, even though it might not be adequate. 
 
QUESTION 2: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Sarah is giving up her legal right to resell the records for a year in 
exchange for John's vintage vinyl record collection. This is part of the 
consideration. 
 
QUESTION 3: 
 
 
 
 
No. 
 
 
 
 
Yes, as third party payment creates a new contract. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Example: 
 
Different thing: 
If you want a debt of £500 to be discharged for £350, you need to 
offer something else in addition, eg. £350 and a cup of tea. It doesn't 
matter if the new consideration does not need to be adequate, 
merely sufficient. 
 
Different place: 
If you want a debt of £500 to be discharged for £350, you can offer 
to pay the £350 at the house of the promisor to give him an 
advantage. 
 
Different time: 
If you want a debt of £500 to be discharged for £350, you can offer 
to pay the £350 at an earlier date. 
Barbara offers to sell her antique watch to Tom for £34, and Tom 
agrees to purchase it and pays Barbara the £34. Barbara tells Tom 
that she will need to go home to collect the watch and will give it to 
Tom later that day. 
 
As she is wrapping the watch, she notices that the watch is actually 
vintage Rolex worth £550,000. She no longer wishes to give Tom the 
watch as she was mistaken as to its value. 
 
Has a valid contract been formed? 
 
Please select the best answer. 
 
A There is a contract in this case as there has been executed 
consideration. 
 
B There is no contract in this case, as the consideration is not 
sufficient in return for the watch. 
 
C 
There is no contract in this case, as the consideration is not 
adequate. 
 
D There is a contract in this case, as sufficient consideration 
was promised in return for the watch. 
 
E 
There is no contract as the consideration promised in return 
for payment was only executory. 
John agrees to sell his vintage vinyl record collection to Sarah for 
£500 and the promises not to resell the records for a year. Sarah 
agrees and pays th £500. 
 
Can John sue Sarah for breach of contract if she resells the records 
after 6 months? 
A debtor owes a creditor £1,000, and they both agree to settle the 
debt for £800. Is this a valid agreement? 
Would your answer differ if the debtor's wife made the promise to 
pay £800 in settlement of the debt?

pages.heading: INTENTION TO CREATE LEGAL RELATIONS · DEFINITION:
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 10 of 30 
INTENTION TO CREATE LEGAL RELATIONS 
 
DEFINITION: 
 
Intention to create legal relations (ICLR) = ‘to create a contract there 
must be a common intention of the parties to enter into legal 
obligations, mutually communicated expressly or impliedly.' – This is an 
objective test. 
 
ICLR requires an objective test and context must also be looked at. 
 
Presumptions: 
Presumptions in law are the starting point and will be upheld unless 
proven wrong. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
COMMERCIAL SITUATIONS: 
 
There is a presumption that the parties had intention to create legal 
relations. 
 
In general, it is not necessary for the parties to have agreed to every 
small point/detail of the contract for there to be intention to create 
legal relations. in commercial situations. 
 
Edwards v Skyways This presumption is rarely rebutted. 
 
A government body's notice promising to reimburse customers who 
lost out and it was not their fault, was seen as a contractual promise 
with ICLR. 
 
The presumption has been rebutted in the following cases: 
 
 
* 
If the agreement was set out in Letters of comfort. 
 Letters of comfort = letter(s) written by a holding company to 
a bank/lender to reassure the bank/lender that the company's 
subsidiary (the company to receive the loan) is in the position 
to repay the loan. 
 
Kleinwort Benson v Malaysia Mining Letters of comfort are not 
legaly binding and do not amount to guarantees. If the 
subsidiary defaults on the loan, the bank cannot chase the 
holding company for the outstanding amount. 
 
 
* 
If the agreement was set out in Letters of intent. 
 Letters of intent = letter(s) written by a person/company to 
another to express their interest in entering into a contract with 
them. 
 
 
* 
If the contract signed contains a clause saying that there is no 
ICLR, the court will uphold this even in the business context. 
 
Rose & Frank v CromptonThe clause might state that there is 
no intention to create legal relations on might say that the 
agreement is to be bound in honour only – these are called 
Honour clauses and will be uphed by the court. 
 
 
* 
If the documents contain a clause that the documents were 
subject to contract. If no contract is ever signed, then there will 
be no binding agreement. 
 
* 
Promotional offers themselves are not binding even if there is 
valid contract. – eg. “Free gift with the purchase” offers are not 
legally binding if the offeror refuses to grant it. 
 
* 
If the agreement is made as a social arrangement. – eg. Where 
the parties promised to divide earnings as part of a bingo group. 
 
* 
In relation to heat of the moment comments/promises, angry 
outbursts. 
 
* 
In relation to jokes. – Pepsi advertised that it would give away 
fighter jets. This was clearly a joke with no ICLR. 
DOMESTIC/SOCIAL SITUATIONS: 
 
There is a presumption that the parties had no intention to create 
legal relations. 
 
Married couples: 
Presumption of no ICLR between married couples. This presumption 
does not apply to separating couples. 
 
Relatives: 
Presumption of no ICLR between a parent and their child. – Jones v 
Padavatton 
 
Presumption of ICLR where there was mutuality of obligations. 
 
Previous conduct can rebut the presumption of no ICLR in social 
settings. 
– 
eg. 
Friends 
sharing 
jackpot 
winnings 
in 
an 
organized/business-like manner. 
 
CAPACITY: 
 
People who are “unable” to enter into contracts are protected by law. 
This is what we call contractual capacity. The reason for this is that 
these people may be unable to understand the consequences of 
entering into a contract. 
 
People who lack capacity: 
1. 
Minors 
2. 
People with mental incapacity 
3. 
Intoxicated people 
 
A contract entered into by someone without capacity renders the 
contract voidable by them when the disability ends. This means that 
the person without capacity have the ability to go back on the contract, 
once they are “able”. – eg. for minors, this is when they reach 18, for 
those who are intoxicated, this is when they sober up or for disabled 
people, this is when the mental disability comes to an end. 
 
 
When the disability comes to an end, the person without capacity 
may: 
1. 
Ratify the contract – decide to adopt it despite making the 
contract without capacity. 
 OR 
2. 
Leave the contract (void) – the contract will be as if it never 
came to existence in the first place. 
 
Minors: 
 
A contract between an adult and a minor (under 18) is not binding on 
the minor, unless the minor ratifies the contract once they reach 18. 
 
Exceptions: 
1. 
Contracts for ‘necessaries': 
• 
Minors are bound where a contract supplies them with 
‘necessaries', or goods that are deemed necessary to 
them. 
• 
Sale of Goods Act 1979 A reasonable price must be paid 
for goods. 
• 
Fancy waistcoats were not necessary for a student 
who was sufficiently clothed. 
 
2. 
Beneficial contracts for service: 
• 
Minors are bound where a contract supplies them 
services which are deemed beneficial to them. 
• 
Although boxing match was not beneficial, minors must 
follow the rules of the match. 
• 
If the facilities of football club are poor, the would be of 
no benefit to a minor. 
• 
If the a minor footballer does not develop under his old 
contract, he can be released from it. 
 
3. 
Contracts for continuing obligations 
 
Mental incapacity: 
 
Someone will lack capacity if: They are ‘unable to make a decision for 
themselves in relation to the matter at the time the contract is made'. 
 
It is not relevant whether the impairment is temporary or permanent, 
the key factor the court will take into account is whether the party to 
the contract was able to make a decision in relation to the subject 
matter of the contract in that moment when the contract was signed. 
 
Those who are mentally incapacitated will still be liable to pay for 
‘necessaries'. 
 
Hart v Connor If the contract is later ratified by the incapacitated party 
at a later date when they are not mentally impaired, the contract will 
be enforceable. 
 
In commercial situations 
There is ICLR 
 
A company hiring a cleaner 
will likely intend to be in a 
legal relationship so the 
cleaner will be able to sue the 
company if they do not pay 
her. 
 
In domestic situations 
There is no ICLR 
 
A 
mother 
asking 
her 
daughter to wash the dished 
will not likely intend to enter 
into a legal relationship so 
the daughter will not be able 
to sue her mother if she does 
not pay her.

pages.heading: Intoxication: · If a party to a contract is intoxicated, the same rules apply as if the
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 11 of 30 
Intoxication: 
 
If a party to a contract is intoxicated, the same rules apply as if the 
person was mentally incapacitated (albeit temporarily). 
 
Matthews v Baxter Ratification of the contract is possible after 
sobering up, however, without ratification, the contract will be void.

pages.heading: PRIVITY OF CONTRACT · GENERAL RULE:
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 12 of 30 
PRIVITY OF CONTRACT 
 
GENERAL RULE: 
 
Privity of contract = asks the question who can sue under a contract 
and who can be sued. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Two rules: 
1. 
The burden of a contract cannot be imposed on a third party. 
2. 
The benefit of a contract cannot be taken by a third party. 
 
A claimant can only make a claim in relation to a contract if he is the 
one who has given the consideration. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
If there is a contract made between two parties to benefit a third party, 
that third party cannot enforce the benefit they were to receive under 
the general rules, if the original parties to the contract refuse to 
perform their obligations. 
 
However, this case will likely fall within the exception under the 
Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 which we will look at 
below. 
 
EXCEPTIONS: 
 
If you have a client who wants to make a claim under a contract to 
which they are not a party, they must look at whether one of the 
exceptions apply. 
 
Main exceptions: 
1. 
Trusts 
2. 
Torts 
3. 
Agency 
4. 
Collateral contract 
5. 
Assignment 
6. 
Judicial activism 
7. 
Contracts (Rights of Third parties) Act 1999 
 
Trust: 
 
In some cases, a third party might be able to successfully argue, that the 
original party to the contract was holding the promise on trust for 
them. 
 
If so, the third party could instruct the party to the contract to enforce 
the promise. Once the money is paid to the party to the contract either 
under the contract or by the court, that money must then be paid to 
the third party, who will be the beneficiary of the trust in this case. 
 
The word “trust” need not have been used to create a trust in this case, 
as the rules on implied trust will imply a trust in this situation. 
 
For equity to operate, it must be inequitable to go back on the promise 
and deprive the beneficiary from the benefit of the contract. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Agency: 
 
Dunlop v Selfridge A third party to a contract may make a claim relying 
on agency if one of the parties to the contract acted as their agent. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
In this case, the agent will simply be acting on the third party's behalf 
and while in theory, the contract is between the agent and the other 
party, the third party is the true party to the contract. 
 
Once the contract is signed, the agent will not be acting on behalf of the 
third party and the third party becomes a party to the contract. 
 
 
 
Scruttons v Midland Silicones 
The courts set out the criteria 
that 
applied 
to 
agency 
situations. 
 
 
 
Lord Reid: There is an agency relationship if: 
• 
The principal was intended to be protected – it must have been 
clear in the contract that there was an agency situation. 
• 
Contracting party was acting as an agent 
• 
They had an authority to act as an agent 
 AND 
• 
Principal has provided consideration 
 
New Zealand Shipping v Satterthwaite (The Eurymedon) The 
principles of agency applied due to the wording of the contract. 
 
Held: The contract stated that 
‘the carrier, its servants, 
agents and employees are 
exempted.' They could rely 
on the principles of agency 
due to the terms of the 
contract. They have also 
provided consideration to the 
shipper 
and 
carrier 
by 
unloading the goods. 
 
Collateral contract: 
 
Creative solutions by the courts to avoid the unfair result that is created 
by strictly following the rules of privity. 
 
The court may find that there is another contract which has not been 
expressly stated between the parties. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
In this case, the court must find that both parties intended for there to 
be a contract between them. 
 
PARTY 
 
THIRD 
PARTY 
 
PARTY 
contract 
help third 
party 
PARTY 
(AGENT) 
 
THIRD 
PARTY 
 
PARTY 
contract 
help third 
party 
Example: 
 
I need my room painted so I reach out to Katy, my gardener and ask 
her if she could do the work for me. If she agrees to paint my room, 
then me and Katy will both be parties to the contract. 
 
If she decides not to take on the work, she may refer me to her son, 
Thomas, the local handyman. If I make a contract with Thomas, then 
Thomas and I will be parties to the contract. – Katy will not be a party 
to the contract in this case. 
 
PARTY 
 
THIRD

contract

pages.heading: Shanklin Pier v Detel While not · an express contract, a new,
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 13 of 30 
 
Shanklin Pier v Detel While not 
an express contract, a new, 
separate contract may arise 
between one of the parties and 
the third party in some cases. 
 
Facts: The owners of a pier 
wanted the pier painted. Detel 
manufactured paints and said 
that if they could ask their contractors to use Detel paints, they would 
guarantee that ‘the paint will last 7 years.' They did that and the 
contractors used Detel paint, but the paint started to peel off after 3-4 
months. The pier owners did not have a contract with Detel. The 
contractor had privity of contract, but the damage was suffered by the 
pier owners. 
 
Held: There was a collateral contract between the pier owners and 
Detel which arose due to a unilateral contract. 
 
Assignment: 
 
If you have a right, you can assign (pass on) the right to a third party. 
 
Two parties have a contract. One of the parties then assigns some or all 
of the rights from his contract to a third party. That third party can now 
sue the original party on the basis of breach of contract if they refuse 
to pay. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Contracts (Rights of Third parties) Act 1999: 
 
Third parties can now sue for a benefit of the contract. 
 
Contracts (Rights of Third Parties) Act 1999 Third party will be able to 
benefit from a contract if: 
• 
The contract expressly provides that they could 
 OR 
• 
The contract purports to confer a benefit 
 
However, the act can be expressly excluded so look out for clauses 
excluding it. 
 
Third parties must also be expressly identified in the contract by name, 
class or description. 
 
Third parties will then be treated as if they were parties to the contract. 
 
Defences may apply. 
 
 
Example: 
 
Thomas paints my room and I owe him £500 for the job he has done. 
He asks me to pay him £300 and pay £200 to his mother, Katy, as he 
owed her £200. 
 
In this case, Thomas assigned some of the benefit of the contract to 
his mother.

pages.heading: CONTRACT TERMS · WHICH STATEMENTS AMOUNT TO TERMS?
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 14 of 30 
CONTRACT TERMS 
 
WHICH STATEMENTS AMOUNT TO TERMS? 
 
Terms = describe the meaning and effect of a contract by setting out 
the rights and obligations contained within it. 
 
Gibson v Manchester CC The terms of a contract must be clear and 
certain otherwise there is no agreement. 
 
Scammell & Nephew v Outson If the court finds that an important term 
of the contract has been missed out from the agreement (written or 
oral), the contract will be to uncertain and unenforceable. 
 
Hillas & Co Ltd v Arcos Ltd If the terms of a contract are uncertain (other 
than key terms in which case the contract is unenforceable), the courts 
may imply terms into the contract using existing trade practices and 
the parties' previous dealings. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
It is important to identify whether the statement in question in relation 
to a contract dispute was a term of the contract. If the statement did 
indeed amount to a term of the contract, then this can give rise to a 
breach of contract claim if the promise is not fulfilled. 
 
Without a breach of contract claim, you may still make a claim for 
misrepresentation (in relation to representations). While this would 
allow you to make a valid claim and receive compensation, the 
compensation will be limited based on whether or not the 
misstatement was intentional and this may limit the recoverable 
compensation. 
 
It is always best to rely on a breach of contract claim where possible, 
and only look into misrepresentation claims where your client cannot 
make a claim for breach of contract. 
 
Not a term: 
 
1. 
Mere puff – mere puffs are not legally recognised and have no 
binding effect, however, they are subject to the Consumer 
Protection Act 1987 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Carlill v Carbolic Smoke Ball Co If a statement is made around 
the time of contracting which amounts to a mere puff, these 
statements can become legally binding if there is evidence in 
the contract or the circumstances that there was intention for 
the mere puff to be binding. 
 
2. 
Representation: 
 Representations = statements of fact made before the contract 
is signed, which convince the other party to sign the contract. 
These representations are not generally terms to the contract, 
but they may become terms in certain circumstances, similarly 
to mere puffs. – eg. “The horse is not vicious.” Or “This antique 
vase belonged to Elvis Presley.” 
 
How a term becomes part of the contract: 
 
1. 
Express terms: 
 Express terms = terms agreed by the parties that they should 
form part of the contract. These are usually written into the 
contract or if the agreement is an oral agreement, then these 
terms have been discussed and agreed to form part of the 
agreement. 
 
2. 
Implied terms: 
 Implied terms = terms that have not been agreed by the parties 
expressly but they also form part of the contract by some 
mechanism. 
 
Terms may be implied into a contract: 
• 
By the courts 
• 
By statute 
 
REPRESENTATION OR EXPRESS TERM? 
 
Whether a statement is simply a representation or a term, can be 
identified by looking at what the contracting parties may have 
intended. 
 
If this is not clear, the court will look at the conduct of the parties and 
infer the parties' intention using the objective test. – What would the 
reasonable person believe by examining the conduct of the parties? 
 
The court will look at the following factors when establishing whether 
something is a term or a representation: 
 
1. 
The timing between the representation and signing the 
contract. 
 
2. 
The importance the parties place on the terms. 
 
3. 
Whether one/both of the parties have some sort of specialist 
knowledge in the subject matter of the contract. 
 
4. 
Whether the purchaser was influenced by the other party not 
to carry out any checks. 
 
The court will not make a decision based on any one of these factors 
alone, all of them will be taken into account and each factor will 
increase or decrease the likelihood that the representation was a term. 
 
Timing: 
 Routledge v McKay The longer the time between the representation 
and signing the contract, the less likely that the representation was 
meant to be a term. – eg. if the statement is made 2 weeks before a 
contract, there is a low chance that the statement was the one which 
induced the party to sing the contract. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Importance: 
 Bannerman v White The parties must have placed importance on the 
truth of the statement. If they did, it is likely that the statement was a 
term. 
 
The court will examine the importance of the statement from the 
perspective of the party to whom it was made. – eg. If the person 
hearing the statement would not have signed the contract without that 
statement, this means high importance. 
 
Specialist knowledge: 
 Dick Bentley Productions v Harold Smith If one of the parties have 
specialist knowledge or if they are expert in the subject matter of the 
contract, then the court will usually decide against them in a dispute. 
This is because they will have had a higher bargaining power and should 
have known what the consequences of the contract were. 
 
If a specialist Seller has made a statement to the other party (who did 
not have specialist knowledge), their statement will be deemed to be 
a warranty by the courts. On the other hand, if the Seller is a private 
Seller without any specialist knowledge, their statement will simply be 
a representation. 
 
 
 
 
 
Example: 
‘Redbull gives you wings' in the Redbull ad is only a joke and 
no one would expect to actually grow wings after drinking a 
redbull. 
Example 1: 
A small shop makes a contract with a supplier to provide the shop 
pre-packaged food and drink. The contract includes the key details, 
except for the price, which is “to be agreed by the parties prior to 
the sale”. The court is unlikely to uphold this contract as valid if 
supplier did not have enough products to sell in December due to 
the high volume of buyers. The price is a key term in a supply of 
goods contract, which was missing in this case, making the contract 
invalid and unenforceable due to uncertainty. 
Example 2: 
A small shop makes a contract with a supplier to provide the shop 
pre-packaged food and drink. The contract includes all the key 
terms, however, for time of delivery, there are no agreed clauses a 
part from the fact that the goods are to be delivered by the supplier 
to the shop's address. If there is a disagreement regarding this 
point, the court would likely uphold the contract, however, it would 
imply a term that the “goods must be delivered within a reasonable 
time”. 
Example: 
Carlos was in the process of selling his specialised bicycle to Dean, 
a potential buyer. Dean asked Carlos whether he knew what the 
year of the bicycle was, as it was difficult to tell this from the serial 
number. Carlos told Dean that was made in 1992. They have signed 
a contract a week later, and the contract did not mention the year 
when the bicycle was made. 
 
A few months later, Dean takes the bicycle to an expert to install 
some new parts, then the expert tells him that the bicycle was 
actually a 1989 model, not a 1992 model. Dean now wants to return 
the bicycle and get his money back. If this case were to be heard by 
the court, the court would take into account the timing of the 
statement versus the signing of the contract, and the 
representation will likely have not become a term of the contract, 
as a week has passed since the statement was made and the signing 
of the contract.

pages.heading: Checks: · If a seller tells the buyer not to carry out checks, then this is effectively
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 15 of 30 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Checks: 
 If a seller tells the buyer not to carry out checks, then this is effectively 
a promise that what they are telling the buyer is true. 
 This does not generally apply to auction sales. 
 
EXPRESS TERMS: 
 
These are terms which have expressly stated to form part of the 
contract, and they will typically be written into the contract. 
 
As we have seen earlier, in some cases, representations may be 
express terms to the contract, if they were of particular significance in 
relation to the agreement. 
 
Construction of terms – What does the term mean? 
 
Unfortunately, not all contractual clauses are clearly drafted. 
 
If the parties cannot agree as to what a particular clause were to mean 
in the contract, the court will identify what the parties' intentions must 
have been at the time of contracting by relying on the objective test. 
 
Parole evidence rule = extrinsic evidence (evidence from outside the 
contract) cannot be taken into account to vary or retract from a written 
contract, where the contract is wholly written. 
 
This means that if the contract is in writing, in most cases, you cannot 
use what was said around the time of making the contract to deny or 
dispute the written terms of the contract. This includes both oral and 
written statements. 
 
What will become the terms of the contract are only the terms 
contained in the written contract. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Exceptions: 
 
• 
Contracts not wholly written: 
 If the contract is one which is part-written, part-oral, then the 
parole evidence rule does not apply. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
• 
Collateral contracts: 
 There was another contract formed, varying or altering the 
original contract. This other contract might be an oral contract. 
 
These contracts run independently of the original contract. 
 
• 
Onerous terms: 
 Onerous terms must be very obvious/pointed out the other 
party, otherwise invalid. 
 
• 
There is ambiguity in the contract: Robertson v Jackson 
 If the contract is not clear on certain points, the court will 
adduce external evidence to clarify the meaning of the contract. 
 
Entire agreement clauses: 
 Entire agreement clauses are inserted into the agreement to exclude 
the parole evidence rule and will be upheld by the court. These clauses 
assert that the contents of the contract form the entire agreement 
between the parties. However, this can sometimes cause unfairness 
and the court do recognise that. 
 
IMPLIED TERMS: 
 
Terms implied into the contract by some mechanism. 
 
The courts/statute will only imply terms into the contract if the parties
