must have intended the term to be a part of the contract, as it was 
necessary for business efficacy (necessary to the essential functioning 
of the contract). 
 
The test of necessity is a lot higher requirement than the test of 
reasonableness. Even if a term would be reasonable to imply into the 
contract, the court will only do so, if it is necessary. 
 
Implied by the courts: 
 
Implied in law: 
 
A term can only be implied into the contract if it is ‘a necessary incident 
of this type of contract'. Terms can be implied for business efficacy, and 
will be based on the nature of the contract. – Liverpool City Council v 
Irwin 
 
Implied in fact: 
 
* 
Implied as a one-off – to ensure business efficacy of the 
contract. The parties did have intention, but it was imputed 
intention that was never discussed. 
 
* 
Rules of trade custom – will be implied terms. 
 
* 
Previous course of dealing – will imply the terms in the new 
contract as used in the old contract. Previous course of dealings 
have to be consistent and regular. Regularity will be a question 
of fact. – eg. when buying ships, buying one per year should be 
enough, but when buying chocolates, buying one every week 
will be regular. 
 
* 
Obvious terms – use the “Officious bystander” test, to see if the 
term was so obvious that the parties must have intended for 
the term to be included. – eg. if a car is being sold, it does not 
need to be discussed that the car will have four wheels, as it is 
so obvious. 
 
Implied by statute: 
 
Sale of Goods Act 1979: *B-to-B* 
 
s.12-15 Sale of Goods Act 1979 Rely on this act if the contract is for the 
sale of goods and it is a contract between two businesses (Business-tobusiness). 
 
Implied terms: s.12-15 Sale of Goods Act 1979 
* 
The seller must have good title to the goods so they are able to 
legally transfer them to the buyer. 
* 
The items sold must be of satisfactory quality. 
* 
The items sold must be fit for the buyer's particular purpose, if 
the buyer told this to the seller. 
* 
If the sale is sale by sample: then the goods must correspond 
with the sample. 
* 
If the sale is sale by description: then the goods must 
correspond with the description. 
 
 
Example 1: 
Callum is a garden specialist with great knowledge in lawnmovers. 
A customer comes into his shop, intending to buy a lawnmover. She 
mentions that she does not know much about lawnmovers, but 
wishes to buy one which will last a long time and will require low 
maintenance. Callum recommends his own brand of lawnmovers 
and tell her that this one is long-lasting and that he highly 
recommends it. 
 
The customer buys the lawnmover which ends up breaking after 6 
months of use. When the customer returns to Callum, he refuses to 
give her a refund, saying that his statement that the lawnmover was 
long-lasting was not a term fo the contract. The court will likely 
disagree with this, and decide that Callum's statement was a 
warranty due to his expertise. 
Example 2: 
Eva is a make-up artist, and she responds to an ad, whereby 
someone is trying to sell their vintage make-up collection. Eva 
meets the seller, Lizzie, in person. Lizzie tells her, that she does not 
know much about the collection or make-up in general, and that 
she inherited the collection from her late mother, and believes that 
it belonged to Marylin Monroe's makeup artist. She tells her that 
she is expecting to sell it for around £3,000. 
 
Eva tells Lizzie that she is a makeup expert and the make-up appears 
to be from the 1970s and could not have been owner by Marylin 
Monroe's makeup artist. Although Eva knows that this is not true 
and is only trying to get a bargain, her statement convinces Lizzie to 
sell the collection to Eva for £110 instead. Later Lizzie realises that 
she had been lied to and make a claim. The court is likely going to 
find that there is no contract and that the makeup collection should 
be returned to Lizzie. 
Example: 
A wholesaler decides to import vapes into the UK. The supplier 
delivers the vapes from Japan so the wholesaler contracts with the 
shipping company, and requests that the products are to be 
shipped below deck. The shipping company promises to ship the 
products below deck, however, there is no mention of this in the 
contract. The products are shipped on deck and the majority of the 
vapes are damaged. The court will likely decide that the oral 
promise was a term in this case, and that the contract was partwritten, part-oral. 
Example: 
If Jonathan, a hairdresser tells you at the time of 
contracting, that the hair dye used on your hair will last you 
7 weeks and it only lasts 2 weeks, the contract will be partwritten, part-oral.

pages.heading: Potential remedies: · Right to reject within 30 days, repair/replacement, price reduction,
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 16 of 30 
Potential remedies: 
Right to reject within 30 days, repair/replacement, price reduction, 
right to reject after 30 days if the fault was discovered after 30 days. 
 
Consumer Rights Act 2015: *B-to-C* 
 
Consumer Rights Act 2015 Rely on this act if the contract is for the sale 
of goods and the buyer is not a business (Business-to-Consumer). 
 
Implied terms: 
* 
Right to supply 
* 
Description 
* 
Satisfactory quality 
* 
Reasonably fit for a particular purpose 
* 
Sample 
 
Same provisions as for the SGA 1979 above, just use a different statute. 
 
Potential remedies: 
Right to reject within 30 days, repair/replacement, price reduction, 
right to reject after 30 days if the fault was discovered after 30 days. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Supply of Goods and Services Act 1982: *B-to-B* 
 
Supply of Goods and Services Act 1982 Rely on this act if the contract 
is for the supply of services and both parties are a business (Businessto-Business). 
 
Implied terms: 
* 
Reasonable care and skill – you must not be negligent while 
supplying the service. 
* 
Within a reasonable time 
* 
Pay reasonable consideration 
 
Same provisions as for the SGA 1979 above, just use a different statute. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Potential remedies: 
Repeat performance of the service, price reduction 
 
Supply of Services Consumer Rights Act 2015: *B-to-C* 
 
Supply of Services Consumer Rights Act 2015 Rely on this act if the 
contract is for the supply of services and the buyer is not a business 
(Business-to-Consumer). 
 
Implied terms: 
* 
Reasonable care and skill – you must not be negligent while 
supplying the service. 
* 
Within a reasonable time 
* 
Pay reasonable consideration 
 
Same provisions as for the SGA 1979 above, just use a different statute. 
 
Digital content: 
 
Implied terms: 
* 
The content must be of satisfactory quality (the court will take 
into account the description of content, the price and how it 
was advertised) 
* 
Must be fit for a particular purpose 
* 
Must be as described 
 
Potential remedies: 
Repair/replacement, if that is not possible, then price reduction 
 
CLASSIFICATION OF TERMS: 
 
Types of term: 
1. 
Conditions 
2. 
Warranties 
3. 
Innominate terms 
 
Conditions = a term in the contract that goes to the root of the contract 
(an important term). 
 
Warranties = a term in the contract that is less important. 
 
Conditions: 
 
The word condition carries a specific legal meaning in this case which is 
an important term to the contract. 
 
There are two phrases: ‘condition precedent' and ‘condition 
subsequent'. These are conditions that are contingent on some event 
to trigger the condition which will then come into effect. 
 
Can be defined by: 
* 
Statute 
* 
The parties 
* 
Courts 
 
Statute: 
 
Sale of Goods Act 1979: 
 
Sale of Goods Act 1979 Rely on this act if the contract is for the sale of 
goods and it is a contract between two businesses (Business-tobusiness). 
 
Sale of Goods Act 1979 s.12-15 are all classed as conditions. 
 
Goods must fit the description size exactly, even if the size of the 
product would not make a difference to the buyer. This is a technical 
breach. Now the rules have changed as this was seen as abuse of the 
rules. 
 
s.15A Sale of Goods Act 1979 The breach of these conditions may be 
treated as a breach of warranty if: 
* 
There is a slight/technical breach of ss.13, 14 or 15 
 AND 
* 
Rejecting the goods would be unreasonable 
 
Consumer Rights Act 2015: 
 
Consumer Rights Act 2015 Rely on this act if the contract is for the sale 
of goods and the buyer is not a business (Business-to-Consumer). 
 
CRA does not classify its terms as either conditions or warranties. 
 
Supply of Goods and Services Act 1982: 
 
The terms implied by this act are treated as innominate terms. 
 
Supply of Services Consumer Rights Act 2015: 
 
The terms implied by this act are treated as conditions. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Parties: 
* 
If a term is defined as a condition in the contract, the courts will 
give effect to this. 
* 
If a term is defined as a condition, but this leads to an 
unreasonable result, the parties must be particularly clear in the 
contract that this is the result they want. 
 
Court: 
 
The courts establish precedents and they held that certain terms will be 
conditions. 
 
'Expected readiness to load' clause will always be a condition. 
This clause means that one party must inform the other when the ship 
is in the dock ready for the goods to be loaded onto it. 
 
Time of performance is always a warranty except when the contract 
says ‘Time is of the essence' in which case it becomes a condition. 
Time of performance is of the essence in all commercial contracts but 
not time of payment. 
 
Innominate terms: 
 
The Hong Kong Fir Innominate term = a term where it is not possible 
to tell if the term goes to the root of the contract. 
 
Once decided whether the term goes to the root of the contract, it will 
then be treated as a condition or warranty. An innominate term does 
not become a condition or warranty it will be simply treated as such. 
Example: 
Laura is a plasterer and she is contracted to plaster a business' head 
office. There is no deadline agreed by which Laura must complete 
the works. Despite this, the SGSA will imply into the contract that 
she must complete the works within a reasonable time using 
reasonable care and skill. 
Example: 
William hired out a catering company to cater for his daughter's 
graduation party. Unfortunately, the catering company did not 
perform as expected. They have arrived late and did not prepare all 
the food that was on the menu. They have also failed to setup the 
tables which had to be done by William himself. The company will 
have breached the terms implied by the SGCRA to supply the service 
with reasonable care and skill. This was a condition that was 
breached. 
Example: 
An airfrier which fails to heat up to the required temperature in 
order to airfry the food placed inside it is not of sufficient quality 
and not fit for purpose, which is to airfry certain food items.

pages.heading: Advertising peas during a memorial service was bad advertising and not · notifying the company of this was seen as a breach of a condition due
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 17 of 30 
 
Advertising peas during a memorial service was bad advertising and not 
notifying the company of this was seen as a breach of a condition due 
to the seriousness. 
 
If the delivery date is wrong in a deliver clause, then the buyer will not 
be able to meet the deadline they might have 
 
If there is no clause in the contract, the default position applies, which 
is that the seller must deliver the goods within a reasonable time. This 
is uncertain, so advise your client to include a delivery clause in the 
contract. 
 
Is time of the essence? 
 
Time of payment: 
 
If no express term for time of payment: time is not of the essence. 
 
Time of delivery: 
 
If there is a clause stating that time is not of the essence, then late 
delivery will be a breach of warranty only. 
 
If there is a clause stating that time is estimated only, then the court 
will interpret this to mean that time of delivery was not important 
for the parties and there is no obligation to deliver on time. 
 
If no clause, default position: 
 
There is no implied term as to whether or not time of delivery is of 
the essence. 
 
If seller is contracted to send the goods to the buyer, then they must 
send the goods within a reasonable time. 
 
The court will rarely imply into a contract that time was of the essence. 
However, the court did imply into a contract that time was of the 
essence if even a small delay would deprive the innocent party of 
substantially the whole benefit of contract. – for example, if the reason 
to contract was to meet the deadline. 
 
EFFECT OF A BREACH: 
 
Breach of a condition: 
 
The innocent party has a choice (right of election) to: 
• 
Terminate the contract and claim damages 
 OR 
• 
Affirm the contract and claim damages 
 
Breach of a warranty: 
 
The innocent party can only claim damages. 
 
Breach of an innominate term: 
 
Rights of the innocent party are uncertain. It depends on how the court 
decides. 
 
If the innocent party believes that this was the breach of a condition 
and decides to terminate the contract, and the court later decides that 
this term was only a warranty, then the other party can sue them for 
wrongful termination. – It is always best to advise your client to treat 
the term as a warranty on in this case, for the purposes of the remedies 
available to them. 
 
Breach of terms implied by CRA 2015 (B-to-C): 
* 
Consumers can use a number of remedies. 
* 
Right to reject in the first 30 days. 
* 
Right to repair/replacement of goods. 
* 
Reduction of price and final right of rejection. 
 
VARIATION OF TERMS: 
 
Business relationships change over time, so occasionally it may be 
necessary to vary the terms of commercial contracts. 
 
Both parties must agree to the variation, preferably in writing. 
 
Unilateral variation (ie where only one party can make a change) is only 
valid under specific circumstances if this has been agreed in advance. 
 
Methods of varying a contract: 
1. 
Written variation 
 
2. 
Oral variation: 
Valid, however, it can be difficult to enforce. Making a recording 
of the oral variation/having witnesses helps enforcement. 
 
3. 
Variation by conduct: 
Often seen in construction contracts or where a contractor has 
deadlines to meet. However, this can lead to an implied change 
in the contract. 
 
In some cases, sustained minor breaches, if the other party 
acquiesced (said nothing), may also lead to an implied change 
of terms, incorporating the conduct amounting to the breach 
into the contract. 
 
4. 
Unilateral variation: 
Generally invalid. However, if both parties agree in the contract 
that unilateral variation is an option, then such variation will be 
valid. This will likely only apply to certain specified terms. 
 
Waiver: 
One party may waive (give up) certain rights under a contract for a set 
period of time. This can be done orally or in writing. Once they have 
agreed to do so, the waiver is binding, even if they change their mind. 
 
Sustained minor breach: 
If one party consistently accepts minor contractual breaches, and a 
dispute then arises regarding these breaches, previous acceptance will 
be taken into account by the court.

pages.heading: EXEMPTION CLAUSES · INTRODUCTION:
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 18 of 30 
EXEMPTION CLAUSES 
 
INTRODUCTION: 
 
Definition: 
 
An exemption clause is a clause that will change a party's obligations to 
pay damages. 
 
Exemption clauses = ‘a term which excludes or modifies an obligation, 
whether primary [or] general secondary.' 
 
Two types of exemption clauses: 
1. 
Exclusion clause – this will exclude liability completely 
2. 
Limitation clause – this will limit a party's liability, so that party 
will only pay a part of the loss. 
 
These types of clauses are put into contracts by a party that has more 
negotiating power over the other. 
 
These are usually seen to be added by large businesses where the 
consumer is not able to negotiate the terms of the contract they are 
signing as they have weaker bargaining power. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
When solving questions on exemption clauses: 
1. 
Identify the liability 
2. 
Only if you have found some form of liability, then look at 
whether the contract has been successful in excluding/limiting 
it. – check whether the contract contains any exemption 
clauses. 
3. 
Check whether the exemption clauses have been incorporated 
into the contract. 
4. 
Check whether a reasonable person would construe the clause 
as such that it would cover the breach. 
5. 
Check whether any of the statutory controls apply to remove 
the binding effect of the clause. 
 
INCORPORATION: 
 
In the past, the courts have not been able to cross out clauses that they 
deemed unfair so when encountering these clauses, they wanted to 
make sure that these clauses were really a part of the contract and have 
been properly incorporated. 
 
Incorporation may happen by: 
* 
Signature 
* 
Notice 
* 
Previous course of dealings 
* 
Trade custom 
 
Incorporation by signature: 
 
General rule: 
If an agreement is signed, in the absence of fraud, it will be immaterial 
whether both parties have read the terms of the agreement. 
 
Exceptions: 
1. 
If there is an overriding oral assurance. 
2. 
If the document given to you is not reasonably expected to have 
a contractual effect, then it won't. – eg. Timesheets. 
3. 
'Non est factum': if you are incapacitated from understanding 
what is in the document, you will not be bound even if you 
signed it. 
 
Incorporation by notice: 
 
Notice = bringing to the attention of the other party what the contract 
will contain. 
 
Reasonable notice: the party relying on the clause must take 
reasonable steps to bring the clause to the other party's attention. 
 
Referring to the term is usually enough for the terms to be 
incorporated. 
 
If the term is particularly onerous terms, then the party relying on the 
term must take more effort to make sure that the other party 
understand the term. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Incorporation by previous course of dealings: 
 
If there had been previous dealings between the parties, then it can be 
assumed that the new contracts will be on the same or at least similar 
terms to the past contracts. 
 
In order to establish previous dealings: 
1. 
The dealing must be consistent 
 AND 
2. 
Regular – Contracting 3-4 times in 5 year was not regular 
enough. 5 similar contracts made in 13 months was regular 
enough. For big contracts, a lower frequency will be enough. 
 
Incorporation by trade custom: 
 
If there is a recognised custom in that industry to use some specific 
implied terms, the court will take those into account. 
 
Other key considerations: 
 
Timing: 
The clause must be a part of the contract before it is signed. 
The clause must be shown to a carpark customer before the automatic 
barrier. 
 
Nature of document: 
If the nature of the document is not one to be expected to be legally 
binding, then it is unlikely to form part of the contract. 
 
CONSTRUCTION: 
 
Would a reasonable person construe the clause as such that it would 
cover the breach? 
The court will interpret the clause using its ordinary, natural meaning. 
Would the clause cover the breach? 
 
Contra proferentem rule: 
* 
If there is any ambiguity in the clause, it will be construed 
against the person relying on the clause. 
* 
The starting point of the court is the ordinary meaning of the 
word. 
 
If the limitation clause in the contract is sensible about the limit, the 
court is more likely to uphold the clause. 
 
When excluding liability for negligence: 
 
You must clearly state that you are to exclude liability for negligence, 
otherwise the wording may be construed to mean something else. 
 
If one of the parties purports to exclude negligence, this is not 
something that the general public would agree to so the wording on 
this must state that what is being excluded is negligence, otherwise the 
court will construe it to mean something else. 
 
STATUTORY CONTROLS: 
 
First, differentiate between Business contracts and consumer contracts 
as different rules apply depending on the type of contract you are 
dealing with. 
 
Business to business – Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 
Business to consumer – Consumer Rights Act 2015 
 
A party is dealing as a consumer if it is not dealing in the course of its 
business. A company may be a consumer if the purchase is not integral 
to their business. 
 
Business = includes a profession and the activities of a public and local 
authority. 
 
UCTA 1977: 
 
The relevant test under the act is the reasonableness test, not 
unfairness as the name would suggest. 
 
Scope: 
Common law controls: 
* 
Incorporation 
* 
Construction 
 
 
Statutory controls: 
* 
Unfair Contract Terms 
Act 1977 
* 
Consumer Rights Act 
2015 
 
Example: 
A woman purchased a ticket to travel by rail from London to 
Birmingham. She received her ticket after her purchase. On the 
back of the ticket, there was a term excluding the train company's 
liability for losses caused to customers as a result of the train being 
delayed. The woman's train was delayed by half an hour and she 
missed a connection as a result, and had to buy another ticket. 
 
In this case, the train company was unsuccessful in excluding 
liability for the delays as the onerous term has not been pointed out 
to the woman and the term was only revealed to her after her 
purchase, and not before.

pages.heading: Only deals with business-to-business contracts · Only deals with exemption clauses and does not deal with any
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 19 of 30 
* 
Only deals with business-to-business contracts 
* 
Only deals with exemption clauses and does not deal with any 
other terms 
* 
Deals with business liability (contractual and tortious) 
* 
Deals with non-contractual notices – eg. where the premises 
have signs trying to limit liability. 
 
It controls clauses which tries to limit/exclude liability for: 
* 
Negligence 
* 
Breach of a contractual term 
* 
Breach of a term implied by SGA or SGSA 
 
Negligence: 
 
Negligence = is a ‘breach of any express or implied contract term to take 
reasonable care or exercise reasonable skill'. 
Eg. A breach of s.13 Supply of Goods and Services Act 1982. 
 
If the term is trying to exclude personal injury or death caused by 
negligence, the exemption clause will be invalid. 
 
If a term is excluding ‘other loss or damage', then the exemption clause 
must be reasonable in order to be valid – look at s.11. 
 
Breach of a contractual term or an implied term: 
 
Breach of a contractual term: 
This means express terms. 
 
If the parties are dealing on the basis of standard terms of business, 
then the reasonableness test in s.11 applies. 
 
If the parties are not dealing on the basis of standard terms of business, 
and the contract is negotiated, then the court will presume that the 
terms are reasonable. 
 
If the general terms of the main agreement are not negotiated, even 
if the other related agreements are negotiated, means contracting on 
general terms. 
 
Breach of a term implied by SGA or SGSA: 
This is an implied term, that cannot be excluded/limited. 
 
Breach of any other implied term: 
Go through the reasonableness test in s.11. 
 
The Reasonableness Test – s.11: 
 
The test for reasonableness must be considered in the circumstances 
existing at the time of contracting. 
 
What is reasonable is a question of fact to the court. 
 
Also look at the non-exhaustive list of guidelines in Schedule 2. 
 
Apply UCTA Reasonableness test: 
 
s.11(2) + Sched 2 Schedule 2 Guidelines – indicative ‘Grey List': 
 
These have a general application to the requirements of 
reasonableness. 
 
Fact pointing to reasonable 
Facts pointing to unreasonable 
Type of clause: 
Limitation of liability 
 
Type of clause: 
Outright exclusion 
Knowledge of clause: 
Buyer must have known of the 
existence of the term because: 
* Capital letters, bold, red or 
underlined to make Buyer 
aware. 
* Knowledge/experience 
with these type of clauses 
Knowledge of clause: 
Buyer did not know of the 
existence of the term because 
* Buyer never contract with 
this Seller before, 
* Clause blends in as to “hide” 
the clause. 
 
But arguably, should read 
contract before signing. 
 
Negotiation? 
Buyer could have insisted on 
amending the clause before 
entering the contract but did 
not do so. 
 
Negotiation? 
No lawyers involved or simply 
signed standard terms. 
Bargaining power? 
Buyer has strong bargaining 
power and could have chosen 
to do business with another 
supplier. 
 
Bargaining power? 
Buyer was in a weaker position, 
never having contracted with the 
Seller before or having no 
solicitors, needing more sales. 
 
Contract inducements: 
Received discounts to accept 
clause 
Contract inducements: 
Received no inducement. 
 
 
Parties' resources and the 
availability of insurance: 
The injured party has insurance 
or resources to pay for the 
losses. 
 
 
Parties' resources and the 
availability of insurance: 
The injured party has no 
insurance nor resources to pay 
for the losses. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The proferens (= party seeking to rely on the clause) must prove 
reasonableness. 
 
What is reasonable is decided on a case-by-case basis: 
 
There could be no appeals made on reasonableness, the finding of 
which is at the discretion of the court. 
 
If businessmen dealing with large companies with equal bargaining 
power would believe that the terms are reasonable, then the courts 
will not intervene. 
Unless the court is satisfied that one of the parties is taking unfair 
advantage of the other or the terms are so unreasonable that they 
would not be properly understood/considered, then the court will not 
interfere with the agreement of the parties. 
 
If the clause is so unreasonable that it contradicts a basic assumption 
of responsibility. 
 
CRA 2015: 
 
Scope: 
Only deals with business-to-consumer contracts but applies to any term 
in the contract, not only exemption clauses. 
 
All terms must be transparent, legible and fair. 
 
Certain exclusions are unfair such as: 
- 
Excluding or limiting liability for death/personal injury caused 
by negligence 
- 
Excluding or limiting the conditions implied by the CRA 
 
If a term is unfair then will not be binding on the consumer. 
 
A term is not binding if it tries to restrict liability for any of the implied 
terms in the Act: 
1. 
Right to supply the goods 
2. 
Goods of satisfactory quality 
3. 
Goods to be fit for a particular purpose 
4. 
Goods to be as described 
5. 
Goods to match any sample examined 
 
Excluding liability when providing services: 
 
An exemption clause is not binding if it is to exclude trader's liability 
arising under s.49 for negligently performing the service. 
 
If the clause is only limiting liability for breach of s.49: then it may be 
binding if it meets the below conditions: 
• 
It does not limit liability for death/personal injury caused by 
breach of duty of skill and care 
• 
It does not limit liability below the purchase price 
 AND 
• 
It passes the fairness test of the act. 
 
Fairness test: 
* 
A contract term must be transparent (expressed in plain and 
intelligible language and, if it is written, legible) and prominent 
(brought to the consumer's attention in such a way that an 
average consumer would be aware of the term). – s.62 CRA 
2015 
* 
A term is unfair if it causes a significant imbalance in the parties' 
rights and obligations under the contract to the detriment of 
the consumer. 
 
The fairness test does not apply to key terms of the contract, such as 
the description of the product or the price, as long as these terms are 
Example: 
A contract to supply a file management software to a grocery store, 
includes a clause limiting the liability of the software company to 
£250,000. The software collapses, losing all of the grocery store's 
data, causing £3.5 million in damages. The insurance of the grocery 
store for this type of damage is limited to £500,000 and the business 
has no other resources. The software company has an insurance 
covering losses up to £5 million. The clause will be unreasonable as 
the grocery store may only pay for the damages by increasing its 
prices and paying less to its staff, while the software company could 
have paid this amount from the insurance payout.

pages.heading: transparent and prominent. However, all other terms can be assessed · for fairness.
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 20 of 30 
transparent and prominent. However, all other terms can be assessed 
for fairness. 
 
The fairness of a term is to be determined by taking into account the 
nature of the goods or services for which the contract was concluded 
and by referring to all the circumstances existing when the term was 
agreed. 
 
Examples of unfair terms: 
* 
Excluding/limiting liability for death/personal injury resulting 
from the act or omission of the business. 
* 
Excluding/limiting the rights of the consumer if there is nonperformance by the business, either partial or total. 
* 
Allowing the business to terminate the contract without 
reasonable notice. 
* 
Binding the consumer to terms they have not agreed to without 
the possibility of opting out. 
* 
Extending the term of a fixed term contract automatically if the 
consumer did not agree to this. 
 
Consequences: 
 If a term is found to be unfair under the fairness test, it is not binding 
on the consumer, though the contract will continue to bind the parties 
if it is capable of existing without the unfair term.

pages.heading: BREACH OF CONTRACT CLAIMS – SALE OF GOODS · CONTRACT FLOWCHART
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 21 of 30 
BREACH OF CONTRACT CLAIMS – SALE OF GOODS 
CONTRACT FLOWCHART 
 
Breach of contract – Structure: 
1. 
Identify claim 
2. 
Identify terms breached 
3. 
Is term breached a condition/warranty? 
4. 
Remedies? 
5. 
Has the right to reject been lost? 
6. 
Exclusion or limitation of liability? 
7. 
Which remedies remain? 
 
IDENTIFY THE CLAIM: 
 
Breach of contract / oral term and what happened – eg. non-delivery 
of goods. 
 
BREACHED EXPRESS/IMPLIED TERM? 
 
Breached terms: Express or implied? Identify term. 
 
Implied terms: 
• 
s.13(1) Sale of Goods Act 1979 The goods will correspond with 
the description 
• 
s.14(2) Satisfactory quality 
Price may be relevant, low price = lower quality expectation. 
s.14(2C) Complainant will have no remedy if testing prior to 
purchase indicates a functional defect but the buyer proceeds 
with the purchase. 
• 
s.14(3) Fitness for Buyer's particular purpose, made known to 
the seller. – eg over the phone. 
 
THE TERM BREACHED A CONDITION OR 
WARRANTY? 
 
s.13(1A) s.13 is a condition 
s.14(6) ss.14(2) and 14(3) are conditions. 
 
REMEDIES: 
 
If a condition was breached, has prima facie choice of 3 remedies: 
1. 
Reject goods, terminate and claim damages 
2. 
Reject goods, affirm contract, contractual performance (to 
deliver the goods 2nd time) 
 OR 
3. 
Accept the goods but still claim damages, by treating the breach 
as a breach of warranty only. 
 
HAS THE RIGHT TO REJECT BEEN LOST? 
 
The right to reject goods is not available if: 
(a) s.15A breach is so slight, it would be unreasonable to do so or 
(b) Buyer has expressly, or by implication, waived the breach; or 
(c) s.35 and s. 11(4) if the buyer has accepted the goods. 
 
If so, only 1 remedy for the buyer: accept the goods but still claim 
damages. 
 
IS THERE AN EXCLUSION OR LIMITATION OF 
LIABILITY? 
 
Identify limitation or exclusion of liability clause. 
 
Direct or indirect and consequential loss? 
 
Exclusion/limitation clause must apply to these types loss, otherwise 
clause is not relevant. 
 
Direct loss: Watford Electronics Direct losses = arise naturally from the 
breach. 
Indirect loss: Hadley v Baxendale Must have been reasonably in 
contemplation when the contract was made. 
Consequential loss: Company and operational expenses. 
 
UCTA: 
 
UCTA applies if: 
1. 
Standard written terms. 
Watford Electronics Court follows the “hands-off” approach 
and not intervene if: negotiated the terms + experienced/of 
equal bargaining power or legal advice. 
 
2. 
Excludes or limits ss. 13-15 SGA implied terms. 
 
This is a B2B contract so the limitation of liability will be valid if it 
satisfies the requirement of reasonableness. If not, the term will be 
void. 
 
s.26(1)-(2) UCTA is not relevant to international supply contracts, it 
only applies to UK contracts. 
 
Apply UCTA Reasonableness test: 
s.11(2) + Sched 2 Factors to assess reasonableness: 
* 
Type of clause 
* 
Knowledge of the clause 
* 
Negotiation 
* 
Bargaining power 
* 
Contract inducement 
* 
Parties' resources 
 
s.11(4) Another factor: Seller's available resources to meet liability + 
insurance cover. 
 
WHICH REMEDIES REMAIN? 
 
If the limitation is held reasonable, limitation is valid, the Buyer can: 
claim money back or receive a replacement or damages for repair costs, 
but no damages – eg. for delay. 
 
If held unreasonable: then the limitation will be void and Buyer's 
remedies remain all those stated above under the “Remedies” heading.

pages.heading: VITIATING FACTORS · While a contract may have been prima facie validly formed, it may
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 22 of 30 
VITIATING FACTORS 
 
While a contract may have been prima facie validly formed, it may 
become void, voidable or unenforceable if one or more vitiating 
factors apply. 
 
Vitiating elements/factors: 
• Misrepresentation 
• Mistake 
• Unfair contract terms 
• Duress and undue influence 
• Illegality 
 
DURESS: 
 
Duress = ‘some form of coercion or threat to the person, property, or 
to a person's financial interests.' 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Effect of duress, if proven: 
 The contract will be voidable (different from void), and the court can 
set it aside. 
 
Voidable = the innocent party has a right to choose whether to keep 
the contract in place or set it aside. If they choose not to go ahead with 
the contract and they then make an application to the court, the court 
will set the contract aside as per their right. 
 
Void = the contract is void from the beginning and the innocent party 
has no choice whether to keep the contract. Proving mistake will render 
the contract void (not voidable). 
 
Types of duress: 
1. 
Duress to the person 
2. 
Duress to goods 
3. 
Economic duress 
 
Duress to the person: 
 
This is their contract was entered into by one party because of threats 
made to their person. – eg. threats to kill or injure them if they do not 
sign a particular contract. 
 
Threat to the person need not be the only reason for entering into a 
contract, but it must be one of the reasons. 
 
Duress to goods: 
 
This comprises of the unlawful detention of someone's goods. 
 
Test for duress to goods is the ‘but for' test. But for the threat, would 
the innocent party have signed the contract. This is a higher 
requirement that we have seen in relation to duress to the person 
(must be one of the reasons). 
 
Economic duress: 
 
Economic duress = a threat to the victim's financial interests. 
 
The test for economic duress: Pakistan International Airline Corp v 
Times Travel (2021) 
1. 
There is a threat/pressure made to the victim. – they may have 
other choices, but those choices would not be practical 
2. 
The threat/pressure is illegitimate, and the Defendant knows it 
is illegitimate. – pressure must be illegitimate, but differentiate 
this from rough negotiations which are acceptable 
3. 
The threat/pressure caused the victim to enter into the 
contract. 
 AND 
4. 
The victim had no reasonable alternative option but to give in 
to the threat/pressure. 
 
Factors to decide whether there has been illegitimate pressure: 
1. 
Pressure is a threatened breach of contract – if so, likely 
illegitimate, unless done in good faith. 
2. 
Pressure is unlawful 
3. 
Pressure is applied in bad faith – if so, likely illegitimate 
4. 
Pressure denied the victim of a practical choice 
5. 
The victim protested – if so, likely illegitimate 
6. 
The victim affirmed – if so, unlikely to be illegitimate 
 
Economic duress is an argument which is rarely accepted by the court 
in the context of commercial contract negotiations as there is an equal 
bargaining power where both parties will enter into a fully negotiated 
contract. 
 
The victim protested or did not affirm the contract: 
 
Protesting after signing the contract is evidence that you were put 
under pressure to sign the contract. – You should advise your client to 
protest as soon as possible and the longer you wait the less likely that 
your protest will be viewed as good evidence. 
 
In particular, the latest you could protest is as soon as the pressure has 
been lifted. 
 
Waiting for 8 months affirms the contract. 
As soon as the invoice is sent, paying the original amount and refusing 
to pay the rest is a sign of protest. 
 
Significant cause: 
 
This is a ‘but for' test. But for the pressure, the victim would not have 
entered into the contract. 
 
UNDUE INFLUENCE: 
 
An equitable doctrine to ensure that when a party enters into a 
contract, their decision has not been unduly influenced. 
 
Typically, duress is easier to establish than undue influence, so duress 
should be the first cause of action to try to establish before looking into 
undue influence. 
 
If undue influence is proved, the contract will be voidable and the 
innocent party may choose to rescind it. 
 
Similar to duress, however, duress is concerned with pressure while 
undue influence is concerned with whether the innocent party made 
their decision through their own free will. 
 
Types of undue influence: 
1. 
Actual undue influence by overt acts 
2. 
Presumed undue influence as a result of the relationship 
between the parties. 
3. 
Third-party undue influence. 
 
Actual undue influence: 
 
Undue influence must have been a factor for entering into to the 
contract, however, it need not be the only factor. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Presumed undue influence: 
 
Elements of presumed undue influence: 
1. 
A relationship of trust and confidence between the parties. 
2. 
When viewed objectively, the resulting transaction requires an 
explanation 
 
This relationship will be presumed in fiduciary relationships: 
* 
Parent and child 
* 
Two partners in a partnership 
* 
Doctor and patient 
* 
Solicitor and client 
 
In most other situations, the relationship of trust and confidence must 
be proven. – eg. in relation to spouses. 
 
Once it has been established that undue influence should be presumed, 
the burden of proof shifts onto the other party to rebut the 
presumption, proving that there was no undue influence. 
 
Third-party undue influence: 
 
Undue influence need not come from the prospective party to the 
contract but may come from a third party. – eg. if a solicitor wishes to 
enter into a contract with their elderly client, the solicitor's wife may 
unduly influence the client to enter into a contract. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Example: 
Where one person threatens that the other will be harmed, they will 
damage something they own or make them bankrupt. This last one 
is a special form of duress called economic duress. 
Example: 
An elderly woman is told by her daughter to sign a contract in 
relation to a family trust or face legal proceedings. She is afraid of 
her daughter and dislikes confrontation. Even though the threat is 
lawful, the contract will be set aside for undue influence.

pages.heading: ILLEGALITY: · Contracts may be void for illegality. – eg. a contract to carry out criminal
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 23 of 30 
ILLEGALITY: 
 
Contracts may be void for illegality. – eg. a contract to carry out criminal 
behaviour is illegal and void. 
 
Contracts illegal by statute: 
 
Where the contract provides for the performance of an act that is 
against a rule set out in a statute. 
 
Contracts illegal at common law: 
 
* 
Any agreements to commit a crime is illegal. – may also be 
illegal under the act that sets out the crime. 
 * 
Any agreements to commit a tort are also illegal. 
 
* 
Contracts prejudicial to the status of marriage and family life. 
– eg. a contract restricting someone's right to marry or choose 
a partner, a contract where someone charges for finding 
another a marriage partner or a contract for the future divorce 
of a couple. 
 
* 
Contracts prejudicial to public safety. – eg. transactions with an 
enemy country during wartime, contracts damaging to foreign 
relations. 
 
* 
Contracts prejudicial to the proper administration of justice: 
1. 
Contracts to pay witnesses for giving witness evidence 
2. 
Contracts with judges relating to the outcome of a case 
3. 
Any agreements to conceal a crime would be illegal 
4. 
Agreements to undermine the court's jurisdiction 
 
Contracts damaging to the government: 
 
Any agreements to trade with the enemy during war times would be 
illegal. 
 
Restraints of trade clauses: 
 
Restraint of trade = a term in the contract which restricts or limits one 
of the parties in the contract in terms of the business they can conduct 
alongside the contract or once the contract has bene terminated. 
 
As a general rule, restraint of trade clauses inserted into agreements 
or employment contracts are void. 
 
However, the restraint of trade clause may be upheld by the court if it 
only limits trade to the degree it is necessary to protect the legitimate 
business interest of the party wishing to rely on the clause.

pages.heading: MISREPRESENTATION · INTRODUCTION:
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 24 of 30 
 
MISREPRESENTATION 
 
INTRODUCTION: 
 
Misrepresentation = a misleading/false statement made to a party to 
the contract before signing the contract that made then enter into it. 
 
Effect: 
Misrepresentation makes the contract voidable. 
Court may undo the contract by rescission. The remedy of rescission is 
available for all types of misrepresentation. 
 
Rescission = an equitable remedy that takes the innocent party to the 
start before the contract was made. 
 
Distinguish from other statement: 
* 
Mere puff 
* 
Terms 
* 
Representations 
* 
Statements of fact – these are somewhere in between mere 
puff and representations. 
 
ELEMENTS OF MISREPRESENTATION: 
 
Actionable Misrepresentation: 
1. 
Unambiguous – the statement should have only one meaning. 
2. 
False – If the statement is not substantially correct, then it is 
false. 
3. 
Statement of fact/law 
4. 
Addressed to the party misled (directly or indirectly via a third 
party) 
5. 
Induces the contract 
6. 
Causes loss 
 
Statement of fact: 
‘A representation is not an undertaking to do, or not to do something. 
It is a statement asserting a given state of affairs.' 
 
Examples of statements of fact/law: 
 
Conduct: 
* 
Conduct could amount to a statement of fact. 
* 
Deliberate concealment of a defect amounted to a false 
statement of fact if the seller did not disclose the defect. 
 
Opinion: 
* 
Opinion could amount to a statement of fact. 
* 
If the party expressing their opinion is an expert or holds out to 
be an expert, then their opinion will be a statement of fact. 
 
Future intention: 
* 
Future intention is not a fact. 
* 
No duty to inform of change of future intention. 
* 
Dishonest statement of intention will amount to misrep. 
 
Silence: 
Silence cannot be a statement of fact. There is no general duty of 
disclosure. 
 
Exceptions: 
• 
Contracts uberrimae fidei: you must disclose all material 
matter when purchasing insurance. 
• 
Fiduciary relationships: you must disclose the truth even if not 
asked. 
• 
Half-truths = something that is true but gives the wrong 
impression. – Dimmock v Hallett 
• 
Continuing representations = something that is true at the time 
but with the false representation that it will continue to be true. 
 
Is the statement material? 
 
Material statement = statement relating to an issue that would 
influence a reasonable man. 
 
Use the objective test. 
 
If the statement is material – then inducement is inferred. 
 
If a reasonable person would be influenced by this statement, then the 
court will infer that the Claimant was actually induced. 
 
Inducement is inferred unless Defendant can prove Claimant was not 
induced (subjective test). 
 
If the statement is not material – then there was no inducement unless 
the Claimant proves that they were induced (subjective test). 
 
 
 
 
Inducement: 
 
The misrepresentation is only actionable if there was material reliance 
on the false statement by the victim of the misrepresentation. 
 
The misrepresentation statement need not be the only inducement. 
There can be no inducement if the Claimant did not actually see/hear 
the misrepresentation. 
No inducement if the Claimant did not actually rely on the 
misrepresentation when signing the contract. 
 
TYPES OF MISREPRESENTATION: 
 
The reason why a Claimant will argue misrepresentation is because they 
want to get out of the contract (rescission). 
 
Four types: 
1. 
Fraudulent – The tort of deceit 
2. 
Negligent misrepresentation – Misrepresentation Act 1967 
3. 
Innocent misrepresentation – Misrepresentation Act 1967 
4. 
Negligent Misstatement – Tort of negligence, use this is the 
statement was made by a third party. 
 
Fraudulent misrepresentation: 
 
A false representation is made: knowing it was untrue or without 
belief in its truth or reckless as to its truth. 
 
Reckless as to the truth of the statement = the person making the 
statement closing its eyes as to the truth of the statement. 
 
Remedies: 
• 
Rescission, Damages (extensive) and possible indemnity. 
• 
Sometimes rescission is not enough, and damages can be 
claimed. 
• 
Damages for fraudulent misrepresentation are extensive, 
meaning that these damages will put the innocent party back 
into the position before the contract was made. 
• 
If, due to the misrep, the innocent party has accrued 
responsibilities to pay to another party, then they can also claim 
indemnities. 
 
Measure of damages is as for the Tort of deceit: 
 
All loss must be ‘directly flowing' from the transaction 
 
Does not need to be foreseeable. 
 
But cannot be rendered too remote by the Claimant. 
 
Negligent misrepresentation: 
 
The court is willing to make a finding of negligent misrepresentation. 
 
Elements of negligent misrep: 
1. 
False statement 
2. 
No reasonable grounds to believe in its truth 
3. 
No need for actual negligence 
 
Burden of proof is on the Defendant to show reasonable grounds for 
belief, effectively disproving negligence. 
 
Remedies: 
• 
Rescission or that is not possible, then damages are possible in 
lieu of rescission and if applicable, indemnity. 
• 
Calculation of damages is the same as for fraudulent 
misrepresentation. 
• 
Claim losses that flow from the misrepresentation (not the 
same as for fraudulent misrep which calculated on losses that 
flow form the transaction). 
 
Innocent misrepresentation: 
 
The person who made the false statement can prove that they believed 
that the statement was true and they had reasonable grounds to 
believe that the facts represented were true. If this cannot be proved, 
then they will be liable for negligent misrep. 
 
Misrepresentation Act 1967 Burden is on the misrepresentor to prove 
that he: ‘had reasonable grounds to believe up to the time the 
contract was made that the facts represented were true.' 
 
Remedies: 
• 
Rescission or that is not possible, then damages in lieu of 
rescission and if applicable, indemnity. 
• 
However, no right to substantive damages so you cannot claim 
the losses you have accrued. Your best outcome will be 
rescission. 
• 
Must inform the other party of intention to rescind.

pages.heading: Negligent misstatement: · Difficult to prove, only use it if you cannot claim for misrepresentation
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 25 of 30 
 
Negligent misstatement: 
 
Difficult to prove, only use it if you cannot claim for misrepresentation 
and you don't need rescission, only damages. 
 
May also use this claim if the false statement that induced you into the 
contract was not the seller but a third party. 
 
Claimant must prove: Hedley Byrne v Heller 
• 
Reliance reasonably foreseeable 
• 
Relationship of proximity between parties 
 AND 
• 
Fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty 
 
REMEDIES TO MISREPRESENTATION: 
 
Rescission: 
 
Bars to rescission: 
 
* 
Third party rights: If a third party acquired rights in the contract 
innocently, then rescission will not be allowed. 
 
* 
Affirmation: Even if a person doesn't want the contract, they 
can affirm it by conduct indicating that they don't wish to 
rescind. 
 
* 
Impossibility: Court cannot allow for rescission if it is 
impossible. – eg. selling a company that no longer exists. 
 
* 
Lapse of time: Court will not allow for rescission if a long time 
has passed. – eg. 5 years may be too long. 
 
Indemnity: 
 
Indemnity is relevant if, after entering into the contract, the wronged 
party wasted money on a service so this amount is to pay off that party. 
– eg. if you purchase a car under misrep and then you make a contract 
for parking arrangements, you can claim indemnity on the parking 
arrangements. 
 
Indemnity is an equitable remedy.

pages.heading: MISTAKE · INTRODUCTION:
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 26 of 30 
MISTAKE 
 
INTRODUCTION: 
 
Mistake = where one/both parties mistake the subject matter or the 
circumstances of the contract. 
 
Types of mistake 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Effect: 
 
Mistake renders the contract void ab initio. 
 
The parties believed that they have made a contract but there was 
never a contract to begin with. This is different from a contract that is 
voidable, because even if ends up voided, that contract have run from 
the date it was made until the date if was voided. 
 
Mutual and Unilateral mistake – Finding of mistake may mean that 
there was no agreement in fact. 
 
Common mistake – Or it may mean that the mistake destroys the 
nature of the agreement. 
 
The mistaken facts must exist before the conclusion of the contract. 
 
MUTUAL MISTAKE: 
 
There must have been such ambiguity that no agreement could be 
found. 
 
The test for agreement is the objective test. 
 
Raffles v Wichelhaus If the court finds, using the objective test, that 
there was no agreement in the first place, the agreement will have 
never been formed. 
 
COMMON MISTAKE: 
 
Can arise in three ways: 
* 
Res extincta 
* 
Res sua 
* 
Mistake as to whether it is possible to perform the contract 
 
Res extincta: 
 
Galloway v Galloway At the time of the contract, both parties believe 
that the subject matter of the contract exists which is not in fact the 
case. – this is usually the item for sale. 
 
If there is a mistake as to the existence of goods, that will fall within the 
claim of common mistake. 
 
Sale of Goods Act 1979 Where there is a contract for specific goods 
and the goods, without knowledge of the seller, perish, the contract 
is void. 
 
Res sua: 
 
At the time of the contract, the buyer already owns the thing they are 
trying to purchase. 
 
Mistake must be operative and affect an essential fundamental 
quality of the contract. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Examples: 
1. 
There was an auction of napkins that were said to have 
belonged to Charles I. Later it turned out that they were not, so 
their value dropped. 
2. 
There was a painting which was painted by the painter 
Constable, but it turned out to be wrong. No mistake here, as 
the court held, the buyer wanted a painting of a cathedral and 
that is what they have received. 
3. 
There was a ship that was struggling on sea and they made a 
contract with the Great Peace to help the crew. Later it turned 
out that the Great Peace was not as close by as they thought 
they were and wanted to terminate the contract. 
 
Mistake as to possibility of performance: 
 
Sheikh Bros Ltd v Ochsner If both parties believe that a specific land 
should produce a set amount crops each year, and the contract is 
subject to the production of this amount of crops, the contract will be 
void if it later turns out that the land is not physically capable of 
producing that amount of crops. 
 
UNILATERAL MISTAKE: 
 
Unilateral mistake can be made due to the expression of intention or 
the nature of document. 
 
Defence – Non est factum: 
 
Incapacity: where the person signing a document does not understand 
the nature of the document. 
 
If a document is signed by fraud, the party signing will not be held to it. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Fraud cannot be argued if there had been negligence. – eg if A lady has 
lost her glasses prior to signing some documents. The court will find 
that she was negligent and could not argue fraud. 
 
Unilateral mistake as to identity: 
 
Unilateral mistake as to identity = where one person mistakes the 
identity of another. 
Eg. A person misrepresenting their identity when making a purchase on 
credit. 
 
Only the identity of the buyer can be essential to the contract, not 
their credit-worthiness. 
 
Distance sales: 
* 
In distance sales, the identity of the buyer is what is essential 
and so mistake will be allowed. 
* 
Mistake will not be allowed if merely the credit-worthiness of 
the buyer is essential to the contract. 
 
Face-to-face sales: 
* 
Mistake will not be allowed if merely the credit-worthiness of 
the buyer is essential to the contract. 
* 
If the wronged party looked up the identity of the buyer, then 
their identity was essential to the contract. – Unlikely to be 
followed. 
* 
Mistake will not be allowed if merely the credit-worthiness of 
the buyer is essential to the contract. 
Example – Unilateral mistake: 
Where one party to a contract lies about their identity on purpose 
so that the other party would enter into the contract. 
Unilateral 
mistake: Only one 
party is mistaken. 
 
Mutual mistake: 
Both parties are 
mistaken in 
different ways. 
 
Common mistake: 
Both parties are 
mistaken in the 
same way. 
 
Example – Mutual mistake: 
Where one party wants to sell some squash, the vegetable, and the 
other person understands squash, the drink. 
Example – Common mistake: 
Where one party wants to sell a car, but while making the sale, the 
car is burnt down. Both parties are mistaken as to the current state 
of the car. 
Example: 
Lever Bros owned a subsidiary in Nigeria. Mr Bell and Mr Snelling 
were chairman and vice chairman of Lever Bros and they paid them 
to resign as they did not want them to continue to be officers. Later 
the company found out that these officers breached their contracts 
and they could have been fired without payment. The company 
sued claiming mistake. The claim failed. 
Example 2: 
Where someone's son was buying a farm and the father signed a 
document to guarantee that his son will be able to pay for the farm. 
The son actually asked him to sign a guarantee for all of his debts. 
The father was illiterate. 
Example 1: 
A man was senile and could not recognise his own signature. He was 
induced to sign a document by fraud and he was not held to it.

pages.heading: TERMINATION · Every contractual obligation gives rise to a corresponding contractual
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 27 of 30 
TERMINATION 
 
Every contractual obligation gives rise to a corresponding contractual 
right. Thus, where the obligation of one party is discharged, the 
corresponding right of the other party is extinguished. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Where all obligations arising from the contract are discharged, all rights 
are thus extinguished, a contract is discharged. 
 
A contract may be discharged by: 
1. 
Performance 
2. 
Agreement 
3. 
Breach 
4. 
Frustration. 
 
TERMINATION BY PERFORMANCE: 
 
Entire obligations rule: a contractual obligation is discharged by 
complete performance. Where the promisor is unable or unwilling to 
give more than partial performance, there is no discharge of the 
contract – this is the case especially for lump sum contracts. 
 
Exceptions: 
1. 
If partial performance is accepted voluntarily by the innocent 
party, the party in default will be entitled to a quantum meruit. 
He must be compensated for the value of the work done 
without profit. 
 
2. 
If the innocent party has no choice but to accept, no payment 
is due. This may be due to: 
* 
A subsequent binding contract (new contract) 
* 
A term in the original contract (condition precedent or 
condition subsequent) 
 
Condition subsequent: 
A contract may contain a condition subsequent upon 
the occurrence of which obligations are discharged. – 
eg. “If my son dies, the contract is discharged.” If the 
event occurs, the contract is automatically discharged. 
Facts: the term of the contract was that the horse must 
hunt with a prescribed type of hound. 
 
Condition precedent: 
A contract may contain a condition precedent upon the 
occurrence of which obligations would commence – eg. 
“If my son is born, the contract commences.” If the 
event never occurs, the contract never comes into 
existence. 
 
A subsequent binding contract: 
* 
An agreement to discharge is effective if 
supported by consideration, if these obligations 
are wholly executory, then it is a mutual waiver. 
Only relevant if none of the parties started the 
performance. 
* 
Pinnel's case If partially performed, then an 
effective agreement to discharge is a deed on 
accord of satisfaction. Part-payment of debt can 
only 
be 
discharged 
by 
providing 
new 
consideration. 
* 
A simple part-performance does not discharge a 
contract. 
 
3. 
An equitable waiver may discharge a contract in certain 
circumstances. – eg. the cases on promissory estoppel. 
 
4. 
Performing the obligations in a way that was completely 
wrong did not amount to substantial performance. 
 
Other rules: 
 
Divisible obligations will allow the contracted party to receive 
payment for each obligation completed. If the contract sets out that 
each individual obligation will warrant the payment of money, then 
even if not all the obligations are performed, payment will be due. – eg. 
there is a difference between a contract saying: ‘I will pay you if you 
paint five paintings' and ‘I will pay you for each painting.' 
 
Performance by third party is not allowed if the person of the party 
carrying out the contract is important. 
 
TERMINATION BY BREACH: 
 
Breach of contract = Where a party, without lawful excuse fails or 
refuses to perform what is due under the contract or performs 
defectively or incapacitates himself from performing. 
 
Types of breach: 
1. 
Breach of condition: In this case, the innocent party has: 
* 
“Immediate right of election” 
* 
A choice to terminate or affirm the contract 
* 
An also claim damages 
 
2. 
Breach of warranty: In this case, the innocent party has the 
right to sue for damages only. 
 
3. 
Breach of an innominate term: In this case, the innocent party's 
rights will depend on the seriousness of the breach. 
 
Anticipatory breach: 
 
Anticipatory breach = a type of breach whereby prior to performance 
one party informs the other they will not fulfill their obligations. In this 
case, the innocent party should argue frustration. 
 
Anticipatory breach may be express or implied by words or conduct. 
 
Right of election – Affirmation: 
 
When an innocent party is faced with a repudiatory anticipatory breach, 
he is under no obligation to sue at once, but can elect to affirm the 
contract and wait for the time of performance. 
 
The innocent party is allowed a period of time to decide between 
affirmation and termination. If after the affirmation, the other party 
continues to refuse to perform, the innocent party can revoke the 
affirmation and terminate the contract. 
 
Once the decision is made, it must be clear and unequivocal. 
 
Obligations and rights remain on both sides, so the innocent party 
needs to carry out their obligations on their end. 
 
Limitations on affirmation: 
* 
Where the other party's cooperation is required, affirmation 
may not be possible. – eg. to let the other party into the gardens 
to carry out the services. 
* 
Affirmation is only allowed if the affirming party has a 
legitimate interest in affirming the contract. 
* 
Legitimate interest means: not wholly unreasonable. 
* 
The legitimate interest test will only be applied in ‘extreme 
cases'. Extreme cases: where it would be unreasonable to 
affirm and damages would be an adequate remedy. 
 
Risks of affirmation: 
* 
Advise your client on the risks of affirmations. 
* 
Client may subsequently breach the contract and may then be 
sued. 
* 
Client may subsequently frustrate the contract and lose their 
rights to damages. 
 
FRUSTRATION: 
 
Frustration is a defence to a claim of breach of contract. 
 
Before going to look at frustration in a question, go through the part on 
terms of contract where you establish the breach and whether a 
condition or warranty has been breached. Then look at frustration as a 
defence. 
 
Definition of Frustration: Law Reform (Frustrated Contracts) Act 1943 
* 
A supervening event – event arising after the formation of the 
contract 
* 
Unforeseeable 
* 
At no fault of either party 
* 
Which renders the contract impossible/illegal/otherwise 
radically different 
 
Effect of frustration: By operation of law, all future obligations will be 
discharged. 
 
Examples of frustration: 
 
Impossibility: 
 
Destruction of the thing: 
1. 
Destruction of the music hall 
2. 
Destruction of a thing that is closely connected to the contract. 
– eg. the factory, where machinery should have been installed. 
 
 
 
Example: 
Under a contract for the provision of services, software access is 
being provided, the corresponding right is to sue the service 
provider if the software is not provided or if it is not up to standard. 
However, once the obligation is discharged, the corresponding right 
to sue is now extinguished.

pages.heading: Unavailability of a thing: · This is a matter of degree so set out a ration of unavailability.
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 28 of 30 
Unavailability of a thing: 
1. 
This is a matter of degree so set out a ration of unavailability. 
Look at the length of unavailability and how long this is relative 
to the contract. 
2. 
Unavailability for 5 months out of a 1 year contract was able to 
frustrate the contract. 
3. 
There was no time limit in the contract, but the contract implied 
a reasonable time. 
4. 
The time approach is only the starting point of the court. 
 
Unavailability of a person: 
1. 
Incapacity: performer was not able to perform his contract due 
to being called to service. 
2. 
Death 
 
Illegality: 
A contract to do what it has been illegal to do cannot be legally 
enforceable. 
 
Government intervention: 
Where the resources were requisitioned by the government, the 
contract was held to have been frustrated. 
 
Frustration of purpose: 
The ‘Coronation cases' However, it must be the common purpose of 
the parties. 
 
Coronation cases: 
1. 
Krell v Henry (1903) 
Facts: Henry hired a flat to watch the procession for the king's 
coronation. The coronation was cancelled so he did not want to 
pay the rent. The court held that the contract was frustrated. 
Krell advertised the flat to watch the coronation and the flat 
was only for day-time hire so this was evidence of his intention. 
 
2. 
Chandler v Webster (1904) 
Facts: Chandler hired a ship so that they could watch the king 
look at the fleet. The court held that the contract was not 
completely frustrated as the fleet was ‘well worth to look at' by 
itself. 
 
3. 
Herne Bay Steamboat (1903) 
Facts: Cab hire ahead of time to make sure that the hirer could 
get to the racecourse. The court held that the cab did not know 
why they were taking the hirer to the racecourse and do not 
usually ask or care. 
 
Leases: 
* 
Leases can never be frustrated even if someone else is 
occupying it. 
* 
There would be some instances when the lease could become 
frustrated. 
* 
In principle, leases can become frustrated, but the court will 
‘hardly ever' make such a finding. When looking at frustration 
of leases, consider ratio of unavailability to total length of lease. 
 
Not frustration: 
 
Commercial impracticality: 
Frustration cannot be used to defend against commercial 
impracticability. 
Example: Contract to ship ground nuts in November. They were to go 
through the Suez Canal but the canal was being nationalised. If it was 
written in the contract that the ship must go through the Suez Canal, 
then the contract will become frustrated due to impossibility. Also if the 
goods are perishable then the longer route would not work and a claim 
would also succeed on frustration. 
 
‘Self-induced' frustration: 
* 
Contracting without having confirmed outcome on the licencing 
where that is required for the contract is self-induced 
frustration and not upheld by the court. 
* 
If the party in breach exercised a choice in any way, they cannot 
argue frustration. 
 
Event foreseeable: 
* 
Government intervention such as the introduction of new 
legislation may be foreseeable if – eg. there are public 
discussions regarding the intervention. 
* 
If there is a provision in the contract dealing with the event that 
happened, then frustration does not apply. 
* 
Many contracts now contain a force majeure clause which lists 
common intervening events and suspends the contract on one 
of the events listed. Other contracts also contain a price 
variation clause. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Consequences of frustration: 
 
At common law: 
 
Claiming consideration: 
 
In cases of partial failure of consideration, money that has already 
been paid cannot be claimed back. 
Partial failure of consideration = cases where parts of the contract 
were satisfied. 
If there was additional consideration provided, then the full amount will 
be due. 
 
In cases of total failure of consideration, the amount paid is 
recoverable. 
 
Expenses: 
 
Expenses incurred before the frustrating event: recoverable only at the 
court's ddiscretion, however, they must have been incurred in 
preparation for the performance of the contract. 
 
Expenses incurred after the frustrating event: no recoverable. 
 
Legislation: 
 
If either party achieved a valuable benefit after the frustrating event 
then a ‘just sum' may be awarded. – eg. in a building contract, although 
the building works were not finished, the job was partially completed 
which the hirer will not have. 
 
Calculate the price of the valuable benefit and the courts will decide 
what would be fair to award in the circumstances. The courts have a 
wide discretion.

pages.heading: REMEDIES · ACTING FOR THE CLAIMANT:
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 29 of 30 
REMEDIES 
 
ACTING FOR THE CLAIMANT: 
 
Damages that a Claimant may claim: 
1. 
Liquidated damages and penalties 
2. 
Compensation 
 
Liquidated damages and penalties: 
 
Liquidated damages = where the parties agree on the damages in case 
of a breach beforehand and set it out in the contract. 
 
If this happens, the contract will set out a specific sum which they can 
pay in case of a breach. If the party in breach refuses to pay, the court 
will enforce this sum of money. 
 
This is beneficial as the parties will know what to expect and this 
reduces the risk of potentially paying out a higher amount than what 
have been agreed. This will also ensure that both parties can take out 
insurance. 
 
Penalty clauses: 
Liquidated damages clauses could be struck out if they are found to be 
a penalty clause. 
 
Legitimate interest test: Ask if the detriment to the contract breaker is 
out of proportion to the legitimate interest of the other party. Look at 
this in the context of the agreement. You will need to find a legitimate 
interest of the party for the clause and it will be valid if proportionate. 
 
Compensation: 
 
If there is no valid liquidated damages clause, then ‘unliquidated 
damages' will be calculated. 
 
The aim in the UK is compensation, not punishment. – the Claimant 
cannot profit from the claim. 
 
Damages aim to put the innocent party into the position they would 
have been in had the contract been performed. 
 
A Claimant can claim either: 
* 
Expectation loss 
* 
Reliance loss 
 OR 
* 
Restitution 
 
Expectation loss: 
 
Damages aim to put the innocent party into the position they would 
have been in had the contract been performed. – Forward looking 
measure, where the Claimant has suffered a loss of expectation. 
 
Three different measures: 
1. 
Difference in value – eg. because of the contract, you have now 
lost out on money. Having a car worth £3,000 but the car would 
have been worth £5,000 due to the contract, the innocent party 
can be awarded £2,000 to reflect the diminution of value. 
2. 
Cost of cure – eg. an amount awarded to reflect how much it 
would cost to fix the defect. 
3. 
Loss of amenity – eg. an amount awarded to reflect the fact that 
the Claimant lost access to something. 
 
Ask for the highest amount and any other available options in the 
alternative. 
 
The court may award loss of amenity if the money to remedy the 
defect would be disproportionate for the benefit achieved by fixing 
the problem. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Other examples: 
• 
Farley wanted a peaceful country residence and contracted 
Skinner to find the ideal property for him. Once he moved in, he 
realised that the area was very noisy due to airplanes constantly 
landing nearby. He was also awarded a loss of amenity. 
 
• 
Loss of amenity is not available in a commercial context. 
 
• 
McGlinn demolished a property built with cosmetic defects, he 
then rebuilt it and sued for cost of cure. This was seen as 
excessive and only loss of amenity was awarded. 
 
Reliance loss: 
* 
These losses aim to put the innocent party back in the position 
had they not made the contract. – Backward looking measure. 
* 
The Claimant may have lost money relying on the proper 
performance of the contract. 
* 
You cannot use reliance loss to get out of a bad bargain. 
* 
Losses that are too speculative will not be allowed under this 
head of loss. Calculating the amount a Claimant could have 
made from a project is too speculative and such compensation 
will not be allowed. 
* 
Pre-contractual expenses could be allowed by the court if any. 
 
Restitution: 
* 
A measure depriving the contract breaker from their profits if 
they made profits from breaching the contract. 
* 
Restitution is only available in exceptional circumstances, 
where contractual damages would be inadequate. 
* 
If you breach your contract as you would make a better deal 
elsewhere, this is allowed, as long as you pay damages. 
 
Damages for mental distress: 
 
This is generally not available. 
The innocent party will always be upset when a contract is breached. 
 
Exception: 
If the contract was for pleasure/relaxation/peace of mind. 
Pleasure/relaxation/peace of mind must have at least been a ‘major 
object of the contract'. 
 
Loss of reputation: 
Claims for loss of reputation can be allowed. 
 
Loss of chance: 
Losing the chance of winning can be claimed. 
 
Quantum meruit: 
Paying for partially completed work will usually be only paying for work 
that had been done. 
 
ACTING FOR THE DEFENDANT: 
 
Limiting damages: 
1. 
Causation – D might agree to a breach but argue that the loss 
was not caused by the breach 
2. 
Remoteness – D might agree that the loss was caused by his 
breach but the loss was too remote 
3. 
Mitigation – D might agree that the loss was caused by his 
breach but claim that C did not mitigate which could have 
reduced its losses. 
4. 
Contributory Negligence – D might argue that his breach of 
contract was due to negligence and may then say that C was 
also negligent so he is not responsible for all the damage 
caused. 
 
Causation: 
 
There must be a causal link between the breach of contract and the 
loss claimed. 
 
The breach must be an effective cause of the loss. 
 
If there is a novus actus interveniens (break in the chain of causation), 
the cause that happened closer to the loss will be deemed to cause it. 
 
Example: A farmer had a trailer which had a faulty coupling. Because of 
this, it went on the other side of the road and caused an accident. The 
farmer argued that the loss was caused by the breach of contract by the 
manufacturer of the trailer. 
 
Held: The loss was not caused by the manufacturers as the farmer knew 
that the trailer was broken when he decided to use it. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Example: 
Mr Forsyth wanted to get a swimming pool built and contracted 
some builders. He wanted the pool to be 7 foot 6 inches deep. When 
the works were completed, it turned out to be 6 foot 9 inches deep 
only. 
 
Contract price 
 
£20,000 
Cost of cure 
 
£21,560 
Difference in value 
£0 – he wouldn't get more money for 
a deeper pool 
Loss of amenity 
 
£2,500 
 
Held: The court was not sure if he was going to use the money to 
remedy the defect. The amount awarded this way would have also 
been disproportionate for the benefit achieved by making the 
swimming pool deeper.

pages.heading: Remoteness: · Some losses are too remote.
pages.text:
Contract law – SQE Prep Book | Page 30 of 30 
Remoteness: 
 
Some losses are too remote. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Hadley v Baxendale When looking at remoteness of a loss, apply the 
two-limb test. 
 
Two-limb test: 
1. 
C can claim for a loss arising naturally in the usual course of 
things. 
Imputed knowledge is required (objective) – eg. mill owners 
should be expected to keep a second mill shaft. 
 
2. 
Reasonably in the contemplation of both parties 
Actual knowledge (subjective) – What did the parties actually 
know about? The claimants in this case should have told the 
defendants at the time of contracting that they did not have 
another mill shaft. 
 
Must be in the contemplation of both parties at the time of 
contracting. 
 
The second limb is not satisfied if the other party to the contract did not 
know about the big contract coming up. 
 
Was the loss one which was ‘not unlikely' to occur? If the loss occurred 
because of a drop in market prices, this was deemed to be 
unforeseeable. 
 
Mitigation: 
 
Strictly speaking no obligation to mitigate, but losses resulting from 
failure to mitigate are unrecoverable. 
 
Only reasonable steps are required to mitigate. 
 
No need to litigate to mitigate. 
 
If cost-effective, innocent party may need to renegotiate the contract. 
 
Mitigation not ‘weighed in nice scales'. Court will not expect the 
innocent party to count pennies. 
 
Contributory negligence: 
 
Contributory negligence may be available if the other party or a third 
party was also negligent and their negligence contributed to the 
damages caused. 
 
Contributory negligence is available where there is: 
i. 
Breach of a contractual duty 
 AND 
ii. 
The breach is also a tort 
 
EQUITABLE REMEDIES: 
 
Specific Performance: 
 
Specific performance = compelling one of the parties to perform their 
obligations under the contract. 
 
Only granted in rare cases and when damages would be insufficient. 
 
Specific performance will not be granted if: 
1. 
Performance would cause undue hardship/unfairness to the 
party in breach 
2. 
Consideration agreed in return for performance is inadequate 
3. 
The innocent party themselves has outstanding obligations 
under the agreement. 
4. 
The contract is an employment contract/contract for personal 
services – the court will not force a person to work for someone. 
5. 
The order would require court supervision. 
 
 
Injunction: 
 
To stop a person from doing something. – eg. prohibiting a party from 
contracting customers. 
 
Rescission: 
 
Rescinds the contract as if it never existed. 
 
Rectification: 
 
If there is a mistake in the contractual document, the court can correct 
the correct it to reflect the true intentions of the parties. 
 
INDEMNITIES AND GUARANTEES: 
 
Indemnities: 
 Indemnity = a contractual obligation by which one party agrees to keep 
another protected from a specific loss. 
 
Liability under an indemnity arises not because of a breach but because 
the parties have stipulated that one shall pay another in specified 
circumstances. 
Eg. if A is sued because of the low quality of the product provided by B, 
B indemnifies A for the lawsuit. 
 
The scope of an indemnity will depend on its wording. 
 
EE Caledonia Ltd v Orbit Valve Co Europe Indemnities do not commonly 
cover losses caused by negligence as this is deemed to be unfair under 
the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977. 
 
Guarantees: 
 Guarantee = a contractual promise made by the guarantor to ensure 
that another person, who is a party to the contract will perform their 
obligations. 
 
UNJUST ENRICHMENT (RESTITUTION): 
 
Restitution = restoring the payment of a sum under a contract where 
the contract was never performed. 
 
Restitution is a concept that is separate from contract law. Restitution 
exists to prevent unjust enrichment. 
 
Unjust enrichment = one party has obtained a benefit at the expense of 
another by mistake, duress or undue influence. 
 
Restitution could be an alternative to contractual damages, however, it 
only applies once the contract has been set aside. Restitution is only 
awarded if other remedies are inadequate. 
 
Requirements: *Awarded to innocent parties only* 
1. 
Innocent party shows a legitimate interest in preventing the 
other party from keeping any of the profits. 
2. 
The other party must have been enriched/benefited 
3. 
The enrichment must have been at the expense of the innocent 
party 
4. 
The enrichment must have been unjust 
5. 
There are no defences. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Remedies: 
* 
Money or property 
 OR 
* 
An order that the party in breach returns any gains they have 
made to the innocent party 
 OR 
* 
If restitution in relation to services: quantum meruit award – an 
order requiring payment of reasonable remuneration for the 
works carried out. 
 OR 
* 
If restitution in relation to goods: quantum valebat award. 
Examples: 
1. 
Work has been carried out but there was no contract 
2. 
One party failed to provide consideration – eg. because one 
of the parties terminated the contract before they have done 
anything at all. 
3. 
If a contract is only partially performed, the innocent party 
then accepts partial performance, however, no price is 
actually agreed 
4. 
Money paid out by mistake 
5. 
Rescinding a contract where there is an outstanding amount 
remaining with the wrong party 
6. 
Transfer of property due to threat/pressure 
7. 
Undue influence 
Example: 
If you fall asleep while driving and drive into another car causing an 
accident, then even if no one dies, the other driver might end up in 
hospital. 
 
Because he broke an arm and was in hospital, he was not able to do 
his job as a shelf stacker at Tesco. 
 
Because he was not able to work, he lost out on money and was not 
able to buy his daughter a textbook she needed to study Contract 
law. 
 
Because she did not get the book, she failed the class and gave up 
on studying law. At some point, these losses will be too remote.
