COURTROOM ETIQUETTE: 
 
* 
Solicitors to wear a formal attire: a dark suit, formal shoes, light 
coloured shirt and modest jewellery. 
 
* 
Solicitor advocates must also wear a gown, collar and bands but 
will not wear a wig. 
 
* 
Electronic devices must be turned off. – a solicitor using a mobile 
phone during a hearing may attract contempt of court 
proceedings. 
 
* 
Do not eat/drink in court 
 
* 
Bow to the judge when entering/leaving the courtroom 
 
* 
Wait until your turn to speak 
 
* 
Refer to the judge by the correct mode of address 
 
* 
Refer to your opponent as ‘my friend'. 
 
COURT ORDERS: 
 
Court order = an official court decision in relation to either a procedural 
or a directional issue. This includes a decision either that one/more of 
the parties do or refrain from doing a specified action. 
 
In most cases the terms judgment and order are used interchangeably. 
 
Types of orders: 
 
A court order may be interim or final. 
 
Order may be made by: 
* 
The operation of the CPR – Deemed orders 
* 
By the court

pages.heading: By the consent of the parties – these are called consent orders · where the parties agree on an outcome and the court makes an
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE notes | Page 16 of 24 
* 
By the consent of the parties – these are called consent orders 
where the parties agree on an outcome and the court makes an 
order to give effect to this. 
 
Deemed orders: 
 
These orders arise by operation of the CPR, rather than a decision of 
the court. 
 
This could be an order setting out that costs are to be paid on a 
standard basis and this would arise in the following situations: 
 
* 
The claim is struck out because the court fees have not been 
paid. – CPR 3.7A 
 
* 
The claim is struck out because the court fees have been paid 
by cheque, however, the cheque is dishonoured. – CPR 3.7B 
 
* 
A Part 36 offer is accepted by one of the parties. – CPR 36.13 
 
* 
The claimant discontinued the claim. – CPR 38.6 
 
For a deemed order to apply, the parties do not need to draft an order 
for this to be enforceable. 
 
Court orders: 
 
The parties may prepare draft orders and send them to the court for 
approval or consideration, however, in most cases, the court has the 
final say as to what goes into the order. 
 
When making an interim application, it is best practice to attach the 
draft order to your application so that the court can consider it and the 
order sought becomes clear. 
 
CPR 40.3 The court will be responsible for drawing up every judgment/ 
order except where: 
* 
The court makes an order for one of the parties to draw it up. 
* 
One of the parties agree to draw it up for the court, with the 
court's permission. 
* 
The court dispenses with the need for an order to be officially 
drawn up. 
* 
The order is a consent order. 
 
CPR 40.7 A judgment/order is effective from the day when it was made 
or a later date, as specified in the order. 
 
Consent orders: 
 
Consent Orders = stay the proceedings on agreed terms. 
 
CPR 40.6(2) An officer of the court may seal a consent order if: 
* 
The judgment/order is an order listed in CPR 40.6(3). 
* 
All of the parties are legally represented. 
 OR 
* 
The CPR/legislation so requires. 
 
 
Tomlin orders – used for confidentiality. This type of order will have a 
public part and a private schedule so specific matters can be kept 
confidential) 
 
Deadline for compliance: 
 
CPR 40.11 The deadline for compliance with a judgment/order where it 
includes the payment of money (including costs), this must be made 
within 14 days of the date of the judgment/order if it is not specified 
on the judgment/order. 
 
If the payment is not made within this time, steps may be taken to 
enforce the judgment. 
 
Exceptions: 
* 
If the judgment/order includes a different date, then that date 
must be followed. 
* 
If the CPR specifies a different deadline. 
* 
If the court has stayed the proceedings/judgment. 
 
Payment by instalment or foreign currency: 
 
CPR 40B.12 If the judgment/order is to be paid by instalments, then 
the judgment/order should include the following: 
* 
The full amount payable and the amount of each instalment. 
* 
The number of instalments 
* 
When to pay each instalment 
* 
Who should receive the payments 
 
CPR 40B.10 If the judgment/order is to be in a foreign currency, the 
judgment/order should include the following wording: 
 
“It is ordered that the defendant pay the claimant (state the sum in the 
foreign currency) or the Sterling equivalent at the time of payment.”

pages.heading: PART 36 OFFERS AND SETTLEMENT · SETTLEMENT (NON-PART 36):
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE notes | Page 17 of 24 
PART 36 OFFERS AND SETTLEMENT 
 
SETTLEMENT (NON-PART 36): 
 
Enforcement: 
 
By court orders: 
• 
Dismiss the claim – stops the Claimant from suing on same issue 
again 
• 
Discontinue claim – the Claimant may sue on same issue again 
• 
Make a consent order – eg. Tomlin order 
 
By a settlement agreement: 
• 
If settlement agreed after Claim Form issued, must notify court 
 
• 
To enforce: 
1. 
Sue for breach of contract, apply for summary judgment 
2. 
If a consent order exists: enforce terms of order in 
addition to breach of settlement agreement. 
 
• 
For confidentiality – use Tomlin orders (this type of order will 
have a public part and a private schedule so specific matters can 
be kept confidential) 
 
Part 36 vs Settlement agreements: 
 
 
SETTLEMENT AGREEMENTS 
 
PART 36 OFFERS 
 
 
* 
No court involvement 
* 
May set own terms for costs, 
although the usual cost rules 
still apply 
* 
Time limits are set by the 
settlement 
agreement 
terms 
* 
May pay in instalments 
* 
No damages award 
 
 
* Court may be involved. – eg. for 
withdrawal which needs court 
permission. 
* Court decides costs consequences 
* Time limit is set = 21 days 
* Must be lump sum 
* If a reasonable offer is refused, 
bonus damages award. 
 
 
PROCEDURE FOR PART 36 OFFERS: 
 
Purpose of Part 36 offers: Financial incentives for opponent to settle. 
When to make a Part 36 offers: at any time, even prior to commencing 
proceedings. 
 
Part 36 offers are treated as ‘without prejudice'. 
 
A Part 36 offer must: 
a. 
Be in writing – eg. in a letter, email. 
b. 
Be clear that it is an offer made under Part 36 
c. 
Must refer to the Relevant period, a period during which the 
offer is open. The offer must be open for a minimum of 21 days. 
 AND 
d. 
Must state if it relates to all/part of the claim and whether it 
includes any counterclaim. 
 
If the above criteria is not satisfied the offer will not amount to a Part 
36 offer. 
 
D must pay within 14 days of deemed service of notice. 
 
VARIATIONS TO A PART 36 OFFER: 
 
If accepted 
the offer, 
cannot 
withdraw 
 
If rejects the 
offer, offer 
remains 
open. 
 
If offer not yet accepted: 
 
1. Before expiry of relevant period: 
 
- Withdrawals need court's permission. 
- Offeror may amend offer only if there is a 
change in circumstances or the interests of 
justice requires amendment: 
 If makes offer less advantageous to offeree, 
the offeror must serve a notice 
 If makes offer more advantageous to 
offeree, it will be treated as a new Part 36 
offer with a new relevant period. 
 
Variation takes effect at end of relevant period. 
If offeree doesn't accept original offer, offeror must 
apply for court's permission to vary or withdraw 
within 7 days of notice of acceptance. 
 
2. After expiry of relevant period: 
Offeror can withdraw or amend at any time 
 
 
 
 
CONSEQUENCES OF REJECTING A PART 36 OFFER: 
 
Structure: 
 
General rule on costs: 
Unsuccessful party pays successful party's costs 
If a Part 36 offer is rejected, court may penalize rejecting party. 
 
Who is the offeror and the offeree? 
Identify the correct heading to use based on who makes the offer 
(offeror) in your scenario. 
 
Compare offer to trial award: 
Identify if the trial award is same, more or less than the offer. 
What is the offer amount and trial amount? 
Eg. Offer = £3,000, Trial award = £5,000, thus final award at trial is more 
than the offer. 
 
Claimant's offer: 
Later the Claimant wins same or more at trial = at least as advantageous 
award 
Later the Claimant wins less at trial = less advantageous award 
 
Defendant's offer: 
Later the Claimant wins same or less at trial = same or less advantageous 
award 
Later the Claimant wins more = more advantageous award 
 
Claimant's offer, Defendant rejects: 
 
Claimant wins same or more at trial (at least as advantageous): 
 
Eg: Claimant's offer = £3,000, Defendant rejects 
Later the Claimant wins £3,000 at trial OR they win more than £3,000 at 
trial 
 
If the Claimant awarded same or more at trial than the offer, the 
Defendant will be punished as he was unreasonable to reject (now 
wasted time/costs). 
 
Penalty for the Defendant for period between end of relevant period 
and trial. 
 
D will pay: 
1. Damages + own costs 
2. Normal costs rules: the Defendant pays all of the Claimant's 
costs until trial. 
3. Penalty. Court's discretion (can decide not to penalize if unjust) 
Maximum penalty: 
- 
Indemnity on costs 
- 
Interest on sums awarded (max 10% interest rate) 
- 
Max 10% of damages awarded up to £75,000 
 
 
 
 Normal costs rules: D pays C's costs 
 Penalty for D 
 
 
 
Claimant wins less at trial (less advantageous): 
 
Eg: Claimant's offer = £3,000, Defendant rejects 
Later the Claimant wins £1,000 at trial 
 
D was reasonable to reject the offer so no penalty. 
 
D will pay: 
1. 
Damages + own costs 
2. 
Normal costs rules: the Defendant pays all of the Claimant's 
costs until trial. 
 
Claimant loses: 
 
The party losing the trial pays to the winner (normal rule). 
The Defendant (winner) will get paid its costs by the Claimant (loser). 
 
The Claimant will pay: 
1. Own costs 
2. Normal costs rules: the Claimant pays all of the Defendant's 
costs until trial.

pages.heading: Defendant's offer, Claimant rejects: · Claimant wins same or less at trial (same or less advantageous):
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE notes | Page 18 of 24 
 
Defendant's offer, Claimant rejects: 
 
Claimant wins same or less at trial (same or less advantageous): 
 
Eg: Defendant's offer = £3,000, Claimant rejects 
Later C wins £3,000 at trial OR C wins less than £3,000 at trial 
 
If Claimant awarded same or less at trial than the offer, the Claimant will 
be punished as they were unreasonable to reject (now wasted 
time/costs). 
 
 ‘Split costs' order: 
1. 
Until relevant period expiry date: the Defendant pays the 
Claimant's costs 
2. 
From relevant period expiry to trial date: the Claimant pays the 
Defendant's costs + interest on costs 
 
The Claimant will get awarded damages but will pay: 
1. 
Own costs 
2. 
‘Split costs' order 
 
 
 D pays C's costs C pays D's costs 
 C pays interest on costs 
 
 
 
 
Claimant wins more at trial (more advantageous): 
 
Eg: Defendant's offer = £3,000, Claimant rejects 
Later C wins £5,000 at trial 
 
The Claimant was reasonable to reject the offer so no penalty. 
 
The Defendant will pay: 
1. 
Damages + own costs 
2. 
Normal costs rules: the Defendant pays all of the Claimant's 
costs until trial. 
 
Claimant loses: 
 
The Claimant was unreasonable to reject the offer. 
 
The Claimant will pay: 
1. 
Normal costs rules: the Claimant (unsuccessful party) pays the 
Defendant's costs. 
2. 
From relevant period expiry to trial date: the Claimant pays 
interest on the Defendant's costs 
3. 
Penalty. Court's discretion (can decide not to penalize if unjust) 
 
 
 
 Normal costs rules: C pays D's costs 
 C pays interest on costs 
 C pays penalty

pages.heading: INTERIM APPLICATIONS · INTRODUCTION:
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE notes | Page 19 of 24 
INTERIM APPLICATIONS 
 
INTRODUCTION: 
 
Applicant = party making the interim application 
Respondent = party against which the application is submitted 
 
Interim applications may be made by either party to the court after 
commencing claim for court orders. – so may be made by the Claimant 
or Defendant. 
 
CPR 1 The overriding objective dictates that costs are to be kept at a 
minimum. Therefore, prior to making any applications to the court, the 
parties should communicate and attempt to resolve any questions they 
may have between themselves. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
PROCEDURE: 
 
This is the procedure we use for interim applications except for summary 
judgments (which has its own procedure timeline), so do use these 
procedures for security for costs applications and all injunctions. 
 
Interim applications may be made: 
1. 
‘With notice': give notice of application to the other party or 
2. 
‘Without notice': Respondent does not find out about the 
application until court makes decision 
 
With notice or without notice? 
 
When to make an application without notice? 
* 
Urgent matter – eg. Freezing injunctions, or protecting 
confidential information from disclosure 
* 
There must be good reasons for not giving notice: such as 
purpose of application is defeated by giving notice etc. freezing 
orders. 
 OR 
* 
There are exceptional circumstances 
 
By not having notice of the application, the Respondent is essentially 
denied an opportunity to present opposing arguments or defend 
application. 
 
Because of inherent unfairness, applicant's duty of full and frank 
disclosure of all material facts (Favourable or adverse) 
 
With notice application procedure: 
 
1. 
Issue the following at court: 
 
Application notice (N244) with the fee 
 
Draft order 
 
Evidence: 
a. 
Claim Form and statements of case. 
b. 
For Interim Prohibitory injunctions only: 
Witness statement 
 
 
Skeleton arguments (only if High Court) 
 
2. 
Applicant serves on Respondent: all above docs 
Min 3 days before hearing 
(For Freezing Order: serve the bank and other 3rd parties first) 
 
3. 
Respondent serves: Evidence in Response 
ASAP = no time limit 
 
4. 
Applicant serves: Evidence in Reply 
ASAP = no time limit 
 
5. 
Both file: Statements of Costs 
Min 24 hours before hearing 
 
For Freezing Orders: 
The Respondent may make an application to vary before the on 
notice hearing or at the on notice hearing 
 
Grounds for a discharge/variation: 
1. 
The order should not have been made. 
2. 
Respondent has provided the required security. 
3. 
The applicant is guilty of non-disclosure. 
4. 
There has been a procedural irregularity. 
 
6. 
Interim hearing 
 
7. 
The order will be served on the parties together with any 
relevant 3rd parties (for Freezing orders: serve on the banks and 
the applicant should go ahead and obtain a bank guarantee in 
support for the undertaking to pay damages) 
 
Without notice application procedure: 
 
1. 
Issue at court: 
* 
N244 Application Notice 
* 
Draft Order: that the applicant wishes the court would 
make 
 
* 
Evidence: 
a. 
Claim Form 
b. 
Full and frank disclosure 
c. 
For Security for costs and IPI: 
Witness statement or Affidavit 
 
* 
Statement of Costs 
* 
Claim Form 
 
In urgent cases, the application notice and evidence can be filed 
with the court on the same or next working day. 
 
2. 
‘Without Notice' Hearing: 
If extreme urgency: telephone hearing. 
 
3. 
If granted, Applicant serves on Respondent: 
* 
Claim Form 
* 
Application Notice 
* 
Copy of Court Order 
* 
Evidence in support of application 
* 
Statement of Costs 
* 
Guarantee supporting undertaking in damages 
* 
Notice of without notice hearing with Respondent's 
right to appeal 
 
4. 
‘With notice' hearing: the court may maintain, discharge the 
order or make an order to pay damages 
 
Interim hearing costs order: 
1. 
Costs in any event: 
* 
Successful party in interim application recovers costs of 
interim application, regardless of who wins at trial. The 
costs recovered run from the date when interim 
application was issued up until the interim application 
hearing. 
* 
If a costs in any event order is made, costs will be 
assessed summarily 
 
2. 
Costs in the case: 
* 
The party who gets his costs at trial will recover its costs 
of the interim application from the other party. 
* 
Interim hearing costs = same as end of trial costs – Argue 
costs in the case if loses application or the judge criticises 
your case. 
 
3. 
No order as to costs: 
* 
Each party bears its own costs at the hearing. 
* 
Awarded when the judge is critical of both parties. 
 
SUMMARY JUDGMENT: 
 
Summary judgment = court decides the claim or issue without a full trial. 
 
SJ is brought for weak cases (no defence or no case), contrast this with 
Judgment in default where the basis is failure to comply with procedural 
rules. 
 
When to apply? 
 
If the Claimant applies: 
After the Defendant served an Acknowledgement of Service or Defence 
up until the trial date, unless the court gives permission to make the 
application before then. 
 
If the Defendant applies: 
Anytime after the commencement of proceedings up until the trial date. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Example: 
 
When the Defendant files their Defence in response to the Particulars 
of Claim, it fails to correctly respond to the allegations in full and the 
Claimant struggles to understand it. 
 
 While a strike out application could be relevant, prior to making an 
application, the Claimant should reach out to the Defendant and 
request further information under CPR 18. If the Defendant fails to 
adequately respond, only then a strike out application should be 
considered.

pages.heading: Grounds: *Take into account overriding objective* · 1. Claimant/Defendant has no real prospect of succeeding on
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE notes | Page 20 of 24 
Grounds: *Take into account overriding objective* 
 
1. Claimant/Defendant has no real prospect of succeeding on 
claim/issue 
 AND 
2. No other compelling reason why case should be disposed of at 
trial: 
Compelling reasons: 
- 
Disputed facts and needs time to investigate 
- 
Very complex case 
- 
Right to trial by jury 
- 
Needs to contact witnesses 
 
Outcomes: 
 
Claimant obtains SJ – Judgment on claim/certain issue. 
General rule on costs at end of trial. 
 
Defendant obtains SJ – Dismissal on claim/certain issue = struck 
out 
 
Dismissal of SJ application – claim continues. 
 
Conditional order – claim may continue if conditions are met. 
 
Procedure: 
 
1. 
Issue the following at court: 
 
Application notice (N244) with the fee 
 
Draft order 
 
Evidence (Witness statement) 
 
2. 
Applicant serves on Respondent: all above docs 
Min 14 days before hearing 
 
 
3. 
Respondent serves: Evidence in Response 
Min 7 days before the hearing 
 
4. 
Applicant serves: Evidence in Reply 
Min 3 days before the hearing 
 
5. 
Both file: Statements of Costs 
Min 24 hours before hearing 
 
6. 
Interim hearing 
 
SECURITY FOR COSTS: 
 
Security for costs = Applications made by the Defendant if it has reason 
to believe that the Claimant does not have sufficient funds to meet the 
costs of the action should the claim be successfully defended (security 
for costs, but not damages). 
 
Use a without notice application procedure. 
 
Grounds: CPR 25.13 
1. 
It is just to make an order, considering all the circumstances of 
the case: 
Balances injustice to the Claimant (right of access to courts) and 
injustice to the Defendant (the need for financial security). 
 
Factors when applying balancing act: 
(a) Respondent's claim = bona fide/not a sham 
If respondent has reasonably good prospects of success 
or the Defendant has admitted liability = likely to be bona 
fide – eg. seeking payment of unpaid invoice = bona fide 
 
(b) D using application oppressively to stifle a genuine 
claim? 
 
Claimant to prove stifling 
 
Court may look at the financial resources of 
parties 
 
Court considers if Respondent can raise money 
from other sources. 
 
D is keen to avoid payment, whilst the Claimant appears 
to have a genuine claim and will potentially be unable to 
pursue that claim if security for costs is ordered. 
 
(c) Delay in making the application? Make the application 
asap. If delayed, reduction/refusal of security for costs. 
 
(d) Does the Respondent have financial difficulties because 
D's actions? 
 
2. 
The Respondent is able to comply with an order for security for 
costs. – The court will not make an order in vain. If the 
Respondent cannot comply with the order, an order is unlikely. 
 
3. 
The court will take into account the overriding objective, which 
sets out the need to deal with the case justly and at a 
proportionate cost to make the order. 
 
 AND 
4. 
At least one condition evidencing the need for an order for 
security for costs apply. 
 
These conditions are as follows: 
 
1. 
The Claimant is a resident out of the jurisdiction but not 
in a state that is bound by the Hague Convention, and 
as a result, it would be difficult to enforce a judgment of 
the English courts if made against the Claimant. 
 
2. 
The Claimant is a company and there is reason to believe 
it will be unable to pay the Defendant's costs if ordered 
to do so. – eg. Limited company and annual accounts or 
newspaper suggest financial difficulties. 
 
D must prove company will not be able to pay not just 
that it may not be able to pay, however, a reason to 
believe is sufficient. This is assessed at the time of 
application but also considering future expectation. 
 
3. 
The Claimant is a nominal claimant (acting on behalf of 
someone else) and there is reason to believe that they 
will be unable to pay the Defendant's costs if ordered to 
do so. 
 
4. 
The Claimant has changed their address since the claim 
began, in the hope to evade a potential judgment. 
 
5. 
The Claimant has not provided their address on the 
Claim Form or provided an incorrect address. 
 
6. 
The Claimant has taken some steps in relation to their 
assets which make it difficult to enforce a potential costs 
order. 
 
The court is not obliged to make an order, even if all the grounds are 
satisfied. 
 
Awards: 
Court's discretion whether or not it makes an order and must consider 
if Respondent realistically able to raise the amount. 
 
Potential orders: 
 
Pay sum into court or give some other form of security 
 
Pay sum to applicant's solicitor 
 
Undertaking to pay D's costs if ordered to do so. 
 
INTERIM PAYMENTS: 
 
The Claimant may make an application for an order requiring the 
Defendant to make a payment to the Claimant in the interim, without a 
judgment made at trial. – CPR 25.6-25.9 
 
This is typically made in relation to personal injury claims and requires 
the Defendant to make a payment in the interim to help the Claimants 
with their costs relating to their injuries so that they can continue with 
their treatment. 
 
An interim payment must only be a reasonable proportion of the whole 
amount likely to be awarded at trial. 
 
Grounds: CPR 25.7 
 
* 
The Defendant must have admitted liability in relation to the 
damages due to the Claimant or some other sum of money. 
 
* 
The Defendant has a judgment entered against them in favour 
of the Claimant for damages or a sum of money (except for costs) 
to be assessed. 
 
 OR 
* 
It is satisfied that, should the claim proceed to trial, the Claimant 
would obtain a substantial amount of damages from the 
Defendant – the Defendant may be the sole Defendant or one of 
a number of Defendants. 
 
APPLICATION FOR SPECIFIC DISCLOSURE: 
 
An order made when standard disclosure has not resulted in the 
disclosure of a specific document that is relevant to the case. – CPR 
31.12 
 
Grounds: 
 The Applicant must show that it is necessary that the Respondent: 
* 
Discloses documents or classes of documents specified in the 
order. 
* 
Carries out a search to the extent set out in the order. 
 OR 
* 
Discloses any documents found

pages.heading: PRE-ACTION DISCLOSURE: · An order made before the proceedings have commenced to obtain
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE notes | Page 21 of 24 
PRE-ACTION DISCLOSURE: 
 
An order made before the proceedings have commenced to obtain 
certain documents or information from the prospective Defendant. – 
CPR 31.16 
 
The test of pre-action disclosure: 
* 
The Applicant and Respondent are prospective parties to an 
anticipated claim. 
* 
Had the proceedings began, the Respondent would have a duty 
under the test of standard disclosure to disclose the documents 
or classes of documents sought by this application. 
 AND 
* 
An order for pre-action disclosure is necessary to dispose of the 
anticipated proceedings fairly, to aid settlement or to otherwise 
save costs. 
 
ORDER TO CALL A WITNESS TO GIVE EVIDENCE AT 
TRIAL: 
 
An order allowing a party to call a specific witness to give oral evidence 
at trial where no witness statement or witness summary was served in 
relation to this specific witness within the prescribed time limits. 
 
Factors the court will take into account: CPR 32.10 Foster 
* 
What is the reason why evidence was not produced and filed 
previously. 
* 
The significance of the evidence 
* 
The prejudice suffered by the Applicant if an order is not made. 
* 
The prejudice suffered by other parties if the order is made. 
* 
The need to be fair and just for all the parties by taking into 
account the overriding objective. 
 
If a witness has not served their witness statement, the automatic 
sanction is that that witness will not be able to give oral evidence at 
court. As this is deemed to be a sanction, the applicant must apply for 
relief from sanctions prior to applying for an order to call the relevant 
witness to give evidence at trial.

pages.heading: INJUNCTIONS · Injunction = an order of the court requiring a party to do something or
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE notes | Page 22 of 24 
INJUNCTIONS 
 
Injunction = an order of the court requiring a party to do something or 
to refrain from doing something. 
 
Breach of an injunction – contempt of court. 
 
Injunctions can be obtained at any point during the proceedings. 
 
Types of Injunctions: 
1. 
Mandatory injunctions: requires the other side to do a specific 
act. 
2. 
Prohibitory injunctions: requires the other side to refrain from 
doing an act. 
3. 
Quia timet injunctions: no wrong is yet committed, merely 
threatened. 
 
There must be a cause of action. – eg. breach of contract. 
 
INTERIM MANDATORY INJUNCTION: 
 
Test (high threshold) – will be granted if: 
* 
The Applicant will suffer serious harm if not granted 
* 
The Applicant is likely to succeed 
 AND 
* 
The Respondent is not required to incur expenditure 
disproportionate to the Applicant's harm. 
 
Damages must not be an adequate remedy: 
* 
The harm is not serious + not likely to continue (One-off) 
* 
The harm is not irreparable. – eg. where privacy was breached 
* 
The harm can be quantified in financial terms. 
* 
The Respondent can pay damages. 
 
INTERIM PROHIBITORY INJUNCTIONS: 
 
American Cyanamid Guidelines (court may depart from it) on how the 
court's discretion should be exercised: 
1. 
Serious question? 
2. 
Damages are adequate remedy for party injured by 
not/granting? 
3. 
Balance of convenience? 
 
Step 1: Is there a serious question to be tried? 
The claim is not frivolous or vexatious + serious question to be tried, the 
claim must have substance. – Yes, if clear breach. Clear terms, no valid 
defence. 
 
Step 2: Would damages be an adequate remedy for a party injured by 
the court's grant of, or failure to grant, an injunction? 
 
Step 2(A): Damages for the applicant + Can the respondent actually 
pay? 
If damages are not adequate or the respondent can't pay then the court 
is likely to grant an injunction. 
 
From Applicant's perspective: 
If the Confidential Information is disclosed so damages will be difficult 
to quantify = inadequate. Even if damages would (in theory) be 
adequate, Respondent is in financial trouble, damages not OK. 
 
Step 2(B): Damages for the respondent + Can the applicant actually 
pay? 
If the injunction were to be granted and it turns out that the injunction 
was wrongly granted, would the Respondent be adequately 
compensated under the Applicant's undertaking as to damages? 
 
From Respondent's perspective: 
Applicant is at an early stage of discussion with Respondent, so will not 
be unduly prejudiced. Even if it turns out that the injunction should not 
have been granted, Applicant is capable of paying damages. 
 
Step 3: Where does the balance of convenience lie? 
If both parties are large multinationals – injunction likely. 
Contrast: one party is a small firm, business might go insolvent – not 
likely. 
 
Factors: 
1. 
Trial is due to be heard soon – likely. 
2. 
Public interest in the injunction being granted or refused. 
3. 
Will one party be disproportionately harmed if the injunction is 
or is not granted? 
4. 
Where evenly balanced, try to maintain the ‘status quo' ante: 
This will be the position before the conduct complained of. 
5. 
Consider the ‘equity' of the situation. 
6. 
If other factors appear to be evenly balanced – merits of the 
case, last resort without conducting a mini-trial. 
 
 
 
 
From Applicant's perspective: 
Damage will be irreparable if the Confidential Information is disclosed. 
Applicant's future business will be severely hindered. Respondent could 
not meet any damages award. 
 
From Respondent's perspective: 
The respondent is not being asked to do anything which it shouldn't be 
doing, it signed the agreement and should comply with it. The 
respondent's deal with the Applicant is at a very early stage so no losses 
there and the Applicant can meet any undertaking in damages. 
 
Conclusion: Balance is in the Applicant's favour. 
 
If you reached a conclusion at this point, don't consider the points on 
Equity and discretionary remedy below. 
 
Equity: 
An injunction is an equitable remedy so all the equitable maxims will 
apply: 
1. 
Court cannot enforce the order: Keep open for trading = not 
enforceable. 
2. 
Must come with clean hands: look at the Applicant's 
wrongdoing 
3. 
Has the Applicant delayed in bringing this application? 
4. 
Equity will not act in vain. Confidentiality has already been 
disclosed so why take further action? 
 
Discretionary remedy: 
An injunction is a discretionary remedy. No right to an injunction. 
 
FREEZING ORDERS (FREEZING INJUNCTIONS): 
 
Freezing injunction is an IPI restraining a party from removing assets 
out of the jurisdiction, or from dealing with assets whether they are 
within the jurisdiction or not. This is to prevent assets being dissipated 
to hinder enforcement. May award against 3rd parties (to police the 
order) – eg. order respondent's bank to stop respondent's access to 
their account. 
 
Effect of a freezing injunction: 
1. 
All assets mentioned in the order are frozen (but would allow 
reasonable expenses per week) 
2. 
The respondent (or anyone else with notice of the order) will be 
in contempt of court if it breaches its terms. 
3. 
It will be in the applicant's best interest to press ahead with the 
action as his assets are frozen until proceedings. 
 
A discretionary and equitable remedy and the usual equitable maxims 
apply. 
 
Mareva Grounds for freezing injunction: 
1. Applicant has substantive cause of action justiciable in 
England and Wales. 
High Court can grant interim relief in foreign jurisdiction cases. 
Here, an order is sought where there is no “related claim”. 
 
2. Applicant has a good arguable case = 50%+ chance of success. 
 
3. Assets within the jurisdiction – UK Bank Account check if assets 
are still in the bank account. 
 
AND 
4. Real risk of respondent dissipating assets to hinder 
enforcement. 
Factors – Evidence of the Respondent's: 
* 
Dishonesty – transferring assets at an undervalue, 
directors' disqualification proceedings 
* 
Debt default 
* 
Removing or disposing of assets 
* 
Residing in a tax haven 
* 
Assets kept in jurisdictions where English judgments not 
easily enforced

pages.heading: APPEALS · GENERAL PRINCIPLES:
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE notes | Page 23 of 24 
APPEALS 
 
GENERAL PRINCIPLES: 
 
There is no automatic right of appeal, and any party hoping to make an 
appeal must first ensure that they have permission to make an appeal. 
 
Appeal the decision of a lower court where: 
1. 
Decision was wrong 
 OR 
2. 
Unjust because of a serious procedural or other irregularity 
 
Court may order the appeal if: 
 Evidence could not be reasonably obtained in lower courts, evidence 
would have an important influence on result and is credible. Also 
consider the overriding objective. 
 
The appeal hearing: 
 Review rather than re-hearing unless the court decides that a re-hearing 
would be in the interest of justice. – CPR 52.21(1) 
 
Court reluctant to interfere with lower court's discretion, unless decision 
was based on error of law, evidence or facts. 
 
Fresh evidence will not be allowed unless the appeal court orders it. 
 
The usual costs rules apply in relation to the appeal hearing. 
 
PERMISSION: 
 
You need permission to appeal. 
 
Applying for permission: 
 
Such an application may be made: 
 
Orally to the lower court directly when the decision is made at 
the hearing. 
 OR 
 
Make the application by filing an appellant's notice with reasons 
to the appeal court within 21 days. 
 
Apart from appeals to Supreme Court, you have 21 days from the 
original decision to appeal. 
 
Test for granting permission: 
 
Appeal must have a real prospect of success 
 OR 
 
Some other compelling reason why appeal should be heard 
 
Respondent's position: 
 
Respondent's notice must be filed and served by a respondent who: 
 
Is seeking permission to appeal from appeal court 
 OR 
 
Asks appeal court to uphold lower court's order for different or 
additional reasons to those given by the lower court. 
 
If no directions on time, file notice (using Form N162) within 14 days 
after the date on which Respondent became aware that appeal was 
going ahead. 
 
Where to apply for permission? 
 
In general, an application for permission to appeal must be made to the 
court that made the decision or the court you want to hear your 
appeal. 
 
APPLICATION FOR PERMISSION TO APPEAL: 
 
In order to be able to appeal a court decision, permission to make an 
appeal must be granted first. 
 
This is because there is no automatic right of appeal, and any party 
hoping to make an appeal must first ensure that they have permission 
to make an appeal. 
 
Court may order the appeal if: 
 
* 
The appeal has a real prospect of success or there is some other 
compelling reason why the appeal should be allowed. 
 AND 
* 
The previous judgment/order was wrong in fact/law or in the 
exercise of discretion or was unjust as a result of a serious 
procedural or other irregularity. 
 
When granting the order to allow an appeal to be made, this order may 
be subject to conditions. 
 
 
 
WHO HEARS THE APPEAL? 
 
 
Original hearing by 
 
Appeal to 
 
 
District Judge (County Court) 
 
 
Circuit Judge (County Court) 
 
Circuit Judge (County Court) 
 
 
Master (High Court) 
 
Master (High Court) 
 
 
Judge (High Court) 
 
Judge (High Court) 
 
 
Lord Justice of Appeal 
(Court of Appeal) 
 
 
Lord Justice of Appeal 
(Court of Appeal) 
 
 
Justice of Supreme Court 
 
A court lower than CoA may transfer first appeal directly to CoA in 
exceptional circumstances. 
 
EFFECT OF AN APPEAL: 
 
Initiating an appeal does not automatically stay the order obtained in 
the lower court. 
 
The effect of the Appeal is to stay the lower court's order if: 
 
Lower court or appeal court so orders 
 OR 
 
The appeal is from the Asylum and Immigration Tribunal 
 
APPEAL HEARINGS: 
 
Composition of the court: 
* 
One judge (either CC Circuit Judge or HC Judge) 
* 
In the Court of Appeal: 2 Lords Justice sit on interim appeals + 3 
on final appeals 
* 
In the Supreme Court: 5-member courts. 
 
Appeal court has the same powers as lower court. 
Second appeals will be heard by the Court of Appeal.

pages.heading: ENFORCEMENT · INTRODUCTION:
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE notes | Page 24 of 24 
ENFORCEMENT 
 
INTRODUCTION: 
 
At the trial, a judgment is made against the losing party, and this includes 
orders to pay the opposing party's legal fees and compensation, if 
necessary. 
 
Any judgment/order will be enforceable for 6 years from the date of the 
judgment/order. 
 
Courts do not enforce judgments automatically when the debtor fails to 
pay. – the judgment creditor will need to commence enforcement 
proceedings. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Interest on the debt: 
 
The interest will be 8% per annum, unless the court decides otherwise. 
Interest will typically accrue from the date of the judgment/order. This 
will depend on what is stated in the order. 
 
For County Court judgments: 
1. 
Judgments for £5,000 or more will be subject to interest. 
2. 
Judgments relating to a qualifying debt under the Late Payment 
of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998 are also subject to 
interest. 
 
For High Court judgments: 
All judgments will be subject to interest. 
 
INVESTIGATING THE DEBTOR'S MEANS: 
 
Before the Claimant commences proceedings for enforcement, they 
should obtain as much information as possible as to the reasons why 
the debtor failed to pay the debt, their circumstances, and assets and 
where these are located. 
 
The debtor's means could be investigated by: 
• 
Asking the debtor themselves 
• 
Instructing an enquiry/tracing agent 
• 
Carrying out a Companies House search 
• 
Obtaining Official Copies from Land Registry (are they the sole 
owner of the property or is the property jointly owned?) 
 
If little knowledge about the debtor and their assets: 
Apply without notice for Order to Obtain information from judgment 
debtor about its assets. 
 
ENFORCEMENT METHODS: 
 
Exam structure: 
1. 
Make a list of all the assets in your scenario. 
2. 
Identify which assets are not possible to enforce the judgment 
against. 
3. 
Select the most appropriate order for the remaining assets. 
 
Key methods of enforcement: 
1. 
Taking control of goods order – use this for goods/vehicle. 
2. 
Third party debt orders – use this in relation to credit in the bank 
account. 
3. 
Charging orders – use this in relation to land or certain securities. 
4. 
Attachment of earnings order – use this in relation to salary. 
5. 
Insolvency proceedings – use if there is no other option. 
 
May use more than one of the below methods. 
 
Taking control of goods order: 
 
Enforcement officer can legally seize the debtor's goods and assets and 
sell them to pay the judgment debt. 
 
Please do not confuse this with goods being sold by businesses, this 
order can be used to seize any items that the debtor may have with a 
few exceptions. 
 
Use this method if the debtor actually owns the goods/assets 
themselves. Goods may be taken even if the judgment debtor owns the 
goods jointly with someone else. – Farrar v Beswick 
Goods that are exempt from seizure: 
 
* 
Tools and necessary items for the debtor's job, trade, profession 
or study up to £1,350 in aggregate value. 
 
* 
Basic domestic items. – eg. clothes, books, telephones, bedding, 
furniture. 
 
Additional considerations: 
 
* 
If the resale value of goods is enough to cover the judgment 
debt, it may not be. 
 
* 
If the market is going well, bad market conditions will make it 
more difficult to sell the goods and to receive fair value for them. 
 
Cannot use TCG against a third party so check any third party claims 
(owners, co-owners, secured creditors) – eg. if judgment debtor uses a 
car owned by a company. Always check who owns the goods. 
 
 
 
Outstanding debt amount 
 
County Court or High Court? 
 
 
Up to £600 
 
 
Only County Court 
 
Between £600 and £5,000 
 
High Court or County Court 
 
 
More than £5,000 
 
 
High Court 
 
 
High Court Procedure: 
 
* 
Obtain a writ of control to be able to seize the debtor's assets. 
 
* 
File a Request for issue of the writ using Form PF 86A together 
with the relevant court fee. 
 
* 
With the form, also file a draft writ of control which the court 
may edit before issuing it. 
 
* 
The writ can only be enforced by an enforcement officer. 
 
County Court Procedure: 
 
* 
Obtain a warrant of control to be able to seize the debtor's 
assets. 
 
* 
File a Request for a warrant of control in the hearing centre 
where the judgment was obtained together with the relevant 
court fee. 
 
Third party debt orders: 
 
CPR 72 If the judgment debtor is owed money by third party, a thirdparty debt order can be made so that this third party pays the debt 
directly to the judgment creditor. 
 
Must be debt due or accruing due. – eg. trade debts, credit in bank 
account, but do not use for overdrafts. 
 
Charging orders: 
 
Do not use this method if the land or assets that are subject to 
mortgages or charges are jointly owned. If co-owned, it is difficult to 
obtain Order for Sale. 
 
If there is a charge on property, bank must be paid off first, then obtain 
Order for Sale. This is expensive and time-consuming. 
 
Attachment of earnings order: 
 
This order ensures that a proportion of the debtor's salary is deducted 
by the employer and paid towards the debt. 
 
This order cannot be made against someone who is self-employed. 
 
Only available in County Court. 
 
Must transfer judgment to County Court, then apply for Attachment of 
Earnings Order. Use against an individual (not company) where the 
person lacks assets but earns a salary. 
 
Insolvency proceedings: 
 
Insolvency proceedings should always be the creditor's last option. 
 
For individuals: 
Must owe creditor more than £5,000 – bankruptcy petition 
 
For companies: 
Must owe creditor more than £750 – winding-up petition 
 
 
JUDGMENT DEBTOR 
 
This is the 
unsuccessful party 
who owes money. 
 
JUDGMENT CREDITOR 
 
This is the successful 
Claimant who is 
enforcing judgment to 
obtain the money 
owed. 
 
££

books.title: Dispute Resolution · SQE Prep Notes（39页版）

pages.heading: METHODS OF DISPUTE RESOLUTION · MAIN METHODS:
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 1 of 39 
METHODS OF DISPUTE RESOLUTION 
 
MAIN METHODS: 
 
 
Non-judicial 
 
 
 
 
 Judicial 
 
Negotiation Mediation Expert Appraisal Arbitration Litigation 
 
 
 + 
 Early Neutral 
 Evaluation 
 
 
In the UK, there are four main processes for resolving disputes: 
* 
Litigation 
* 
Negotiation 
* 
Arbitration 
* 
Mediation 
 
Negotiation, arbitration, and mediation are all alternative dispute 
resolution procedures (ADR) which means alternative to litigation. 
 
Other types of alternative dispute resolution: 
 
Early neutral evaluation = Independent evaluator meets with parties to 
assess dispute. Non-binding and confidential. 
 
Expert appraisal = Parties appoint independent expert on subject 
matter. Non-binding decision. 
 
Expert determination = Parties appoint independent expert on subject 
matter. It is binding, but cannot make a costs order 
 
LITIGATION: 
 
Legal action that will proceed through the court system. Litigation 
requires the parties to comply with the formal rules surrounding 
procedures and evidence. The judge is the one making the final decision 
over the dispute. 
 
NEGOTIATION: 
 
Informal discussions that take place between the parties to resolve the 
dispute. This may take place at any time and the parties resolve their 
own dispute by agreement. 
 
– 
Any correspondence and discussions that is part of the 
negotiation may be marked ‘without prejudice'. 
 
Without prejudice communications = discussions which cannot 
be relied on/referred to in court. 
 
– 
The parties may also hold round-table discussions where the 
parties and their representatives try to settle the dispute after 
they have disclosed all witness statements and evidence. 
 
ARBITRATION: 
 
Semi-formal procedure similar to litigation, however, the final decision 
is made by a neutral third party (the arbitrator) that resolves dispute by 
granting a final award. 
 
– 
The parties may decide on the procedures to use. 
 
– 
The formal rules on evidence such as seen in litigation do not 
apply. 
 
– 
The parties are contractually bound to comply with the award 
and the award is as binding as litigation. However, the arbitral 
award is not binding on third parties. 
 
– 
Just as contentious and adversarial as court proceedings. 
 
 
 
PROS 
 
CONS 
 
 
* Can choose arbitrator, but not 
the judge in case of litigation. 
Might choose a specialist. 
* Can choose where arbitration 
takes place, choose the 
mechanism of the process. 
* Private hearings – sign NDAs. 
* Final and binding unlike court 
appeals procedure. 
* New York Convention ensures 
decision is enforced abroad. 
 
 
* 
Slow but may speed it up by 
changing process 
mechanisms. 
* 
No precedent value. 
* 
Can be expensive as parties 
pay for arbitrator + premises. 
* 
Powers are more limited than 
that of the court. 
* 
Not as effective for interim 
applications. 
 
 
 
 
Private hearings: 
While there is third party involvement with arbitration, the only third 
party is the arbitrator, it is generally private and there is no reporting of 
the matter (unlike litigation). 
 
Arbitration clauses: 
 
Typically, an arbitration clause within a contract is the common 
method by which parties agree to resolve their disputes through 
arbitration. The arbitration clause is agreed upon when the contract is 
formed, and it usually outlines the rules, the seat of arbitration, and 
sometimes the appointing body or specific arbitrators. 
 
However, parties can agree to arbitrate a dispute even without a preexisting arbitration clause in their contract. This can be done by 
entering into a separate arbitration agreement after a dispute has 
arisen. This post-dispute agreement would similarly define the terms 
and procedures of the arbitration process. 
 
MEDIATION/CONCILIATION: 
 
Informal dispute resolution process where the decision is made by the 
parties with the assistance of a neutral third party (the mediator) 
without looking at the merits of the case. 
 
Confidentiality: 
The mediation process is confidential and without prejudice. 
 
Process: 
 
– 
The process of mediation includes sessions held with each party 
separately and joint sessions at a later stage. The procedure is 
structure with a set number of sessions required. 
 
– 
Parties can discuss and resolve anything they wish. – eg. even 
hurt feelings, and could request an apology. 
 
– 
The parties come to a solution themselves and result of 
mediation is non-binding on the parties. As a result, the parties 
must sign an agreement to have a binding decision. 
 
– 
Any decision that is made during mediation is final and cannot 
be appealed. 
 
– 
If mediation does not lead to settlement, the mediator could 
invite the parties to pursue mediation again at a later stage. 
 
 
PROS 
 
CONS 
 
 
* Cheaper + quicker than litigation 
* Promotes an amicable solution, 
preserves commercial 
relationship 
* If ends in a consent order, 
becomes enforceable 
* Confidential so allows for 
private discussions. 
* Without prejudice so it is not 
admissible in court if parties 
decide to make a claim. 
* Allows for creative solutions. 
 
 
* Solution is not imposed on 
either party, may waste time 
and money. 
* Although commercial 
resolution, may not be legally 
correct. Injustice to one party. 
* Only effective if both parties 
genuinely intend to resolve 
* Flexible, may leave if not going 
as expected. 
 
 
Conciliation: 
 
* 
The conciliation procedure is very similar to mediation with a 
few differences between the two procedures. 
 
* 
Instead of a mediator, the consolation is led by the conciliator 
who will have a more active role in suggesting solutions to the 
parties and they can also advise the parties in relation to the 
dispute including both matters of fact and law they may also 
provide recommendations as to how to resolve the issue. 
 
* 
The procedure is more flexible to suit the parties. 
 
In practice, the terms mediation and conciliation are sometimes used 
interchangeably, and the distinction is subtle. 
 
If the parties are unsure as to the outcome they require and need more 
guidance, conciliation may be more suitable. 
 
DUTY TO ENCOURAGE: 
 
Duty to encourage clients to attend ADR: 
 
The Court of Appeal has made a direction directed towards legal 
professionals to encourage clients to try ADR prior to taking legal action. 
 
Even though ADR is not required prior to commencing litigation, clients 
should consider it. – ADR is a voluntary process, and the parties must 
consent to it before it can go ahead. 
 
Expert 
Determi
nation

pages.heading: The court has a duty to – ensure that all cases are dealt with justly, fairly, · and proportionately (the overriding objective) and considering/
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 2 of 39 
The court has a duty to – ensure that all cases are dealt with justly, fairly, 
and proportionately (the overriding objective) and considering/ 
attempting ADR may achieve this. 
 
Legal professionals have a duty to – tell their clients about their option 
to attempt ADR instead of/before litigation 
 
Parties have a duty to – consider whether ADR would be appropriate 
throughout the proceedings. 
 
If the parties fail to consider/participate ADR, they might not be able to 
recover the costs of the proceedings (at all or in part). 
 
Unreasonable refusal to engage in ADR: 
 
When the parties receive a request for ADR, they must respond to it and 
if they refuse ADR, they must set out the reasons for why they consider 
that ADR would be inappropriate in this case. 
 
If the court believes that refusal was unreasonable or the party ignored 
the request for ADR completely, they may penalise the party refusing it 
in respect of payment/recovery of legal costs depending on whether 
the outcome of their claim is successful.

INTRODUCTION TO LITIGATION 
 
PROCEDURE TIMELINE:

applications 
and ADR 
 
 
 May begin from before the claim form is filed until 
the start of trial. – CPR 23-25 
 Settlement 
and Part 36 
offers 
 
 May be made from commencement up until the 
start of trial. 
 
PRE-ACTION 
 
 
* Interview Claimant client 
* Claimant sends Letter of Claim 
* Consider ADR 
* Defendant sends Letter of 
Response 
 
 
 
 
 
14 days from 
Letter of Claim 
 
MAKING A 
CLAIM 
 
 
* Issue Claim form 
* Serve Claim form on Defendant 
– CPR 7.5 
* Serve Particulars of Claim (PoC) 
with Claim form or separately 
* File Certificate of Service 
 
 
 
 
4 months from 
issue date 
14 days from 
Claim form 
21 days from 
Claim form

RESPONSE 
 
 
* File Acknowledgement of 
Service 
* File Defence and Counterclaim 
 
 
 
14 days from

THE CASE

CPR 26.4 
* Directions Questionnaire 
* Allocation hearing 
* Case and Cost management 
conference 
 
 
 
 
CLAIMANT 
REPLY 
 
 
* Reply to Defence and 
Counterclaim – CPR 15.8 
 
 
 EVIDENCE 
 
 * Instruct experts 
* Disclosure and inspection 
* Parties exchange witness 
statements – CPR 32 
* Parties exchange expert reports 
– CPR 35 
 
 
 PRE-TRIAL 
 
 * Court sends Pre-trial checklist 
* Pre-trial hearing 
* Claimant files trial bundles 
* Prepare skeleton arguments 
and list of authorities 
* Consider Notice to admit facts 
* Prepare a case summary 
* Summon reluctant witnesses 
* Prepare Brief to counsel

3 days pre-trial 
 
 
TRIAL
