POST-TRIAL 
 
 
* Appeals – CPR 52 
* Enforce judgment – CPR 70 
 
 
 
There are two stages to be considered when starting court 
proceedings. The first is issue of proceedings, the term used for 
commencing proceedings. The second is service of proceedings, which 
means getting the documents into the defendant's hands in a way the 
court recognises as valid. 
 
It is worth noting at this stage that ‘file' means providing the court with 
a document and ‘serve' means providing the other side with the 
document. 
 
Proceedings are started when the court issues a claim form at the 
request of the claimant (CPR 7.2 (1), subject to 7APD 5.1 & 5.2). Upon 
issue, the court will stamp the claim form with the court seal and give 
the action a claim number. 
 
Service of the claim form 
Once the claim form has been issued, it must be served on the 
defendant within four months of issue CPR 7.5(1) (or within six months 
if it is to be served out of the jurisdiction: CPR 7.5(2)). If it is not 
possible to serve within this time limit, the claimant may apply for an 
extension under CPR 7.6 (although this is not easy to obtain because 
the rules are very strict). 
 
Who serves the claim form? 
Under CPR 6.4, a claim form may be served either by the court or by 
the claimant's solicitor. 
If the court serves, service will usually be by first class post. Once the 
court has effected service, it will send the claimant a notice of issue 
stating the deemed date of service. If the court is unable to serve the 
claim form for any reason, the claimant will be sent a notice of nonservice. It is then up to the claimant to try to serve the claim form on 
the defendant. 
If the claimant's solicitor wishes to serve the claim form, it must notify 
the court when it issues the claim form that it does not wish the court 
to serve it. The court will then give or send the claimant's solicitor the 
issued claim form with sealed copies for service on the defendant(s). 
The claimant's solicitor then effects service using any of the methods of 
service in CPR 6.3. The claimant's solicitor must then file a certificate of 
service at court within 21 days of service, confirming that the 
document has not been returned undelivered and certifying details of 
the date on which the claim was posted/delivered/transmitted (see 
CPR 6.17). It is not necessary to file a certificate of service if all of the 
defendants have filed an acknowledgment of service within that time. 
NOTE: The claimant will not be permitted to obtain judgment in default 
under CPR 12 unless it has filed a certificate of service 
 
Service (CPR 6) 
Service is the process of giving the document to the other parties in an 
action in a way which is recognised by the court. 
 
Service must be by a method recognised as valid by the CPR. If it is not, 
service may be invalid and the claimant may be unable to obtain 
judgment or enforce any judgment obtained. 
 
CPR 6.3 lists various permitted methods of serving the claim form: 
• 
personally by the claimant 
• 
delivering or leaving the document at a permitted address 
• 
by first class post 
• 
by fax 
• 
by document exchange (DX) 
• 
by any electronic method (e.g. email) 
 
Service by a contractually agreed method 
If a contract specifies a method of service of a claim form, CPR 6.11 
provides that service is valid if effected in accordance with that 
contractual method. 
 
Solicitor authorised to accept service 
Where a solicitor is authorised by his/her client to accept service on 
behalf of a party and has notified the other party in writing, the 
document must be served on the solicitor and not on the party (CPR 
6.7(1)). 
 
Alternative service (CPR 6.15) 
The court may permit service by an alternative method if there is good 
reason to do so, i.e. where the other available methods of service 
would be ineffective or impossible. 
An application must be made to court setting out why service in 
accordance with the methods listed in the CPR are not possible or why 
attempts to serve in accordance with these methods have been 
unsuccessful. The application should state the alternative method 
proposed. Examples of alternative service methods are: (i) serving on 
solicitors acting for a party where the solicitor has not been authorised 
to accept service; and (ii) placing an advert in a newspaper notifying 
the defendant that proceedings have been commenced against it. 
Alternative service cannot be used retrospectively and it cannot be 
used to remedy irregular service. 
 
Service of the particulars of claim 
If the particulars of claim is either contained in the claim form or 
attached to the claim form as a separate document and contained in 
the same envelope, then CPR 6.14 applies. In such circumstances, it is 
treated as part of the claim form for the purposes of these rules of 
service and is deemed served at the same time as the claim form. 
If the particulars of claim is served separately from the claim form, i.e. 
served within 14 days after service of the claim form (CPR 7.4(1)(b)) 
then CPR 6.26 applies to service of the particulars of claim, 
 
The defendant's response 
The defendant does not (apart from in the Commercial Court) have to 
react to the claim at all until it receives the particulars of claim. Once 
the defendant has been served with the particulars of claim, the 
defendant's time to respond starts running. (CPR 9.1) 
The defendant must then respond in one of three ways within 14 days 
of deemed service of the particulars of claim: 
1. 
admit part or all of the claim; 
2. 
file a defence; or 
3. 
file an acknowledgment of service (this will give the 
defendant longer to prepare its defence). (CPR 9.2) 
 
Admission 
A defendant may respond to the particulars of claim by admitting 
either the whole or part of the claim or by requesting time to pay. You 
can find details of admissions in CPR 14. The permission of the court is 
required to amend or withdraw an admission (14.1(5)).

pages.heading: Defence · A defendant contesting a claim must file a defence which sets out why
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 4 of 39 
 
Defence 
A defendant contesting a claim must file a defence which sets out why 
the claim is disputed. A defence must be filed at court and served on all 
parties (CPR 15.6) within 14 days of the deemed date of service of the 
particulars of claim (CPR 15.4). 
 
Acknowledgment of service 
CPR 10 sets out the relevant rules relating to acknowledging service. 
This step is not compulsory. However, the defendant will file an 
acknowledgment of service either: 
1. 
if it is unable to file the defence in time and needs longer than 
14 days from the deemed date of service of the particulars of 
claim in which to serve a defence; or 
2. 
if it wishes to dispute that the court has jurisdiction to hear the 
claim. 
 
The form for acknowledging service (Form N9) is sent to the defendant 
in the response pack. 
The general rule is that the period for filing an acknowledgment of 
service is 14 days after service of the particulars of claim, whether or 
not it is served with the claim form (see CPR 10.3). 
 
Once the defendant has filed an acknowledgment of service, the court 
will notify the claimant in writing that this has been done (CPR 10.4). 
The filing of an acknowledgment of service extends the time for filing a 
defence, as set out in CPR 15.4: 
* 
If the defendant does not file an acknowledgement of service, it 
must file and serve a defence within 14 days of the deemed 
date of service of the particulars of claim. 
* 
If the defendant does file an acknowledgment of service 
indicating an intention to defend the claim, it extends the 
deadline for serving the defence to 28 days after the deemed 
date of service of the particulars of claim. 
 
 
GLOSSARY: 
 
The claim: 
 
Litigation and application are two different legal procedures. 
 
Litigation: 
This is the main claim or legal action that is being brought. You can start 
a claim by filing a claim form at the court. A Claimant must have a cause 
of action to bring a claim. 
 
Application: 
These are specific requests being made to the court for a particular order 
or relief. 
 
Two types of applications: 
 
1. 
Interim applications: smaller requests/applications can be made 
to the curt that relate to the main claim but relate to one specific 
issue that can be decided by the court before the main hearing. 
 
2. 
Stand-alone applications: Some main claims are called 
applications such as Judicial review applications, probate 
applications, family law applications. 
 
As you learn about a specific matter/area of law, you will learn about the 
different types of claims and applications that can be brought and what 
these are called. 
 
Parties: 
 
Parties to litigation: 
Claimant = person making the claim. 
Defendant = person defending the claim made against them. 
 
Parties to interim applications: 
Applicant = person making the application. 
Respondent = person defending the application made against them. 
 
Litigation documents: 
 
Letter of Claim (Letter Before Action) = a letter sent by a potential 
Claimant to a potential Defendant setting out the details of the claim 
before they file the Claim form. 
 
Claim form = the form a Claimant must fill in, file with the court and 
serve it on all the parties to start litigation. There are various different 
types of claim forms and the Claimant must select the most appropriate 
form. 
 
Particulars of Claim = when starting litigation, the Claimant will also send 
out a Particular of Claim either with the Claim Form or separately. This 
document is a statement of case that details the Claimant's case and 
identifies all the relevant issues. The court will read this document to 
understand what the claim is about. 
 
Certificate of service = the Claimant may fill in and file a Certificate of 
service that will inform the court who the Claimant served the 
Particulars of Claim and Claim form on. 
 
Acknowledgement of Service = the Defendant may decide to file an 
Acknowledgement of Service with the court, to extend the 14-day 
deadline for filing the Defence. If they do file an Acknowledgement of 
Service, their deadline will be extended to 28 days, and this essentially 
serves as a notice to the Claimant that the Defendant has received the 
Particulars of Claim and is now preparing its defence. 
 
Defence = a statement of case filed by the Defendant in response to the 
Particulars of Claim, essentially defending the claim. In some cases, a 
Defence will also contain a counterclaim. 
 
Reply = a non-essential statement of case. The Claimant may decide to 
respond to the Defence and file their Reply, however, this is not a 
compulsory. 
 
PRE-ACTION CONSIDERATIONS: 
 
Before commencing proceedings, the claimant must consider a number 
of different questions. This will help the claimant identify what is the 
best direction to take with the claim and whether it is worth bringing a 
claim in the first place. 
 
Pre-action considerations to take into account: 
 
1. 
Which jurisdiction is the appropriate place to bring the claim? 
 
2. 
If the correct jurisdiction is England and Wales, which court is 
the correct court for bringing the claim? 
 
3. 
Whether both the claimant and the defendant have legal 
capacity. 
 
4. 
Whether the claim can be brought within the limitation period. 
 
5. 
Whether there is a valid cause of action to bring the claim. 
 
LEGAL CAPACITY OF BOTH PARTIES: 
 
There can be no claim without a Claimant capable of making a claim 
and a party capable of being a Defendant. 
 
Please note that the words “claimant” and “defendant” are only 
capitalised to help you memorise the rules relating to them. In practice, 
these words are not capitalised. 
 
Make sure to identify who the Claimant and Defendant is in your 
question. 
 
Mental capacity: 
CPR 21 Children under 18 or a party who lacks mental capacity to 
conduct litigation (a protected party) must have a litigation friend to 
bring a claim. 
 
Incorporated bodies: 
* 
Companies may bring a claim as they are legal persons under 
the Companies Act 2006. 
* 
Limited Liability Partnerships (LLPs) may also bring a claim. 
* 
Sole traders can be sued in their trading name but they cannot 
use their trading name when bringing a claim. 
 
THE USE OF WELSH LANGUAGE: 
 
Welsh Language Act 1993 Welsh language should be treated no less 
favourably than English in public life in Wales. 
 
The CPR has created a number of rules and considerations to take into 
account in relation to the use of Welsh language in civil proceedings. 
 
These rules exist to allow for Welsh speakers to be able to fully 
participate in the proceedings without being disadvantaged. 
 
This is the case for both English and Welsh court proceedings. – To 
determine the correct rules to use, consider the following test to identify 
whether the case should be heard in the English or Welsh courts. 
 
Criteria for identifying where proceedings should be brought: 
 
* 
Georgraphical connection to Wales – whether the case involves 
events, acts taking place in Wales. – eg. if the contract was to be 
delivered in Wales or the accident took place in Wales. 
 
* 
Whether the proceedings fall under the jurisdiction of the Welsh 
courts – it automatically will if the case involved Welsh 
legislation. 
 
* 
If any of the parties (Claimant or Defendant) are based in Wales. 
 
* 
Whether the applicable law is Welsh – eg. if the contract was to 
be delivered in Wales or the accident took place in Wales.

pages.heading: Whether any of the documents submitted during the · proceedings are in Welsh or relate to Welsh matters. – this could
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 5 of 39 
* 
Whether any of the documents submitted during the 
proceedings are in Welsh or relate to Welsh matters. – this could 
include a Letter of Claim, Claim Form etc. 
 
Count each factor to identify whether the case is more closely 
connected to England or Wales. 
 
Depending on whether you have decided that the case should go to the 
Welsh court or English court, the following rules will apply. 
 
For proceedings either at English or Welsh courts: 
 
The parties must inform the court if Welsh will be used, to ensure 
proper management and that appropriate arrangements can be made. 
 
Documents can be submitted in either English or Welsh, and the court 
should be notified in advance if a Welsh document will be presented. 
HMCTS provides Welsh-language forms and translation services. 
 
Allocation questionnaires: 
 
For allocation questionnaires, parties must include details about the 
possible use of Welsh, such as Welsh-speaking witnesses and Welsh 
documents. This information must also be included in the directions 
questionnaire, even if previously communicated. 
 
Case management: 
 During case management and interim hearings, parties should inform 
the court of any Welsh language use, and confirm this in pre-trial 
checklists. 
 
Evidence: 
 
Parties are able to submit written evidence ins Welsh. 
 
Non-compliance: 
 If either parties fail to comply with these rules, non-compliance may 
lead to a cost order against the non-compliant party or their 
representative. 
 
Welsh court proceedings only: 
 
These rules only apply to civil proceedings in Wales or related to 
Wales. 
 
Hearings: 
 It allows hearings to be conducted entirely in Welsh if all parties and 
witnesses consent. 
 
Cases where Welsh is to be used will be listed, where possible, before a 
Welsh-speaking judge and at courts with translation facilities if 
required. Court managers will ensure the availability of approved 
interpreters when needed. 
 
Witnesses can choose to take oaths or affirmations in Welsh or English. 
In jury trials, jurors are informed they may take the oath or affirmation 
in either language. 
 
If necessary, an interpreter will be hired and paid for by the court. 
 
Who bears the costs? 
 If the use of Welsh leads to additional costs, these costs are managed 
within the court's procedures. 
 
English court proceedings only: 
 
Hearings: 
 If Welsh is used in hearings, the court will make arrangements for 
translation, if needed. 
 
If necessary, an interpreter will be hired. 
 
Who bears the costs? 
 
If the use of Welsh in English courts leads to additional costs due to 
translation or other arrangements, these costs may be allocated as per 
the court's decision, similar to how they are managed in Welsh courts.

pages.heading: TORT AND CONTRACT CLAIMS · LIMITATION PERIODS:
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 6 of 39 
TORT AND CONTRACT CLAIMS 
 
LIMITATION PERIODS: 
 
There are set limitation periods for different types of claims within 
which the claim must be brought. 
 
Most limitation periods are set out in a statute. If a Claimant runs out of 
this limitation period, they will be “statute-barred” from bringing a 
claim. 
 
If a Claimant goes ahead and commences legal action after the expiry of 
the limitation period, the Defendant can raise the fact that the limitation 
period has passed as a defence. If the court accepts this defence, the 
claim will be struck out. 
 
Why do we need limitation periods? 
It becomes harder to collect evidence and call witnesses if a long time 
period has passed since the act/breach. 
 
Key limitation periods: 
 
There is a lot of variation to the limitation period depending on the type 
of claim or application being brought to the court. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Other rules on limitation periods: 
 
Time for the limitation period will stop running once the Claimant 
delivers the correctly completed claim form and the correct fee to the 
court, issuing proceedings. 
 
If the Defendant has been correctly identified, but their name is 
incorrect, it is possible to change their name even if the limitation period 
expired. 
 
If the Claimant is a minor: 
The limitation period runs from the Claimant's 18th birthday. 
 
If the Claimant lacks mental capacity at the accrual date: 
The limitation period runs from when the Claimant produces a 
certificate that they are of sound mind. 
 
If the Claimant loses mental capacity after the accrual date: 
The limitation period stops running from when the Claimant loses 
capacity. 
 
For cases of fraud/concealment: 
The limitation period runs from then the Claimant discovers/reasonably 
should have discovered the fraud/concealment. 
 
TORT – LIMITATION PERIODS: 
 
General rule: 
 
General rule: tort claims must be brought within 6 years from the cause 
of action date (when the tortious act occurred/accrual date) even if the 
Claimant is unaware of breach and the damages occurred later. 
 
Accrual date = the date when the tortious act occurred. 
 
If the tort was not yet apparent on the accrual date: 
Then 6 years from when the Claimant gained knowledge of the tort and 
knowledge of who caused the tort. 
 
Personal injury claims: 
 
If the claim is a personal injury claim: 
 
The claim must be brought within 3 years from the accrual date/ 
knowledge. 
 
If the victim died because of the tort within 3 years of the accrual date, 
the claim must be brought within: 
1. 
3 years from the date of death 
 OR 
2. 
3 years from when the personal representatives of the deceased 
gained knowledge of the tort. 
When is a tort claim a personal injury claim? 
 
In order to identify whether your claim is a personal injury claim, you 
must look at the damage claimed by the Claimant. The Claimant may 
make a claim for personal injury and/or property damage. 
 
If there is a claim for both in one proceedings: 
* 
One part of the claim will relate to compensation for personal 
injury due to physical or psychological harm suffered. The 
limitation period for personal injury claims is three years from 
the date of the injury or the date of knowledge – Limitation Act 
1980 
* 
The second part of the claim will relate to compensation for 
damage to or loss of property (vehicles, buildings, personal 
belongings). The limitation period for property damage claims is 
generally six years from the date of the incident. 
 
These claims are called mixed claims. The limitation period will remain 
valid in respect of each element of the claim. 
 
If the Claimant is running out of time for the personal injury claim (3 year 
deadline is approaching), it is best to make both claims together. 
However, if time has already run out on the personal injury claim, the 
Claimant is still free to make the claim for the property damage. 
 
Latent defects in property: 
 
If the claim is a negligence claim for latent defects in property due to a 
fault in design/materials/workmanship that existed at the time when 
construction of the property/item was completed but was not apparent 
at completion – the claim can be brought up until (whichever is later): 
1. 
6 years from accrual of the action 
 OR 
2. 
3 years from the earliest date on which the Claimant knew or 
ought to have known the material facts necessary to bring a 
negligence action 
 
Longstop date: 
 
There is a longstop date of 15 years – no action can be brought after 
more than 15 years after the act/omission alleged to have caused the 
damage. 
 
CONTRACT – LIMITATION PERIODS: 
 
General rule: 
 
General rule: contract claims must be brought within 6 years from the 
date of the breach. 
 
Construction contracts: 
 
For claims in relation to construction contracts: there is a shorter 
limitation period allowing the party in breach to ‘make good' any 
defects in the building, however this does not prevent the party that 
suffered a loss to make a simple contract claim within the usual 6-year 
period. – The shorter period (which will be set out in the contract) will 
only apply to the requirement to ‘make good' the defects. – Look out for 
‘make good' clauses in the contract. 
 
CAUSE OF ACTION IN TORT AND CONTRACT: 
 
Claim concurrent duties (sue for both tort and contract) and if limitation 
period is tight, one claim might still fall within the period. 
 
Tort – Cause of action structure: 
 
1. Duty of care: Reasonably competent advice from reasonably 
competent solicitor. – If you have a lawyer who gave negligent 
legal advice, sue the lawyer in tort and the LLP for breach of 
contract (LLP has deeper pockets and possibly insurance so they 
are more likely to be able to pay compensation). 
 
2. Breach: Did the Defendant breach their duty? – eg. What was 
the solicitor's specialism? Would a similarly qualified property 
lawyer advise differently? Would a reasonable lawyer have 
caveated their advice? 
 
3. Causation: Did the defendant's breach cause the Claimant's 
loss? – eg. Did the solicitor's breach cause the loss suffered? Did 
X rely on this advice? What would X have done if caveated 
advice? Is there a chance that they would have acted differently? 
 
4. Remoteness: Was the damage suffered reasonably foreseeable? 
 
5. Loss suffered: Must be foreseeable not too remote. 
 
6. Damages: 
 
Measure of damages: 
 
CONTRACT 
 
 6 years from the breach of 
contract, not from when the 
contract was signed. – eg. did 
not satisfy obligations. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
TORT 
 
 6 years from cause of action 
date (when the tortious act 
occurred) 
even 
if 
the 
Claimant was unaware of the 
breach and/or any damages 
occurred later. – eg. date of 
poor advice, not date of 
retainer.

pages.heading: 1. Put the Claimant back in the position had the tort not · occurred. Be wary of remote damages and contributory
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 7 of 39 
1. Put the Claimant back in the position had the tort not 
occurred. Be wary of remote damages and contributory 
negligence. 
2. Contributory negligence: if the loss has been partly 
caused by the Claimant's own negligence – damages 
received by the Claimant will be reduced. 
 
7. Remedies 
 
Contract – Cause of action structure: 
 
1. Duty: The duties of both parties is set out in the contract 
governing the parties' relationship. – Look at any express and 
implied terms. 
 
Implied terms: 
s.13 Supply of Goods and Services Act 1982 The person 
performing services must act with reasonable care and skill. 
 
If contract is for Sale of goods also look at the below: 
* 
The goods must be of satisfactory quality. – s.14(2) Sale 
of Goods Act 1979 
* 
The goods must be fit for the particular purpose of the 
buyer. – s.14(3) SGA 1979 
* 
If the sale is sale by description: any products sold by 
description must match the description. – s.13 SGA 
1979 
 
2. Breach: Did the Defendant breach a term of the contract? – eg. 
Express or implied term. 
 
3. Loss: Did the Claimant suffer loss as a result of the breach? 
 
4. Damages: 
 
Measure of damages: 
1. 
Contract claims: Put injured party in position had the 
contract been properly performed. The Claimant must 
mitigate. 
2. 
Debts: it is a claim for a sum owed. No need to mitigate. 
 
5. Remedies 
 
COMPENSATION AND OTHER REMEDIES: 
 
Remedies in contract and tort: 
 
 
CONTRACT 
 
TORT 
 
 
 Common law remedies: 
The purpose of these remedies 
is to put the Claimant into the 
position they would have been 
had the contract been properly 
performed. – the Claimant 
cannot profit from the claim. 
 
Damages (expectation loss, 
reliance loss, restitution) 
 
Liquidated damages (if available 
as set out in the contract) 
Equitable remedies: 
 
Specific performance (enforcing 
one of the parties to perform 
their duties under the contract) 
 
Rescission (rescinds the 
contract) 
 
Rectification (correcting a 
mistake in the contract to reflect 
the intention of the parties) 
 
Restitution (restoring the 
payment of a sum under a 
contract where the contract was 
never performed) 
 
Declaration (an interim/final 
declaration as to the finding of a 
fact or legal right – CPR 40.20) 
 
Injunction (Prohibitory or 
Mandatory injunction requiring 
a party to do something or 
 
 Common law remedies: 
The purpose of these 
remedies is to compensate the 
victim for their losses and the 
put them back into the 
position they would have 
been had the tort never 
occurred. 
Damages: 
* Nominal damages 
 
* Aggravated damages 
where additional 
compensation is 
required due to 
aggravating conduct 
 
* General damages which 
are assessed at court 
 
* Special damages 
calculated based on 
actual monetary loss 
until trial 
refraining from doing 
something) 
 
 
Specified sum or unspecified sum? 
 
Specified sum claims = these are claims that can be quantified. 
 
Unspecified sum claims = these are claims that cannot be quantified. 
 
A claim may include a claim for a specified and an unspecified sum, it 
does not have to be one or the other. 
 
Claimants have a general duty mitigate their losses, otherwise the court 
may reduce their damages award. 
 
When to specify the amount claimed: 
 
* 
Quantified claims: If the claim can be precisely quantified, such 
as a specific amount owed under a contract or a defined sum of 
money, it should be clearly stated in the 'amount claimed' box. 
This includes any specific losses, costs, or expenses that can be 
calculated prior to filing the claim. 
 
* 
Fixed costs claims: In cases where statutory costs, fixed fees, or 
agreed expenses are involved, these should also be included in 
the amount claimed if they can be specifically determined at the 
time of filing. 
 
When not to specify exact amounts: 
 
* 
Unliquidated damages: where damages are unliquidated (not 
predetermined by agreement) and depend on a court's 
assessment, such as claims for pain and suffering or other 
general damages in tort, the claim form should indicate that the 
exact amount is to be determined by the court. This is often 
marked as 'to be assessed. 
 
* 
For complex cases where the full extent of damages cannot be 
ascertained immediately or depends on further developments 
(e.g., ongoing business losses, future medical expenses in 
personal injury cases), the form should state that damages are 
to be assessed. 
 
* 
Interim or provisional claims: Sometimes, you might only be 
ready to claim for part of the losses, or you anticipate needing 
further assessments or evidence to support additional claims. 
 
 
QUESTION 1 – LIMITATION PERIODS: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
General rule: tort claims must be brought within 6 years from the cause 
of action date (when the tortious act occurred/accrual date) 
 
If the tort was not yet apparent: 
6 years from gaining knowledge of the tort and who caused the tort. 
 
Personal injury claims: 
3 years from the tort/knowledge. 
 
If the victim died because of the tort within 3 years of the accrual date, 
the claim must be brought within: 
1. 
3 years from the date of death 
 OR 
2. 
3 years from when the personal representatives of the deceased 
gained knowledge of the tort. 
 
There is a longstop date of 15 years – no action can be brought after 
more than 15 years after the act/omission alleged to have caused the 
damage. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Salma was employed at a chemical manufacturing plant. She has 
died 2 years ago, and at the time, her death was thought to be 
caused by heart failure. 
 
A few months ago, another death occurred at the manufacturing 
plant, which has led to investigations into the safety protocols at the 
plant. It turned out that the employed had been negligent in 
implementing safety protocols, causing several deaths within the 
team working with toxic substances. 
 
Further examination into Salma's medical records had confirmed 
that her heart failure was likely caused by the long-term exposure to 
toxic chemicals at work.

pages.heading: QUESTION 2 – LIMITATION PERIODS: · TORT:
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 8 of 39 
QUESTION 2 – LIMITATION PERIODS: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
TORT: 
 
General rule: tort claims must be brought within 6 years from the cause 
of action date (when the tortious act occurred/accrual date) 
 
If the tort was not yet apparent: 
6 years from gaining knowledge of the tort and who caused the tort. 
 
Personal injury claims: 
3 years from the tort/knowledge. 
 
If the claim is a negligence claim for latent defects in property that was 
not apparent at the time – the limitation period is (whichever is later): 
1. 
6 years from accrual of the action 
 OR 
2. 
3 years from the earliest date on which the Claimant knew or 
ought to have known the material facts necessary to bring a 
negligence action 
 
CONTRACT: 
 
General rule: contract claims must be brought within 6 years from the 
date of the breach. 
 
 
Harvey has purchased a used car last year and has suffered an 
accident earlier this month. He is now in hospital in a coma with a 
fractured arm. 
 
His brother, Adrien took the car to a specialist, who examined the 
car and found no issues. When Harvey woke up from the coma last 
week, he explained to his brother that he lost control of the car and 
he felt that the accident was caused by a mechanical problem. 
 
Adrien takes the car to another specialist, who discovers that the car 
was faulty and that this was likely due to the negligent 
manufacturing of the car. 
 
Harvey is now unable to work.

pages.heading: FUNDING CIVIL CLAIMS · LEGAL AID FUNDING:
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 9 of 39 
FUNDING CIVIL CLAIMS 
 
LEGAL AID FUNDING: 
 
Which type of claims might qualify? 
 
The following will not be funded – alternative funding needed: 
1. Personal injury or death – but injury due to clinical negligence 
is not excluded. 
2. Conveyancing, boundary disputes, defamation, wills/trust 
law, company/partnership law, contract claims 
3. Employment cases negligence and consumer cases 
 
What type of funding is available? 
 
Legal help: helping with preparing a case, but not litigation 
Help at court: allows advocates to speak for the client at a court hearing 
without acting formally – one-off help for one trial. 
Legal representation: covers preparation + litigation + representation. 
 
Assessing whether a client qualifies for help: 
 
Only available to individuals. Must pass both the merits + means test. 
 
Merits test: 
 
Moderate prospect of success is enough. 
 
Will be refused funding if: 
 
Unlikely to win more than the case costs 
 
Alternative funding available 
 
Suitable for the small claims track 
 
Complaints procedure/ADR is not exhausted 
 
Unreasonable for the public to fund the case 
 
Means test: 
 
If the client or their partner receives benefit they are eligible. – eg. 
income support or other benefits. 
 
If no benefits, then consider client's capital and income: 
1. 
Capital: disposable capital is max. £8,000. (and also look at 
partner's capital) 
 AND 
2. 
Income: gross monthly income is max. £2,657 + disposable 
income is max £733 per month. (and also look at partner's 
income) 
 
Costs consequences of legal aid funding: 
 
If a client keeps/gains money or property at the end of their case, then 
they may have to repay some or all of the legal aid costs. This is done 
through a statutory charge. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
If legal aid funding is not available: 
 
Consider: 
* 
Entering into a no win no fee agreement with the law firm 
* 
Takin out/relying on existing insurance 
* 
Self-funding 
 
No win no fee agreements: 
 
 
Conditional fee agreements 
(CFA) 
 
 
Damages based agreements 
(DBA) 
 
 
If the client wins the case: 
 
Pays to the solicitor: 
 
Basic fee 
 
Disbursements 
 
Success fee (pays out of 
pocket) 
 
Insurance premium (pays 
out of pocket) 
 
Recovers from the other side: 
 
Solicitor's basic fee 
 
Disbursements 
 
Damages 
If lawyers lose the case, they do 
not recover any fees. 
 
If lawyers win the case, the max 
recoverable amount is capped: 
1. at 25% of the damages in 
personal injury cases 
2. 35% 
of 
damages 
in 
employment tribunal cases 
 AND 
3. 50% of damages in all 
other cases. 
 
 
If the client loses the case: 
 
Pays to the solicitor: 
 
Disbursements 
 
insurance premium 
 
Damages (if there is a 
successful counterclaim) 
 
Recovers from the other side: 
Nothing 
 
 
Insurance: 
 
If the policy was entered into after 1 Apr 2013: Insurance premium is 
not recoverable from the other side if the policy-holder then wins at 
trial and is awarded its costs. 
 
 
Before the event (BTE) 
insurance 
 
 
After the event (ATE) 
insurance 
 
 
BTE insurance provides the 
client with an indemnity for the 
cost of any legal fees incurred 
as a result of any such future 
litigation. 
 
BTE premiums are relatively 
low (less than 1% of the 
insurance cover). 
 
Criteria: merits of the case + the 
level of cover required, i.e. 
whether a particular insurance 
company is willing to take on the 
risk and on what terms. 
 
ATE 
premiums 
are 
more 
expensive (more than 25% of the 
insurance cover). 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Example of statutory charge on the money/property: 
 
If client wins damages of £20,000 
Court orders costs of £4,000, LAA costs of £5,000 
Statutory charge on damages: £5,000 - £4,000 = £1,000

pages.heading: COMMENCING PROCEEDINGS · Statements of case are:
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 10 of 39 
COMMENCING PROCEEDINGS 
 
Statements of case are: 
* 
Claim Form 
* 
Particulars of Claim (if separate from Claim Form) 
* 
Defence 
* 
Counterclaim 
 
PRE-ACTION PROTOCOLS: 
 
Steps that the parties/their representatives must take before starting 
legal action. 
 
Parties must: 
• 
Exchange adequate info to understand each other's position 
• 
Consider ADR 
• 
Lessen the costs of resolving the dispute 
 
Standard procedure: 
1. 
Claimant will send out a Letter of Claim to the Defendant 
 
2. 
The Defendant need not send out an Acknowledgement of 
Service, but must send a Letter of Response: 
• If there is a deadline in the Letter of Claim, within the 
deadline 
• If no deadline and the claim is a simple claim, within 14 
days of the date of the Letter of Claim 
• If no deadline and the claim is complex, within 3 months 
from the date of the Letter of Claim 
 
3. 
Parties should disclose key documents, whether they are 
planning on using a single joint expert. 
4. 
Parties should consider ADR. 
 
Professional negligence pre-action rules: 
 
For claims against professionals only. 
 
If reasonable chance of bringing claim against potential D, send 
Preliminary Notice. Acknowledge this within 21 days. 
 
When Claimant decides on the grounds, sends Letter of Claim 
 
Other side has 3 months to investigate claim, then sends: 
• 
Letter of Response with response to allegations and/or 
• 
Without prejudice (WP) Letter of Settlement 
 
If offers to settle or admits part of the claim, parties negotiate for max 6 
months from Letter of Acknowledgement. 
 
If the Claimant does not agree, Claimant sends written notice 14 days 
before issuing proceedings. 
 
Personal injury pre-action rules: 
 
The Letter of Claim should contain: 
* 
Summary of the facts 
* 
Details as to how the Claimant's injuries impact on their daily life 
* 
The hospital they attended and any reference numbers 
* 
An indication of financial losses – usually an estimate only. 
 
Response to Letter of Claim: 
The Defendant has 21 days to respond – this response will likely indicate 
whether the Defendant wishes to investigate the matter. 
 
If so, they have 3 months to admit/deny the claim. 
 
If the Defendant does not reply within 21 days, the Claimant may issue 
the Claim form. 
 
The letters sent from each party should include reference to documents 
that will be disclosed during the proceedings. 
 
Instructing an expert: 
* 
If the Claimant will be instructing an expert, the Claimant should 
aim to choose a single-joint expert together with the Defendant, 
and discussions should start at this stage. 
* 
The Claimant must send a list of proposed experts to the 
Defendant who may disagree within 14 days. 
* 
If the Defendant disagrees, each party must instruct their own 
expert. 
 
Other pre-action protocol rules: 
 
If you fail to follow the pre-action protocols: 
* 
The court may order that the proceedings is stayed to allow the 
Practice Direction/the pre-action protocols to be complied with. 
* 
The court may order the non-compliant party to pay the costs 
or part of it of the other party. 
 
It may be acceptable to issue proceedings without compliance with the 
protocols if: 
* 
The limitation period is about to expire 
* 
A court order is needed to preserve evidence/assets 
 OR 
* 
The Defendant may issue proceedings in another country to 
avoid the UK courts. 
 
Pre-action application for disclosure: 
Either party may make a pre-action application for disclosure of certain 
documents. 
 
This can only be done if: 
1. 
The documents requested would be disclosed under standard 
disclosure. 
 AND 
2. 
Disclosure would now assist in disposing of the claim without 
having to issue proceedings and thus saving costs. 
 
Application to inspect property: 
 
Either party might make a pre-action application to inspect property if: 
• 
The property is/may become the subject matter of the 
proceedings 
 OR 
• 
It is relevant to the issues in the proceedings. 
 
WHICH COURT? 
 
Do not confuse this question with allocation to tracks! 
 
Which Court to choose? 
 
Identify the value of claim. PD7A para 2.1 
 
Less than £100,000 even if complex – 
County Court. If deemed complex, case 
will be transferred later. 
 
£100,000 or more – client has a choice: 
County Court and High Court has 
concurrent jurisdiction. 
 
 
If there is a choice, consider the factors in PD 7A para 2.4: 
 
1. 
Financial value – over £100,000 by much? CPR 16.3(5) 
CPR 16.3(6) CPR 26.8 Financial value = how much we expect to 
recover minus interest and costs for any counterclaim. 
£125,000 is only £25,000 above the High Court threshold of 
£100,000 – commence the case in the County Court. 
 
2. 
Complexity: 
 
Simple claims: 
* 
Breach of contract – eg. non-payment of an invoice is a 
simple debt claim. 
* 
Parking charge appeals 
* 
Simple negligence claims 
 
Complex claims: 
* 
International cases – eg. the Claimant is based in the 
UK, the Defendant is based in Singapore. 
* 
Cases with differing jurisdiction and law – English 
jurisdiction but Spanish law. 
* 
Multiple parties 
* 
Expert witnesses will be required 
 
3. 
Importance to the public – not public interest 
 
Which High Court division? 
* 
King's Bench Division – contract, tort 
* 
Chancery Division – IP, land 
* 
Family Division – family law cases 
 
The high court in London is the Royal Courts of Justice. 
 
What if the case is brought in the wrong court? 
 
CPR 30.3 If the case is brought in the wrong court, transfer is likely. 
 
CPR 30.3(2) Transfer order factors: 
* 
Financial value, complexity, public interest factors as above 
* 
Convenience, fair to transfer 
* 
Availability of specialist judge in regional specialist court 
* 
Facilities for disabled/potential witnesses 
 
Sanctions: 
* 
The court may order C to pay the costs of the transfer. 
* 
Additional sanction for wrongly bringing a claim in the High Court 
instead of the County Court. – s.51 SCA 1981 
County Court: 
* Simple facts/law 
* Lower value 
High Court: 
* Complex facts/law 
* High value

pages.heading: COUNTING TIME: *POPULAR EXAM Q* · What is the document served?
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 11 of 39 
 
COUNTING TIME: *POPULAR EXAM Q* 
 
What is the document served? 
 
Is the document being served a Claim form or some other document? 
 
If the Particulars is not served with the Claim Form it must be served 
within 14 days of service of the Claim Form. 
 
If Claim form – how has it been served? 
 
Service of Claim Form (CF)? *Only mention if asked* 
Serve the Claim Form by sending it to court with one copy for each 
Defendant, one for Claimant, one for court + court fee 
 
Sealing Claim Form = starts proceedings and stops the limitation period. 
 
Where to serve CF? 
Serve the Claim Form at the solicitors' address. 
If sending to solicitor, they must be authorised to accept service. 
 
If no solicitor: 
* 
D's last known place of residence or company's principal office. 
– it will not matter if the Claim Form has not been actually 
received. 
* 
If the serving party had a reason to believe other party was no 
longer there – then serving party must take reasonable steps to 
find address. 
 
Who serves the CF? 
* 
The court by post or the Claimant. 
* 
File certificate of service within 21 days of service of the Claim 
Form, unless all Defendants filed an Acknowledgement of 
Service. 
 
How to serve the CF? 
The Claim Form must be served by taking ‘relevant step' within 4 
months of issue of the Claim Form. Serve the Particulars of Claim at 
same time as the Claim Form. 
 
 
Method of service 
Relevant Step 
First class post 
Post or leave with postal service 
Delivery or leaving at address 
Delivered or left at address 
Personal service 
Leave with individual or partner 
at company 
Fax (if other party accepts fax) 
Fax transmitted 
Electronic service – eg. email 
Email sent 
 
 
If the Claimant is to serve the claim form late, apply for an extension 
before the period ends. 
 
Good to know the deemed date of service of the CF: 
• 
For Claimants: the time limit for serving the Particulars of Claim 
runs from the deemed date of service of the claim form. 
• 
For Defendants: the deadline for serving a response to the claim 
form runs from the deemed date of service of the claim form. 
 
Claim Form is deemed served on 2nd business day after the relevant 
step. – eg. If posted on Friday, deemed served on Tuesday 
 I 
If only dealing with CF, skip the next heading and start counting time. 
 
If documents other than a claim form – how has it been served? 
 
Service of any document other than Claim Form: 
 
 
Method of service 
Deemed served 
First class post 
2nd business day after posting 
Delivery or leaving at address 
If served before 4.30pm on a 
business day, then same day, 
otherwise next business day. 
Personal service 
Fax (if other party accepts fax) 
Electronic service 
 
 
Particulars of Claim: 
Serve the Particulars within 4 months of taking relevant step 
 
If Particulars served same time as the CF: 
It will be deemed served at the same time as the Claim form. 
 
If Particulars served separately from CF: 
Above rules on service apply to the Particulars of Claim. 
Must serve the Particulars 14 clear days after CF served. 
 
Particulars of Claim – How to respond? 
D must respond in one of 3 ways within 14 days of deemed service of 
the Particulars: 
1. 
Admit part or all of the claim 
2. 
File defence within 28 clear days of deemed service of 
Particulars 
 OR 
3. 
File Acknowledgment of service using Form N9. Do this if: 
1. You need more than 14 days to prepare the defence 
 OR 
2. If it wishes to dispute that the court has jurisdiction to 
hear the claim. 
 
File an acknowledgment of service within 14 days after service 
of the Particulars 
 
Acknowledgement of Service + Defence: 
File the Acknowledgement of Service 14 days after Particulars deemed 
served: 
– 
File the Acknowledgement of Service together with the defence 
 OR 
– 
File the Acknowledgement of Service separately 
 
File the defence 14 days after Particulars or if acknowledged service, file 
the defence 28 clear days after the Particulars of Claim. 
 
Counting time: 
 
Days = always 'clear days' not incl. first day. If last day ends with event 
(hearing), then add 1 day. Therefore, the day of deemed service is 
always treated as 0, then stop counting on the 14th day. If 14th is a 
hearing date, skip that day and stop at the 15th day. 
 
If period is 5 days or less ≠ incl. weekends + bank holidays 
Notice served at least 3 days before hearing (Friday 20 Oct) - last date of 
service = Monday 16 Oct 
 
If period is > 5 days = incl. weekends + bank holidays 
Eg. Particulars served within 14 days of CF. If CF deemed served on 3 Feb, 
last date of service = 17 Feb 
 
TIME EXTENSIONS: 
 
The Defendant may agree with the Claimant to extend the deadline for 
service if they cannot serve the defence in time. 
 
The parties can agree among themselves to extend the deadline by up 
to 28 clear days from the deemed service of Claim Form, so that the 
Defendant has 56 days in total to serve its defence. The parties must 
notify the court in writing. 
 
If the Defendant needs more time than 28 days, the Defendant should 
make an interim application to extend time: 
The court will ensure that the overriding objective is furthered in 
deciding whether to grant an extension of time. The court may accept or 
reject the application.

pages.heading: JUDGMENT IN DEFAULT · Judgment in default = Judgment without trial in the Claimant's favour
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 12 of 39 
JUDGMENT IN DEFAULT 
 
Judgment in default = Judgment without trial in the Claimant's favour 
due to the Defendant's default. This is done at the early stages of a claim 
where the Defendant has not submitted an Acknowledgement of 
Service and/or the Defence in time or at all. 
 
REQUIREMENTS: 
 
Claimant may apply if: the Defendant did not file the 
Acknowledgement of Service or defence within the time limits. 
 
The Claimant must apply promptly. 
 
The Claimant must show that: 
* 
The Claimant filed a certificate of service 
* 
Application was made on notice and with all the relevant 
evidence 
* 
The claim has not been admitted or satisfied 
 AND 
* 
No application made for summary judgment or strike out. 
 
THE DEFENDANT'S OPTIONS: 
 
Once the default judgment has been entered, the defendant has the 
option to apply to have the default judgment set aside. – CPR 13.2 
 
This application may be made on mandatory or discretionary grounds. 
 
Grounds: 
 
Mandatory grounds (court must set aside judgment in default if): 
* 
Acknowledgement of Service/Defence was served within time 
limit. – CPR 13.2(a) 
* 
D applied for summary judgment or strike out before the default 
judgment was entered. – CPR 13.2(b) 
* 
D has satisfied/admitted claim before the application. – CPR 
13.2(c) 
 
Discretionary remedy (court may set aside if): 
* 
The Defendant has real prospect of defending the claim. 
* 
The is a good reason to set aside the judgment. – eg. length and 
reasons for D's delay 
 
Test for setting aside default judgment: 
 
FXF v English Karate (2023) The Denton test also applies to applications 
setting aside default judgment. 
 
Denton Test for relief from sanctions. Relief will be granted if: 
 
* 
The breach is not serious/significant 
 * 
There is a legitimate reason for the breach – Defendants must 
explain what the reason was for their non-compliance. 
 
* 
Other circumstances that suggest relief should be allowed, in 
particular, whether the application to for relief was made 
promptly by the applicant.

pages.heading: STATEMENTS OF CASE · Statements of case are as follows:
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 13 of 39 
STATEMENTS OF CASE 
 
Statements of case are as follows: 
– 
Claim Form 
– 
Particulars of Claim (if separate from Claim Form) 
– 
Defence and Counterclaim 
 
PARTICULARS OF CLAIM: 
 
The Claimant must send out a Particulars of Claim detailing their case 
and must disclose enough information to identify all issues. 
 
The Particulars of Claim must include: 
 
* 
For contract claims: 
1. 
The parties to the contract 
2. 
The nature of the contract 
3. 
The terms that have been breached 
4. 
Fact pattern showing the breach and losses 
5. 
Prayer for relief (the remedy sought) 
6. 
Statement of truth 
 
* 
For Road accident claims: 
1. 
Date, time, place and description of the collision 
2. 
Details of negligence 
3. 
Any relevant convictions 
4. 
Details of any injuries 
5. 
Schedule of past and future losses 
6. 
Prayer for relief 
7. 
Statement of truth 
 
* 
For personal injury claims: 
1. 
Date, time, place and description of the accident 
2. 
Details of negligence 
3. 
Any relevant convictions 
4. 
Details of any injuries 
5. 
Schedule of past and future losses 
6. 
Prayer for relief 
7. 
Statement of truth. 
 
* 
For employer liability tort claims: 
1. 
Facts that establish the employer-employee relationship 
2. 
Circumstances and details of the injury 
3. 
Breach 
4. 
Schedule of past and future losses 
5. 
Prayer for relief 
6. 
Statement of truth 
 
If you are claiming interest, include: 
1. 
The basis for the claim, the applicable percentage 
2. 
The date on which the interest ends (usually the day when the 
Particulars of Claim was drafted) 
3. 
The total amount claimed 
 
Other points to include, if relevant: 
1. 
Any illegality surrounding the case 
2. 
Allegations of fraud 
3. 
Misrepresentation 
4. 
Breach of trust 
5. 
Notices of knowledge of a fact 
6. 
Unsoundness of mind 
7. 
Undue influence of either party 
8. 
Details of wilful default 
9. 
Defendant's failure to mitigate loss or damage 
 
DEFENCE: 
 
A Defendant should then prepare a defence in response (however, they 
do not need to if they do not wish to defend the claim). Once a defence 
is prepared, it should be served on every other party to the claim. 
 
The Claimant may then send a Reply to the defence if they wish to. 
 
Admit, deny, require proof: 
 
In the defence, the Defendant must respond to each paragraph in the 
Particulars of Claim by: 
1. 
Admitting it 
2. 
Denying it 
 OR 
3. 
Requiring proof of the statement (also called a non-admission) 
 
Admit: 
Admit anything that is not disputed or non-controversial. In a contract 
action, it is usual to admit the existence of the contract and sometimes 
its performance and its terms. 
 
 
 
Deny: 
Denials are used to dispute any facts which, if they had occurred, would 
have been within the defendant's knowledge. If a defendant denies an 
allegation it must give reasons or put forward a different version of 
events. 
 
In a contract claim, it may be possible to deny that: 
a) The debt is due, or 
b) The term relied upon exists, explaining why – eg. because the 
sale was not in the course of business. 
 
Require proof: 
This term is used if the Defendant is unable to either admit or deny 
because the fact that is alleged is something about which the Defendant 
did not and could not know. In contract claims, the Defendant usually 
requires proof of the amount of the alleged loss and damage. 
 
Specific rules: 
 
If the Defendant disputed the Claimant's statement of value, they should 
state the reasons why and state their own value. 
 
For personal injury claims: 
The defence must state whether the Defendant agrees with the medical 
report served with the Particulars of Claim. 
 
A Defendant may admit damages subject to liability – thus a Defendant 
may admit the amount of damages but deny liability. If this is the case, 
the Claimant will recover the agreed damages if they prove liability. 
 
Example: 
 
Respond to each paragraph of the Particulars of Claim – example 
paragraphs: 
• 
At all material times paragraph – admit. There is nothing 
controversial in this paragraph. In fact, the comment that ‘the 
Defendant was a manufacturer of cat furniture' helps Pets's case 
that this was a sale in the course of a business. 
 
• 
The Claimant entered into a contract with the Defendant on 11 
October 2024 and the price for the Goods was £200,000 – 
admit. There is nothing which Pets disputes here. The parties 
entered into the contract and Pets does not dispute that the 
price agreed was £200,000. 
 
• 
It was an express term of the Contract that payment for all 
services and goods provided would be due 30 days from the 
date of the invoice and that interest would be payable at 8% 
per annum on late payment. – admit. Again none of this is 
controversial and it describes what happened. The fact that the 
invoice was not paid (breach) is separate so use a separate 
paragraph. 
 
• 
In breach of the express term of the Contract, no payment has 
been made by the Defendant. – this would be denied by saying 
that there was no breach of contract. The Defendant could deny 
liability to pay the invoice for example if the products 
malfunctioned or were not as described which meant that there 
had been a breach of the implied term in the contract that the 
goods were of satisfactory quality. 
 
• 
As a result of the breach, the Claimant claims the sum of 
£200,000 – the loss figure here would be admitted or denied 
depending on whether you are disputing the figure or not. 
 
• 
The paragraphs claiming interest – this should be denied. 
 
DIFFERENT TYPES OF CLAIMS: 
 
There are three key types of claims the SQE may test you on: 
 
1. 
Part 7 Claims – your usual claim where the Claimant and the 
Defendant are in dispute of facts. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
2. 
Part 8 Claims – a claim where the Claimant and the Defendant 
are not disputing any of the facts (relatively rare). 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Example: 
Jessabelle makes a claim for breach of contract against 
Aubrey, in relation to works that have not been carried out 
to the required standard. Aubrey says that this is not correct, 
and he has performed the contract according to the 
specification. 
Example: 
Molly is the personal representative of her father, who has 
passed away last week. She requires guidance from the 
court, as she is unsure how to interpret her father's will. 
There are no facts in dispute here, so the claim will be made 
under Part 8.

pages.heading: Part 20 Claims – claims that are additional to the principal claim. · PART 20 CLAIMS:
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 14 of 39 
3. 
Part 20 Claims – claims that are additional to the principal claim. 
 
PART 20 CLAIMS: 
 
Part 20 claims include: 
 
* 
The Defendant's claims against third parties who are potentially 
liable to pay compensation to the Claimant/Defendant 
* 
The Defendant's counterclaims against the Claimant 
 
The Defendant must obtain court permission to file: 
1. 
A counterclaim 
2. 
A third-party claim 
3. 
Indemnity/contribution 
4. 
Counterclaim against another third party 
 
If the counterclaim, third party claim or indemnity/contribution is filed 
together with the defence, then the Defendant does not need to obtain 
court permission. 
 
Thus, if the Defendant wishes to make these claims at another time, they 
must obtain court permission. 
 
Serving the Claim: 
* 
If court permission is not required, a Part 20 claim must be 
served on each party to the claim when the defence is filed. 
* 
If an additional claim is issued by the court later, it must be 
served on the person against whom it is made within 14 days of 
issue. 
 
Defences to Part 20 claims: 
Defences must be served within 14 days of the deemed date of service 
of the Part 20 claim. 
 
Counterclaim: 
 
Counterclaim = when a Defendant makes a claim against the Claimant in 
the defence where this claim is arising from the same set of 
circumstances as the Claimant's claim. 
 
Counterclaims must be brought within the same proceedings. – typically, 
as part of the defence. 
 
Counterclaims are monetary claims in their own right. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Third-party claims: 
 
Third-party claim = a Defendant claims that a third party (who is not 
party to the claim) has caused the Claimant's losses. 
 
The Particulars of Claim must be served with the third-party claim. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Counterclaim against another third party: 
 
A Defendant counterclaims a third party (who is not party to the claim) 
for compensation. These counterclaims must arise out of the same 
proceedings as the main claim. 
 
These claims may only be made after obtaining a court order. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
REQUESTS FOR FURTHER INFORMATION: 
 
Either party may send a request for further information to any of the 
other parties to clarify a matter in dispute/get additional information. 
 
If the other party does not respond within a reasonable time, the 
requesting party may make an application to the court. 
 
The other party may object – grounds for objection: 
* 
The request is unnecessary/irrelevant/improper 
* 
The information is protected by privilege 
* 
The responding party is unable to provide the information 
requested 
* 
The responding party was given insufficient time to respond 
* 
The costs of complying with the request would be 
disproportionate to the claim 
* 
Complying with the request would be contrary to the overriding 
objective 
 
AMENDMENTS TO STATEMENTS OF CASE: 
 
Once the Statements of case is served, it can be amended by written 
consent of all the parties/court permission. 
 
A new party can be added to the proceedings, if it is shown that adding 
the party will allow the court to resolve the matters in dispute/resolve a 
connected matter. 
 
A court may order a person to cease to be a party, if it would not be 
desirable for them to be a party to the proceedings. 
 
A party may be substituted for an existing party, if: 
* 
The existing party's interest/liability has passed to the new party 
 AND 
* 
It is desirable to substitute the new party so that the court can 
resolve the matters in dispute.

DEFENDANT'S ADDITIONAL CLAIMS 
 
Part 20 governs the Defendant's claims, and therefore, none of the 
Claimant's additional claims fall within Part 20. 
 
Any additional parties the Claimant might add is done under Part 19. 
In this case, all the Claimant needs to do is add in any additional 
Defendants or Claimants onto the Claim Form and Particulars of Claim 
before it is served or change them after service with the court's 
permission. 
 
Please note: all of these claims made by the Defendant are treated as 
substantive claims and a Defence must also be filed in response to these 
within the time limits. 
 
COUNTERCLAIM AGAINST THE CLAIMANT: 
 
Recognise this claim: 
 
CPR 20.4 In many cases, the Defendant may submit a counterclaim with 
their defence (or later), a separate claim against the Claimant. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The rules in relation to this claim: 
 
How can the Defendant submit this type of counterclaim? 
 
The Defendant may submit their counterclaim: 
1. 
When Defence is filed – permission is not needed. – CPR 20.4(2) 
2. 
After Defence is filed – court permission is required. 
 
PD 20(6.1) Defence and Counterclaim is usually in one document but 
counterclaim can follow the defence. 
 
COUNTERCLAIM AGAINST A THIRD PARTY: 
 
Recognise this claim: 
 
CPR 20.5 Instead of a simple counterclaim against the Claimant, the 
Defendant might submit a counterclaim against both the Claimant and 
a third party. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The terminology might change depending on the point of view. 
 
If you are looking at the situation from the point of view of the Original 
Claimant, then the Defendant will be the Defendant. 
 
The rules in relation to this claim: 
 
How can the Defendant submit this type of counterclaim? 
 
Counterclaim against someone other than Claimant: 
* 
There must be substantive connection between Claimant and 
the third party. 
* 
In this case, court permission is always required. – CPR 20.5(1) 
* 
Apply to the court pursuant to both CPR 19 and 20 as the 
Defendant making the counterclaim is now also the Claimant. 
* 
Document to use: N211 claim form 
 
Substantive connection with the Claimant – examples: 
* 
Employee-employer where the employer is vicariously liable, so 
the employer should have been sued. 
* 
Work carried out together but only one of them is being sued. 
* 
Someone else was the wrongdoer who wronged the Claimant 
even if that third party had no relationship with the Defendant. 
 
CONTRIBUTION/INDEMNITY AGAINST 
CO-DEFENDANT: 
 
Recognise this claim: 
 
CPR 20.6 The Defendant may make a claim for contribution/indemnity 
against a Co-Defendant. 
 
Contribution = A right to recover from a third person all/part of the 
amount which they themselves are liable to pay. 
 
Indemnity = A right to recover from a third person the whole amount 
which they themselves are liable to pay. 
 
Co-Defendant = another Defendant to the case who has been included 
as a Co-Defendant when the Claimant made the original claim. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Claimant

Example: 
Larry has recently bought his first home. He hires Thomas, a builder 
to install his kitchen. Larry later finds out that the sink is leaking 
and the kitchen surface around the sink was not installed properly. 
He refuses to pay Thomas' invoice for the installation. 
 
Thomas makes a claim for non-payment of the invoice and when 
Larry files his defence, he also files a counterclaim against Thomas 
as he now cannot use his kitchen and has suffered a loss as a result. 
Example: 
Larry has recently bought his first home. He hires Thomas, a builder 
and Anthony, a plumber, to install his kitchen. Larry later finds out 
that the sink is leaking and the kitchen surface around the sink was 
not installed properly. He refuses to pay Thomas' invoice for the 
installation. (Notice that it is Thomas' invoice that is unpaid and he 
is the one who makes the claim not Anthony.) 
 
Thomas makes a claim for non-payment of the invoice and when 
Larry files his defence, he also files a counterclaim against Thomas 
and also Anthony as a third party to the claim as he now cannot use 
his kitchen and has suffered a loss as a result.

pages.heading: Claims for indemnity/contribution will always be made by the · wrongdoer. If the Defendant in your claim has not done anything wrong
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 16 of 39 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Claims for indemnity/contribution will always be made by the 
wrongdoer. If the Defendant in your claim has not done anything wrong 
apart from refusing the pay an outstanding amount, then they cannot 
make a claim for contribution/indemnity. 
 
Refusing payment will not make one party the wrongdoer, this is usually 
done as a response of a wrongdoing. 
 
The rules in relation to this claim: 
 
How can the Defendant submit this type of contribution/indemnity? 
 
Contribution or indemnity (100%) from co-Defendant: 
1. 
When Defence is filed – permission is not needed. – CPR 20.6(2) 
2. 
After Defence is filed – Court permission is required. 
3. 
Document to use: D's claim for contribution or indemnity will 
be set out in a contribution notice. There is no set form for this. 
 
How this works in practice: 
1. 
If C is successful, C will have a judgment against D which they 
will enforce. 
2. 
If D is also successful in their Part 20 claim against co-D, D will 
have a separate judgment against co-D, so they will claim their 
contribution or indemnity from co-D. 
 
CONTRIBUTION/INDEMNITY AGAINST 
THIRD PARTY: 
 
Recognise this claim: 
 
CPR 20.7 The Defendant may make a claim for contribution/indemnity 
against a third party. 
 
However, this is also a “catch-all category” for any claims that do not fit 
into the previous three categories. 
 
Contribution = A right to recover from a third person all/part of the 
amount which they themselves are liable to pay. 
 
Indemnity = A right to recover from a third person the whole amount 
which they themselves are liable to pay. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The rules in relation to this claim: 
 
How can the Defendant submit this type of contribution/indemnity? 
 
Other additional claims for contribution or indemnity against third 
party who is not already part to the claim: CPR 20.7 
1. 
When Defence is filed – permission is not required. – CPR 
20.7(3) 
2. 
After Defence is filed – court permission is needed. 
Counterclaims are usually not filed together with the Defence. 
3. 
Document to use: N211 claim form 
 
COUNTERCLAIM VS CLAIM FOR INDEMNITY: 
 
When someone makes an indemnity claim against another, the 
Claimant (in that situation) will want to receive the money they would 
be paying for the claim as the Defendant. 
 
If this is the case, how is making a claim for indemnity different from a 
counterclaim? 
 
A claim for indemnity can only be made if there is some form of contract 
between the parties allowing one of the parties to make a claim for 
indemnity in certain circumstances. 
 
Indemnity – Examples: 
1. 
If someone is vicariously liable in tort, for example in relation 
to an employer-employee relationship, they may receive a 
claim for indemnity under the contract. 
 
2. 
If there is a breach of contract that triggers the operstion of an 
indemnity clause in a contract. 
 
A counterclaim is a completely separate claim existing in its own right. 
– could be a claim for breach of statutory duty, tortious claim for 
negligence etc. 
 
You can make a claim for contribution in relation to tort claims, however, 
for indemnity claims, you will need to have a contract with an indemnity 
clause, otherwise you would need to make a counterclaim
