pages.heading: CASE MANAGEMENT · CPR 1.1 Overriding objective: the court must ensure that cases are
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 17 of 39 
CASE MANAGEMENT 
 
CPR 1.1 Overriding objective: the court must ensure that cases are 
dealt with justly, fairly and proportionately. 
 
CPR 1.2 The court must give effect to the overriding objective when 
exercising its case management powers. 
 
CPR 1.3 Solicitors and parties to a claim have a positive duty to help the 
court achieve its overriding objective. 
 
Case and costs management are interlinked and are both dealt with at 
the allocation stage. The CMC often doubles as a costs management 
hearing and is referred to as the costs and case management conference 
(CCMC). 
 
THE COURT'S POWERS: 
 
It is the court's duty to manage cases actively, dealing with cases: 
* 
Justly and at proportionate cost 
* 
Within a reasonable time 
 AND 
* 
By proportionate use of court and party resources 
 
Powers: 
Court has general case management powers to: 
1. 
Extend/shorten time limits for compliance with a rule/practice 
direction/court order 
2. 
Adjourn/change hearing dates 
3. 
Require a party/their legal representative to attend court 
4. 
Exclude an issue from the proceedings and direct that part to be 
dealt with in a separate proceedings 
5. 
Stay the whole/part of the proceedings 
6. 
Try 2 or more claims at the same trial 
7. 
Order a party to file/serve an estimate of costs 
8. 
Contact the parties to monitor compliance with directions 
 AND 
9. 
Take any other step/make any other order to manage the case 
and further the overriding objective 
 
Court has the power to make an order of its own initiative regardless 
of hearing or representations. 
 
SANCTIONS: 
 
Key sanctions: 
 
Consider court sanctions eg. if 1 party doesn't comply with pre-action 
protocol because may have avoided litigation if complied. 
 
Failure to comply with the rules/court orders will attract a sanction. 
 
Sanction = punishment imposed by the court. 
Seeking to obtain 'relief from sanctions' = Trying to persuade the court 
not to impose a sanction where due. 
 
Key sanctions the court can impose: Broad powers! 
1. 
Making an order subject to conditions 
2. 
Setting out consequences for failure to comply with an order. 
3. 
When giving directions, court may take into account compliance 
with the pre-action protocols 
 AND 
4. 
Ordering a party to pay the court for failure to comply with a 
rule/practice direction/pre-action protocol 
 
Additional powers: 
• 
Make a costs order in relation to either party 
• 
Prevent a party from adducing evidence on an issue (debarring 
evidence) 
• 
Limit interest on a claim/increase the interest amount payable 
• 
Impose an unless order: unless party complies with the relevant 
rule, sanction will be enforced. 
 
• 
Strike out whole or part of the case – rare. 
Once deleted, the party cannot rely on it in the proceedings. This 
power is used to strike out inappropriately drafted paragraphs 
or as a sanction for abuse of court process. 
 
Relief from sanctions: 
 
If a party has a good reason for non-compliance, the court may grant 
relief from sanctions. 
 
Test for relief from sanctions. Relief will be granted if: 
1. 
The breach is not serious/significant – Does the breach imperil 
future hearing dates? – eg. filing late by 45 mins is not serious, 
but repeat offenders are more likely to be serious. Significant if 
trial had to be vacated because of it. 
 OR 
2. 
There is a legitimate reason for the breach – eg. solicitor or 
party overworked is not legitimate reason 
 
UNLESS ORDER: 
 
An order that unless the party that has not complied with the CPR 
complied with the CPR requirements within the time limits set out by 
the order, the court will order the strike out of that party's case. 
 
Grounds: CPR 3.1(3) and CPR 23 
* 
The Respondent in an interim application has failed to comply 
with the previous order or the overriding objective. 
 OR 
* 
The courts believe that it is likely that the Respondent is not 
acting in good faith. 
 
When an order is made: 
 The court will specify the sanction to be received by the Respondent 
should they not comply with the unless order within the prescribed time 
limits. 
 
EXTENDING THE DEADLINE: 
 
Exam Structure – Extending the deadline: 
1. 
Which CPR was breached? 
2. 
Deadline for compliance passed/extended? 
State the deadline start and end date here. 
3. 
Has the deadline expired? Is the application in time or out of 
time? 
4. 
CPR + Any relevant case law 
 
In time: 
* 
Applicant's reason for an extension 
* 
Delay in making the application? 
* 
Overriding objective 
* 
Will it cause any disruption? 
 
Out of time: 
* 
CPR 3.9 
* 
Denton 
 
5. 
Apply 
6. 
Conclude 
 
In-time applications: 
 
If you applied for extension before the deadline, use this procedure. 
 
Chartwell v Fergies For in-time applications, the relief from sanctions 
procedure won't apply, irrespective of when the court deals with the 
application. 
Teresa Baker Reasonable in-time applications will be allowed, if 
doesn't disrupt conduct of litigation – eg. hearing date stays the same. 
 
Full example – application to facts: 
1. 
Is the application in time or out of time? In time – 21 days 
before the CCMC (this is enough if you don't have the dates) 
 
2. 
CPR + Any relevant case law + Apply 
In time: 
* 
Applicant's reason for an extension 
Expert witness is on holidays 
 
* 
Delay in making the application? 
Applicant argues no delay as only 2 days passed since 
witness went on holidays but Respondent will argue that 
they have learned the expert witness would be on 
holidays 3 weeks ago. 
 
* 
Overriding objective 
No delay in proceedings. 
 
* 
Will it cause any disruption? 
The CCMC is on the 19th. Applicant asked for extension 
till the 11th. We are asking for the Precedent H to be due 
in the same time as Precedent R. The counsel gets back 
on 3rd or 4th so could extent till then. The court will 
never want to move the other dates. 
 
3. 
Apply: considering the above, another week is acceptable. 
4. 
Conclude: application should be allowed 
 
Out of time application: 
 
If you applied for extension after the deadline has passed, use this 
procedure. 
Brutal sanction for out of time: it is treated as if you only filed the court 
fees. 
 
CPR 3.9(1) Apply for relief from sanctions, as late application.

pages.heading: Denton Test for relief from sanctions. Relief will be granted if: · The breach is not serious/significant
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 18 of 39 
Denton Test for relief from sanctions. Relief will be granted if: 
3. 
The breach is not serious/significant 
Test: Does the breach imperil future hearing dates? 
eg. filing late by 45 mins is not serious, but repeat offenders are 
more likely to be serious. Significant if trial had to be vacated 
because of it. 
4. 
There is a legitimate reason for the breach 
eg. solicitor or party overworked is not legitimate reason 
5. 
Other circumstances that suggest relief should be allowed, with 
particular weight to CPR 3.9(1) criteria: 
- 
Litigation must be conducted efficiently and at 
proportionate cost, and 
- 
Enforce compliance with the rules, PDs and orders. 
 
If one applies, likely to approve relief. The breach must be minor and not 
delay hearing date. 
 
Full example – applying to the facts: 
1. 
Is the application in time or out of time? 
21 Nov = deadline, should have applied by then. – out of time. 
 
2. 
CPR + Any relevant case law 
Out of time: 
(a) CPR 3.9 
(b) Denton (go through Denton in the exam) 
 
Denton Factors: 
- Seriousness of the breach 
Failing to exchange witness statements on time is serious. 
 
- Why the default occurred 
Francis was sick, how severely sick? Has he got a cold or is he 
unconscious unable to write the statement? 
 
- Evaluate all the circumstances. 
Mainly look at: CPR 3.9(1) 
Litigation is important. No other person to be a witness? 
 
3. 
Apply: only 1 day late, but not a good reason. 
4. 
Conclude: appl. should be allowed as 1 day would not affect the 
proceedings. 
 
ALLOCATION: 
 
Once the defence has been filed, the County Court will allocate every 
case to a particular track. 
 
Allocation is, however, in the direction of the court, so they may 
ultimately decide to allocate a case which was meant to be allocated to 
the multi-track, to the intermediate track or another track. 
 
Four tracks: 
1. 
Small claims track 
2. 
Fast track 
3. 
Intermediate track 
4. 
Multi-track 
 
Small claims track: 
 
Value of the claim is less than £10,000. 
For personal injury claims: value must be less than £1,000. 
 
Recoverable costs will be limited to fixed costs (what the court deems 
reasonable for the type of case). 
 
Fast track: 
 
Between £10,000 and £25,000. 
 
 AND 
 
Other factors to consider for fast track: 
 
Trial should be expected to take less than 5 hours 
 AND 
 
There will only be one expert per party. 
 
Intermediate track: 
 
Cases between £25,000 and £100,000 
 
 AND 
 
Other factors to consider for intermediate track: CPR 26.9(7) 
 
Trial is not expected to last longer than 3 days. 
 
There will only be up to 2 experts per party. 
 AND 
 
There is a maximum of 3 parties to the claim. 
 
Multi-track: 
 
All other types of cases 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
PROCEDURE: 
 
STEP 1 – Notice of Proposed Allocation (NPA) – All tracks: 
 
CPR 26.4(1) After the defence is filed, court assigns the case to suitable 
track + sends NPA. Parties can then fill in the Directions Questionnaire 
and accept the allocation or argue for a different track. 
 
CPR 26.8(1)-(2) Lists all additional factors for allocation – eg. likely 
complexity, number of parties, nature of remedy. 
 
STEP 2 – Directions Questionnaire (DQ) – All tracks except the small 
claims track: 
 
CPR 26.4(6)(b)(ii) DQ is filed 28 days using Form N181 after NPA deemed 
served (4.30pm business day rule, except for post). 
 
The document will contain: 
 
Which court to allocate case 
 
Number of witnesses/experts 
 
Estimated trial length 
 
Directions asked for 
 
CPR 29.4 Agreed proposed directions order or if disagree, proposed 
directions (adapted standard directions) must be filed within 7 days 
before CMC Statement. 
 
STEP 3 – Disclosure Report (DR) – Intermediate track and multi track 
cases only: 
CPR 31.5(3)-(8) Both parties produce a DR max 14 days before the first 
CMC. 
 
STEP 4 – Allocation – All tracks: 
Once all parties have filed their DQ: 
CPR 26.7 Court will allocate claim to a track 
CPR 26.4 Court will send parties a Notice of Allocation 
 
CASE MANAGEMENT CONFERENCE: 
 
Case Management Conference (CMC): 
 
CMC = Meeting to approve of directions for conduct prior to trial + 
narrow any issues. 
 
File case summary before CMC if this helps court to understand the case 
better. 
 
Representative attending a CMC must be familiar with the case and have 
sufficient authority to deal with the case. If contravened and CMC is 
postponed, the court may make a wasted costs order (solicitor pays). 
 
Directions: 
 
Directions = court instructions on how to prepare for case – eg. how to 
exchange witness statements, deadlines, hearings. 
 
• 
If parties do not agree directions: must conduct case and costs 
management conference. 
 
• 
If parties agree: no CMC but separate costs management 
conference. 
 
 
Example: 
Four people are injured in a car accident, injured in the same 
vehicle. All four of them make a claim against the negligent driver 
who caused the incident. Even if the value of the claim is only 
£38,000, the claim will have to be allocated to the multi-track 
because there would be five parties involved (four claimants and 
one defendant).

pages.heading: COSTS MANAGEMENT · COSTS BUDGETS:
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 19 of 39 
COSTS MANAGEMENT 
 
COSTS BUDGETS: 
 
Parties must deal with costs at the allocation stage – this involves the 
legal costs of a cases (legal fees and disbursements). 
 
Costs and case management conference (CCMC) happens where CMC 
doubles as a costs management hearing. 
 
Costs budget = a budget estimate of reasonable and proportionate costs 
that party expects to incur during litigation. – Tactical point: high budget 
will convince opponent into mediation, leading to early settlement. 
 
Costs budget – Precedent H: 
 
Who needs to file a costs budget? 
 
All parties to an intermediate track or multi-track case must file and 
exchange costs budgets setting out estimated costs for each stage in the 
proceedings. 
 
Exceptions to the need for preparing a costs budget: 
1. 
Litigants in person need not file a costs budget. 
2. 
No need to file a costs budget if the court orders not to file it. 
3. 
If the value of the claim exceeds £10 million. 
4. 
If the claim is brought by or on behalf of a minor (under 18). 
 
Precedent H = prescribed form for the costs budget. May lead to Costs 
Management Order (CMO) and secure early settlement. 
 
Precedent H must contain assumptions on which the budget is based 
and will contain the costs already incurred and an estimate of future 
costs. 
 
What type of costs budget to file? 
 
Use the first page of Precedent H if: 
 
The value of the claim is less than £50,000 
 OR 
 
The budgeted costs of that party do not go over £25,000. 
 
In any other cases, use must use the full Precedent H. 
 
What is the deadline for filing? 
 
If the value of the claim is less than £50,000: 
1. 
Not later than 21 days before the first CMC. The deadline is set 
out in the notice of proposed allocation. – Count back 22 days 
from the CMC date, because clear day rule does not include the 
hearing date. 
 OR 
2. 
If the claim is a multi-track claim: The costs budgets should be 
filed and exchanged with the parties' Directions Questionnaire. 
– CPR 3.13(a) 
 
Budget discussion report – Precedent R: 
 
If a costs budget has been filed, a budget discussion report must also be 
filed at a later date. 
 
Precedent R = prescribed form for budget discussion report. 
 
The budget discussion report must include: 
 
The figures that are agreed and not agreed for each phase of the 
proceedings 
 AND 
 
A summary of the grounds. 
 
The parties must file and exchange a budget discussion report no later 
than 7 days before the first CMC. 
 
Failure to file a budget: 
 
Sanction: 
 
CPR 3.14 If there is a delay in filing or no filing of the budgets at all, the 
court may treat the parties as having filed a budget containing only the 
court fees. 
 
This means that the party will not be able to recover any of their costs 
above court fees even if wins at trial and awarded its costs. 
 
Revising costs budgets: 
 
Each party can revise costs if significant developments in the litigation 
warrant a revision. Send to other parties for agreement. If not agreed, 
submit amended budget to court. 
 
If there is no revision, the court will not depart from the costs budget 
without a good reason. Successful party risks not recovering extra costs 
incurred. – eg. to prepare extra witness statements. 
Retrospective approval is not allowed – the court only has the power to 
manage future costs. 
 
The recoverability of costs incurred in preparing costs budgets: 
The costs of preparing a Precedent H can max be the higher of £1,000 or 
1% of the approved costs budget. All other recoverable costs of 
budgeting shall not exceed 2% of the costs budget. 
 
Costs capping orders: 
If court is concerned re disproportionate costs, court can make a costs 
capping order limiting the future costs which a party can recover. 
 
STATEMENT OF COSTS: 
 
Low value cases/interim applications: 
* 
Parties must file the statement of costs 24 hours before a 
hearing or 2 days before a trial. 
* 
At the end of the hearing, the judge makes a summary 
assessment of costs that would be payable at the end of the 
hearing. 
 
Large value cases: 
 
OPTION 1 – Detailed assessment of costs: 
* 
The court will likely order a detailed assessment of costs. Most 
likely option. 
* 
The successful party will prepare a bill of costs within 3 months 
of the judgment/order. 
* 
If the bill is more than 20% above the figures in the costs budget, 
the Claimant must file a statement of costs with reasons 
included. 
* 
The paying party must file points of dispute within 21 days. 
 
OPTION 2 – Provisional assessment of costs: 
* 
Or, instead of a detailed assessment, the judge may enter a 
provisional assessment based on the bills – this will essentially 
indicate an amount that the judge is willing to approve. 
* 
If the party receiving the assessment does not agree with the 
assessment, it can challenge it within 21 days. 
* 
They can also ask for the matter to be listed for a detailed 
assessment hearing instead. 
 
Once the parties agree/follow the assessment, a final costs certificate is 
issued. 
 
The costs must be paid within 14 days from the date when the costs 
certificate is issued by the court. 
 
COST CALCULATIONS AND ASSESSMENTS: 
 
Retainer = contract between solicitor and client. Client must instruct 
solicitor who must then agree to act. Initial interview = not retainer. 
 
Solicitors' costs: 
1. 
Profit costs (hourly rate x numbers of hours spent) plus VAT 
2. 
Disbursements 
 
Bill your time every 6 minutes. 
 
Who pays costs? 
 
General rule: the party who loses the litigation will pay the winner's 
costs and disbursements. – the court will make an inter-partes costs 
order to effect this. 
 
Court considers: 
* 
The parties' conduct: 
Including whether they complied with the pre-action protocols. 
 
* 
Whether either party succeeded on whole/part of its case – ie. 
if the Claimant wins, the court is likely to award them costs. 
 
* 
Whether any offers have been made to settle. 
Part 36 offers will not be taken into account as special rules 
apply. 
 
Solicitor/client costs: The client is responsible for their solicitor's costs. 
Court will take into account the conduct of the parties. 
 
Party/party costs: unsuccessful party pays successful party's costs 
 
Amount of costs: 
 
Costs must be reasonably incurred + proportionate in amount – 
unreasonable/disproportionate cost requests will be denied. 
 
Neither party will ever recover 100% of its costs.

pages.heading: Standard basis: · Any doubt whether something is proportionate will be resolved in favour
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 20 of 39 
Standard basis: 
Any doubt whether something is proportionate will be resolved in favour 
of paying party. Receiving party recovers 60-70% of costs. 
 
Indemnity basis: 
Any doubt resolved in favour of receiving party. 
* 
Punishes paying party – eg. for conduct. 
* 
Receiving party recovers 80% of costs 
 
Court will look at receiving party's last approved budget to decide the 
right amount of reasonable costs that will then be awarded. 
 
When costs are payable: 
 
When making a costs order, the court will indicate the basis of 
assessment. 
 
Two types of assessments: 
* 
Summary assessment: 
If trial is expected to last 1 day or less. 
 OR 
* 
Detailed assessment: 
For all other trials, a detailed assessment will be prepared by a 
specialist costs judge. 
 
Interim costs orders: 
 ⇒ 
Costs in the case – Costs follow the order at trial 
 ⇒ 
No order as to costs – Each party bears their own costs 
 ⇒ 
Costs in any event – The party awarded costs gets its costs of the 
interim application. 
 ⇒ 
Costs reserved – The issue of costs is to be decided at a later 
stage, typically after trial. 
 ⇒ 
Costs thrown away – A party has wasted costs due to their 
conduct, and this party will be required to pay for these costs 
themselves. 
 
Security for costs: 
 
The Defendant may be concerned that the Claimant may not be able to 
pay their costs at the end of the proceedings and they have the option 
to make an application for security for costs. 
 
This is because even if the Defendant wins the case, their costs may not 
be covered if the Claimant is unable to pay.

pages.heading: DISCLOSURE AND INSPECTION · There is no duty of automatic disclosure and/or inspection of relevant
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 21 of 39 
DISCLOSURE AND INSPECTION 
 
There is no duty of automatic disclosure and/or inspection of relevant 
documents. Such duty will only arise by court order. 
 
Two-stage process: 
1. 
Disclosure – ie. here is the list of documents which exist or have 
existed. 
 AND 
2. 
Inspection – ie. these are the documents you can actually look 
at and make photocopies. There is no requirement to show 
originals, sometimes only copies are shown. 
 
DISCLOSURE PROCEDURE: 
 
Standard Disclosure: 
 
The disclosure statement: 
1. 
Every list of documents must include a disclosure statement. 
This: 
* 
Sets out the extent of the search made and state that it 
is reasonable + proportionate. 
* 
Certifies the party understands its duty to disclose the 
documents 
 AND 
* 
Certifies that, to the best of the party's knowledge, he 
has carried out that duty. 
 
2. 
The disclosure statement must be made (signed) by the 
disclosing party. If a company is making the statement, the 
statement must be made by an appropriate officer. 
 
Inspection: 
 
A party wishing to inspect documents must send a written notice of its 
wish to do so to the other side and the other side must allow inspection 
within 7 days of receipt of the notice. 
 
It is possible to ask for copies instead, with an undertaking to pay 
reasonable photocopying charges (but it is usually better to inspect 
original documents as well as to request copies). 
 
Challenging the disclosure: 
 
The disclosure can be challenged by either party. – eg. if it logically 
appears that a document is missing. 
 
Ways to challenge the disclosure: 
– 
Apply for specific disclosure 
– 
Serve a Notice to Admit Facts 
– 
Make a Request for Information to obtain the missing 
information 
 OR 
– 
If the opposing party continues to disregard their obligations 
under the CPR – Apply for an unless order. 
 
Disclosure report: 
 
If the claim is a multi-track claim that is not related to personal injury, 
the court requires each party to draft a Disclosure Report (Form N263). 
 
This disclosure report must be filed: 
* 
At least 14 days before the first Case Management Conference 
 OR 
* 
File it with the Directions Questionnaire. 
 
An interim application for specific disclosure: 
 
Either party may start an interim application for specific disclosure. 
 
This application would require another party to the proceedings to 
disclose specific documents and it is usually done where there is a 
reason to believe that the disclosure made was not adequate. – eg. 
there are documents missing. 
 
The application for specific disclosure should include: 
– 
Written request for information – this request should include: 
* 
A description of the documents sought and why they 
are relevant 
* 
Why it is reasonable and proportionate for this to go 
ahead 
* 
The document is not in their control 
 
 AND 
– 
Evidence in support. 
 
Pre-action disclosure: 
 
Before issuing proceedings, a person who is likely to become a party to 
the proceedings may make an application for disclosure so that they 
have information as to the evidence the other side has and their likely 
chances of success. 
 
New documents are discovered: 
 
If new documents are discovered after disclosure and after service of 
the List of Documents, the disclosing party must serve a Supplemental 
List including the new documents. 
 
STAGE 1 – STANDARD DISCLOSURE: 
 
Parties to litigation have a duty to disclose all documents (in physical 
or electronic form) relevant to the litigation. 
 
Electronic documents: 
* 
E-mail and other electronic messaging – eg. text/Whatsapp 
* 
Databases 
* 
Documents stored on servers, deleted docs and clouds. 
* 
Metadata (= data about data) such as the date/time of creation 
* 
Content of social media websites – eg. Facebook and Twitter 
 
This duty extends to your client if the documents were in their control: 
 
Control is defined widely: 
a) 
The document is/was in the physical possession of the party 
b) 
The party has (or has had) a right to possession of the document 
 OR 
c) 
The party has/has had a right to inspect or take copies of the 
document. 
 
Standard disclosure requires a party to disclose only: 
 
(a) The documents on which they rely – Board minutes to prove a 
strong case, offer to settle letter relied upon to obtain 
favourable costs orders. 
 
(b) The documents which: 
(i) Adversely affect their own case 
(ii) Adversely affect another party's case 
 OR 
(iii) Support another party's case 
 
 AND 
 
(c) The documents which they must disclose under a relevant 
practice direction. 
 
Reasonable search: 
 
A party need only carry out a reasonable search for documents that fall 
into categories (b) or (c) of the standard disclosure definition. This is an 
obligation which falls within the duty of standard disclosure. 
 
Reasonable search factors: CPR 31.7 
1. 
The approximate number of documents 
2. 
The nature and complexity of the proceedings 
3. 
How difficult/expensive it will be to retrieve some docs, and 
4. 
The significance of the docs likely to be found. 
 
The court will also take into account the proportionality principle and 
the overriding objective. – Thus, the search could be limited to a specific 
transaction or docs created on or after a given date. 
 
A party need not search for a document if it would be disproportionate 
to do so. If so, the party must state this in its disclosure statement and 
why the search would be unreasonable. 
 
STAGE 2 – INSPECTION: 
 
Can the document be withheld from inspection? 
 
Yes if: 
– 
The document is privileged 
– 
The document is no longer in their control 
– 
Allowing inspection would be disproportionate 
 
Types of privilege: *Learn all definitions by heart* 
 
Legal advice 
 
Litigation 
 
‘Without prejudice' 
 
Legal professional privilege includes both legal advice and litigation 
privilege. 
 
Legal advice privilege (legal professional privilege): 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Definition: 
A document which is a confidential communication between a 
lawyer and a client and was prepared for the purpose of giving/ 
receiving legal advice.

pages.heading: A solicitor's attendance note of a conversation between lawyer and · client is subject to legal advice privilege.
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 22 of 39 
A solicitor's attendance note of a conversation between lawyer and 
client is subject to legal advice privilege. 
 
Parry v Newsgroup Newspapers A solicitor's attendance note of a 
conversation between parties is not privileged (open communications). 
 
Balabel v Air India Legal advice need not be strictly legal, it can be 
presentation of legal advice and wider communications. 
 
Three Rivers DC Legal advice is defined broadly: ‘presentational advice' 
is covered by legal advice privilege. However, lawyers must be giving 
such advice through legal spectacles. 
 
The Good Luck Case Client's internal repetition of the advice is 
privileged. Contrast this with client's own opinion is not privileged. – 
eg. if client received legal advice and repeats this information to the 
team, this is privileged. Once he starts adding comments to the advice, 
his comments are not privileged. 
 
Prudential Plc Advice given by non-lawyers is not privileged even if the 
advice is of a legal or quasi-legal nature. 
 
Civil Aviation Authority v Jet2.com Anyone claiming legal advice 
privilege over a doc must prove that the doc was created for the 
dominant purpose of giving/receiving legal advice. – eg. in relation to 
emails, the court will look at the dominant purpose of each email sent. 
 
Litigation privilege (legal professional privilege): 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Confidential: 
Information must have been confidential for litigation privilege to 
apply. 
 
Communication between lawyer and third party: 
For example: 
* 
Solicitor and witness: litigation privilege – witness statements 
 and/or 
* 
Solicitor and expert: litigation privilege – eg. expert reports 
 
A solicitor's attendance note of a conversation between lawyer and 
client – subject to litigation privilege. 
 
Parry v Newsgroup Newspapers A solicitor's attendance note of a 
conversation between parties is not privileged (open communications). 
 
Waugh v BRB If a document has two purposes, litigation must be the 
dominant purpose (more than 50%). 
 
Re Highgrade Traders Whose purpose? When establishing the 
dominant purpose of the document, ask the commissioner, not the 
author of the document (if these are two separate people). – Eg. for 
insurance report, it is the person who asked the insurer to write the 
report. 
 
USA v Philip Morris Litigation must be a real likelihood not a mere 
possibility. Not sufficient = apprehension of future litigation. 
 
Without prejudice communications: 
 
Includes documents with the purpose being a genuine attempt to 
settle a dispute (whether the claim is in process or only contemplated 
is irrelevant). 
 
Simply marking the letter as “without prejudice” will not make it 
without prejudice if the contents of the letter are not related to 
settlement. 
 
Best practice: mark these documents as “without prejudice”, however, 
the court does look at the content of the letters, if the contents are a 
genuine attempt to settle, the documents will be treated as without 
prejudice. 
 
Rush and Tompkins The court will look to substance rather than form. 
 
If marked as being “Without prejudice save as to costs” – judge can look 
to the document to decide the costs. 
 
Waiver and redaction: 
 
Waiver: 
A party may deliberately disclose and allow inspection of a privileged 
doc if that doc will likely help its case. In this case, privilege is waived. 
 
But, you cannot ‘cherry pick' certain parts of a privileged document to 
reveal to the other side/the court. Waiving privileged in part of a 
document will lead to privilege being waived over the whole document. 
 
If a document is mentioned in a statement of case, affidavit or a 
witness statement – this would waive privilege. 
 
Redaction: 
If a document is not privileged (disclosable), but includes privileged 
material, the privileged information can be redacted. – eg. in a note of 
conversation with other's solicitor + client, redact client's conversation. 
 
PROFESSIONAL CONDUCT RULES: 
 
Solicitor's duty to ‘endeavour to ensure' that the disclosing party 
understands duty of disclosure. – eg. do this by sending out a client care 
letter. 
 
If client knowingly signs a false disclosure statement = contempt of 
court – this may mean fine/imprisonment for client 
 
Not deceive or knowingly or recklessly mislead the court. 
 
Not be complicit in another person deceiving/misleading court. 
Cease to act for client if becomes aware client (attempted to) misled 
the court in any material matter, unless client agrees to disclose truth 
to the court. 
 I 
If the client doesn't want to disclose you would cease to act. 
 
What if a privileged document is inspected by mistake? 
 
Clearly a mistake and privileged. 
Immediately cease reading the documents, inform the other side and 
return the documents. 
 
Where the mistake is not obvious, the document can only be used by 
the party who inspected it with the court's permission. 
 
Must disclose all material information but do not tell the client or the 
court the information in this case. Tell them you received it but not the 
content. 
 
If you wish to rely on a privileged document which has been disclosed 
by mistake, you must seek and obtain the permission of the court first. 
 
WHICH PART? 
 
The list of documents for disclosure should be made using Form N265 
and divided into three sections. 
 
Which part of the list of documents should the relevant document go? 
 
For the question of privilege: 
Part 1 – Available for inspection: For documents that are not 
privileged 
Part 2 – Not available for inspection: For privileged documents 
Part 3 – Documents no longer in the party's control 
 
Redaction: 
Part 1 – Redacted version of document 
Part 2 – Unredacted version of document 
Part 3 – Documents no longer in the party's control 
 
DISCLOSURE AND PRIVILEGE EXAMPLES: 
 
Letter of instruction of an expert report: 
 
Instructions are not privileged from inspection. 
No privileged material should be attached or referred to in the 
instructions as this would waive privilege over these docs. 
 
Expert report: 
 
Privileged until served on the other side. 
Draft expert report (not final) is subject to litigation privilege. Privilege 
will be waived in the final version of the report when it is served. 
 
1. Attendance Note – version 1: 
 
Disclosure: Must be disclosed as it is adverse to the party's case. 
 
Inspection: This attendance note was of a meeting at which both 
parties were present so not privileged. 
 
Which part? Part 1 of the List of Documents. 
 
2. Attendance Note – version 2 with two notes: 
 
Two notes within the doc. The first note was a lawyer's attendance 
note of a telephone conversation with client. The second was an 
Definition: 
Confidential communications between a client and solicitor or 
between either one of them and a third party, with the dominant 
purpose to obtain legal advice/evidence/information for use in 
the conduct of litigation reasonably in prospect at the time when 
the document was created.

pages.heading: attendance note of telephone conversation with the other side's · solicitor.
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 23 of 39 
attendance note of telephone conversation with the other side's 
solicitor. 
 
Disclosure: 
1. First note: Adverse, as it shows that D's case was weak. 
2. Second note: A reliance document because it shows good 
conduct on the part of the D. 
 
Privilege: 
1. First note: This was subject to litigation privilege. 
2. Second note: No privilege applies as it was not a confidential 
communication under the rule in Parry v Newsgroup. 
 
Attendance note overall: The page is part privileged and part 
unprivileged, the doc must be redacted. Refuse inspection and redact 
the first note and allow inspection of the second note. 
 
Which part? Redacted version of doc goes in Part 1, unredacted version 
goes in Part 3. 
 
3. Contract: 
 
Disclosure: Contract between the parties. C would rely on this to show 
breach of contract, must be disclosed. 
 
Inspection: Open for both parties to inspect, not privileged. 
 
Which part? Part 1 of the List of Documents. 
 
4. Letter of claim: 
 
Disclosure: Must be disclosed as a reliance document. It shows good 
pre-action conduct on behalf of the C. 
 
Inspection: Open letter between the parties, only pre-action. Not priv. 
 
Which part? Part 1 of the List of Documents. 
 
5. Email: 
 
Disclosure: Must be disclosed as a reliance document, it is evidence of 
communications relevant to the case. 
 
Inspection: 
Litigation 
privilege 
applies. 
This 
document 
is 
communication between the client and the service engineer with the 
dominant purpose of obtaining the notes of the engineer's site visit in 
July 2018. This will provide evidence for litigation. The email was sent 
after the litigation had commenced and refers to the litigation. 
 
Which part? Part 3 of the List of Documents. 
 
6. Draft Witness Statement: 
 
Disclosure: Must be disclosed as a reliance doc for C, if well-drafted or 
adverse doc if badly-drafted. Disclose either way. 
 
Inspection: Litigation privilege applies as not signed and not filed and 
therefore, confidential. Privilege is waived if signed and served. 
 
Which part? Part 3 of the List of Documents. 
 
7. Internal Memorandum: 
 
Disclosure: Repeats legal advice given by solicitor. Must be disclosed as 
a reliance doc for C. 
 
Inspection: The Good Luck case, repetition of legal advice is privileged. 
This paragraph may be redacted. 
 
Which part? Part 3 of the List of Documents or if redacted, part 1 and 
3.

pages.heading: SEARCH ORDERS · CPR 25.1(1)(h) Search order/Anton Piller order = an order requiring a
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 24 of 39 
SEARCH ORDERS 
 
CPR 25.1(1)(h) Search order/Anton Piller order = an order requiring a 
party to admit another party to premises to preserve evidence. t is a 
discretionary, interim remedy. 
 
APPLICATION PROCEDURE: 
 
May make an application either prior to or after issuing a claim. 
 
Pre-Action Documents: 
* 
Draft/Issued Claim Form 
* 
N244 Application 
* 
Affidavit in support – Applicant has duty of good faith for full 
and frank disclosure – PD 25A(7.3) 
* 
Draft Order – You will find a Standard Search Order in the 
PD25A Standard Search Order (SSO) 
* 
Skeleton Argument 
 
Without notice hearing: 
* 
Hearing participants: judge and Applicant only. Respondent 
does not take part in the hearing. 
* 
Apply search order conditions as above (Anton Piller guidelines) 
* 
Used where the purpose of the Order would be defeated by 
giving notice – there is a need for secrecy. – eg. evidence of 
deception and destruction of evidence. 
 
If Order is granted, it will be served on Respondent in a pack: 
* 
Search Order 
* 
Claim Form (if not yet issued) 
* 
Note of ‘without notice' hearing 
* 
Return date details for on notice hearing 
* 
Skeleton Argument 
 
On Notice Hearing: 
* 
Hearing participants: judge, Applicant and Respondent 
* 
3 outcomes: order can be maintained, varied or discharged. 
 
APPLYING FOR A SEARCH ORDER: 
 
Identify makes the application against which party. A search order 
application will be made by the Applicant against the Respondent. 
 
An application for search order needs to satisfy the below conditions: 
Anton Piller v Manufacturing Processes 
 
1. 
Strong prima facie case of a civil cause of action. – yes if there 
is a likely breach of contract, infringement of intellectual 
property, breach of statutory duties as director. State breached 
terms (implied/express?) Which clause? If intellectual property 
breach, state the type. Is the claim certain or merely likely? 
 
If breach of confidentiality: 
Faccenda Chicken v Fowler Employee is and remains under a 
duty to keep information obtained during employment 
confidential and not to use it against employer. 
 
2. 
The damage, potential or actual, must be serious. – yes if there 
were there losses in the past and they would continue into the 
future. State the likely amount lost. 
 
3. 
Clear evidence of Respondent's possession of incriminating 
documents. List potential evidence. If merely circumstantial 
evidence and no concrete evidence, you will need more 
evidence. – eg. by Respondent having access to details of 
Applicant's design system or “staff have done a lot of 
photocopying this week”. 
 
4. 
Real possibility that docs will be destroyed or removed before 
any on notice application for disclosure. 
25A PD7.3(2) Must be probable (= more than mere possibility) 
Previous examples of dishonesty by Respondent suggests a risk 
of destroying documents. – eg lying or deleting files. 
 
5. 
The harm likely caused to Respondent's business by the search 
must not be excessive or disproportionate to the legitimate 
object of the order. 
Which one is greater? Harm to Respondent or the potential 
financial loss to the Applicant? 
 
Pointing to not excessive if: 
* 
The losses likely to be significant in the case 
* 
Search is for relatively specific docs and thus it would 
not be too disruptive. 
 
Pointing to excessive if: 
* 
Applicant can find potentially confidential information 
during the search. 
 
There is an underlying principle of necessity: the order must be 
necessary for the proper administration of justice. 
 
A search order is a discretionary and equitable remedy. 
 
All the equitable maxims will apply: 
1. 
Applicant must come with clean hands – look at the Applicant's 
wrongdoing: eg. no lying, pretending to be someone else. What 
is the evidence based on? Is it the statement of a disgruntled 
employee? 
2. 
Has the applicant delayed in bringing his application? 
3. 
Equity will not act in vain. – eg. Confidentiality has already been 
disclosed so why take further action? 
 
Para 16-18 What information must Respondent give to the Applicant's 
solicitor and when? 
• 
Where the listed items are; who provided him with them and 
where he has sent them 
• 
Must be provided immediately 
 
What is the respondent prevented from doing before return date? 
• 
Para 20 Warning anyone about the order 
• 
Para 21 Destroy, tamper with, cancel or part with possession, 
power, custody or control of the listed items 
 
Conclude: 
Weighing the factors above, argue whether this is an arguable or good 
case for a search order. 
Due to the nature of the order being a discretionary remedy, avoid 
saying that the application is either certain or hopeless. 
 
If search order is unlikely: 
CPR 25.1(1)(c)(i) An alternative is to apply for the “detention, custody 
or preservation” of evidence. 
L v L & H Such an application has a much lower threshold of evidence, 
given that it is a less intrusive order although much less extensive. 
 
VARIATION/DISCHARGE OF THE ORDER: 
 
Identify makes the application against which party. A discharge/ 
variation application will be made by the Respondent to the search 
order against the Applicant. 
 
Respondent may apply: 
1. 
To have the search order discharged/varied 
 AND/OR 
2. 
For damages (either as a result of the discharge or for the way 
in which the search order was executed). 
 
Supervising solicitor's report will be available for inspection by Court at 
‘on notice' hearing. 
 
If successfully discharged – ‘on notice' hearing date is adjourned. 
 
Respondent may apply for costs or damages if application is frivolous – 
Schedule C Applicant must give undertaking to cover damages prior to 
the granting of an order. 
 
When to apply: 
At or before on notice' hearing return date. 
 
Grounds for variation: 
1. 
Applicant had no grounds for obtaining a Search Order 
2. 
Order is drawn too widely 
3. 
Insufficient safeguards for execution 
 
Grounds for discharge: 
Select the most likely ground for discharge in your scenario. 
 
1. 
The Search Order should not have been granted: 
There is no legal or factual basis for the order when applying the 
Anton Piller guidelines. – apply the guidelines to find out. 
 
2. 
Applicant is guilty of material non-disclosure: 
* 
Applicant failed to make full + frank disclosure 
* 
Breaches of CPR25 and 25A PD – eg. “inexcusable nondisclosure”. 
 
3. 
Disclosure of material searched for would breach privilege 
 
4. 
Procedural Irregularity – The Gadget Shop 
Search will be discharged if the search was procedurally 
irregular and was executed in an oppressive way. 
 
Example failings: 
* 
Breach of Search Order – If the search was not executed 
in accordance with the Search Order. – Check how 
search was actually executed and what search order 
said. Contract and compare. Check members listed for 
search and members who actually carried out the

pages.heading: search. · You might be given the Search Order in the exam, in that
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 25 of 39 
search. 
 
You might be given the Search Order in the exam, in that 
case, read the Search Order, if not, then rely on the 
Standard Search Order under CPR 25 in your statute 
book. – PD25A Standard Search Order (SSO) 
 
* 
The order was not in the Standard Form and changes 
from standard form were not drawn to judge's 
attention at without notice hearing. 
 
* 
Breach started not at a time described in the search 
order: 25A PD 7.4(6) and para 25 SSO 
 
Search may have started too early/too late. The 
Standard Search Order does not specify the time/date 
of the search, this will be filled in by the judge granting 
the order. 
 
However, in general, only executed during working 
hours 
 
* 
All-male team was used. If the premises are occupied 
by an unaccompanied woman, the search team cannot 
be all-male – 25A PD 7.4(5) and footnote 8 SOO 
 
* 
No one from the search team should be someone who 
could make a gain personally/commercially from 
anything which they might read or see on premises, 
unless their presence is essential – Footnote 9 to para 
6 SSO – eg. by knowing what documents to look for. 
 
* 
Causing damage on the premises – eg. to the 
Respondent's computer system. Should not have 
searched as they did not have the skills to safely do so. 
 
* 
Taking away the Respondent's items except for 
disputed documents which will be retained by the 
Supervising Solicitor. – eg. taking Respondent's laptop 
or documents that were irrelevant to the search. 
 
* 
Privileged documents are excluded from the search 
and these must be retained by someone other than by 
the Supervising Solicitor. – eg. by the Applicant's 
solicitor or the Applicant themselves. 
 
* 
Supervising solicitor failed to follow the rules 
applicable to them during the search: 
 
* 
Search team must have permission to search. – Para 67 SSO 
 
* 
Too many people in the search team may be oppressive. 
 
* 
Search team must know what they are searching for. – 
the documents will be listed in the order. 
 
* 
Search Order must be served personally by the 
Supervising Solicitor. – Para 26 and 25A PD 7.4(1) 
 
* 
Respondent may ask Supervising Solicitor to delay 
search to seek legal advice. May delay for up to 2 hours 
or a longer period as permitted by the Supervising 
Solicitor. – Para 10-11 
 
* 
Check premises to be searched for breach – Schedule A 
* 
Check Listed Items (items searched for) for breach – 
Schedule B 
 
Conclude: Collective irregularities likely to lead to discharge 
 
5. 
Search Order was executed in breach of undertakings: 
Solicitor's breach of undertaking. Automatic undertakings by 
Supervising solicitor under a Search Order: 
 
* 
The Supervising Solicitor should have explained to 
the Respondent: 
• 
What was in the order in plain English 
• 
That they had the right to take legal advice – 
Schedule E 
• 
That the search could be delayed for 2 hours to 
take legal advice – 25A PD7.4(4) Para 9-10 SSO 
 
* 
Provide supervisor's report within 48 hours. 
 
6. 
Applicant infringed Respondent's human rights by the 
improper execution. 
Specific breach of Article 8 ECHR the right to private + family 
life. 
 
 
 
Damages: 
Seek damages as compensation for losses caused by Search Order 
 
Losses can include: 
* 
Lost business from disruption caused by the search – eg. 
because the employees lost work or the meetings were 
disrupted 
* 
Cost of repairing an IT system damage caused by the search 
* 
Harm to reputation 
* 
Compensation for potential breach of the Respondent's human 
rights under Art 8. 
 
Respondent might apply for (and the court might, in exceptional 
circumstances, grant) aggravated damages and/or exemplary damages. 
 
Aggravated Damages = additional damages which court may award due 
to objectionable behaviour providing compensation for injury to 
feelings. Cannot be claimed by companies. 
 
Exemplary Damages = Damages which go beyond compensating for 
actual loss and are awarded to show the court's disapproval of 
Applicant's behaviour. 
 I 
Only available in certain categories of case, e.g. oppressive, arbitrary or 
unconstitutional behaviour by government servants and solicitors 
acting when undertaking a search order. 
 
Conclude: 
There is a good chance of Applicant's application for discharge of the 
search order and his application for damages being successful. 
 
If the search order already carried out: 
* 
It would be incorrect to discharge the order and this would be 
an empty gesture as already carried out. 
* 
Adjourn the discharge application until trial. – Dormeuil Freres

pages.heading: WITNESS AND EXPERT EVIDENCE · These rules relate to evidence at civil trials only. The rules in relation to
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 26 of 39 
 
WITNESS AND EXPERT EVIDENCE 
 
These rules relate to evidence at civil trials only. The rules in relation to 
criminal trial will be different and you will find them in the Criminal 
litigation notes. 
 
ADMISSIBLE/INADMISSIBLE EVIDENCE: 
 
Evidence, which is inadmissible cannot be taken into account by the 
court at trial. 
 
General rule: all relevant evidence is admissible. 
 
Court may exclude evidence even if that evidence is admissible. 
 
Two types of witness evidence: 
1. 
Evidence of witnesses of fact 
 AND 
2. 
Evidence of expert witnesses 
 
Inadmissible Evidence: 
* 
Irrelevant 
* 
Opinion evidence: what a witness thinks, believes, or infers in 
relation to facts. Exceptions: Perceived facts and expert opinion 
* 
Privileged evidence: admissible only if privilege is waived. 
 
Admissible Evidence: 
* 
Perceived facts 
This is where the witness' opinion is a shorthand for facts. – eg. 
“The car was driving fast”. “Bob was drunk”. 
 
* 
Expert evidence 
The opinion of an expert will be admissible. 
 
* 
Hearsay – admissible in civil proceedings subject to procedural 
issues. 
 
HEARSAY EVIDENCE: 
 
Hearsay evidence = An oral or written statement that has been made 
out of court that which is later adduced in court to prove the truth of a 
matter. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
When to use hearsay evidence? 
 
* 
When the original witness cannot be located. 
 
* 
When the original witness has died. 
 
* 
May use the witness statement of someone else who heard 
what the original witness said as hearsay evidence. 
 
* 
May use the witness statement of the original witness as 
hearsay if the original witness can no longer attend trial. – Oral 
evidence at trial is direct evidence, as it allows for the witness to 
be cross-examined and strengthens the evidence if the witness 
can answer any questions without casting doubt on their version 
of the events. Without oral evidence, a witness statement is only 
hearsay evidence. 
 
Procedure for hearsay evidence: 
 
1. 
All hearsay evidence is inadmissible, however, there are certain 
procedures that can be used to admit hearsay evidence. 
 
To admit hearsay evidence, the following conditions must be 
satisfied: Criminal Justice Act 2003 
 
* 
The original statement would be admissible evidence if 
the person who made the statement was able to attend 
trial and give oral evidence. – s.116(1)(a) 
 
* 
The person who made the original statement can be 
identified to the satisfaction of the court. – s.116(1)(b) 
 
 AND 
 
* 
The party relying on the evidence has taken reasonable 
steps to find the person who made the original 
statement, however, despite these efforts, they cannot 
be found. – s.116(2)(d) 
 
If hearsay evidence is admitted to trial, it will be indirect 
evidence only, so whilst it is taken into account, it is less reliable 
than direct evidence. 
 
 
2. 
If intends to rely on hearsay evidence, serve notice of intention 
on the other side. 
 
Serving a witness statement is deemed notice of 
intention and no separate notice is required. 
 
If witness is not coming to trial, must explain why and 
inform the other party. 
 
If there is no witness statement served and a party 
wishes to rely on hearsay evidence at trial, then the 
other party must be given notice. 
 
3. 
When other side receives notice, they have 4 options: 
1. Request particulars 
2. Call for cross-examination within 14 days of notice being 
served. 
3. Challenge the weight of the hearsay evidence at the trial 
4. If witness is not called to trial, attack their credibility by 
pointing out past contradictory statements but notify 
other side within 14 days. 
 
4. Court decides on weight: 
Factors: court considers: 
a. Reasonable and practicable for witness to attend trial 
b. If original statement was made at the same time as the 
matters stated 
c. Multiple hearsay involved 
d. Motive to misrepresent matters 
e. Whether circumstances suggest an attempt to prevent 
proper evaluation of its weight 
 
WITNESS STATEMENTS: 
 
Oral evidence is direct evidence, the witness statement itself will be 
hearsay if the witness does not attend trial. 
 
Service of witness statements: 
 A witness statement, once served on the other side, will be prior notice 
of what the witness will say at trial. 
 
If you intend to rely on a Witness Statement at trial, you must serve it on 
the opposing If not served, the witness cannot give oral evidence at trial. 
 
Contents of a witness statement: 
 
The witness statement will contain evidence that help prove the facts in 
issue – eg. duty, breach, causation. 
 
The witness statement cannot include: 
* 
Inadmissible evidence 
* 
Irrelevant information 
 
What should you do if you are not able to exchange on time? 
 
1. 
Depends, if the application is in time or out of time. 
2. 
Parties can agree in writing extensions of up to 28 days for the 
filing + serving of witness statements, without court approval, if 
any such extension does not put a hearing at risk. 
3. 
If a witness statement is not served on time, the witness may not 
be called to give oral evidence unless the court gives permission. 
 
If the witness does not want to give evidence: 
 
If witness refuses to give a witness statement and/or cannot attend trial 
to give evidence, serve a witness summons at least 7 days before trial. 
 
Ensure that the witness summons is properly served on the witness, as 
it will not be binding without proper service (look at the rules on 
counting time). 
 
Once properly served, the witness must attend the court trial and give 
evidence, otherwise, the witness will be in contempt of court. 
 
However, once received, the witness has the right to make an 
application to the court to set aside the witness summons if the witness 
is unable to provide information in their evidence which would be 
relevant to any of the matters in issue. 
 
EXPERT EVIDENCE: 
 
Court has a duty to restrict expert evidence. Need permission of the 
court to use expert evidence but not for expert advisors. It is ultimately 
up to the court whether expert evidence is allowed. 
 
The expert's primary duty is owed to the court, not the paying party. 
 
 
 
Example: 
 
Mr Brown sees the Defendant breaking into the victim's house and 
removing items through the back door. He rushes back home to call 
the police and he tells his daughter, Alice, what he saw. Mr Brown has 
had a stroke and is now recovering in the local hospital, so he is 
unavailable to give evidence. 
 
As Mr Brown is not able to give evidence, his daughter, Alice may give 
witness evidence of what her father said to her, and this may be 
admissible in court as hearsay.

pages.heading: Adducing expert evidence: · Parties need permission to call experts.
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 27 of 39 
Adducing expert evidence: 
 
Parties need permission to call experts. 
 
At the direction stage, provide the court with: 
* 
The experts' names 
* 
Their field of expertise 
* 
A cost estimate for calling the experts 
* 
The issues the experts will address 
 
Parties should try to agree a Single Joint Expert (SJE) to save costs. 
 
Expert reports must be exchanged. Failure to exchange report would 
mean the reports cannot be relied on at trial unless court permits. 
 
Letter of instruction and expert report – privilege status: 
 
Letter of instruction of an expert report – Instructions are not 
privileged from inspection. 
No privileged material should be attached or referred to in the 
instructions as this would waive privilege over these docs. 
 
Expert report – Privileged until served on the other side. 
Draft expert report (not final) is subject to litigation privilege. Privilege 
will be waived in the final version of the report when it is served. 
 
What steps should experts take after exchange of reports? 
 
Questions to experts: Written questions can be put to an expert once 
only within 28 days of service of the expert's report. 
 
Discussions between experts: The court can direct that discussions take 
place between experts to identify, narrow and if possible, agree issues. 
– any meeting between experts will be without prejudice. 
 
Joint statement: A joint statement must be prepared by the experts. 
 
Experts have the right to ask the court for directions. 
 
PROFESSIONAL CONDUCT: *POPULAR EXAM Q* 
 
Witness puts forward false evidence: 
 
If statement is false and it is verified by statement of truth without 
honest belief in its truth = contempt of court proceedings 
Not deceive or knowingly or recklessly mislead the court. 
Not be complicit in another person deceiving/misleading court. 
 
Cease to act if becomes aware client (attempted to) misled the court in 
any material matter, unless client agrees to disclose truth to court. 
 
Cannot call witness whose evidence you know is not true. 
 
If finds inconsistency in witness's story: 
 
If during proceedings, solicitor aware he's inadvertently misled court, he 
must immediately inform court with client's consent. 
If client doesn't consent, cease to act 
 
Witness changes statement: 
 
Do not place yourself in contempt of court. 
Cannot influence witness's statement 
Cannot tamper with evidence or persuade witness to change evidence

pages.heading: TRIAL · PREPARATIONS FOR TRIAL:
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 28 of 39 
TRIAL 
 
PREPARATIONS FOR TRIAL: 
 
1. 
Pre-trial checklist (Listing Questionnaire): 
* 
Sent out by the court 
Must be sent to each party at least 14 days before 
 
* 
Must be completed and filed by both parties. 
 
Filing date is set by the court and it will be at least 8 
weeks before the trial date. 
 
Consequences of non-compliance: 
- 
If both parties fail to file checklist on time: court 
will likely grant an unless order: 
 
Parties must file within 7 days of order 
 OR 
 
Strike out 
 
- 
If one party fails to file on time: court gives 
further directions, but unlikely to strike out 
 
* 
Check whether cost management directions have been 
complied with. 
 
2. 
Attend pre-trial hearing: 
The court will review the case, gives directions on trial date and 
other matters. 
 
3. 
Trial bundle must be filed 3-7 days before trial. 
* 
The Claimant's solicitor must prepare 6 trial bundles as 
a minimum for all civil litigation trials. 
* 
The Claimant's solicitor must approach the Defendant's 
solicitor and seek their agreement as to what is to be 
included in the bundle. 
 
* 
The trial bundle will include: 
 
All statements of case 
 
The case summary 
 
Information about the parties 
 
A schedule of issue 
 
Witness statements and expert reports. 
 
4. 
Skeleton arguments + list of authorities 
* 
For High Court trials, this will be prepared by both parties 
* 
Summarises parties' legal arguments and includes a list 
of authorities 
 
5. 
Settlement: 
Assess strengths and weaknesses of case, reconsider whether to 
settle/make a Part 36 offer. 
 
6. 
Parties consider Notices to admit facts/documents 
 
7. 
Prepare the case summary: 
Case summary must: 
* 
Not be more than 500 words 
* 
Clearly specify the issues and facts that have been 
agreed and those that are in dispute. 
* 
Provide a synopsis of evidence that will be needed at 
trial. 
 
8. 
Summon reluctant witnesses: 
Witness summons = requires witness to attend to give 
evidence/produce docs for court. 
 
9. 
Brief to Counsel: 
Doc given to counsel with their instructions. 
 
10. Secure attendance of experts/witnesses. 
 
11. Update costs if needed. 
 
TRIAL: 
 
General rule: all hearings are held in public. 
If the is confidential information in the matter, the hearing will be held 
in private. 
 
The trial is held to decide on an outcome for the dispute. The litigants 
in the case might have a different view of the events and the dispute 
might be due to a misunderstanding or one or both of them might be 
lying to the court. 
 
The judge will look at the evidence presented and decide which side's 
evidence is more convincing. 
 
 
 
Stages of a trial: 
1. 
Opening statements by both advocates (first the Claimant then 
the Defendant) 
 
2. 
Calls Claimant's evidence: 
* 
Evidence in chief 
* 
Cross-examination 
* 
Re-examination – eg. to restore credibility of a witness. 
 
3. 
Calls Defendant's evidence: 
* 
Evidence in chief 
* 
Cross-examination 
* 
Re-examination 
 
4. 
Closing submissions by advocates (first the Claimant then the 
Defendant) 
 
5. 
Judgment – the judge may give judgment immediately or at a 
later date. The judge may allow the Claimant's claim or dismiss 
it. 
 
6. 
Arguments on costs 
 
7. 
Costs judgment/order 
 
Leading questions are permitted during cross-examination; however, 
they are not permitted during re-examination. 
 
Leading question = a question prompting the responding party to give a 
desired answer. 
 
THE JUDGE: 
 
The judge and decision-making: 
 
The judge will be familiar with the codes of conduct as they were 
solicitors and barristers before becoming judges. 
 
The civil courts have no jury, and therefore, the judge will decide both 
questions of fact and questions of law. 
 
The judge will look at the evidence presented and decide which side's 
evidence is more convincing. 
 
The judge will be guided by the code of conduct for solicitors and/or 
barristers when making a decision. 
 
The judge will be legally trained and should not ask help from a legal 
advisor when making decisions, as they will have their own experience 
within the legal profession. 
 
Addressing the judge: 
 
You must know how to properly address people in and outside of court.

pages.heading: COURTROOM ETIQUETTE: · Solicitors to wear a formal attire: a dark suit, formal shoes, light
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 29 of 39 
COURTROOM ETIQUETTE: 
 
* 
Solicitors to wear a formal attire: a dark suit, formal shoes, light 
coloured shirt and modest jewellery. 
 
* 
Solicitor advocates must also wear a gown, collar and bands but 
will not wear a wig. 
 
* 
Electronic devices must be turned off. – a solicitor using a mobile 
phone during a hearing may attract contempt of court 
proceedings. 
 
* 
Do not eat/drink in court 
 
* 
Bow to the judge when entering/leaving the courtroom 
 
* 
Wait until your turn to speak 
 
* 
Refer to the judge by the correct mode of address 
 
* 
Refer to your opponent as ‘my friend'. 
 
COURT ORDERS: 
 
Court order = an official court decision in relation to either a procedural 
or a directional issue. This includes a decision either that one/more of 
the parties do or refrain from doing a specified action. 
 
In most cases the terms judgment and order are used interchangeably. 
 
Types of orders: 
 
A court order may be interim or final. 
 
Order may be made by: 
* 
The operation of the CPR – Deemed orders 
* 
By the court 
* 
By the consent of the parties – these are called consent orders 
where the parties agree on an outcome and the court makes an 
order to give effect to this. 
 
Deemed orders: 
 
These orders arise by operation of the CPR, rather than a decision of 
the court. 
 
This could be an order setting out that costs are to be paid on a 
standard basis and this would arise in the following situations: 
 
* 
The claim is struck out because the court fees have not been 
paid. – CPR 3.7A 
 
* 
The claim is struck out because the court fees have been paid 
by cheque, however, the cheque is dishonoured. – CPR 3.7B 
 
* 
A Part 36 offer is accepted by one of the parties. – CPR 36.13 
 
* 
The claimant discontinued the claim. – CPR 38.6 
 
For a deemed order to apply, the parties do not need to draft an order 
for this to be enforceable. 
 
Court orders: 
 
The parties may prepare draft orders and send them to the court for 
approval or consideration, however, in most cases, the court has the 
final say as to what goes into the order. 
 
When making an interim application, it is best practice to attach the 
draft order to your application so that the court can consider it and the 
order sought becomes clear. 
 
CPR 40.3 The court will be responsible for drawing up every judgment/ 
order except where: 
* 
The court makes an order for one of the parties to draw it up. 
* 
One of the parties agree to draw it up for the court, with the 
court's permission. 
* 
The court dispenses with the need for an order to be officially 
drawn up. 
* 
The order is a consent order. 
 
CPR 40.7 A judgment/order is effective from the day when it was made 
or a later date, as specified in the order. 
 
Consent orders: 
 
Consent Orders = stay the proceedings on agreed terms. 
 
CPR 40.6(2) An officer of the court may seal a consent order if: 
* 
The judgment/order is an order listed in CPR 40.6(3). 
* 
All of the parties are legally represented. 
 OR 
* 
The CPR/legislation so requires. 
 
 
Tomlin orders – used for confidentiality. This type of order will have a 
public part and a private schedule so specific matters can be kept 
confidential) 
 
Deadline for compliance: 
 
CPR 40.11 The deadline for compliance with a judgment/order where it 
includes the payment of money (including costs), this must be made 
within 14 days of the date of the judgment/order if it is not specified 
on the judgment/order. 
 
If the payment is not made within this time, steps may be taken to 
enforce the judgment. 
 
Exceptions: 
* 
If the judgment/order includes a different date, then that date 
must be followed. 
* 
If the CPR specifies a different deadline. 
* 
If the court has stayed the proceedings/judgment. 
 
Payment by instalment or foreign currency: 
 
CPR 40B.12 If the judgment/order is to be paid by instalments, then 
the judgment/order should include the following: 
* 
The full amount payable and the amount of each instalment. 
* 
The number of instalments 
* 
When to pay each instalment 
* 
Who should receive the payments 
 
CPR 40B.10 If the judgment/order is to be in a foreign currency, the 
judgment/order should include the following wording: 
 
“It is ordered that the defendant pay the claimant (state the sum in the 
foreign currency) or the Sterling equivalent at the time of payment.”

pages.heading: PART 36 OFFERS AND SETTLEMENT · SETTLEMENT (NON-PART 36):
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 30 of 39 
PART 36 OFFERS AND SETTLEMENT 
 
SETTLEMENT (NON-PART 36): 
 
Enforcement: 
 
By court orders: 
• 
Dismiss the claim – stops the Claimant from suing on same issue 
again 
• 
Discontinue claim – the Claimant may sue on same issue again 
• 
Make a consent order – eg. Tomlin order 
 
By a settlement agreement: 
• 
If settlement agreed after Claim Form issued, must notify court 
 
• 
To enforce: 
1. 
Sue for breach of contract, apply for summary judgment 
2. 
If a consent order exists: 
* 
Enforce terms of order in addition to breach of 
settlement agreement. 
* 
Set out timescales for compliance, but without 
contrary agreement, it will be 14 days. – CPR 
40.11 
* 
The claim could be stayed, discontinued or 
dismissed. 
 
• 
For confidentiality – use Tomlin orders (this type of order will 
have a public part and a private schedule so specific matters can 
be kept confidential) 
 
Part 36 vs Settlement agreements: 
 
 
SETTLEMENT AGREEMENTS 
 
PART 36 OFFERS 
 
 
• 
No court involvement 
• 
May set own terms for costs, 
although the usual cost rules 
still apply 
• 
Time limits are set by the 
settlement agreement terms 
• 
May pay in instalments 
• 
No damages award 
 
 
• 
Court may be involved. – eg. for 
withdrawal which needs court 
permission. 
• 
Court decides costs consequences 
• 
Time limit is set = 21 days 
• 
Must be lump sum 
• 
If a reasonable offer is refused, 
bonus damages award. 
 
 
PROCEDURE FOR PART 36 OFFERS: 
 
Part 36 offers = a formal offer to settle the case. – an offer which does 
not comply with the formalities of a Part 36 offer will be a simple offer 
to settle. 
 
Purpose of Part 36 offers: 
 Financial incentives for opponent to settle. 
 
When to make a Part 36 offers: 
 At any time, including before and during the proceedings. A Part 36 may 
also be made at the appeal stage. – CPR 36.1 and CPR 36.4 
 
However, if a Part 36 offer is to be accepted during trial, the permission 
of the court is required to accept the offer. – CPR 36.11(3)(d) 
 
A Part 36 offer must: CPR 36.5 
a. 
Be in writing – eg. in a letter, email or Form N242A. 
b. 
Clearly state that it is an offer made under Part 36 
c. 
Must refer to the Relevant period, a period during which the 
offer is open. The offer must be open for a minimum of 21 days. 
 AND 
d. 
Must state if it relates to all/part of the claim and whether it 
includes any counterclaim. 
 
If the above criteria is not satisfied, the offer will not amount to a Part 
36 offer. 
 
Part 36 offers are treated as ‘without prejudice'. 
 
Acceptance: 
 A Part 36 offer is accepted by serving a written notice on the offeror. 
D must pay within 14 days of deemed service of notice. 
 
It can be accepted at any point within the relevant period, unless it has 
been withdrawn. It makes no difference that the offeror has made a new 
offer, a new offer will not withdraw the previous offer. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
VARIATIONS TO A PART 36 OFFER: 
 
If accepted 
the offer, 
cannot 
withdraw 
 
If rejects the 
offer, offer 
remains 
open. 
 
If offer not yet accepted: 
 
1. Before expiry of relevant period: 
 
- Withdrawals need court's permission. 
- Offeror may amend offer only if there is a 
change in circumstances or the interests of 
justice requires amendment: 
 If makes offer less advantageous to offeree, 
the offeror must serve a notice 
 If makes offer more advantageous to 
offeree, it will be treated as a new Part 36 
offer with a new relevant period. 
 
Variation takes effect at end of relevant period. 
If offeree doesn't accept original offer, offeror must 
apply for court's permission to vary or withdraw 
within 7 days of notice of acceptance. 
 
2. After expiry of relevant period: 
Offeror can withdraw or amend at any time 
 
 
CONSEQUENCES OF REJECTING A PART 36 OFFER: 
 
Structure: 
 
General rule on costs: 
Unsuccessful party pays successful party's costs 
If a Part 36 offer is rejected, court may penalise rejecting party. 
 
Who is the offeror and the offeree? 
Identify the correct heading to use based on who makes the offer 
(offeror) in your scenario. 
 
Compare offer to trial award: 
Identify if the trial award is same, more or less than the offer. 
What is the offer amount and trial amount? 
Eg. Offer = £3,000, Trial award = £5,000, thus final award at trial is more 
than the offer. 
 
Claimant's offer: 
Later the Claimant wins same or more at trial = at least as advantageous 
award 
Later the Claimant wins less at trial = less advantageous award 
 
Defendant's offer: 
Later the Claimant wins same or less at trial = same or less advantageous 
award 
Later the Claimant wins more = more advantageous award 
 
Claimant's offer, Defendant rejects: 
 
Claimant wins same or more at trial (at least as advantageous): 
 
Eg: Claimant's offer = £3,000, Defendant rejects 
Later the Claimant wins £3,000 at trial OR they win more than £3,000 at 
trial 
 
If the Claimant awarded same or more at trial than the offer, the 
Defendant will be punished as he was unreasonable to reject (now 
wasted time/costs). 
 
Penalty for the Defendant for period between end of relevant period 
and trial. 
 
D will pay: 
1. Damages + own costs 
2. Normal costs rules: the Defendant pays all of the Claimant's 
costs until trial. 
3. Penalty. Court's discretion (can decide not to penalize if unjust) 
Maximum penalty: 
- 
Indemnity on costs 
- 
Interest on sums awarded (max 10% interest rate) 
- 
Max 10% of damages awarded up to £75,000 
 
 
 
 Normal costs rules: D pays C's costs 
 Penalty for D

pages.heading: Part 36 offer · Claimant wins less at trial (less advantageous):
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 31 of 39 
 
 
 
 
 Part 36 offer 
 
Claimant wins less at trial (less advantageous): 
 
Eg: Claimant's offer = £3,000, Defendant rejects 
Later the Claimant wins £1,000 at trial 
 
D was reasonable to reject the offer so no penalty. 
 
D will pay: 
1. 
Damages + own costs 
2. 
Normal costs rules: the Defendant pays all of the Claimant's 
costs until trial. 
 
Claimant loses: 
 
The party losing the trial pays to the winner (normal rule). 
The Defendant (winner) will get paid its costs by the Claimant (loser). 
 
The Claimant will pay: 
1. Own costs 
2. Normal costs rules: the Claimant pays all of the Defendant's 
costs until trial. 
 
Defendant's offer, Claimant rejects: 
 
Claimant wins same or less at trial (same or less advantageous): 
 
Eg: Defendant's offer = £3,000, Claimant rejects 
Later C wins £3,000 at trial OR C wins less than £3,000 at trial 
 
If Claimant awarded same or less at trial than the offer, the Claimant will 
be punished as they were unreasonable to reject (now wasted 
time/costs). 
 
 ‘Split costs' order: 
1. 
Until relevant period expiry date: the Defendant pays the 
Claimant's costs 
2. 
From relevant period expiry to trial date: the Claimant pays the 
Defendant's costs + interest on costs 
 
The Claimant will get awarded damages but will pay: 
1. 
Own costs 
2. 
‘Split costs' order 
 
 
 D pays C's costs C pays D's costs 
 C pays interest on costs 
 
 
 
 
Claimant wins more at trial (more advantageous): 
 
Eg: Defendant's offer = £3,000, Claimant rejects 
Later C wins £5,000 at trial 
 
The Claimant was reasonable to reject the offer so no penalty. 
 
The Defendant will pay: 
1. 
Damages + own costs 
2. 
Normal costs rules: the Defendant pays all of the Claimant's 
costs until trial. 
 
Claimant loses: 
 
The Claimant was unreasonable to reject the offer. 
 
The Claimant will pay: 
1. 
Normal costs rules: the Claimant (unsuccessful party) pays the 
Defendant's costs. 
2. 
From relevant period expiry to trial date: the Claimant pays 
interest on the Defendant's costs 
3. 
Penalty. Court's discretion (can decide not to penalize if unjust) 
 
 
 
 Normal costs rules: C pays D's costs 
 C pays interest on costs 
 C pays penalty 
 
 
 
1. 
Eg: Claimant's offer = £3,000, Defendant rejects 
Later the Claimant wins £4,000 
 
Unreasonable 
 
2. 
Eg: Claimant's offer = £3,000, Defendant rejects 
Later the Claimant wins £1,000 at trial 
 
Reasonable 
 
3.

C loses

4. 
Eg: Defendant's offer = £3,000, Claimant rejects 
Later C wins £2,000 at trial

5. 
Eg: Defendant's offer = £3,000, Claimant rejects 
Later C wins £5,000 at trial 
 
Reasonable 
 
6. 
Eg: Defendant's offer = £3,000, Claimant rejects 
C loses 
 
Unreasonable 
 
 
QUESTION 1: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Claimant = Isabella 
Defendant = Diligent Ltd. 
 
1. 
If Isabella were awarded £300,000 at trial. 
 
Claimant makes an offer for £300,000. Defendant rejects. 
Claimant wins same or more at trial (at least as advantageous) 
Unreasonable to reject. 
 
Defendant pay: 
* 
Damages + own costs 
* 
Normal costs rules apply: D will pay the costs of litigation to 
the C for the entirety of the trial period 
* 
Penalty: from the expiry of the relevant period until the trial 
date, indemnity on costs (10%) and interest on all sums 
awarded (10%) 
 
Defendant makes on offer for £150,000. Claimant rejects. 
Claimant was awarded £300,000 at trial. 
Isabella has made a part 36 offer saying that she would accept 
£300,000, exclusive of interest, from Diligent Ltd. Diligent rejects 
the offer and makes its own offer under part 36 whereby it says that 
it is prepared to pay Isabella £150,000, exclusive of interest. Isabella 
rejects this offer. By the time of the trial of the case, neither offer is 
withdrawn. Accordingly, both offers remain open at trial. 
 
Explain fully, referencing relevant CPR provisions, the costs 
consequences of both offers in three alternative situations. 
 
i 
If Isabella were awarded £300,000, exclusive of interest, at 
trial. 
 
ii 
If Isabella were awarded £250,000, exclusive of interest, at 
trial. 
 
iii If the judge accepted Diligent's defence and gave judgment 
to the defendant, Diligent. 
 
You do not need to set out the form or content of the offer but did 
need to explain the costs consequences (without referring to 
procedure).

pages.heading: If Isabella were awarded £250,000 at trial. · Claimant makes an offer for £300,000. Defendant rejects.
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 32 of 39 
 
2. 
If Isabella were awarded £250,000 at trial. 
 
Claimant makes an offer for £300,000. Defendant rejects. 
 
Defendant makes on offer for £150,000. Claimant rejects. 
 
3. 
If the judge accepted Diligent's defence and gave judgment to the 
defendant, Diligent. 
 
Claimant makes an offer for £300,000. Defendant rejects. 
 
Defendant makes an offer for £150,000. Claimant rejects. 
 
RULES FOR WHEN THE PART 36 OFFER IS MADE 
AFTER THE COSTS MANAGEMENT CONFERENCE: 
 
A Part 36 offer may be made at any time during the proceedings, 
including after the costs management conference. 
 
By that stage, there will be approved costs budgets, which the court 
will have to take into account. 
 
Costs budgets serve as the framework for assessing the reasonable and 
proportionate costs of the litigation. – So these budgets are used as the 
basis for what costs are anticipated and deemed to be reasonable. The 
court has already approved of these costs at the costs management 
conference. 
 
The court evaluates whether the refusal of the Part 36 offer was 
reasonable. If the costs significantly exceed the budgets, the court might 
view refusing a Part 36 offer more critically. 
 
 
Example: 
 
Personal injury claim 
 
Commencing proceedings 
 
 
Each party serves statements of case 
 
 
 
Case and costs management hearing 
(judge approves of costs budgets) 
 
 
 
 
 
 
At this stage, the parties learn that the costs of the case will be 
exceptionally high, £400,000 (legal fees). 
 
Defendant wants to make an offer. They look at the possible damages 
for the type of injury and severity (head injury) and see that the Claimant 
may win £1,000,000. 
 
Defendant make an offer to pay £800,000, Claimant rejects. 
 
Goes to trial. Witnesses are heard, turn out the claimant was also 
contributorily negligent and the Claimant is awarded only £700,000 at 
trial 
 
Claimant was unreasonable. 
 
‘Split costs' order: 
1. 
Until relevant period expiry date: the Defendant pays the 
Claimant's costs 
2. 
From relevant period expiry to trial date: the Claimant pays the 
Defendant's costs + interest on costs 
 
The Claimant will get awarded damages but will pay their own cost and 
the ‘Split costs' order. 
 
Because the court will be aware that the Claimant knew that there would 
be high legal fees involved, they should have accepted the offer and 
therefore will now receive a higher percentage as penalty than usual.

pages.heading: INTERIM APPLICATIONS · INTRODUCTION:
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 33 of 39 
INTERIM APPLICATIONS 
 
INTRODUCTION: 
 
CPR 1 The overriding objective dictates that costs are to be kept at a 
minimum. Therefore, prior to making any applications to the court, the 
parties should communicate and attempt to resolve any questions they 
may have between themselves. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Who can make an application? 
 
Interim applications may be made by either party to the court for court 
orders. – so may be made by the Claimant or Defendant. 
 
Applicant = party making the interim application 
Respondent = party against which the application is submitted 
 
When can an application be made? 
 
Before the proceedings begin or after, up until the trial date. 
 
Pre-action injunctions are also a possibility, if the test of the relevant 
injunction is satified. 
 
PROCEDURE: 
 
This is the procedure used for all interim applications except for 
summary judgments (which has its own procedure timeline), so this
