procedure is relevant in relation to security for costs applications and all 
injunctions. 
 
Interim applications may be made: 
1. 
‘With notice': give notice of application to the other party or 
2. 
‘Without notice': Respondent does not find out about the 
application until court makes decision 
 
With notice or without notice? 
 
When to make an application without notice? 
* 
Urgent matter – eg. Freezing injunctions, or protecting 
confidential information from disclosure 
* 
There must be good reasons for not giving notice: such as 
purpose of application is defeated by giving notice etc. freezing 
orders. 
 OR 
* 
There are exceptional circumstances 
 
By not having notice of the application, the Respondent is essentially 
denied an opportunity to present opposing arguments or defend 
application. 
 
Because of inherent unfairness, applicant's duty of full and frank 
disclosure of all material facts (Favourable or adverse) 
 
With notice application procedure: 
 
1. 
Issue the following at court: 
 
Application notice (N244) with the fee 
 
Draft order 
 
Evidence: 
a. 
Claim Form and statements of case. 
b. 
For Interim Prohibitory injunctions only: 
Witness statement 
 
 
Skeleton arguments (only if High Court) 
 
2. 
Applicant serves on Respondent: all above docs 
Min 3 days before hearing 
(For Freezing Order: serve the bank and other 3rd parties first) 
 
3. 
Respondent serves: Evidence in Response 
ASAP = no time limit 
 
4. 
Applicant serves: Evidence in Reply 
ASAP = no time limit 
 
5. 
Both file: Statements of Costs 
Min 24 hours before hearing 
 
For Freezing Orders: 
The Respondent may make an application to vary before the on 
notice hearing or at the on notice hearing 
 
 
Grounds for a discharge/variation: 
1. 
The order should not have been made. 
2. 
Respondent has provided the required security. 
3. 
The applicant is guilty of non-disclosure. 
4. 
There has been a procedural irregularity. 
 
6. 
Interim hearing 
 
7. 
The order will be served on the parties together with any 
relevant 3rd parties (for Freezing orders: serve on the banks and 
the applicant should go ahead and obtain a bank guarantee in 
support for the undertaking to pay damages) 
 
Without notice application procedure: 
 
1. 
Issue at court: 
* 
N244 Application Notice 
* 
Draft Order: that the applicant wishes the court would 
make 
 
* 
Evidence: 
a. 
Claim Form 
b. 
Full and frank disclosure 
c. 
For Security for costs and IPI: 
Witness statement or Affidavit 
 
* 
Statement of Costs 
* 
Claim Form 
 
In urgent cases, the application notice and evidence can be filed 
with the court on the same or next working day. 
 
2. 
‘Without Notice' Hearing: 
If extreme urgency: telephone hearing. 
 
3. 
If granted, Applicant serves on Respondent: 
* 
Claim Form 
* 
Application Notice 
* 
Copy of Court Order 
* 
Evidence in support of application 
* 
Statement of Costs 
* 
Guarantee supporting undertaking in damages 
* 
Notice of without notice hearing with Respondent's 
right to appeal 
 
4. 
‘With notice' hearing: the court may maintain, discharge the 
order or make an order to pay damages 
 
COSTS ORDERS FOR INTERIM APPLICATIONS: 
 
There are three main types of costs orders for interim applications: 
1. 
Costs in any event 
2. 
Costs in the case 
3. 
No order as to costs 
 
Costs in any event: 
 
Successful party in interim application recovers costs of interim 
application, regardless of who wins at trial. The costs recovered run from 
the date when interim application was issued up until the interim 
application hearing. 
 
If a costs in any event order is made, costs will be assessed summarily. 
 
Costs in the case: 
 
The party who gets his costs at trial will recover its costs of the interim 
application from the other party. 
 
In this case, the interim hearing costs will be the same as end of trial 
costs – Argue costs in the case if loses application or the judge criticises 
your case. 
 
No order as to costs: 
 
Each party bears its own costs at the hearing. 
 
Awarded when the judge is critical of both parties. 
 
 
 
 
 
Example: 
 
When the Defendant files their Defence in response to the Particulars 
of Claim, it fails to correctly respond to the allegations in full and the 
Claimant struggles to understand it. 
 
While a strike out application could be relevant, prior to making an 
application, the Claimant should reach out to the Defendant and 
request further information under CPR 18. If the Defendant fails to 
adequately respond, only then a strike out application should be 
considered.

pages.heading: SUMMARY JUDGMENT: · Summary judgment = court decides the claim or issue without a full trial.
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 34 of 39 
SUMMARY JUDGMENT: 
 
Summary judgment = court decides the claim or issue without a full trial. 
 
SJ is brought for weak cases (no defence or no case), contrast this with 
Judgment in default where the basis is failure to comply with procedural 
rules. 
 
When to apply? 
 
If the Claimant applies: CPR 24.4(1)(a) 
After the Defendant served an Acknowledgement of Service or Defence 
up until the trial date, unless the court gives permission to make the 
application before then. 
 
If the Defendant applies: 
Anytime after the commencement of proceedings up until the trial date 
without the need for court permission. 
 
Grounds: *Take into account overriding objective* 
 
1. Claimant/Defendant has no real prospect of succeeding on 
claim/issue 
 AND 
2. No other compelling reason why case should be disposed of at 
trial: 
Compelling reasons: 
- 
Disputed facts and needs time to investigate 
- 
Very complex case 
- 
Right to trial by jury 
- 
Needs to contact witnesses 
 
Outcomes: 
 
 
The Claimant succeeds and obtains summary judgment in their 
favour – Judgment on claim/certain issue and the Claimant's 
costs will be assessed using the general rule on costs. 
 
 
The Defendant succeeds and obtains summary judgment in 
their favour – Dismissal on claim/certain issue, the claim will be 
struck out/dismissed. 
 
 
Dismissal of SJ application – claim continues. 
 
 
Conditional order – claim may continue if conditions are met. 
 
Procedure: 
 
1. 
Issue the following at court: 
 
Application notice (N244) with the fee 
 
Draft order 
 
Evidence (Witness statement) 
 
2. 
Applicant serves on Respondent: all above docs 
Min 14 days before hearing 
 
3. 
Respondent serves: Evidence in Response 
Min 7 days before the hearing 
 
4. 
Applicant serves: Evidence in Reply 
Min 3 days before the hearing 
 
5. 
Both file: Statements of Costs 
Min 24 hours before hearing 
 
6. 
Interim hearing: 
This hearing is not a trial, there will be no cross-examination of 
evidence. The court will not take a long time to dissect the 
evidence and will simply decide the case on the face of it on the 
papers. 
 
STRIKE OUT: 
 
A party to a claim may make an application to strike out whole or part 
of the case. 
 
Once deleted, the party cannot rely on it in the proceedings. This power 
is used to strike out inappropriately drafted paragraphs or as a sanction 
for abuse of court process. 
 
Grounds for strike-out: 
3. 
The statement of case discloses no reasonable grounds for 
bringing/defending the claim (High standard). – legally 
unrecognizable/no cause of action, makes no sense, set out no 
facts, lacking information proving duty, breach and causation. 
4. 
Abuse of court process/obstructing just disposal of claim – eg. 
vexatious claims 
 OR 
5. 
Failed to comply with a rule/practice direction/court order – eg. 
late service of docs, late exchange 
 
 
 
Strike out is different from summary judgment: 
 
Strike out is used for cases/issues that are wrongly pleaded or are an 
abuse of process. Summary judgment is used for cases that are weak on 
the facts and have no real prospect of success. 
 
Strike out is different from dismissing the claim: 
 
A claim can only be dismissed at trial, strike out will happen before trial 
for one of the grounds for strike out without the court having the chance 
to properly consider the claim at trial. 
 
SECURITY FOR COSTS: 
 
Security for costs = Applications made by the Defendant if it has reason 
to believe that the Claimant does not have sufficient funds to meet the 
costs of the action should the claim be successfully defended (security 
for costs, but not damages). 
 
Security for costs applications are mostly used by companies. 
 
Use a without notice application procedure. 
 
Grounds: 
1. 
Claimant is a resident out of the jurisdiction but not in a state 
that is bound by the Hague Convention: 
* 
If Claimant is a company, it resides = where its place of 
central management and control. 
* 
Out of jurisdiction = jurisdictions where it would be 
difficult to enforce judgments 
* 
Claimant not residing in Brussels Regulation MSs 
 
2. 
Claimant is an impecunious company: 
* 
Claimant is a company/other body 
 AND 
* 
There is reason to believe it won't be able to pay D's 
costs if ordered to do so – eg. Limited company and 
annual accounts and/or newspaper suggest financial 
difficulties. 
 
D must prove company will not be able to pay not just that it may not be 
able to pay. This is assessed at the time of application but taking into 
account of future expectation. 
 
Need only have ‘reason to believe' that the Claimant will be unable to 
pay. This is less than balance of probabilities (even if the Claimant has 
evidence to the contrary), lower hurdle. 
 
Court's discretion: 
1. 
Court is not obliged to make an order, despite all grounds 
satisfied. 
 
2. 
Main consideration: is the Respondent able to comply with an 
order for security for costs? If not, an order is unlikely. 
 
3. 
Take into account the overriding objective 
Overriding objective: deal with the case justly and at a 
proportionate cost to make the order. 
 
4. 
Considers all circumstances of the case: 
Balances injustice to the Claimant (right of access to courts) and 
injustice to the Defendant (the need for financial security). 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Factors when applying balancing act: 
(a) Respondent's claim = bona fide/not a sham 
If respondent has reasonably good prospects of success 
or the Defendant has admitted liability = likely to be bona 
fide – eg. seeking payment of unpaid invoice = bona fide 
 
(b) D using application oppressively to stifle a genuine 
claim? 
 
Claimant to prove stifling 
 
Court may look at the financial resources of 
parties 
 
Court considers if Respondent can raise money 
from other sources. 
 
D is keen to avoid payment, whilst the Claimant appears 
to have a genuine claim and will potentially be unable to 
pursue that claim if security for costs is ordered. 
 
Claimant's need to 
access the courts 
Defendant's need 
for financial security 
The application 
will not be granted

pages.heading: (c) Delay in making the application? Make the application · asap. If delayed, reduction/refusal of security for costs.
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 35 of 39 
(c) Delay in making the application? Make the application 
asap. If delayed, reduction/refusal of security for costs. 
 
(d) Does the Respondent have financial difficulties because 
D's actions? 
 
Awards: 
 
Court's discretion whether or not it makes an order and must consider 
if Respondent realistically able to raise the amount. 
 
Potential orders: 
 
Pay sum into court or give some other form of security 
 
Pay sum to applicant's solicitor 
 
Undertaking to pay D's costs if ordered to do so. 
 
What happens if the Claimant is unable to pay the security? 
 
The court will stay the claim until the security is provided. Once security 
is given, the proceedings continue. 
 
If the security is not paid within a time period specified by the court, the 
claim may be struck out (ending the claim). 
 
INTERIM PAYMENTS: 
 
The Claimant may make an application for an order requiring the 
Defendant to make a payment to the Claimant in the interim, without a 
judgment made at trial. – CPR 25.6-25.9 
 
This is typically made in relation to personal injury claims and requires 
the Defendant to make a payment in the interim to help the Claimants 
with their costs relating to their injuries so that they can continue with 
their treatment. 
 
An interim payment must only be a reasonable proportion of the whole 
amount likely to be awarded at trial. 
 
Grounds: CPR 25.7 
 
* 
The Defendant must have admitted liability in relation to the 
damages due to the Claimant or some other sum of money. 
 
* 
The Defendant has a judgment entered against them in favour 
of the Claimant for damages or a sum of money (except for costs) 
to be assessed. 
 
 OR 
* 
It is satisfied that, should the claim proceed to trial, the Claimant 
would obtain a substantial amount of damages from the 
Defendant – the Defendant may be the sole Defendant or one of 
a number of Defendants. 
 
APPLICATION FOR SPECIFIC DISCLOSURE: 
 
An order made when standard disclosure has not resulted in the 
disclosure of a specific document that is relevant to the case. – CPR 
31.12 
 
Grounds: 
 The Applicant must show that it is necessary that the Respondent: 
* 
Discloses documents or classes of documents specified in the 
order. 
* 
Carries out a search to the extent set out in the order. 
 OR 
* 
Discloses any documents found 
 
PRE-ACTION DISCLOSURE: 
 
An order made before the proceedings have commenced to obtain 
certain documents or information from the prospective Defendant. – 
CPR 31.16 
 
The test of pre-action disclosure: 
* 
The Applicant and Respondent are prospective parties to an 
anticipated claim. 
* 
Had the proceedings began, the Respondent would have a duty 
under the test of standard disclosure to disclose the documents 
or classes of documents sought by this application. 
 AND 
* 
An order for pre-action disclosure is necessary to dispose of the 
anticipated proceedings fairly, to aid settlement or to otherwise 
save costs. 
 
ORDER TO CALL A WITNESS TO GIVE EVIDENCE AT 
TRIAL: 
 
An order allowing a party to call a specific witness to give oral evidence 
at trial where no witness statement or witness summary was served in 
relation to this specific witness within the prescribed time limits. 
 
Factors the court will take into account: CPR 32.10 Foster 
* 
What is the reason why evidence was not produced and filed 
previously. 
* 
The significance of the evidence 
* 
The prejudice suffered by the Applicant if an order is not made. 
* 
The prejudice suffered by other parties if the order is made. 
* 
The need to be fair and just for all the parties by taking into 
account the overriding objective. 
 
If a witness has not served their witness statement, the automatic 
sanction is that that witness will not be able to give oral evidence at 
court. As this is deemed to be a sanction, the applicant must apply for 
relief from sanctions prior to applying for an order to call the relevant 
witness to give evidence at trial.

pages.heading: INJUNCTIONS · Injunction = an order of the court requiring a party to do something or
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 36 of 39 
INJUNCTIONS 
 
Injunction = an order of the court requiring a party to do something or 
to refrain from doing something. 
 
Breach of an injunction – contempt of court. 
 
Injunctions can be obtained at any point during the proceedings. 
 
Types of Injunctions: 
1. 
Mandatory injunctions: requires the other side to do a specific 
act. 
2. 
Prohibitory injunctions: requires the other side to refrain from 
doing an act. 
3. 
Quia timet injunctions: no wrong is yet committed, merely 
threatened. 
 
There must be a cause of action. – eg. breach of contract. 
 
INTERIM MANDATORY INJUNCTION: 
 
Test (high threshold) – will be granted if: 
* 
The Applicant will suffer serious harm if not granted 
* 
The Applicant is likely to succeed 
 AND 
* 
The Respondent is not required to incur expenditure 
disproportionate to the Applicant's harm. 
 
Damages must not be an adequate remedy: 
* 
The harm is not serious + not likely to continue (One-off) 
* 
The harm is not irreparable. – eg. where privacy was breached 
* 
The harm can be quantified in financial terms. 
* 
The Respondent can pay damages. 
 
INTERIM PROHIBITORY INJUNCTIONS: 
 
American Cyanamid Guidelines (court may depart from it) on how the 
court's discretion should be exercised: 
1. 
Serious question? 
2. 
Damages are adequate remedy for party injured by 
not/granting? 
3. 
Balance of convenience? 
 
Step 1: Is there a serious question to be tried? 
The claim is not frivolous or vexatious + serious question to be tried, the 
claim must have substance. – Yes, if clear breach. Clear terms, no valid 
defence. 
 
Step 2: Would damages be an adequate remedy for a party injured by 
the court's grant of, or failure to grant, an injunction? 
 
Step 2(A): Damages for the applicant + Can the respondent actually 
pay? 
If damages are not adequate or the respondent can't pay then the court 
is likely to grant an injunction. 
 
From Applicant's perspective: 
If the Confidential Information is disclosed so damages will be difficult 
to quantify = inadequate. Even if damages would (in theory) be 
adequate, Respondent is in financial trouble, damages not OK. 
 
Step 2(B): Damages for the respondent + Can the applicant actually 
pay? 
If the injunction were to be granted and it turns out that the injunction 
was wrongly granted, would the Respondent be adequately 
compensated under the Applicant's undertaking as to damages? 
 
From Respondent's perspective: 
Applicant is at an early stage of discussion with Respondent, so will not 
be unduly prejudiced. Even if it turns out that the injunction should not 
have been granted, Applicant is capable of paying damages. 
 
Step 3: Where does the balance of convenience lie? 
If both parties are large multinationals – injunction likely. 
Contrast: one party is a small firm, business might go insolvent – not 
likely. 
 
Factors: 
1. 
Trial is due to be heard soon – likely. 
2. 
Public interest in the injunction being granted or refused. 
3. 
Will one party be disproportionately harmed if the injunction is 
or is not granted? 
4. 
Where evenly balanced, try to maintain the ‘status quo' ante: 
This will be the position before the conduct complained of. 
5. 
Consider the ‘equity' of the situation. 
6. 
If other factors appear to be evenly balanced – merits of the 
case, last resort without conducting a mini-trial. 
 
 
 
 
From Applicant's perspective: 
Damage will be irreparable if the Confidential Information is disclosed. 
Applicant's future business will be severely hindered. Respondent could 
not meet any damages award. 
 
From Respondent's perspective: 
The respondent is not being asked to do anything which it shouldn't be 
doing, it signed the agreement and should comply with it. The 
respondent's deal with the Applicant is at a very early stage so no losses 
there and the Applicant can meet any undertaking in damages. 
 
Conclusion: Balance is in the Applicant's favour. 
 
If you reached a conclusion at this point, don't consider the points on 
Equity and discretionary remedy below. 
 
Equity: 
An injunction is an equitable remedy so all the equitable maxims will 
apply: 
1. 
Court cannot enforce the order: Keep open for trading = not 
enforceable. 
2. 
Must come with clean hands: look at the Applicant's 
wrongdoing 
3. 
Has the Applicant delayed in bringing this application? 
4. 
Equity will not act in vain. Confidentiality has already been 
disclosed so why take further action? 
 
Discretionary remedy: 
An injunction is a discretionary remedy. No right to an injunction. 
 
FREEZING ORDERS (FREEZING INJUNCTIONS): 
 
Freezing injunction is an IPI restraining a party from removing assets 
out of the jurisdiction, or from dealing with assets whether they are 
within the jurisdiction or not. This is to prevent assets being dissipated 
to hinder enforcement. May award against 3rd parties (to police the 
order) – eg. order respondent's bank to stop respondent's access to 
their account. 
 
Effect of a freezing injunction: 
1. 
All assets mentioned in the order are frozen (but would allow 
reasonable expenses per week) 
2. 
The respondent (or anyone else with notice of the order) will be 
in contempt of court if it breaches its terms. 
3. 
It will be in the applicant's best interest to press ahead with the 
action as his assets are frozen until proceedings. 
 
A discretionary and equitable remedy and the usual equitable maxims 
apply. 
 
Mareva Grounds for freezing injunction: 
1. Applicant has substantive cause of action justiciable in 
England and Wales. 
High Court can grant interim relief in foreign jurisdiction cases. 
Here, an order is sought where there is no “related claim”. 
 
2. Applicant has a good arguable case = 50%+ chance of success. 
 
3. Assets within the jurisdiction – UK Bank Account check if assets 
are still in the bank account. 
 
AND 
4. Real risk of respondent dissipating assets to hinder 
enforcement. 
Factors – Evidence of the Respondent's: 
* 
Dishonesty – transferring assets at an undervalue, 
directors' disqualification proceedings 
* 
Debt default 
* 
Removing or disposing of assets 
* 
Residing in a tax haven 
* 
Assets kept in jurisdictions where English judgments not 
easily enforced

pages.heading: JURISDICTION OVER FOREIGN MATTERS · PRELIMINARY CONSIDERATIONS:
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 37 of 39 
JURISDICTION OVER FOREIGN MATTERS 
 
PRELIMINARY CONSIDERATIONS: 
 
When is foreign jurisdiction an issue? 
Foreign jurisdiction becomes an issue if one of the parties or the subject 
matter of the case is located abroad. – eg. if one party lives abroad or 
the contract is to be performed abroad. 
 
In all of these cases, there will be no express jurisdiction clause in the 
contract. If there is an express jurisdiction clause deciding in favour of 
a jurisdiction, then the clause must be followed. 
 
When discussing jurisdiction over foreign matters, apply either: 
(1) 
Hague Convention on Choice of Court Agreements 2005 
 OR 
(2) 
The Common Law Rules – The Hague convention is nonexaminable so state it does not apply and thus the Common law 
rules will be relevant. 
 
THE COMMON LAW RULES: 
 
Under the Common Law Rules, the courts of England and Wales will 
have jurisdiction over a foreign Defendant in the following 
circumstances: 
 
 
 
Presence OR 
Submission OR Permission 
 
 
STEP 1 – Presence: 
 
If foreign D is present in jurisdiction when Claim form is served then 
the courts of England & Wales will have jurisdiction. 
 
Must have either: 
1. 
Permanent presence – eg. company having a Birmingham office 
2. 
Temporary presence – eg. D was visiting for a week 
 
Onus is on D to prove English courts are not ‘forum conveniens' (= 
proper place to bring claim). Use Proper Place test to prove different 
jurisdiction is more suitable. 
 
Proper Place Test: *all circumstances of the case* 
1. Is England the natural forum: 
Spiliada Maritime Corp Forum conveniens is: forum in which 
the case can be most suitably tried in the interests of all the 
parties and for the ends of justice. 
 
Spiliada Maritime Corp Factors: 
* Applicability of the law to the contract – English law was 
the proper law of the contract 
* D's Residence or place of business 
* Availability of witnesses – if all the witnesses come from 
England, then England is more likely to be the proper 
place 
* Local knowledge if this would help the case 
* Cost, delay or inconvenience of bringing proceeding – is 
it necessary to fly out witnesses/experts? 
 
Court will give different weight to each factor based on the 
circumstances of the case. 
 
If England is the natural forum, then England is the proper place 
to bring the claim and permission will be granted. 
 
2. If England is not the natural forum, apply second step: Does 
substantial justice require case to be tried in England? If so, 
grant permission. 
 
STEP 2 – Submission: 
 
A foreign defendant will be subject to the jurisdiction of the courts of 
England and Wales if they submit to it. 
 
Two ways in which a Defendant can submit to the jurisdiction of the 
court: 
1. 
Appoint agent to accept service on its behalf – eg. instructing 
an English solicitor 
2. 
Takes part in proceedings: D takes a step in the proceedings – 
eg. files defence or applies for an order. 
 
STEP 3 – Permission: 
 
CPR 6.36 If D is not in the jurisdiction and has not submitted to the 
jurisdiction, C must apply for court permission to serve proceedings on 
foreign D. 
 
 
3-stage test: 
1. 
6B PD 3.1 CPR 6.37(1)(a) Jurisdictional gateway (grounds for 
the application) 
 
• 
6B PD 3.1(2) Injunction: The claim is made regarding an 
injunction in respect of D. 
 
• 
6B PD 3.1(3) Necessary or proper party (co-Ds): 
- A claim is made against someone on whom the 
claim form has been/will be served 
- It must be a real issue to be tried 
 AND 
- C wants to serve the claim form on another D who 
is a necessary or proper party to that claim. 
 
• 
6B PD 3.1(6)-(7) Contract – satisfy one of three: 
- Contract was made or breach of contract 
occurred within England & Wales 
- Made via agent trading or residing within England 
& Wales 
 OR 
- Governed by English law 
 
2. 
CPR 6.37(1)(b) Reasonable prospect of success for the claim 
low threshold 
 
3. 
CPR 6.37(3) Proper place: Forum conveniens 
D will dispute English court's jurisdiction by arguing England 
is not the proper place to bring the claim. Onus on C to prove 
England & Wales is forum conveniens. 
 
Spiliada Maritime Corp Forum conveniens is: forum in which 
the case can be most suitably tried in the interests of all the 
parties and for the ends of justice. 
 
Spiliada Maritime Corp Factors: 
* Applicability of the law to the contract – English law was 
the proper law of the contract 
* D's Residence or place of business 
* Availability of witnesses – if all the witnesses come from 
England then England is more likely to be the proper 
place 
* Local knowledge if this would help the case 
* Cost, delay or inconvenience of bringing proceeding - is 
it necessary to fly out witnesses/experts? 
 
Court will give different weight to each factor based on the 
circumstances of the case. 
 
Conclude: Court has a discretion whether to grant permission. 
If England is the natural forum, then England is the proper place to bring 
the claim and permission will likely be granted. 
 
EFFECT ON PROCEEDINGS: 
 
Timeframes 
 
 
Domestic D 
 
Foreign D – Common Law 
 
Claim Form 
CPR 7.5(1) Must 
serve on D within 
4 months of issue 
CPR 7.5(2) Must serve on D within 
6 months of issue 
 
AoS/Defence 
CPR 10.3 + 15.4 
File within 
14 days of serving 
Particulars 
Different for each country. For 
USA – 22 days. 
CPR 6.37(5) 6B PD 6.2-6.4 Table 
with rules per country 
 
Defence if AoS 
submitted 
CPR 15.4 Must file 
within 28 days of 
AoS 
6B PD 6.4 Look at the day in the 
table and add 14 days 
 
 
Permission to serve? 
C may or may not need permission from the court to serve proceedings 
on a D outside the jurisdiction. 
 
No permission needed: CPR 6.33 
CPR 6.33(2B)(b) If C properly served the claim form, they will not need 
permission if: 
1. 
They rely on a jurisdiction clause in favour of the courts of 
England and Wales 
 AND 
2. 
The Hague Convention does not apply. 
 
CPR 6.34 If C relies on this provision: C must file with the claim form a 
Notice containing a statement of the grounds on which C is entitled to 
serve the claim form out of the jurisdiction and serve a copy of that 
Notice with the claim form. 
 
Permission needed: CPR 6.36-6.37 
If common law rules apply and D is not physically in English jurisdiction, 
Claimant needs court permission before serving the Claim form on 
foreign D.

pages.heading: APPEALS · GENERAL PRINCIPLES:
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 38 of 39 
APPEALS 
 
GENERAL PRINCIPLES: 
 
There is no automatic right of appeal, and any party hoping to make an 
appeal must first ensure that they have permission to make an appeal. 
 
Appeal the decision of a lower court where: 
1. 
Decision was wrong 
 OR 
2. 
Unjust because of a serious procedural or other irregularity 
 
Court may order the appeal if: 
 Evidence could not be reasonably obtained in lower courts, evidence 
would have an important influence on result and is credible. Also 
consider the overriding objective. 
 
The appeal hearing: 
 Review rather than re-hearing unless the court decides that a re-hearing 
would be in the interest of justice. – CPR 52.21(1) 
 
Court reluctant to interfere with lower court's discretion, unless decision 
was based on error of law, evidence or facts. 
 
Fresh evidence will not be allowed unless the appeal court orders it. 
 
The usual costs rules apply in relation to the appeal hearing. 
 
PERMISSION: 
 
You need permission to appeal. 
 
Applying for permission: 
 
Such an application may be made: 
 
Orally to the lower court directly when the decision is made at 
the hearing. 
 OR 
 
Make the application by filing an appellant's notice with reasons 
to the appeal court within 21 days. 
 
Apart from appeals to Supreme Court, you have 21 days from the 
original decision to appeal. 
 
Test for granting permission: 
 
Appeal must have a real prospect of success 
 OR 
 
Some other compelling reason why appeal should be heard 
 
Respondent's position: 
 
Respondent's notice must be filed and served by a respondent who: 
 
Is seeking permission to appeal from appeal court 
 OR 
 
Asks appeal court to uphold lower court's order for different or 
additional reasons to those given by the lower court. 
 
If no directions on time, file notice (using Form N162) within 14 days 
after the date on which Respondent became aware that appeal was 
going ahead. 
 
Where to apply for permission? 
 
In general, an application for permission to appeal must be made to the 
court that made the decision or the court you want to hear your 
appeal. 
 
APPLICATION FOR PERMISSION TO APPEAL: 
 
In order to be able to appeal a court decision, permission to make an 
appeal must be granted first. 
 
This is because there is no automatic right of appeal, and any party 
hoping to make an appeal must first ensure that they have permission 
to make an appeal. 
 
Court may order the appeal if: 
 
* 
The appeal has a real prospect of success or there is some other 
compelling reason why the appeal should be allowed. 
 AND 
* 
The previous judgment/order was wrong in fact/law or in the 
exercise of discretion or was unjust as a result of a serious 
procedural or other irregularity. 
 
When granting the order to allow an appeal to be made, this order may 
be subject to conditions. 
 
 
 
WHO HEARS THE APPEAL? 
 
 
Original hearing by 
 
Appeal to 
 
 
District Judge (County Court) 
 
 
Circuit Judge (County Court) 
 
Circuit Judge (County Court) 
 
 
Master (High Court) 
 
Master (High Court) 
 
 
Judge (High Court) 
 
Judge (High Court) 
 
 
Lord Justice of Appeal 
(Court of Appeal) 
 
 
Lord Justice of Appeal 
(Court of Appeal) 
 
 
Justice of Supreme Court 
 
A court lower than CoA may transfer first appeal directly to CoA in 
exceptional circumstances. 
 
EFFECT OF AN APPEAL: 
 
Initiating an appeal does not automatically stay the order obtained in 
the lower court. 
 
The effect of the Appeal is to stay the lower court's order if: 
 
Lower court or appeal court so orders 
 OR 
 
The appeal is from the Asylum and Immigration Tribunal 
 
APPEAL HEARINGS: 
 
Composition of the court: 
* 
One judge (either CC Circuit Judge or HC Judge) 
* 
In the Court of Appeal: 2 Lords Justice sit on interim appeals + 3 
on final appeals 
* 
In the Supreme Court: 5-member courts. 
 
Appeal court has the same powers as lower court. 
Second appeals will be heard by the Court of Appeal.

pages.heading: ENFORCEMENT · INTRODUCTION:
pages.text:
Dispute Resolution – SQE Book | Page 39 of 39 
ENFORCEMENT 
 
INTRODUCTION: 
 
At the trial, a judgment is made against the losing party, and this includes 
orders to pay the opposing party's legal fees and compensation, if 
necessary. 
 
Any judgment/order will be enforceable for 6 years from the date of the 
judgment/order. 
 
Courts do not enforce judgments automatically when the debtor fails to 
pay. – the judgment creditor will need to commence enforcement 
proceedings. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Interest on the debt: 
 
The interest will be 8% per annum, unless the court decides otherwise. 
Interest will typically accrue from the date of the judgment/order. This 
will depend on what is stated in the order. 
 
For County Court judgments: 
1. 
Judgments for £5,000 or more will be subject to interest. 
2. 
Judgments relating to a qualifying debt under the Late Payment 
of Commercial Debts (Interest) Act 1998 are also subject to 
interest. 
 
For High Court judgments: 
All judgments will be subject to interest. 
 
INVESTIGATING THE DEBTOR'S MEANS: 
 
Before the Claimant commences proceedings for enforcement, they 
should obtain as much information as possible as to the reasons why 
the debtor failed to pay the debt, their circumstances, and assets and 
where these are located. 
 
The debtor's means could be investigated by: 
• 
Asking the debtor themselves 
• 
Instructing an enquiry/tracing agent 
• 
Carrying out a Companies House search 
• 
Obtaining Official Copies from Land Registry (are they the sole 
owner of the property or is the property jointly owned?) 
 
If little knowledge about the debtor and their assets: 
Apply without notice for Order to Obtain information from judgment 
debtor about its assets. 
 
ENFORCEMENT METHODS: 
 
Exam structure: 
1. 
Make a list of all the assets in your scenario. 
2. 
Identify which assets are not possible to enforce the judgment 
against. 
3. 
Select the most appropriate order for the remaining assets. 
 
Key methods of enforcement: 
1. 
Taking control of goods order – use this for goods/vehicle. 
2. 
Third party debt orders – use this in relation to credit in the bank 
account. 
3. 
Charging orders – use this in relation to land or certain securities. 
4. 
Attachment of earnings order – use this in relation to salary. 
5. 
Insolvency proceedings – use if there is no other option. 
 
May use more than one of the below methods. 
 
Taking control of goods order: 
 
Enforcement officer can legally seize the debtor's goods and assets and 
sell them to pay the judgment debt. 
 
Please do not confuse this with goods being sold by businesses, this 
order can be used to seize any items that the debtor may have with a 
few exceptions. 
 
Use this method if the debtor actually owns the goods/assets 
themselves. Goods may be taken even if the judgment debtor owns the 
goods jointly with someone else. – Farrar v Beswick 
Goods that are exempt from seizure: 
 
* 
Tools and necessary items for the debtor's job, trade, profession 
or study up to £1,350 in aggregate value. 
 
* 
Basic domestic items. – eg. clothes, books, telephones, bedding, 
furniture. 
 
Additional considerations: 
 
* 
If the resale value of goods is enough to cover the judgment 
debt, it may not be. 
 
* 
If the market is going well, bad market conditions will make it 
more difficult to sell the goods and to receive fair value for them. 
 
Cannot use TCG against a third party so check any third party claims 
(owners, co-owners, secured creditors) – eg. if judgment debtor uses a 
car owned by a company. Always check who owns the goods. 
 
 
 
Outstanding debt amount 
 
County Court or High Court? 
 
 
Up to £600 
 
 
Only County Court 
 
Between £600 and £5,000 
 
High Court or County Court 
 
 
More than £5,000 
 
 
High Court 
 
 
High Court Procedure: 
 
* 
Obtain a writ of control to be able to seize the debtor's assets. 
 
* 
File a Request for issue of the writ using Form PF 86A together 
with the relevant court fee. 
 
* 
With the form, also file a draft writ of control which the court 
may edit before issuing it. 
 
* 
The writ can only be enforced by an enforcement officer. 
 
County Court Procedure: 
 
* 
Obtain a warrant of control to be able to seize the debtor's 
assets. 
 
* 
File a Request for a warrant of control in the hearing centre 
where the judgment was obtained together with the relevant 
court fee. 
 
Third party debt orders: 
 
CPR 72 If the judgment debtor is owed money by third party, a thirdparty debt order can be made so that this third party pays the debt 
directly to the judgment creditor. 
 
Must be debt due or accruing due. – eg. trade debts, credit in bank 
account, but do not use for overdrafts. 
 
Charging orders: 
 
Do not use this method if the land or assets that are subject to 
mortgages or charges are jointly owned. If co-owned, it is difficult to 
obtain Order for Sale. 
 
If there is a charge on property, bank must be paid off first, then obtain 
Order for Sale. This is expensive and time-consuming. 
 
Attachment of earnings order: 
 
This order ensures that a proportion of the debtor's salary is deducted 
by the employer and paid towards the debt. 
 
This order cannot be made against someone who is self-employed. 
 
Only available in County Court. 
 
Must transfer judgment to County Court, then apply for Attachment of 
Earnings Order. Use against an individual (not company) where the 
person lacks assets but earns a salary. 
 
Insolvency proceedings: 
 
Insolvency proceedings should always be the creditor's last option. 
 
For individuals: 
Must owe creditor more than £5,000 – bankruptcy petition 
 
For companies: 
Must owe creditor more than £750 – winding-up petition 
 
JUDGMENT DEBTOR 
 
This is the 
unsuccessful party 
who owes money. 
 
JUDGMENT CREDITOR 
 
This is the successful 
Claimant who is 
enforcing judgment to 
obtain the money 
owed. 
 
££

books.title: Ethics and Professional Conduct · SQE Notes（9页版）

pages.heading: CODE OF CONDUCT · The 2011 Code of Conduct has been replaced by two new shorter
pages.text:
Ethics – SQE notes | Page 1 of 9 
 
 
CODE OF CONDUCT 
 
The 2011 Code of Conduct has been replaced by two new shorter 
codes: 
1. 
SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, Registered European 
Lawyers (RELs) and Registered Foreign Lawyers (RFLs) (CCS) 
2. 
SRA Code of Conduct for Firms (CCF) 
 
Together, the new rules and regulations are known as the SRA 
Standards and Regulations 2019. 
 
THE PRINCIPLES: 
 
You must act: 
 
Principle 1 In a way that upholds the rule of law and proper 
administration of justice (public interest). 
 Principle 2 In a way that upholds public trust and confidence in the 
profession and in legal services provided by authorised persons (public 
interest). 
 Principle 3 With independence 
 Principle 4 With honesty 
 Principle 5 With integrity 
 Principle 6 In a way that encourages equality, diversity, and inclusion 
 Principle 7 In the best interests of each client. 
 
Difference between honesty and integrity: 
Integrity is wider than dishonesty. It is possible to behave without 
integrity without being dishonest. – eg. misleading, taking unfair 
advantage of or causing distress to clients/third parties. 
 
Lack of integrity = willful/reckless disregard of standards, rules, or 
ethics, an indifference to the consequences of a breach. 
 
Conflict between the principles: 
 
If there is a conflict, those principles which safeguard public interest 
will avail over those protecting client interests. 
 
Inform client of your duty to the court and other professional duties 
outweigh your duty to them. 
 
Breach of the principles: 
 
Clients may report a solicitor's conduct to the SRA. Non-compliance 
may lead to the SRA taking regulatory action against the solicitor. 
 
THE CODES: 
 
Compliance with CCS: 
 
Solicitors are personally accountable for compliance with CCS, and 
with other regulatory requirements set by the SRA. A failure to meet 
the standards or a serious breach of the SRA requirements may result 
in regulatory action against the solicitor. 
 
Compliance with CCF: 
 
CCF describes the standards and business controls expected of Firms. 
A serious failure to meet the standards or a serious breach of regulatory 
requirement may lead to regulatory action against the firm or its 
managers/compliance officers/employees. 
 
In addition, SRA enforces the requirements relating to referral fees set 
out in s.56 Legal Aid, Sentencing and Punishment of Offenders Act 
2012. 
 
Definitions: 
 
Meaning of ‘you' in CCS = solicitors, RELs (registered European lawyers) 
and RFLs (registered foreign lawyers). 
 
Meaning of ‘you' in CCF = firm authorised by SRA to provide legal 
services. 
 
Client = individual/company for whom you act (former + future) 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
CLIENT CARE, SERVICE AND COMPETENCE: 
 
Before accepting instructions – identify your client: 
 
You must identify who you are acting for. You must comply with the 
law and the Codes (including MLR) when deciding to act for a potential 
client. 
 
Accepting instructions: 
 
CCS 1.1 and CCF 1.1 You are free to decide whether to take on a 
particular client, provided you do not unlawfully discriminate. 
 
A solicitor or Firm must not accept instructions when acting would 
involve you in a breach of law, CCS or CCF. 
 
For example: 
1. 
If there is a conflict of interest between you and a client, or two 
or more clients. 
2. 
If money laundering is suspected. 
 
NEW CLIENT AND CLIENT CARE LETTERS: 
 
Must cover the following matters with new clients: 
1. 
Identity check 
2. 
Conflict of interest check – CCS 6 Avoid conflict of interest 
3. 
Money-laundering check, report anything suspicious to the 
MLRO. – Money Laundering Regs 2017 
4. 
Provide a Client Care letter (include fees, complaints procedure, 
matter's supervisor, scope of the work) and ask client to sign it 
and send it back 
5. 
Open a file for the client's case 
 
Client care letters: 
 
No obligation in the code for law firms to send client care letters to 
clients. 
 
CCS 8 Solicitors must provide information on costs and their complaints 
procedure at the time of first engagement. 
 
CCS 1.1 and CCF 1.1 You must treat your clients fairly. To comply with 
this, you should send a client care letter (= engagement letter or 
retainer letter) to client setting out the terms & conditions of your 
service. However, a client care letter is not compulsory. 
 
SRA Guidelines on Client Care Letters It is recommended that law firms 
will send one each time when they begin work for a new client. This will 
also ensure compliance with CCS 8. 
 
No prescribed form for client care letters but should include: 
 
* 
Scope of work: explaining the scope of the work, confirmation 
of what is included in and excluded from scope and next steps. 
 
* 
Clear/concise cost breakdown and explanation of potential 
additional costs. 
 
CCS 8.7 Ensure that the client receives best possible information 
as to pricing and both at the time of engagement and when 
appropriate as the matter progresses, about the likely overall 
cost of the matter and any costs incurred. 
 
* 
Likely timescales for the agreed work 
 
* 
Action required from client 
 
* 
Details of a named contact and how to get in touch 
 
* 
Inform client of the right to complain to the solicitor about their 
service and charges, how a complaint can be made – CCS 8.3 
 
Compliance with the Code: 
 
Service and competence: 
 
The below standards should be met in providing legal advice. 
 
These can be added to the client care letter: 
 
1. 
Only act on instructions from client, or from someone 
authorised to provide instructions on their behalf. If you 
suspect that the instructions do not represent client's wishes, 
do not act. Protect your client's best interests even if you 
cannot obtain/ascertain client's instructions. 
 
2. 
Ensure that the service you provide to clients is competent and 
delivered on time. 
 
3. 
Maintain your competence and keep your professional 
knowledge and skills up to date.

pages.heading: Ensure that your managers and employees/those who you · manage are competent and keep their professional knowledge
pages.text:
Ethics – SQE notes | Page 2 of 9 
 
 
4. 
Ensure that your managers and employees/those who you 
manage are competent and keep their professional knowledge 
and skills and understanding of their legal/ethical/regulatory 
obligations up to date. 
 
5. 
Have an effective system for supervising clients' matters. 
 
6. 
Consider your client's attributes, needs and circumstances. 
 
7. 
Where you supervise/manage others providing legal services: 
you remain accountable for the work carried out. 
 
Client Info and Publicity: 
 
There are rules regulating how information is provided to clients. 
These rules also apply to Firms. 
 
The below should be observed, and can be stated in the client care 
letter: 
• 
Ensure clients are informed about the services they need, how 
their matter is handled and their options. 
 
• 
Ensure that clients understand how your services are 
regulated: 
- 
Explain that you are an authorised person and which 
part of the work you will carry out. 
- 
Explain which services provided by you, the firm or 
other regulated businesses. 
 AND 
- 
Do not represent firms which is not authorised by the 
SRA, as being regulated by the SRA. 
 
• 
Ensure that clients understand the regulatory protections 
available to them. 
 
Inform your client of all this as soon as practicable after instructions. 
 
Costs Standards – solicitors must be transparent regarding their fees: 
 
These rules also apply to Firms. 
 
The below should be in the client care letter and discussed with client: 
 
1. 
Inform clients about the cost of matter and other costs, at the 
time of engagement and as the matter progresses. 
 
2. 
The advertisement of your practice must be accurate and not 
misleading. It must include info relating to your charges and/or 
when interest is payable by or to clients. 
 
Rules setting out how client monies are handled: 
 
• 
Properly account for financial benefits you receive as a result of 
their instructions, except if otherwise agreed. 
• 
Safeguard money and assets entrusted to you by clients and 
others. 
• 
Do not personally hold client money unless: 
- 
Permitted under the Authorisation of Individuals 
Regulations 
- 
You work in an authorised body/organisation. 
 
Complaints: 
 
These rules also apply to Firms. 
 
The rules relating to complaints are below: 
1. 
Establish and maintain, or participate in, a procedure for 
handling complaints in relation to the legal services you 
provide. 
 
2. 
Inform clients in writing at the time of engagement: 
• 
they have a right to complain about your services/ 
charges 
• 
how a complaint can be made and to whom 
 AND 
• 
they have a right to make a complaint to the Legal 
Ombudsman and when they can make any such 
complaint. 
 
3. 
If client made a complaint to you, and no resolution to client's 
satisfaction within 8 weeks, write to them: 
• 
Stating their right to complain to the Legal Ombudsman, 
the time frame and full details of how to contact them 
 AND 
• 
If a complaint has been brought and your complaints 
procedure has been exhausted, stating: 
- 
That you cannot settle the complaint 
- 
The name and website of an ADR approved 
body which is competent to deal with the 
complaint 
 AND 
- 
Whether you agree to use the scheme of that 
body. 
 
4. 
Deal with complaints properly, fairly, and free of charge. 
 
Ongoing obligations: 
 
The above obligations last throughout the retainer. Keep clients 
informed as the matter progresses, such as if info in the client care 
letter becomes superseded. – eg. if a costs estimate changed. 
 
Repeat business and client care letters: 
 
If you are carrying out repeat work on agreed terms for an established 
client, it may be inappropriate to provide all the above information 
each time a new file is opened. Instead, send annual client care letters 
and shorter letters once a new matter is opened. 
 
Contents of a client care letter: 
 
Client's instructions and options: 
• 
Client's objectives 
• 
Explain the issues and their options 
• 
Agree on the next steps 
• 
Agree on level of service/how client will be informed of 
progress 
 
General information: 
• 
Your responsibilities 
• 
Explain client's responsibilities 
• 
Explain anything which may limit the steps you can take on their 
behalf – eg. a potential conflict with another client 
 AND 
• 
Explain that you may be entitled to a lien (right to retain 
possession of files) if there are any unpaid costs. 
 
Costs information: 
Explain who will be dealing with their matter: name, status, and 
supervisor. 
 
Complaints: 
Explain how they and to whom they can complain if they are unhappy 
with the service and details of the firm's complaints procedure. 
 
Termination of the retainer: 
Good reasons to terminate your retainer with a client: 
• 
You cannot obtain clear instructions – eg. if partners from a 
two-partner firm give you conflicting instructions. 
• 
No termination would break the law or breach the Codes – eg. 
conflict of interest. 
• 
Your client has failed to pay its bills. – ie. an interim bill. 
 
You cannot terminate a retainer on grounds of self-interest. 
 
CCF 1.1 Treat your client fairly. 
 Principles 4 and 5 Act with honesty and integrity. 
 Principle 7 Act in the best interests of each client. 
 
Terminating on these grounds amounts to repudiatory breach of 
contract, so you must pay back all the fees already paid. 
 
Example: 
 
Jess Watts from Libro Ltd instructed you and said that she would not 
instruct you if the firm had a connection with Festive Books. A week 
later, Anne Festive of Festive Books called you hoping to instruct you 
on a different matter. You now wish to terminate your retainer with 
Libro Ltd and act for Festive Books as Festive Books is paying you 
more. 
 
The firm's proposed termination of Libro Ltd's retainer is motivated by 
the firm's own commercial interests. 
 
You cannot terminate a retainer on grounds of self-interest. 
 
CCF 1.1 Treat your client fairly. 
 Principles 4 and 5 Act with honesty and integrity. 
 Principle 7 Act in the best interests of each client. 
 
You cannot treat Libro Ltd fairly if you terminate the retainer for a more 
lucrative proposition. 
 
Termination of the retainer on grounds of self-interest is not reasonable 
and would breach the Code and Principles. 
 
Moreover, it would be a repudiatory breach of contract, so you may 
need to pay back any fees already paid. You must continue to act for 
Libro Ltd without taking on Festive Books as a client.

pages.heading: CONFLICTS AND CONFIDENTIALITY · CONFLICT OF INTEREST:
pages.text:
Ethics – SQE notes | Page 3 of 9 
 
 
CONFLICTS AND CONFIDENTIALITY 
 
CONFLICT OF INTEREST: 
 
General rule: 
 
You must not act for a client where: 
I. 
CCS 6.1 and CCF 6.1 There is an own interest conflict. 
 
Own interest conflict = where your duty to act in the best 
interests of the client conflicts with your own interests. – eg. 
where you seek to buy a property from client or borrow money 
from client. 
 
II. 
CCS 6.2 and CCF 6.2 There is a conflict of interest. 
 
Conflict of interest = where your separate duties to act in the 
best interests of two or more clients in relation to the same or 
related matters conflict. – eg. instructed by opposing parties in 
litigation. 
 
Significant risk of conflict is enough for conflict of interest to exist. 
Unless an exception applies, you must cease acting for client (1 or both). 
 
Exceptions – when can you act? 
 
The exceptions below only apply when there is a client conflict, or 
significant risk of a conflict, between two clients. The exceptions won't 
apply in case of an own interest conflict. 
 
Exception 1: Substantially Common Interest (SCI): 
Eg. when two clients want to instruct you to advise them on a purchase 
or setting up of a business as partners, or taking out a lease, as joint 
tenants. 
 
CCS 6.2(a) and CCF 6.2(a) This exception will apply if there is: 
• 
A clear common purpose between the clients. – clients want the 
deal to succeed. 
 AND 
• 
A strong consensus on how this is to be achieved. – parties have 
agreed the key terms of the deal or likely no/little negotiation. 
 
AND 
 
CCS 6.2(b)(i) – (iii) and CCF 6.2(b)(i) – (iii) All of the following apply: 
1) 
All clients give informed consent in writing, to you acting. 
 
2) 
If appropriate, you put in place effective safeguards to protect 
clients' confidential information: 
Where there is a conflict of interest, you may not be able to pass 
info relevant to the matter from one client to another. If there 
is a risk of this situation arising, do not act for both clients. 
 
3) 
It is reasonable for you to act for all the clients: 
Factors: 
* 
Knowledge and bargaining power of each client. Is one 
party vulnerable or in a relatively weak position and 
should be referred for independent advice? – eg. one 
client is an individual and the other is a company 
* 
The likely extent of negotiations between clients. 
* 
Benefits to clients if you act for both clients. – eg. speed, 
lower cost, specialist knowledge 
 
Example: 
A stadium is financed by a secured loan from Bank A and Bank Z. A 
and Z have agreed that A will rank in priority ahead of Z and the banks 
have agreed the form of the deed of priority. Z has just instructed you 
to draft the security documents. You have already received similar 
instructions from A in this matter. Can you accept Z's instructions? 
 
Potential client conflict as both lenders instruct you in connection with 
the same matter and lenders will not rank equally against the Borrower. 
 
CCS 6.2 You cannot act for both parties where there is a client conflict 
or a significant risk of one. – Under the default position, you must 
decline acting for Z. 
 
Z and A have a clear common purpose, the lending of the money. 
 
As lenders have agreed their respective rankings and the form of the 
deed of priority, the is a low risk of conflict. Also, you would do similar 
jobs for Z and A in relation to the same part of the transaction and both 
clients will benefit from the lower cost of instructing only one firm. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
As they are both banks, they are sophisticated clients who will 
understand the risks, you may act if: 
1. 
Both clients give written informed consent to you 
2. 
You have put in place effective safeguards as to the protection 
of confidential info 
 AND 
3. 
You are satisfied it is reasonable for you to act. 
 
Exception 2: Clients competing for the same objective (CCSO): 
 
Eg. acting for more than one creditor on the insolvency of a company 
or acting for different tenderers tendering for the same contract. 
 
Does not apply if clients are on the opposite sides: if they are a 
Claimant and Defendant in litigation or the Seller and Buyer in a 
transaction. CCSO exception is rare and will only apply where clients 
are sophisticated clients. 
 
CCS 6.2(b) and CCF 6.2(b) This exception will apply if: 
2 or more clients are competing for the same objective, an objective 
which, if attained by one client, will make it unattainable to the other. 
– eg. a lender and borrower are not competing for the objective (the 
property). 
 
Objective = asset, contract, or business opportunity which 2 or more 
clients seek to acquire/recover through a private auction/offer. 
 
AND 
 
All of the following apply: 
• 
All clients give informed consent in writing, to you acting. 
• 
Where appropriate, you put in place effective safeguards to 
protect your clients' confidential info 
 AND 
• 
It is reasonable for you to act for the clients. 
 
Steps to take to avoid conflict: 
 
You must have effective systems and controls in place to enable you 
to identify and assess potential conflicts of interests. 
 
Conflict search: 
• 
Client name (and its parent or subsidiary companies) 
• 
Client's company number (also for parent company or 
subsidiaries) 
• 
Name(s) of any counterparties to the matter 
 
CONFIDENTIALITY AND DISCLOSURE: 
 
Duty of confidentiality: 
 
CCS 6.3 and CCF 6.3 You must keep the information and affairs of 
client confidential. This confidentiality continues after the retainer is 
terminated and extends to the PRs of a client if a client dies. 
 
Exceptions: 
• 
Client consents to disclosure 
 OR 
• 
Disclosure is permitted/required by law: 
1. 
Some statutes empower government and other bodies 
(HMRC) to require disclosure 
 
2. 
Statutory/regulatory reporting requirements – eg. 
those in the Money Laundering Regulations 2017, the 
Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 and anti-terrorism 
legislation. 
 
3. 
You must reveal the info to support a defence in a 
prosecution or if a negligence claim brought against you 
by a client. 
 
4. 
You must reveal to an appropriate authority if: 
- 
You discover that a child has been sexually or 
physically abused. 
 OR 
- 
You believe that the child's health (mental or 
physical) is in danger. 
 
Duty of disclosure: 
 
CCS 6.4 and CCF 6.4 Solicitors have a personal duty to disclose to client 
all information which is material to their matter. The duty does not 
extend to information of which others in the firm may be aware. 
 
Material = information which might reasonably be expected to 
significantly affect the client's decision-making with regard to their 
matter. 
 
The duty of confidentiality to another current or former client (A) might 
prevent solicitors from disclosing material info that they obtained in 
relation to A's case to a new client (B).

pages.heading: Stop acting for B unless you obtain B's informed consent. · Exceptions:
pages.text:
Ethics – SQE notes | Page 4 of 9 
 
 
Stop acting for B unless you obtain B's informed consent. 
 I 
Exceptions: 
(a) the disclosure is prohibited by legal restrictions imposed in the 
interests of national security or the prevention of crime. 
(b) the client gives informed consent in writing, to the information 
not being disclosed to them. 
(c) The solicitor has reason to believe that serious physical or 
mental injury will be caused to the client or another if the 
information is disclosed. 
 OR 
(d) The information is contained in a privileged document that the 
solicitor has knowledge of only because it has been mistakenly 
disclosed. 
 
Conflict between confidentiality and disclosure: 
 
You may also owe a duty of confidentiality to another client in respect 
of the same information. 
 
Where there is a conflict between the duties of confidentiality and 
disclosure, confidentiality takes precedence. 
 
However, you cannot rely on a duty of confidentiality to excuse a 
failure to disclose material information. 
 
In this case, you must: 
(a) Renegotiate the terms of the retainer with the client, so they 
know you have information, but you cannot reveal it; or 
(b) You should refuse to act for the client if you have not already 
started acting or cease to act if you have. 
 
Adverse interests and confidential information: 
 
Client A wishes to instruct you for advice in relation to a dispute over a 
lease that he has taken from B. The search of X and Co's database 
reveals that another employee of your firm gave B some advice on the 
lease in relation to a dispute with A last year. Your firm is no longer 
acting for B. 
 
You do not act for a client where that client has an interest adverse to 
the interest of another current or former client of you or your firm, for 
whom you or your firm holds confidential info which is material to that 
matter, unless 6.5(a) or (b) applies. 
 
Adverse interest = where one party is, or is likely to become, the 
opposing party on a matter, whether in negotiations or some form of 
dispute resolution. 
 
Two exceptions: CCS 6.5(a)-(b) and CCF 6.5 (a)-(b) 
(a) Effective measures have been taken which result in there 
being no real risk of disclosure of the confidential information: 
 – eg. setting up an information barrier, high standard 
 
Factors: 
• 
Burden is on the firm to show that there is no real risk 
that the info will come into the possession of those 
acting for the other party 
• 
Information barriers means an established system that 
should not rely on individuals 
• 
Information barriers between departments will likely 
pass the test, but not barriers within one team 
 
Effective measures examples: 
• 
Systems identifying potential confidentiality issues 
• 
Separate departments handling the cases 
• 
Info held on separate servers 
• 
Info is encrypted and password protected 
• 
Individuals being aware of the information barrier 
• 
Policies and training for staff 
 
(b) The current/former client, whose information you hold gives 
informed consent in writing, to you acting, including to the 
protective measures. 
 
If the firm puts in measures to protect the client's information, 
someone else in the firm must seek that consent, as you will be 
unable to do so without disclosing the client's confidential info. 
 
If the info is not material but there is an adverse interest? 
You can continue acting for client, if you comply with 6.5(a) or (b). 
 
If someone else in the firm holds info likely material to my client? 
Solicitors have no duty to find out if anyone else in the firm has info 
which might be material to client's matter, but good practice to check 
for client conflict. This may reveal that others in the firm may have 
material confidential info. If so, it may not be reasonable for you to 
continue acting.

pages.heading: CRIMINAL CONDUCT ISSUES · Relevant code: Code of Conduct for Solicitors (CCS)
pages.text:
Ethics – SQE notes | Page 5 of 9 
 
 
CRIMINAL CONDUCT ISSUES 
 
Relevant code: Code of Conduct for Solicitors (CCS) 
 
Refuse/cease to act by giving reasonable notice if: 
* 
Acting would involve you in a breach of the law/breach of 
professional conduct rules. 
* 
There is a breakdown in confidence between you and client 
 OR 
* 
You are unable to obtain proper instructions. 
 
Exam Structure – Conduct Issues: 
1. 
Identify the Issue – this will determine if you can act for the 
client such as misleading the court or conflict of interest. 
2. 
State the relevant Principles – only state the ones that apply. 
3. 
Identify the relevant CCS to be achieved 
4. 
Discuss and apply CCS to the facts. 
 
Select the relevant Issue – you may have more than one: 
1. 
Duty to the client 
2. 
Duty to the court 
3. 
Conflict of interest and confidentiality – interlinked 
4. 
Third party instructions 
 
DUTY TO THE CLIENT: 
 
Solicitors can decide whether or not to take on a client provided that 
they do not unlawfully discriminate. 
 
You must: 
• 
Give clients competent advice in a timely manner. 
• 
Advise on any plea, costs, and other implications. 
• 
Advise your client of the likely costs at the outset. 
• 
Explain to the client how the complaints procedure works. 
 
DUTY TO THE COURT: *POPULAR EXAM Q* 
 
Issue: 
 
Whether acting on client's instructions would amount to misleading the 
court. 
 
Principles: 
 
Principle 1 Uphold the law and the proper administration of justice. 
Principle 2 Act in a way that maintains the public trust. 
Principle 5 Act with integrity. 
Principle 7 Act in your client's best interests. 
 
Inform your client when your duty to the court overrides your 
obligations to the client. – eg. If client instructs you to withhold evidence 
which must be disclosed. 
 
CCS: 
 
You must: 
Not deceive or knowingly/recklessly mislead the court. 
Not be complicit in another person deceiving/misleading court. 
Keep the affairs of clients confidential. 
 
Not a breach of the Code if the solicitor interviews and takes statements 
from a witness or prospective witness. 
 
However you must not: 
Make a payment to a witness where payment is dependent on 
their evidence or the outcome of the case. 
Put forward arguments to the court that are not properly 
arguable. 
Fail to comply with court orders. 
Place yourself in contempt of court. 
 
You might mislead the court if: 
• You submit inaccurate information to the court by: 
1. 
Lying – eg. say that client is a man of unblemished 
character, but he has previous convictions. 
2. 
Agreeing with information which you know is false. 
 
• You call a witness whose evidence you know is untrue. 
• You do not immediately disclose a document, which you have 
become aware of, that it should previously have been disclosed. 
• You misuse/tamper with evidence or attempt to do so. 
• You try to influence witness evidence when taking a statement 
or try to persuade a witness to change their evidence. 
• You do not draw to the court's attention relevant cases/ 
statute/procedural irregularities which you are aware and likely 
to have a material effect on the outcome of the case. 
• You waste the court's time. 
 
 
 
Practical Examples: 
 
1. The solicitor inadvertently misled the court. 
This is not a breach of the Code. However, you must get your 
client's consent and immediately inform the court about this as 
soon as you become aware of it. 
If the client does not consent – stop acting. 
 
2. Client tells you: ‘I did steal the bike, but I will plead not guilty.' 
OR tells you: ‘I am innocent, but I will plead guilty.' 
You can act for the client, but you must not be complicit in them 
misleading the court. 
You must not make any false submissions to the court. 
 
3. Client tells you: ‘I did steal the bike, but I will remain silent.' 
Client is entitled to remain silent and put the prosecution to 
proof. 
P(7) This will be in the client's best interest if the evidence is 
weak. 
D cannot assert their innocence in the proceedings/ police 
interview, nor can you do so without misleading the court. You 
can continue to act if D remains silent. 
 
4. Client tells you: ‘I did steal the bike, but I am going to say I found 
the bike in front of my house.' 
You cannot allow the client to lie to the court/police interview. 
– you are not in breach of the Code if you did not know they were 
going to lie. 
If they insist that they are going to lie, then you cannot continue 
to act to avoid breaching P(1) and P(2). 
If you must withdraw, keep the affairs of your client confidential. 
 
5. Client tells you: ‘My previous convictions are incomplete as 
they do not include a recent conviction. Please point out to the 
court that I have been out of trouble for over a year.' 
 
OR 
 
Client tells you: ‘My mother will provide me a false alibi.' 
 
You can act for client provided you are not complicit in them 
misleading the court. – you cannot comply with the client's 
instructions. 
You would be breaching P(1) and P(2). 
Although it would be in client's best interests to lie under P(7), if 
two principles conflict, the one which takes precedence is the 
one which best serves the public interest. 
 
You are unable to disclose the relevant conviction to the court 
without the client's consent. – Get client's consent. 
 
 
If client does not consent: 
 
The decision to withdraw rests with you. 
 
 
 
Continue to act, however you 
will be greatly limited: 
- You cannot advance a 
positive case for your 
client – eg. that your client 
was out of trouble for a 
year. 
- If the court were to ask you 
a question you must tell 
them the truth. 
 
Explain these limitations to 
client. 
 
If you decide to stop acting: 
- Do not disclose the 
confidential info. 
- Tell the court that your 
professional duties 
prevent your continuing 
to act. 
 
CONFLICT OF INTEREST AND CONFIDENTIALITY: 
 
Issue: 
 
There may be a conflict of interest between the parties. This will also 
involve issues of confidentiality and disclosure. 
 
Principles: 
 
P(5) Act with integrity. 
P(7) Act in our client's best interests.

pages.heading: CCS: · Conflict of interest:
pages.text:
Ethics – SQE notes | Page 6 of 9 
 
 
CCS: 
 
Conflict of interest: 
You cannot act where there is a conflict or a significant risk of conflict. 
– You can act if risk is not significant. 
 
Two types of conflict: *Select which one applies* 
1. 
Own interest conflict – If your own interest conflicts with the 
interest of the client. In this case, do not act. 
 
2. 
Client conflict – If there is a conflict between clients, you cannot 
act for either one of them. 
 
Examples: 
* 
If one client blames the other for the crime 
* 
If one client says both of them were involved and the 
other client denies involvement. 
 
If, during the course of proceedings, a conflict of interest arises 
between clients, only continue to act for one client. 
 
Disclosure and Confidentiality: 
You must keep the affairs of clients/former clients confidential except 
where disclosure is required or permitted by law/client. 
You must disclose all material information to your client and make sure 
that the client understands the information. 
 
Where confidentiality to one client comes into conflict with your duty 
of disclosure to another client, confidentiality takes precedence. 
 
Solicitor has no duty to disclose information that may be negative unless 
the client is to give evidence that is untrue/misleading. 
 
The duty of confidentiality lasts forever. 
 
Co-defendants: 
Only act if both clients tell the same story and clients have a substantially 
common interest in relation to the matter and both clients give 
informed consent for you acting. 
 
Before obtaining your clients' written consent, you must bring all 
relevant issues to clients' attention and have a reasonable belief that 
clients understand these issues. 
 
Practical Examples: 
 
1. 
Jack and Jill are arrested for robbery as co-defendants. You 
have a private consultation with Jill who tells you that both of 
them were involved. You then have a private consultation with 
Jack who denies involvement. 
 
Can you act for Jack? 
 
P(7) Ask whether you can act in the best interests of each client. 
You cannot act if there is a client conflict. Here, Jill has implicated 
Jack while Jack denies involvement. If there is a conflict between 
clients, you cannot act for either one of them. 
 
P(7) You cannot act for Jack as you are unable to act in both 
Jill's and Jack's best interests. 
You cannot tell Jack what Jill has said as we owe Jill a duty of 
confidentiality and cannot tell Jack without Jill's consent. Advise 
Jack to seek representation from another firm. 
 
Can you continue to act for Jill? 
 
You now have: 
* 
Information from Jack – he denies all involvement. 
* 
Which is material to Jill's case – Jill says she carried out 
the robbery with Jack. 
 
You have a duty to disclose this to Jill. 
You also have a duty of confidentiality to Jack, which continues 
even though you no longer act for him. Confidentiality overrides 
disclosure and lasts forever. 
 
P(7) You cannot act for Jack and now you are also unable to act 
in Jill's best interests as you are unable to disclose material 
information to her. 
 
Cease to act for both. 
 
Always ask each client before taking instructions whether there 
might be a conflict. This would have enabled us to act for Jill. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
2. 
Ron has been arrested for ABH on his girlfriend, Sophie. You 
have your consultation with Ron and he denies the assault. He 
says that Sophie lied to the police. Later on, you discover that 
Sophie instructed your firm months ago, relating to an 
allegation against her then boyfriend, which she withdrew. 
 
Can you continue to act for Ron? 
You have taken instructions from Ron who has accused his 
girlfriend of lying. 
You have now discovered that Sophie previously withdrew an 
allegation. 
 
This info is material to Ron's case and should be disclosed to him. 
You cannot do so without Sophie's consent because of your duty 
of confidentiality to her. 
 
P(7) You thus cannot act in Ron's best interests and must cease 
to act as there is a conflict between your duties to each client. 
 
3. 
Jim, aged 32 years, has been arrested together with his cohabiting girlfriend, Trisha aged 18 years. Jim says, ‘When you 
see Trisha, tell her I said that she should go for self-defence.' 
 
Should you act for Trisha? 
We cannot act if there is a significant risk of a conflict. Jim's 
request that you pass on this message to his girlfriend raises a 
conflict of interest. You cannot act for Trisha. 
 
In cases where there is inequality between the parties and there 
is an indication of influence, stop acting. – Here, Jim is 14 years 
older than Trisha and they live together. 
 
P(7) If convicted, Trisha might blame Jim for involving her which 
would be contrary to Jim's interests. Also, Jim could be trying to 
get Trisha to concoct a defence. 
 
Acting for Trisha amount to: 
* 
Misleading the court 
* 
P(1) P(5) You would not be acting with integrity or 
upholding the administration of justice. 
* 
In addition to acting, passing on such a message, might 
also result in you committing a criminal offence. 
 
4. 
Client tells his solicitor that he is not going to attend his trial. 
This is covered by legal professional privilege and cannot be 
disclosed without client's consent. Advise D that the trial may go 
ahead in their absence. 
 
5. 
Can a court force a solicitor to reveal confidential information? 
Yes, some matters that are confidential may be disclosed 
following an order from the court. Confidential information may 
be disclosed by court order, while privilege is absolute. 
 
THIRD PARTY INSTRUCTIONS: 
 
Issue: 
 
Whether acting on third party instructions would ensure that you are 
acting in the client's best interest and whether you can keep client's 
information confidential. 
 
Principles: 
 
P(1) Uphold the law and the proper administration of justice. – Access to 
a solicitor cannot be delayed on grounds that the solicitor was instructed 
by third party. 
P(7) Act in our client's best interests. 
 
CCS: 
 
You must keep the affairs of clients/former clients confidential except 
where disclosure is required/permitted by law or by client. 
 
Where instructed by third party, you cannot act unless you check that 
the instructing person has authority to do so on behalf of the client. – 
Especially true if client is disabled/blind and thus vulnerable.

pages.heading: MAINTAINING TRUST AND DISPUTE RESOLUTION · MAINTAINING TRUST AND ACTING FAIRLY:
pages.text:
Ethics – SQE notes | Page 7 of 9 
 
 
MAINTAINING TRUST AND DISPUTE RESOLUTION 
 
MAINTAINING TRUST AND ACTING FAIRLY: 
 
CCS 1.1 and CCF 1.1 Do not unfairly discriminate by allowing your 
personal views to affect your professional relationships and your work. 
CCS 1.2 and CCF 1.2 Do not abuse your position by taking advantage of 
clients or others. 
 
Undertakings: 
 
Undertaking = a promise that you or a third party will do/not do 
something or cause something to be done. The word ‘undertaking' 
need not be included in the statement to amount to an undertaking. 
 
An undertaking can be given by solicitors, junior or unqualified staff, 
secretaries, and trainee solicitors. 
 
Undertakings are specifically enforceable. The right to enforce an 
undertaking is taken against the firm and not the firm's client. 
 
Examples of ‘everyday' undertakings: 
• 
Undertaking by seller's solicitor in a property transaction to 
forward part of the sale proceeds to discharge the seller's 
mortgage on the property 
• 
Undertaking to the court that a document will be filed on behalf 
of a client by a given date 
• 
Undertaking to hold money to another firm's order prior to the 
occurrence of a specific event 
 
Form of Undertakings: *SMART* 
• 
Specific: be clear as to what is involved – ambiguity in an 
undertaking will be construed in favour of the recipient. 
• 
Measured: it must be capable of quantification 
• 
Agreed: both sides must agree the wording 
• 
Realistic: within solicitor's control – Never promise something 
which is outside your control. 
• 
Timed: must not be of unlimited duration 
 
Standard rules: 
You must perform all of your undertakings within the agreed timescale 
or if no timescale, within a reasonable time. 
 
Failure to do so is a serious disciplinary offence, and SRA will likely 
investigate the solicitor for professional misconduct. 
 
Advice to law firms: 
- 
Record when undertakings have been given and discharged 
- 
Set up procedures to procure that undertakings are complied 
with 
 
COOPERATION AND ACCOUNTABILITY: 
 
CCS 7 and CCF 3 You must meet the standards of cooperation and 
accountability: 
• 
Keep yourself updated with the changes in law governing the 
way you work and follow the rules. 
• 
Cooperate with the SRA, Legal Ombudsman and other legal 
services bodies/regulators. 
• 
Be honest with clients if things go wrong, aim to put matters 
right and explain promptly what happened and the likely 
impact. 
 
• 
If the SRA requests: 
- 
Take remedial action promptly. 
- 
Show that you complied with your SRA rules by being 
able to justify your decisions/actions. 
- 
Investigate if anyone may have a claim against you, 
prepare a report to the SRA, and notify relevant persons 
that they may have a claim. 
 
Obligations regarding the provision of information: 
• 
Full and accurate explanations, info and docs are to be provided 
in response to an SRA request. 
• 
Info is to be available to the SRA for inspection. 
• 
Neither solicitors nor Firms are to attempt to prevent anyone 
from providing information to the SRA. 
 
• 
Keep SRA up to date: 
- 
With criminal charges 
- 
With financial difficulty indicators, firm insolvency 
events, if the Firm will cease operating as a legal 
business and of any change to info in the register. 
- 
Prompt report must be made to SRA if there is a serious 
breach of the rules, and if instructed to do so a solicitor 
or Firm must investigate these serious breaches. 
- 
An info report must be provided to SRA on an annual 
basis (or whatever period the SRA specifies) in the 
prescribed form. 
 
DISPUTE RESOLUTION, PROCEEDINGS, INQUIRIES: 
 
Solicitors Act 1974 A solicitor is an officer of the court. 
These rules also apply to Firms. 
 
Do not waste the court's time. 
CCS 2.5 Do not place yourself in contempt of court. 
CCS 2.4 Only make assertions, statements, representations or 
submissions to the court which are properly arguable. 
 
CCS 1.4 and CCF 1.4 Do not to mislead/attempt to mislead the court: 
• 
You are not guilty of misconduct if misled the court 
inadvertently. If you become aware that you had inadvertently 
misled the court, you must, with client's consent, immediately 
inform the court. If the client does not consent, stop acting. 
• 
If you become aware that a client committed perjury/misled 
the court or attempted to do so, cease to act unless client 
agreed to disclose the truth to court. 
 
How might you mislead the court? 
• 
Draft documents/construct facts supporting your client's case 
which are not properly arguable. 
• 
Make any allegation of crime/misconduct/fraud unless it is 
material to your client's case and done on reasonable grounds 
• 
You call a witness whose evidence you know is untrue. 
 
Other important standards: 
These rules also apply to Firms. 
 
• 
You must not misuse/tamper with evidence or attempt to do 
so. 
• 
You must not influence evidence, including generating false 
evidence or persuading witnesses to change their evidence. 
• 
You will not breach the Codes if you interview and take 
statements from any (prospective/actual) witness, even if that 
witness has been interviewed or called by another party. 
However, you must not provide or offer to provide any benefit 
to witnesses (including payments) if the benefit is dependent 
on the nature of the evidence or the outcome of the case. 
 
COMPLIANCE WITH BUSINESS SYSTEMS: 
 
Firms must have effective governance structures, arrangements, 
systems, and controls in place that ensure: 
(a) You comply with SRA's regulatory arrangements, as well as with
