Residue powers which remain vested in the Crown, is exercisable by the 
ministers. 
 
The Ram Doctrine: 
 
Government shall have the power to carry on ordinary business even 
if the power is not explicitly set out by statute/royal prerogative. 
 
Constitutional conventions: 
 
Constitutional conventions = the unwritten rules about how people 
should act in certain circumstances. 
 
 
 
 
 
Key conventions: 
* 
Royal Assent is necessary for a bill to become statute. However, 
although the Monarch may technically deny giving Royal 
Assent, under constitutional conventions, the Monarch will 
always give Royal Assent to a bill passed by Parliament. 
* 
The Monarch will always act on the advice of the Prime 
Minister. 
* 
Government ministers and leadership of the executive branch 
can be appointed only from among the members of the 
Parliament. 
* 
Government ministers must take responsibility for policy 
failure. – this means that they must resign if there has been a 
policy failure. 
* 
The government is accountable to the Parliament by 
government ministers appearing in Parliament to answer 
questions and to take part in debates. 
 
Devolution: 
 
The UK includes: 
1. 
England 
2. 
Wales 
3. 
Northern Ireland 
 AND 
4. 
Scotland 
 
The UK Parliament may legislate for all four nations. However, statute 
has now set out that Northern Ireland, Scotland, and Wales also has 
separate powers to legislate and the power to operate their own 
government to develop their own laws. 
 
The UK's devolution is asymmetric, as the extent of devolution to each 
nation is not equal. 
 
CONSTITUTIONAL PRINCIPLES: 
 
The doctrine of Parliamentary Sovereignty: 
* 
Parliament has the power to make/unmake any law 
whatsoever. 
* 
No person or body is recognised as having the right to override/ 
set aside an Act of Parliament, not even the judiciary. 
 AND 
* 
No Parliament can bind its successors. 
 
The Enrolled Bill Rule: 
The courts cannot question the validity of an Act of Parliament and 
must give effect to them. 
 
Fundamental rights: 
Certain rights exist to give effect to the rule of law and these rights are 
collectively called fundamental rights. 
 
Rule of law = laws should not be applied retrospectively and should be 
applied fairly. 
 
Two key rules in relation to fundamental rights: 
1. 
Only Parliament may interfere with the fundamental rights 
through statute expressly allowing for these fundamental rights 
to be breached in certain circumstances. 
 OR 
2. 
If the statute that is being examined by the court does not state 
this, then the court will interpret the act in a way to make sure 
it complies with the rule of law and fundamental common law 
rights. 
 
The Human Rights Act: Human Rights Act 1998 
The Human Rights Act requires statute to be interpreted in a way which 
is compatible with the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR). 
– which ensures that human rights are protected from breach by a 
public body. 
 
If this is not possible, given the wording of the statue, then the court 
will make a declaration of incompatibility. 
 
This declaration will not make the law invalid, but simply acts as a 
signal to Parliament that they should consider amending the statute to 
make sure that it is compatible with the ECHR. 
 
Judicial review: 
The actions/decisions of public authorities can be reviewed by the court 
in a judicial review action. This is a review of whether the public body 
arrived at the decision following the correct procedure. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Parliament 
Government 
Judiciary

pages.heading: CONSTITUTIONAL LAW – PARLIAMENT · MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT:
pages.text:
The Legal System – SQE notes | Page 5 of 14 
CONSTITUTIONAL LAW – PARLIAMENT 
 
MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT: 
 
The UK Parliament has a two-house/two-chamber system. 
 
House of Commons: 
* 
The House of Commons is the first chamber of the UK 
Parliament. 
 
* 
Members of the House of Commons are elected for 5 years 
unless: 
× 
A motion of no confidence is passed before the expiry 
of the 5-year period. 
 OR 
× 
At least 66% of the MPs vote in favour of an early 
general election. 
 
* 
MPs must be at least 18 
 
* 
MPs cannot be: 
× 
Civil servants 
× 
Members of the House of Lords 
× 
Members of the Judiciary 
× 
Members of the armed forces 
× 
Members of the police force 
 
House of Lords: 
* 
The House of Lords is the second chamber of the UK Parliament. 
 
* 
It is independent from the House of Commons. The Lords shares 
the task of making laws and checking the work of the 
government. 
 
* 
The House of Lord is unelected. 
 
* 
The House of Lords include: 
× 
92 hereditary peers (persons at the rank of Duke, Earl, 
Viscount or Baron) 
× 
Life peers appointed by the Monarch on the advice of 
the Prime Minister 
 AND 
× 
Lords Spiritual (the 26 most senior bishops of the 
Church of England) 
 
Speaker of the House of Commons: 
* 
Their role is to maintain order in the House of Commons during 
debates. 
* 
The Speaker is chosen by the MPs and is expected to be 
impartial. 
 
STEPS OF PASSING A BILL: 
 
Each session of Parliament (a period of 12 months) begins with the 
King's Speech, in which the King reads out a speech prepared by the 
government outlining the government's legislative proposals for the 
following session. 
 
Types of bills: 
* 
Public bills – change the law as it applies to the general 
population 
* 
Private Members' Bills – introduced by MPs and Lords who 
are not government ministers 
* 
Money Bills – solely concerns taxation or government 
spending, cannot be vetoed by the House of Lords 
* 
Secondary legislations 
 
To become law, a bill must: 
1. 
Pass through and be approved by the House of Commons 
2. 
Pass through the House of Lords 
 AND 
3. 
Receive Royal Assent before the end of the session. 
 
Steps of passing a bill: 
1. 
First reading: this reading will formally introduce the bill and 
explain its intentions. 
2. 
Second reading: the principles of the bill are debated. 
3. 
Committee stage: the Committee scrutinises the bill line-byline. They can receive evidence and may make amendments. 
4. 
Report stage: the bills is reconsidered by the whole house in 
light of the amendments and comments of the committee. 
5. 
Third reading: the bill's final review before being sent to the 
House of Lords. 
6. 
Bill goes through the same process in the House of Lords 
7. 
Amendment Ping Pong: the House of Lords will request 
amendments from the House of Commons, and they will send 
it back to the House of Lords for approval. 
8. 
Royal Assent: once approved by the House of Lords, the bill 
must receive Royal Assent to become law. 
 
Salisbury Convention: 
If a government bill is implementing a commitment that the party 
elected into government made in their manifesto, then the House of 
Lords will automatically grant a second reading to the bill. 
 
Suspensory Veto: Parliament Act 1911-1949 
If the House of Lords blocks statute already passed in the Commons and 
the bill is passed the next year by the House of Commons again, the bill 
will be sent for Royal Assent even if the House of Lords blocks it again. 
 
This will essentially suspend the House of Lords' veto on the bill. 
 
Commencement: 
Bills will include a commencement date later when it actually received 
Royal Assent so that the government is given time to make 
commencement orders and regulations bringing the law into effect. 
 
One statute may have different parts with different commencement 
dates. 
 
PRIMARY LEGISLATION (STATUTE): 
 
Implementation: 
 
Once the bill passes through Parliament and receives Royal Assent, the 
act will be implemented. 
 
Implementation happens by the act being published and made 
available to the public and it will become enforceable in the UK on its 
commencement date. 
 
Once published, the courts, individuals and public authorities must 
follow the act and apply the law set out within it. 
 
The repeal of primary legislation: 
 
Laws will remain in effect until repealed. 
 
In some cases, statute may include a sunset provision which provides 
and expiration date for the law, and in that case, the law will stop being 
valid on the expiration date. 
 
 
EXPRESS REPEAL 
 
 
IMPLIED REPEAL 
 
A later Parliament has the right 
to expressly repeal the act of an 
earlier Parliament by publishing 
a new statute with wording to 
expressly repeal a previous one. 
 
In this case, the act will no longer 
be valid and enforceable. – eg. 
the Companies Act 1985 was 
repealed when the Companies 
Act 2006 was published. 
 
 
A later Parliament may impliedly 
repeal an earlier act if there is 
inconsistency 
between 
the 
earlier act and a new statute. 
 
In this case, these is no need for 
express wording to repeal the 
previous statute. 
 
The doctrine of “implied repeal” 
does not apply to constitutional 
statutes. 
 
 
 
SECONDARY LEGISLATION: 
 
In some cases, the act will also include a clause delegating specific 
authority (giving power) to an executive branch to make more specific 
laws (secondary legislation) under the principal act. 
 
Secondary legislation = legislation made by the government under the 
authority granted to it under a statute. – eg. commencement orders 
and regulations. 
 
There are two types of procedures that might be used for enacting 
secondary legislation: the negative resolution or affirmative resolution 
procedure. 
 
 
NEGATIVE RESOLUTION 
PROCEDURE 
 
 
AFFIRMATIVE RESOLUTION 
PROCEDURE 
 
A draft for secondary legislation 
will be laid in both Houses and it 
will take effect unless either 
House rejects the legislation 
within 40 days. 
 
 
A draft for secondary legislation 
will be laid in both Houses and it 
will take effect only if both 
House votes in favour. 
 
 
 
Whichever procedure is used, amendments cannot be made to the 
draft secondary legislation by either House.

pages.heading: As secondary legislation is made by the government and not · Parliament, the court may strike this legislation down for not following
pages.text:
The Legal System – SQE notes | Page 6 of 14 
As secondary legislation is made by the government and not 
Parliament, the court may strike this legislation down for not following 
the rule of law. 
 
PARLIAMENTARY PRIVILEGE: 
 
Freedom of speech and debates or proceedings in Parliament ought not 
to be impeached or questioned in any court or place out of Parliament. 
 
However, parliamentary privilege does not pose any bar to the 
prosecution of defendants charged with false accounting who, while 
serving as MPs, made false expenses and allowance claims. 
 
Parliamentary privilege applies to all members of Parliament and 
provides that no member of Parliament may be challenged in the court 
for anything said in Parliament. 
 
Sub judicie rule: 
This rule is a convention that prohibits MPs and peers from referring to 
cases that are currently being heard by the courts during debates. 
 
GOVERNMENT ACCOUNTABILITY: 
 
Collective ministerial responsibility: 
Ministers are expected to toe party line in Parliament and in public. 
 
Individual ministerial responsibility: 
Ministers responsible for decisions of their department.

pages.heading: CONSTITUTIONAL LAW – THE ROYAL PREROGATIVE · INTRODUCTION:
pages.text:
The Legal System – SQE notes | Page 7 of 14 
CONSTITUTIONAL LAW – THE ROYAL PREROGATIVE 
 
INTRODUCTION: 
 
The Crown = includes the Monarch, the ministers forming His Majesty's 
Government, the Privy Council, the secretaries of state and civil 
servants. 
 
Parliament has the power to abolish the royal prerogative powers – no 
new prerogative powers can be created. 
 
If Parliament decides to replace a prerogative power, the prerogative 
power is abolished and only the statutory power will exist. 
 
If statute and prerogative powers overlap, statute will take 
precedence. 
 
Government cannot choose to never implement an act and instead 
rely on their existing prerogative powers. 
 
Prerogative powers cannot be used to change the law or the sources 
of law. 
 
Statutes are not binding on the Crown unless: 
* 
The statute expressly states so 
 OR 
* 
If it binds the Crown by implication 
 
TYPES OF PREROGATIVE POWERS: 
 
Royal prerogative powers: 
The Crown's powers and also a source of government power that is 
recognised at common law by the courts. 
 
Ministerial prerogative powers: 
Powers exercised by ministers on behalf of the Crown. – eg. deploying 
troops, granting passports/pardons, acquiring territories, negotiating/ 
ratifying treaties. 
 
Although ministers still have prerogative powers, since 2003, the 
government will customarily seek support of the House of Commons 
before deploying troops. 
 
Personal prerogative powers: 
Powers that are personally exercised by the Monarch. – eg. dismissing 
the government, appointing the Prime Minister, granting Royal Assent. 
 
Legislative prerogative powers: 
Powers of the Privy Council to pass Orders of Council (statutory 
instruments) 
 
Judicial prerogative powers: 
Powers to hear appeals from Commonwealth nations to the Judicial 
Committee of the Privy Council. 
 
Miscellaneous prerogative powers: 
* 
The right to mine precious minerals 
* 
The right to construct harbours 
* 
The right to claim ownership over any sturgeon/dolphin/whales 
/swans over parts of the River Thames 
 
RATIFICATION OF TREATIES: 
 
The ratification of treaties is within the prerogative powers of the 
Crown. However, by act of Parliament, the draft treaty must be laid 
before both Houses of Parliament they have 21 days to vote against 
ratification. 
 
If either one of the houses vote against ratification, the government 
will have a right to explain why they want the treaty to be ratified and 
the House of Commons will have 21 days to reject the treaty. 
 
In exceptional circumstances, the government may bypass this 
requirement and accept the treaty. The act does not define exceptional 
circumstances. 
 
APPOINTING MINISTERS: 
 
The Crown has the power to appoint ministers, including the Prime 
Minister. By convention, the Monarch will appoint the leader of the 
party with the majority of seats in the House of Commons. 
 
After a general election, if a different party gains a majority in the House 
of Commons, the Prime Minister is expected to resign, and the new 
majority party will select a leader who will then be appointed to be 
Prime Minister. 
 
Prime Ministers remain in office until they lose the confidence of the 
members of the House of Commons. 
 
Cardinal Convention: 
A convention that limits the power of the Monarch to appoint ministers 
by requiring them to only act on the advice of ministers, and mainly, 
the Prime Minister. 
 
If the Monarch does not agree with the Prime Minister's choice on any 
matter, they may encourage/warn them privately. In public, the 
Monarch must always show support towards the Prime Minister's 
decisions.

pages.heading: CONSTITUTIONAL LAW – GOVERNMENT · CENTRAL GOVERNMENT AND ACCOUNTABILITY:
pages.text:
The Legal System – SQE notes | Page 8 of 14 
CONSTITUTIONAL LAW – GOVERNMENT 
 
CENTRAL GOVERNMENT AND ACCOUNTABILITY: 
 
Prime Minister (also called the First Lord of the Treasury): 
 
Prime Minister = Leads central government supported by a Cabinet 
which includes the most senior ministers. 
 
Prime Minister's duties: 
* 
Prime Minister forms the government. 
* 
This is done by the Prime Minister recommending to the 
Monarch the ministers to lead the departments that make up 
central government. 
* 
Prime Minister meets weekly with the Monarch. 
* 
Responsible for national security measures and intelligence 
matters. 
 AND 
* 
Responsible for deploying troops. 
 
Prime Minister's powers: 
* 
May change the organisation of government by abolishing/ 
merging/creating new departments. 
 
The Cabinet: 
* 
The Cabinet make government decisions collectively. 
* 
Subcommittees sit beneath the Cabinet. These are established 
by the Prime Minister who will determine their membership. 
* 
Subcommittee decisions have the same authority as Cabinet 
decisions. 
 
Ministers: 
 
Individual responsibility: 
Ministers have an individual responsibility for their own actions and 
must also take responsibility for the operation/conduct of their 
government. 
 
Collective responsibility: 
Ministers have collective responsibility in relation to government 
decisions. 
 
Confidentiality: 
Discussions within the 
government regarding policy 
matters are confidential. – this 
includes ministers' positions 
expressed in Cabinet/ 
committees. 
Unanimity: 
When a decision is reached by 
government, all ministers must 
publicly support the decision. If 
they cannot do that, they must 
resign. 
 
 
Minister's duties: 
* 
Account to Parliament (report on actions of their department 
and respond to criticism) 
* 
Must not mislead Parliament 
* 
Must behave appropriately in their private life and resign if they 
fail to do so. 
 
* 
Must personally take responsibility for the failures of their 
department: 
1. 
Policy failures (if so, resign) – eg. implementation of 
policies that did not work. 
2. 
Operational failures (if so, report it and ensure that this 
will not reoccur) – eg. where civil servants failed to 
follow procedures. 
 
Members of Parliament: 
* 
During the Prime Minister's Question Time, members of 
Parliament may ask questions about the conduct of 
government irrespective of political party. 
 
* 
Every day, Members of Parliament may ask questions from 
ministers on a rotating basis: 
× 
Questions may also be asked in writing, and if so, the 
department has 7 days to answer. 
× 
Questions cannot be regarding local authorities, the 
Monarch, cases heard in court, the affairs of other 
countries (including Northern Ireland, Scotland and 
Wales). 
 
Secretary of State: 
* 
The Secretary of State can administer legislative schemes, this 
power is granted to them by statute. 
* 
Carltona Doctrine: civil servants within the relevant Secretary 
of State's department can exercise the power granted to the 
Secretary of State. 
 
 
 
 
 
Privy Council: 
* 
Privy Council meetings are held in secret. 
* 
Although the Privy Council appears to be an important body, it 
plays only a minor role in government today. 
* 
Appointments to the council are for life and made by the 
Monarch on the advice of the Prime Minister. 
 
Privy Council's duties: 
* 
Advises the Monarch on how to exercises their royal 
prerogative powers. 
* 
Issues statutory instruments called Orders of Council. 
* 
The Judicial Committee of the Privy Council hears appeals from 
independent Commonwealth nations and British Overseas 
Territories that used to be part of the British Empire. Justices of 
the Supreme Court are members of this committee. 
* 
Approves the text of Royal Charters creating new public 
institutions. – eg. universities and learned societies. 
 
Orders of Council: 
* 
May be primary legislation, if made pursuant to the Royal 
Prerogative 
* 
May be secondary legislation, if made pursuant to statute. 
 
DEVOLUTION: 
 
The UK Parliament may legislate for all four nations. However, statute 
has now set out that Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales also has 
separate powers to legislate over certain subject areas. 
 
Scotland and Wales: 
 
The act sets out that these institutions are permanent parts of the UK 
constitution, and they cannot be abolished unless the citizens of 
Scotland or Wales vote to abolish them at a referendum. 
 
Northern Ireland: 
 
The Northern Irish government is a devolved government established 
by a treaty – the 1998 Good Friday Agreement. 
 
After this Agreement, Northern Ireland established the Northern 
Ireland Assembly and the Northern Ireland Executive. 
 
The Agreement allows for the citizens of Northern Ireland to leave the 
UK to join Ireland by referendum – and act of Parliament is not needed. 
 
Sewel Convention: 
 
If the UK Parliament is planning on legislating on a matter that is 
devolved to Scotland/Wales/Northern Ireland, the consent of the 
affected institutions will be required via a ‘legislative consent motion'. 
– even if consent is not given, Parliament will still be able to adopt the 
legislation. 
 
Legislative consent motion = the means by which a devolved legislature 
indicates that it agrees for the UK Parliament to pass law on a devolved 
matter. 
 
Review of legislation passed by devolved legislature: 
* 
If a court from one of the devolved nations believed that the 
nation's legislature/executive exceeded their authority by 
legislating beyond their power, they may refer the matter to the 
UK Supreme Court. 
* 
The legislature from each nation may also refer a bill to the UK 
Supreme Court before the bill is submitted for Royal Assent.

pages.heading: ADMINISTRATIVE LAW – JUDICIAL REVIEW · DEFINITION:
pages.text:
The Legal System – SQE notes | Page 9 of 14 
ADMINISTRATIVE LAW – JUDICIAL REVIEW 
 
DEFINITION: 
 
A judicial process allowing the courts to scrutinise the actions of the 
executive agencies/government bodies. When carrying out judicial 
review, the courts do not scrutinise the merits of the decision made by 
government bodies, but rather, look to see whether the correct process 
was used in arriving at the decision. 
 
Two stages of a judicial review claim: 
1. 
STAGE 1 – Permission stage 
2. 
STAGE 2 – Full hearing stage 
 
Applications must be filed in the Administrative Court. 
 
JUDICIAL REVIEW REQUIREMENTS: 
 
To bring a judicial review claim, the below requirements must be 
satisfied: 
1. 
Judicial review is only available against decisions made by public 
bodies. 
2. 
Ruling in the applicant's favour must change their outcome. 
3. 
The application must be made within the time limit. 
4. 
The applicant must have standing to bring the claim. 
5. 
Must be a public law issue. 
 AND 
6. 
One of the grounds for judicial review must apply. 
 
Public bodies: 
 
The decision complained of must have been made by public body, or 
another body exercising a public function. 
 
Decisions of private businesses, private associations and charities 
cannot be subjected to judicial review. – eg. private employers. 
 
Bodies that exercise both a public and private function can be subjected 
to judicial review, but only if in making the decision complained of, they 
exercised a public function. 
 
If the person seeking judicial review has a contract with the public body, 
then contract law will govern their relationship and judicial review is 
not available. 
 
Change of outcome: 
 
Ruling in the applicant's favour must substantially change their 
outcome. – eg. if the public body would have come to the same 
conclusion using the correct procedures, which is a possibility, then the 
claim will not be allowed. 
 
Time limit: 
 
Applications for judicial review must be made promptly but not later 
than 3 months after the issue first arose. 
 
All other remedies must be exhausted first. 
 
For judicial review of planning decisions: 
The application must be brought within 6 weeks from the decision. 
 
Time limits cannot be extended by the parties. 
 
Standing: 
 
The applicant must have sufficient standing to bring a claim. 
 
Standing is reviewed during the permission stage. 
 
Sufficient interest test: The applicant must show sufficient interest. 
 
The Human Rights Act uses a different test for standing – the Victim 
test which is more limited. Do not confuse the two tests. 
 
Groups usually do not have standing, but the court is likely to find 
sufficient interest if there is an association or group that is: 
* 
Responsible 
* 
Well resourced 
* 
Has expertise 
 AND 
* 
There is unlikely to be an alternative claimant 
 
Public law issue: 
 
The review must be for a public law issue and public law issues can only 
be reviewed via judicial review. 
 
Exception: if there are mixed issues: private and public law in one 
matter, the case can be heard at the private law courts. 
GROUNDS FOR JUDICIAL REVIEW: 
 
Illegality: 
 
A claim of illegality may be based on any of the following assertions: 
 
* 
The public body acted ultra vires: 
 
Decision of a public authority can be set aside if it exceeds the 
powers delegated to it by Parliament. 
 
* 
The public body failed to comply with a specific legal duty: 
 
Public bodies will have a legal duty to take into account equality 
considerations, therefore, they must take into consideration the 
following: 
× 
Eliminating discrimination 
× 
Advancing equality 
 AND 
× 
Minimising/removing disadvantages suffered by those 
who share a protected characteristic. – eg. age, race, 
disability, gender reassignment, pregnancy, religion, sex, 
sexual orientation. 
 
* 
Took into account irrelevant considerations: 
 
× 
The public body may only consider factors that are 
relevant to the power granted to them. 
× 
Powers being used for the wrong purpose, improper 
purpose or irrelevant consideration must materially 
influence the decision. 
 
* 
Acted under an error of law: 
 
Ouster clauses seek to exclude the jurisdiction of the court. If 
there are ouster clauses in the statute granting power to the 
public body the applicant will be limited in the type of judicial 
review claim they can bring. 
 
Ouster clause = a clause stating that the decisions of the public 
body pursuant to the statute cannot be challenged by way of 
judicial review. 
 
If the statute delegating power to the public body includes an 
ouster clause, the court will construe the clause narrowly to 
interpret it to mean that only legal decisions cannot be 
challenged. They can still review decisions to see if there was 
any illegality. – the courts will then review the decision to see if 
it was legal. If there are ouster clauses in your question, this is 
the only ground that applies. 
 
* 
Unlawful delegation: 
 
Unlawfully delegated its power to another. This cannot be 
justified by administrative convenience. 
 
Procedural impropriety: 
 
A claim of procedural impropriety focuses on whether the decisionmaker followed the procedures that are laid down in the statute 
delegating the power. 
 
A decision may be found invalid for: 
 
* 
Failure to follow mandatory requirements: 
 
Mandatory requirements: 
The decision will be set aside if 
the mandatory requirements 
were not followed, even if there 
is no denial of natural justice. – 
these will be ‘must' or ‘shall' 
requirements in the statute. 
Discretionary/directory 
requirements: 
The decision will be 
deemed valid, if not 
followed. 
 
 
* 
Failure to follow the common law/natural justice: 
 
× 
Failed to provide for the right to be heard: 
The applicant was not given a right to be heard before 
the decision-maker made the decision. 
 
Example 1: 
If a person is removed from the country as a result of a 
public law decision, they must be given an opportunity 
to respond and have their case heard. 
 
Example 2: 
If a company's licence is withdrawn without any 
investigation when the decision-maker hears rumours 
that the company is in breach, then this means that the 
company's right to be heard and respond was breached.

pages.heading: Failed to stay unbiased: · Nobody may be a judge of their own cause
pages.text:
The Legal System – SQE notes | Page 10 of 14 
× 
Failed to stay unbiased: 
– 
Nobody may be a judge of their own cause 
– 
Bias is present even if it is not demonstrated that 
the interest has influenced the decision. 
– 
If bias is found, the decision will automatically 
be disqualified and if there is apparent bias, the 
decision will subsequently be disqualified after 
such a finding is made. 
 
 
The decisionmaker will be deemed biased if they: 
1. 
Have a financial interest in the subject matter 
 OR 
2. 
Have a non-financial interest which is closely 
connected to the issues raised by the decision. 
 
The court may find apparent bias if: 
A fair-minded and informed observer, informed of the 
facts, would conclude that there was a real possibility of 
bias. 
 
× 
Failed consult: 
Those, who may be affected by the decision have a right 
to be consulted and comment on the decisions of the 
local authority. 
 
The product of consultation must be taken into account 
when the ultimate decision is taken. 
 
Right to consult arises when: 
1. 
There is a statutory duty to consult 
2. 
There has been a promise to consult 
3. 
There is an established practice to consult 
 OR 
4. 
The failure to consult would lead to conspicuous 
unfairness. 
 
× 
Failed to give reasons for the decision: 
No general duty to give reasons for a decision of a public 
authority. 
 
Duty to give reasons arises when: 
1. 
The subject matter/interest is important – such 
as any decisions involving the question of 
personal liberty. 
 OR 
2. 
The decision appears to be aberrant (unusual, 
non-standard). 
 
Legitimate expectations: 
 
Failure to meet the legitimate expectation of the applicant could also be 
grounds for remedies under judicial review. 
 
This can be due to: 
1. 
An explicit promise/assurance 
 OR 
2. 
Previous actions by the local authority 
 
Examples: 
* 
If the decision maker has formerly carried a certain policy one 
way, it is legitimate to expect that it will do so in the future. 
* 
The decision maker promised a benefit, it would be unfair to 
dishonour it, even if there were public interest grounds for doing 
so. 
* 
The decision maker made a clear and unambiguous promise or 
representation that gives rise to an expectation. 
* 
The affected party has an interest in some eventual benefit that 
it expected to attain or retain. 
* 
The decision maker possesses the power to make such 
representation, and the affected party reasonably acted in 
reliance upon it to their detriment. 
 
Irrationality: 
 
Making an irrational/unreasonable decision will also be a ground for 
invalidating the decision under judicial review. 
 
Test: 
The decision must be so outrageous in its defiance of logic or of 
accepted moral standards that no sensible person would have arrived 
at it. 
 
Two types: 
 
Wednesbury unreasonableness: 
* 
No sensible person who had applied his mind to the question 
would have arrived at it. 
* 
Courts look at the merits of the decision, rather than at the 
procedure by which it was arrived at or legal basis on which it 
was founded. 
Proportionality: 
Human Rights Act 1998 Recognised where issues of EU law and ECHR 
are involved. 
 
REMEDIES: 
 
Quashing Order: 
* 
Nullifies decision by public body. 
* 
Court can send case back to original decision maker – direction 
to remake the decision. 
 
Prohibiting order: 
* 
Acts prospectively 
* 
Obliges the public authority not to do something 
 
Mandatory order: 
* 
Compels public authority to fulfil their duties 
* 
Addresses wrongful failure to act 
* 
Failure to comply is punishable as a contempt of court 
 
Declaration: 
* 
Clarifies the respective rights and obligations of parties to the 
proceedings 
* 
Parties not obliged to do anything 
* 
Resolves legal position of parties in proceedings 
 
Injunction: 
* 
Order may be made by court to stop a public body from acting 
in an unlawful way 
* 
Must be mandatory 
 
Damages: 
There must either a recognised private law cause of action or a claim 
under EU law or the Human Rights Act. 
 
Procedural issues concerning remedies: 
* 
Remedies are discretionary – even if a court finds a public body 
has acted wrongly, it does not have to grant remedy 
* 
Relief is not granted if the court finds that the lawful action by 
the public authority would have led to the substantially same 
outcome.

pages.heading: EUROPEAN UNION LAW · THE PLACE OF EU IN UK LAW:
pages.text:
The Legal System – SQE notes | Page 11 of 14 
EUROPEAN UNION LAW 
 
THE PLACE OF EU IN UK LAW: 
 
Dualist and Monist principles: 
 
Dualist Principle: 
The theory treats international 
law 
and 
domestic 
law 
as 
separate. International law only 
forms part of a domestic law, if 
accepted by statute or judicial 
decisions. 
 
Monist Principle: 
There is a direct application of 
international law into domestic 
law, without the need for 
ratification. 
 
The effects of Brexit: 
 
European Union (Withdrawal) Act 2018 European Union (Withdrawal 
Agreement) Act 2020 All EU law that was part of the UK's legal system 
at the end of the transition period was converted into new UK law, 
collectively known as retained EU law. 
 
Previous rules: 
 
Doctrine of Direct Applicability: allows EU law to take immediate 
effect in Member States 
 
Doctrine of Direct Effect: parties can enforce it in national courts 
 
Incorporated EU law: 
 
Pre-Brexit legislation (both primary and secondary), implementing EU 
directives has been preserved as UK law and it is now called EUderived domestic legislation. 
 
Automatically binding EU regulations have been retained as direct EU 
legislation. 
 
EU law with direct applicability, such as treaties, have been retained 
as directly effective EU law. 
 
Retained decisions of the Court of Justice of the EU (CJEU) are binding 
on the UK domestic courts except for the Supreme Court and Court 
of Appeal and have been retained as retained EU case law. 
 
The UK has the right to repeal and amend retained EU law. 
 
Supremacy and Retained EU law: 
 
If there is conflict between UK law that was enacted before the end of 
the transition period and retained EU law, then retained EU law will 
prevail. 
 
However, statute enacted after the transition period is not subject to 
the principle of supremacy, meaning that the UK can create legislation 
contrary to EU law. 
 
HUMAN RIGHTS ACT: 
 
Human Rights Act 1998 The ECHR has been incorporated into UK law 
so that the UK courts may invoke the ECHR when making decisions. 
 
Types of rights under the ECHR: 
1. 
Absolute rights – rights which cannot be limited at all. – the 
rights to life and prohibition of torture. 
2. 
Limited rights – which can be limited under the circumstances 
described in the act. – the right to liberty and the right to a fair 
trial. 
3. 
Qualified rights – which can be limited to achieve a legitimate 
interest. – the right to privacy, freedom of thought, religion, 
expression, assembly, marriage, the ban on discrimination. 
 
The key human rights and freedoms in the ECHR: 
 
Right to life – Art 2 
Everyone's right to life is protected by law. No one shall be deprived of 
his life intentionally. 
 
Prohibition of torture – Art 3 
No one shall be subjected to torture or to inhuman or degrading 
treatment or punishment. 
 
Prohibition of slavery and forced labour – Art 4 
No one should be held in slavery/servitude. 
 
Right to liberty and security – Art 5 
Everyone has the right to liberty and security of person. 
 
Right to a fair trial – Art 6 
Everyone is entitled to a fair and public hearing within a reasonable 
time by an independent court/tribunal. 
Right to respect for private and family life – Art 8 
Everyone has the right to respect for his private and family life and their 
home. 
 
Freedom of thought, conscience and religion – Art 9 
Everyone has the right to freedom of thought, conscience and religion; 
this right includes freedom to change religion/belief and freedom, 
either alone or as part of a community, in public /private, to manifest 
their religion/belief, in worship, teaching, practice and observance. 
 
Freedom of expression – Art 10 
Everyone has the right to freedom of expression. This right shall include 
freedom to hold opinions and to receive and impart information and 
ideas without interference by public authority. 
 
Freedom of assembly and association – Art 11 
Everyone has the right to freedom of peaceful assembly and to freedom 
of association with others, including the right to form and to join 
trade unions for the protection of their interests. 
 
Right to marry – Art 12 
Men and women of marriageable age have the right to marry and to 
found a family. 
 
Prohibition of discrimination – Art 14 
The enjoyment of rights/freedoms set forth in this Convention shall be 
secured without discrimination on any ground such as sex, race, 
colour, language, religion, political or other opinion, national or 
social origin, association with a national minority, property, birth or 
other status. 
 
Can a qualified right be restricted? 
 
Proportionality test: 
 
The proportionality test is used when deciding whether action of a 
public authority that restricts a qualified right is justified: 
× 
The restriction must be designed to meet a legitimate aim 
sufficiently important to justify interference. 
× 
The restriction must be reasonably connected to achieving its 
aim. 
 AND 
× 
The restriction must interfere with the right no more than 
necessary to achieve its aim, so it must be the least onerous way 
of achieving the aim. 
 
Judicial deference: 
 
If an issue is politically controversial, when applying the proportionality 
test, the courts should defer the issue to the government or Parliament. 
 
If the actions of a public authority are challenged at the European Court 
of Human Rights (ECtHR), the public authority might argue that they are 
entitled to a margin of appreciation – this is similar to judicial 
deference. 
 
Margin of appreciation: 
× 
The ECtHR will likely apply a narrow margin of appreciation 
when there is a consensus among the member states on an 
issue 
× 
The ECtHR will likely broader margin of appreciation when 
there is no consensus. 
 
Derogation: 
 
The states may derogate (= deviate from) the rights provided by the 
ECHR. Derogation is allowed to the extent it is necessary in the event of 
war/other public emergencies threatening the nation. 
 
Derogation is not allowed in relation to the prohibition of torture, 
slavery and retrospective criminal offences. 
 
How will the courts apply the ECHR/HRA? 
 
Human Rights Act 1998 The courts must interpret statute in a way 
which is compatible with the ECHR to the extent that this is possible. – 
the UK court must also follow the interpretation of the ECtHR, where 
there is a clear line of authority. 
 
If a UK court finds that it is not possible to interpret a statute in a way 
to make it compatible with the ECHR, the court will not be able to strike 
down the legislation but may make a declaration of incompatibility. 
 
A declaration of incompatibility will have no effect on the statute, it 
merely serves to alert the Parliament that the statute should be 
amended to make it compatible with the ECHR.

pages.heading: Remedies: · When the court makes a declaration of incompatibility:
pages.text:
The Legal System – SQE notes | Page 12 of 14 
Remedies: 
 
When the court makes a declaration of incompatibility: 
 
Fast track remedial orders: 
1. 
Non-urgent procedure: amendments to the law are approved 
by both Houses of Parliament and they become law 60 days 
thereafter. 
2. 
Urgent procedure: this is the procedure to use if the matter is 
declared urgent by a government minister. The amendments in 
this case are immediately effective but must be laid before both 
House of Parliament and will cease to be effective unless both 
Houses approve the remedial order within 120 days. 
 
s.6 Human Rights Act 1998 When a public authority has acted in a way 
which is incompatible with ECHR: They should seek judicial review. 
 
Requirements: 
1. 
The act must have been carried out by a public authority. – this 
includes a court/tribunal, but members of the House of 
Commons and House of Lords are excluded. 
2. 
Only the victim of the unlawful action can bring a claim and the 
victim cannot ask someone else to bring a claim for them. 
3. 
Such HRA claims may be brought within 1 year from the act 
complained of. – even though this is a judicial review claim that 
has a 3 month deadline, in this case, the time limit is extended 
to 1 year. 
 
Remedies for human rights violation are discretionary. 
 
EQUALITY ACT: 
 
Equality Act 2010 In addition to the ECHR's ban on discrimination, 
there is statutory protection against discrimination laid down in this 
act. 
 
The act protects from discrimination based on: 
× 
Sex/sexual orientation/gender reassignment 
× 
Race 
× 
Disability/age 
× 
Religion/belief 
× 
Marital/partnership status 
 AND 
× 
Pregnancy/maternity 
 
Why to claim under the Equality Act? 
× 
Claims for violations of the ECHR right to be free from 
discrimination under the HRA can only be brought if it is 
attached to the breach of another Convention right. However, 
a claim under the Equality Act can be brought by itself. 
 AND 
× 
Claims for discrimination under the act may be brought against 
private employers, not only public bodies. 
 
Claims for discrimination may be for: 
 
1. 
Direct discrimination – where the victim was treated less 
favourably because of their protected status. 
 
2. 
Indirect discrimination – where a policy, practice or procedure 
unfavourably affects a protected group of people. 
 
PUBLIC ORDER LAW: 
 
Public authorities (such as the police) have: Public Order Act 1986 
1. 
The power to limit the right to protest. 
2. 
The power to arrest persons who violate public order. 
 AND 
3. 
The power to maintain the King's Peace – meaning: to ensure 
that citizens can go about their ordinary business without 
undue interference from other citizens. 
 
These powers must be interpreted in a way that it gives effect to the 
ECHR and HRA rights to freedom of expression, assembly and 
association. 
 I 
So restriction on these rights must only be for the purposes of: 
* 
National security 
* 
Public safety 
 OR 
* 
Prevention of crime. 
 
Elements of breach of peace: 
 
Breach of the peace occurs when: 
* 
When someone genuinely is in fear of harm to themselves or to 
their property in their presence as a result of an assault/affray/ 
riot or other disturbance. 
* 
When harm has actually been done to someone or to property 
in their presence. 
 OR 
* 
When harm is likely to be done to someone or to property in 
their presence. 
 
Can occur on public or private property. 
 
Police officers may take reasonable steps to terminate a breach of the 
peace or to prevent a likely breach of peace. – this includes arresting 
someone or forcing entry into private premises. 
 
Types of breach of peace: 
 
Riot: 
12 or more persons who are present together use or threaten unlawful 
violence for a common purpose and the conduct of them (taken 
together) is such as would cause a person of reasonable firmness present 
at the scene to fear for their personal safety. 
 
Violent disorder: 
3 or more persons who are present together use of threaten unlawful 
violence, and the conduct of them taken together is such as would cause 
a person with reasonable firmness present at the scene to fear for his 
personal safety. 
 
Affray: 
A person is guilty of affray if he threatens unlawful violence towards 
another and their conduct would cause person of reasonable firmness 
present at the scene to fear for his personal safety. 
 
Causing fear or provocation of violence: 
Words must be used in the presence and earshot of the person to whom 
they are directed in a public or private place. 
 
Intentional harassment, alarm of distress: 
Public or private place, using threatening abusive or insulting words of 
behaviour, or disorderly behaviour. 
 
Using threatening/abusive words or behaviour likely to cause 
harassment, alarm or distress: 
Within the hearing or sight of a person likely to be caused harassment, 
alarm of distress in a public or private place. 
 
Public Gatherings: 
 
Public procession: 
 
Public Order Act 1986 If the public plans a parade or march, there are 
a number of conditions they must follow, otherwise, the parade/march 
will be banned. 
 
Advance written notice of 6 clear days must be given to the police if 
the procession is intended to achieve one of the following: 
× 
To demonstrate support for/opposition to the views or actions 
of any person. 
× 
To publicise a cause/campaign 
 OR 
× 
To mark/commemorate an event. 
 
The notice must: 
× 
Specify date, time, proposed route, name and address of the 
persons proposing to organise the procession 
× 
Be delivered to the police station located in the area where the 
procession will be held 
 AND 
× 
Notice is not required for processions commonly held such as 
funeral marches or Remembrance Sunday parades. 
 
A senior police officer of the area or the most senior police officer 
present at the march may impose conditions if they reasonably 
believe: 
1. 
The procession will result in serious damage to property 
 AND 
2. 
The procession's purpose is to intimidate others 
 
The conditions can relate to the route or exclusion from any public 
place. 
 
If no condition can prevent serious disorder, the chief constable can 
apply to ban all/a specified class of processions for up to 3 months: 
× 
If the procession is to take place in London or Greater London, 
by applying to the Home Secretary. 
× 
If the procession is to take place elsewhere, by applying to the 
local council. 
 
Public Assembly: 
 
The regulation surrounding public assemblies is similar to the regulation 
of public processions. 
 
Public assembly = 2 or more persons in a public place in open air.

pages.heading: No prior notice required. Conditions may be imposed regarding number · of people, location and maximum duration.
pages.text:
The Legal System – SQE notes | Page 13 of 14 
No prior notice required. Conditions may be imposed regarding number 
of people, location and maximum duration. 
 
The senior police officer may impose conditions – grounds: 
* 
Serious public disorder 
* 
Serious damage to property 
* 
Intimidation 
 OR 
* 
Serious disruption to the life of community 
 
Trespassory Assemblies: 
 
Trespassory assembly = 20 or more person on land in the open air on 
private land without the permission, or in excess of permission from 
occupier which may result in serious disruption to the community or 
cause significant damage. – It includes assemblies obstructing traffic 
and assemblies at Stonehenge. 
 
If the chief constable believes that such an assembly is likely to take 
place, they can apply to local council for a ban prohibiting all 
trespassory assemblies. – In London or Greater London, an application 
must be made to the Home Secretary. 
 
The police may stop anyone they reasonably believe to be on their 
way to a trespassory assembly which has been banned and direct them 
not to attend the assembly.

pages.heading: FUNDING CIVIL CLAIMS · LEGAL AID FUNDING:
pages.text:
The Legal System – SQE notes | Page 14 of 14 
FUNDING CIVIL CLAIMS 
 
LEGAL AID FUNDING: 
 
Which type of claims might qualify? 
 
The following will not be funded – alternative funding needed: 
1. Personal injury or death – but injury due to clinical negligence 
is not excluded. 
2. Conveyancing, boundary disputes, defamation, wills/trust law, 
company/partnership law, contract claims 
3. Employment cases negligence and consumer cases 
 
What type of funding is available? 
 
Legal help: helping with preparing a case, but not litigation 
Help at court: allows advocates to speak for the client at a court hearing 
without acting formally – one-off help for one trial. 
Legal representation: covers preparation + litigation + representation. 
 
Assessing whether a client qualifies for help: 
 
Only available to individuals. Must pass both the merits + means test. 
 
Merits test: 
Moderate prospect of success is enough. 
 
Will be refused funding if: 
× 
Unlikely to win more than the case costs 
× 
Alternative funding available 
× 
Suitable for the small claims track 
× 
Complaints procedure/ADR is not exhausted 
× 
Unreasonable for the public to fund the case 
 
Means test: 
If the client or their partner receives benefit they are eligible. – eg. 
income support. 
 
If no benefits, then consider client's capital and income: 
1. 
Capital: disposable capital is max. £8,000. (+ also look at 
partner's capital) 
 AND 
2. 
Income: gross monthly income is max. £2,657 + disposable 
income is max £733 per month. (+ also look at partner's 
income) 
 
Costs consequences of legal aid funding: 
 
If a client keeps/gains money or property at the end of their case, then 
they may have to repay some or all of the legal aid costs. This is done 
through a statutory charge. 
 
Example of statutory charge on the money/property: 
 
If client wins damages of £20,000 
Court orders costs of £4,000, LAA costs of £5,000 
Statutory charge on damages: £5,000 - £4,000 = £1,000 
 
NO WIN NO FEE AGREEMENTS: 
 
Conditional fee agreements (CFA): 
 
If the client wins the case: 
 
Pays to the solicitor: 
* 
Solicitor's basic fee and disbursements 
* 
Success fee (pays out of pocket) 
* 
Insurance premium (pays out of pocket) 
 
Recovers from the other side: 
* 
Solicitor's basic fee and disbursements 
* 
Damages 
 
If the client loses the case: 
 
Pays to the solicitor: 
* 
Disbursements 
* 
Insurance premium 
* 
Damages if there is a successful counterclaim 
 
Recovers from the other side: nothing 
 
Damages based agreements (DBA): 
 
If lawyers lose the case, they do not recover any fees. 
If lawyers win the case, the max recoverable amount is capped: 
1. at 25% of the damages in personal injury cases 
2. 35% of damages in employment tribunal cases and 
3. 50% of damages in all other cases. 
INSURANCE: 
 
If the policy was entered into after 1 Apr 2013: Insurance premium is 
not recoverable from the other side if the policy-holder then wins at 
trial and is awarded its costs. 
 
 
Before the event (BTE) 
insurance 
 
BTE insurance provides the 
client with an indemnity for the 
cost of any legal fees incurred as 
a result of any future litigation. 
 
BTE premiums are relatively low 
(less than 1% of the insurance 
cover). 
 
 
After the event (ATE) 
insurance 
 
Criteria: merits of the case + the 
level of cover required. – ie. 
whether a particular insurance 
company is willing to take on the 
risk and on what terms. 
 
ATE 
premiums 
are 
more 
expensive (more than 25% of the 
insurance cover). 
 
 
FUNDING CRIMINAL CLAIMS 
 
At the police station: 
 
At the police station all suspects are entitled to free legal advice. In 
addition to this, suspects may pay for solicitors privately. 
 
To determine level of free advice – use the ‘Sufficient benefit' test: 
1. 
It is reasonable for the suspect to be provided with help 
2. 
Advice is likely to be sufficient benefit to the suspect 
 
If the matter passes the test: solicitor advises face-to-face at police 
station, attends interviews, identity parades and public hearing. 
Passes eg. if there has been serious maltreatment by the police 
 
If the matter fails the test: only entitled to telephone advice. 
Fails eg. minor offence, non-imprisonable or to do with drunkenness. 
 
At the Magistrates' Court: 
 
Apply for a representation order as soon as possible to get funding for 
representation at the hearing. 
 
To obtain this order: D must pass both means test + merits test. 
 
Means test: 
 
D will pass this test if: 
* 
D is under 18 
* 
D receives unemployment benefits 
 OR 
* 
D receives an income below £12,475 or capital is below £12,475. 
 
Merits test: 
 
s.17 LASPO 2012 D's solicitor will complete a form demonstrating that it 
is in the interest of justice that D is legally represented. 
 
Are the below factors likely? 
* 
Is a prison sentence likely? – eg. a prison sentence will always be 
likely for serious offences 
* 
D losing their livelihood? – if a custodial sentence is likely, then 
D will also likely lose their livelihood. 
* 
D suffering serious damage to reputation? – eg. if D was a lawyer 
or if D is of previous good character. 
* 
Is it in the interest of another person that D is represented? – 
eg. if it was a violent/sexual offence, the victim will want to be 
cross-examined by a lawyer rather than the accused. 
* 
Does the matter involve a substantial question of law? 
 
* 
The proceedings requiring: 
1. The tracing or interviewing a prosecution witness? 
2. Cross-examination of experts/witnesses? 
 
If the D fail these tests: 
* 
D may consult the duty solicitor on one occasion if D is in 
prison/custody. 
* 
D may pay for representation privately.

pages.heading: INTENTIONAL TORTS · This topic is commonly examined in terms of Occupiers' liability and
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Notes | Page 1 of 14 
 
INTENTIONAL TORTS 
 
This topic is commonly examined in terms of Occupiers' liability and 
Burglary (Criminal law). 
 
Torts that arise from the intentional actions of the Defendant: 
 
1. Trespass to property – Three separate torts: 
i. Trespass to land 
ii. Trespass to goods 
iii. Conversion 
 
2. Trespass to the person – Three separate torts: 
i. Battery 
ii. Assault 
iii. False imprisonment 
 
 
TRESPASS TO PROPERTY: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
TRESPASS TO LAND: 
 
Connection to occupiers' liability: 
 Trespass to land is commonly seen in occupiers' liability questions which 
you will read about in one of the later chapters. Establishing whether 
someone was a trespasser will be necessary for that. 
 
Connection to land law: 
 Trespass to land is commonly used in relation to boundary disputes in 
land law. The parties usually also make a claim for the tort of trespass to 
land to seek a remedy in relation to the claims made for proprietary 
rights in land. 
 
Definition: 
 
Trespass to land = unlawful, unjustifiable, and direct interference with 
the Claimant's possession of land. – the Claimant has a proprietary right 
in land and therefore, a right to keep people off the land. 
 
This tort includes the intentional entering or wrongfully remaining on 
someone else's land. 
 
Elements: 
 
Elements of trespass to land: 
 
1. 
Possession of the land – the Claimant bringing an action for 
trespass must have exclusive possession of the land. 
 
2. 
Land includes the usable space above and below and the surface 
of the land. – a drone flying over the land is trespass, but not 
aircraft flying at reasonable height. An overhanging crane can 
constitute trespass. 
 
3. 
Direct physical interference with the land by person, the 
machines they control or animals. – allowing the roots of your 
tree to extend under the land is indirect interference so not 
trespass. 
 
4. 
Intent to enter the land/negligence as to animals/machines 
entering the land – no need for intent to trespass, intent must 
be to simply enter the land. A person will also be liable if they 
negligently allow animals/machines in their control to enter the 
land. 
 
Each day an object or person remains unlawfully on land, a fresh cause 
of action arises. 
 
Even if a person has permission to be on the land because they have 
been invited to enter, they may become a trespasser if they enter for a 
different purpose than what the invitation entailed or if they enter a 
different area of the land where they have not been invited. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Direct interference: 
 The interference is only actionable if it is direct. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Indirect interference is not actionable. – a tree branch leaning over onto 
someone else's land is indirect interference. 
 
If smells/noises/vibrations enter your land from the neighbouring land, 
this will give rise to a nuisance claim, not trespass. 
 
Defences: 
 
Lawful entry: 
If the Defendant's presence is lawful, there is no trespass. 
 
Necessity: 
If the Defendant can prove that it was necessary for them to enter the 
land to preserve life or property, there is no trespass. 
 
TRESPASS TO GOODS: 
 
Definition: 
 
Trespass to goods = wrongful physical interference with goods that are 
in the possession of another. 
 
Elements: 
 
Trespass to chattels is actionable per se – actual damage is not required. 
 
Defences: 
 
Defending a person/property: 
Goods are in real or imminent danger and interference is reasonable in 
the circumstances, and the Defendant considered that there was no 
other practical means of protecting the property. 
 
Consent: 
Liability negated if consent extended to the conduct complained of 
 
Recovery of goods: 
Recovery of goods by claimant removed by the Defendant due to 
unlawful distress. 
 
CONVERSION: 
 
Definition: 
 
Conversion = the intentional dealing with goods which is seriously 
inconsistent with the use and possession or right to immediate 
possession of another person. 
 
Elements: 
1. 
Conversion is actionable per se. 
2. 
Conversion is a strict liability tort, which does not require the 
claimant to show the Defendant had a wrong intention, the 
Defendant may assert as a defence that he acted honestly. 
3. 
Only applies to corporeal personal property. – does not apply to 
intangible property such as a contractual right, copyright or 
electronic documents. 
4. 
Possession or immediate right to possession required to have 
standing to sue for conversion. – ownership is not a critical 
factor. 
 
Defences: 
 
Co-ownership: 
 A co-owner has no right to bring action against another co-owner for 
interfering with his right of possession. 
 
Cheques Act: 
 Cheques Act If cheque incorrectly paid into customer's account in good 
faith and without negligence, the bank has a defence. 
Example: 
* 
If they have been invited over for tea and they proceed to 
steal items from the house, they will be deemed to be 
trespassers as the purpose of the invitation was not stealing. 
* 
If someone is invited into the garden, they become trespasser 
if they enter the house. The permission was given to them to 
enter the garden only. 
 Trespass to land 
 
 Unlawful direct 
interference with 
another's land and 
right to possess it. 
 
 Trespass to goods 
 
 The intentional and 
unlawful 
interference with 
another's lawful 
use or possession 
of goods (personal 
property). 
 
 
 
Conversion 
 
 The intentional 
dealing with goods 
which is inconsistent 
with the use and 
possession of 
another. 
 
 
Examples of direct interference: 
* 
Taking possession of the land 
* 
Wrongfully entering or staying on the land 
* 
Placing anything on the land 
* 
Crossing the land or driving over the land 
* 
Allowing animals on the land.

pages.heading: Insolvency Act: · Insolvency Act A person who deals with the bankrupt's property when
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Notes | Page 2 of 14 
 
 
Insolvency Act: 
 Insolvency Act A person who deals with the bankrupt's property when 
unaware of the bankruptcy is not liable. 
 
Pawnbrokers: 
 Pawnbrokers are not liable for failing to confirm the pledged goods are 
being returned to the true owner. 
 
Abandonment: 
 The test for purposes of ascertaining whether there has been 
abandonment is whether there has been both an intention to abandon 
and some physical act of relinquishment. 
 
The finder must establish a reasonable entitlement to conclude that no 
one is interested in the goods and they can therefore be disposed of. 
 
TRESPASS TO THE PERSON: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
BATTERY: 
 
 
 
 
 
Battery will likely be relevant in questions where a doctor or another 
medical professional does more to a person's body than authorized. 
 
Definition: 
 
Battery = the intentional and direct application of force to another 
person. 
 
Elements: 
1. 
Unlawful force against another person – this includes unwanted 
physical contact of any kind that is not generally acceptable in 
the ordinary conduct of life. 
2. 
Which is direct and immediate physically. 
3. 
The act must be intentional; however, the harm need not be. 
 AND 
4. 
The Claimant is not required to demonstrate physical injury. 
 
The contact need not be from one person to another, it can be through 
clothes or throwing something. 
 
ASSAULT: 
 
 
 
 
 
Definition: 
 
Assault = an act which causes another person to apprehend the infliction 
of immediate, unlawful force on their person. 
 
Elements: 
1. 
The Defendant intends that Claimant apprehends the 
application of unlawful force on the Claimant. 
2. 
The Defendant reasonably apprehends the direct and immediate 
application of unlawful force. 
3. 
The Defendant has no lawful justification/excuse. 
 AND 
4. 
No requirement of direct application of force – words which 
instil a reasonable fear of unlawful force amount to assault. 
 
FALSE IMPRISONMENT: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Definition: 
 
False imprisonment = Depriving the Claimant of freedom of 
movement, without a lawful justification for doing so. 
 
 
Elements: 
* 
The Defendant must intend to completely restrict Claimant's 
freedom of movement. 
 AND 
* 
The Defendant has no lawful justification/excuse. 
 
Strict liability: if the Defendant intentionally performs an act that leads 
to the imprisonment of Claimant, then liability attaches even in 
circumstances if the Defendant did not know this act would result in false 
imprisonment. 
 
Defences to trespass against the person: 
 
Volenti non fit injuria: 
In relation to sports: If the injuries suffered were not from the Claimant's 
participation in the sport but inadequate safety measures, that is a 
defence. 
 
 
Self defence: 
Self-defence is a valid defence to trespass against the person, assuming 
that it constituted the use of reasonable force which they honestly and 
reasonably believe is necessary to protect themselves or someone else, 
or property. 
 
Consent: 
* 
Consent is not always a defence. 
* 
Consent must be valid to be taken into account. 
 
Necessity: 
* 
The act must be necessary to avoid inevitable, irreparable evil. 
* 
No more may be done than is necessary to achieve purpose. 
* 
The harm inflicted must not be disproportionate to evil avoided. 
 
 
 
INTENTIONAL + DIRECT APPLICATION OF FORCE 
 
INTENTIONAL + APPREHENSION OF BATTERY 
 
INTENTIONAL + UNLAWFUL + DEPRIVATION OF LIBERTY 
 
Battery 
 
 The intentional and 
direct application of 
physical force to 
another. 
 
 
 
 
 
Assault 
 
 An intentional act 
which causes 
another to 
apprehend the 
infliction of 
immediate, 
unlawful force. 
 
 False imprisonment 
 
 Depriving another of 
freedom of 
movement, without 
a lawful justification 
for doing so.

pages.heading: NEGLIGENCE – DUTY AND BREACH · INTRODUCTION:
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Notes | Page 3 of 14 
 
NEGLIGENCE – DUTY AND BREACH 
 
INTRODUCTION: 
 
The most common action in tort is negligence, where the Claimant aims 
to recover compensation for the damage caused to the Claimant if this 
damage was caused by negligence where a duty of care was owed to the 
Claimant. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Negligence is essentially caused by carelessness and covers all sorts of 
issues from road traffic accidents to product liability and medical 
treatment. 
 
Unlike in relation to contract law, privity to the contract is not required, 
so tort allows for third parties to a contract to make a claim. In fact, to 
make a tort claim, no contract is required at all. 
 
Elements of negligence: *You need all of these to establish a claim* 
1. 
Duty of care – the Defendant owed a duty of care to the 
Claimant. 
2. 
Breach of duty – the Defendant breached their duty of care. 
3. 
Causation – the Defendant's negligence was the cause of the 
Claimant's damage. 
4. 
Remoteness – the damage suffered is not too remote 
 AND 
5. 
Lack of defences 
 
DUTY OF CARE: 
 
Was the relationship between the Claimant and the Defendant such that 
the Defendant was obliged to take care for the Claimant's safety? 
 
Establishing duty of care: 
 
Was the relationship between the Claimant and the Defendant such that 
the Defendant was obliged to take care for the Claimant's safety? 
 
There are a number of established duties of care, where case law has 
already established that a duty is owed. 
 
Established duties: 
* 
Drivers of motor vehicles owe 
a duty of care to pedestrians 
and other road users 
* 
Doctors owe a duty to their 
patients 
* 
Employers owe a duty to their 
employees 
* 
Manufacturers owe a duty to 
their consumers 
* 
Teachers owe a duty of care to 
students 
* 
Solicitors owe a duty of care to 
their clients 
 
There is generally less likely for a duty 
of care to arise where psychiatric 
injuries have been caused by accidents. 
 
 
Novel duty situations: 
 
There are also situations where a duty of care has not previously been 
decided. In these cases, the court decide whether a duty of care is owed 
by using the incremental approach. 
 
The courts will only imply a duty of care if: Caparo v Dickman 
*Important* 
 
1. 
The Claimant is a foreseeable Claimant – the Defendant's 
conduct must have caused a foreseeable risk of harm. Use the 
objective test. 
 
2. 
There must be a relationship of proximity between the 
Defendant and the Claimant: the Claimant must be a person who 
is so closely and directly affected by my act that I ought 
reasonably to have them in contemplation as being so affected. 
This is called the ‘Neighbour principle'. – Donoghue v Stevenson 
 
3. 
It is fair, just and reasonable to impose a remedy – applied by 
courts to look at broader implications of awarding a remedy. 
 
 
 
The Claimant must be a foreseeable Claimant: 
 
Palsgraf v Long Island Railroad A duty can only exist if it was reasonably 
foreseeable that damage or injury would be caused to a particular 
person or a class of people. 
 
Langley v Dray Civilians failing to stop for police officers and engaging in 
a police chase will owe a duty of care not to commit acts which would 
reasonably create a risk or cause harm to the police officer chasing 
them. 
 
Proximity: 
 
Donoghue v Stevenson Use the Neighbour Principle to determine 
whether there has been proximity between the parties. There is a 
general duty that people must take reasonable care to avoid acts or 
omissions which can be reasonably foreseen to likely cause injury to 
their neighbour. 
 
Neighbour = someone closely and directly affected by the tortfeasor's 
acts/omissions. 
 
Caparo v Dickman Proximity simply refers to situations where the 
Defendant must have reasonably expected that their actions would 
cause damage to the Claimant. – This includes either physical, 
circumstantial or causal closeness. 
 
Fair, just and reasonable: 
 
Where the court refers to fairness in relation to their refusal to allow for 
a duty of care to arise, this is the care there is an underlying public policy 
consideration to protect. 
 
McFarlane v Tayside Health Board Claimants cannot bring a claim for 
the costs of bringing up a child where the reason for getting pregnant 
was the failure of a vasectomy or similar procedure. 
 
West Bromwich Albion v Medhat El-Safty Doctors are only responsible 
to their patients and when advising them on procedures, they have to 
advise the patient as to what is best for them, rather than what is best 
for their professional career. 
 
Mitchell v Glasgow City Council Public policy generally protects councils 
from liability for harm caused by third parties. The court does not 
impose a duty on landlords and social workers to warn affected tenants 
that they have scheduled a meeting with tenants who have shown 
antisocial behaviour. 
 
Robinson v West Yorkshire Police Public policy generally protects police 
officers from liability for harm caused to third parties. This is because 
there is public interest in arresting criminals. 
 
Liability for omissions: 
 
There is no general duty to act so there is no general liability for 
omissions. – no duty to save someone in danger. 
 
Exceptions: 
 
* 
If there is a special relationship between the parties – eg. 
parent-child relationship, doctor and patient. 
 
* 
If the Defendant has control over the victim – Dorset Yacht – eg. 
a police officer will have control over a suspect in custody. 
 
 
* 
If the harm/danger is caused by a third party who is within the 
Defendant's control – eg. a parent has control over their child so 
they may owe a duty of care not to allow their child to hurt other 
children. 
 
* 
If a person attempts to rescue someone, they will have a duty 
not to make the situation worse. – East Suffolk Rivers v Kent – 
this is the case even if the person does not complete the rescue. 
 
Scope: 
 
When looking at duty of care, ensure that the harm suffered is within 
the scope of the Defendant's duty of care because if not, then the 
Defendant cannot be held liable, even if there was negligence. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Example: 
Selling a faulty car which then bursts into flames. Even if no one is 
injured in the accident, the owner of the car and the passengers may 
be able to claim for psychiatric damage. 
 
Special relationships 
creating a duty of care

Teacher 
 
 
Student
