pages.heading: DUTY OF CARE – PUBLIC BODIES: · The police:
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Notes | Page 4 of 14 
 
DUTY OF CARE – PUBLIC BODIES: 
 
The police: 
 
Duty of care in relation to positive acts: 
 
Robinson If a police officer has been negligent and this negligence 
creates a positive risk of injury where there was a relationship of 
proximity, the police officer will be liable. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Duty of care in relation to omissions: 
 Michael v Chief Constable of South Wales Police The police will owe a 
duty of care to a person if they have assumed responsibility for that 
person's safety and security or if the police has created the danger 
themselves. 
 
R v Dytham If a police officer is on duty, they will be liable for omissions 
if they fail to protect members of the public. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Fire service: 
 
Hampshire If the fire service attends a fire, they will have a duty not to 
make the situation worse. – eg. by turning the sprinkler system off or 
spreading the fire. 
 
If the fire service creates a danger, it will have a duty to take positive 
steps to fight that danger, as much as reasonable. 
 
BREACH OF DUTY: 
 
What standard of care was the Defendant obliged to hold themselves to 
that they breached? 
 
Reasonable man test: 
 The standard of care expected of the Defendant is that of the ordinary 
reasonable person in the Defendant's position. – the Defendant will 
have breached their duty if the court finds that a reasonable person 
would not have fallen below the standard of care. 
 
The reasonable man is also known as the man on the Clapham omnibus. 
 
In assessing whether the care used was reasonable, consider: 
 The likelihood of harm arising and the seriousness of that potential 
harm. If there is a high chance of potential harm/serious harm in any 
given situation, greater caution should be exercised. 
 
When the court decides on reasonability, they will look at factors: 
a. 
The court will take into account all the circumstances of the case. 
b. 
The Defendant's position – eg. if they were part of a particular 
profession or had some form of expert knowledge, they will be 
held to a higher standard. 
c. 
Foreseeability of harm – if the harm is foreseeable, then more 
precaution must be taken to avoid the harm. 
d. 
Magnitude of risk – the greater the harm, the greater the 
precautions that will need to be taken. 
e. 
Cost and practicality in overcoming any risk – courts expect 
people to take only reasonable precautions in guarding against 
harm to other. 
f. 
Purpose and utility of the Defendant's activity – emergencies or 
if it is taken for the benefit of society. 
 
Professionals: *Special duties* 
 
Professionals will be held to a higher standard, the standard expected 
of a reasonable member of that profession. – eg. a doctor will be held 
to the standard of a reasonably competent doctor. 
 
Bolam Bolam test: Professionals will be judged by the standard of 
ordinary skilled man exercising and/or professing to have that special 
skill. – This is the case even if they do not in fact have the skill they say 
they have. 
 
Bolitho The court will not find a doctor not liable simply because other 
doctors testify that they agree with what that particular doctor did in 
that specific situation. 
 
Wells v Cooper The fact that the professional is inexperienced, 
incompetent or a junior member of the team do not lower the standard 
expected of them. If a person decides to carry out an activity they do not 
have the competence to do, this will be a sign of negligence. 
 
The Wells v Cooper standard applies to: 
 
* 
Junior doctors – a junior doctor will have to meet the standard 
of a reasonably competent doctor in their department. – 
Wilshire v Essex Area Health Authority 
 
* 
Learner drivers – learner drivers should meet the standard of a 
competent and experienced driver. – Nettleship v Weston 
 
Additional duties for doctors: Montgomery 
 
* 
Doctors must warn patients of material risks of treatment. 
 
* 
The professional must have taken reasonable care to explain any 
materials risks involved in any particular choice, and any 
reasonable alternatives. What is material in any given case will 
depend on the patient. 
 
* 
The doctors cannot argue that a failure to warn is based on a 
responsible body of professional opinion. 
 
Children: *Lower standard* 
 
Mullin v Richards Children are held to a lower standard, which will be 
the standard expected of an ordinary child of the same age. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Orchard v Lee High degree of carelessness is acceptable in relation to 
children and will generally not amount to negligence. 
 
Exception: 
 If a child carries out acts typically carried out by adults, they will be held 
to the standard of a reasonable adult. – eg. driving a car, smoking a 
cigarette. 
 
Illness: *No change in standards* 
 
Anyone who is ill while carrying out certain activities, will be held to the 
same standard as a healthy person. Someone who suffered a stroke 
while driving, causing an accident was held to the standard expected of 
a reasonably competent driver. 
 
BREACH OF DUTY – PROVE THE BREACH: 
 
Proving that there has been a breach of duty can sometimes be difficult. 
 
Common types of evidence used to prove that there has been a breach: 
1. 
Witness evidence 
2. 
The doctrine of “Res Ipsa Loquitur” 
 
Witness evidence: 
 
In order to prove the breach, it is important to find witnesses to give 
evidence. 
 
This should include either witnesses of fact to describe the events or 
expert witnesses to describe the correct procedures that should have 
been used. 
 
Res Ipsa loquitur: 
 
Res Ipsa loquitur = the thing speaks for itself. 
 
This doctrine is used in situations where there is no evidence, but the 
circumstances are such, that negligence is obvious. 
 
Elements: 
1. 
The Defendant must be shown to have been in control of the 
thing which caused the injury to the Claimant. 
2. 
Accident must be of such a nature that it would not have 
occurred in the ordinary course of events without negligence. 
 AND 
3. 
There is no explanation as to how the accident occurred. 
 
 
Example: 
A police officer on duty wearing a uniform should help an old lady 
being violently assaulted, even if the police officer is on break as 
they have a duty to protect members of the public. 
Example: 
Two police officers are chasing a suspected thief in a busy urban 
area with a lot of pedestrians around. During the chase, an officer 
attempts to tackle the suspect but does so recklessly, and he knocks 
over a pedestrian, causing them serious injury. In this case, the 
pedestrian might have a claim against the police for negligence. 
Example: 
A 6-year old is not found to be negligent for not understanding that 
certain situations can be dangerous such as walking across a busy 
road without looking both ways.

pages.heading: NEGLIGENCE – CAUSATION, REMOTENESS · AND DEFENCES
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Notes | Page 5 of 14 
 
NEGLIGENCE – CAUSATION, REMOTENESS 
AND DEFENCES 
 
CAUSATION: 
 
In addition to establishing a duty of care and a breach of duty, a Claimant 
must also establish causation and remoteness. 
 
Did the Defendant's breach of duty cause the harm the Claimant 
suffered? The Defendant will not be liable unless their negligence has 
caused the Claimant's injury/loss. 
 
Consider causation in two stages: 
1. 
Causation in fact 
 AND 
2. 
Causation in law 
 
STAGE 1 – Causation in fact: 
 
But for test: 
 Claimant must show that their loss was caused by the Defendant's 
negligence. – But for the Defendant's breach, the Claimant would not 
have suffered harm. 
 
If the harm would have occurred if the Defendant did not breach their 
duty, then the breach will not have caused the harm suffered and the 
Claimant cannot have a claim for negligence. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Successive injuries: 
 
Performance Cars v Abraham If there are successive injuries, the 
Claimant may recover from each Defendant for each injury caused by 
them. – eg. if one of the Defendant's caused a broken rib and the other 
one caused a broken leg right after. 
 
Concurrent causes: 
 
 Bonnington Castings v Wardlaw If the injury could have resulted from a 
number of different causes acting together, the Claimant need only 
show that the Defendant's breach materially contributed to the 
Claimant's harm. 
 
Divisible injuries: 
 If the injury is divisible and each Defendant's contribution is clear to the 
court, then each Defendant is liable for the proportion they caused. – eg. 
if one of them caused 30%, and the other 70%. 
 
Indivisible injuries: 
 If two or more Defendants breached a duty which leads to an injury 
which cannot be attributed to either one of the Defendants alone, the 
Claimant can recover full compensation from either Defendants. – eg. 
if the Claimant was hit by a bus and another car, thus suffering a broken 
leg, with no way to tell which one caused the injury, as it was likely 
caused by both collisions. 
 
If one of the Defendants can prove that they have paid more than their 
share of the fault, they will be able to seek contribution from the other 
Defendant. 
 
STAGE 2 – Causation in law: 
 
The Claimant must show that there was no new intervening act 
breaking the chain of causation. 
 
If there is a new, intervening act, this may break the chain of causation 
starting from the Defendant's breach to the Claimant's harm. Where this 
is the case, the Defendant will not be liable for the harm suffered by the 
Claimant. 
 
The new intervening act will break the chain if: 
* 
The intervening act was unforeseeable 
* 
A doctor's gross negligence when treating the Claimant will have 
been unforeseeable. – However, ordinary negligence will have 
been foreseeable. 
* 
The Claimant's own actions may break the chain of causation if 
they acted unreasonably. 
 
Proof of causation: 
 
This will be proof on the balance of probabilities that the Defendant's 
breach of duty caused the harm. 
 
REMOTENESS OF DAMAGE: 
 
Even if all the other elements are satisfied, the Defendant may escape 
liability if the damage was too remote a consequence of the breach of 
duty. 
 
Test for remoteness: 
 
Wagon Mound The damage must have been reasonably foreseeable by 
the Defendant. If the damage was not reasonably foreseeable, it will be 
deemed to be too remote. 
 
Armstead v Royal & Sun Alliance (2024) The burden of proof that one/ 
more of the losses are too remote to be recovered is on the Defendant. 
 
 
Exceptions: 
 
The Egg-shell skull rule: 
Defendants will be liable, as long as the 
type of harm and its manner was 
reasonably foreseeable, even if the extent 
of the harm was not foreseeable. – even if 
they intend a lesser harm, if the harm 
ends up being worse than expected, they 
will still be liable. 
 
Defendants will take the victim as they 
find them, even if the victim has any 
weaknesses or ailments. – if they hit the 
victim, and the victim has an underlying 
condition, killing them, they will be liable 
for their death, even if that was not 
intended. 
 
The Similar in type rule: 
If the Claimant suffers 
the type of harm which 
would be reasonably 
foreseeable, but the way 
in which it occurs is 
unforeseeable, it will not 
be too remote. 
 
 
 
DEFENCES: 
 
The Defendant will seek to establish a defence to the claim as having a 
valid defence may reduce/extinguish their liability to pay compensation. 
 
Contributory Negligence: *Most common defence* 
 
* 
The Claimant was in part responsible for the harm they suffered, 
due to their own negligence, which will result in a reduction of 
damages payable by the Defendant. 
 
* 
Contributory negligence is a partial defence. 
 
Voluntary assumption of risk (Volenti non fit injuria): 
 
Where the Claimant had full knowledge of the risk and they freely and 
voluntarily consented to it, the Defendant will not be held liable. 
 
It is not sufficient to show that the Claimant knew of the risk, the 
Claimant must actually consent to it. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
This is a complete defence. 
 
The court will rarely find that this defence applies in practice, high 
threshold. The court is more likely to find contributory negligence, 
where the Claimant failed to take reasonable care of their own safety. 
 
Exclusion of liability: 
 
If there is a contractual exclusion of liability for death or personal injury 
arising from negligence, this will not be enforced by the court and 
negligence claim is still valid. 
 
Other exclusions of liability for negligence will be enforced only if they 
are reasonable. 
 
 
 
 
 
Example 1: 
In the medical context, patients must be made aware of material 
risks involved prior to undergoing any medical procedures. 
Example 2: 
Where Claimant breaks his leg in a rugby match, the Claimant will 
have voluntarily assumed a risk in the ordinary course of the game. 
Example: 
 
Beryl goes to the A&E, complaining of a headache. The doctor on 
duty examines her and finds that the headache is likely caused by 
lack of sleep. Beryl is sent home, where she dies of a brain 
haemorrhage a few hours later. 
 
Even if there is a finding that the doctor was negligent when 
examining Beryl, if Beryl would have died even after a proper 
examination, then the doctor will not have caused her death and 
Beryl's estate will not have a claim against the doctor.

pages.heading: Criminal activity: · If a Defendant negligently injures a Claimant whilst that Claimant was
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Notes | Page 6 of 14 
 
Criminal activity: 
 
If a Defendant negligently injures a Claimant whilst that Claimant was 
undertaking criminal activity, this will serve as a complete defence. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Example: 
 
The Claimant and the Defendant were stealing a car together and due 
to the Defendant's negligent driving, the Claimant is injured in an 
accident. 
 
The fact that the injury happened whilst carrying out a crime will 
absolve the Defendant of liability for the tort and the Claimant will 
not be able to make a claim.

pages.heading: VICARIOUS LIABILITY · Vicarious liability = the Employer is liable for the torts committed by
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Notes | Page 7 of 14 
 
VICARIOUS LIABILITY 
 
Vicarious liability = the Employer is liable for the torts committed by 
employee, even if employer has not been guilty of any personal 
negligence. 
 
Where vicarious liability is owed, the Claimant may make a claim against 
both the tortfeasor (the person who committed the tort) and their 
Employer. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
REQUIREMENTS: 
 
Requirements for vicarious liability to apply: 
1. 
The tortfeasor must be an employee 
2. 
Act must have been closely connected to the task the employee 
was employed to carry out. 
 AND 
3. 
The tort must have been committed in the course of 
employment. 
 
The duty may arise for an employee's tort committed against 
customers, other employees and any third parties even if they had no 
connection to the employer's business. 
 
Who is an employee? 
 
Employee = a person who undertakes to do work for another under a 
contract of service. 
 
Independent contractor = a person who undertakes to do work for 
another under a contract for services. 
 
The employer will not generally be liable for any torts committed by their 
independent contractors. – However, if the breach of duty was in 
relation to a duty owed by the employer which was simply delegated to 
the independent contractor, then the employer remains liable. 
 
Tests to establish whether the Defendant was an employee: 
 
– 
Control Test: 
Court considers the degree of control exercised by the employer 
over the work. 
 
More likely to be an employee if: 
The Employer has control over how, where and when work is 
carried out. 
 
– 
Integration test: 
The test considers whether the tortfeasor was an integral part of 
the employer's business, or someone who is merely ancillary to 
it. 
 
– 
Mutuality of obligations test: 
Is there an obligation to provide work and to perform work? – 
eg. must accept work when offered. 
 
More likely to be an employee if: 
Tortfeasor has not worked elsewhere and/or has been provided 
with work continuously for years. 
 
– 
No particular factor is decisive and all circumstances are 
considered, including control, integration as well as whether 
wages, taxes and national insurance are paid through the 
employer. 
 
Employees agrees to provide their work and skill to the employer in 
return for remuneration. 
 
Employees agrees, expressly or impliedly, to be directed as to the mode 
of performance to such a degree as to make the other their employer. 
 
Other terms of the contract are consistent with there being a contract of 
employment. 
 
Borrowed employees: 
Proper test is whether the hirer did or did not have the authority to 
control the manner in which the act involving negligence was performed. 
 
Relationships akin to employment: 
Where the Defendant and the tortfeasor are not bound by a contract of 
employment, but their relationship has the same features, the 
relationship can properly give rise to vicarious liability for reasons that it 
is akin to between an employer and employee. 
 
 
Closely connected: 
 
Close Connection test: 
There must have been a sufficiently close and direct connection between 
what the employee was employed to do, and the tort was committed by 
the employee. 
 
Torts committed in the course of employment: 
 
Negligent and careless act: 
Employer will be liable where the employee commits a tortious act but 
was still acting within the authority given to him by the employer. 
 
Diversions and detours: 
Employees who make a detour from an authorised route will be 
considered as acting within in the course of their employment, as long 
as they are still engaged in the business of their employer. 
− 
However, a new and independent journey which is solely undertaken for 
the selfish purposes of the employee should not give rise to vicarious 
liability. 
 
Disobedience: 
− 
If the employee disobeyed the employer's instructions, that means that 
the act they committed was outside of the course of employment and the 
employer will not be liable. 
 
Disobedience does not take the matter outside the scope of employment, 
if they simply carried out what was asked of them in a different manner. 
– eg. if a driver also took passengers on their journey of delivering mail, 
when they were not supposed to. 
 
The act of an employee will fall outside of ordinary course of employment 
if they have acted on a frolic of their own. – they must have done 
something majorly different from what was expected of them. – eg. 
deviating from the usual route in a major way. 
 
OTHER SITUATIONS: 
 
Criminal acts: 
− 
 
In some cases, tortious liability will also attach to criminal acts, and a 
Claimant might have a claim in tort. If that is the case, the employer 
might be liable for the criminal acts of their employees well. 
 
Agency: 
− 
 
When one party is under a duty to act for or give advice for the benefit 
of another on matters within the scope of their relationship, a fiduciary 
relationship is created. This will give rise to vicarious liability. 
 
Partnership: 
 
Partnership Act 1980 A partnership and each partner is vicariously liable 
for the wrongful acts or omissions of another partner, as long as the 
partner was acting within his authority, or whilst in the ordinary course 
of the firm's business. 
 
 
Example: 
If you are injured due to the negligence of a driver, then you can sue 
both the driver and their employer if they were employed and hit you 
during work hours.

pages.heading: EMPLOYERS' LIABILITY · Employers owe a duty of care to their employees.
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Notes | Page 8 of 14 
 
EMPLOYERS' LIABILITY 
 
Employers owe a duty of care to their employees. 
 
Employer's duty of care covers – the provision of: 
* 
Safe equipment 
* 
A safe place of work 
* 
A safe system of work 
 AND 
* 
Competent fellow staff members (the employer must take 
reasonable care to ensure competency, by providing training, 
disciplining staff, hiring competent employees/contractors) 
 
The employer's duty is non-delegable. Employers cannot outsource 
their obligations and must take reasonable care themselves and ensure 
that all staff that they delegate to also exercises reasonable care. If the 
employees breach their duty, the employer will be liable. 
 
The duty of the employer is to take reasonable care, not to ensure 
absolute safety. 
 
Adequate plant and equipment – an employer must ensure that: 
* 
Machinery/equipment are safe, and safety features/protective 
clothing are provided 
* 
Machinery/equipment are properly maintained 
* 
Premises are safe and free from defects – eg. floor should not be 
slippery. 
 
This duty extends to other premises to which employees are sent but 
only to the extent that employer is aware of a specific danger at the 
other premises. 
 
Employer's Liability (Defective Equipment Act) 1969 If an employee is 
injured by equipment with a latent defect due to the negligence of a 
third party, the employer will also be deemed negligent. – eg. 
manufacturer. 
 
Competent fellow workers: 
 Employers must hire staff members who are competent by carrying out 
checks into their background and level of experience and education. If 
necessary, the employer must provide adequate training. 
 
Staff members must be sufficiently competent so as not to put other 
employees at risk. – eg. cleaners should be competent in cleaning and 
should check for and clean spillages throughout the workday. 
 
Defence: 
 If the employee voluntarily assumes risk – high standard and the court 
will rarely agree to this defence.

pages.heading: OCCUPIERS' LIABILITY · DEFINITION:
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Notes | Page 9 of 14 
 
OCCUPIERS' LIABILITY 
 
DEFINITION: 
 
Occupiers may be held liable if someone suffers injury or damage is 
caused to items due to the state of their premises. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Occupier: 
 
Occupier = someone who has control of the premises. They will be the 
Defendant in these claims. 
 
Occupier need not have physical possession of the property and need 
not be the owner of the property. 
 
The occupier is the person who has sufficient legal control of the 
property to allow people to access the property or prevent them from 
entering. 
 
There may be multiple occupiers in relation one land, and if that is the 
case, all of them could be liable in respect of the damage. 
 
The occupier will be the Local Authority for the following: 
* 
Public parks 
* 
Highways 
* 
Schools 
 
Who has control? 
 
The level of control exercised will be a question of fact. 
 
Mathewson v Crump (2020) The legal owner may not be the occupier 
if they do not have sufficient control over the premises. – only visiting 
for inspection of the premises if there is a tenant means that there is 
insufficient control. 
 
Premises: 
 
Premises = include the buildings on the land and the land itself and 
includes vehicles and fixtures as well. 
 
Visitors: 
 
Visitor = someone who invited onto or given permission to be on the 
premises. 
 
If a visitor enters the premises for their own calling, they will be 
expected to appreciate and guard against any special risks. – eg. 
electricians. 
 
RISK CREATED BY THIRD PARTIES: 
 
The risk may have been created by a third party, rather than the 
occupier. 
 
Risk created by an independent contractor: 
 
If there is an independent contractor who works on the premises and 
a visitor is injured because of the independent contractor, the occupier 
will have met their duty if they took reasonable care in entrusting the 
work of the contractor and could reasonably conclude that the 
contractor was competent. 
 
Risk created by a stranger: 
 
Wheat v E Lacon If the risk has been created by a stranger, the occupier 
will not be responsible for the injuries/losses caused. 
 
DUTY OWED TO LAWFUL VISITORS: 
 
Occupiers' Liability Act 1957 Duty owed by the occupier to lawful 
visitors. The occupier must take reasonable care to ensure that visitors 
can safely use the premises. 
 
If there has been a breach of occupiers' duties, the rules on causation 
will apply. 
 
Duty owed to children: 
 
The occupier must take into account when looking after the premises 
that children visiting will be less careful than adults. 
 
The occupier should not have areas where children would easily injure 
themselves near a playground or an area where children's shows are 
commonly performed. – eg. sharp, hard edges near a playground. 
 
The occupier should not keep fixtures or chattels on the land which are 
dangerous but would attract children. Identify whether it was 
foreseeable that the fixture or chattel would attract children. – eg. an 
old boat with a rotting floor, old tree house. 
 
Duty owed to skilled visitors: 
 
Professional, or skilled visitors are expected to anticipate certain 
special risks and avoid accidents. 
 
Defences: 
 
Contributory negligence: 
 Visitors ought to be responsible for their own safety, allows for the 
defence of contributory negligence. 
 
Warning notices: 
 Occupiers may be able to exclude liability by placing warning notices 
on the premises. 
 
s.2(4)(a) OLA 1957 Warning does not automatically absolve an 
occupier from liability. It must enable the visitor to be reasonably safe 
in order to discharge the occupier's duty of care. 
 
Note the difference between a warning notice and a notice seeking to 
exclude or limit liability – former seeks to discharge an occupier's duty 
while the latter seeks to prevent it from arising in the first place. 
 
DUTY OWED TO TRESPASSERS: 
 
Occupiers' Liability Act 1984 Duty owed by the occupier to persons who 
are not visitors. 
 
Non-visitors = anyone who is not invited/permitted to be on the 
premises by the occupier. This includes trespassers, although the duty 
owed to trespassers is limited. 
 
 
Requirements for this duty to arise in relation to trespassers: 
* 
The occupier must be aware of the danger and aware that a 
trespasser might encounter it. 
* 
The occupier must take reasonable care to ensure that the 
trespasser does not suffer personal injury. Risk of injury must be 
due to the state of the premises rather than as a result of an 
activity on them. 
 
Defences: 
 
Contributory negligence: 
 Trespasser ought to be responsible for their own safety, allows for the 
defence of contributory negligence. 
 
Warning notices: 
 Occupiers may be able to exclude liability by placing warning notices 
on the premises. 
 
s.1(5) OLA 1984 A warning notice will discharge the occupiers' duty if 
the occupier took reasonable steps to warn trespassers of the danger 
on the premises or discourage them to take the risk. 
 
Note the difference between a warning notice and a notice seeking to 
exclude or limit liability – former seeks to discharge an occupier's duty 
while the latter seeks to prevent it from arising in the first place. 
 
ADDITIONAL DUTIES – LANDLORDS: 
 
Defective Premises Act 1972 A landlord is obliged/permitted to carry 
out repairs to the premises and so has a duty of care in respect of the 
state of the premises. – this duty of care is to take such care as 
reasonable in the circumstances to see that they are reasonably safe 
from personal injury/damage to their property. 
 
This duty covers defects: 
1. 
Within the scope of the landlord's repair obligations/rights 
 AND 
2. 
Which the landlord knew/ought to have known about. 
 
This duty is owed to anyone who might reasonably be expected to be 
affected by this defect. 
 
 
 
Example: 
Anne visited Lina's house one afternoon for tea. Lina has spilled 
some tea onto the floor earlier and Anne slipped and fell, breaking 
her arm. Anne may make a claim for Occupiers' Liability and Lina will 
likely have to compensate her for her injuries.

pages.heading: PRODUCT LIABILITY · If a person is injured by a faulty product, they can:
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Notes | Page 10 of 14 
 
PRODUCT LIABILITY 
 
If a person is injured by a faulty product, they can: 
* 
Bring a claim under the Sale of Goods Act 1979 
* 
Claim for negligence 
 OR 
* 
Make a claim under the Consumer Protection Act 1987 
 
The contract law claim requires privity of contract which might be a 
problem in many cases. 
 
The tort claim is fault-based, so fault of the Defendant must be proven. 
 
COMMON LAW NEGLIGENCE: 
 
Product liability = a manufacturer's legal responsibility for injury or 
damage caused by a product that they have made or sold. 
 
This type of liability applies when a product is defective or dangerous, 
and it causes harm to a consumer. 
 
Manufacturers are liable in respect of injuries sustained because of 
defective products. – The retailer of the product is not liable. 
 
Requirements: 
* 
Breach of duty: 
– 
The standard in negligence applies. The manufacturer 
must have fallen below the standard of care expected of 
them. 
– 
A manufacturer must take reasonable care to the 
consumer who uses the manufacturer's product if the 
manufacturer doesn't expect the product to be 
examined after leaving the manufacturer and before 
reaching the customer (which is common for 
manufactured goods). 
– 
The Claimant must show that there has been a 
manufacturing or design defect. 
 
* 
Causation: 
Damage must have been caused by the faulty product. 
 
To whom the duty is owed? 
– 
The duty is owed to anyone whom the manufacturer could 
reasonably foresee as likely to be affected by a defect in the 
product. 
– 
This includes people who might come into contact with the 
product. – eg. members of the consumer's family. 
 
What is covered? 
– 
Damages for personal injury 
– 
Damage to property 
– 
Consequential economic losses 
 
CONSUMER PROTECTION ACT 1987: 
 
As it is difficult to prove fault on behalf of the manufacturer, the 
Consumer Protection Act introduces strict liability in relation to 
defective products and the Claimant will not need to show that the 
Defendant was at fault. 
 
However, do not confuse strict liability with absolute liability. The 
Claimant need not prove fault, but simply that there has been a defect 
in the product. 
 
Consumer Protection Act 1987 Establishes that liability is imposed in 
respect only of damage caused by a defect in a product. A product is 
defective if its safety does not reach the level a reasonable person is 
entitled to expect. 
 
Defective = being below the standard of safety which one is generally 
entitled to expect. 
 
Persons liable: 
* 
Manufacturers – includes manufacturers of final products or 
components 
* 
Abstractors 
* 
Persons who are neither manufacturers or abstractors but 
who give agricultural products an essential characterisation by 
means of industrial process es – such as frozen peas. 
* 
EU Importers − Where the producer is in the EU, the liability for 
the product lies on the manufacturer. However where the 
manufacturer A is from Japan and it is imported into Germany 
by B and then reimported into UK by C, A and B will be strictly 
liable under the Act. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The supplier of the product is only liable if: 
* 
The Claimant requests the name of one of the above parties 
from the supplier. 
* 
It is not reasonably practicable for the Claimant to identify 
those persons independently. 
 AND 
* 
The supplier does not identify the manufacturer/importer. 
 
Time limits: 
Must be brought within 3 years from the date on which the action 
accrued, or the date of knowledge – this is subject to a 10-year 
overriding limit. 
 
For non-personal injury or death claims: action must be brought within 
10 years from the relevant time. 
 
Defence: 
* 
The damage did not exist when the product was supplied 
* 
The Defendant was not acting in the course of business when 
they supplied the product 
* 
The State-of-the-art defence: could not have supplied a better 
product because the knowledge/scientific advancements at the 
time did not allow for the creation of a better product. 
* 
Contributory negligence 
 
Liability cannot be excluded/limited under the CPA 1987. 
 
Remedies: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Damages are recoverable for: 
* Personal injury and death 
* Damage to private property 
(if it is more than £275) 
 
 
Recovery is NOT allowed for: 
* Damage to the defective 
product itself 
* Damage to business 
property 
* Damage to private 
property below £275.

pages.heading: NUISANCE AND THE RULE IN RYLANDS V FLETCHER · PUBLIC NUISANCE:
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Notes | Page 11 of 14 
 
NUISANCE AND THE RULE IN RYLANDS V FLETCHER 
 
PUBLIC NUISANCE: 
 
Public nuisance = nuisance that disturbs the comfort and convenience 
of life for a section of the public. 
 
Public nuisance is not limited to the protection of interest in land. 
 
Elements of public nuisance: 
* That the persons affected by the nuisance constitutes a public or 
a section of the public. 
 AND 
* If an individual claimant is making a claim, they can only do so if 
they have suffered special and particular damage, over and 
above the inconvenience suffered by the public at large. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
PRIVATE NUISANCE: 
 
Private nuisance = violation of real property rights involving either an 
interference with proprietary rights of the occupier, including a legal 
interest such as an easement, or unreasonable interference with the 
occupier's right to use and enjoy it, which is an inherent facet of a right 
of exclusive possession. 
 
Requirements: 
 
Elements of private nuisance: 
* Violation of proprietary rights/the occupier's right to use and 
enjoy the land 
* The interference must be unreasonable 
 AND 
* The interference must be continuing – cannot simply be one 
isolated event. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
While damage may be sufficient, it is not an essential requirement to 
assert a claim in nuisance through interference with the amenity of the 
occupier's land. 
 
Damage must be a foreseeable result of the Defendant's actions. – 
damage cannot be too remote. 
 
Nuisance may be caused by inaction or omission as well as some positive 
activity – this must lead to an unreasonable interference, which goes 
beyond the normal. – such as depriving neighbours of sleep. 
 
Factors to look at when determining unreasonability: 
a. 
Intensity and duration of interference – the shorter the duration 
of the act, the less likely that the use will be found to be 
unreasonable. 
b. 
Sensitivity – No nuisance where damage was result of unusual 
sensitivity. 
c. 
Location – including the character of the neighbourhood. 
d. 
Utility of the Defendant's conduct – where cricket balls entered 
the Claimant's garden several times a year, the court held that 
the social utility of the cricket club outweighed the Claimant's 
inconvenience. 
e. 
Malice 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Liability: 
 
Creator of the 
nuisance: 
The creator of the 
nuisance needs 
neither own nor 
occupy the land 
from where the 
nuisance originates. 
 
Occupier of the land: 
The occupiers must 
have had the 
knowledge of the 
existence of a drain 
laid by a trespasser, 
without the consent 
of the occupier, which 
caused the risk of 
flooding into the 
neighbours' land – the 
occupier was 
therefore liable for 
nuisance as he had 
continued and 
adopted the nuisance. 
 
Owners of the land: 
Council which 
granted permission 
to a go-kart club to 
use their land for 
the purpose of 
using go-karts were 
held liable in 
nuisance for noise 
caused to the 
claimant who lived 
close to the go-kart 
track. 
 
 
Defences: 
 
Prescription: 
A person can be exempt from liability for a nuisance if the conduct that 
caused the nuisance has been ongoing for a sufficient length of time 
and the person who is complaining about the nuisance has known 
about it and failed to take action. 
 
Defence of prescription can be raised if nuisance remains actionable but 
is never claimed for at least 20 years. 
 
Statutory authority: 
Where parliament authorised an activity which creates the nuisance, it 
is not actionable as long as all due care and skill has been taken to avoid 
it. 
 
Lawful use of land 
 
Non-defences: 
* That planning permission was granted for the use 
* That nuisance was in existence before the Claimant moved in. 
 
Remedies: 
 
Damages may be awarded to compensate the victim of the nuisance and 
for the damage caused. 
 
The Claimant may force the Defendant to stop the activity by applying 
for an injunction. – however, please note that it is in the court's 
discretion whether to grant this remedy. 
 
RYLANDS V FLETCHER: 
 
Rylands v Fletcher The rule in Rylands v Fletcher: The rule imposes strict 
liability on a person who brings onto their land something that is likely 
to do harm if it escapes. – viruses or hazardous chemicals. 
 
Requirements: 
 
Rylands v Fletcher Requirements: 
1. 
The Defendant used the land in a non-natural way for their own 
purposes. 
2. 
As part of this non-natural use, the Defendant brings something 
onto the land, which, if it escapes, is it likely to do damage. 
3. 
The hazardous thing escaped, and the victim suffered a damage 
as a result. 
4. 
This does not need to be a continuing state of affairs. – an 
isolated escape is sufficient. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Strict liability – Claimant only needed to show that the damage was 
caused by the Defendant, no need to prove negligence. 
 
Defences: 
 
* 
The escape was caused by an unforeseeable act of a stranger. 
* 
The escape was caused by an unforeseeable natural 
circumstance. – eg. an earthquake. 
* 
The Claimant's contributory negligence 
* 
Statutory authority. 
 
 
 
Examples of private nuisance: 
* 
Encroachment on a neighbour's land such as overhanging tree 
branches. 
* 
Damage to a neighbour land. 
* 
Nuisance by interference with a neighbour's quiet enjoyment 
of their land. 
Examples of public nuisance: 
* Creating danger on/obstructing the highway 
* Carrying on an offensive trade 
* Selling food unfit for consumption 
Examples: 
If, due to the operation of a factory, hazardous chemicals escape and 
contaminate the groundwater or nearby rivers, the person who 
operates the factory may be liable under the rule in Rylands v 
Fletcher.

pages.heading: BREACH OF STATUTORY DUTY · INTRODUCTION:
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Notes | Page 12 of 14 
 
BREACH OF STATUTORY DUTY 
 
INTRODUCTION: 
 
These statutes may or may not prescribe whether non-performance of 
the duties set out in the statute will amount to tortious or other liability. 
 
If any statute imposes a duty in the circumstances where the Claimant 
was injured, the breach of that duty can be used to prove liability 
instead of the duty owed under negligence. 
 
Your Claimant client will attempt to establish a tortious liability in order 
to allow them to bring a claim for compensation. 
 
ESTABLISH A TORT CLAIM FOR BREACH OF 
STATUTORY DUTY: 
 
The general rule: 
 
X v Bedfordshire County Council By simply having breached a statutory 
duty, the Defendant is not automatically liable in tort. 
 
When is it possible to bring a tort claim? 
 
Two routes to bring an action for breach of statutory duty in tort: 
 
1. 
If there is express wording in the act to say that the Claimant 
could bring a claim. 
2. 
Parliament has shown an intention that the Claimant should be 
able bring a claim. – X v Bedfordshire County Council 
 
Identify this intention by considering the following factors: 
1. 
Who was meant to benefit from the statute 
2. 
Whether there are alternative remedies available for the breach 
3. 
The level of detail in the statute itself 
4. 
The background to the legislation 
 AND 
5. 
The type of harm involved 
 
Who was meant to benefit from the statute: 
 
The court will consider whether the statute was meant to confer a 
benefit to the general public or individuals. A claim for statutory duty 
can only be brought if the statute aimed to confer a benefit to 
individuals or a class of individuals. 
 
The Claimant must show that they fall within the class of persons 
intended to be protected by the statute. – eg. for an act that was passed 
for the protection of doctors, the Claimant must be a doctor. 
 
Whether there are alternative remedies available for the breach: 
 
If there is an alternative remedy provided in the act, the court will 
generally understand that Parliament will have meant for this remedy to 
be the only possible remedy. 
 
Todd v Adams Where the statute allows for criminal liability, giving rise 
to fines, it is unlikely that the statute will have also intended for a 
separate civil claim to be brought in addition to the fine. 
 
In some cases, even if the act does not set out an alternative remedy, if 
the Claimant were to have an alternative remedy due to the nature of 
their situation, the court is unlikely to allow for a tort claim. – eg. the 
Claimant may have a judicial review claim or may use the Defendant's 
complaints or appeals procedure. 
 
Groves v Winbourne If the alternative remedy is the payment of a fine 
which is inadequate compared to the harm caused, the court may 
decide that a claim could be made in tort. 
 
The level of detail in the statute itself: 
 
The more detailed the statutory provisions, the more likely that the 
courts will imply a liability in tort. 
 
The background to the legislation: 
 
When the courts are attempting to work out Parliament's intention, they 
will look at the background of the legislation to find clues. 
 
The type of harm involved: 
 
Where the type of harm is inconsistent with the type of harm typically 
recovered in tort law, the court is also unlikely to allow for a claim in 
tort. – eg. loss of liberty is not something that tort law would allow 
Claimants to claim for. 
 
 
 
 
 
ELEMENTS OF THE TORT: 
 
After the court decides that a particular statutory provision has been 
breached, allowing for a cause of action in tort, the court must decide 
whether there has been a breach, and whether the damage suffered by 
the Claimant falls within the damage envisioned by the statute. 
 
Breach of duty: 
 The court will read the wording of the act to identify what the duty set 
out in the statute was and whether it has been breached. 
 
Damage: 
 Gorris v Scott The damage suffered by the Claimant must also be the 
type which the statute was passed to prevent. 
 
Defences: 
 Voluntary assumption of risk and contributory negligence both apply as 
defences.

pages.heading: REMEDIES · INTRODUCTION:
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Notes | Page 13 of 14 
 
REMEDIES 
 
INTRODUCTION: 
 
The key remedy for tortious liability is compensation for the loss and 
damage caused as a result of the tort. 
 
The Claimant may seek compensation for the following types of losses: 
1. 
Loss caused to a person (loss in terms of loss of value to property 
or financial loss) 
2. 
Personal injury 
3. 
Reputational damage (if quantifiable). 
 
PURE ECONOMIC LOSS: 
 
Pure economic loss = financial loss suffered by a person/company which 
is not accompanied by any physical damage to their person or property. 
 
Compensation for pure economic loss includes: 
 
* 
Compensation for financial losses made as a result of a bad 
financial decision (however, this may be recoverable if this is 
due to negligent misstatement). 
 
* 
Compensation for financial loss which does not directly flow 
from damage to the Claimant or their property. 
 
* 
Compensation for loss of profits if there is no physical damage 
to property. – eg. damage to a computer system. 
 
* 
Compensation for damage to property which does not belong to 
the Claimant. 
 
* 
Lost opportunity 
 
* 
In relation to product liability claims: compensation for damage 
to the defective product itself. – Murphy v Brentwood District 
Council 
 
 
However, consequential economic loss may be recovered along with 
damages for physical injury/damage to property. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Pure economic loss may be caused by: 
* 
A negligent act – eg. by accidentally cutting through the 
electricity supply to a factory, thus shutting the entire factory 
down. 
 OR 
* 
A negligent misstatement – eg. by giving negligent financial 
advice to the Claimant where the Claimant loses out as a result 
of the negligent advice. 
 
General rule: 
 
No duty is care is owed in relation to pure economic losses, so no 
negligence claim may be lodged in relation to these types of losses. 
 
Exception: 
 
Hedley Byrne v Heller Pure economic loss may be recoverable if caused 
by negligent misstatements and if there has been a special relationship 
between the Defendant and the Claimant. 
 
Elements of negligent misstatement: 
1. 
The Defendant knew that the Claimant was likely to rely on the 
Defendant's advice without independent enquiry. 
 AND 
2. 
The advice is required for a purpose which is made known to the 
Defendant. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
PSYCHIATRIC HARM: 
 
In a negligence action, the Claimant may recover compensation for 
personal injury which includes the physical impact of the injury and its 
mental consequences. – eg. anxiety, distress, any other psychiatric harm. 
 
General rule: damages are not payable for psychiatric harm where there 
has been no physical impact. However, there are some exceptions. 
 
There are two different types of victims in relation to psychiatric harm. 
 
In either case, damages will only be recoverable if the psychiatric harm 
is a medically recognised psychiatric condition. – eg. post-traumatic 
stress syndrome. 
 
If a Claimant suffers psychiatric harm together with a physical injury, the 
psychiatric harm will be labelled as consequential psychiatric harm and 
the ordinary rules of recovery will apply. 
 
Primary victims: 
 
Primary victim = a victim in the actual event who experiences risk of 
physical injury. 
 
A primary victim may recover remedies: 
 
* 
If they have suffered a physical injury themselves in addition to 
their psychiatric injury. In this case, they can recover their losses 
for both physical and psychiatric injuries. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
* 
If there was a foreseeable risk of physical injury to them, but the 
primary victim was ultimately not harmed, then they may 
recover their losses for their psychiatric injuries only. 
 
Dulieu v White Psychiatric injury may only be claimed in this case 
if it was caused by the Claimant's reasonable fear for their own 
safety. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The Egg shell skull rule also applies to these Claimants. 
 
Note that where a passer-by joins in as a rescuer they will be considered 
a primary victim. 
 
Secondary victims: 
 
Secondary victim = a victim who is not in the actual area of danger, but 
suffers harm nevertheless. 
 
A secondary victim is only owed a duty of care if a number of conditions 
are satisfied: Alcock 
1. 
Must have been present at the scene or its immediate 
aftermath. 
2. 
Must be foreseeable to the Claimant that a person of 'ordinary 
phlegm' might suffer psychiatric injury by shock (the closer the 
ties are the more likely). 
3. 
Sudden shock must have been suffered in immediate aftermath. 
 AND 
4. 
There must have been a proximity of relationship between the 
Claimant and those endangered – requires close ties of love and 
affection 
 
Proximity in time and space is required. – Seeing the event on television 
or reading it on newspaper is not sufficient, unless you are able to spot 
the loved one on the television. 
 
No recovery for police officers either as rescuers or employees. Rescuers 
must be exposed to some danger. 
Example: 
If the Claimant asks their accountant for a report, and the accountant 
negligently makes an error on the report, if the Claimant then relies 
on the report and loses out, they will be able to make a claim. 
Example: 
A restaurant suffers a short circuit due to the work of a negligent 
electrician. As a result, the fridge is now damaged and all the food 
spoils in the fridge. 
 
The following losses arise: 
1. 
The fridge is damaged – This is damage to property and 
recoverable. 
2. 
The food in the fridge is spoilt. – damage to property and 
recoverable. 
3. 
The restaurant will not be able to operate or even purchase 
a new fridge until the short circuit is ongoing and will. Lose 
out on profits – this is consequential economic loss and also 
recoverable. 
4. 
The restaurant will have suffered a loss of reputation – this 
could be quantified and may be recoverable. 
5. 
As a result of the loss of reputation, the restaurant has less 
customers and the restaurant estimate that they will have 
lost out on £300,000 worth of profits per annum. – this is 
pure economic loss and not recoverable. 
Example: 
Harold was involved in a car accident. He ends up with a head 
injury due to another road user's negligent driving. He now 
suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder as a result of the 
incident. He may recover his losses for his head injury and 
PTSD. 
Example: 
Harold was involved in a car accident. He believed he was 
about to die or be severely injured, however, he only suffers 
a minor scrape to his knee. He now suffers from posttraumatic stress disorder as a result of the incident. He may 
recover his losses for his PTSD, despite not suffering any 
substantial physical injuries.

pages.heading: DAMAGES FOR PERSONAL INJURY: · If the tortfeasor causes personal injury or death, different rules apply
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Notes | Page 14 of 14 
 
DAMAGES FOR PERSONAL INJURY: 
 
If the tortfeasor causes personal injury or death, different rules apply 
in relation to the remedies that can be recovered. 
 
Two different scenarios to consider in relation to personal injury: 
* 
If the victim is alive 
* 
If the victim dies 
 
The damages granted in tort will aim to put the injured party in the 
position they would have been in had the tort never occurred. – 
financially speaking. 
 
Tort victims must ensure that they mitigate their losses to limit the 
damages they suffer. 
 
Types of damages 
 
 
If there is a living Claimant: 
 
Damages can be claimed for the Claimant's pain, suffering and loss of 
amenity caused by the accident. 
 
Loss of amenity = the effect of the injury on the Claimant's enjoyment 
of life. 
 
Damages can also be awarded for financial loss caused by the injury 
itself. – eg. not being able to work will allow a Claimant to claim for loss 
of earnings in addition to medical treatments. 
 
Recoverable pecuniary (financial) losses: 
* 
Loss of past income – between the injury and trial/settlement 
based on the net wages lost. 
 
* 
Loss of future income – if the Claimant will lose out on earnings 
in the future due to the injuries: 
– 
Measure this as the difference in income before and 
after the injury multiplied by the number of years the 
income will be lost. 
– 
Add contingencies of life – eg. any possibilities that the 
Claimant would have lost their job. 
– 
This will be awarded as a lump sum reflecting the present 
value of the amount awarded 
– 
If the injury have likely shortened the Claimant's life 
expectancy, loss of future income will be reduced to 
reflect this. 
 
* 
Cost of medical treatment – both past and future. Do not count 
treatment provided by the NHS. 
 
* 
Recoverable nonpecuniary losses – including past and future 
pain and suffering and loss of amenity. – a person in coma will 
not recover for this while they were in coma. 
 
* 
Damage to property – measure this by the replacement costs. 
 
If the Claimant dies from the injuries caused by the tort before the 
damages are paid out, their claim for damages will be paid out to the 
Claimant's estate. 
 
If the victim dies: 
 
Where the victim dies as a result of their injuries caused by the tort, the 
Claimants have a separate cause of action for bereavement. 
 
Funeral expenses will also be recoverable. 
 
Requirements for a bereavement claim: 
* 
The Claimant must show, that had the victim survived, they 
would have been able to bring a successful claim. 
* 
The Claimant must have been financially dependent on the 
victim. 
* 
The Claimant must fall within the statutory list of eligible 
relationships. 
 
Statutory list includes only: 
– 
The deceased's spouse/civil partner 
– 
The deceased's cohabitant of more than 2 years 
 OR 
– 
The deceased's parents if the deceased was under 18 and never 
married. 
 
The deceased's children are not entitled to bereavement payments. 
 
Bereavement Claimants can only recover a fixed statutory sum which 
is £15,120.

pages.heading: INTRODUCTION TO TORT · WHAT IS A TORT?
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Prep notes | Page 1 of 27 
 
INTRODUCTION TO TORT 
 
WHAT IS A TORT? 
 
Tort law covers a wide range of circumstances, including road traffic 
accidents, a patient suffering injury due to medical negligence, wrongful 
defamation, or a visitor claiming damages if they suffered an accident on 
someone's land. 
 
Tort = a breach of one/more of the general duties set by civil law. 
 Tortfeasor = the person committing the tort. 
 Victim = the person suffering an injury/damage as a result of the tort. 
 
When a tort occurs, the law permits the affected party to seek 
compensation or damages from the responsible party. Depending on 
the case, additional remedies may also be available. 
 
THE CLASSIFICATION OF TORT LAW: 
 
Tort law allows the victim who has suffered a damage as a result of a 
tortious act, bring a claim, even if they do not have a claim for breach of 
contract or a claim in criminal law. 
 
Tort law and Criminal law: 
 
 
 
Tort law 
 
 
Criminal law 
 Standard of 
proof 
 Balance of 
probabilities 
 
 Beyond reasonable 
doubt 
 Purpose 
 
 Compensation 
 
 Punishment 
 Interests 
infringed 
 
 Victim's interests 
 Public interest 
 
Tort is different from Criminal law in a number of respects, and in most 
cases, even if a criminal offence has been committed, it is more 
beneficial for the victim to bring a claim in tort for compensation. 
 
Not only because criminal compensation is a lot lower than tortious 
compensation, but also because tort claims are often covered by 
insurance which allows for quick and predicable payments. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Tort law and Contract law: 
 
 
 
Tort law 
 
 
Contract law 
 Standard of 
proof 
 Balance of 
probabilities 
 
 Balance of 
probabilities 
 Duties owed 
 
 People in general 
 
 The parties 
 Duties 
infringed 
 
 Duties fixed by 
law 
 Duties agreed by 
the parties 
 
A tort is an infringement of a general duty established by law, while a 
breach of contract involves violating a duty that a party has voluntarily 
accepted. 
 
In relation to contract claims, obligations are typically limited to the 
parties involved in the contract. In contrast, tort law imposes duties 
towards the general public or specific groups such as employees. 
 
The primary goal of tort actions is to provide compensation for damages, 
whereas contract law mainly enforces agreements. 
 
It is possible for someone to be liable for both a tort and a breach of 
contract simultaneously. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
GENERAL PRINCIPLES OF TORT: 
 
The key principles in tort law involve establishing the following: 
 
1. 
The Claimant's interest – this must be an interest which 
requires protection. 
 
2. 
The Defendant's act interfered with the Claimant's interest – 
either intentionally or unintentionally, causing a consequence 
to the Claimant for which the Defendant should be held 
responsible. 
 
 AND 
3. 
The Claimant must have suffered a loss as a result of the 
Defendant's acts – this includes causation, typically both 
factual and legal causation must be satisfied. 
 
Intentions: 
 Unlike Criminal law (except for strict liability crimes), the intentions of 
the Defendant will be irrelevant as long as they had a duty of care 
towards the Claimant which they have breached. 
 
Instead of the requirement of intention that could be seen in criminal 
cases, tort law relies on “fault”. When negligent, the tortfeasor was at 
fault in some way. On the other hand, there are also no-fault torts, these 
are also called strict liability torts. 
 
Compensation: 
 The purpose of compensation for tort is to put the victim back in the 
position they would have been had the tort never been committed. 
 
TORT CLAIMS: 
 
There are a number of different torts which are all actionable by the 
victim. The most common and important tort is negligence. 
 
Other common claims: 
 
1. 
Intentional torts – conversion and trespass to land, to the 
person and to goods. 
 
2. 
Employers' liability – the liability of the employer towards their 
employees. 
 
3. 
Vicarious liability – the liability of the employer where the tort 
has been committed by their employee during the course of 
employment. 
 
4. 
Occupiers' liability – the liability of an occupier for injury/ 
damage suffered due to disrepair on their premises. 
 
5. 
Product liability – claims made in relation to defective products 
where the defects lead to losses/injuries. 
 
6. 
Nuisance – allowing the occupiers of land to remedy activities 
which stop them from enjoying the land. 
 7. 
Defamation – enables victims to recover compensation for loss 
of reputation where a false statement has been made in relation 
to them. 
 
Alternative to tort claims: 
 
* 
Social security benefits – where victims of an accident have no 
valid claim in tort or do not wish to bring a claim, they have to 
rely on benefits for financial support while recovering from their 
injuries. 
 
* 
Insurance cover – insurance may help victims in situations 
which are covered by their policies. 
 
It is a criminal offence to not have insurance for drivers and for 
employers to be without insurance. – Road Traffic Act 1988 
Employers' Liability (Compulsory Insurance Act 1969 
 
It is also common to take out household insurance to cover 
occupiers' liability claims. 
 
* 
Compensation for victims of crime – the Criminal Injuries 
Compensation Scheme provides compensation for injuries 
suffered as a result of violent crimes. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Example: 
Car accident claims commonly attract both tortious and criminal 
liability. If this is the case, the negligent driver may be prosecuted by 
the Crown Prosecution Service and sued by the victim for 
compensation for their injuries. 
Example: 
The sale of goods and provision of services commonly allow for the 
parties to bring a claim both in contract and tort. A breach of 
contract for sale of goods will also open doors for product liability 
claims in relation to defective products and a breach of contract for 
the provision of services will also allow for negligence claims.

pages.heading: INTENTIONAL TORTS · Torts that arise from the intentional actions of the Defendant:
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Prep notes | Page 2 of 27 
 
INTENTIONAL TORTS 
 
Torts that arise from the intentional actions of the Defendant: 
 
1. Trespass to property – Three separate torts: 
i. Trespass to land 
ii. Trespass to goods 
iii. Conversion 
 
2. Trespass to the person – Three separate torts: 
i. Battery 
ii. Assault 
iii. False imprisonment 
 
 
 
TRESPASS TO PROPERTY: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
TRESPASS TO LAND: 
 
Connection to occupiers' liability: 
 Trespass to land is commonly seen in occupiers' liability questions which 
you will read about in one of the later chapters. Establishing whether 
someone was a trespasser will be necessary for that. 
 
Connection to land law: 
 Trespass to land is commonly used in relation to boundary disputes in 
land law. The parties usually also make a claim for the tort of trespass to 
land to seek a remedy in relation to the claims made for proprietary 
rights in land. 
 
Definition: 
 
Trespass to land = unlawful, unjustifiable, and direct interference with 
the Claimant's possession of land. – the Claimant has a proprietary right 
in land and therefore, a right to keep people off the land. 
 
This tort includes the intentional entering or wrongfully remaining on 
someone else's land. 
 
Elements: 
 
Elements of trespass to land: 
1. 
Possession of the land – the Claimant bringing an action for 
trespass must have exclusive possession of the land. 
 
2. 
Land includes the usable space above and below and the surface 
of the land. – a drone flying over the land is trespass, but not 
aircraft flying at reasonable height. An overhanging crane can 
constitute trespass. 
 
3. 
Direct physical interference with the land by person, the 
machines they control or animals. – allowing the roots of your 
tree to extend under the land is indirect interference so not 
trespass. 
 
4. 
Intent to enter the land/negligence as to animals/machines 
entering the land – no need for intent to trespass, intent must 
be to simply enter the land. A person will also be liable if they 
negligently allow animals/machines in their control to enter the 
land. 
 
Each day an object or person remains unlawfully on land, a fresh cause 
of action arises. 
 
Even if a person has permission to be on the land because they have 
been invited to enter, they may become a trespasser if they enter for a 
different purpose than what the invitation entailed or if they enter a 
different area of the land where they have not been invited. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Direct interference: 
 The interference is only actionable if it is direct. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Indirect interference is not actionable. – a tree branch leaning over onto 
someone else's land is indirect interference. 
 
If smells/noises/vibrations enter your land from the neighbouring land, 
this will give rise to a nuisance claim, not trespass. 
 
Defences: 
 
Lawful entry: 
If the Defendant's presence is lawful, there is no trespass. 
 
Necessity: 
If the Defendant can prove that it was necessary for them to enter the 
land to preserve life or property, there is no trespass. 
 
TRESPASS TO GOODS: 
 
Definition: 
 
Trespass to goods = wrongful physical interference with goods that are 
in the possession of another. 
 
Elements: 
 
Trespass to chattels is actionable per se – actual damage is not required. 
 
Defences: 
 
Defending a person/property: 
 Goods are in real or imminent danger and interference is reasonable in 
the circumstances, and the Defendant considered that there was no 
other practical means of protecting the property. 
 
Consent: 
 The Defendant cannot be held liable for trespass to goods if the Claimant 
had consented to the Defendant's interference. 
 
Types of consent: 
* 
Express consent 
* 
Implied consent 
 
In most cases, while there might not be express consent, there may be 
consent implied from the conduct of the owner of the goods or customs 
relating to the goods. 
 
Consent is only valid if the owner of the goods had capacity to consent 
– look at mental and legal capacity. 
 
Recovery of goods: 
 Recovery of goods by claimant removed by the Defendant due to 
unlawful distress. 
 
CONVERSION: 
 
Definition: 
 
Conversion = the intentional dealing with goods which is seriously 
inconsistent with the use and possession or right to immediate 
possession of another person. 
 
Elements: 
1. 
Conversion is actionable per se. 
2. 
Conversion is a strict liability tort, which does not require the 
claimant to show the Defendant had a wrong intention, the 
Defendant may assert as a defence that he acted honestly. 
3. 
Only applies to corporeal personal property. – does not apply to 
intangible property such as a contractual right, copyright or 
electronic documents. 
4. 
Possession or immediate right to possession required to have 
standing to sue for conversion. – ownership is not a critical 
factor. 
 
Defences: 
 
Co-ownership: 
 A co-owner has no right to bring action against another co-owner for 
interfering with his right of possession. 
 
Example: 
* 
If they have been invited over for tea and they proceed to 
steal items from the house, they will be deemed to be 
trespassers as the purpose of the invitation was not stealing. 
* 
If someone is invited into the garden, they become trespasser 
if they enter the house. The permission was given to them to 
enter the garden only. 
 Trespass to land 
 
 Unlawful direct 
interference with 
another's land and 
right to possess it. 
 
 
Trespass to goods 
 
 
The intentional and 
unlawful 
interference with 
another's lawful 
use or possession 
of goods (personal 
property). 
 
 
 
Conversion 
 
 
The intentional 
dealing with goods 
which is inconsistent 
with the use and 
possession of 
another. 
 
 
Examples of direct interference: 
* 
Taking possession of the land 
* 
Wrongfully entering or staying on the land 
* 
Placing anything on the land 
* 
Crossing the land or driving over the land 
* 
Allowing animals on the land.

pages.heading: Cheques Act: · Cheques Act If cheque incorrectly paid into customer's account in good
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Prep notes | Page 3 of 27 
 
Cheques Act: 
 Cheques Act If cheque incorrectly paid into customer's account in good 
faith and without negligence, the bank has a defence. 
 
Insolvency Act: 
 Insolvency Act A person who deals with the bankrupt's property when 
unaware of the bankruptcy is not liable. 
 
Pawnbrokers: 
 Pawnbrokers are not liable for failing to confirm the pledged goods are 
being returned to the true owner. 
 
Abandonment: 
 The test for purposes of ascertaining whether there has been 
abandonment is whether there has been both an intention to abandon 
and some physical act of relinquishment. 
 
The finder must establish a reasonable entitlement to conclude that no 
one is interested in the goods and they can therefore be disposed of. 
 
TRESPASS TO THE PERSON: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
BATTERY: 
 
 
 
 
 
Battery will likely be relevant in questions where a doctor or another 
medical professional does more to a person's body than authorized. 
 
Definition: 
 
Battery = the intentional and direct application of force to another 
person. 
 
Elements: 
1. 
Unlawful force against another person – this includes unwanted 
physical contact of any kind that is not generally acceptable in 
the ordinary conduct of life. 
2. 
Which is direct and immediate physically. 
3. 
The act must be intentional; however, the harm need not be. 
 AND 
4. 
The Claimant is not required to demonstrate physical injury. 
 
The contact need not be from one person to another, it can be through 
clothes or throwing something. 
 
ASSAULT: 
 
 
 
 
 
Definition: 
 
Assault = an act which causes another person to apprehend the infliction 
of immediate, unlawful force on their person. 
 
Elements: 
1. 
The Defendant intends that Claimant apprehends the 
application of unlawful force on the Claimant. 
2. 
The Defendant reasonably apprehends the direct and immediate 
application of unlawful force. 
3. 
The Defendant has no lawful justification/excuse. 
 AND 
4. 
No requirement of direct application of force – words which 
instil a reasonable fear of unlawful force amount to assault. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
FALSE IMPRISONMENT: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Definition: 
 
False imprisonment = Depriving the Claimant of freedom of 
movement, without a lawful justification for doing so. 
 
Elements: 
* 
The Defendant must intend to completely restrict Claimant's 
freedom of movement. 
 AND 
* 
The Defendant has no lawful justification/excuse. 
 
Strict liability: if the Defendant intentionally performs an act that leads 
to the imprisonment of Claimant, then liability attaches even in 
circumstances if the Defendant did not know this act would result in false 
imprisonment. 
 
Defences to trespass against the person: 
 
Volenti non fit injuria: 
 In relation to sports: If the injuries suffered were not from the Claimant's 
participation in the sport but inadequate safety measures, that is a 
defence. 
 
Self defence: 
 Self-defence is a valid defence to trespass against the person, assuming 
that it constituted the use of reasonable force which they honestly and 
reasonably believe is necessary to protect themselves or someone else, 
or property. 
 
Consent: 
* 
Consent is not always a defence. 
* 
Consent must be valid to be taken into account. 
 
Necessity: 
* 
The act must be necessary to avoid inevitable, irreparable evil. 
* 
No more may be done than is necessary to achieve purpose. 
* 
The harm inflicted must not be disproportionate to evil avoided. 
 
 
 
 
INTENTIONAL + DIRECT APPLICATION OF FORCE 
 
INTENTIONAL + APPREHENSION OF BATTERY 
 
INTENTIONAL + UNLAWFUL + DEPRIVATION OF LIBERTY 
 
Battery 
 
 
The intentional and 
direct application of 
physical force to 
another. 
 
 
 
 
 
Assault 
 
 An intentional act 
which causes 
another to 
apprehend the 
infliction of 
immediate, 
unlawful force. 
 
 False imprisonment 
 
 Depriving another of 
freedom of 
movement, without 
a lawful justification 
for doing so.

pages.heading: NEGLIGENCE – DUTY OF CARE · INTRODUCTION:
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Prep notes | Page 4 of 27 
 
NEGLIGENCE – DUTY OF CARE 
 
INTRODUCTION: 
 
The most common action in tort is negligence, where the Claimant aims 
to recover compensation for the damage caused to the Claimant if this 
damage was caused by negligence where a duty of care was owed to the 
Claimant and the Defendant has breached this duty. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Negligence is essentially caused by carelessness and covers all sorts of 
issues from road traffic accidents to product liability and medical 
treatment. 
 
Unlike in relation to contract law, privity to the contract is not required, 
so tort allows for third parties to a contract to make a claim. In fact, to 
make a tort claim, no contract is required at all. 
 
Elements of negligence: *You need all of these to establish a claim* 
1. 
Duty of care – the Defendant owed a duty of care to the 
Claimant. 
2. 
Breach of duty – the Defendant breached their duty of care. 
3. 
Causation – the Defendant's negligence was the cause of the 
Claimant's damage. 
4. 
Remoteness of damages – the damage suffered is not too 
remote 
 AND 
5. 
Lack of defences 
 
ESTABLISHING DUTY OF CARE: 
 
Was the relationship between the Claimant and the Defendant such that 
the Defendant was obliged to take care for the Claimant's safety? 
 
There are a number of established duties of care, where case law has 
already established that a duty is owed. 
 
Where you find an established duty that corresponds to the duty in your 
scenario, rely on that established duty, as the courts will always aim to 
rely on existing cases and develop the law by analogy. 
 
Established duties: 
* 
Drivers of motor vehicles owe 
a duty of care to pedestrians 
and other road users 
* 
Doctors owe a duty to their 
patients 
* 
Employers owe a duty to their 
employees 
* 
Manufacturers owe a duty to 
their consumers 
* 
Teachers owe a duty of care to 
students 
* 
Solicitors owe a duty of care to 
their clients 
 
There is generally less likely for a duty 
of care to arise where psychiatric 
injuries have been caused by accidents, 
the work of the council and arrests. 
 
 
NOVEL DUTY SITUATIONS: 
 
There are also situations where a duty of care has not previously been 
decided. In these cases, the court decide whether a duty of care is owed 
by using the incremental approach. 
 
The courts will only imply a duty of care if: Caparo v Dickman 
*Important* 
 
1. 
The Claimant is a foreseeable Claimant – the Defendant's 
conduct must have caused a foreseeable risk of harm. Use the 
objective test. 
 
2. 
There must be a relationship of proximity between the 
Defendant and the Claimant: the Claimant must be a person who 
is so closely and directly affected by my act that I ought 
reasonably to have them in contemplation as being so affected. 
This is called the ‘Neighbour principle'. – Donoghue v Stevenson 
 
3. 
It is fair, just and reasonable to impose a remedy – applied by 
courts to look at broader implications of awarding a remedy. 
 
The court will review each one of these three factors in turn to see if a 
duty of care should be owed by the Defendant. If either one of these 
parts of the test is not satisfied, the courts will decide that the Defendant 
did not owe a duty of care in the circumstances. 
 
The Claimant must be a foreseeable Claimant: 
 
Palsgraf v Long Island Railroad A duty can only exist if it was reasonably 
foreseeable that damage or injury would be caused to a particular 
person or a class of people. There is no duty of care owed to the general 
public. – eg. it is not reasonably foreseeable that kicking someone in the 
foot would cause injury to someone outside of the immediate vicinity. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Langley v Dray Civilians failing to stop for police officers and engaging in 
a police chase will owe a duty of care not to commit acts which would 
reasonably create a risk or cause harm to the police officer chasing 
them. The police officer, other road users, pedestrians or the owners of 
nearby houses would all be foreseeable Claimants. 
 
Haley v London Electricity Board Despite the need for foreseeability that 
a particular person would be injured, it is sufficient that the Claimant 
falls within a particular class of people who would be injured by the 
Defendant's acts or omissions. – eg. the need to take into account blind 
people where the population is large enough to warrant additional 
precautions. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Proximity: 
 
The ordinary meaning of “proximity” is closeness. In relation to the rules 
of duty of care, we examine closeness in terms of the parties' 
relationship. – This includes either physical, circumstantial or causal 
closeness. 
 
Donoghue v Stevenson Use the Neighbour Principle to determine 
whether there has been proximity between the parties. There is a 
general duty that people must take reasonable care to avoid acts or 
omissions which can be reasonably foreseen to likely cause injury to 
their neighbour. 
 
Neighbour = someone so closely and directly affected by the 
tortfeasor's acts/omissions that the tortfeasor ought reasonably to have 
them in contemplation when carrying out those relevant acts/omissions. 
 
Muirhead v Industrial Tank Proximity does not mean that the Claimant 
and Defendant must have known each other. 
 
Caparo v Dickman Proximity simply refers to situations where the 
Defendant must have reasonably expected that their actions would 
cause damage to the Claimant. 
 
 
Example: 
Selling a faulty car which then bursts into flames. Even if no one is 
injured in the accident, the owner of the car and the passengers may 
be able to claim for psychiatric damage. 
 
Special relationships 
creating a duty of care 
 Parent 
 Child 
 
Teacher 
 
 
Student 
 School 
 
 Student 
 Drivers 
 
 Road user 
 
 Doctors 
 
 Patient 
 
 Employer 
 
 Employee 
 
 Occupier 
 
 Visitor 
 
 Solicitor 
 
 Client 
 
 Accountant 
 
 Client 
 
 Ambulance 
 
 Patient 
 
Example: 
Craig is a railway worker, who is called to attend the tills urgently. 
He starts running towards the tills, and bumps into a passenger, 
Ismail, carrying a box. Unknown to Craig, the box contained 
fireworks, and it exploded immediately, hitting a wooden beam 
several feet away. This beam fell onto another passenger, Holly who 
she got injured as a result. The court would find that Craig could not 
have reasonably foreseen that bumping into Ismail would injure 
Holly, standing several feet away. 
Example 1: 
 A company was carrying out street repair works in London. During 
these repairs, the workmen would dig holes in the ground and put 
up signs to ensure that the people walking by would see not fall into 
these holes. Ronnie was blind, and did not see the sign, so he fell 
into one of the holes and suffered an injury. 
 
The court would likely decide whether this was foreseeable based 
on the likelihood that a blind of partially sighted person would walk 
by. In London, there are a large number of blind people walking on 
the streets due to the high population numbers, so further 
precautions to guard against the risk of them falling in the holes 
should have been taken. 
Example 2: 
 A British research team carries out research to prepare a report in 
relation to the cleanliness of the drinking water found in the local 
wells in Pakistan. They test for e-coli, bacteria and common viruses 
and produce a report. 
 
Zakariya is taken to hospital and is told by the doctor that his 
symptoms appear to be caused by arsenic contamination in the local 
wells. Zakariya makes a claim for negligence against the research 
team, arguing that they should have tested the water for arsenic. 
The court will not decide for Zakariya in this case, as Zakariya has 
never read the report produced by the team and the research team 
cannot owe a duty to the whole population of Pakistan.

pages.heading: Fair, just and reasonable: · There is an overlap between proximity, reasonable foreseeability and
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Prep notes | Page 5 of 27 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Fair, just and reasonable: 
 
There is an overlap between proximity, reasonable foreseeability and 
fairness. 
 
Where the court refers to fairness in relation to their refusal to allow for 
a duty of care to arise, this is the care there is an underlying public policy 
consideration to protect. 
 
Even if the case fulfils the criteria of foreseeability and proximity, the 
court may still decide to reject the claim based on public policy. 
 
McFarlane v Tayside Health Board Claimants cannot bring a claim for 
the costs of bringing up a child where the reason for getting pregnant 
was the failure of a vasectomy or similar procedure. – the court views 
the birth of a healthy child as a blessing, not something where 
compensation should be due. 
 
West Bromwich Albion v Medhat El-Safty Doctors are only responsible 
to their patients and when advising them on procedures, they have to 
advise the patient as to what is best for them, rather than what is best 
for their professional career. – eg. when deciding whether to advise on 
procedures that aid with longevity rather than short-term performance. 
 
Mitchell v Glasgow City Council Public policy generally protects councils 
from liability for harm caused by third parties. The court does not 
impose a duty on landlords and social workers to warn affected tenants 
that they have scheduled a meeting with tenants who have shown 
antisocial behaviour. Imposing such liability would deter landlords and 
social workers from dealing with antisocial tenants. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Robinson v West Yorkshire Police (2014) Public policy generally protects 
police officers from liability for harm caused to third parties. This is 
because there is public interest in arresting criminals. The court is 
unlikely to impose a duty where the police officers were negligent in 
arresting someone and as a result, a third party is injured. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
LIABILITY FOR OMISSIONS: 
 
There is no general duty to act so there is no general liability for 
omissions. There is no duty to actively help. – no duty to save someone 
in danger. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
However, there are certain situations where the court imposes a duty to 
actively act. 
 
Exceptions: 
 
* 
If there is a special relationship between the parties – eg. 
parent-child relationship, doctor and patient. 
 
* 
If the Defendant has control over the victim – Dorset Yacht – eg. 
a police officer will have control over a suspect in custody. 
 
 
* 
If the harm/danger is created by a third party who is within the 
Defendant's control – eg. a parent has control over their child so 
they may owe a duty of care not to allow their child to hurt other 
children. 
 
* 
If a person has created a risk or made an existing risk worse, 
they have a duty to resolve the danger that has been created. – 
Capital and Counties 
 
* 
If a person attempts to rescue someone, they will have a duty
