not to make the situation worse. – East Suffolk Rivers v Kent – 
this is the case even if the person does not complete the rescue. 
 
* 
If one of the parties have voluntarily assumed responsibility 
over the other, a duty will be implied. 
 
Control: 
 
If the Defendant had a high degree of control over the victim, they will 
likely have a duty to look after them. 
 
Reeves v Commissioner of Police for the Metropolis The police has a 
positive duty to prevent suicide attempts in prisons as the police will 
have control over the suspects in custody and inmates in prisons. 
 
Voluntary assumption of responsibility: 
 
There is generally no duty to help others under English law. 
 
However, the duty to help will be implied if: 
1. 
There is a contract between the parties implying such 
responsibility. 
2. 
Responsibility arises due to the nature of the Defendant's job. 
 OR 
3. 
One of the parties has assumed responsibility by conduct. 
 
Voluntary assumption via contract: 
 
There is a contract (which is not an employment contract) between the 
parties which implies that one of the parties will owe a duty of care 
towards certain classes of people. There may be a requirement to help 
while on or off-duty, depending on what the contract prescribes. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Voluntary assumption via the Defendant's job: 
 
The Defendant has signed an employment contract which imposes a 
duty on the Defendant to help others only while on duty. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Voluntary assumption via conduct: 
 
A person or organization may voluntarily assume responsibility by 
conduct if they start providing assistance when in need. From that point 
onwards, they are required to assist until the danger has passed. 
 
Barrett v Ministry of Defence An authority or company will be held liable 
if someone is ill, drunk or drugged and someone arrives to pick up them 
up. At that stage, the authority or company will have voluntarily 
assumed responsibility for making sure that that person is taken care of 
while their illness or condition lasts. – eg. this includes someone staying 
with them or taking them to the hospital if needed. 
 
If the Defendant has signed an employment contract which imposes a 
duty on the Defendant to help others while on duty, the Defendant is 
not required to help others off-duty. However, if the Defendant starts 
providing assistance, at that stage, there will be voluntary assumption 
of responsibility by conduct. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Example: 
During a company acquisition, if the Buyer company is to rely on the 
audits of the Target company (the company to be purchased), the 
auditors will only owe a duty of care to the Target company and its 
shareholders, and not to potential buyers, unless the audit was 
specifically prepared for the purpose to be used in a company 
acquisition to value the Target company. 
Example: 
Remi had an antisocial neighbour, James, who would regularly send 
him death threats in the post. James lived in a council housing, so 
Remi let the council know of these threats and as a result, the 
council scheduled a meeting with James, where he was told that if 
the threats do not stop, he would be evicted. After the meeting, 
James broke into Remi's home and attacked him, leaving a scar on 
his face and multiple items in the home were broken. Remi's claim 
against the council, that they should have warned him of the 
meeting, would be rejected on public policy grounds. 
Example: 
PC Harman and PC Goodfellow were arresting a dangerous criminal 
gang. The criminals resisted the arrest, and the police officers used 
reasonable force. Unfortunately, Ewan, who was a passer-by, was 
also arrested. During the arrest, Ewan resisted and was forced to the 
floor where he was handcuffed. When the police grappled him and 
handcuffed him, he kept trying to break free and broke his right arm. 
Later, he made a claim for negligence against the police officers, 
however, he was unsuccessful on grounds of public policy. 
Example: 
Christian is on his way home from work when he sees an old woman 
being attacked by a fox. He looks at the woman and walks away. The 
woman is seriously injured and claims that Christian was a strong 
man with a backpack, he could have easily helped her when she was 
attacked. The court will likely decide that Christian's refusal to help 
will not make him liable, even if it would have been easy for him to 
help the woman. 
Example: 
Nathan is a freelance swimming instructor at a local pool. He signed 
a contract with the pool management company, which includes a 
clause that he would provide life-saving assistances to swimmers as 
and when needed. 
Example: 
Sophia is an on-duty doctor at the A&E at a hospital. During her shift, 
a patient arrives at the emergency room with severe injuries. Sophia 
will be required to provide medical assistance by the nature of her 
job. 
Example: 
Sophia is a doctor at the A&E at a hospital. She is at a concert during 
her day off, when a woman collapses in front of her. She is not 
legally required to help, however, if she attends the woman, she will 
be required to assist using reasonable care and skill.

pages.heading: Creation of a risk: · If the Defendant themselves created a dangerous situation or made an
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Prep notes | Page 6 of 27 
 
Creation of a risk: 
 
If the Defendant themselves created a dangerous situation or made an 
existing risk worse, they will have a positive duty to extinguish the risk 
or danger. 
 
Capital and Counties v Hampshire County Council The fire brigade owe 
a duty to the owners of the property not to make the fire worse. – eg. 
by switching off the internal sprinkler system. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Creation of a risk, third party caused the harm: 
 
If the Defendant created a risk, they may be liable if a third party's 
actions harm/injure the Claimant. 
 
Haynes v Harwood If horses are left unattended in a busy area and a 
third party agitates the horses, the person leaving them unattended will 
be responsible for the damage caused by the horses. – in this case, the 
horses could have become agitated without third party intervention. 
 
Topp v London Country Bus If a bus is left unattended on the street, with 
the keys in ignition, this will not make the person leaving it unattended 
responsible for the harm caused by a third party's dangerous driving. – 
in this case, the active negligence of the third party was needed for the 
risk to materialise. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
SCOPE OF DUTY: 
 
When looking at duty of care, ensure that the harm suffered is within 
the scope of the Defendant's duty of care because if not, then the 
Defendant cannot be held liable, even if there was negligence. 
 
Professional negligence: 
 
South Australia Asset Management v York Montague A negligent 
surveyor who overvalues property which is to be offered as security for 
a loan owes a duty to the lender. 
 
Always check the reason why the professional was hired. The breach 
must fall within extent of the work expected at the point of hiring the 
professional. 
 
If a surveyor is hired to provide property valuation, they will only owe 
a duty of care in relation to the valuation of the property and will owe 
no duty of care in relation to the information they share as to future 
trends. Their duty of care will only extend to the advice for which they 
have been employed. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Manchester Building Society v Grant Thornton (2021) A negligent 
accountant who gives ineffective accounting and financial advice will be 
held liable for all the advice and information that was given to the client 
for the purpose of the duty (to give financial advice). This is judged by 
the standard of the reasonable person (objective test). 
 
While accountants and financial advisors are more likely to be hired to 
provide financial strategies for the future, you must always look at the 
reason why the professional was hired. If they have been hired to 
provide financial strategies, then they will owe a duty of care both in 
relation to future predictions. 
 
While the financial advisor cannot be responsible for unforeseen future 
events, they must use the correct calculations, taking into account all 
the vital aspects of the company. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
PUBLIC BODIES: 
 
The police: 
 
Duty of care in relation to positive acts: 
 
Robinson (2018) If a police officer has been negligent and this negligence 
creates a positive risk of injury where there was a relationship of 
proximity, the police officer will be liable. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Langley v Dray Civilians failing to stop for police officers and engaging in 
a police chase will owe a duty of care not to commit acts which would 
reasonably cause harm to the police officer chasing them. 
 
 
Example: 
Two police officers are chasing a suspected thief in a busy urban 
area with a lot of pedestrians around. During the chase, an officer 
attempts to tackle the suspect but does so recklessly, and he knocks 
over a pedestrian, causing them serious injury. In this case, the 
pedestrian might have a claim against the police for negligence. 
Example: 
 Margot is a surveyor, and she has been instructed by Universal Bank 
to carry out a valuation of the current value of Unit 1 492 Waldram 
Crescent. Unit 1 was a warehouse building and it was owned by a 
third party, Sustaina Build Limited. Sustaina applied for a loan from 
Universal Bank and unit 1 were to be used as the security for the 
loan. 
 
Margot has visited the premises and prepared her valuation report, 
where she had stated that the estimated value of Unit 1 was 
£450,000 and that with the future trend, whereby property prices 
go up, Unit 1 could potentially be worth £600,000 within the next 5 
years. 
 
As a result of this advice, Universal Bank grants a loan of £600,000 
to Sustaina for a term of 5 years. After a year, there is an economic 
crash, the value of Unit 1 plummets to £280,000, Sustaina goes 
insolvent and Universal Bank can only recover £280,000 by selling 
Unit 1. Universal Bank's claim for negligence would be limited to the 
value of Unit 1 at the time of the valuation report, as this is what 
Margot was contracted to do, and Margot would not be liable for a 
negligent advice as to the future market trends even if the bank 
relied on it. 
Example: 
 Clear View Consulting Ltd is a company of accountants and financial 
advisors. Grandiose Ltd is a company which engages Clear View to 
provide financial and accounting advice. 
 
Clear View, led by its senior accountant, John, advises Grandiose to 
enter into an interest rate swap arrangement to protect Grandiose 
against potential future interest rate increases and instability. John 
assures Grandiose that the interest rate swap is a sound financial 
decision, providing detailed projections and assurances. Relying on 
this advice, Grandiose enters into the agreement. 
 
A year later, the swap results in an £1,000,000 loss due to 
unforeseen interest rate movements. Grandiose discovers that John 
had failed to consider critical aspects of the company's financial 
position and as a result, the plan was not suitable for Grandiose. 
 
Grandiose will have a claim for negligence in this case. If the case 
went to trial, the court would evaluate whether John, failed to meet 
the standard of care expected of a reasonable accountant in 
providing financial advice. The court would assess whether John 
breached this duty by failing to consider critical financial aspects. 
Given that the advice led to significant financial losses, it is likely that 
this would be considered a breach of duty. 
Example: 
 A director hired a contractor, called Ashish to perform a safety 
assessment and general maintenance on the electrical systems of an 
office building. While performing his work, Ashish accidentally 
damages a gas pipe, causing a gas leak. If he, decides to leave the 
premises at this stage, anyone injured in the building will be able to 
make a negligence claim against him for damages. 
 
By creating the risk, he had a positive duty to take steps to either 
attempt to repair the pipe himself (if he has the expertise) or 
immediately inform the building management or emergency 
services so that it can be addressed. 
Example: 
 Freddie's is smoking a cigarette while driving down the motorway. 
He accidentally drops his cigarette onto the floor, however, he 
continues driving, despite the carpet starting to burn, switching on 
the AC to stop the fire. He continues to drive until his trousers start 
burning, when he stops the car in the middle of the motorway to get 
out of the car. At this stage, the car is on fire. 
 
Drivers are noticing the burning car and are slowing down as they 
approach it. Two teenagers pick up wooden sticks and use the fire 
to set them alight. They start throwing the sticks at cars. Lilly is in 
one of those cars, and one of the sticks hit her in the face, leaving a 
burn mark. In this case, both Freddie and the teenagers could be 
liable for causing the injury.

pages.heading: Duty of care in relation to omissions: · Michael v Chief Constable of South Wales Police The police will owe a
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Prep notes | Page 7 of 27 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Duty of care in relation to omissions: 
 Michael v Chief Constable of South Wales Police The police will owe a 
duty of care to a person if they have assumed responsibility for that 
person's safety and security or if the police has created the danger 
themselves. 
 
R v Dytham If a police officer is on duty, they will be liable for omissions 
if they fail to protect members of the public. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Fire service: 
 
Hampshire If the fire service attends a fire, they will have a duty not to 
make the situation worse. – eg. by turning the sprinkler system off or 
spreading the fire. 
 
If the fire service creates a danger, or makes it worse it will have a duty 
to take positive steps to fight that danger, as much as reasonable. 
 
 
 
 
Example: 
A police officer on duty wearing a uniform should help an old lady 
being violently assaulted, even if the police officer is on break as 
they have a duty to protect members of the public. 
Example: 
Beatrice is driving a stolen car, when a police officer asks her to stop 
the car to carry out a stop and search. Instead of stopping the 
vehicle, Beatrice drives off, and police officer started chasing her. 
Knowing this, Beatrice decides to speed up and the police officer 
crashes through the fence of a house next to the road. 
 
Even though, it was the police officers' act of chasing Beatrice that 
caused the accident, both the homeowner and the police officer will 
have a case for negligence against Beatrice, as she owed a duty of 
care to the police officer and other road users and had a duty not to 
speed up, creating a risk of injury.

pages.heading: NEGLIGENCE – BREACH OF DUTY · STANDARD OF CARE AND BREACH:
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Prep notes | Page 8 of 27 
 
NEGLIGENCE – BREACH OF DUTY 
 
STANDARD OF CARE AND BREACH: 
 
It is not sufficient to simply establish that a duty of care existed in the 
circumstances, we also need to identify whether there has been a 
breach of that duty. This is the care if the Defendant fails to take 
reasonable care to the standard expected of them. 
 
What standard of care was the Defendant obliged to hold themselves to 
that they breached? 
 
Reasonable man test: 
 Blyth v Birmingham Waterworks The standard of care expected of the 
Defendant is that of the ordinary reasonable person in the Defendant's 
position. – the Defendant will have breached their duty if the court finds 
that a reasonable person would not have fallen below the standard of 
care. 
 
The reasonable man is also known as the man on the Clapham omnibus. 
 
Nettleship v Weston New drivers will be held to the standard of a 
reasonable person without the court looking at their characteristics. This 
includes inexperience, which will be ignored. – the court will hold the 
new driver to the standard expected of a reasonably competent driver. 
 
In assessing whether the care used was reasonable, consider: 
 The likelihood of harm arising and the seriousness of that potential 
harm. If there is a high chance of potential harm/serious harm in any 
given situation, greater caution should be exercised. 
 
When the court decides on reasonability, they will look at factors: 
a. 
The court will take into account all the circumstances of the case. 
b. 
The Defendant's position – eg. if they were part of a particular 
profession or had some form of expert knowledge, they will be 
held to a higher standard. 
c. 
Foreseeability of harm – if the harm is foreseeable, then more 
precaution must be taken to avoid the harm. 
d. 
The seriousness of any potential harm – the greater the harm, 
the greater the precautions that will need to be taken. 
e. 
Magnitude of risk 
f. 
Cost and practicality in overcoming any risk – courts expect 
people to take only reasonable precautions in guarding against 
harm to other. 
g. 
Purpose and utility of the Defendant's activity – emergencies or 
if it is taken for the benefit of society. 
h. 
Common practice at the time 
i. 
State of knowledge at the time 
 
PROFESSIONALS: *HIGHER STANDARD* 
 
Professionals will be held to a higher standard, the standard expected 
of a reasonable member of that profession. – eg. a doctor will be held 
to the standard of a reasonably competent doctor. 
 
Bolam Bolam test: Professionals will be judged by the standard of 
ordinary skilled man exercising and/or professing to have that special 
skill. – This is the case even if they do not in fact have the skill they say 
they have. 
 
Bolitho The court will not find a doctor not liable simply because other 
doctors testify that they agree with what that particular doctor did in 
that specific situation. 
 
Wells v Cooper The fact that the professional is inexperienced, 
incompetent or a junior member of the team do not lower the standard 
expected of them. If a person decides to carry out an activity they do not 
have the competence to do, this will be a sign of negligence. 
 
The Wells v Cooper standard applies to: 
 
* 
Junior doctors – a junior doctor will have to meet the standard 
of a reasonably competent doctor in their department. – 
Wilshire v Essex Area Health Authority 
 
* 
Learner drivers – learner drivers should meet the standard of a 
competent and experienced driver. – Nettleship v Weston 
 
Additional duties for doctors: Montgomery 
 
* 
Doctors must warn patients of material risks of treatment. 
 
* 
The professional must have taken reasonable care to explain any 
materials risks involved in any particular choice, and any 
reasonable alternatives. What is material in any given case will 
depend on the patient. 
 
* 
The doctors cannot argue that a failure to warn is based on a 
responsible body of professional opinion. 
 
 
 
 
CHILDREN: *LOWER STANDARD* 
 
Mullin v Richards Children are held to a lower standard, which will be 
the standard expected of an ordinary child of the same age. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Mullin v Richards 15-year-old girls may not foresee that sword-fights 
with plastic rulers pose a risk of injury, if they have not been warned by 
the school. 
 
Orchard v Lee High degree of carelessness is acceptable in relation to 
children and will generally not amount to negligence. 
 
Exception: 
 If a child carries out acts typically carried out by adults, they will be held 
to the standard of a reasonable adult. – eg. driving a car, smoking a 
cigarette. 
 
ILLNESS: *NO CHANGE IN STANDARDS* 
 
Anyone who is ill while carrying out certain activities, will be held to the 
same standard as a healthy person. 
 
Roberts v Ramsbottom Someone who suffered a stroke while driving, 
causing an accident was held to the standard expected of a reasonably 
competent driver. The reason for this decision was that the driver could 
make an insurance claim to cover the compensation. 
 
PROVING THE BREACH: 
 
Proving that there has been a breach of duty can sometimes be difficult. 
 
Common types of evidence used to prove that there has been a breach: 
1. 
Witness evidence 
2. 
The doctrine of “Res Ipsa Loquitur” 
 
Witness evidence: 
 
In order to prove the breach, it is important to find witnesses to give 
evidence. 
 
This should include either witnesses of fact to describe the events or 
expert witnesses to describe the correct procedures that should have 
been used. 
 
Res Ipsa loquitur: 
 
Res Ipsa loquitur = the thing speaks for itself. 
 
This doctrine is used in situations where there is no evidence, but the 
circumstances are such, that negligence is obvious. 
 
Elements: 
1. 
The Defendant must be shown to have been in control of the 
thing which caused the injury to the Claimant. 
2. 
Accident must be of such a nature that it would not have 
occurred in the ordinary course of events without negligence. 
 AND 
3. 
There is no explanation as to how the accident occurred. 
 
 
Example: 
A 6-year old is not found to be negligent for not understanding that 
certain situations can be dangerous such as walking across a busy 
road without looking both ways.

pages.heading: NEGLIGENCE – CAUSATION AND REMOTENESS · CAUSATION – INTRODUCTION:
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Prep notes | Page 9 of 27 
 
NEGLIGENCE – CAUSATION AND REMOTENESS 
 
CAUSATION – INTRODUCTION: 
 
In addition to establishing a duty of care and a breach of duty, a Claimant 
must also establish causation and remoteness. 
 
Did the Defendant's breach of duty cause the harm the Claimant 
suffered? The Defendant will not be liable unless their negligence has 
caused the Claimant's injury/loss. 
 
Consider causation in two stages: 
 
1. 
Causation in fact – Was the Claimant's loss/injury caused by the 
negligence of the Defendant? 
 AND 
2. 
Causation in law – Was the Claimant's loss/injury too remote? 
 
Claimants must prove that their injuries/losses were caused both in fact 
and in law (so ensure that you address both stages of the test). 
 
Burden of proof: 
 The Claimant has the burden of proof to show that, on the balance of 
probabilities, the damage/injury suffered by the Claimant has been 
caused by the Defendant's negligent actions/omissions. 
 
CAUSATION IN FACT: 
 
The General rule – the “But for” test: 
 
Claimant must show that their loss was caused by the Defendant's 
negligence. – But for the Defendant's breach, the Claimant would not 
have suffered harm. This is called the “But for” test, and this is the test 
to use where the injury had one single cause. 
 
If the harm would have occurred even if the Defendant did not breach 
their duty, then the breach will not have caused the harm suffered and 
the Claimant cannot have a claim for negligence. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Successive injuries: 
 
However, if the injury/loss was caused as a result of multiple causes, 
identify whether the causes resulted in successive injuries or whether 
there has only been one single injury suffered by the Claimant as a result 
of the multiple causes. 
 
Successive injuries = two or more causes that took place one after 
another, causing different injuries. 
 
Performance Cars v Abraham If there are successive injuries, use expert 
evidence to determine the cause of each injury. In this case, the Claimant 
may recover from each Defendant for each injury caused by them. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Concurrent causes, indivisible injuries: 
 
If the Claimant has suffered an injury or multiple injuries which could 
have resulted from a number of different causes acting together to 
cause the injury/injuries, then you need to look at the following rules. 
 
Bonnington Castings v Wardlaw In this case, the Claimant need only 
show that the Defendant's breach has materially contributed to the 
Claimant's harm. – this means a contribution of more than 50%. 
 
Sienkiewicz v Greif If the acts of the Defendant have materially 
increased the risk of harm, then the Defendant should be held liable for 
the harm, even if the exact contribution of their negligence to the 
causation of the harm cannot be quantified. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Divisible injuries: 
 
Holtby v Brigham and Cowan Ltd If the Claimant has suffered an injury 
or multiple injuries in one accident which resulted from multiple 
causes, however, the cause of the injury is divisible (clearly identifiable), 
the court will typically provide that each Defendant is liable in 
accordance with the proportion of harm each of them caused. – eg. if 
one of them caused 30%, and the other 70%. 
 
indivisible injuries: 
 
If two or more Defendants breached a duty which leads to an injury 
which cannot be attributed to either one of the Defendants alone, 
meaning that the injury or injuries are indivisible, the Claimant can 
recover full compensation from either Defendants. 
 
This is because, without this limitation, there would be a risk that the 
Claimant were to recover the same damages twice or more. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Civil Liability (Contribution) Act 1978 The court will identify what 
percentage each Defendant should pay based on how they should share 
responsibility for the Claimant's injuries/losses. 
 
If one of the Defendants can prove that they have paid more than their 
share of the fault, they will be able to seek contribution from the other 
Defendant. 
 
CAUSATION IN LAW: 
 
The Claimant must show that there was no new intervening act (novus 
actus interveniens) breaking the chain of causation. 
 
If there is a new, intervening act, 
caused by a third party, this may 
break the chain of causation starting 
from the Defendant's breach to the 
Claimant's harm. 
 
Where this is the case, the Defendant will not be liable for the harm 
suffered by the Claimant. 
 
The new intervening act will break the chain if: 
 
* 
The intervening act was unforeseeable. 
 
 
* 
The Claimant's own actions may break the chain of causation if 
they acted unreasonably. 
 
* 
If the intervening act is committed by a third party, it must have 
been either intentional or reckless. – this new act must have 
been independent of the negligence of the Defendant. 
 
* 
A doctor's gross negligence when treating the Claimant will have 
been unforeseeable. – However, ordinary negligence will have 
been foreseeable. 
 
* 
An act of nature will break the chain of causation if it causes the 
damage/injury in itself. 
 
The Claimant's own actions: 
 The Claimant's own actions will only break the chain of causation if the 
Claimant acted in a way which was so reckless and unreasonable that 
their injury can no longer be attributed to the acts/omissions of the 
Defendant. 
 
In this case, the court will decide that the Claimant will be responsible 
for their own injuries. 
 
The new intervening act does not break the chain of causation if: 
 
* 
The negligence of the third party was foreseeable. – Rouse v 
Squires 
 
Example: 
 Beryl goes to the A&E, complaining of a headache. The doctor on 
duty examines her and finds that the headache is likely caused by 
lack of sleep. Beryl is sent home, where she dies of a brain 
haemorrhage a few hours later. 
 
Even if there is a finding that the doctor was negligent when 
examining Beryl, if Beryl would have died even after a proper 
examination, then the doctor will not have caused her death and 
Beryl's estate will not have a claim against the doctor. 
Example: 
 
Omonike has worked for a company where she had been exposed 
to small amounts to asbestos as a result of the company's 
negligence. She has later developed mesothelioma, a disease that 
could be potentially caused by asbestos among other causes. 
 
As the company's negligence has materially increased the risk of 
Omonike contracting mesothelioma, the court would likely find the 
company liable. 
Example: 
 Jacob has been involved in a car accident where a negligent driver 
has hit his car from the back, causing a broken leg. If a few seconds 
later, a negligent motorbike rider crashes into Jacob's car from the 
right-hand side, resulting in a broken rib, Jacob will likely have a 
claim for both injuries. The negligent driver will be liable for the 
broken leg and the negligent motorbike rider will be liable for the 
broken rib. 
Example: 
 If Kyle was hit by a bus and then also a car, thus suffering a broken 
leg, with no way to tell which one caused the injury even by using 
expert evidence, the court will likely decide that the injury was 
caused by both collisions, rather than one or the other.

pages.heading: The intervening act took place as an instinctive reaction to what · was happening at the time. – Scott v Shepherd
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Prep notes | Page 10 of 27 
 
* 
The intervening act took place as an instinctive reaction to what 
was happening at the time. – Scott v Shepherd 
 
REMOTENESS OF DAMAGE: 
 
Even if all the other elements are satisfied, the Defendant may escape 
liability if the damage was too remote a consequence of the breach of 
duty. – if this is the case, the damage will be unrecoverable. 
 
Test for remoteness: 
 
Wagon Mound The damage must have been reasonably foreseeable by 
the Defendant. If the damage was not reasonably foreseeable, it will be 
deemed to be too remote. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Armstead v Royal & Sun Alliance (2024) The burden of proof that one/ 
more of the losses are too remote to be recovered is on the Defendant. 
This means the Defendant must prove that the loss or type of loss was 
not reasonably foreseeable. 
 
This is the general rule that applies to all cases apart from a few 
exceptions, listed below. 
 
Exceptions: 
1. 
The Egg-shell skull rule 
2. 
The Similar in type rule 
3. 
Loss of a chance 
 
The Egg-shell skull rule: 
 
Defendants will take the victim as they find them, even if the victim has 
any weaknesses or ailments. – if the victim drinks a drink which contains 
e-coli, and the victim has an underlying condition, killing them, the 
manufacturer will be liable for their death, even if that was not intended. 
 
Smith v Leech Brain Defendants will be liable, as long as the type of harm 
and its manner was reasonably foreseeable, even if the extent of the 
harm was not foreseeable. – even if they intend a lesser harm, if the 
harm ends up being worse than expected, they will still be liable. 
 
The Similar in type rule: 
 
Hughes v Lord Advocate If the Claimant suffers the type of harm which 
would be reasonably foreseeable, however the specific manner in which 
it occurs or the actual damage suffered is unforeseeable, it will not be 
too remote. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Loss of a chance: 
 
Stovold v Barlows Where the loss of the Claimant is a loss of a change, 
the Claimant must prove that there was a real/substantial chance, 
rather than mere speculation. 
 
This exception relates to the acts of a third party, where the Claimant 
themselves had no substantial control over that third party's actions. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Example: 
 AB Shipping Ltd is a company repairing ships. One day, they are 
called out to fix the side of an oil tanker which is in the middle of 
delivering large quantities of oil. The workers replace a part of the 
ship to ensure that the side is stronger and more durable to enable 
the ship to complete its voyage safely. Unfortunately, one of the 
parts have not been properly attached during the repairs. 
 
As the ship leaves the harbour, the oil starts leaking, and it drifts to 
an area of the harbour where workmen from another company are 
welding metal. A spark from the welding catches fire from the oil 
and the fire spreads to the wharf causing substantial damage. In this 
case, AB Shipping cannot be held responsible for the damage, as it 
was not reasonably foreseeable when the negligence occurred and 
therefore, would be too remote. 
Example: 
 
Tom is an electrician who leaves an open manhole covered with a 
tent and lit by warning lamps at a construction site. Sarah, a 
pedestrian, decides to explore the tent out of curiosity. As she 
stands next to the manhole, and one of the lamps is knocked over 
by a gust of wind, causing a small explosion. Sarah is thrown into the 
manhole and suffers severe burns and a broken leg from the fall. 
 
The type of harm (injury from falling into the manhole) is reasonably 
foreseeable due to the open manhole. However, the exact way in 
which the injury occurred (the explosion) was unforeseeable. 
However, Tom can still be held liable because the type of harm was 
foreseeable. 
Example: 
 
Gabriella purchases a new fan, which explodes when she turns it on. 
She is now in hospital, and it appears that she will be unable to work 
for at least 8 months in her current role as a marketing manager. 
She decides to make a claim against the manufacturer of the fan for 
negligence and in addition to her usual salary covering the 8 months 
loss of work, she also claims for her loss of bonus. 
 
This may not be too remote if she had a real/substantial chance of 
receiving this bonus. She will need to show evidence of the previous 
performances bonuses she has receives, and positive performance 
reviews and internal communications indicating that she would be 
a strong contender from a bonus.

pages.heading: NEGLIGENCE – DEFENCES · INTRODUCTION:
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Prep notes | Page 11 of 27 
 
NEGLIGENCE – DEFENCES 
 
INTRODUCTION: 
 
The Defendant will seek to establish a defence to the claim as having a 
valid defence may reduce/extinguish their liability to pay compensation. 
 
While the Claimant has the burden of proof, showing that the Defendant 
has been negligent, the Defendant has the burden of proof showing that 
on the balance of probabilities, one or more of the following defences 
apply. 
 
Key defences that the Defendant may rely on: 
 
1. 
The Claimant was contributorily negligent 
 
2. 
The Claimant has voluntarily assumed a risk 
 
3. 
The Defendant has validly excluded/limited their liability 
 
4. 
The Claimant was undertaking a criminal activity when they 
were injured 
 
5. 
The damage was caused as a result of a necessity. 
 
6. 
The negligent act was making a negligent misstatement and the 
Defendant had simply made a mistake and had an honest belief 
in the truth of their statement. 
 
CONTRIBUTORY NEGLIGENCE: 
 
The Defendant may use the defence of contributory negligence where 
the Claimant or a third party was, in part, responsible for the harm they 
suffered, due to their own negligence. – s.1 Law Reform (Contributory 
Negligence) Act 1945 
 
A finding of contributory negligence will result in a reduction of damages 
payable by the Defendant. 
 
This is the most common defence to negligence. When there is an 
accident, the Claimant themselves will likely have been negligent in 
some way, therefore, contributing to the accident. 
 
Contributory negligence is a partial defence and will not extinguish 
liability completely but will reduce the damages payable by the 
Defendant. Contribution can never pay for 100% of the losses. 
 
There are two ways in which contributory negligence can be claimed: 
either against the Claimant themselves or a third party. 
 
Contributory negligence claims against the Claimant: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The Defendant need not show that the Claimant owed them a duty of 
care in the circumstances. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Contributory negligence claims against a third party: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Establishing the standard of care: 
 
While the Defendant need to establish that the Claimant or third party 
owed them a duty of care, they must establish what the standard of care 
would have been reasonably expected of the Claimant/third party to 
identify whether had been negligent. 
 
When doing this, the court will always look at what was reasonable in 
the circumstances. 
 
Children: 
 Gough v Thorne Children could also be potentially held liable for 
contributory negligence if they have reached the age where the court 
believes it would have been reasonable of them to take precautions. 
 
Employees: 
 In relation to employers' liability, employees may also be found to be 
contributorily negligent if they have been negligent in their own right, 
contributing to their own injuries. 
 
In determining the standard expected of employees, the court will take 
into account all the circumstances of the case. 
 
Rescuers: 
 Baker In some cases, the Claimant will claim that both the original 
tortfeasor and their rescuer was negligent, if the rescuer's negligence 
contributed to their injuries. In this case, the standard expected of 
rescuers is the standard of a reasonable rescuer. 
 
Heat of the moment decisions: 
 Where the Defendant's negligence causes an emergency situation, and 
the Claimant finds themselves in an imminent danger as a result, the 
court will lower the standard expected of Claimants, who may be 
making decisions in the heat of the moment. 
 
VOLUNTARY ASSUMPTION OF RISK (VOLENTI NON 
FIT INJURIA): 
 
Where the Claimant had full knowledge of the risk and they freely and 
voluntarily consented to it, the Defendant will not be held liable. 
 
It is not sufficient to show that the Claimant knew of the risk, the 
Claimant must actually consent to it. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Example: 
 
Samuel ordered 120 sets of curtains from Dreamy Curtains Ltd for a 
hotel renovation project. The curtains, which were custom made, 
turned out to be the wrong colour, instead of teal, they were 
cornflower blue. The contract did not specify the colour. 
 
Samuel made a claim against Dreamy Curtains. Dreamy Curtains, in 
their defence, made a counterclaim against Samuel for contributory 
negligence, claiming that he selected the wrong colour, royal blue on 
the website when he made the order. While the colour the curtains 
turned out to be was not royal blue, cornflower blue is closer to royal 
blue than teal on the colour wheel. 
C 
D 
Claim 
Counterclaim 
(in the Defence) 
If the Claimant was themselves 
negligent, thus contributing to their 
own losses, the Defendant can make 
a counterclaim against them in their 
defence. 
 
The Defendant must show that: 
1. The Claimant did not take 
reasonable care. 
 AND 
2. This has contributed to the 
losses they have suffered. 
C 
D 
Claim 
Counterclaim, add 
as additional D 
If a third party was negligent, they, 
can be added to the claim as a joint 
tortfeasor, 
as 
an 
additional 
Defendant to the claim. 
 
If you struggle to identify whether 
the counterclaim should be made 
against the Claimant or a third 
party, ask, who was the one who 
suffered a loss and will thus be 
making the claim? 
TP 
Example: 
 
Samuel ordered 120 sets of curtains from Dreamy Curtains Ltd for a 
hotel renovation project. The curtains, which were custom made, 
turned out to be the wrong colour, instead of teal, they were 
cornflower blue. The contract did not specify the colour. 
 
Samuel made a claim against Dreamy Curtains. Dreamy Curtains, in 
their defence, made a counterclaim against another company, 
Luscious Fabrics Ltd, as they were the ones who sourced the fabric 
for the curtains. 
Example 1: 
 
In the medical context, patient must be made aware of material risks 
involved in their surgeries. If Adam is to have a surgery to his 
eustachian tube, he must be informed of all the risks involved and 
must sign a consent form before the surgery could be performed. In 
this case, if one of the risks materialises, Adam will have no claim 
against the surgeon. 
Example 2: 
 Dom broke his leg while playing in rugby match. He believes that this 
was caused by a negligent tackle by the opposing team. If he were 
to make a claim, the court would likely decide that Dom voluntarily 
assumed risk in the ordinary course of the game by participating.

pages.heading: The test for consent to apply – the Defendant must show that: · The Claimant was fully aware of the nature and extent of the risk
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Prep notes | Page 12 of 27 
 
The test for consent to apply – the Defendant must show that: 
 
1. 
The Claimant was fully aware of the nature and extent of the risk 
involved in the activities. – Dann 
 
 AND 
2. 
The Claimant has freely consented to the risk either expressly 
(by making a statement or signing a consent form) or impliedly 
(by way of the actions). 
 
Consent is not freely given if there is a relationship of dominance 
between the parties. – such as employer-employee relationship 
or the relationship between married couples. 
 
Smith Baker In cases where there is unequal power in the 
relationship, the courts are not likely to find consent. 
 
This is a complete defence to negligence. 
 
However, the court will rarely find that this defence applies in practice. 
The court is more likely to find contributory negligence, where the 
Claimant failed to take reasonable care of their own safety. 
 
Illegal activities: 
 The court will not accept the argument of voluntary assumption of a risk 
or even contributory negligence where the Defendant was engaging in a 
clearly illegal activity. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
EXCLUSION OF LIABILITY: 
 
If there is a contractual exclusion of liability for death or personal injury 
arising from negligence, this will not be enforced by the court and 
negligence claim is still valid. 
 
Other exclusions of liability for negligence will be enforced only if they 
are reasonable. 
 
In order to establish whether the clause was reasonable, use: 
– 
The reasonability test under the Unfair Contract Terms Act 1977 
(for business-to-business transactions). 
– 
The fairness test in the Consumer Rights Act 2015 (for businessto-consumer transactions). 
 
CRIMINAL ACTIVITY (ILLEGALITY): 
 
If a Defendant negligently injures a Claimant whilst that Claimant was 
undertaking criminal activity or immoral conduct, this will serve as a 
complete defence. 
 
This defence is also called “Illegality” or “Ex turpi causa non oritur”, 
meaning that no claim may arise from an illegal/disgraceful cause. 
 
Ashton If the Claimant and Defendant were both parties to a burglary, 
and the Claimant is injured due to the negligent driving of the Defendant 
of the getaway car while driving away from the crime scene, the 
Claimant will not have the right to make a claim for negligence. 
 
Potential criminal activities that may apply in these scenarios: 
1. 
Stealing a car together and due to the Defendant's negligent 
driving, the Claimant is injured in an accident. 
2. 
Street racing 
3. 
Drink driving 
4. 
Theft 
5. 
Burglary 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
NECESSITY: 
 
There might be emergency situations, where a reasonable person might 
decide that causing some damage is a worthy sacrifice in order to 
prevent a much greater harm. 
 
Cope However, these situations must be of sufficient scale in 
comparison to the harm caused by the Defendant. The more serious the 
emergency situation, and the smaller the harm caused, the more likely 
that the Defendant's actions will be justified by the circumstances. 
 
If the argument is accepted by the court, it is a complete defence to 
negligence. 
 
Medical cases: 
 Re A (Children) (Conjoined Twins: Surgical Separation) Use the 
following test in relation to the application of necessity in the medical 
context: 
 
1. 
The act which has caused the harm was necessary to avoid an 
inevitable and irreparable evil. 
 
2. 
There was no more done than what was reasonably necessary 
to achieve this purpose. 
 AND 
3. 
The harm caused must not be disproportionate to the evil 
avoided. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
MISTAKE: 
 
This defence can only apply to negligent misstatements where the 
Defendant truly believed that the statement they have made was 
correct and has made an honest mistake. 
 
However, mistake does not apply to ordinary negligence cases. 
 
 
 
 
 
Example 1: 
 Two men are at the pub, drinking. One of them offers to drive the 
other home, the other man accepts and gets in the car with him, 
despite knowing that the man was drunk. On the way home, the 
drunk driver crashes the car into a tree, causing serious injuries to 
the other man. 
 
The injured man can now make a claim for negligence against the 
drunk driver, and the drunk driver cannot rely on the argument that 
the other man consented or was contributorily negligent for getting 
in the car. 
Example 2: 
 A group of chemistry students decide to create and detonate 
homemade fireworks without a permit. During the setup process, 
one of the students accidentally detonates one of the fireworks 
early, injuring the students standing nearby. 
 
The students standing nearby may make a claim against the 
students setting up the fireworks. While they may have consented 
to the risk by watching, this will not mitigate the student's liability. 
Example: 
 Gabriel and Harry decide to engage in street racing at night. Gabriel 
drives too fast and loses control of the vehicle, crashing into the 
Harry, driving his car. Gabriel's vehicle also crashes into a car parked 
on a driveway. Unbeknownst to them, a woman was sleeping in the 
car, and she is now seriously injured. 
 
In this case, Harry cannot make a claim against Gabriel as he was 
also part of the criminal activity (street racing). However, the injured 
woman may potentially have a claim against Gabriel. 
Example: 
 
Elizabeth is a surgeon, operating on Herman, when his heart stops 
on the operative table. The medical team manages to resuscitate 
him, leaving a number of broken ribs behind, which would 
potentially take an additional 4 months to heal. When Herman 
wakes up, and decides to make a claim, he will argue that he has 
never signed a consent form to be resuscitated. However, as he 
would have died without the resuscitation, the court would likely 
accept the defence of necessity in this case.

pages.heading: ROAD TRAFFIC ACCIDENT CLAIMS · COMMON LAW DUTY OF CARE:
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Prep notes | Page 13 of 27 
 
ROAD TRAFFIC ACCIDENT CLAIMS 
 
COMMON LAW DUTY OF CARE: 
 
Motorist owe a common law duty of care to other road users/ 
pedestrians/those occupying property adjacent to the highway to drive 
or conduct themselves with reasonable care and skill expected of a 
reasonably competent driver. 
 
This duty includes: Highway Code 
1. 
The duty to drive with reasonable care and attention. – Rule 
144 
2. 
The duty not to drive under the influence of alcohol – Rule 95 
3. 
The duty to signal to warn other users of the intention to stop – 
Rule 103 
4. 
The duty to obey traffic lights signals and they must not proceed 
through the green lights if there is obvious danger. – Rule 109 
5. 
The duty not to exceed the speed limit. – Rule 124 
6. 
The duty to be considerate and to not become agitated while 
driving. – Rule 147 
7. 
The duty to check surroundings and blind spot before moving 
off. – Rule 159 
8. 
The duty not to overtake a vehicle approaching a crossing. – Rule 
191 
 
Breach of the highway code is not punishable, but it helps to prove a 
breach of duty which is necessary to make a claim in tort. 
 
BREACH OF DUTY: 
 
Rear end shunt cases: 
 
Go through this section if the accident was caused by a read end shunt. 
 
If a driver drives into the rear of another, there is a strong inference of 
negligence and the following vehicle will be held liable. 
 
Identify the breach. 
The rear end of of the C's car was hit by D's car. 
 
Identify what D should have done to comply with their duty: 
* 
Keeping adequate distance after C's car and 
* 
Driving within the speed limit so that they can stop on time. 
* 
Not diverting their attention by using mobile phone 
* 
Not driving under the influence of alcohol 
 
Defences and Contributory negligence: 
1. 
If the accident is wholly caused by the abrupt and immediate halt 
of a vehicle in front – this is not foreseeable. 
2. 
If the front car performs an emergency stop but both parties 
were negligent, a finding of contributory negligence may be 
made reducing the damages payable by D. 
3. 
If a car was overtaking another vehicle and suddenly cut in front 
of them, the front car will be liable. – Luffman v Coshall 
 
Collision: 
 
Go through this section if the injury was due to a collision in the centre 
of the road. 
 
Identify the breach. 
D's car colliding with C'car in the centre of the road. 
 
Liability: 
If there is a collision in the centre of the road and there is no other 
evidence, both will be liable 50-50%. 
 
Defences and Contributory negligence: 
If there is evidence to suggest negligence such as losing control of the 
vehicle or negligent driving, the court will follow rely on that evidence to 
find one party liable. 
 
Traffic Signal cases: 
 
Go through this section if the collision was immediately after passing the 
traffic lights. 
 
Identify the breach. 
D proceeded through the red light or D proceeded through the green 
light when there was obvious danger in proceeding. 
 
Identify what D should have done to comply with their duty: 
* 
Obeying the traffic lights 
* 
Driving within the speed limits 
* 
Paying undivided attention to the road to notice any dangers 
 
Defences and Contributory negligence: 
In a case where a taxi proceeded through a green light and a cyclist went 
through a red light collided, liability was split 80/20 in the taxi's favour. 
This was because although the taxi driver passed through the green light, 
collision could have been avoided if they paid attention. 
 
Road rage cases: 
 
Go through this section if the accident was due to road rage. 
 
Identify the breach. 
Drivers caused an accident due to their road rage. 
 
Identify what D should have done to comply with their duty. 
Keeping calm and considerate at all times as to not become agitated. 
 
Defences and Contributory negligence: 
In a case where more than one drivers are at fault, the driver that 
demonstrated road rage will likely have an increased percentage 
towards damages. 
 
Influence of alcohol: 
 
Go through this section if the accident was caused by driving under the 
influence of alcohol. 
 
Identify the breach. 
Driving under the influence of alcohol. 
 
Identify what D should have done to comply with their duty. 
Not to driver under the influence of alcohol and drive with reasonable 
care and attention. 
 
CONTRIBUTORY NEGLIGENCE: 
 
Duty to wear a seat belt: 
 
Drivers: 
 
Failure to wear a seatbelt may constitute to contributory negligence: 
Froom v Butcher 
* 
if injuries would have been prevented by wearing the seatbelt – 
damages should be reduced by 25%. 
* 
if medical evidence only shows that not wearing a seatbelt made 
a considerable difference – damages should be reduced by 15%. 
 
Passengers: 
 
The duty to wear a seatbelt extends to passengers. The percentage 
awarded will follow the rule in Froom v Butcher. 
 
Emergency services: 
 
If road users fail to react to the signs of an approaching emergency 
vehicle (sirens/flashing light) and the emergency vehicle causes an 
accident, the driver of the emergency vehicle will not be liable. 
 
Pedestrians: 
 
Drivers have a duty to anticipate dangers on the road and should drive 
more carefully if they see that a dangerous situation could potentially 
arise. 
 
This includes: 
* 
A pedestrian walking in the centre of the road. – If the pedestrian 
is struck, the pedestrian will likely be found 40% contributory 
negligent. 
* 
A child is walking on the side of the road. – The child might 
suddenly run across the road. 
 
Drivers will not be held liable if they could not have anticipated the 
pedestrian's actions. – eg. jumping in front of the car. However, if a child 
jumps in front of the car, then it is arguably something the driver could 
have anticipated. 
 
But pedestrians will not be held more responsible than the driver unless 
they suddenly moved into the vehicle's path. 
 
Examples of contributory negligence: 
* 
A pedestrian walking in the centre of the road. 
* 
A parent not holding their child's hand next to a busy road will 
be held to be negligent. 
 
There can be no contributory negligence: 
* 
A 6-year-old child walking on the side of the road, suddenly 
running across the street is unlikely to be found negligent. 
Children at that age cannot appreciate the danger of running 
across the street on a busy road. However, 10-year-olds are 
more likely to be found negligent when running across the street 
without looking both ways first.

pages.heading: CAUSATION: · The onus is on the Claimant to prove that their injuries were caused by
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Prep notes | Page 14 of 27 
 
CAUSATION: 
 
The onus is on the Claimant to prove that their injuries were caused by 
the breach of duty which is not too remote. C must show that but for 
D's breach, the injuries would not have occurred. 
 
D can dispute causation by: 
1. 
Arguing that they did not cause the accident or 
2. 
Arguing contributory negligence. 
 
s.1 Law Reform (Contributory Negligence) Act 1945 If anyone who 
suffers an injury partly due to his own fault, damages will be reduced to 
such an extent as court thinks just and equitable.

pages.heading: VICARIOUS LIABILITY · Vicarious liability = the Employer is liable for the torts committed by
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Prep notes | Page 15 of 27 
 
VICARIOUS LIABILITY 
 
Vicarious liability = the Employer is liable for the torts committed by 
employee, even if employer has not been guilty of any personal 
negligence. 
 
Where vicarious liability is owed, the Claimant may make a claim against 
both the tortfeasor (the person who committed the tort) and their 
Employer. – eg. if you are injured due to the negligence of a driver, then 
you can sue both the driver and their employer if they were employed 
and hit you during work hours. 
 
REQUIREMENTS: 
 
Requirements for vicarious liability to apply: 
– 
The tortfeasor must be an employee 
– 
Act must have been closely connected to the task the employee 
was employed to carry out. 
 AND 
– 
The tort must have been committed in the course of 
employment. 
 
The duty may arise for an employee's tort committed against 
customers, other employees and any third parties even if they had no 
connection to the employer's business. 
 
Who is an employee? 
 
Employee = a person who undertakes to do work for another under a 
contract of service. 
 
Independent contractor = a person who undertakes to do work for 
another under a contract for services. 
 
Barclays Bank plc (2020) The employer will not generally be liable for 
any torts committed by their independent contractors. – However, if the 
breach of duty was in relation to a duty owed by the employer which 
was simply delegated to the independent contractor, then the employer 
remains liable. 
 
Tests to establish whether the Defendant was an employee: 
* 
Control test 
* 
Integration test 
* 
Mutuality of obligations test 
* 
Other factors 
 
Control Test: Yewens v Noakes 
 Court considers the degree of control exercised by the employer over 
the work. 
 
More likely to be an employee if: 
The Employer has control over how, where and when work is carried out. 
 
Integration test: Stevenson 
 The test considers whether the tortfeasor was an integral part of the 
employer's business, or someone who is merely ancillary to it. This 
includes a number of factors, whether they attend work events, wear a 
uniform, and have a designated work station. 
 
Mutuality of obligations test: Ready Mixed Concrete 
 Is there an obligation to provide work and to perform work? – eg. must 
accept work when offered. 
 
More likely to be an employee if: 
Tortfeasor has not worked elsewhere and/or has been provided with 
work continuously for years. 
 
Additional factors: 
– 
Whether wages, taxes and national insurance are paid through 
the employer. 
– 
Whether tools and equipment are provided by the employer or 
the worker. 
– 
Whether the worker is being directed as to the mode of 
performance and to what degree. 
– 
Whether the worker is required to wear a uniform. 
– 
Whether the worker receives a pension. 
– 
Whether the employer controls the work hours and where the 
work is being carried out. 
– 
Whether the worker has a financial risk. 
 
No particular factor is decisive, and all circumstances are considered. 
 
Borrowed employees: 
 In some cases, employees may be lent our hired by or to another 
company. 
 
Mersey Docks and Harbour Board Proper test is whether the hirer did 
or did not have the authority to control the manner in which the act 
involving negligence was performed. 
 
 
Relationships akin to employment: 
 Where the Defendant and the tortfeasor are not bound by a contract of 
employment, however their relationship has the same features, the 
relationship can properly give rise to vicarious liability for reasons that it 
is akin to between an employer and employee. 
 
Barclays Bank plc (2020) In this case, the relationship between the 
employer and the tortfeasor must be analogous to an employment 
relationship. 
 
In order to identify whether there was a relationship analogous to 
employment, the court must look at the practical reality of the 
relationship between the parties. 
 
Closely connected: 
 
Close Connection test: Lister v Hesley Hall 
There must have been a sufficiently close and direct connection between 
what the employee was employed to do, and the tort was committed by 
the employee. 
 
Torts committed in the course of employment: 
 
Negligent and careless act: 
 Employer will be liable where the employee commits a tortious act but 
was still acting within the authority given to him by the employer. 
 
Diversions and detours: 
 Employees who make a detour from an authorised route will be 
considered as acting within in the course of their employment, as long 
as they are still engaged in the business of their employer. 
− 
However, a new and independent journey which is solely undertaken 
for the selfish purposes of the employee should not give rise to vicarious 
liability. 
 
Disobedience: 
 
− 
If the employee disobeyed the employer's instructions, that means that 
the act they committed was outside of the course of employment and the 
employer will not be liable. 
 
However, simply because the employer has placed an express prohibition 
on certain behaviour, it does not mean that carrying out that act will fall 
outside of the ambit of vicarious liability. When carrying out that act, they 
will still be acting within the course of employment. 
 
Disobedience does not take the matter outside the scope of employment, 
if they simply carried out what was asked of them in a different manner. 
– eg. if a driver also took passengers on their journey of delivering mail, 
when they were not supposed to. 
 
Joel v Morrison The act of an employee will fall outside of ordinary course 
of employment if they have acted on a frolic of their own. – they must 
have done something majorly different from what was expected of them. 
– eg. deviating from the usual route in a major way. 
 
OTHER SITUATIONS: 
 
Criminal acts: 
 
In some cases, tortious liability will also attach to criminal acts, and a 
Claimant might have a claim in tort. If that is the case, the employer 
might be liable for the criminal acts of their employees well. 
 
Agency: 
 
 When one party is under a duty to act for or give advice for the benefit 
of another on matters within the scope of their relationship, a fiduciary 
relationship is created. This will give rise to vicarious liability. 
 
Partnership: 
 Partnership Act 1980 A partnership and each partner is vicariously liable 
for the wrongful acts or omissions of another partner, as long as the 
partner was acting within his authority, or whilst in the ordinary course 
of the firm's business.

pages.heading: EMPLOYERS' LIABILITY · Employers owe a duty of care to their employees to ensure that they
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Prep notes | Page 16 of 27 
 
EMPLOYERS' LIABILITY 
 
Employers owe a duty of care to their employees to ensure that they 
are safe while they are at their place of work. This duty has been laid 
out both in common law and statute, and a claim may be made under 
both. 
 
STATUTORY DUTIES: 
 
There are a number of different regulations which apply to the 
workplace, setting out the duties of an employer. 
 
Workplace Regs 1992: 
 
Reg. 5 The workplace shall be maintained in an efficient state, efficient 
working order and good repair. 
 Reg. 6 Ventilation 
 
Reg. 7 Temperature in indoor workplaces 
 
Reg. 8 Lighting 
 Reg. 10 Room dimensions and space 
 
Reg. 11 Workstations and seating 
 Reg. 13 Falls and falling objects. 
 Reg. 14 Windows, and transparent or translucent doors, gates and walls. 
 
Reg. 17 Organisation of traffic routes 
 Reg. 20 Sanitary conveniences 
 
Reg. 21 Washing facilities 
 Reg. 22 Drinking water 
 Reg. 24 Facilities for changing clothing 
 
Cleanliness: Reg. 9 
 
Reg. 9(2) The surfaces shall be kept sufficiently clean. 
 
Conditions of floors and traffic routes: Reg. 12 
 
Every floor in a workplace must: 
* 
Be suitably constructed for the purpose for which it is used. – eg. 
Floor that is in constant use must be constructed using more 
sturdy materials than floor that is rarely used. 
* 
Have no hole or slope or be uneven or slippery. 
* 
Be kept free from substances which may cause a person to slip. 
 
Reg. 12(5) Employers must provide a suitable and sufficient handrail for 
staircases. 
 
Management of Health & Safety at Work Regs 1999: 
 
Risk assessment: Reg. 3 
 Employers must carry out risk assessments, assessing: 
(a) Health and safety risks to its employees to which they are 
exposed while at work. 
 AND 
(b) Health and safety risks to persons not in its employment arising 
out of or in connection with their conduct. 
 
Evidence of risk assessment: Accident report book to note past 
accidents and committee meeting minute to see if risks were discussed. 
 
Principles of prevention: Reg. 4 
 
If an employer identifies a risk, they should look at Sched 1 which sets 
out the order for implementing preventative measures. 
 
Hierarchy of control measures: 
a) 
Avoid the risk 
b) 
Evaluate the unavoidable risks 
 AND 
c) 
Combat risks at source – eg. by adapting processes 
 
Health and safety arrangements: Reg. 5 
 Employers must prepare and implement suitable health and safety 
measures. In assessing the necessary measures, employers must have 
regard to the nature and size of the business. 
 
Information for employees: Reg. 10 
 Employers must give information that is comprehensible to employees 
on health and safety risks and protective measures that should be 
adopted. 
 
Employee capabilities and health and safety training: Reg. 13 
Employers must provide employees with adequate health and safety 
training. Training should be repeated periodically and kept up to date. 
 
 
Employees' duties: Reg. 14 
(i) 
To use machinery as per the training/instructions 
 
 AND 
(ii) To inform employer of dangers 
 
Manual Handling Operations Regs 1992: 
 
Reg. 2(1) Manual handling = an operation involving the transportation 
of load including lifting, carrying, pushing, pulling, using force. 
 
Duties of employers: Reg. 4 
Reg. 4(1) Each employer shall: 
(a) so far as is reasonably practicable, avoid the need for his 
employees to undertake any manual handling operations or 
work which involve a risk of their being injured; or 
(b) where it is not reasonably practicable: 
(i) 
Assess manual handling operation, and 
(ii) Take appropriate steps to reduce the risk of injury. 
 
Reg. 4(2) The assessment shall be reviewed by the employer if: 
a) 
there is reason to suspect that it is no longer valid; or 
b) 
there has been a significant change in the manual handling 
operations. 
 
Reg. 4(3) To determine if the manual handling required involves a risk 
of injury and the steps to reduce that risk, consider: 
(a) the physical suitability of the employee 
(b) the clothing, footwear or other personal effects they are wearing 
(c) his knowledge and training 
(d) the results of any risk assessment 
(e) if the employee is within the group identified by the assessment 
as being especially at risk; and 
(f) the results of health surveillance 
 
Duty of employees: Reg. 5 
Employees must make full and proper use of any system of work 
provided by the employer in compliance with Reg. 4(1)(b)(ii). 
 
PUWER 1998: 
 
Suitability of work equipment: Reg. 5 
Employers must ensure that work equipment is constructed/adapted 
as to be suitable for the purpose for which it is used/provided. 
 
Work equipment = any machine, apparatus, tool or installation used at 
work and includes any equipment used at work. 
 
In selecting work equipment employers must have regard to: 
1. 
the working conditions and 
2. 
the health and safety risks in the premises/undertaking where 
work equipment is to be used and 
3. 
additional risks posed by the use of that work equipment. 
 
Maintenance: Reg. 5 
Employers must ensure that work equipment is maintained in an 
efficient state, in efficient working order and in good repair. 
 
Inspection: Reg. 6 
Employers should set up an inspection regime as appropriate. The 
concept of risk assessment comes into play here as the inspection should 
be at suitable intervals. – evidence of this: record of system of inspection 
and record of risk assessment to establish whether the risk has been 
identified and that preventative measures were put in place. 
 
Specific risks: Reg. 7 
Employers must ensure that machinery, with a specific risk to health and 
safety, is only used by employees who are trained and who constantly 
use the machine. This is also the case for repairs, modifications and 
maintenance. 
 
Information and instructions: Reg. 8 
Employers must provide adequate health and safety information to 
employees who use their work equipment. 
 
Training: Reg. 9 
Employers must ensure that all persons who use work equipment have 
received adequate training as to how to use work equipment for the 
purpose of health and safety. The training should be kept up to date. 
 
Dangerous part of machinery: Reg. 11 
Employers must prevent their employees having contact with any 
dangerous part of, or a piece of work equipment. All guards and 
protective devices must be suitable for the purpose for which they are 
provided. 
 
Health and Safety (Display Screen Equipment) Regs 1992: 
 
Reg. 2 Employers must perform a suitable analysis of the workstations 
which they have provided to their staff members to be used for work 
purposes.

pages.heading: Reg. 4 Employers must plan the daily work routines of users so that their · users' work on screen equipment is periodically interrupted by
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Prep notes | Page 17 of 27 
 
Reg. 4 Employers must plan the daily work routines of users so that their 
users' work on screen equipment is periodically interrupted by 
breaks/changes of activities to reduce the effect of these equipment on 
their health. 
 
Personal Protective Equipment Regs 1992: 
 
Use these regulations as a last resort. 
 
Provision of personal protective equipment (PPE): Reg. 4 
Reg. 4(1) Employers must provide employees with suitable personal 
protective equipment (PPE). – eg. eye protectors, gloves, footwear etc. 
 
Evidence of this could be: record of issue of PPE equipment 
 
Assessment of PPE: Reg. 6 
Before choosing PPE, an employer/self-employed person must ensure 
that an assessment is made to determine whether the PPE he intends to 
provide is suitable and compatible with other work equipment. 
 
Maintenance and replacement of PPE: Reg. 7 
Employers must ensure that any PPE equipment provided to his 
employees is maintained in an efficient state, in efficient working order 
and in good repair. 
 
Information, instruction and training: Reg. 9 
The employer must ensure that the employee is provided with such 
information and training as is adequate to enable the employee to 
know: 
* 
The risk(s) which the PPE will avoid or limit 
* 
The purpose for which PPE is to be used 
* 
How to use the equipment and 
* 
Any action to be taken by the employee to ensure that the PPE 
remains in an efficient state, in efficient working order and in 
good repair as required by Reg. 7(1). 
 
Use of PPE: Reg. 10 
* 
Employers must take all reasonable steps to ensure that any PPE 
provided to their employees under Reg. 4(1) is effectively use. –
evidence of this could be: record of warning that employee 
should use PPE. 
* 
Employers must take reasonable measures to ensure that its 
employees use the equipment. 
 
COMMON LAW: 
 
Primary liability: 
 
Duty of care and breach: 
 
Employer's duty of care covers – to provide employees with: 
Wilsons and Clyde Coal v English 
* 
Safe equipment 
* 
A safe place of work 
* 
A safe system of work 
 AND 
* 
Competent fellow staff members (the employer must take 
reasonable care to ensure competency, by providing training, 
disciplining staff, hiring competent employees/contractors) 
 
The employer's duty is non-delegable. While employers may outsource 
certain tasks related to discharging their obligations to an appointed 
agent and must take reasonable care themselves and will remain 
personally liable. 
 
If the employees or the appointed agent breaches their duty and fails 
to exercise reasonable care, the employer will be vicariously liable. 
 
The duty of the employer is to take reasonable care, not to ensure 
absolute safety. 
 
Adequate plant and equipment – an employer must ensure that: 
 
* 
Machinery/equipment are safe, and safety features/protective 
clothing are provided 
* 
Machinery/equipment are properly maintained 
* 
Premises are safe and free from defects – eg. floor should not be 
slippery. 
 
This duty extends to other premises to which employees are sent but 
only to the extent that employer is aware of a specific danger at the 
other premises. 
 
Employer's Liability (Defective Equipment Act) 1969 If an employee is 
injured by equipment with a latent defect due to the negligence of a 
third party, the employer will also be deemed negligent. – eg. 
manufacturer. 
 
If employer fails to provide adequate premises, they may also be liable 
under occupiers' liability. 
 
Safe system of work – employers should implementing a safe system, 
considering: 
* 
The sequence/method by which work is carried out 
* 
The physical layout of the job 
* 
Providing special instructions, warnings and notices 
* 
Taking any safety precautions 
 
An employer can also be held liable if the stress levels at work are high, 
contributing to a higher risk to employees. – Barber v Somerset County 
Council 
 
Competent fellow workers: Latimer v AEC 
 
Employers must hire staff members who are competent by carrying out 
checks into their background and level of experience and education. If 
necessary, the employer must provide adequate training. 
 
Staff members must be sufficiently competent so as not to put other 
employees at risk. – eg. cleaners should be competent in cleaning and 
should check for and clean spillages throughout the workday. 
 
An employer can be held liable for practical jokes but only to the extent 
that they knew/ought to have known that employee was a prankster. 
 
Causation: 
 
Usually not an issue in these cases, if the employer breached its duty and 
the employee suffered an injury as a result, the employer will likely be 
held negligent. – Ask what caused C's injury? Was it the negligence? 
 
Vicarious liability: 
 
Duty of care and breach: 
 
Employers are primarily liable for their employees at common law. It 
may also be vicariously liable for the torts of its other employees. 
 
Where an employee injures a fellow worker, the employer will be held 
liable for the negligent acts/omissions of its employees, if the employee 
was acting within the scope of their employment. 
 
Acting in the course of employment: 
Their actions must be closely connected to employment to be held to 
be carried out in the course of employment. 
 
Wallbank v Wallbank Fox Designs Acting with spontaneous force in 
response to instructions in relation to work will be deemed as acting in 
the course of his employment. 
 
Graham v Commercial Bodyworks Ltd Employers creating/enhancing a 
risk does not give rise to a sufficiently close connection between that risk 
and the wrongful act. – eg. employee spraying co-worker's overalls with 
thinning agent and setting them alight is separate from the employer as 
all the employer did was provide the thinning agent for work reasons. 
 
Factors: Graham v Commercial Bodyworks Ltd 
* 
The wrongful act furthers the employer's aims 
* 
The wrongful act is related to friction, confrontation or intimacy 
inherent in the employer's enterprise. – including horseplay and 
more serious acts such as assault. 
* 
The employment requires the exercise of force 
 
Causation: 
 Usually not an issue in these cases, if an employee breached its duty and 
another employee suffered an injury as a result, the employer will likely 
be held negligent. – Ask what caused C's injury? Was it the negligence? 
 
Defence: 
 
If the employee voluntarily assumes risk – high standard and the court 
will rarely agree to this defence.

pages.heading: OCCUPIERS' LIABILITY · DEFINITION:
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Prep notes | Page 18 of 27 
 
OCCUPIERS' LIABILITY 
 
DEFINITION: 
 
Occupiers may be held liable if someone suffers injury or damage is 
caused to items due to the state of their premises under the Occupiers' 
Liability Acts (which includes the 1957 and 1984). 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Definition of “Premises”: 
 Premises = include the buildings on the land and the land itself and 
includes vehicles and fixtures as well. 
 
Disrepair that could potentially give rise to claims: 
* 
Disrepair 
* 
Bad lighting 
* 
Unsafe furniture or items 
* 
Dangerous gases/chemicals 
 
OCCUPIER: 
 
Occupier = someone who has control of the premises. They will be the 
Defendant in these claims. 
 
None of the acts define “occupier”, so we must rely on the common law 
to identify who the occupier is. 
 
Occupier need not have physical possession of the property and need 
not be the owner of the property. 
 
The occupier is the person who has sufficient legal control of the 
property to allow people to access the property or prevent them from 
entering. 
 
There may be multiple occupiers in relation one land, and if that is the 
case, all of them could be liable in respect of the damage. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Who has control? 
 
The level of control exercised will be a question of fact. 
 
Mathewson v Crump (2020) The legal owner may not be the occupier 
if they do not have sufficient control over the premises. – only visiting 
for inspection of the premises if there is a tenant means that there is 
insufficient control. 
 
Harris v Birkenhead Corp Where a house has been purchased and the 
new owner fails to enter the house or take board up the premises, the 
legal right to control will be with the new owners, who will be in the 
best position to prevent accidents. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Wheat v E Lacon In relation to commercial buildings, even if there is an 
appointed manager managing the building and the business, the owner 
will also remain in control of the premises (in addition to the manager 
who will also have control). 
 
Revill v Newbery The occupier is not liable in every situation where an 
incident happens on the land. Occupiers' liability only applies if the 
harm is caused by the dangerous conditions on the land or dangerous 
conduct which constitutes a continuing source of danger on the land. 
 
If the harm is caused by the one-off actions of the occupier, there can 
be no claims for occupiers' liability, although there may be a claim for 
negligence. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The occupier will be the Local Authority for the following: 
* 
Public parks 
* 
Highways 
* 
Schools 
 
VISITORS: 
 
Visitor = someone who invited onto or given permission (either express 
or implied) from the occupier to be on the premises. 
 
If someone enters without permission, that person will be a trespasser 
rather than a visitor. 
 
If a visitor has been given permission to enter, however, that 
permission is withdrawn while the visitor is still on the premises, this 
implies that they have a reasonable time to leave the premises, and if 
they do not do so, that visitor will become a trespasser. 
 
If a visitor enters the premises for their own calling, they will be 
expected to appreciate and guard against any special risks. – eg. 
electricians. 
 
Implied permission: 
 Even if an entrant does not receive express permission, permission may 
be implied from the conduct of the occupier or the circumstances. If 
someone has implied permission, they will be legally classed as a visitor. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Legal rights to enter: 
 Anyone who has a legal right to enter will also be classed as a visitor, 
despite not being given permission by the occupier. However, they 
must enter in order to allow them to carry out their legal duties. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Walkers and ramblers: 
 Countryside and Rights of Way Act 2000 The public has a general right 
to walk over open lands classed as “mountains, moors, heaths or 
downs”, this right is called the right to roam. While walkers and rambles 
are exercising a legal right to roam when walking across these open 
lands, they will be deemed to be trespassers under the acts. 
 
Public rights of way: 
 McGeown v Northern Ireland Housing Anyone walking across public 
areas, exercising their public right of way (walking on the street) is not 
defined as a visitor, and will be deemed to be trespassers under the 
acts. 
 
The reason for this is because it is impossible to predict every type of 
person who may use these rights of way, and it is impossible to allow 
each one of them to safely use the right of way. 
 
RISK CREATED BY THIRD PARTIES: 
 
In some cases, the risk is created by a third party, rather than the 
occupier. If this is the case, we need to look at the rules that apply 
depending on who has created the risk. 
 
Risk created by an independent contractor: 
 
If there is an independent contractor who works on the premises and 
a visitor is injured because of the independent contractor, the occupier 
will have met their duty if they took reasonable care in entrusting the 
work of the contractor and could reasonably conclude that the 
contractor was competent. 
 
 
 
Example: 
Anne visited Lina's house one afternoon for tea. Lina has spilled 
some tea onto the floor earlier and Anne slipped and fell, breaking 
her arm. Anne may make a claim for Occupiers' Liability and Lina will 
likely have to compensate her for her injuries. 
Example: 
If a landlord rents a room to a tenant in a shared house, the tenant 
will have everyday control of the room and the landlord will also be 
the occupier by having the right to enter the room to carry out 
repairs. If the room is in disrepair, both the landlord and tenant could 
be liable for any injuries this may cause to visitors/trespassers. 
Example: 
A compulsory purchase order has been served on the owners of a 
house by the council. After the purchase, the residents move out, and 
the council fails to board up the house. Harvey, a five-year old boy 
wanders into the house through the door and falls from the first floor. 
In this case, the legal occupier will be the council, the new buyers, 
despite the disrepair being caused by the original owners. 
Example: 
 Joseph is an elderly man, whose home is commonly visited by
