vandals and thieves, as a result, he decides to start sleeping in his 
shed with a shotgun. David sneaks onto Joseph's land, intending to 
steal. Joseph hears movements from outside the shed, so he wakes 
up and fires his gun through a small hole, shooting David in the arm. 
In this case, the fact that Joseph was an occupier does not make him 
liable for occupiers' liability, however, David may have a claim for 
ordinary negligence. 
Examples of entrants with implied permission: 
* 
Deliverymen 
* 
Postmen 
* 
Door-to-door salespeople 
* 
Meter readers 
* 
Repairmen 
Examples of entrants with legal right to enter: 
* 
Police officers 
* 
Ambulance workers 
* 
Firefighters

pages.heading: Risk created by a stranger: · Wheat v E Lacon If the risk has been created by a stranger, the occupier
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Prep notes | Page 19 of 27 
 
Risk created by a stranger: 
 
Wheat v E Lacon If the risk has been created by a stranger, the occupier 
will not be responsible for the injuries/losses caused. 
 
DUTY OWED TO LAWFUL VISITORS: 
 
s.2(2) Occupiers' Liability Act 1957 Duty owed by the occupier to lawful 
visitors. The occupier must take reasonable care to ensure that visitors 
can safely use the premises. 
 
There is no requirement to provide absolute safety, however, the 
occupier must have taken reasonable steps to protect visitors against 
harm. – eg. this would include giving warning of danger. 
 
If there has been a breach of occupiers' duties, the rules on causation 
will apply. 
Ward v The Ritz Hotel While taking into safety standards is simply a 
recommendation and not a legal requirement, failing to follow safety 
standards could show that the occupier had not taken reasonable care. 
 
Darby v National Trust There is no requirement to warn about obvious 
risks. Land with ponds and rivers on them do not need to have a sign 
warning about the danger of drowning. 
 
Clare v Perry When deciding which steps are reasonable for an occupier 
to take to discharge their duty, look at the behaviour reasonably 
expected of a visitor. – occupiers need not guide against unusual or 
erratic behaviour such as climbing over fences/walls. 
 
Duty owed to children: 
 
s.2(3)(a) Occupiers' Liability Act 1957 The occupier must take into 
account when looking after the premises that children visiting will be 
less careful than adults. 
 
Perry v Butlins Holiday World The occupier should not have areas 
where children would easily injure themselves near a playground or an 
area where children's shows are commonly performed. – eg. sharp, 
hard edges near a playground. 
 
Jolley v London Borough of Sutton The occupier should not keep 
fixtures or chattels on the land which are dangerous but would attract 
children. Identify whether it was foreseeable that the fixture or chattel 
would attract children. – eg. an old boat with a rotting floor, old tree 
house. 
 
Glasgow Corp v Taylor Bushes/shrubs with poisonous berries should 
be fenced off with a warning notice because it would attract children. 
The occupier must know that the berries are poisonous, otherwise they 
would not have a duty to warn against the risk. 
 
Duty owed to skilled visitors: 
 
s.2(3)(b) Occupiers' Liability Act 1957 Professional, or skilled visitors 
are expected to anticipate certain special risks and avoid accidents. 
 
Roles v Nathan Chimney sweeps must anticipate the risk of carbon 
monoxide gas if they work on the chimney while it is alight. 
 
Ogwo v Taylor Fire-fighters may have a claim for occupiers' liability if 
the fire was caused by the negligence of the owner and the fire-fighter 
is injured while trying to put out the fire. This argument can only be 
relied on by the firefighter if the fire is so severe that there is no amount 
of care or expertise that could have protected the fire-fighter. 
 
Defences: 
 
Contributory negligence: 
 Visitors ought to be responsible for their own safety, allows for the 
defence of contributory negligence. 
 
Warning notices: 
 Occupiers may be able to exclude liability by placing warning notices 
on the premises. 
 
s.2(4)(a) OLA 1957 Warning does not automatically absolve an 
occupier from liability. It must enable the visitor to be reasonably safe 
in order to discharge the occupier's duty of care. 
 
Note the difference between a warning notice and a notice seeking to 
exclude or limit liability – former seeks to discharge an occupier's duty 
while the latter seeks to prevent it from arising in the first place. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
DUTY OWED TO TRESPASSERS: 
 
Occupiers' Liability Act 1984 Duty owed by the occupier to persons who 
are not visitors. 
 
Non-visitors = anyone who is not invited/permitted to be on the 
premises by the occupier. This includes trespassers, although the duty 
owed to trespassers is limited. 
 
Requirements for this duty to arise in relation to trespassers: 
* 
The occupier must be aware of the danger and aware that a 
trespasser might encounter it. 
* 
The occupier must take reasonable care to ensure that the 
trespasser does not suffer personal injury. Risk of injury must be 
due to the state of the premises rather than as a result of an 
activity on them. 
 
Defences: 
 
Contributory negligence: 
 Trespasser ought to be responsible for their own safety, allows for the 
defence of contributory negligence. 
 
Warning notices: 
 Occupiers may be able to exclude liability by placing warning notices 
on the premises. 
 
s.1(5) OLA 1984 A warning notice will discharge the occupiers' duty if 
the occupier took reasonable steps to warn trespassers of the danger 
on the premises or discourage them to take the risk. 
 
Note the difference between a warning notice and a notice seeking to 
exclude or limit liability – former seeks to discharge an occupier's duty 
while the latter seeks to prevent it from arising in the first place. 
 
ADDITIONAL DUTIES – LANDLORDS: 
 
Defective Premises Act 1972 A landlord is obliged/permitted to carry 
out repairs to the premises and so has a duty of care in respect of the 
state of the premises. – this duty of care is to take such care as 
reasonable in the circumstances to see that they are reasonably safe 
from personal injury/damage to their property. 
 
This duty covers defects: 
1. 
Within the scope of the landlord's repair obligations/rights 
 AND 
2. 
Which the landlord knew/ought to have known about. 
 
This duty is owed to anyone who might reasonably be expected to be 
affected by this defect.

pages.heading: PRODUCT LIABILITY · If a person is injured by a faulty product, they can:
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Prep notes | Page 20 of 27 
 
PRODUCT LIABILITY 
 
If a person is injured by a faulty product, they can: 
 
* 
Bring a breach of contract claim for breach of one or more 
implied terms of the contract under the Sale of Goods Act 1979 
(business to business contracts) or the Consumer Rights Act 
2015 (business to consumer contracts) 
 
* 
Claim for negligence under the common law 
 OR 
* 
Make a claim under the Consumer Protection Act 1987 
 
The contract law claim requires privity of contract which might be a 
problem in many cases, however, if the Claimant was a party to the 
contract, then it is easier to bring a claim for breach of contract than to 
establish negligence. 
 
The tort claim is fault-based, so fault of the Defendant must be proven, 
which will require a lot of evidence to be provided by the Claimant. 
 
COMMON LAW NEGLIGENCE: 
 
Product liability = a manufacturer's legal responsibility for injury or 
damage caused by a product that they have made or sold. 
 
This type of liability applies when a product is defective or dangerous, 
and it causes harm to a consumer. 
 
Manufacturers are liable in respect of injuries sustained because of 
defective products. 
 
Requirements: 
* 
Breach of duty: 
– 
The standard in negligence applies. The manufacturer 
must have fallen below the standard of care expected of 
them. 
– 
A manufacturer must take reasonable care to the 
consumer who uses the manufacturer's product if the 
manufacturer doesn't expect the product to be 
examined after leaving the manufacturer and before 
reaching the customer (which is common for 
manufactured goods). 
– 
The Claimant must show that there has been a 
manufacturing or design defect. 
 
* 
Causation: 
Damage must have been caused by the faulty product. 
 
Who may be liable? 
– 
The manufacturer 
– 
The retailer of the product is not liable. 
 
To whom the duty is owed? 
– 
The duty is owed to anyone whom the manufacturer could 
reasonably foresee as likely to be affected by a defect in the 
product. 
– 
This includes people who might come into contact with the 
product. – eg. members of the consumer's family. 
 
What is covered? 
– 
Damages for personal injury 
– 
Damage to property 
– 
Consequential economic losses 
 
CONSUMER PROTECTION ACT 1987: 
 
As it is difficult to prove fault on behalf of the manufacturer, the 
Consumer Protection Act introduces strict liability in relation to 
defective products and the Claimant will not need to show that the 
Defendant was at fault. 
 
However, do not confuse strict liability with absolute liability. The 
Claimant need not prove fault, but simply that there has been a defect 
in the product. 
 
Consumer Protection Act 1987 Establishes that liability is imposed in 
respect only of damage caused by a defect in a product. A product is 
defective if its safety does not reach the level a reasonable person is 
entitled to expect. 
 
Product = includes physical goods and electricity. Does not include 
services. – s.1(2)(c) CPA 1987 
 
Defective = being below the standard of safety which one is generally 
entitled to expect. 
 
Who may be liable? s.2 CPA 1987 
 
* 
The manufacturer/producer – includes: 
– 
Manufacturers of the final product 
– 
Manufacturers of components – if the defective element 
if that component. 
– 
Anyone extracting materials to obtain nonmanufactured product 
– 
Anyone carrying out a process to obtain a nonmanufactured product 
 
* 
Abstractors 
 
* 
Persons who are neither manufacturers or abstractors but 
who give agricultural products an essential characterisation by 
means of industrial processes. – such as frozen peas. 
 
* 
EU Importers − Where the producer is in the EU, the liability 
for the product lies on the manufacturer. However where the 
manufacturer (A) is from Japan and it is imported into 
Germany by B and then reimported into UK by C, A and B will 
be strictly liable under the Act. 
 
* 
Own-branders – A supplier who does not manufacture or 
produce the product, but simply brands them to make it 
appear as if they have manufactured/produced the product. 
 
The supplier of the product is only liable if: 
* 
The Claimant requests the name of one of the above parties 
from the supplier. 
* 
It is not reasonably practicable for the Claimant to identify 
those persons independently. 
 AND 
* 
The supplier does not identify the manufacturer/importer. 
 
Time limits: 
 Must be brought within 3 years from the date on which the action 
accrued, or the date of knowledge – this is subject to a 10-year 
overriding limit. 
 
For non-personal injury or death claims: action must be brought within 
10 years from the relevant time. 
 
Defence: 
 
* 
The damage did not exist when the product was supplied. 
 
* 
The Defendant was not acting in the course of business when 
they supplied the product. 
 
* 
The State-of-the-art defence or “Development risk” defence: 
could not have supplied a better product because the 
knowledge/scientific advancements at the time did not allow 
for the creation of a better product. 
 
* 
The defect was caused as a result of fulfilling a statutory 
requirement. 
 
* 
The injury/damage was caused, partially as a result of the 
Claimant's own contributory negligence. – this is a partial 
defence. 
 
* 
The Claimant has voluntarily assumed the risk after becoming 
aware of the defect by deciding to choose the product despite 
the risk. – this is also a partial defence. 
 
Exclusion of liability: 
 s.7 CPA 1987 Liability cannot be excluded/limited under the CPA 1987 
by including a contractual term in the contract or giving notice to the 
Claimant. 
 
Consequences of the tort: 
 The CPA 1987 imposes a strict liability offence, meaning that there no 
need to establish that the tortfeasor intended to cause a harm. 
 
The Claimant does not need to prove negligence, all that needs to be 
established is that the product was defective and caused the damage. 
 
Remedies: 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Damages are recoverable for: 
* Personal injury and death 
* Damage to private property 
(if it is more than £275) 
 
 
Recovery is NOT allowed for: 
* Damage to the defective 
product itself 
* Damage to business 
property 
* Damage to private 
property below £275.

pages.heading: NUISANCE AND · THE RULE IN RYLANDS V FLETCHER
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Prep notes | Page 21 of 27 
 
NUISANCE AND 
THE RULE IN RYLANDS V FLETCHER 
 
PUBLIC NUISANCE: 
 
Public nuisance = nuisance that disturbs the comfort and convenience 
of life for a section of the public. 
 
Public nuisance is not limited to the protection of interest in land. 
 
Elements of public nuisance: 
* That the persons affected by the nuisance constitutes a public or 
a section of the public. 
 AND 
* If an individual claimant is making a claim, they can only do so if 
they have suffered special and particular damage, over and 
above the inconvenience suffered by the public at large. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Consequences of the tort: 
 While public nuisance is a tort, it is also a criminal offence, and 
therefore, carrying out this tort might attract criminal prosecution and 
related penalties, including a prison sentence. 
 
Public nuisance is a strict liability offence, meaning that there no need 
to establish that the tortfeasor intended to commit public nuisance, all 
that needs to be established is that the act has been committed. 
 
PRIVATE NUISANCE: 
 
Private nuisance = violation of real property rights involving either an 
interference with proprietary rights of the occupier, including a legal 
interest such as an easement, or unreasonable interference with the 
occupier's right to use and enjoy it, which is an inherent facet of a right 
of exclusive possession. 
 
Requirements: 
 
Elements of private nuisance: 
* Violation of proprietary rights/the occupier's right to use and 
enjoy the land 
* The interference must be unreasonable 
 AND 
* The interference must be continuing – cannot simply be one 
isolated event. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
While damage may be sufficient, it is not an essential requirement to 
assert a claim in nuisance through interference with the amenity of the 
occupier's land. 
 
Damage must be a foreseeable result of the Defendant's actions. – 
damage cannot be too remote. 
 
Nuisance may be caused by inaction or omission as well as some positive 
activity – this must lead to an unreasonable interference, which goes 
beyond the normal. – such as depriving neighbours of sleep. 
 
Factors to look at when determining unreasonability: 
a. 
Intensity and duration of interference – the shorter the duration 
of the act, the less likely that the use will be found to be 
unreasonable. 
b. 
Sensitivity – No nuisance where damage was result of unusual 
sensitivity. 
c. 
Location – including the character of the neighbourhood. 
d. 
Utility of the Defendant's conduct – where cricket balls entered 
the Claimant's garden several times a year, the court held that 
the social utility of the cricket club outweighed the Claimant's 
inconvenience. 
e. 
Malice 
 
 
 
 
 
Liability: 
 
Creator of the 
nuisance: 
The creator of the 
nuisance needs 
neither own nor 
occupy the land 
from where the 
nuisance originates. 
 
Occupier of the land: 
The occupiers must 
have had the 
knowledge of the 
existence of a drain 
laid by a trespasser, 
without the consent 
of the occupier, which 
caused the risk of 
flooding into the 
neighbours' land – the 
occupier was 
therefore liable for 
nuisance as he had 
continued and 
adopted the nuisance. 
 
Owners of the land: 
Council which 
granted permission 
to a go-kart club to 
use their land for 
the purpose of 
using go-karts were 
held liable in 
nuisance for noise 
caused to the 
claimant who lived 
close to the go-kart 
track. 
 
 
DEFENCES: 
 
Even if a claim for nuisance is made against the tortfeasor, the tortfeasor 
may be able to rely on one of the following defences. 
 
Prescription: 
 A person can be exempt from liability for a nuisance if the conduct that 
caused the nuisance has been ongoing for a sufficient length of time 
and the person who is complaining about the nuisance has known 
about it and failed to take action. 
 
Defence of prescription can be raised if nuisance remains actionable but 
is never claimed for at least 20 years. 
 
Statutory authority: 
 Where Parliament authorises an activity which creates the nuisance, 
the claim for nuisance is not actionable as long as all due care and skill 
has been taken to avoid the nuisance. – Allen 
 
In this case, the tortfeasor will claim that they have been given authority 
by Parliament by relying on a specific statute. 
 
On the other hand, it is also important that they are not exercising their 
statutory powers negligently, because if that is the case, they can no 
longer rely on this defence. 
 
Lawful use of land: 
 If the tortfeasor is able to successfully argue that the nuisance took 
place as a result of the lawful use of the land, then they will also have a 
defence to the nuisance action. 
 
Non-defences: 
 
* That planning permission was granted for the use. – Although 
this appears to fall within one of the defences, whereby the 
nuisance was due to the “lawful use of the land”, this is not 
acceptable in cases where planning permission was granted for 
the use, because despite this, the tortfeasor will have an 
additional duty to not cause nuisance. 
 
* That nuisance was in existence before the Claimant moved in. 
 
REMEDIES: 
 
There are a number of different remedies that can be awarded to the 
victim of nuisance (private or public). 
 
Key remedies: 
1. 
Injunction – best option 
2. 
Damages 
3. 
Abatement 
 
Your client may apply for more than one of these at once as the most 
effective method to further their interests. – eg. instead of simply 
applying for damages, apply for an interim and a final injunction together 
with damages. 
 
Injunction: 
 
The Claimant may force the Defendant to stop the activity by applying 
for an injunction. – however, please note that it is in the court's 
discretion whether to grant this remedy. 
 
In any event, applying for an injunction is the Claimant's best option. 
 
Test for an injunction: 
1. 
Damages must be an inadequate remedy. – eg. if the nuisance is 
disruptive to someone's quality of life or business operations. 
 AND 
2. 
The nuisance is continuing. – it is constant rather than a one-off 
event. 
Examples of public nuisance: 
* Creating danger on/obstructing the highway 
* Carrying on an offensive trade 
* Selling food unfit for consumption 
* Releasing toxic fumes into the air 
Examples of private nuisance: 
* 
Encroachment on a neighbour's land such as overhanging tree 
branches. 
* 
Damage to a neighbour land. 
* 
Nuisance by interference with a neighbour's quiet enjoyment 
of their land.

pages.heading: Types of injunctions to apply for: · Quia timet injunction – apply for this injunction if the damage/
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Prep notes | Page 22 of 27 
 
 
Types of injunctions to apply for: 
 
* 
Quia timet injunction – apply for this injunction if the damage/ 
nuisance has not yet occurred, but the Claimant is expecting that 
it would occur. This injunction would prevent the nuisance. – 
Hext v Gill 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
* 
Interim prohibitory injunction – apply for this injunction to stop 
an existing nuisance while the final hearing is pending. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
* 
Final prohibitory injunction – apply for this injunction to stop an 
existing nuisance at the final hearing. Typically, the tortfeasor 
will be required to stop the nuisance within 14 days from the 
injunction, however, the court may decide that the nuisance 
must stop immediately once the order is granted. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
* 
Final mandatory injunction – apply for this injunction to require 
the tortfeasor to carry out certain positive acts to reduce/stop 
the nuisance. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Damages: 
 
Damages may be awarded to compensate the victim of the nuisance and 
for the damage caused. 
 
In order for damages to be granted, the damage caused by the nuisance 
must be quantifiable. 
 
Damages may also be too remote in some cases, so the court must 
consider the remoteness of damages rule when calculating the damages 
to be granted. The damage that has occurred to the Claimant must have 
been reasonably foreseeable by the tortfeasor. 
 
Damages for public nuisance: 
 One of the requirements for a public nuisance claim is that the Claimant 
must have suffered special damage as a result of the nuisance. 
 
Damages for private nuisance: 
 Private nuisance claims allow for damages to be granted where there 
has been a direct interference with the land. 
 
Damages that may be claimed for private nuisance include: 
1. 
Loss of enjoyment of the property – owner has a right to quiet 
enjoyment. 
2. 
Injury to the land 
3. 
Economic loss 
4. 
Past losses/inconvenience 
 
Abatement: 
 
The Claimant may remedy the nuisance themselves (self-help), by 
carrying out certain works. – eg. installing soundproof wall panels. 
 
Give notice to the tortfeasor prior to carrying out the works so that they 
are given an opportunity to stop the nuisance before spending money. 
 
Later, the Claimant could claim the money spent to remedy the nuisance 
back from the tortfeasor. 
THE RULE IN RYLANDS V FLETCHER: 
 
Rylands v Fletcher The rule in Rylands v Fletcher: The rule imposes strict 
liability on a person who brings onto their land something that is likely 
to do harm if it escapes. – viruses or hazardous chemicals. 
 
Requirements: 
 
Requirements: Rylands v Fletcher 
1. 
The Defendant used the land in a non-natural way for their own 
purposes. 
2. 
As part of this non-natural use, the Defendant brings something 
onto the land, which, if it escapes, is it likely to do damage. 
3. 
The hazardous thing escaped, and the victim suffered a damage 
as a result. 
4. 
This does not need to be a continuing state of affairs. – an 
isolated escape is sufficient. 
 
If, due to the operation of a factory, hazardous chemicals escape and 
contaminate the groundwater or nearby rivers, the person who operates 
the factory may be liable under the rule in Rylands v Fletcher. 
 
Strict liability – Claimant only needed to show that the damage was 
caused by the Defendant, no need to prove negligence. 
 
Consequences of the tort: 
 Rylands v Fletcher imposes a strict liability offence, meaning that there 
no need to establish that the tortfeasor intended to cause a harm, all 
that needs to be established is that the act has been committed. 
 
Liability is also personal to the person who has committed. 
 
Defences: 
 
There are a number of defences that may apply in this case as well. 
 
Possible defences: 
 
* 
The escape was caused by the unforeseeable acts of a stranger 
(however, this cannot be an independent contractor the 
Defendant has hired). 
 
* 
The escape was caused by an unforeseeable natural 
circumstance. – eg. an earthquake. 
 
* 
The Claimant's contributory negligence, contributing to their 
own loss. 
 
* 
Statutory authority. 
 
 
Example: 
A construction company obtains planning permission to carry 
out extensive construction work on a land next to residential 
houses. These works include excavation works, and the 
residents apply for a quia timet injunction to prevent noise, 
air and dust pollution and vibration damage. 
Example: 
Abbie's neighbour is making loud noises by using industrial 
printing machinery at night, so she struggles to fall asleep. 
After asking them to stop (without success), she makes a 
claim. While the hearing is pending, she applies for an interim 
injunction to stop the noise in the meantime. 
Example: 
Abbie's neighbour is making loud noises by using industrial 
printing machinery at night, so she struggles to fall asleep. She 
makes a claim asking the court to grant a final prohibitory 
injunction, requiring her neighbour to stop using the 
machinery at certain times of the day. 
Example: 
George's neighbour installs a drainage system that redirects 
water onto George's land, causing flooding. George could 
make a claim requesting the court to grant a mandatory 
injunction requiring his neighbour to alter the drainage 
system to stop the flooding on George's land.

pages.heading: BREACH OF STATUTORY DUTY · INTRODUCTION:
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Prep notes | Page 23 of 27 
 
BREACH OF STATUTORY DUTY 
 
INTRODUCTION: 
 
There are numerous statutes imposing duties on private individuals, 
companies and/or public bodies. 
 
These statutes may or may not prescribe whether non-performance of 
the duties set out in the statute will amount to tortious or other liability. 
 
Some breaches of statutory duty may not even give rise to a cause of 
action under the statute itself. As a result, the court has made decisions 
as to which statutory duties should attract liability for a breach. 
 
If any statute imposes a duty in the circumstances where the Claimant 
was injured and prescribes that the person in breach should be liable in 
tort, the breach of that duty can be used to prove liability instead of the 
duty owed under negligence, making the court process simpler. 
 
ESTABLISH A TORT CLAIM FOR BREACH OF 
STATUTORY DUTY: 
 
You may be acting for a Claimant client who has suffered an injury as a 
result of a breach of statutory duty. If this is the case, they would want 
you to bring a claim in tort to recover compensation on their behalf. 
 
The general rule: 
 
The statute itself may or may not prescribe whether a claim in tort may 
be brought for breach of the duty. 
 
In some cases, an act may provide that breach of the duty cannot be 
used in a civil case, and it that is the case, you cannot sue in tort for the 
breach. 
 
s.69 Enterprise and Regulatory Reform Act 2013 Any breach of duty 
which arises out of the health and safety regulations that applies to 
employers, cannot give rise to tortious liability unless the legislation 
itself specifically allows Claimant to make civil claims. 
 
X v Bedfordshire County Council By simply having breached a statutory 
duty, the Defendant is not automatically liable in tort. 
 
When is it possible to bring a tort claim? 
 
Two routes to bring an action for breach of statutory duty in tort: 
 
1. 
If there is express wording in the act to say that the Claimant 
could bring a claim. 
2. 
Parliament has shown an intention that the Claimant should be 
able bring a claim. – X v Bedfordshire County Council 
 
Identify this intention by considering the following factors: 
1. 
Who was meant to benefit from the statute 
2. 
Whether there are alternative remedies available for the breach 
3. 
The level of detail in the statute itself 
4. 
The background to the legislation 
 AND 
5. 
The type of harm involved 
 
No single factor alone may be used a conclusive factor in establishing 
statutory duty, but rather, all the factors should be taken into account 
together. 
 
Who was meant to benefit from the statute: 
 
The court will consider whether the statute was meant to confer a 
benefit to the general public or individuals (in which case it would create 
individual rights). 
 
Ex parte Island Records Ltd A statute providing that it was a criminal 
offence to record the live performances of musicians without their 
consent was deemed to benefit musicians. – in this case, musicians 
would have the right to bring a civil tort action in addition to reporting 
this activity to the police. 
 
A claim for statutory duty can only be brought if the statute aimed to 
confer a benefit to individuals or a class of individuals. 
 
X v Bedfordshire County Council In some cases, even if the statute is 
aimed at protecting certain classes of individuals, there court may find 
that the case was aimed to benefit society as a whole. A statute aimed 
to protect children from abuse and provide improved education services 
was deemed to benefit society and not only children. 
 
The Claimant must show that they fall within the class of persons 
intended to be protected by the statute. – eg. for an act that was passed 
for the protection of doctors, the Claimant must be a doctor. 
 
 
 
Whether there are alternative remedies available for the breach: 
 
The statute itself may or may not provide for alternative remedies as a 
result of a breach of duty. 
 
If there is an alternative remedy provided in the act, the court will 
generally understand that Parliament will have meant for this remedy to 
be the only possible remedy and the courts will not allow for a separate 
tort claim to be brought. 
 
Todd v Adams Where the relevant statute allows for criminal liability of 
the person in breach, giving rise to fines, it is unlikely that the statute will 
have also intended for a separate civil claim to be brought against the 
Defendant in addition to the fine. 
 
Alternative remedy due to the nature of the Claimant's situation: 
 In some cases, even if the act does not set out an alternative remedy, if 
the Claimant were to have an alternative remedy due to the nature of 
their situation, the court is unlikely to allow for a tort claim. 
 
Olotu v Home Office Where the statutory limit on how long a suspect 
may be kept in custody has been breached, a tort claim was not allowed, 
because the suspect will have other remedies to use, such as a bail 
application or the judicial review procedure. 
 
Phelps v Hillingdon Borough Council In the case of misdiagnosed 
dyslexia, a tort claim was not allowed, as parents would be able to go 
through any appeals procedures and make an application for judicial 
review. 
 
Where the alternative remedy is inadequate: 
 Groves v Winbourne If the alternative remedy is the payment of a fine 
which is inadequate compared to the harm caused, the court may 
decide that a claim could be made in tort. However, it is important to 
note there have been other cases after this one, which seem to suggest, 
that this case is less likely to be applied by the courts, unless there is a 
large discrepancy between the harm caused and the compensation. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The level of detail in the statute itself: 
 
X v Bedfordshire County Council The more detailed the statutory 
provisions, the more likely that the courts will imply a liability in tort. It 
is unlikely that Parliament intended to create tortious liability where 
they have used general language such as “safeguard” and “protect”. 
 
The background to the legislation: 
 
When the courts are attempting to work out Parliament's intention, they 
will look at the background of the legislation to find clues. 
 
Ziemniak v ETPM Deep Sea The courts will look at earlier legislation and 
Hansard to establish what the legislation intended and if tortious liability 
arose in the earlier legislation, it is likely that the courts would allow for 
this liability to arise again in the new legislation. 
 
The type of harm involved: 
 
Cullen v Chief Constable Tort law exists to protect victims from personal 
injury, property damage or economic loss. Where the type of harm is 
inconsistent with the type of harm typically recovered in tort law, the 
court is also unlikely to allow for a claim in tort. – eg. loss of liberty is not 
something that tort law would allow Claimants to claim for. 
 
ELEMENTS OF THE TORT: 
 
After the court decides that a particular statutory provision has been 
breached, allowing for a cause of action in tort, the court must decide 
whether there has been a breach, and whether the damage suffered by 
the Claimant falls within the damage envisioned by the statute. 
 
Breach of duty: 
 
The court will read the wording of the act to identify what the duty set 
out in the statute was and whether it has been breached. 
 
R v East Sussex County Council, ex parte T Where certain sections in the 
statute mention a list of considerations that the council is allowed to 
take into account when making decisions, however, the specific section 
which the Claimant is relying on does not mention these considerations, 
it is unlikely that Parliament will have intended the council to take into 
account these considerations when making decisions. 
Example: 
A factory worker gets his arm amputated by an unfenced machine. 
There is a statute providing for these particular types of machines to 
be fenced due to the high risk of harm these machines could cause. 
The same statute provided that the remedy for a breach would be a 
£100 fine which could be used to compensate anyone who suffers a 
harm due to the breach. In this case, the court may deem the remedy 
inadequate and allow for a separate tort claim.

pages.heading: In addition to considering whether there has been a breach of duty, the · court is also going to consider the degree of fault required by the statute
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Prep notes | Page 24 of 27 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
In addition to considering whether there has been a breach of duty, the 
court is also going to consider the degree of fault required by the statute 
to constitute a breach. 
 
If a statute imposes an absolute duty, and the court finds tortious 
liability, this liability will be strict liability and the Defendant will be liable 
even if they could not have prevented the injury/harm. 
 
Damage: 
 
Gorris v Scott The damage suffered by the Claimant must also be the 
type which the statute was passed to prevent. 
 
Defences: 
 
Voluntary assumption of risk and contributory negligence both apply as 
defences. 
 
 
 
 
 
Example: 
 The council has been providing home tuition to a child who was 
unable to go to school as she has had a long-term illness. This home 
tuition involved five contact hours per week. To save costs, the 
council decided to reduce the contact hours to three hours per week. 
When deciding whether the council was in breach of their duty, the 
court will look at the wording of the statute. 
 
In the statute providing for home education for children with longterm illness, there is mention of financial considerations in several 
different sections, except for the one which set out the way in which 
the council should decide how many hours are required to provide 
suitable education. The court held in this case, that finances should 
not have been taken into account by the council in this case.

pages.heading: REMEDIES · INTRODUCTION:
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Prep notes | Page 25 of 27 
 
REMEDIES 
 
INTRODUCTION: 
 
The key remedy for tortious liability is compensation for the loss and 
damage caused as a result of the tort. 
 
The Claimant may seek compensation for the following types of losses: 
1. 
Loss caused to a person (loss in terms of loss of value to property 
or financial loss) 
2. 
Personal injury 
3. 
Reputational damage (if quantifiable). 
 
PURE ECONOMIC LOSS: 
 
Pure economic loss = financial loss suffered by a person/company which 
is not accompanied by any physical damage to their person or property. 
 
Compensation for pure economic loss includes: 
 
* 
Compensation for financial losses made as a result of a bad 
financial decision (however, this may be recoverable if this is 
due to negligent misstatement). 
 
* 
Compensation for financial loss which does not directly flow 
from damage to the Claimant or their property. 
 
* 
Compensation for loss of profits if there is no physical damage 
to property. – eg. damage to a computer system. 
 
* 
Compensation for damage to property which does not belong to 
the Claimant. 
 
* 
Lost opportunity 
 
* 
In relation to product liability claims: compensation for damage 
to the defective product itself. – Murphy v Brentwood District 
Council 
 
These claims must be brought in contract by the other party to 
the contract rather than tort, and it is done under the Sale of 
Good Act 1979 or Consumer Rights Act 2015. 
 
 
However, consequential economic loss may be recovered along with 
damages for physical injury/damage to property. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Pure economic loss may be caused by: 
* 
A negligent act – eg. by accidentally cutting through the 
electricity supply to a factory, thus shutting the entire factory 
down. 
 OR 
* 
A negligent misstatement – eg. by giving negligent financial 
advice to the Claimant where the Claimant loses out as a result 
of the negligent advice. 
 
General rule: 
 
No duty is care is owed in relation to pure economic losses, so no 
negligence claim may be lodged in relation to these types of losses. 
 
Exception: 
 
Hedley Byrne v Heller Pure economic loss may be recoverable if caused 
by negligent misstatements and if there has been a special relationship 
between the Defendant and the Claimant. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Elements of negligent misstatement: 
1. 
The Defendant knew that the Claimant was likely to rely on the 
Defendant's advice without independent enquiry. 
 AND 
2. 
The advice is required for a purpose which is made known to the 
Defendant. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
PSYCHIATRIC HARM: 
 
In a negligence action, the Claimant may recover compensation for 
personal injury which includes the physical impact of the injury and its 
mental consequences. – eg. anxiety, distress, any other psychiatric 
harm. 
 
General rule: 
 Damages are not payable for psychiatric harm where there has been no 
physical impact. However, there are some exceptions. 
 
There are two different types of victims in relation to psychiatric harm. 
 
In either case, damages will only be recoverable if the psychiatric harm 
is a medically recognised psychiatric condition. – eg. post-traumatic 
stress syndrome. 
 
If a Claimant suffers psychiatric harm together with a physical injury, the 
psychiatric harm will be labelled as consequential psychiatric harm and 
the ordinary rules of recovery will apply. 
 
Primary victims: 
 
Primary victim = a victim in the actual event who experiences a risk of 
physical injury. – eg. Emily, seeing a block of concrete falling right next 
to her will be a primary victim even if not injured. 
 
A primary victim may recover remedies: 
 
* 
If they have suffered a physical injury themselves in addition to 
their psychiatric injury. In this case, they can recover their losses 
for both physical and psychiatric injuries. 
 
Page v Smith In this case, once physical injury was foreseeable, 
there is no requirement to prove that the psychiatric injury was 
also foreseeable. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
* 
If there was a foreseeable risk of physical injury to them, but 
the primary victim was ultimately not harmed, then they may 
recover their losses for their psychiatric injuries only. 
 
Page v Smith In this case, once physical injury was foreseeable, 
there is no requirement to prove that the psychiatric injury was 
also foreseeable. 
 
Dulieu v White Psychiatric injury may only be claimed in this case 
if it was caused by the Claimant's reasonable fear for their own 
safety. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
The Egg shell skull rule also applies to these Claimants. 
 
Note that where a passer-by joins in as a rescuer, they will be considered 
a primary victim. 
Example: 
A restaurant suffers a short circuit due to the work of a negligent 
electrician. As a result, the fridge is now damaged and all the food 
spoils in the fridge. 
 
The following losses arise: 
1. 
The fridge is damaged – This is damage to property and 
recoverable. 
2. 
The food in the fridge is spoilt. – damage to property and 
recoverable. 
3. 
The restaurant will not be able to operate or even purchase 
a new fridge until the short circuit is ongoing and will. Lose 
out on profits – this is consequential economic loss and also 
recoverable. 
4. 
The restaurant will have suffered a loss of reputation – this 
could be quantified and may be recoverable. 
5. 
As a result of the loss of reputation, the restaurant has less 
customers and the restaurant estimate that they will have 
lost out on £300,000 worth of profits per annum. – this is 
pure economic loss and not recoverable. 
Example: 
If the Claimant asks their accountant for a report, and the accountant 
negligently makes an error on the report, if the Claimant then relies 
on the report and loses out, they will be able to make a claim. 
 
Example: 
Harold was involved in a car accident. He ends up with a head 
injury due to another road user's negligent driving. He now 
suffers from post-traumatic stress disorder as a result of the 
incident. He may recover his losses for his head injury and 
PTSD. 
Example 1: 
Harold was involved in a car accident. He believed he was 
about to die or be severely injured, however, he only suffers 
a minor scrape to his knee. He now suffers from posttraumatic stress disorder as a result of the incident. He may 
recover his losses for his PTSD, despite not suffering any 
substantial physical injuries. 
Example 2: 
Phoebe, washing the dishes in her home will be able to claim 
damages if a car crashes into her kitchen and she suffers a 
shock leading to a miscarriage. This is the case even if she is 
unharmed.

pages.heading: Where the primary victim only suffers pure psychiatric harm: · If you client is claiming that they have suffered a psychiatric injury only,
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Prep notes | Page 26 of 27 
 
Where the primary victim only suffers pure psychiatric harm: 
 
If you client is claiming that they have suffered a psychiatric injury only, 
without any physical damage, there is a higher threshold that they need 
to meet. 
 
A primary victim can only recover remedies for psychiatric injury if the 
psychiatric injury was: 
 
* 
A medically recognised psychiatric illness 
 AND 
* 
Caused by a sudden shock 
 
A medically recognised psychiatric illness: 
 
Your client will need to obtain a formal medical diagnosis to claim for 
these illnesses. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Caused by a sudden shock: 
 
Alcock Sudden shock = a person realising that a horrifying event is about 
to happen by their own senses (sight, sound). 
 
The condition caused by the sudden shock may either be a mental or 
physical condition. – miscarriage, heart attack or PTSD as a result of the 
shock. 
 
Where the primary victim suffers both a physical injury and psychiatric 
harm: 
 
If your client has suffered a physical injury, there is no need to rely on 
the fact that the psychiatric injury was a recognised injury. There is no 
need for a formal diagnosis. – as a result, simple mental distress is 
sufficient (upset, anxiety). 
 
This is because the presence of a physical injury supports the victim's 
claim that they have suffered a psychiatric trauma, making it much more 
straightforward to establish a link between the incident and the resulting 
psychological impact. 
 
Secondary victims: 
 
Secondary victim = a victim who is not in the area of danger where they 
could have apprehended a risk of physical injury, but suffers a harm, 
nevertheless. 
 
Historically, secondary victims could not claims compensation, however, 
exceptions to this rule have been developed, allowing for secondary 
victims to recover compensation in some circumstances. 
 
A secondary victim is only owed a duty of care if all of the following 
conditions are satisfied: Alcock Paul v Royal Wolverhampton (2024) 
 
1. 
The Claimant suffered a medically recognised psychiatric injury. 
 2. 
This injury has been suffered as a result of seeing or hearing 
the accident or its immediate aftermath. 
 
3. 
There was a relationship of love and affection between the 
Claimant and the primary victim. 
 
4. 
It must have been reasonably foreseeable to the tortfeasor that 
the Claimant might suffer psychiatric injury by shock. 
 
5. 
There is causal link between witnessing the accident and the 
psychiatric injury. 
 
 AND 
6. 
There must have been proximity between the Claimant and the 
accident or its immediate aftermath in both time and space. 
 
A medically recognised psychiatric illness: 
 
Your client will need to obtain a formal medical diagnosis to claim for 
these illnesses. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Relationship of love and affection: 
 Paul v Royal Wolverhampton (2024) Proximity means proximity of 
relationship between the claimant and the victims or those who have 
been endangered. This requires a relationship of love and affection. – 
This means a close family member or other loved one. 
 
McFarlane v EE Caledonia Bystanders cannot make a claim, despite the 
fact that they have suffered an injury. 
 
Proximity: 
 Accident = an unexpected incident caused unintentionally whereby 
violent causes result in injuries or a risk of injuries. 
 
Proximity in time and space between the Claimant and the accident or 
its immediate aftermath is a key requirement. – The Claimant must have 
had a physical sense of the accident. 
 
McFarlane v EE Caledonia Being told about the accident does not qualify 
a victim to make a claim. 
 
Simply seeing the event on television or reading it on newspaper is also 
not sufficient, unless the victim is able to spot the loved one on the 
television as one of the primary victims. 
 
Being at the scene of the accident and witnessing its immediate 
aftermath will be sufficient to make a claim. 
 
Paul v Royal Wolverhampton (2024) There is no requirement that the 
Claimant has suffered a sudden shock or that they were themselves 
exposed to the accident. 
 
The Claimant must have experienced the event as one single event 
rather than a number of separate events (even if linked to the accident), 
unless the separate events were very close in time to each other and 
close in time to the accident. 
 
Taylor v A Novo No claims can be made for injuries suffered at a second 
event (relating to the first event) if the second event happened at a 
different time from the first accident. 
 
Excluded categories of claimants: 
 There is generally recovery for psychiatric injury for police officers, 
rescuers, firemen and medical professionals who attend the scene. 
Rescuers must be exposed to some danger, and they are expected to be 
of the fortitude of a reasonable person. 
 
Rescuers who attend the scene will be classed as primary victims, and 
rescuers who did not attend the scene will be classes as secondary 
victims. 
 
Paul v Royal Wolverhampton (2024) If a doctor was negligent in failing 
to diagnose a patient, causing the death or medical emergency, they 
owe a duty to the patient but not the patient's loved ones or close 
family members. This is the case even if those loved ones or close family 
members apprehended their loved one's death or medical emergency as 
a result of the doctor's negligence. 
 
DAMAGES FOR PERSONAL INJURY: 
 
If the tortfeasor causes personal injury or death, different rules apply 
in relation to the remedies that can be recovered. 
 
Two different scenarios to consider in relation to personal injury: 
* 
If the victim is alive 
* 
If the victim dies 
 
The damages granted in tort will aim to put the injured party in the 
position they would have been in had the tort never occurred. – 
financially speaking. 
 
Tort victims must ensure that they mitigate their losses to limit the 
damages they suffer. 
 
 
Types of damages 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Examples of recognised psychiatric illnesses: 
* Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) 
* Acute stress disorder (ASD) 
* Adjustment disorders 
* Depression and mood disorders 
* Major depressive episodes 
* Specific phobias – including vehophobia, the fear of driving 
which could be caused by a car accident.

pages.heading: If there is a living Claimant: · Damages can be claimed for the Claimant's pain, suffering and loss of
pages.text:
Tort law – SQE Prep notes | Page 27 of 27 
 
If there is a living Claimant: 
 
Damages can be claimed for the Claimant's pain, suffering and loss of 
amenity caused by the accident. 
 
Loss of amenity = the effect of the injury on the Claimant's enjoyment 
of life. 
 
Damages can also be awarded for financial loss caused by the injury 
itself. – eg. not being able to work will allow a Claimant to claim for loss 
of earnings in addition to medical treatments. 
 
Recoverable pecuniary (financial) losses: 
* 
Loss of past income – between the injury and trial/settlement 
based on the net wages lost. 
 
* 
Loss of future income – if the Claimant will lose out on earnings 
in the future due to the injuries: 
– 
Measure this as the difference in income before and 
after the injury multiplied by the number of years the 
income will be lost. 
– 
Add contingencies of life – eg. any possibilities that the 
Claimant would have lost their job. 
– 
This will be awarded as a lump sum reflecting the present 
value of the amount awarded 
– 
If the injury have likely shortened the Claimant's life 
expectancy, loss of future income will be reduced to 
reflect this. 
 
* 
Cost of medical treatment – both past and future. Do not count 
treatment provided by the NHS. 
 
* 
Recoverable nonpecuniary losses – including past and future 
pain and suffering and loss of amenity. – a person in coma will 
not recover for this while they were in coma. 
 
* 
Damage to property – measure this by the replacement costs. 
 
If the Claimant dies from the injuries caused by the tort before the 
damages are paid out, their claim for damages will be paid out to the 
Claimant's estate. 
 
If the victim dies: 
 
Where the victim dies as a result of their injuries caused by the tort, the 
Claimants have a separate cause of action for bereavement. 
 
Funeral expenses will also be recoverable. 
 
Requirements for a bereavement claim: 
* 
The Claimant must show, that had the victim survived, they 
would have been able to bring a successful claim. 
* 
The Claimant must have been financially dependent on the 
victim. 
* 
The Claimant must fall within the statutory list of eligible 
relationships. 
 
Statutory list includes only: 
– 
The deceased's spouse/civil partner 
– 
The deceased's cohabitant of more than 2 years 
 OR 
– 
The deceased's parents if the deceased was under 18 and never 
married. 
 
The deceased's children are not entitled to bereavement payments. 
 
Bereavement Claimants can only recover a fixed statutory sum which 
is £15,120.
